flashcards.q: What are the three circuit breaker states?
flashcards.a: CLOSED (pass through) -> OPEN (fail fast, no thread spent) -> HALF_OPEN (limited probes) -> back to CLOSED on success, or OPEN on any probe failure.

flashcards.q: Correct nesting order of the four resilience patterns?
flashcards.a: Bulkhead -> CircuitBreaker -> Retry -> Timeout (outermost to innermost). Timeout innermost because you retry a timed-out attempt; retry inside the breaker so one logical failure = one breaker outcome; bulkhead outermost so rejection costs no thread.

flashcards.q: Why does minimumNumberOfCalls exist on a circuit breaker?
flashcards.a: Without it, 1 failure out of 1 call is a 100% failure rate and trips the breaker instantly on low-traffic endpoints. Typical value: 20.

flashcards.q: Why failure RATE and not failure COUNT?
flashcards.a: A count trips on volume: high-traffic endpoints trip constantly, low-traffic ones never do. Rate normalises across traffic levels.

flashcards.q: Formula for full jitter backoff?
flashcards.a: sleep = rand(0, min(cap, base * 2**attempt)). The default choice - lowest contention and good spread.

flashcards.q: Formula for decorrelated jitter?
flashcards.a: sleep = min(cap, rand(base, prev * 3)). Slightly better completion time under heavy contention.

flashcards.q: Why is jitter necessary at all?
flashcards.a: Plain exponential backoff synchronises clients - everyone fails at T and retries at T+1, T+2, T+4 together. Jitter breaks the synchronisation so the recovering service is not hit by waves.

flashcards.q: Retry amplification math?
flashcards.a: 3 attempts against a fully-failing downstream = 3x offered load. Two layers of retrying services = 9x. This is why retry needs a circuit breaker.

flashcards.q: Retry budget vs maxAttempts?
flashcards.a: maxAttempts is per-request and does not bound aggregate load. A retry budget caps retries as a fraction of total fleet requests (~10%), which is the only mechanism that directly bounds amplification. Envoy, gRPC and Finagle implement it.

flashcards.q: Which HTTP statuses are retryable?
flashcards.a: Retry: connection errors, timeouts, 429, 502, 503, 504. Never retry: 400, 401, 403, 404, 422.

flashcards.q: Three preconditions for safe retry?
flashcards.a: 1) The operation is idempotent or carries an idempotency key. 2) The error is actually retryable. 3) There is a budget bounding total retries.

flashcards.q: How do you size a bulkhead?
flashcards.a: Little's Law: concurrency = throughput x latency. 100 rps at 50ms p99 = 5 slots; provision ~2x for burst, so 10. Then verify under load.

flashcards.q: Semaphore vs thread-pool bulkhead?
flashcards.a: Semaphore: cheap counter, work runs on the caller's thread, cannot interrupt a blocking call - use in async code. Thread-pool: true isolation and an enforceable timeout on blocking clients, at the cost of context switches.

flashcards.q: Dependency returns 200s but takes 30 seconds. Does a failure-rate breaker trip?
flashcards.a: No - every call succeeds. You need slowCallRateThreshold with slowCallDurationThreshold (e.g. trip if >50% of calls exceed 2s). Slow success exhausts threads exactly like failure.

flashcards.q: How do you set a read timeout?
flashcards.a: From the downstream's p99, not a guess: timeout ~= p99 x 1.5, then verify against your own SLO. Connect timeout separately at 1-3s.

flashcards.q: What does a client-side timeout NOT protect you from?
flashcards.a: Server-side work continuing after you give up. Unless cancellation is propagated (gRPC cancellation, context, asyncio cancellation) the server keeps holding its DB connection - a capacity leak, and a correctness bug for writes.

flashcards.q: Why propagate deadlines instead of durations?
flashcards.a: Timeout budget must shrink with call depth. A fixed 3s at every layer lets the innermost call consume the whole user-facing budget, leaving no time to fall back. Pass an absolute deadline; each layer takes min(remaining, its own max).

flashcards.q: If you could only add ONE resilience pattern, which?
flashcards.a: Timeout. Everything else assumes a bounded call: an unbounded call never returns to retry, never records a breaker outcome, and holds a bulkhead slot forever.

flashcards.q: Fallback quality ranking?
flashcards.a: Stale cache > degraded response > default value > queue-for-later > fast 503 with Retry-After. Never let a fallback call another unprotected remote service.

flashcards.q: Which circuit breaker library for Java?
flashcards.a: Resilience4j. Hystrix has been in maintenance mode since 2018 - naming it as a current recommendation is an interview red flag.

flashcards.q: Resilience4j's documented decorator order?
flashcards.a: Bulkhead -> TimeLimiter -> RateLimiter -> CircuitBreaker -> Retry. Note retry is outermost there, which permits retrying after a breaker rejection when the retry can be routed to a different instance.

flashcards.q: Circuit breaker granularity - per what?
flashcards.a: Per (service, route-template). Too coarse and one bad endpoint blocks healthy ones; too fine and no breaker reaches minimumNumberOfCalls. Key on route templates, not raw URLs, or memory grows with path parameters.

flashcards.q: Your breaker flaps open/closed every few seconds. Diagnose.
flashcards.a: minimumNumberOfCalls too low or window too small (tiny sample = 100% rate); or waitDurationInOpenState too short so probes hit a service still restarting; or permittedCallsInHalfOpen = 1 so one sample decides everything.

flashcards.q: Should resilience live in the service mesh or in application code?
flashcards.a: Both. Mesh (Envoy outlier detection, retry budgets, pool limits) gives uniform transport-level defaults with no redeploy. But the mesh does not know if an operation is idempotent, cannot express business fallbacks, and cannot do per-tenant policy.

flashcards.q: How do you make a retried write safe?
flashcards.a: Idempotency key per logical operation; server stores (key -> response) in a dedup store and returns the stored response on repeat. Must be atomic - INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING checking affected rows, not read-then-write. TTL must exceed the max retry window.

flashcards.q: Resilience strategy for an LLM agent calling 5 tools?
flashcards.a: Per-tool bulkheads and timeouts derived from the agent's total budget; retry only transient transport errors and 429, never semantic tool errors; per-tool breaker with a structured 'tool unavailable' observation so the model routes around it; token/cost and step-count caps as the outermost bulkhead; and checkpointed state so failures resume rather than restart.

flashcards.q: Rank the four patterns by how often their absence causes a real incident.
flashcards.a: 1) Missing timeout 2) Missing bulkhead 3) Retry without breaker/budget 4) Missing breaker alone. This is roughly the inverse of how often they get discussed.

flashcards.q: How do you test a circuit breaker without sleeping?
flashcards.a: Inject a clock. FakeClock.advance() drives the OPEN -> HALF_OPEN transition deterministically. Tests that call time.sleep() are broken tests.

flashcards.q: What IS an agent, mechanically?
flashcards.a: A loop around a stateless model: send messages + tool schemas, model returns text (done) or tool calls, execute them, append results, repeat. ~40 lines.

flashcards.q: Why is agent cost quadratic in turns?
flashcards.a: The model is stateless. Every turn re-sends the entire message history, so turn N pays for turns 1..N. Total cost grows as the square of turn count.

flashcards.q: The six stop conditions for an agent loop?
flashcards.a: 1) model returns no tool call 2) step cap (10-25) 3) token budget 4) cost budget 5) wall-clock deadline 6) no-progress detector.

flashcards.q: Which stop condition fires most often in production?
flashcards.a: The no-progress detector. The common failure isn't infinite exploration, it's the model repeating an identical tool call that will never succeed.

flashcards.q: How do you implement no-progress detection?
flashcards.a: Hash (tool_name, sorted args) into a counter. At 3 repeats, return a tool RESULT telling the model to change approach - not an exception.

flashcards.q: What happens when a tool throws?
flashcards.a: Catch it and return a readable error string as the tool result, so the model can route around it. Propagating the exception discards all prior work in the run.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT catch a tool exception?
flashcards.a: When it's a bug in your harness rather than the tool's dependency. A model cannot fix your KeyError - crash loudly instead of shipping an agent that looks merely stupid.

flashcards.q: Agent reliability math at 95% per step?
flashcards.a: 0.95^10 is about 60%. At 85% per step, 10 steps is about 20%. 0.95^50 is 8%. Reliability is multiplicative.

flashcards.q: What fixes compounding agent failure?
flashcards.a: Not a better model. Fewer steps, checkpointing so failures resume instead of restart, and human approval at consequential points.

flashcards.q: Three context-management levers, in order?
flashcards.a: 1) Truncate tool results at the tool boundary (highest leverage) 2) Compact at ~70% of window: recap old turns, keep recent verbatim 3) Externalise to file/store so state survives compaction.

flashcards.q: What must never be compacted away?
flashcards.a: messages[0] / the system prompt, the original task statement, and any pending obligation. Carry an explicit open-items list through every compaction.

flashcards.q: What does a framework like LangGraph actually give you?
flashcards.a: Persistence and checkpointing (the real reason), streaming, interrupt()/HITL, per-node retry semantics, observability hooks, subgraph composition. NOT the loop.

flashcards.q: When is an agent the WRONG choice?
flashcards.a: When the steps are known in advance - write the pipeline. When one prompt suffices. When work is long-running or multi-party - use a durable workflow engine.

flashcards.q: Difference between ReAct and the agent loop?
flashcards.a: ReAct is the prompting pattern (interleave reasoning and action). The loop is the harness executing it. ReAct originally parsed Thought/Action/Observation text; native tool calling replaced that.

flashcards.q: How do you make a mutating tool safe to retry?
flashcards.a: Idempotency keys: client generates a key per logical operation, server stores (key to result) and returns the stored result on repeat. Read-only tools are naturally safe.

flashcards.q: How do you test a nondeterministic agent?
flashcards.a: Separate layers. Harness (stops, budgets, dispatch, compaction) is deterministic - unit test against a scripted fake model. Tools tested independently. Only end-to-end needs eval-style golden trajectories.

flashcards.q: Why does human-in-the-loop force durable execution?
flashcards.a: A human may take a day to approve. You must persist loop state before the consequential action and rehydrate on approval - an in-process loop cannot survive that wait.

flashcards.q: Single agent with 20 tools, or 5 specialists with 4 each?
flashcards.a: Start with one agent and good tools. Multi-agent costs routing errors, handoff context loss, harder debugging, more latency. Split only for parallelisable subtasks, needed context isolation, or differing permissions.

flashcards.q: What is the scaled dot-product attention formula?
flashcards.a: softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V -- Q and K scored via dot product, scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k), softmaxed into weights, then used to weight-average V.

flashcards.q: Derive why attention scores are divided by sqrt(d_k), not d_k or nothing.
flashcards.a: If Q,K components are iid mean-0 variance-1, the dot product over d_k terms has variance d_k (sum of d_k independent unit-variance products), so std dev grows as sqrt(d_k). Dividing by sqrt(d_k) restores unit variance regardless of d_k; dividing by d_k over-shrinks variance below 1 and pushes softmax toward uniform.

flashcards.q: What happens if attention scores are not scaled at large d_k?
flashcards.a: Large-variance scores saturate softmax toward one-hot output, and softmax's own gradient factor softmax_i(1-softmax_i) collapses toward zero almost everywhere, stalling gradient flow.

flashcards.q: What is the time and memory cost of naive self-attention, and which one is the practical bottleneck?
flashcards.a: O(n^2 d_k) time, O(n^2) memory per head (the QK^T matrix). Memory is the practical limiter -- at n=8192 fp16, one head's score matrix is ~128MB.

flashcards.q: What is the KV cache size formula per token?
flashcards.a: 2 * n_kv_heads * d_head * bytes_per_element (the 2 accounts for storing both K and V).

flashcards.q: How does MQA reduce KV cache size versus MHA?
flashcards.a: MQA (Shazeer, 2019) shares one KV head across all query heads, dividing KV cache size by h (the number of query heads), at a measurable quality cost on summarization and long-context retrieval.

flashcards.q: How does GQA reduce KV cache size versus MHA, and what config does Llama-family 70B use?
flashcards.a: GQA (Ainslie et al., 2023) groups query heads into g groups sharing one KV head each, dividing cache by h/g. Llama-family 70B uses 64 query heads over 8 KV heads -- an 8x reduction, recovering nearly all MHA quality.

flashcards.q: What is Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) and how does it differ from GQA?
flashcards.a: MLA (DeepSeek-V2/V3) compresses K and V into a shared low-rank latent vector via learned projections rather than sharing discrete heads. GQA reduces the COUNT of KV heads; MLA reduces the DIMENSIONALITY stored per cached position. DeepSeek-V3 reports ~70KB/token vs 192-328KB/token for comparable GQA models.

flashcards.q: What is the worked KV-cache example for a 70B model (80 layers, GQA-8, head_dim=128, BF16) at 4k and 128k context?
flashcards.a: 0.32 MB/token (2*80*8*128*2 bytes). At 4,096 tokens: ~1.3GB per sequence. At 128,000 tokens: ~42GB per sequence -- larger than many single GPUs' total VRAM.

flashcards.q: Why is FlashAttention described as exact rather than approximate?
flashcards.a: It computes the mathematically identical softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V output -- it changes memory access order (tiling + online/running softmax), not what is computed. Approximate methods (Linformer, sparse attention) change the computed function itself.

flashcards.q: Does FlashAttention change the asymptotic time complexity of attention?
flashcards.a: No -- it stays O(n^2) time (same FLOP count). It changes memory from O(n^2) to O(n) by never materializing the full score matrix in HBM, and improves constant-factor speed via better hardware utilization.

flashcards.q: What are FlashAttention-3's reported speedups on H100?
flashcards.a: 1.5-2.0x faster than FlashAttention-2 in FP16, reaching up to 740 TFLOPs/s (~75% of peak) FP16, 840 TFLOPs/s (~85%) BF16, and ~1.2-1.3 PFLOPs/s in FP8.

flashcards.q: What three techniques does FlashAttention-3 use to hit its H100 numbers?
flashcards.a: Warp-specialized async overlap of Tensor Core matmuls with TMA data movement, interleaved block-wise matmul/softmax scheduling, and FP8 support with incoherent processing to control quantization error.

flashcards.q: Can GQA or MLA be added to an existing pretrained MHA checkpoint as a serving-time optimization?
flashcards.a: No -- both are architecture decisions baked in during pretraining (or continued pretraining); they cannot be retrofitted at inference time the way PagedAttention or quantization can.

flashcards.q: Why is prefill compute-bound and decode memory-bandwidth-bound?
flashcards.a: Prefill processes all prompt tokens in one parallel pass, reusing each loaded weight matrix across many positions -- high arithmetic intensity, compute-bound. Decode processes one token per step but still loads the full weight matrices and KV cache from HBM for that single position -- arithmetic intensity drops ~5x, so the GPU waits on memory bandwidth, not FLOPs.

flashcards.q: What is the KV cache size formula, derived?
flashcards.a: bytes/token = 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * d_head * bytes_per_element. Multiply by seq_len * batch_size for total footprint. The leading 2 accounts for storing both K and V.

flashcards.q: Worked example: 70B model, 80 layers, GQA-8, head_dim=128, BF16 -- what's the KV cache at 4k and 128k tokens?
flashcards.a: 0.32 MB/token. At 4,096 tokens: ~1.3GB per sequence. At 128,000 tokens: ~42GB per sequence -- larger than many single GPUs' entire VRAM, for one sequence.

flashcards.q: What problem does PagedAttention solve and how?
flashcards.a: Fragmentation: naive contiguous per-request KV-cache allocation sized for worst-case length wastes 60-80% of memory. PagedAttention partitions the cache into fixed-size blocks (e.g. 16 tokens) with a per-sequence block table (logical->physical), allocated on demand -- reduces waste to under 4%, enabling 2-4x more throughput via larger batches.

flashcards.q: What is continuous (in-flight) batching and why does it beat static batching?
flashcards.a: Static batching waits for the whole batch's slowest (longest) sequence before reusing any slot, idling finished slots. Continuous batching (from Orca, adopted by vLLM/SGLang/TGI) evicts finished sequences and admits new queued ones at every decode iteration, keeping GPU utilization near-constant regardless of output-length variance.

flashcards.q: What is chunked prefill and what problem does it fix?
flashcards.a: Splitting a long prompt's prefill into fixed-size chunks (vLLM default 2,048 tokens) interleaved with other sequences' decode steps, instead of running the whole prefill uninterrupted. Fixes head-of-line blocking, where one long prefill would otherwise stall every other in-flight request's decode (raising their TPOT) for the whole prefill duration.

flashcards.q: How does SGLang's RadixAttention differ from vLLM's automatic prefix caching?
flashcards.a: vLLM hashes fixed-size blocks by content and reuses a block on exact hash match, reference-counted. RadixAttention organizes the ENTIRE KV-cache pool as a radix tree keyed by token sequence, automatically discovering and sharing any prefix across any requests (not just explicitly grouped ones), with LRU eviction over tree leaves.

flashcards.q: What's the reported throughput gap between SGLang and vLLM, and how does it change with model scale?
flashcards.a: On an 8B model with ShareGPT-style traffic, SGLang ~16,200 tok/s vs vLLM ~12,500 tok/s (~29% higher), driven by RadixAttention's prefix reuse. The gap narrows to 3-5% at 70B scale, since compute increasingly dominates over cache-reuse benefits at larger model sizes.

flashcards.q: Define TTFT and TPOT precisely.
flashcards.a: TTFT (time to first token): wall-clock time from request arrival to first generated token, dominated by queueing + prefill compute, scales with prompt length and load. TPOT (time per output token / inter-token latency): average time per subsequent token, memory-bandwidth-bound, scales with total KV cache read per decode step across the batch.

flashcards.q: How does batch size trade off TTFT, TPOT, and throughput?
flashcards.a: Increasing batch size raises throughput (amortizes weight-load cost across more sequences, better arithmetic intensity) but raises TPOT (more total KV cache read per step, more memory-bus contention) and can raise TTFT for new arrivals competing with a larger active batch. No single batch size minimizes all three simultaneously -- it's a genuine three-way tradeoff surface.

flashcards.q: What is the cost model formula for dollars per million tokens?
flashcards.a: $/M tokens = (GPU $/hr) / (tokens/sec * 3600) * 1,000,000. Increasing batch size raises tokens/sec, lowering this number, up to the point where KV-cache capacity or memory bandwidth saturates.

flashcards.q: What does vLLM's chunked prefill default chunk size default to?
flashcards.a: 2,048 tokens.

flashcards.q: What are LangChain's base TextSplitter defaults for chunk_size and chunk_overlap?
flashcards.a: chunk_size=4000 characters, chunk_overlap=200 (character-level; most teams override to token counts sized to the embedding model's context limit).

flashcards.q: What is Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval and when was it published?
flashcards.a: Published Sept 19, 2024. Prepends a 50-100 token LLM-generated context sentence to each chunk before embedding and BM25 indexing, so decontextualized chunks ("the company grew 3%") get their missing anchor restored.

flashcards.q: What retrieval failure-rate reduction does Contextual Retrieval achieve, at each stage?
flashcards.a: Baseline 5.7% top-20 failure -> 3.7% with contextual embeddings (35% cut) -> 2.9% with contextual embeddings + BM25 (49% cut) -> 1.9% with reranking added (67% cut).

flashcards.q: What is the one-time cost of Contextual Retrieval with prompt caching?
flashcards.a: $1.02 per million document tokens, assuming 800-token chunks, 8k-token documents, 50 tokens of instruction, 100 tokens of generated context per chunk.

flashcards.q: What is late chunking (Jina AI, arXiv:2409.04701) and how does it differ from contextual retrieval?
flashcards.a: Embed the WHOLE document first with a long-context model (~8k tokens, e.g. jina-embeddings-v2/v3), THEN mean-pool token embeddings within each chunk's span. No LLM call needed, unlike contextual retrieval which uses an LLM to generate an explicit context sentence.

flashcards.q: What is LlamaIndex's SemanticSplitterNodeParser default breakpoint threshold?
flashcards.a: buffer_size=1, breakpoint_percentile_threshold=95 -- cuts occur only at the most severe 5% of sentence-embedding similarity drops.

flashcards.q: What chunk-size starting points make sense for FAQ/support corpora vs narrative/legal/financial documents?
flashcards.a: FAQ/support: 200-500 tokens (answer usually in one paragraph). Narrative/legal/financial: 800-1000 tokens (meaning depends on surrounding clauses). Always validate against a recall@k eval.

flashcards.q: What overlap percentage is a reasonable starting point, and why not more?
flashcards.a: 10-20% of chunk size. Enough to avoid severing a sentence at a boundary; more than that mostly re-embeds duplicate text and dilutes the corpus with near-identical vectors competing for top-k slots.

flashcards.q: Which tools are best for extracting tables from PDFs for RAG, and why?
flashcards.a: Unstructured (open-source + API, detectron2 layout analysis) is the general-purpose industry standard; LlamaParse (vision-based layout analysis) is the stronger choice specifically for complex/merged-cell tables. Both should serialize tables to Markdown, not flatten them to plain text.

flashcards.q: Why shouldn't code be split by character count?
flashcards.a: A character-count split can cut a function or class in half, guaranteeing an unusable retrieval. Use language-aware recursive separators (e.g. LangChain's Language.PYTHON splits before class/def) instead.

flashcards.q: When should you skip RAG/chunking entirely, per Anthropic's own guidance?
flashcards.a: If the knowledge base is under ~200,000 tokens (~500 pages), just put the whole thing in a cached prompt -- no retrieval infrastructure needed.

flashcards.q: What is the "over-compression" failure mode of chunks that are too large?
flashcards.a: A chunk covering multiple subtopics produces one embedding averaged across all of them, so a query about any single subtopic scores lower similarity than it would against a focused chunk -- the vector is diluted.

flashcards.q: What are BM25's k1 and b defaults, and what does each control?
flashcards.a: k1=1.2 (Lucene/Elasticsearch default) controls term-frequency saturation, capping how much repeated term occurrences inflate score. b=0.75 controls document-length normalization, penalizing term matches in longer documents relative to shorter ones.

flashcards.q: Why does dense retrieval fail on exact matches like error codes or IDs?
flashcards.a: Embedding models compress text into a fixed-size vector optimized for semantic similarity; rare, low-frequency tokens get weakly differentiated representations because the model saw few or no training examples anchoring their exact meaning. Anthropic's example: querying "Error code TS-999" finds content about error codes generally but can miss the exact string.

flashcards.q: What is the Reciprocal Rank Fusion formula and what is k?
flashcards.a: RRF_score(d) = sum over retrievers of 1/(k + rank_r(d)). k=60 is the empirical constant from Cormack, Clarke & Buttcher's 2009 TREC experiments; k in [40,80] performs comparably across benchmarks.

flashcards.q: Why does rank fusion (RRF) beat naive score fusion?
flashcards.a: Different retrievers produce scores on incompatible scales (unbounded, corpus-dependent BM25 vs bounded cosine similarity). Averaging raw scores lets whichever retriever has larger magnitude dominate. RRF discards scores and uses only rank position, which is comparable across any two retrievers by construction.

flashcards.q: What is weighted score fusion's formula and its main failure mode?
flashcards.a: fused = alpha*normalize(dense_score) + (1-alpha)*normalize(bm25_score). Failure mode: BM25 score distributions shift whenever corpus statistics (avgdl, IDF) change on reindex, silently invalidating a previously-tuned alpha and normalization scheme.

flashcards.q: What is ColBERT's MaxSim scoring function?
flashcards.a: MaxSim(Q,D) = sum over query tokens of [max over doc tokens of (q_i . d_j)]. For each query token, find its single best-matching document token by dot product, sum those maxima across all query tokens.

flashcards.q: What is ColBERT's storage cost for 1 million documents, compared to a bi-encoder?
flashcards.a: ~200 tokens/doc at 128 dims float32: 1M x 200 x 128 x 4 bytes ~= 102 GB, vs ~3 GB for a single-vector 768-dim bi-encoder index -- roughly 34x more. ColBERTv2's residual/2-bit compression brings this to ~6 GB (~2x the bi-encoder).

flashcards.q: What does the PLAID engine do for ColBERTv2?
flashcards.a: Summarizes documents into "bags of centroids," computing query-centroid dot products once per query to prune most candidates before running full MaxSim only on the reduced candidate set, making ColBERTv2 practical to serve at scale.

flashcards.q: Does reranking remove the need for hybrid retrieval?
flashcards.a: No. A reranker only reorders candidates stage-1 retrieval already surfaced; if the relevant document never entered that candidate set, no reranker downstream can recover it. Retrieval and reranking solve recall and precision respectively, and neither substitutes for the other.

flashcards.q: Which production systems support native hybrid search?
flashcards.a: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch (native hybrid queries + built-in RRF), Weaviate (alpha weighted fusion or RRF ranking), Qdrant (sparse+dense), Vespa (also native ColBERT-style multi-vector tensor ranking), Milvus.

flashcards.q: In a worked 2-second RAG budget, roughly how is time allocated across stages?
flashcards.a: ~75ms embedding, ~100ms ANN retrieval, ~250ms rerank (top~100), ~75ms buffer, leaving ~1500ms (~75% of total) for generation, which dominates because it's the least compressible stage.

flashcards.q: What is the cascade retrieval pattern and why is it structured that way?
flashcards.a: Stage 1: cheap, wide hybrid ANN retrieval (top 50-150) optimized for recall. Stage 2: expensive, narrow cross-encoder rerank (top 3-20) optimized for precision. Works because stage-1 cost is roughly independent of top-k, while stage-2 cost scales linearly with candidate count and can't run over the whole corpus at interactive latency.

flashcards.q: What are typical latencies for query embedding and cross-encoder reranking?
flashcards.a: Query embedding: 50-100ms (e.g. Voyage lite ~52ms/query). Cross-encoder rerank: 100-300ms via Cohere's hosted API, or ~50ms/pair for self-hosted BGE-reranker-v2-m3 on an L40S GPU.

flashcards.q: What three costs does retrieving more candidates (higher top-k) incur?
flashcards.a: 1) Reranker latency/cost scales linearly with candidate count. 2) Generation context-token cost scales linearly with candidates passed to the LLM. 3) Quality can drop past a threshold via the "lost in the middle" effect -- more context doesn't guarantee better attention to the right part of it.

flashcards.q: Do retrieval-quality techniques (hybrid, contextual retrieval, reranking, reformulation) stack additively in accuracy?
flashcards.a: No. Evidence shows rerank-over-hybrid often matches rerank-over-dense-only, meaning the reranker's gain subsumes much of the hybrid leg's contribution. Precision returns flatten while latency costs of each added stage stay additive.

flashcards.q: When should you cut the reranking stage?
flashcards.a: When stage-1 recall is already sufficient (eval-verified), when the latency budget can't afford 100-300ms (sub-500ms targets), when the corpus is small/low-noise, or when reranking cost at your actual QPS doesn't pencil out economically.

flashcards.q: What is Cohere Rerank's approximate pricing and latency?
flashcards.a: Roughly $0.001-$0.0025 per search of up to 100 documents (documents over 500 tokens split into additional billed sub-chunks); typical latency 100-300ms.

flashcards.q: What's the discipline for deciding a retrieval-pipeline change is actually an improvement?
flashcards.a: 1) Offline eval (recall@k/nDCG) to gate cheaply. 2) Shadow/canary deployment to measure real p50/p99 latency under load. 3) Online A/B test on a user-facing metric (task success, feedback, follow-up-query rate) since offline recall improving doesn't guarantee the online metric moves.

flashcards.q: Why does generation typically dominate the RAG latency budget?
flashcards.a: Generation latency is driven by output token count and model size/architecture, mostly outside retrieval's control -- often 60-75% of total budget vs the much smaller slices spent on embedding, ANN search, and reranking.

flashcards.q: What is the "lost in the middle" effect and why does it matter for retrieval budget decisions?
flashcards.a: Models exhibit degraded attention to information buried in the middle of a long context. It means blindly adding more retrieved chunks "to be safe" can measurably hurt answer quality, not just waste latency/cost/tokens.

flashcards.q: What are pgvector's HNSW defaults?
flashcards.a: m=16, ef_construction=64, hnsw.ef_search=40.

flashcards.q: What are Weaviate's HNSW defaults?
flashcards.a: DefaultMaxConnections=32 (lowered from 64), DefaultEFConstruction=128, search-time ef=-1 (dynamic: query_limit * dynamicEfFactor(8), clamped between dynamicEfMin=100 and dynamicEfMax=500).

flashcards.q: What does each HNSW knob (M, efConstruction, efSearch) cost when increased?
flashcards.a: M: more memory, slower build/search, better recall. efConstruction: slower build only (no query cost), better recall. efSearch: linearly more query latency, better recall, must be >= k.

flashcards.q: What is the HNSW memory formula and what does it give for 10M vectors at 768 and 1536 dims (M=16)?
flashcards.a: bytes/vector ~= 1.1*(4*dim + 8*M). At 768d: 3,520 B/vec -> 35.2 GB for 10M vectors. At 1536d: 6,899 B/vec -> 69.0 GB for 10M vectors.

flashcards.q: What is the IVF nlist rule of thumb, and what does nprobe control?
flashcards.a: nlist ~= sqrt(N) centroids (coarse k-means partition). nprobe = number of cells actually searched per query; directly trades recall for latency. Starting point: nprobe=8-16 for 1-10M vectors, tuned to recall plateau.

flashcards.q: How does product quantization (PQ) compress vectors, and what's the accuracy cost?
flashcards.a: Splits each vector into m subspaces, quantizes each against a codebook of 2^nbits centroids (typically nbits=8, 256 centroids), storing only the index -- e.g. 768d/m=96 -> 96 bytes vs 3072 bytes raw (~32x compression). Cost: quantization error is baked in at index time; no amount of nprobe tuning recovers it.

flashcards.q: What does ScaNN's anisotropic vector quantization do differently from plain PQ?
flashcards.a: Instead of minimizing uniform reconstruction error, it penalizes quantization error parallel to the database vector more heavily than error orthogonal to it, because parallel error is what actually shifts ranking under MIPS/dot-product similarity -- giving better recall-per-byte for ranking-sensitive tasks.

flashcards.q: What is DiskANN's Vamana graph and what performance does it achieve on SIFT1B?
flashcards.a: A single-layer (non-hierarchical) directed graph built via randomized init + two-pass alpha-pruning (~1.2). PQ-compressed vectors cached in RAM guide search; full vectors + graph live on SSD. On SIFT1B: 5000+ QPS, <3ms mean latency, 95%+ recall@1 on a 16-core/64GB-RAM machine.

flashcards.q: Why is filtered vector search genuinely hard?
flashcards.a: ANN indexes assume any indexed vector is a valid target. Pre-filtering degenerates to brute force over the filtered subset (no index over it). Naive post-filtering can under-return on selective filters because the unfiltered search never routed toward filter-valid regions of the graph.

flashcards.q: How does Weaviate's ACORN solve filtered search?
flashcards.a: Two-hop graph expansion so the search radius covers enough of the graph to find filter-valid neighbors regardless of selectivity; since v1.34 it's the default, auto-choosing between multi-hop exploration (selective filters), broader relaxed traversal (broad filters), or flat scan (tiny result sets).

flashcards.q: Can you cleanly delete a vector from an HNSW index?
flashcards.a: No -- deleted vectors are typically tombstoned, not physically removed (removing a node requires re-linking its neighbors, expensive to do online). Heavy churn degrades graph quality until a rebuild.

flashcards.q: Name the four types of agent memory and what each stores.
flashcards.a: WORKING = the context window itself (system prompt, task, recent turns, tool output); volatile, re-sent every turn. EPISODIC = what happened on past runs (task signature, trajectory, OUTCOME, cost); append-only. SEMANTIC = durable facts as (subject, predicate, value); upserted with conflict resolution. PROCEDURAL = how to act (rules, skills, tool-ordering); files under version control.

flashcards.q: Why should episodic and semantic memory not share one index?
flashcards.a: Different retrieval keys (task signature vs subject-predicate), different read patterns (rare exemplar vs every-turn fact), different decay rates, different failure modes. One index means you retrieve a stale trajectory when you wanted a fact.

flashcards.q: Five reasons naive vector search over past conversation turns performs badly.
flashcards.a: 1) Turns are not self-contained ('yes, do that one'). 2) Embeddings encode topic not truth: 'I want to cancel' ~ 'I decided not to cancel'. 3) Precision collapses at volume (8 of 50k on a weak signal). 4) No temporal reasoning. 5) Injected memories are treated as authoritative, unlike a visibly-irrelevant RAG chunk.

flashcards.q: Give the composite memory retrieval score.
flashcards.a: 0.55*cosine + 0.20*0.5^(age_days/half_life) + 0.15*importance + 0.10*log1p(hit_count). Generative-Agents style: relevance + recency + importance + usage. Weights are tuned against a golden set; the structure is the point.

flashcards.q: Why must the tenant/user filter go INSIDE the ANN query rather than after it?
flashcards.a: Post-filtering is both a quality bug (another tenant's near-duplicates crowd the correct tenant's facts out of the top-50) and a cross-tenant leak waiting for one code path to omit the filter. Enforce it in a repository layer that cannot issue an unfiltered query.

flashcards.q: What is the default write decision for a memory extractor, and what is the write gate?
flashcards.a: Default is NOOP; an empty list is the most common correct output. Gate: 'would this change how I answer a FUTURE, UNRELATED question?' Confidence >= 0.7. Never store anything with a system of record. Target under 1 durable fact per 10 turns, with a hard per-user cap (200-500) to force eviction.

flashcards.q: How does a wrong memory die? Name the mechanisms.
flashcards.a: Per-class TTL (identity none, stable_pref 365d, entitlement 30d, project_state 14d, task_local 0). Contradiction supersession: close valid_to, never hard-overwrite. Continuous decay in the ranking function. Capacity eviction on lowest composite score. Hard delete only for user/GDPR requests, cascading to embeddings and derived summaries.

flashcards.q: What should never be stored in memory?
flashcards.a: Anything with a system of record: plan tier, balance, ticket status, quotas, feature flags. Read them from the API. Remembering them is how you tell a downgraded customer they still have premium support.

flashcards.q: What is bi-temporal memory and why isn't updated_at enough?
flashcards.a: Two axes: event time (when the fact became true) and ingestion time (when you learned it), plus a validity window [valid_from, valid_to). updated_at records only ingestion, so last-write-wins lets a stale-but-recently-ingested fact beat a fresh-but-earlier-ingested one, and you cannot reconstruct historical state for 'what plan was I on in March'.

flashcards.q: Working memory ladder: buffer vs window vs summary vs hybrid.
flashcards.a: Buffer: perfect fidelity, O(n^2) cumulative cost, degrades via lost-in-the-middle before the hard limit. Window(k): O(k), forgets turn 2. Rolling summary: O(1), drops IDs/dates/exact constraints first. Hybrid (summary + last-k verbatim + a PINNED structured state block the summariser never sees) is the defensible default, plus externalising long artefacts to files.

flashcards.q: Mem0's reported LOCOMO numbers.
flashcards.a: 26% relative uplift in LLM-as-judge score over OpenAI's memory (66.9% vs 52.9%), p95 latency 1.44s vs 17.12s for full-context (91% lower), and ~1.8K tokens per conversation vs 26K (90% fewer). Vendor-reported; LOCOMO is ~300 turns / ~9K tokens / up to 35 sessions, which may not resemble your workload.

flashcards.q: Zep/Graphiti's reported numbers and what it is good at.
flashcards.a: DMR 94.8% vs MemGPT's 93.4%; up to 18.5% accuracy improvement on LongMemEval with ~90% lower latency than full-context. Model is a bi-temporal knowledge graph. Genuinely wins multi-hop and temporal reasoning over long histories; expensive to construct, with LLM extraction on every write.

flashcards.q: What did Anthropic report for the memory tool and context editing (Sept 29, 2025)?
flashcards.a: Memory tool + context editing = +39% over baseline on an internal agentic search eval; context editing alone = +29%. On a 100-turn web search eval, context editing cut token consumption 84% and enabled runs that previously failed on context exhaustion. Key read: most of the gain came from REMOVING content, not adding recall.

flashcards.q: Why is procedural memory the highest-blast-radius memory type?
flashcards.a: A wrong semantic fact affects one user; a wrong procedural rule affects every run, silently, until someone reads the prompt. That is why procedural memory lives in files under version control with a human approval gate, and why the agent may propose rules but not commit them.

flashcards.q: What is the anti-example trick in episodic memory?
flashcards.a: Inject ONE past failure, explicitly labelled as a failure with a one-line reason. It reduces repeat failures more than injecting two more successes, and it is the cheapest learning an agent can do without touching weights. Requires storing the outcome, not just the trajectory.

flashcards.q: Why is memory a precision problem rather than a recall problem?
flashcards.a: Injected memories are treated as authoritative. A missing memory produces a clarifying question; a wrong memory produces a confident error. One wrong item is worse than ten missing ones, so use a relevance floor (returning nothing is valid), per-predicate diversity, and a strict write gate rather than a bigger k.

flashcards.q: How do you evaluate a memory system?
flashcards.a: A/B with memory on vs off on CROSS-SESSION golden tasks, plus an adversarial slice of superseded/retracted facts. Track task success delta, injected-memory precision (fraction of injected facts a human judges relevant and correct; alert under 0.7), tokens added per turn, and write rate (facts per 1,000 turns; a floor alert catches a silently dead background job).

flashcards.q: The honest production picture of agent memory.
flashcards.a: The median shipped system is a typed user-profile table, a rolling session summary, and last-N-turns. Not a temporal knowledge graph. If the facts have a schema, use columns. Vendors supply storage; you still supply the write policy, the invalidation rules, and the tenancy model, which are the actual work.

flashcards.q: The citation strength ladder, and where the real gap is.
flashcards.a: fabricated → well-formed → resolves → topically relevant → ENTAILED → entailed + located. The 2026 deep-research audit (arXiv:2605.06635) measured link-works at 94-100%, topical relevance at 80-96%, and FACT CHECK at 24-77%. Everything below 'entailed' is a decoration, and the gap between 'relevant' and 'entailed' is the whole problem.

flashcards.q: State the AIS criterion and its two load-bearing clauses.
flashcards.a: Rashkin et al. 2021: sentence x is attributable to source s if a generic reader would agree that 'According to s, x' is true, with x interpreted in the context of the full response. Clause 1 ('according to s') means truth in the world is NOT the test — attribution is not truth. Clause 2 ('in context') is why you must decontextualise a sentence before checking it.

flashcards.q: Define ALCE citation recall and citation precision.
flashcards.a: Recall(s) = 1 if concat(cited docs) entails s, else 0 — 'is this sentence supported at all by what it cites?' Precision(d) = d alone entails s, OR removing d breaks entailment of the remainder — 'is each citation pulling its weight?' Headline metric = unsupported-sentence rate = 1 − mean recall.

flashcards.q: Why does citation precision exist as a metric?
flashcards.a: Because recall is trivially gameable: cite five documents per sentence and recall rises while the user's ability to check anything falls. Precision penalises the shotgun. Practically also cap citations per sentence at 2-3, since a citation list is only useful if a human will actually click it.

flashcards.q: Five mechanisms by which post-hoc citation produces confident wrong citations.
flashcards.a: 1) The answer already exists, so retrieval is evidence-SEEKING for a fixed conclusion. 2) Retrieval scores similarity, not entailment — negation barely moves an embedding, so the most similar chunk often states the opposite. 3) 'Cite your sources' makes citation mandatory, so 'nothing supports this' is unreachable. 4) The verifier is the generator, so errors are correlated. 5) The citation marker is just a token; the decoder cannot distinguish supported from unsupported.

flashcards.q: Post-hoc citation vs grounded generation, in one line each.
flashcards.a: Post-hoc asks 'what supports what I already said?' — that question has an answer for every claim, true or false. Grounded generation asks 'what can I say given this evidence?' — that question can have no answer, which is exactly why it is safer.

flashcards.q: The four levels a citation fails at, and which dominates.
flashcards.a: 0 fabricated (invented DOI/case number) — rare with retrieval, resolve the id. 1 wrong locator (right doc, wrong section) — common with document-level citations. 2 RELEVANT BUT UNSUPPORTING — the DOMINANT mode, 24-77% fact-check accuracy, only NLI catches it. 3 supports but misleading (superseded, cherry-picked, contradicted elsewhere) — underreported, needs corpus hygiene not more entailment.

flashcards.q: Grounded generation techniques, weakest to strongest.
flashcards.a: 1) Ids in context plus a soft 'cite only these' instruction — routinely violated. 2) Citation-CONSTRAINED DECODING over the in-context id set — kills fabricated ids structurally, near-free. 3) ATTRIBUTE FIRST then generate (arXiv:2403.17104) — extract spans, then generate from the spans only with raw chunks removed; costs 2 calls, ~1.4-1.8x tokens, lower fluency, lower coverage. 4) Structured claims carrying evidence id + quote, with a verbatim substring check.

flashcards.q: The verbatim quote check: what is it and what does it catch that NLI misses?
flashcards.a: An exact normalised substring comparison of the quoted span against the cited document. Cost ~0. It catches paraphrased-quote fabrication, which NLI happily entails because the paraphrase captures the gist. Free deterministic checks that catch what probabilistic checks miss always go first.

flashcards.q: Hard ceiling on grounded generation.
flashcards.a: You cannot cite what you did not retrieve. Grounding converts a hallucination problem into a retrieval-recall problem: if the answer is in the doc ranked 40th, grounded generation abstains and post-hoc citation confabulates. Abstention is better, but the fix is retrieval, not attribution.

flashcards.q: Attribution granularity: three options and the default.
flashcards.a: Response-level = 1 verification call and meaningless ('some of this is supported' is not a claim). SENTENCE-level = ~8-25 calls per answer, the DEFAULT, matches how users check. Claim-level (atomic decomposition, FActScore-style) = 3-8x sentence cost, for medical/legal/financial.

flashcards.q: Decontextualisation: what is it and what breaks without it?
flashcards.a: Resolving references in a sentence against the preceding response before checking it. Without it, 'It was raised to 4.5% in March' is not an evaluable hypothesis, so the NLI model returns neutral and you get a FALSE 'unsupported' flag. This is the single most common cause of a verifier flagging 40% of good sentences. Fix with a heuristic subject-prepend or one LLM rewrite per RESPONSE (not per sentence).

flashcards.q: Why must you split long premises for NLI, and what do you get for free?
flashcards.a: NLI models are trained on premise/hypothesis pairs of a couple of sentences; feed a 1,200-1,500 token chunk and entailment drifts toward neutral. Split into overlapping 3-sentence windows, score each, and MAX-POOL. Free bonus: the winning window is your span-level locator, which is what the UI needs anyway.

flashcards.q: Which entailment checker, and why not just prompt a frontier model?
flashcards.a: MiniCheck-FT5 (~770M, flan-t5-large) matches Claude 3 Opus and approaches GPT-4 on LLM-AggreFact at a fraction of the cost; AlignScore-large is 355M on RoBERTa-large; HHEM-2.1-open is smaller still and beats several larger models; LettuceDetect flags unsupported SPANS. A frontier judge is 10-100x cost and, if same family as the generator, has correlated errors. Cascade: small checker everywhere, frontier judge only near the threshold band.

flashcards.q: Why does more search make attribution worse?
flashcards.a: Attention dilution during synthesis. The 2026 deep-research audit ablated search depth: GPT-5.4 fact-check accuracy fell from 79% at 2 tool calls to 17% at 150, while link validity and relevance stayed above 92%. Provider pattern matched: models generating the MOST citations had the LOWEST fact-check accuracy. Selective citation beats exhaustive citation.

flashcards.q: A citation passes entailment and the answer is still wrong. Name the ways.
flashcards.a: The cited document is SUPERSEDED (v1.4 entails it, v2.1 overrides). The span is CHERRY-PICKED (the exception, not the rule). The corpus is internally inconsistent and retrieval silently picked a side. Or the source itself is wrong — AIS is 'according to s', so attribution says nothing about truth. Fixes are corpus and retrieval fixes: effective_from / superseded_by metadata filtered at retrieval, plus a contradiction sweep.

flashcards.q: How do you detect cherry-picking or corpus conflict automatically?
flashcards.a: Run the NLI checker in the CONTRADICTION direction across the other retrieved chunks. If one retrieved chunk contradicts the generated sentence at high confidence while another entails it, the correct output is 'your documents disagree, here are both', not a confident answer. Costs another k entailment calls.

flashcards.q: Does RAG solve hallucination? Give the numbers.
flashcards.a: No, it reduces it. Stanford RegLab (Magesh et al., J. Empirical Legal Studies 2025): commercial legal RAG products hallucinated 17% (Lexis+ AI) to 33% (Westlaw AI-AR) versus 43% for GPT-4, while one vendor marketed '100% hallucination-free linked legal citations'. RAG moves the failure from parametric fabrication to mis-attribution, mis-ranking, and stale corpus content.

flashcards.q: The benchmark pair to quote when someone says hallucination is solved.
flashcards.a: Vectara HHEM summarisation 2026: frontier models ~1.0-2.5% (from 3-8% in 2023) on 7,700+ articles — the EASIEST grounding task, source in context. FACTS Benchmark Suite (Grounding v2 + parametric + search + multimodal): NO model breaks 70%, Gemini 3 Pro leads at 68.8%. Same models, two orders of difficulty.

flashcards.q: Why is your internal citation-precision number not comparable to a paper's?
flashcards.a: 2026 audit work (arXiv:2606.23915, 'Do LLM Attribution Metrics Transfer?') finds metric-human agreement varies substantially across datasets and constructs. Your number is a RELATIVE instrument for tracking your own regressions. Anchor it with a human audit of ~100 sentences per release.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT show citations?
flashcards.a: When there is exactly one source (highlight the span in the doc viewer instead — citation is disambiguation among sources). When the output is creative or synthesis-heavy (section-level provenance plus an on-demand sources view). When the claim comes from general knowledge and no source is being asserted (mark it unsourced rather than finding a plausible source). And when you cannot verify, since an unverified citation is a false trust signal.

flashcards.q: Verifying citations for a web-browsing agent: what changes?
flashcards.a: Page content is mutable, paywalled, or JS-rendered. So: SNAPSHOT at fetch time with a content hash and verify against the snapshot, not a re-fetch; cite snapshot id + URL + retrieval timestamp, since 'the page said this on date X' is the only supportable claim; verify per section during synthesis rather than once at the end; cap sources per section; and treat 'link works' as a fetcher health check, never as an attribution metric.

flashcards.q: State the core claim of context engineering in one sentence.
flashcards.a: Context is a budget with diminishing marginal returns, not a buffer: adding tokens usually makes an agent worse, so the job is finding the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximises the likelihood of the desired outcome.

flashcards.q: Why is attention a finite budget? Name three mechanisms.
flashcards.a: 1) A transformer lets every token attend to every other, giving n^2 pairwise relationships, so attention mass per relationship thins as n grows. 2) Training corpora are dominated by short sequences, so there are fewer parameters specialised for context-wide dependencies. 3) Position-encoding interpolation extends the window at a cost to positional precision. Result: a performance gradient, not a cliff.

flashcards.q: What did Chroma's context rot research measure?
flashcards.a: Across 18 frontier models, accuracy drops 20-50% from 10k to 100k+ input tokens, non-uniformly. Needle-question semantic similarity and the presence of near-miss DISTRACTORS matter more than raw length, and coherent well-structured input degrades attention MORE than shuffled input.

flashcards.q: The four context levers, in the order you reach for them.
flashcards.a: 1) Truncate tool results AT THE TOOL (free, biggest win, lossless where it matters). 2) Clear stale tool results (free, no LLM call, but breaks the prompt cache). 3) Compact older turns into a structured recap (one LLM call, lossy). 4) Isolate: subagents with fresh windows returning 1-2k distilled tokens, plus progress files that were never in the window.

flashcards.q: Derive the cost of a 40-turn run with a 6k prefix and 4k of growth per turn.
flashcards.a: cumulative_input = turns*base + growth*turns*(turns-1)/2 = 240,000 + 3,120,000 = 3.36M input tokens (~$10 at $3/Mtok). Cut per-turn growth to 1k and it is 240k + 780k = 1.02M (~$3). Same task, 3x cheaper, and the lever was the tool, not the model. Cost is quadratic in turns because the prefix re-sends every turn.

flashcards.q: List the seven things that must never be compacted.
flashcards.a: The task and success criteria; hard constraints and prohibitions; open obligations; identifiers and exact values; the user's most recent correction; any pending tool call; approval/permission state. The mechanism matters: they are regenerated from durable state into a protected block, so the summariser never sees them.

flashcards.q: What are the six sections of a good compaction schema?
flashcards.a: Task (request, success criteria, constraints), State (done, files changed, artefacts), Discoveries (facts, decisions with reasons, errors resolved), FAILED APPROACHES (without it the agent retries what already failed), Open items (a checklist, never silently dropped), Verbatim values (a flat list of every identifier/path/version/amount).

flashcards.q: At what fraction of the window should you trigger compaction, and why not later?
flashcards.a: 55-65%. The compaction call itself must fit both the region being summarised and the summary output, so triggering at 90-95% means the compaction request fails at the worst possible moment.

flashcards.q: How do you verify a compaction did not lose anything?
flashcards.a: Mechanically: regex every identifier-shaped token (tickets, hashes, versions, paths, amounts) out of the compacted region and assert each appears in the recap; assert every open item survived. Retry once naming the omissions; if it fails again, DO NOT COMPACT and keep more verbatim instead of shipping a lossy recap.

flashcards.q: Give the real Anthropic context-editing config parameters and defaults.
flashcards.a: Beta header context-management-2025-06-27. clear_tool_uses_20250919: trigger (default 100,000 input tokens), keep (default 3 tool use/result pairs), clear_at_least (cache-break floor), exclude_tools, clear_tool_inputs (default false, so the CALL stays visible and only the RESULT is cleared). clear_thinking_20251015: keep {thinking_turns: N} or 'all', and it must be listed FIRST in the edits array.

flashcards.q: How does context editing interact with prompt caching?
flashcards.a: Clearing tool results mutates the prefix and invalidates the cache from that point, so you pay a cache write. Cache reads run at ~0.1x base input, so a large stable prefix is nearly free and repeated small clears destroy that. clear_at_least exists for this: clear only if reclaimed * turns_until_next_clear * input_rate > prefix_tokens * cache_write_rate. Keeping thinking blocks preserves the cache; clearing them invalidates from the clear point.

flashcards.q: What is the subagent compression ratio and the return contract?
flashcards.a: A subagent may burn tens of thousands of tokens in a fresh window and return only 1,000-2,000 distilled tokens (~20-40x compression). Return contract: Answer (1-3 sentences), Evidence (file:line or URL plus the exact quoted span), Confidence and what would change it, and NOT FOUND / NOT CHECKED so gaps are explicit rather than silently omitted.

flashcards.q: What does subagent isolation cost you, and how do you mitigate it?
flashcards.a: An unauditable lossy handoff: if the 1.4k summary omitted the thing that mattered, the main agent cannot tell and cannot ask without re-running the subtask. Mitigations: require pointers (file:line, URL, stored query id) so the main agent can re-read on demand; require a 'not checked' section; and forbid subagents from acting. Keep writes single-threaded and let extra agents contribute intelligence, not actions.

flashcards.q: Why does a progress file beat compaction, and what are its three requirements?
flashcards.a: It was never in the context window, so compaction cannot lose it (and a human can read it mid-run). Requirements: 1) structure it with the same schema as the recap; 2) APPEND with timestamps rather than rewriting, because rewriting is a summary of a summary and reintroduces brevity bias; 3) the harness must INJECT the open-items section every turn after a compaction. 'Remember to read progress.md' is not a mechanism.

flashcards.q: The compaction / server-side tool token-accounting bug.
flashcards.a: With server-side tools like web search, cache_read_input_tokens accumulates across the tool's internal API calls: a response can show input_tokens 63,000 and cache_read_input_tokens 270,000. A client summing all usage fields sees 334k and compacts a conversation whose real context is 63k. Symptom: compaction firing every other turn on an obviously short conversation. Fix: the token-counting endpoint, exclude cache reads from the threshold, or use server-side compaction.

flashcards.q: Why is the protected constraints list a security control, not a nicety?
flashcards.a: 'Governance decay': compaction silently erasing constraints like 'read-only on prod' or 'never contact the customer directly' turns a quality issue into an unauthorised action, and it fails silently since nothing errors, the agent simply stops being constrained. It needs an assertion test in CI, not a code review.

flashcards.q: Why is 'retrieve 20 documents to be safe' negative-value?
flashcards.a: You did not hedge, you added 17 near-miss distractors, and distractors are the highest-damage category in context rot. Use a relevance floor where returning nothing is a valid result, rather than a fixed k.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT compact?
flashcards.a: Tasks needing precise recall of early detail (legal review, reconciliation, forensic transcript analysis) - keep verbatim, chunk, or externalise and re-read. Short runs under ~30% of the window. Client-side compaction alongside heavy server-side tools until token accounting is fixed. And remember context editing is within-session deletion, not memory.

flashcards.q: How would you falsify 'more tokens makes agents worse'?
flashcards.a: Pad the same golden task set with plausible-but-irrelevant retrieved content to 8k / 30k / 100k / 200k and plot task success. If success is flat or rising, the claim is wrong for that workload. In practice it falls, steepest on tasks needing precise retrieval from the middle. Naming the experiment is the difference between a measurement and a slogan.

flashcards.q: Server-side or client-side compaction, and why?
flashcards.a: Server-side by default (compact_20260112): less code, correct token accounting, and context editing applies before the prompt reaches the model so your client keeps the full unmodified history and your logs stay complete. The client-side SDK compaction_control is deprecated. Go client-side only when you need domain-specific control over what survives, and accept that you then own orphaned tool pairs, premature triggers, and recursive summarisation.

flashcards.q: Interpretability vs explainability — one sentence each.
flashcards.a: Interpretability is a property of the MODEL: how far its mechanism is human-understandable (global, intrinsic). Explainability is a property of an ACCOUNT OF ONE OUTPUT: why this input produced this output (local, usually post-hoc). For LLM systems interpretability is a research programme; explainability is an engineering deliverable made of traces and citations.

flashcards.q: The four-layer explanation stack. Which layers do you ship?
flashcards.a: L1 mechanistic (circuits, attribution graphs) = research only. L2 model-behavioural (SHAP/LIME/IG) = tabular components only. L3 SYSTEM TRACE = ship it, faithful by construction. L4 user rationale + citations = ship it, derived from L3 only. Chain-of-thought lives at L4, NOT L3.

flashcards.q: Faithfulness vs plausibility, and why the distinction is a product risk.
flashcards.a: Faithfulness = the explanation matches the process that produced the output. Plausibility = a human finds it convincing. They are independent axes and only plausibility is visible to users, PMs, and human raters, so RLHF and A/B tests optimise the wrong one. Plausible explanations raise acceptance of WRONG outputs.

flashcards.q: Cite the CoT unfaithfulness evidence with numbers.
flashcards.a: Turpin et al. 2023 (arXiv:2305.04388): biasing features drop accuracy up to 36% on 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks while CoT rationalises without mentioning the bias. Anthropic 2025 (arXiv:2505.05410): hint-verbalisation faithfulness 25% Claude 3.7 Sonnet / 39% DeepSeek R1, falling to 20% / 29% on harmful hints and worsening as tasks get harder. Arcuschin 2025 (arXiv:2503.08679): unfaithful on natural prompts with NO injected bias.

flashcards.q: Why exactly is chain-of-thought not an explanation of the computation?
flashcards.a: The CoT tokens are sampled autoregressively from the same distribution as the answer. Nothing in training ties them to the forward-pass computation that determined the answer, and RLHF rewards them for being convincing. Keep two claims separate: CoT is often causally load-bearing (erase it, accuracy drops) but is NOT a faithful description of the computation (25-39% on the standard test).

flashcards.q: Why is a trace faithful when CoT is not?
flashcards.a: Because emitting a trace is a DIFFERENT ACT from doing the work. A retrieval span is written by the retrieval code as a side effect; it cannot rationalise because it is not generated by a policy optimised for plausibility. A log is a record; a chain of thought is a story about a record.

flashcards.q: Give the arithmetic that rules SHAP out for LLMs.
flashcards.a: Exact Shapley = 2^|F| coalitions. KernelSHAP needs roughly 2|F| + 2048 samples, so ~3k forward passes per explained output at 512 tokens, and real prompts are 10-50k tokens. Plus: tokens are correlated so the marginal reference puts mass off-manifold, and SHAP explains a SCALAR while an LLM emits a sequence.

flashcards.q: Where does SHAP still belong, and what is TreeSHAP's complexity?
flashcards.a: On the non-generative models in the pipeline: the reranker's feature-based scorer, CTR or fraud models, the router. TreeSHAP is exact and O(T·L·D²) for T trees, L leaves, D depth, so it is cheap there. The point is scoping, not dismissal.

flashcards.q: Name LIME's two known failure modes.
flashcards.a: 1) Seed instability: different random perturbation samples give different top-k features for the same input, so you must run it n>=10 times and report only stable features. 2) Kernel width sigma is a free parameter with no principled default and no cross-validation objective, so changing it changes which features look important.

flashcards.q: Why does integrated gradients not transfer to text?
flashcards.a: IG needs a neutral baseline x'. For images, all-black works. For text there is none: the zero embedding is off-manifold, [PAD] and [MASK] carry learned meaning, and the baseline choice can flip attribution signs. It also needs white-box gradients (20-300 Riemann steps; check completeness sum ≈ f(x)−f(x') within ~5%), which you do not have for API models.

flashcards.q: The honesty ladder of LLM attribution: what can you claim, and at what cost?
flashcards.a: Provenance ('these tokens were in context') cost ~0, always on. NLI entailment ('this passage entails this sentence') one small-model call per sentence. Leave-one-out ('removing this chunk changes the answer') k+1 generations, audit path. SHAP on tabular: 100s-1000s of evals, batch. Attribution graphs: research. CoT: cost ~0 and it is the only rung that is a lie.

flashcards.q: Chunk occlusion says a chunk has zero influence. What do you conclude?
flashcards.a: Only that it was not NECESSARY given everything else present. Either it was irrelevant, or the fact was redundantly available in another chunk or in the weights. Occlusion measures necessity, not sufficiency. To disambiguate, run sufficiency (that chunk alone) and a closed-book baseline: three numbers are interpretable, one is not. Cost at k=10 is ~22 generation calls, so it is an audit-path technique.

flashcards.q: What must a trace pin for an explanation to be replayable?
flashcards.a: model@version, prompt template@version, tool schema version, index snapshot id. Plus retrieval query after rewrite, top-k doc ids with scores, rerank input/output order, tool arguments, guardrail verdicts, decision branches with budget remaining. Store result HASH + bounded prefix, not the full payload.

flashcards.q: Model card vs system card, and who owns each?
flashcards.a: Model card (Mitchell et al. 2019) documents the trained artefact: intended and out-of-scope use, training data summary, evaluation disaggregated by subgroup, caveats. For a frontier API model it is the provider's; for your fine-tune it is yours. System card documents the deployed composition — model + retrieval + tools + guardrails + human oversight — and the failure modes that only exist in the composition. That one is always yours.

flashcards.q: What the EU AI Act actually requires on explanation, and when.
flashcards.a: Not 'explainable models'. Article 13 requires transparency sufficient for deployers to interpret and use output appropriately; Article 14 requires oversight persons be able to correctly interpret output and override it. High-risk obligations plus Article 50 transparency and the GPAI documentation stack (internal docs, public model card, deployer package, training-data summary) apply from 2 August 2026, with penalties to €35M or 6-7% of global turnover depending on provision.

flashcards.q: Why is an explanation an attack surface, and what is the pattern?
flashcards.a: It leaks system-prompt structure, corpus composition, and threshold behaviour, so for adversarial decisions (fraud, abuse, pricing, moderation) a faithful explanation is a specification for evading the system. Pattern: two tiers — full trace to the internal reviewer, a fixed audited reason code plus an appeal route to the subject. No scores, no feature ordering, no 'you were 0.02 away', and rate-limit the endpoint since perturbed repeat queries are model extraction.

flashcards.q: How do you test whether an explanation actually helps?
flashcards.a: Error injection on the HUMANS, not the model: take N real outputs, corrupt a specific claim in a random half, show explanation and no-explanation arms to reviewers, and measure detection rate and time-to-decision. If detection does not improve, the explanation is decoration. Almost nobody runs this eval.

flashcards.q: Attention weights as explanation — the 2019 verdict.
flashcards.a: No. Jain & Wallace (NAACL 2019) constructed adversarial attention distributions producing the same prediction with completely different weights, so attention is not identifiable as the explanation. Wiegreffe & Pinter (EMNLP 2019) pushed back on the strongest reading without restoring it. In deep transformers it is worse: layer-7 attention is over representations that already mixed everything. Rollout/flow help coarse localisation and are still not causal.

flashcards.q: Where is mechanistic interpretability today, operationally?
flashcards.a: Anthropic's circuit tracing with cross-layer transcoders builds attribution graphs and was open-sourced as circuit-tracer in May 2025; MIT Tech Review named mech interp a 2026 Breakthrough Technology. Legitimate uses today: post-incident forensics on open-weights models you control, and safety research. Not a production explanation path — you need a transcoder per model and graph construction costs orders of magnitude more than the generation it explains.

flashcards.q: Verification instead of explanation — the two managed examples and what they buy.
flashcards.a: Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding filters over 75% of hallucinated responses on RAG and summarisation by checking output against source. Bedrock Automated Reasoning checks (GA Aug 2025) encode a policy into formal logic and validate outputs with claimed up to 99% accuracy. Note precisely what that is: a soundness claim over a FORMALISED policy, not an explanation, and it only exists where someone did the formalisation.

flashcards.q: The two orthogonal axes of the hallucination taxonomy, and the engineering consequence.
flashcards.a: Faithfulness (consistency with the PROVIDED source/instruction) vs factuality (consistency with the WORLD); and intrinsic (contradicts the source) vs extrinsic (source is silent). Consequence: faithfulness is testable this quarter with the source in hand via NLI; factuality is a fact-checking product with its own corpus, freshness, and dispute problems. Scope to faithfulness.

flashcards.q: Map each taxonomy cell to a detector and an action.
flashcards.a: Intrinsic faithfulness → NLI CONTRADICTION vs cited chunk → DROP the sentence, log a corpus conflict. Extrinsic faithfulness → NLI neutral (no entailment above tau) → flag unsupported or abstain. Intrinsic factuality → retrieve then NLI → correct or abstain. Extrinsic factuality → search/KB/human → mark unverified, usually out of scope.

flashcards.q: Three independent reasons hallucination is structural, not a bug.
flashcards.a: 1) NO NULL TOKEN — decoding must emit a distribution every step, so 'I don't know' is a learned sequence, not an escape hatch. 2) Lossy fact storage means approximate recall returns a plausible NEIGHBOUR — right shape, wrong value — which is why hallucinations are never absurd. 3) Kalai & Vempala (STOC 2024): a CALIBRATED model must hallucinate arbitrary facts at a rate >= monofact rate − miscalibration, independent of architecture and data quality.

flashcards.q: What is the monofact rate and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: The fraction of facts appearing exactly ONCE in the training corpus, related to the Good-Turing missing-mass estimator. Kalai & Vempala (arXiv:2311.14648) proved a calibrated model's hallucination rate on arbitrary facts is bounded below by it minus miscalibration; a 2026 PNAS study (arXiv:2502.08666) validated the prediction empirically. It is why 'zero hallucination' is not available for facts recalled from weights.

flashcards.q: Why does post-training make hallucination worse rather than better?
flashcards.a: score(guess) = p(correct) > 0 while score('I don't know') = 0, so any process optimising binary accuracy selects FOR guessing — Kalai et al. arXiv:2509.04664 and the Nature 2026 follow-on. And RLHF degrades calibration, so the guess arrives sounding certain. A single hallucination benchmark cannot outvote hundreds of accuracy benchmarks.

flashcards.q: Why is fluency a trap when reviewing for hallucination?
flashcards.a: Because lossy parametric recall returns items from the plausible neighbourhood: a fabricated section number looks like a section number, a fabricated year looks like a year. 'It read fine to me' is not a QA process, and human review without the source document open is worthless.

flashcards.q: Quote four hallucination rates with the task attached.
flashcards.a: Vectara HHEM summarisation 2026 frontier: ~1.0-2.5% (from 3-8% in 2023) — the easiest task, NOT a production number. FACTS Benchmark Suite: no model above 70%, leader 68.8%. AA-Omniscience (6k questions, 6 domains, refusal free, error penalised): most frontier models score BELOW ZERO. PersonQA (o3/o4-mini system card): o1 16% → o3 33% → o4-mini 48%.

flashcards.q: Does a newer/bigger model hallucinate less?
flashcards.a: Not automatically. OpenAI's o3/o4-mini system card (April 2025) reports PersonQA hallucination at 16% for o1, 33% for o3, 48% for o4-mini, noting the newer models make more claims overall so produce both more accurate and more inaccurate ones, and that 'more research is needed'. AA-Omniscience shows knowledge and reliability are partly decoupled. Gate upgrades on your own hallucination suite.

flashcards.q: Detection methods ranked by effectiveness per dollar.
flashcards.a: 1) NLI grounding vs the provided source — best value; MiniCheck-FT5 ~770M ≈ Claude 3 Opus on LLM-AggreFact, 10-40ms batched; Bedrock contextual grounding filters >75% of hallucinated RAG responses. 2) Semantic entropy — n generations + O(n·|C|) NLI, ~0.60 AUROC on hard sets, blind to consistent falsehood. 3) SelfCheckGPT — n=20, AUC-PR ~0.53-0.67. 4) Retrieval verification — only method for FACTUALITY, 1+ retrieval per claim. 5) Internal-state probes — 1 forward pass, white-box, distribution-specific. 6) LLM judge — 10-100x, correlated if same family.

flashcards.q: Gate vs router: why does it matter for an imperfect detector?
flashcards.a: A gate suppresses below threshold; at ~0.6 AUROC that costs many correct answers per error prevented, and the loss is invisible because suppressed correct answers generate no complaints. A router picks among actions — answer, answer+flags, deeper verification, clarify, escalate — so a weak signal degrades into 'spend more compute' rather than 'withhold a correct answer'. Prove it with the risk-coverage curve at equal risk and equal coverage.

flashcards.q: The honest ranking of what reduces hallucination.
flashcards.a: 1) Grounding in retrieval (+ relevance filter). 2) Constrained decoding / schema / citation-id grammar — eliminates CLASSES, near-free. 3) Verification passes (drop contradictions, flag unsupported). 4) Abstention. 5) Decomposition + tools for arithmetic/dates/lookup/aggregation. 6) Abstention fine-tuning. 7) Decoding interventions (CAD/DoLa/ITI). 8) Prompting, last.

flashcards.q: Why is constrained decoding ranked above verification?
flashcards.a: Because it is a STRUCTURAL impossibility rather than a probabilistic improvement, and it is nearly free. A schema with enums makes an out-of-vocabulary category impossible; a citation grammar over in-context ids makes a fabricated doc id impossible; a regex-constrained field makes a malformed identifier impossible. It does not touch free-text factual claims, which is why it is second, not first.

flashcards.q: Give the numbers proving 'be accurate' prompting is insufficient.
flashcards.a: A clinical adversarial study measured hallucination at 65.9% under the default prompt and 44.2% with a mitigation prompt — a real 22-point improvement and still 44%. Prompting cannot create knowledge the model lacks or install a null token.

flashcards.q: Why does temperature 0 not reduce hallucination?
flashcards.a: Same clinical study: 66.5% at zero temperature versus 65.9% default — statistically indistinguishable; broader work finds temperature in 0.0-1.0 has no significant effect on problem-solving accuracy. The failure is not sampling noise: the model's MODE is frequently the plausible falsehood. Greedy decoding buys reproducibility, which matters for debugging and evals, not truth.

flashcards.q: Full list of things that do NOT work.
flashcards.a: 'Be accurate' / 'don't hallucinate' instructions (65.9% → 44.2%, still 44%); temperature 0 alone (66.5% vs 65.9%); a bigger or newer model (PersonQA 16% → 33% → 48%); more context (context rot; deep-research fact check 79% → 17% from 2 to 150 tool calls); self-verification by the same model (correlated errors); RLHF (degrades calibration); and a single detector used as a hard gate.

flashcards.q: Name and explain RAG-induced distraction.
flashcards.a: Irrelevant retrieved chunks make output WORSE than no retrieval, so more k is not more grounding. Observable signature: an eval sweep where accuracy at k=10 is worse than at k=3, per-chunk relevance scores showing a long low-relevance tail, and traces where the answer references a chunk unrelated to the question. A relevance filter on retrieved chunks is part of grounding, not an optional extra.

flashcards.q: The three ways hallucination behaves worse inside an agent loop.
flashcards.a: 1) It COMPOUNDS — a fabricated intermediate becomes the premise of step 7, which is internally coherent and wrong. 2) Fabricated TOOL ARGUMENTS execute: a well-formed but invented record id, path, or filter runs with no reader to catch it. 3) Uncertainty is LAUNDERED at subagent handoffs — a summary reads as fact to the supervisor. Fix: check on the OBSERVATION path before results enter context, and again before any side-effecting call.

flashcards.q: The eval trap that makes internal scores rise while complaints rise.
flashcards.a: A binary-accuracy internal leaderboard pays your own team to guess, exactly as Kalai et al. describe for the industry. Also: a golden set drawn from happy-path traffic with no false premises, underspecified questions, or genuinely unanswerable cases; and response-level rather than claim-level scoring, so nine right claims plus one fabrication scores well. Fix: AA-Omniscience-style scoring (reward correct, penalise wrong, refusal neutral) plus adversarial cases plus claim-level metrics.

flashcards.q: The production mitigation pipeline, in order.
flashcards.a: 1) Retrieve + relevance-filter chunks. 2) Constrain the output shape (schema, enums, citation-id grammar). 3) Generate with an explicit prefer-context instruction. 4) Verify per sentence with an NLI gate and drop contradictions. 5) Route on the ensemble signal. 6) BOUNDED regeneration, max 2, then abstain. 7) Log with versions and sample for human audit.

flashcards.q: Where is hallucination acceptable or desirable, and what is the boundary rule?
flashcards.a: Brainstorming, naming, fiction, marketing variants, hypothesis generation, synthetic training data, adversarial test-case generation — where producing plausible content absent from the source IS the feature and a human is the filter. Boundary rule: nothing downstream may treat the output as fact, so creative-surface outputs carry a provenance marker and factual surfaces treat unmarked pasted content as unverified.

flashcards.q: Decoding-time interventions: name three and the measured effect.
flashcards.a: Context-Aware Decoding (CAD, arXiv:2305.14739) contrasts logits with and without context to force trust in the context, reporting ≈14.3% factuality gain for LLaMA on summarisation and being especially strong on knowledge conflicts. DoLa contrasts early vs late layer logits. ITI shifts activations along truthfulness directions. All need white-box access, deliver modest gains, and rank seventh.

flashcards.q: What do you tell an executive who asks when hallucinations will be fixed?
flashcards.a: 'Not fixed, bounded — here is the bound and the plan.' Then: it is structural with a proven statistical floor for facts recalled from weights, so the goal is an error budget like latency or availability; our measured unsupported-sentence rate is X% at Y% coverage on our own golden set, measured this way; the next three interventions in priority order with expected effect and cost; and the human gate on irreversible actions stays regardless of the model, because the residual rate will never be zero.

flashcards.q: Define an agent harness in one sentence, and give the analogy.
flashcards.a: Everything in an agent except the model: the runtime control plane of loop, instruction assembly, context building, tools, permissions, execution, state, memory, compaction, planning, approvals and traces. Agent = Model + Harness. Analogy (Schmid, Jan 2026): the model is the CPU, the context window is the RAM, the harness is the operating system, the agent is the application.

flashcards.q: State the four necessary and sufficient conditions for a system to be an agent harness.
flashcards.a: T1 a reasoning/action/observation loop at runtime. T2 a tool interface that can ALTER an external environment, not merely read it.
