T3 active management of what enters and leaves context. T4 at least one control mechanism whose effectiveness does not depend on the model cooperating. Yes to all four = harness. Memory, verification, observability and retry are specializations of T1-T4, not a fifth condition.

flashcards.q: Why does size-based truncation fail T3, and a log line fail T4?
flashcards.a: T3 requires the decision about what enters and leaves context to depend on the CONTENT of the task or current observation, not merely on buffer size; a mechanical cut by size does some context handling but is not active management. T4 requires the mechanism to alter or contain execution independently of the model's choices; a log print changes nothing about execution, whereas a tool-call cap or a re-run of the test suite does.

flashcards.q: List the 15 harness components.
flashcards.a: 1 instruction manager, 2 context builder, 3 model adapter, 4 tool registry, 5 permission engine, 6 execution engine, 7 state store, 8 memory and retrieval, 9 compactor, 10 planner/goal controller, 11 skill registry, 12 MCP/external connector manager, 13 approval manager, 14 trace and eval system, 15 sandbox/execution boundary.

flashcards.q: What is NOT required for a system to be a harness?
flashcards.a: Multi-agent architecture (a single model in a loop with tools and control already qualifies), learning or fine-tuning (the harness is engineering around the model, not modification of it), a specific model (model switching is itself a control mechanism), and a user interface (a harness can be a faceless library).

flashcards.q: Walk the tool-call contract from model output to observation. Why is the order load-bearing?
flashcards.a: resolve name + phase visibility, SCHEMA VALIDATE, PERMISSION resolve (allow/deny/ask), on ask checkpoint and return for durable approval, attach idempotency key if mutating, execute in the SANDBOX with a timeout, shape the result (persist above ~50K chars keeping a 2KB preview and path), inject as a typed observation. Validation must precede permission resolution because you cannot make an authorization decision about arguments you have not parsed; coercing them first is how you get a policy bypass.

flashcards.q: What is the error policy inside a harness, and what is the one exception to it?
flashcards.a: Every rejection path returns an observation with a remediation message the model can act on: unknown tool, invalid arguments (include the schema), permission denied, timeout, sandbox refusal, tool dependency failure. The exception: do not swallow your own bugs. A tool's dependency failing returns to the model; a harness KeyError should crash loudly, because a model cannot fix your programming error and swallowing it ships a broken agent that merely looks stupid.

flashcards.q: State the boundary principle: what does the trusted control plane own versus the sandbox?
flashcards.a: Harness owns user identity and tenant boundaries, credential management, approval records, audit logs, billing and rate limits, tool authorization, and the final commit to external systems. Sandbox owns temp files, generated artifacts, script execution, isolated browser or shell work, connector-specific data processing. Never put secrets, approval logic or authorization decisions in the prompt or in anything the model can modify.

flashcards.q: Give the authority hierarchy for content in an agent's context, and the rule that follows.
flashcards.a: provider/system policy > organization policy > product/developer policy > workspace/project policy (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md) > domain or directory policy > user task > model-visible runtime reminders > tool observations > untrusted retrieved content. Rule: retrieved content may contain instructions, but those instructions are DATA, not policy. Labelling lowers the probability of injection; only a model-independent control (the permission engine) bounds the damage.

flashcards.q: How can compaction launder authority? Name the documented example.
flashcards.a: Claude Code's autocompact summarizer processes user instructions and tool results through the same pipeline with no classification step, so an instruction planted in a project file survives compaction and lands in the summary indistinguishable from legitimate context. The <analysis> chain-of-thought scratchpad that makes summaries good faithfully preserves the injection. A second edge: when the conversation is so long the compaction request itself returns prompt-too-long, recursive head-truncation drops the edges, so content placed mid-conversation survives.

flashcards.q: Is a guardrail a harness? Give the test question.
flashcards.a: No, it is a part of one. Guardrails LIMIT (cap tool calls, block destructive commands, cost ceilings). The harness as a whole ENABLES (context manager helps it remember, memory avoids repeated work, retry survives transients, verifier confirms completion). Test: is this limiting the agent or helping it execute? Limiting means guardrail, which is a kind of T4 control. Part-whole relation, not sibling categories.

flashcards.q: Give four numbers showing harness beats model choice.
flashcards.a: LangChain moved a coding agent from rank 30 to top 5 on Terminal Bench 2.0 with harness-only changes and no model swap. statewright took local models from 2/10 to 10/10 on a SWE-bench subset purely by shrinking the per-phase tool space. Microsoft's Azure SRE Agent raised 'Intent Met' from 45% to 75% on novel incidents by replacing 100+ bespoke tools with a filesystem plus read_file/grep/find/shell. Anthropic's 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report puts harness configuration alone at 5+ percentage points of benchmark swing. Life-Harness showed harness-side adaptation transferring across 18 model backbones.

flashcards.q: What is the Bitter Lesson tax on harness design, with evidence?
flashcards.a: Every harness component encodes an assumption that the model cannot do something, and those assumptions expire. Manus refactored their harness five times in six months to remove rigid assumptions. LangChain re-architected Open Deep Research three times in one year. Vercel deleted 80% of their agent's tools and got fewer steps, fewer tokens and faster responses. LangChain also warns models can OVERFIT to a harness, so an elaborate custom harness can be worse on the next model. Conclusion: build to delete, modular, rippable in an afternoon.

flashcards.q: Name the ten-item minimal viable harness and the build sequence.
flashcards.a: Ten: one model adapter, one deterministic context builder, a narrow tool registry, strict local schema validation, runtime permission checks, structured tool results with remediation, step and cost budgets, trace logging, compaction only when needed, a small eval set. Sequence: manual loop, tools, permissions, structured observations, budgets, tracing, planning, context/memory, compaction, skills/connectors, goal loop, subagents. Each later component is undebuggable without the earlier ones.

flashcards.q: Give the six harness maturity levels.
flashcards.a: 0 answer-only assistant (no tools). 1 retrieval agent (reads trusted resources, no side effects). 2 drafting agent (proposes, cannot commit). 3 approval-gated actor (executes after explicit approval). 4 policy-bounded autonomous actor (low-risk actions within scopes, budgets, audit). 5 long-running goal worker (multi-session progress; needs durable state, compaction, budgets, checkpoints, evaluation). Move up only when evals show the simpler level is insufficient.

flashcards.q: Why is a shell deny-list not a security boundary?
flashcards.a: Microsoft's own Agent Framework docs state it: the deny-list is a UX pre-filter, not a security boundary. Shell syntax has too many equivalent encodings (variable expansion, base64 piped into sh, find -exec, writing then executing a script) for pattern matching to hold against intent. Patterns catch accidents; the boundary is capability-based, namely what filesystem, network and credentials the sandboxed process actually has, plus a permission engine that does not consult the model.

flashcards.q: What are the three documented enterprise MCP gaps, and their mitigations?
flashcards.a: 1 No identity propagation: the server cannot tell who the request is ultimately for, breaking per-user authorization and audit. Mitigate with JWT-enriched tool calls. 2 No adaptive tool budgeting: nothing negotiates call count or latency, so one slow tool blows the wall-clock budget. Mitigate with per-tool timeout contracts enforced harness-side. 3 Unstructured error semantics: errors arrive as prose so the harness cannot map them to retry/deny/escalate. Mitigate with a standardized error-to-action mapping.

flashcards.q: Is MCP an agent protocol?
flashcards.a: No, it is a TOOL protocol, and it is component 12 of 15. OpenAI built a separate Item/Turn/Thread protocol over JSON-RPC/JSONL on stdio for the Codex harness precisely because approval flows, streaming diffs and thread persistence needed more than a tool-oriented model could express. Also note the transport issue: Streamable HTTP replaced HTTP+SSE in the 2025-11-25 spec and unlocks remote servers, but the stateful Mcp-Session-Id header fights load balancers and horizontal scaling.

flashcards.q: Why is the state store the highest-priority component, arithmetically?
flashcards.a: At 85% per-step reliability a ten-step run completes about 20% of the time; at 95%, about 60%. So most multi-step runs fail somewhere, and without checkpoints every failure is a full restart that pays the whole token bill again. A state store converts restart into resume. Store typed events (user_message, assistant_message, tool_call, tool_result, approval_request/result, plan_update, goal_update, skill_invocation, memory_load, context_compaction, connector_call, error, final_answer) rather than a message array; the prompt is not a database.

flashcards.q: One trace attribute to add first, and why?
flashcards.a: The hash of the fully assembled request prefix. It makes the two most expensive silent bugs visible at once: unintended prompt drift (hash changed and nobody meant it to) and cache breakage (hash changes every turn, so cache_read_input_tokens is zero and you pay 5-10x). It also makes runs reproducible, which is the precondition for snapshot testing, resumability and bisecting a regression.

flashcards.q: How do you tell a model regression from a harness regression?
flashcards.a: You cannot without harness versioning plus an eval gate: harness config in git, one change per PR, a golden eval set in CI, and traces recording model version, reasoning-effort setting, cache configuration, prompt hash and tool-registry hash per run. Then a regression is a bisect. Anthropic's April 2026 postmortem is the canonical case: Claude Code degradation traced to three independent harness-level changes (a default reasoning-effort downgrade, a caching bug dropping thinking history from stale sessions, and an overly aggressive verbosity-limiting prompt) with no model change at all.

flashcards.q: What is the 'lethal trifecta' and what does it imply for a permission engine?
flashcards.a: Private data access + exposure to untrusted content + the ability to communicate externally. Each tool can be individually safe while the SET exfiltrates, so per-tool risk analysis is insufficient. The implication: the permission engine needs a session-level property, not just per-call rules. If a session has read private data and ingested untrusted content, egress tools require approval regardless of their individual MCP annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint), which are hints feeding the decision rather than enforced contracts.

flashcards.q: How do you test a harness given a nondeterministic model?
flashcards.a: Layer it: the registry, permission engine, execution engine, budgets, compactor and context builder are deterministic code, so unit-test them against a scripted fake model. Assert INVARIANTS not outputs: a bad-arg call yields an observation containing the schema and the loop continues; a denied call yields an observation and the loop continues; messages[0] and the open-items list survive compaction; the assembled request is byte-identical across two runs of the same fixture. Tools tested independently. Only end-to-end needs evals: 10-20 golden tasks with trajectory and outcome assertions, tracked as a distribution.

flashcards.q: When is building a harness the wrong call?
flashcards.a: Single-turn tasks (classification, extraction, summarizing provided content): level 0, no loop, and a harness buys latency, cost and nondeterminism for nothing. Deterministic workflows: write the pipeline, since fifteen components maintaining a state machine an if-statement expressed better is strictly worse. Long-running multi-party work needing retries across hours, day-long approvals and exactly-once side effects: a hand-rolled state store plus approval manager is a worse Temporal, so use Temporal or Step Functions with LLM calls as activities.

flashcards.q: Computational versus inferential controls, and the ordering rule.
flashcards.a: Bockeler's distinction. Computational controls are deterministic and cheap: linters, type checkers, tests, schema validators, re-running the suite. Inferential controls are probabilistic: LLM-as-judge, 'does this match our architectural conventions'. Exhaust computational first; use inferential only where no computational check exists. An inferential control alone does not robustly satisfy T4, because its effectiveness partly depends on the same class of system that produced the output.

flashcards.q: What is the harness engineering loop as an operating model?
flashcards.a: Agent fails or slows down, identify the missing capability, context, validator or permission rule, encode the fix into docs, tools, policies, schemas or evals, rerun and measure, keep the improvement as part of the harness. The mature model is: humans steer, agents execute, and the harness turns human judgment into reusable constraints and feedback loops. Corollary: most agent failures are not insufficient autonomy but weak harness boundaries (broad tools, vague instructions, missing approval gates, unstructured tool results, poor context hygiene, no evals).

flashcards.q: What is a gate a function of?
flashcards.a: gate = f(irreversibility, blast radius, externality), with rate risk handled independently as a cap. NOT a function of how scary the tool's name is, and never a function of what the model asked for — prompt injection's whole purpose is to make the agent believe an action is authorised.

flashcards.q: The gate ladder from reversible-small to unbounded-destructive.
flashcards.a: reversible + small → AUTO + LOG (+ audit sample). reversible + bounded → NOTIFY-AND-PROCEED + undo window. irreversible OR external-visible OR financial → SYNCHRONOUS APPROVAL with a diff. irreversible + multi-record or high value → DUAL APPROVAL (four-eyes). unbounded destructive → PROHIBITED, not in the toolset. Delete stays gated at every autonomy level.

flashcards.q: Why does externality dominate reversibility?
flashcards.a: Because anything a third party observes — email, payment, public post, filed document — is irreversible in practice even when the database row can be rolled back. You cannot un-send. So an action that is reversible in your data model but sends an email is tiered as irreversible.

flashcards.q: Five properties to register per tool, at registration time not call time.
flashcards.a: Class (read_only | write | financial | destructive); reversibility (trivial | compensating | none); max blast radius (one | bounded | unbounded); externality (none | internal | external_visible); rate risk plus a cap. The four-tier class vocabulary alone is insufficient because 'write' spans a draft edit and a production config overwrite.

flashcards.q: The most under-used oversight pattern, and why it beats an approval.
flashcards.a: Dry run + diff + deterministic invariant checks. The agent computes the exact change and a validator asserts invariants — row count in bounds, no rows outside the tenant, no field crossing a threshold, target matches a pattern. Most of what a reviewer would catch is expressible as an assertion, so it runs in milliseconds on 100% of actions instead of 90 seconds on 10%.

flashcards.q: Second-best pattern: reversibility instead of approval.
flashcards.a: Soft delete with a 7-day tombstone, a staged email that sends after 10 minutes unless cancelled, a config change behind a feature flag. Each converts an approval into an undo, which costs a human nothing in the normal case. Approvals scale linearly with volume; undo windows do not.

flashcards.q: Six requirements for a review to be meaningful.
flashcards.a: 1) Show the DIFF, not the intent. 2) Evidence inline at the decision point. 3) 'No' is one click, has a reason code, and is respected (no instant re-propose). 4) Bounded queue within computed review capacity. 5) Time budgeted, and NO bulk-approve affordance on irreversible classes. 6) Measured by error injection — corrupt a small random percentage of proposals and track catch rate.

flashcards.q: Four telemetry signals that detect rubber-stamping.
flashcards.a: Approval decision p50 latency under ~5s on a decision designed to take 45-90s. Override/rejection rate near 0%, meaning the gate is decorative. Gated volume above computed review capacity, which is unplanned sampling with unknown coverage. Any bulk-approve usage on an irreversible class, which is a design bug because the affordance should not exist.

flashcards.q: The alert-fatigue base rates that predict gate decay.
flashcards.a: ~2,992 security alerts per day with 63% unaddressed (Vectra 2026); 46% of alerts are false positives (Microsoft SOC 2026); 73% of security teams name false positives as their top detection challenge and 76% cite alert fatigue (SANS 2025); ~90% of SOCs report backlog overwhelm; 71% of analysts report burnout (Tines). Approval queues obey the same physics.

flashcards.q: Why is error injection the only real test of a gate, and how do you run it ethically?
flashcards.a: Because a gate with a low catch rate is not oversight, it is a latency tax plus accountability laundering — the human's signature transfers blame without transferring scrutiny. Run it disclosed as part of the role, agreed with people managers, never used for individual performance management, and reported only in aggregate. Framed as a fire drill it is standard practice; framed as gotcha surveillance it destroys the trust the control depends on.

flashcards.q: Six escalation decisions you must make explicitly.
flashcards.a: 1) Timeout default per tier — FAIL-CLOSED for irreversible/financial, fail-open only for reversible+bounded and logged as timeout not approval. 2) Request expiry with preconditions re-validated at execution. 3) Who may approve, with separation of duties. 4) Tiering with target response times and fallbacks. 5) Batching rules — per-item for irreversible, never select-all across a heterogeneous batch. 6) A tested kill switch.

flashcards.q: Why does an approval bind to a diff rather than an intent?
flashcards.a: Because approving a 40-minute-old proposal is approving a stale world state. Requests carry an expiry, and preconditions are re-validated at execution time with a failure if they moved. Otherwise an approved action executes against changed data, which is a classic incident.

flashcards.q: Separation of duties for agents — three concrete rules.
flashcards.a: The requester cannot approve. The agent cannot approve itself, so any 'agent:' principal is rejected as an approver in the broker. The approver must hold the permission for the underlying action in their own right. And the agent must never hold the credential that grants approval.

flashcards.q: The audit record field everyone forgets, and the second one.
flashcards.a: First: THE EVIDENCE BUNDLE THE REVIEWER WAS SHOWN (or its hash). Without it you cannot distinguish informed approval from a rubber stamp, and it catches the bug where the UI showed something different from the request. Second: DECISION LATENCY, which is your rubber-stamp detector. Also store the policy id + version, or 'why was this gated this way' is unanswerable.

flashcards.q: What EU AI Act Article 14 actually requires, and when.
flashcards.a: High-risk systems from 2 August 2026 must be DESIGNED so oversight persons can: understand the system's capacities and limitations; remain aware of the tendency to over-rely on it (automation bias is named in the text); correctly interpret output; decide not to use, or disregard, override, or reverse it; and intervene or halt via a stop button or comparable procedure. Article 26 adds deployer duties. Penalties to €35M or 6-7% of global turnover depending on provision.

flashcards.q: Why does Article 14 being a DESIGN obligation matter to an engineer?
flashcards.a: Because a UI that makes override impractical is non-compliant even with a human present. A rubber-stamped queue is a compliance finding, not just a quality problem. Staffing a queue does not discharge the obligation; the interface has to make meaningful review and override realistic.

flashcards.q: What is actually on an enterprise buyer's oversight checklist?
flashcards.a: A tested kill switch; scoped short-lived per-agent credentials rather than a shared service account; an exportable immutable audit log with defined retention; RBAC with separation of duties on approvals; documented risk tiers and which actions require human approval; data residency and retention for prompts, traces, and evidence bundles; and a named accountable owner.

flashcards.q: The gates-versus-value arithmetic.
flashcards.a: net = S − g·R − wait_cost, break-even at g = S/R, where S is minutes saved, R is minutes of review, g is the gated fraction. S=10 R=1.5 → gate everything and keep 85%. S=10 R=5 → keep 50%. S=2 R=1.5 → keep 25% and rubber-stamping is CERTAIN because the economics force speed. wait_cost is the forgotten term: a synchronous gate blocks the run.

flashcards.q: Why is durable checkpointing a prerequisite for approval gates?
flashcards.a: Because a synchronous mid-run gate means the run must suspend to storage and resume, not sit in memory holding a connection through a lunch break or a deploy. LangGraph interrupt() plus a Postgres checkpointer, or Temporal signals, is the reference shape. Without it, approval latency turns into lost runs and held resources.

flashcards.q: How do you resolve the gates-versus-velocity argument without politics?
flashcards.a: Evidence-based autonomy ratcheting: start gated per action class, measure the error rate and the reviewer catch rate, and graduate a class from approval to notify-and-proceed after a defined volume of clean executions, with automatic demotion on incident. Validate a proposed loosening by shadow-running it first. Deletes and unbounded-blast-radius actions never graduate.

flashcards.q: When is a human gate the WRONG answer?
flashcards.a: When a deterministic check does the same job in milliseconds on 100% of actions. When the action can be made reversible instead. When the reviewer lacks the expertise to judge, since the gate then transfers liability without adding scrutiny. When the queue would exceed review capacity, where explicit sampling with known coverage beats an over-capacity queue. And when latency is structurally intolerable — redesign the action rather than faking a 200ms gate.

flashcards.q: Who is accountable when an agent does something wrong?
flashcards.a: A named human. Every agent has an owner; actions attribute through the delegation chain to a person — the principal it acted for, the reviewer who approved, the owner who deployed it with those permissions. 'The AI did it' is never a resolution, and deployer duties under Article 26 cannot be delegated to a vendor or a model. A 3-second approval is the DESIGN's failure, not the reviewer's.

flashcards.q: Rank oversight investments by protection per unit of cost.
flashcards.a: 1) Remove the action from the toolset. 2) Scoped short-lived per-agent credentials, so unpermitted actions fail at the API. 3) Deterministic invariants + dry-run diffs. 4) Reversibility. 5) Rate caps — the only thing that bounds a runaway loop. 6) Narrow, well-designed approval gates on the genuinely irreversible set. 7) Immutable audit with evidence digest and decision latency. 8) Error-injection catch-rate measurement. Dead last: adding more gates.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph I: StateGraph, Reducers, Conditional Edges, Send
flashcards.q: What execution model does LangGraph use internally, and what is a super-step?
flashcards.a: Pregel-style bulk-synchronous message passing (Google, 2010). A super-step is one tick: every scheduled node runs (possibly in parallel), all their writes are reduced into the channels, a checkpoint is written, then the next tick is scheduled from nodes with inbound messages. Halts when no node has inbound messages.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph I: StateGraph, Reducers, Conditional Edges, Send
flashcards.q: What is the default reducer for a state key, and what happens if two nodes write it in the same super-step?
flashcards.a: The default is LAST WRITE WINS (overwrite). Two writes in ONE super-step raise `InvalidUpdateError: At key 'k': Can receive only one value per step. Use an Annotated key to handle multiple values.` Two writes on CONSECUTIVE super-steps raise nothing and silently discard the first.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph I: StateGraph, Reducers, Conditional Edges, Send
flashcards.q: What is a reducer's signature, and why does `Annotated[list, operator.add]` exist?
flashcards.a: `(current, update) -> new`. It exists because a channel without a reducer accepts exactly one write per super-step, so any parallel fan-out or Send map-reduce writing a shared channel is broken by construction. It is the fan-in contract, not typing decoration.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph I: StateGraph, Reducers, Conditional Edges, Send
flashcards.q: How is `add_messages` different from `operator.add`?
flashcards.a: `operator.add` concatenates blindly. `add_messages` matches on message `id` and REPLACES an existing message with the same id, and coerces `{"role":..,"content":..}` dicts into LangChain message objects. The id-matching is why HITL edits and `update_state` correct a message instead of duplicating it.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph I: StateGraph, Reducers, Conditional Edges, Send
flashcards.q: How do you bypass a reducer and set a channel directly?
flashcards.a: `Overwrite(value)` from `langgraph.types`, e.g. `return {"messages": Overwrite([summary])}`. Constraint: only one node may Overwrite a given key per super-step, otherwise `InvalidUpdateError`.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph I: StateGraph, Reducers, Conditional Edges, Send
flashcards.q: What is the default `recursion_limit` in current LangGraph, what did it used to be, and where does it go in config?
flashcards.a: 1000 super-steps as of langgraph 1.0.6; it was 25 for the framework's first two years. It is a TOP-LEVEL config key: `config={"recursion_limit": 40}`. Nested under `configurable` it is silently ignored. Exceeding it raises `GraphRecursionError`.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph I: StateGraph, Reducers, Conditional Edges, Send
flashcards.q: What does `Send` do, and how is it different from a conditional edge returning a list of node names?
flashcards.a: `Send(node, per_call_state)` runs the SAME node N times on N DIFFERENT states, returned as a list from a conditional edge. A conditional edge returning `["a","b"]` runs two DIFFERENT nodes on the SAME state. Send requires a reducer on the fan-in channel and a `max_concurrency` bound.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph I: StateGraph, Reducers, Conditional Edges, Send
flashcards.q: Your fan-in node sees only some of the fan-out results and no error is raised. Cause and fix?
flashcards.a: Unequal branch lengths: the fan-in node's inbound edges were satisfied before the longer branch finished, so it ran on a partial channel. Fix: `add_node("synthesise", fn, defer=True)`, which delays it until all pending tasks complete. Symmetric test fixtures never trigger it.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph I: StateGraph, Reducers, Conditional Edges, Send
flashcards.q: When do you use `Command` instead of a conditional edge, and what are the two gotchas?
flashcards.a: When you need to update state AND route in one decision: `Command(update=..., goto=...)`. Gotchas: (1) you must annotate the return type `-> Command[Literal["a","b"]]` or the runtime can't render the graph or know destinations; (2) `goto` ADDS a dynamic edge and does not override a static `add_edge`, so both destinations run. One routing mechanism per node.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph I: StateGraph, Reducers, Conditional Edges, Send
flashcards.q: What belongs in graph state, and where do dependencies and large blobs go instead?
flashcards.a: State is serialised into a checkpoint at every super-step, so keep it small and serialisable: ids, decisions, counters, messages. Dependencies (DB connections, model name, tenant id) go in runtime context via `context_schema` + `Runtime[Ctx]`, which is NOT checkpointed. Large blobs go in the `Store` or object storage with only the key in state.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph I: StateGraph, Reducers, Conditional Edges, Send
flashcards.q: Name the seven LangGraph stream modes and which require a checkpointer.
flashcards.a: `values`, `updates`, `messages`, `custom`, `checkpoints`, `tasks`, `debug`. `checkpoints`, `tasks`, and `debug` require a checkpointer. `debug` = checkpoints + tasks + metadata.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph I: StateGraph, Reducers, Conditional Edges, Send
flashcards.q: What do `version="v2"` and `version="v3"` change about streaming?
flashcards.a: v1 (still default) changes shape by options: raw dict, `(mode,data)` tuples, `(ns,data)` for subgraphs, triples for both. `version="v2"` (needs >=1.1) makes every chunk a uniform `StreamPart` `{type, ns, data}` and makes `invoke` return a `GraphOutput` with `.value`/`.interrupts`. `version="v3"` on `stream_events` (1.2, beta) gives typed per-channel projections: `.messages`, `.values`, `.interrupts`, `.output`.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph I: StateGraph, Reducers, Conditional Edges, Send
flashcards.q: Three subgraph persistence modes via `compile(checkpointer=...)` and their tradeoffs?
flashcards.a: `None` (per-invocation, default): interrupts YES, memory across calls NO, parallel calls safe YES. `True` (per-thread): memory YES, own checkpoint history so inner time travel works, but parallel calls to the SAME subgraph conflict on the namespace. `False` (stateless): plain function call, no interrupts, no durable execution.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph I: StateGraph, Reducers, Conditional Edges, Send
flashcards.q: What are `RetryPolicy`'s defaults, and which exceptions does it deliberately NOT retry?
flashcards.a: `max_attempts=3`, `initial_interval=0.5s`, `backoff_factor=2.0`, `max_interval=128s`, `jitter=True`. Default `retry_on` retries any exception EXCEPT ValueError, TypeError, ArithmeticError, ImportError, LookupError, NameError, SyntaxError, RuntimeError, ReferenceError, StopIteration, StopAsyncIteration, OSError. For requests/httpx it retries 5xx only.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph I: StateGraph, Reducers, Conditional Edges, Send
flashcards.q: In what fixed order do per-node timeout, retry policy, and error handler compose?
flashcards.a: timeout raises `NodeTimeoutError` -> the retry policy decides whether to retry -> only after retries are exhausted does `error_handler` run (receiving a typed `NodeError`, and it can return a `Command` for Saga compensation). `interrupt()` bypasses both retries and the error handler. Timeouts and error handlers require langgraph>=1.2 and are async-node-only.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph I: StateGraph, Reducers, Conditional Edges, Send
flashcards.q: Honestly, what does the graph abstraction buy you over a 40-line agent loop?
flashcards.a: Exactly three things: a checkpoint boundary at every super-step (turning restart into resume, which matters because 0.85^10 ~= 20%), declared merge semantics for parallel writes via reducers, and an inspectable/streamable topology with per-node retry, timeout, and cache policies. For a simple model->tool->model loop it buys almost none of that and costs you a framework in the stack trace plus a migration every couple of quarters.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph I: StateGraph, Reducers, Conditional Edges, Send
flashcards.q: Which LangGraph versions introduced what, and when?
flashcards.a: 1.0.0 on 2025-10-20 (GA). 1.1.0 on 2026-03-10: `version="v2"` unified StreamPart streaming and typed invoke. 1.2.0 on 2026-05-12: per-node timeouts, node-level `error_handler`, graceful shutdown via `RunControl.request_drain()`, `DeltaChannel` (beta), and `version="v3"` event streaming.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: What four methods does `BaseCheckpointSaver` implement, and what does each surface as?
flashcards.a: `.put` (store a full snapshot; one write per super-step), `.put_writes` (per-task intermediate writes = pending-writes recovery), `.get_tuple` (surfaces as `graph.get_state()`), `.list` (surfaces as `graph.get_state_history()`). Async twins: `.aput`, `.aput_writes`, `.aget_tuple`, `.alist`, used automatically by `ainvoke`/`astream`.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: What does `put_writes` protect against?
flashcards.a: Within one super-step, each node's writes are persisted as task rows before the super-step's snapshot commits. If A, B, C run in parallel and C throws, A and B's writes are already durable and are NOT re-executed on resume. Only C re-runs. It protects siblings, NOT the failing node itself.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: Why does `InMemorySaver` not survive a deploy, and what is the second failure people miss?
flashcards.a: It is a Python dict on the process heap: a rolling deploy, K8s SIGTERM, autoscaler eviction, spot reclaim, or OOM kill destroys it. Second failure: it breaks at TWO REPLICAS even with no restart — the resume request load-balances to a pod with an empty dict. Symptom: `Command(resume=...)` on an unknown thread, so the graph silently starts over and the approval is ignored.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: What is `ShallowPostgresSaver` and what do you lose?
flashcards.a: A Postgres checkpointer that keeps only the LATEST checkpoint per thread. Durable and resumable, but `get_state_history()` is empty — no time travel, no forking, no audit trail of how the thread got here. Choose it deliberately, not by accident.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: List the `StateSnapshot` fields.
flashcards.a: `values` (channel values), `next` (tuple of nodes to run; `()` = complete), `config` (thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id), `metadata` (`source` in input|loop|update, `writes`, `step`), `created_at`, `parent_config` (None for the first), `tasks` (PregelTask: `id`, `name`, `error`, `interrupts`, optional `state`).

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: What are the possible values of `checkpoint_ns`?
flashcards.a: `""` for the root graph; `"node_name:uuid"` for a subgraph invoked as that node; nested subgraphs join with `|`, e.g. `"outer:uuid|inner:uuid"`. Readable inside a node via `config["configurable"]["checkpoint_ns"]`. Renaming a node changes the namespace and breaks interrupted threads about to enter it.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: What does `graph.invoke(None, prior_snapshot.config)` do, and what is the trap?
flashcards.a: Replay: nodes before that checkpoint are skipped (results already saved), nodes after it re-execute. The trap is that it is NOT a cached read — LLM calls, API calls, and interrupts all fire again and may return different results. Replaying from the final checkpoint (`next == ()`) is a no-op.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: What does `graph.update_state(...)` actually do, and what are its two subtleties?
flashcards.a: It FORKS: creates a new checkpoint branching from the specified one, leaving the original history intact. It does not roll back. Subtleties: (1) values pass through REDUCERS, so an `operator.add` channel accumulates your 'replacement' — wrap in `Overwrite` to replace; (2) `as_node=` attributes the update to a node, controlling which node runs next.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: When must you pass `as_node` explicitly to `update_state`?
flashcards.a: Three cases: parallel branches wrote in the same step so LangGraph can't infer which was last (otherwise `InvalidUpdateError`); the thread has no execution history (setting up state in a test); or you want to skip a node by making the graph think it already ran.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: Mechanically, what happens when a node calls `interrupt()`?
flashcards.a: It raises a special `GraphBubbleUp` exception the runtime catches; the runtime writes the checkpoint, surfaces the JSON-serialisable payload, and waits INDEFINITELY. Read it via `result["__interrupt__"]` (v1 invoke), `result.interrupts` (v2), or `stream.interrupts`/`stream.interrupted` (`stream_events(version="v3")`). Resume with `Command(resume=value)` on the same `thread_id`; that value becomes the return of `interrupt()`.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: State the four rules of writing a node that contains `interrupt()`.
flashcards.a: 1) No mutating side effects before the interrupt — move them after or into their own node, because the node re-runs from its first line on every resume. 2) Never wrap `interrupt()` in a bare `try/except`; it works by raising, so `except Exception` swallows the pause. 3) Never conditionally skip or reorder interrupts — resume values are matched STRICTLY BY INDEX within the task. 4) Payloads must be JSON-serialisable: no functions, no class instances.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: What happens to in-flight tool side effects on resume, and what are the four mitigations in order?
flashcards.a: Sibling that completed in a failed super-step: safe (pending writes). The node that failed or interrupted: everything before that point RE-RUNS, because resume restarts the node from line one. Mitigations: (1) move the side effect after the interrupt or into its own node; (2) make it naturally idempotent (upsert, not insert); (3) idempotency key derived deterministically as `f"{thread_id}:{checkpoint_id}:{op}"` with TTL > the approval window; (4) wrap it in a `@task` so a completed result is retrieved on replay.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: Does LangGraph give you exactly-once side effects?
flashcards.a: No. It documents at-least-once and instructs you to make side effects idempotent: if a task starts but fails to complete, resumption re-runs it. Exactly-once is a property of the downstream system or of an idempotency layer you own, never of the orchestrator. Claiming otherwise fails the question.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: Name the three durability modes and what each loses on a crash.
flashcards.a: `"exit"`: writes only on exit (success, error, or interrupt) — a mid-run crash loses everything since the start; HITL still works because an interrupt counts as an exit. `"async"`: writes asynchronously while the next step runs — small window of loss; good default. `"sync"`: writes before the next step starts — nothing lost, highest overhead; use it around steps with external side effects.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: Why must a custom Postgres connection/pool use `autocommit=True` and `row_factory=dict_row`?
flashcards.a: `autocommit=True` is required or `.setup()` may not persist the DDL, so your tables silently never get created. `row_factory=dict_row` is required because the saver reads columns by name (`row["col"]`); the default `tuple_row` raises `TypeError: tuple indices must be integers or slices, not str` on every read.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: What does `PostgresSaver.setup()` create, and where should you call it?
flashcards.a: `checkpoints`, `checkpoint_blobs`, `checkpoint_writes`, and a `checkpoint_migrations` table. It is idempotent but belongs in a migration job, not on every worker boot: N workers racing DDL on cold start is avoidable, and in a locked-down environment the app role may not have DDL rights.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: Two security settings every production checkpointer needs, and why.
flashcards.a: `serde=EncryptedSerializer.from_pycryptodome_aes()` (reads `LANGGRAPH_AES_KEY`) because checkpoints hold full prompts, tool arguments, and outputs in PLAINTEXT by default. And `LANGGRAPH_STRICT_MSGPACK=true` (or an explicit `allowed_msgpack_modules` list) so a compromised checkpoint store isn't a code-execution path into your workers via deserialisation.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: State the reliability arithmetic that justifies checkpointing.
flashcards.a: Reliability is multiplicative: p^n. 0.95^10 ~= 60%, 0.85^10 ~= 20%, 0.95^50 ~= 8%. At 0.85 over 10 steps, four runs in five fail somewhere; un-checkpointed, each retry re-pays the whole trajectory, so expected cost per success is ~5x a clean run. Checkpointing makes a failure at step 8 cost the remaining steps, not all of them. Retry raises p; checkpointing makes failure cheap. They are complements.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: How do you handle SIGTERM mid-run in langgraph >= 1.2, and what does drain NOT guarantee?
flashcards.a: Create a `RunControl`, register `signal.signal(SIGTERM, lambda *_: control.request_drain("sigterm"))`, pass `control=control` to `invoke`, and catch `GraphDrained`; resume later with `invoke(None, config)`. Drain is COOPERATIVE and applies at the next super-step boundary. It does NOT cancel asyncio tasks or kill threads, so pair it with per-node timeouts and a hard supervisor deadline.

flashcards.topic: LangGraph II: Checkpointers, interrupt()/HITL, Durable Resume
flashcards.q: Which graph and state changes are safe with live threads?
flashcards.a: For threads at the END of the graph: any topology change (add, remove, rename nodes and edges). For INTERRUPTED threads: all topology changes EXCEPT renaming or removing nodes, since a thread may be about to enter one. For state: adding and removing keys is fully compatible; RENAMING a key loses its saved state; incompatible type changes can break threads holding old values. Ship renames expand/contract.

flashcards.q: Name the two distinct token quantities in an agent loop and how they behave differently.
flashcards.a: context_tokens is what is in THIS agent's window right now: it drives compaction, is per-agent, and DECREASES when you compact. billed_tokens is everything the run has ever paid for, including every subagent's isolated context and every summarizer call: it drives cost, is per-run, and only increases. Compaction lowers the first and raises the second, so enforcing a cost budget against context_tokens makes spend appear to fall while you pay more.

flashcards.q: How do cost, steps and wall-clock compose across nested subagents?
flashcards.a: Cost and billed tokens are additive and must be RESERVED before dispatch, not checked, because check-then-spend is a TOCTOU bug that lets N parallel children overshoot by up to Nx. Steps need TWO counters: local_steps (this loop's cap) and tree_steps (run-wide), because a child's steps must not terminate the parent early but must consume the run's total. Wall-clock is inherited as an ABSOLUTE monotonic timestamp; passing a duration gives each nested level its own full timeout, so three levels of 600s becomes 1,800s.

flashcards.q: Describe the budget reservation pattern and its diagnostic symptom when missing.
flashcards.a: At delegation time the parent pessimistically debits the child's maximum from its own remaining budget, hands the child a budget capped at that reservation, and credits back (reservation - actual) on return. Because the debit happens once in the parent's thread before any child starts, no lock is needed. Symptom when missing: p99 run cost sits at roughly fanout x the configured cap while every individual subagent trace shows it stayed under budget.

flashcards.q: List the nine stop conditions.
flashcards.a: 1 verified natural termination (no tool call AND verification passes). 2 local step cap. 3 tree step cap. 4 billed-token budget. 5 cost budget. 6 absolute wall-clock deadline. 7 no-progress detector. 8 compaction circuit breaker. 9 external interrupt (user cancel, kill switch, policy revocation, parent cancellation), cooperative at a tool boundary.

flashcards.q: Describe the five-level compaction cascade with triggers and costs.
flashcards.a: 1 Tool-result budget: single result over ~50,000 chars, persist to disk keeping a 2 KB preview and path, zero cost, reversible. 2 Snip: stale scaffolding, zero cost, must report tokens freed. 3 Microcompact: cold path (cache expired, ~5 min TTL) rewrites old tool results; hot path uses API-level cache_edits to preserve a 100K+ cached prefix; zero API calls. 4 Context collapse: ~90% utilisation, projection-based folding, zero cost, REVERSIBLE. 5 Autocompact: ~87% utilisation, forks a summarizer, one API call, IRREVERSIBLE. Collapse active suppresses autocompact.

flashcards.q: Cheap compaction freed 30K tokens and expensive autocompact fired anyway. Why?
flashcards.a: The autocompact threshold is computed from the last assistant message's usage, which still reflects the pre-snip context size. The freed tokens were not credited to the trigger. Claude Code threads snipTokensFreed into the threshold calculation for exactly this. General rule: every cheap shaper must report tokens_freed and every later trigger must compute from the corrected number.

flashcards.q: How does compaction interact with tool-result truncation, and which is higher leverage?
flashcards.a: Truncation changes the RATE of context growth; compaction changes the LEVEL. Truncating at the tool boundary is strictly higher leverage because those tokens never enter context, so compaction fires less often and you make fewer irreversible summarizer calls. A high compaction rate means the bug is upstream: fix the tool. Also: compaction must preserve persisted-output pointers verbatim, or Level 1's disk path gets paraphrased away and the artifact becomes unreachable.

flashcards.q: Why does microcompact have two code paths?
flashcards.a: Cache state. Any modification to old messages invalidates the cached prefix from that point. When the cache is already cold (user idle past the ~5-minute TTL) the rebuild is inevitable, so it directly rewrites message content to a placeholder. When the cache is hot, holding 100K+ tokens, direct modification is a large cost hit, so the edit is expressed as API-level cache_edits blocks that delete tool-result references server-side while the local message array is returned unchanged. The paths are mutually exclusive and cold takes priority.

flashcards.q: What must happen immediately after a heavy compaction, and why?
flashcards.a: Post-compaction recovery, because the immediate failure is the agent re-reading files it just edited or making contradictory changes. Concretely: restore the last ~5 recently-read files at up to 5K tokens each, restore activated skills at up to 25K tokens total, re-announce deferred tools, agent lists and MCP directives, reset context-collapse state, and restore plan-mode state if it was active.

flashcards.q: Why does compaction need a circuit breaker? Give the incident numbers.
flashcards.a: Because if the context is irrecoverably over limit, the fourth attempt fails too. Anthropic's March 2026 telemetry showed 1,279 sessions with 50+ consecutive autocompact failures, the worst hitting 3,272, wasting roughly 250,000 API calls per day globally. The fix was MAX_CONSECUTIVE_AUTOCOMPACT_FAILURES = 3. General principle: any self-healing mechanism inside a loop needs a breaker, or the fix becomes the new failure mode.

flashcards.q: How should you count context tokens, and what is the error rate of the naive approach?
flashcards.a: Anchor on the usage field returned by the most recent API response as ground truth and estimate only the messages added since. That yields under 5% error with no tokenizer round-trip. Pure client-side tokenizer estimation carries 30%+ error, which is enough to fire the compaction cascade too early (wasting the cache) or too late (413 prompt-too-long).

flashcards.q: Argument-hash repeat detection never fires but the agent is stuck. Why, and what replaces it?
flashcards.a: The model varies its arguments while making no progress: search('clickhouse OOM'), search('clickhouse out of memory'), search('clickhouse memory error') are three distinct hashes and zero progress. Replace with a state-delta signature: dirty-file hashes, passing-test count, closed-todo count, artifact count. Unchanged for K about 4 steps is evidence, not a heuristic.

flashcards.q: Give the three-stage no-progress escalation.
flashcards.a: K about 4: nudge, naming the specific absence ('no file modified, no test outcome changed, no todo closed in 4 steps'), ask for the current hypothesis, require a different approach. K about 7: constrain, shrinking the visible tool registry to the phase-relevant subset. K about 10: escalate, stop with stop_reason='no_progress' and hand the trajectory to a human rather than burning the remaining budget. All interventions are delivered as observations, never exceptions.

flashcards.q: Why inject the remaining budget into the model's context?
flashcards.a: Because temporal awareness appears orthogonal to reasoning capability: explicit temporal feedback in the loop measurably improves performance on deadline-constrained tasks. An agent that knows it has six steps and 240 seconds left triages; an agent that does not, explores. Harness-side enforcement alone wastes capability. LangChain ships this as time-budget warnings injected into context.

flashcards.q: Name five loop invariants and the symptom each violation produces.
flashcards.a: messages[0] byte-identical across iterations, else cache_read near zero and cost 5-10x. Every tool_use id has exactly one matching tool_result before the next model call, else API 400 after a partial failure or cancellation. thinking blocks preserved when returning tool results, else silent multi-step reasoning degradation with no error. Task, open_items and persisted-output paths survive every compaction, else turn-40 amnesia or an unreachable artifact. context_tokens strictly decreases across a successful compaction, else you paid for a no-op.

flashcards.q: Which loop invariant should you build first, and why?
flashcards.a: Determinism of context assembly: replaying the event log to step k must produce a byte-identical assembled request. It is the precondition for everything else, since without it you cannot snapshot-test, cannot resume correctly, and cannot bisect a regression. It fails for boring reasons: a dict whose iteration order varies, a datetime.now() in the prompt, tools listed in set order, or an injected file whose contents changed.

flashcards.q: What are the three requirements for a resumable loop?
flashcards.a: 1 A typed append-only event log rather than a message array, with messages derived from events. 2 Deterministic reconstruction, so rehydrate(events[:k]) is byte-identical to the original step k: logical clock rather than now(), stable ordering, versioned prompt templates recorded in the event, resolved file contents stored rather than paths. 3 Checkpoint boundaries chosen around side effects: checkpoint after appending the tool result, and make the execution-to-persistence gap safe with idempotency keys.

flashcards.q: What is hibernate-and-wake, and how is it stronger than checkpointing?
flashcards.a: The loop must be able to end deliberately, write a handoff artifact, and be resumed by a FRESH context that never saw the earlier turns. Meta's Ranking Engineer Agent does this to resume interrupted 6-hour tasks across multi-day pipelines; Anthropic's version is an initializer agent handing off to a coding agent with feature lists, git commits and test gates as cross-session state. Design rule: the handoff artifact must be sufficient alone. Test: kill the process, start a fresh one, see whether it makes progress.

flashcards.q: Give the worked reliability table for a 12-step task and state which controls buy the most.
flashcards.a: Bare loop p=0.90: 0.90^12 = 28%. Plus errors-as-observations p=0.94: 48%. Plus no-progress detection: about 55%. Omitting compaction (0.94^8 x 0.85^4): 32%, showing compaction removes a floor rather than raising a ceiling. Plus checkpoint-and-resume with up to 2 retries, collapsing transient failure (0.036^3 about 0) to p=0.976: 0.976^12 = 75%. Plus a deterministic verifier: reported drops 75% to 72% but TRUE-correct rises about 67% to 72%. Biggest wins: errors-as-observations and resume, roughly +19 points each.

flashcards.q: Why won't a better model remove the need for loop controls?
flashcards.a: It moves p, which is exponentiated, so it genuinely helps: 0.98^12 = 79% with no controls. But it does not address the failure classes structurally. A better model still hits a 503, still exceeds the context window at turn 40, still occasionally claims success on a red suite. And the evidence points to spending on the harness: LangChain moved a coding agent from rank 30 to top 5 on Terminal Bench 2.0 with harness-only changes and no model swap. Controls compose with model quality, they do not compete with it.

flashcards.q: Give the reference numbers for Claude Code's production loop.
flashcards.a: A 1,729-line async generator with a 1,421-line while(true) body and 9 distinct named continue points. State machine rather than recursion, because recursion blew the call stack on long conversations. Token budget checked TWICE per iteration, before the model call and after. Streaming tool execution: a 5-tool-call turn goes from 30s sequential to 18s, a 40% latency win from architecture alone. And stop_reason === 'tool_use' is not reliably set, so detect tool calls by watching for tool_use blocks during streaming.

flashcards.q: Why check the budget twice in one loop iteration?
flashcards.a: The checks answer different questions. Before the model call: should we spend the next request at all given what is left? After: did this response push us over, and should we inject a 'you have N steps left' nudge or stop? Skipping the pre-call check means you always pay for one more request than the budget allowed, which at large output sizes is not a rounding error.

flashcards.q: What should you log per iteration, and which two fields matter most?
flashcards.a: run and parent-run id, iteration, phase, model/version/reasoning-effort, prompt_prefix_hash, full usage including cache read/write, context_tokens before and after, cumulative billed tokens and USD, compaction levels fired with tokens freed and compaction cost, per-tool-call name/decision/validation/latency/bytes, progress_signature, steps_without_progress, transition_reason, and latency split into TTFT/total/tool-wall. The two that matter most: prompt_prefix_hash (catches prompt drift and cache breakage) and transition_reason (turns 'it looped' into 'it took the reactive_compact transition 40 times').

flashcards.q: cost_budget is your most common stop_reason. Raise the cap?
flashcards.a: No. That means the agent does not work and the budget is hiding it. Budgets are backstops, not design. Fix it with fewer steps or better tools: truncate tool results at the source, give one good tool instead of three weak ones, cache aggressively, route simple turns to a smaller model. Raising the cap converts a bounded failure into an unbounded one, and it is the easiest wrong decision in the space because it is a one-line config change.

flashcards.q: p99 step count is 24 and the mean is 4. Diagnose.
flashcards.a: A bimodal distribution: most tasks finish fast, a tail hits the step cap. This is why you alert on p99 for steps and cost, since the mean hides runaways entirely. Segment the tail by stop_reason and transition_reason. local_step_budget with flat progress_signature means stuck runs, so fix progress detection and tools. A single dominant transition_reason like reactive_compact means fix upstream truncation. Correlation with one tool's error rate means fix the tool. Do not just lower the cap; that converts slow failures into fast ones and silently drops tasks that legitimately needed 15 steps.

flashcards.q: Streaming tool execution: what does it buy and what does it cost?
flashcards.a: Buys roughly 40% latency: a 5-tool-call turn goes from 30s sequential to 18s when tool 1 starts while the model is still generating call 3. Costs correctness surface: cancellation, ordering and partial-failure semantics get materially harder, and the specific failure is a cancelled or partially-failed turn leaving a tool_use with no matching tool_result, which is an API 400 on the next call. Prerequisite: your 1:1 pairing invariant plus synthesizing a 'cancelled' tool result on the cancel path.

flashcards.q: Agent-controlled versus harness-controlled compaction: which and when?
flashcards.a: Harness-controlled at a token threshold is the default and the correct starting point. Agent-controlled (the model calls a compression tool when it judges the moment safe) is better in principle because it avoids reactive-at-limit compaction interrupting a subtask mid-flight and corrupting in-flight reasoning; the Active Context Compression result is 22.7% token reduction with no accuracy loss on long-horizon tasks. But it adds a failure mode where the model never calls the tool and you hit the wall anyway. Ship threshold-based first, add the tool second, keep the threshold as the backstop.

flashcards.q: When should you not build the full loop apparatus?
flashcards.a: Short read-only tasks: a step cap and a deadline suffice; the nine conditions and five-level cascade are a response to long runs. Deterministic workflows: write the pipeline. When Temporal or Step Functions already exists in the org: event log, deterministic replay, checkpointing, idempotent retries and day-long human pauses IS a workflow engine and you will build a worse one, so keep loop POLICY (compaction, progress detection, verification) and buy loop DURABILITY. When a managed harness already ships it, for example Agent Framework's iteration limit, compaction strategy, per-call history persistence, approvals and OpenTelemetry.

flashcards.q: What two axes generate every multi-agent topology?
flashcards.a: Who decides what happens next (central router vs distributed peers) and what context crosses the boundary (full history vs distilled summary). Central + distilled = orchestrator with subagents, which is the shape that usually wins. Central + full = supervisor. Distributed + full = swarm. Distributed + distilled = blackboard.

flashcards.q: Name the five real costs of multi-agent decomposition.
flashcards.a: 1) Routing errors, silent and compounding: 92% accuracy over 3 hops is 0.92^3 ~ 78%. 2) Context handoff loss, with no third option between 'everything crosses' (no isolation, N x cost) and 'a summary crosses' (undetectable loss). 3) Latency multiplication: coordination is sequential and fan-out latency is the slowest branch. 4) Cost multiplication, ~15x in Anthropic's own reported system. 5) Debugging difficulty, because the failure lives in the seam and never surfaces as an error.

flashcards.q: What is MAST and what did it find?
flashcards.a: Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy (Cemri et al., arXiv:2503.13657). MAST-Data annotates 1,600+ traces across 7 popular MAS frameworks; the taxonomy was derived from 150 traces at inter-annotator kappa = 0.88, giving 14 failure modes in 3 categories: system design issues, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification. Headline: MAS gains on popular benchmarks are often minimal, and failures come from DESIGN rather than model capability.

flashcards.q: Supervisor vs swarm: state the tradeoff precisely.
flashcards.a: The swarm is faster and cheaper (no intermediary, direct handoffs, fewer LLM calls). The supervisor is easier to reason about (one routing node, explicit control flow, every decision visible in the trace, routing accuracy measurable). Choose the swarm when latency beats observability and the handoff graph is small and linear; the supervisor when you will debug this at 3am.

flashcards.q: What crosses on a handoff in the OpenAI Agents SDK, and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: The entire message history: the receiving agent sees the whole conversation as if it had been there from the start. So you get zero context isolation and pay full prompt cost at every agent. Also security-relevant: input guardrails apply only to the first agent in a handoff chain and output guardrails only to the agent producing the final output, so mid-chain agents can be unguarded.

flashcards.q: How is a handoff implemented in LangGraph?
flashcards.a: A tool that returns Command(goto=target, graph=Command.PARENT, update={...}). goto names the node in the parent graph, and the update payload is what crosses, so unlike the OpenAI SDK you control isolation - at the cost of engineering a lossy summary with required fields (reason, context_summary, latest correction).

flashcards.q: Describe the blackboard pattern and its named failure mode.
flashcards.a: Agents never address each other; they read and write typed, versioned slots in a shared store, and a controller schedules whichever agent's preconditions are satisfied (from HEARSAY-II). Failure mode: LOST UPDATE - two agents read v3, both write, one silently wins, and the trace shows both succeeding. Fix: optimistic concurrency with an explicit Conflict, plus a write journal. Never use an untyped shared text scratchpad.

flashcards.q: Does multi-agent debate work?
flashcards.a: Less than Du et al. (2023) suggested. Controlled follow-ups in the 7-8B instruction-tuned class find a 2.1x-3.4x token multiplier for accuracy statistically comparable to or worse than isolated self-correction, with three failure modes: sycophantic conformity (abandoning a correct answer to agree with a confident peer), contextual fragility (order/phrasing dependence), and consensus collapse (early convergence so extra rounds cost nothing but tokens). The value comes from independence and aggregation, so prefer self-consistency.

flashcards.q: Which decomposition has the strongest prior in its favour?
flashcards.a: An asymmetric verifier: one separate agent with a different prompt and a checklist, run once over the primary agent's output. That is verification, not debate, and MAST's third failure category is task verification, so a dedicated verifier beats any symmetric debate scheme. Add a verifier before you add a second worker.

flashcards.q: Name the six conditions that justify splitting into multiple agents.
flashcards.a: 1) Parallel read-heavy subtasks where intermediate volume >> returned volume. 2) Mandatory context isolation. 3) A different permission/trust tier. 4) A different model/latency tier. 5) Independent deployment ownership across teams or organisations (what A2A is for). 6) Untrusted content quarantine behind a tool-less agent. NOT reasons: 30 tools, the org chart, a tidy diagram.

flashcards.q: The agent has 30 tools and picks the wrong one. Four fixes before splitting.
flashcards.a: 1) Rewrite descriptions with explicit use-this-when / do-not-use-this-when. 2) Remove overlap - if a human engineer cannot say definitively which tool applies, the model will not do better. 3) Group fine-grained tools behind fewer higher-level ones. 4) Add a tool-search step so only relevant schemas are in context. Splitting replaces a selection problem with a routing problem PLUS a handoff problem.

flashcards.q: What is the single-writer principle?
flashcards.a: Only one agent mutates state; every other agent contributes information, not actions. Concurrent writers give conflicting actions with no serialisation point, no way to reason about final state, and partially-applied non-idempotent side effects. It also means there is exactly one place for an approval gate, an idempotency key, and an audit record. If parallel work must write, workers PROPOSE structured changes and the orchestrator validates and applies them in order.

flashcards.q: Quote the evidence on BOTH sides of the multi-agent debate.
flashcards.a: For: Anthropic's Research feature (orchestrator + parallel subagents with isolated windows) beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on research tasks, at ~15x the tokens, with token usage alone explaining ~80% of performance variance on browsing evals. Against: Cognition's 'Don't Build Multi-Agents' (June 2025) argues single-threaded linear agents plus a compression model, because subagents have no context of each other's work. Both are right about the task shapes they built for.

flashcards.q: What is the discriminating variable between one agent and many?
flashcards.a: Task shape. Parallel BREADTH with independent branches and small distilled returns favours decomposition. Sequential DEPTH with shared evolving context favours one agent. Say that sentence and you have answered the question.

flashcards.q: How do orchestration and choreography map onto agent topologies, and what is the LLM-specific twist?
flashcards.a: Orchestration = supervisor; choreography = swarm. The tradeoffs transfer from microservices: explicit testable control flow with a bottleneck, vs autonomy and lower latency with emergent behaviour. The twist: the 'orchestrator' here is a probabilistic classifier that can be wrong, so the case for choreography is WEAKER than in microservices, because you lose the one place where routing accuracy was measurable.

flashcards.q: What is A2A and how does it differ from MCP?
flashcards.a: Agent2Agent: Google-announced April 2025, donated to the Linux Foundation, 1.0 in April 2026 with 150+ organisations, signed Agent Cards for cryptographic identity, a defined task lifecycle, multi-tenancy, and SDKs in five languages. MCP connects an agent to tools and data; A2A connects an agent to another AGENT with its own reasoning and goals. A tool returns data you asked for; a remote agent returns what it decided to produce - hence identity, task lifecycle, and output distrust are first-class.

flashcards.q: What multi-agent-specific observability do you need?
flashcards.a: One trace id spanning every agent; a span per agent invocation carrying the subtask in, the structured return out, tokens, cost, and outcome; the routing decision with the model's stated reason; the handoff payload logged verbatim. Two metrics that only exist here: route distribution / route accuracy against labels, and handoff count per run (a rising count is the earliest signal of ping-ponging).

flashcards.q: How do you prove a multi-agent design was the right call?
flashcards.a: A single-agent baseline on the same golden task set with the same tools, measuring success, tokens, p50/p99 latency, and cost per task. Then the multi-agent version. Then the comparison people skip: the single agent given the SAME budget (bigger model, more steps, self-consistency). Break results down by task shape. No single-agent baseline means you made no architecture decision, only a bigger bill.

flashcards.q: How many model calls does a 4-worker supervisor task cost, minimum?
flashcards.a: Nine: 4 routing calls + 4 worker calls + 1 synthesis. Every hop costs a supervisor LLM call, which is pure coordination tax. A three-level hierarchy adds ~1.5s of routing latency per level before any work starts.

flashcards.q: Two agents return contradictory facts. What should happen?
flashcards.a: By default something invisible: whichever result the synthesis step weighted wins silently. Design it: structured returns with confidence and evidence pointers so disagreement is detectable; an explicit conflict path that either sends each agent the other's evidence for ONE reconciliation round or applies a documented tiebreak (prefer primary sources); and when unresolved, surface the conflict to the user rather than silently picking.

flashcards.q: What single axis separates ReAct, Plan-Execute, Reflexion and ToT?
flashcards.a: Where the decision point sits relative to the observations. ReAct decides AFTER each observation; Plan-Execute decides BEFORE any observation; Reflexion decides AGAIN after a failed attempt; ToT decides ACROSS parallel branches.

flashcards.q: What are the three parts of ReAct in 2026, and what replaced what?
flashcards.a: Thought = the model's reasoning/thinking content block. Action = a structured tool_use block from the API. Observation = a tool_result block keyed by tool_use_id. Native tool calling replaced regex-parsing `Thought:/Action:/Observation:` out of free text. Parse-failure rate went from ~2-8% of turns to 0.

flashcards.q: What happens if you drop the reasoning block when appending the assistant turn?
flashcards.a: You have re-implemented act-only, which is the exact ablation the ReAct paper showed FAILS on identical observations. Symptom: the agent stops adapting to surprises and repeats the previous action. With some providers it also invalidates the thinking-block signature and errors, which is the better outcome.

flashcards.q: Give a mechanism (not 'it thinks more') for why a reasoning trace improves action selection.
flashcards.a: Four: (1) Locality - the thought puts a compressed task-relevant summary adjacent to the decision point instead of making the decode re-derive it from 20k tokens. (2) Factorisation - replaces hard P(action|history) with P(thought|history) then P(action|thought,history). (3) Exception handling - a surprising observation needs somewhere to be processed; without a thought slot the only output channel is the action, so it repeats. (4) Steerability - thoughts are text, so a human can edit two and change downstream behaviour.

flashcards.q: What does a ReAct reasoning trace cost, as a formula?
flashcards.a: Extra input tokens = thought_len x n(n+1)/2, because every thought is re-sent on every subsequent turn. At 120 tokens over 10 steps: 120 x 55 = 6,600 extra input tokens. Quadratic, which is why 'make the thoughts longer' is not a strategy.

flashcards.q: ReAct's headline numbers from Yao et al. (arXiv Oct 2022 / ICLR 2023)?
flashcards.a: +34% absolute success rate on ALFWorld and +10% on WebShop over imitation and RL baselines, with only one or two in-context examples. Motivation: CoT alone hallucinates (ungrounded); act-only cannot synthesise (their ablation had identical observations and still failed).

flashcards.q: What are the three (four) components of Plan-and-Execute, and which does everyone forget?
flashcards.a: Planner (ordered steps, optionally a dependency DAG), Executor (runs step i with a SMALL context), Solver (synthesises from plan + all outputs), plus an optional Replanner edge. People forget the Solver, and they forget that the replan edge is where the entire cost saving goes.

flashcards.q: Quantify the Plan-Execute saving, and the point at which it disappears.
flashcards.a: 8-step task, 1,500-token system prompt, 800-token observations: ReAct re-sends everything each turn = ~38,880 input tokens; Plan-Execute = 1 planner + 8 small stateless executors + 1 solver = ~15,000. About 2.6x cheaper and the executors parallelise. But one replan at step 4 costs ~+4,700 tokens plus re-running the tail, and TWO replans make Plan-Execute more expensive than ReAct with worse adaptivity.

flashcards.q: What are the three real reasons to use Plan-and-Execute?
flashcards.a: Cost (~2-3x fewer input tokens), latency (executors parallelise, so 8 sequential round trips collapse to ~3), and auditability (the plan is a diffable artifact a human can review before anything executes). NOT intelligence.

flashcards.q: Name the plan lock-in failure mode and its observable symptom.
flashcards.a: Plan lock-in: the plan was committed before any observation, so a mid-trajectory failure never changes it. Symptom in the trace: plan_hash constant across every step, replan_count == 0, and the final answer references an entity that an earlier observation reported as missing. Classic shape: step 3 returns 'relation does not exist', steps 4-8 aggregate over an empty set, solver describes zero rows as a trend.

flashcards.q: Fix for plan lock-in: add a replanner?
flashcards.a: No. Add a deterministic GATE: after each step, a cheap non-LLM check on whether the observation invalidates any downstream step's precondition, and pay for an LLM replan only when the gate fires. A blanket replan-after-every-step is just ReAct with extra latency and a worse name.

flashcards.q: What is ReWOO and what does it save?
flashcards.a: Reasoning WithOut Observation: the planner emits ALL tool calls up front with variable substitution (#E2 refers to step 2's output), so the executor is a dumb runtime with no LLM in the orchestration loop and only the solver sees results. Reported 30-50% fewer tokens than ReAct on equivalent multi-step tasks. Breaks when tool results are unexpected, because it committed before seeing any observation.

flashcards.q: Reflexion's four pieces?
flashcards.a: Actor (produces a trajectory, typically a ReAct agent), Evaluator (scores it: unit tests / game engine / EM / heuristic / LLM judge), Self-reflection (turns trajectory + score into VERBAL feedback), Memory (episodic buffer of reflections injected into attempt k+1). The 'policy update' is a paragraph appended to the prompt - verbal reinforcement learning, no gradients.

flashcards.q: Reflexion's headline numbers, and the column that matters?
flashcards.a: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4's 80%; ALFWorld 130/134 (~97%) in 12 trials vs ReAct's 75%; HotpotQA 61% -> 75% EM on 100 sampled questions. The column that matters is the verdict source: unit tests, game engine success flag, exact match vs ground truth. Every headline gain is verifier-backed, so mechanically it is retry-with-a-grounded-failure-explanation, not introspection.

flashcards.q: What did Huang et al. (ICLR 2024) find about self-correction?
flashcards.a: INTRINSIC self-correction (model critiques itself with no external feedback) fails to reliably improve reasoning on GSM8K, CommonSenseQA and HotpotQA, and sometimes degrades it. Sharpest finding is methodological: several published self-correction gains were artifacts of a deliberately weak INITIAL prompt - strengthen the first prompt and the benefit largely evaporates.

flashcards.q: Three metrics for a reflection loop.
flashcards.a: Help rate (wrong -> right), harm rate (right -> wrong), and cost per net-correct answer. Log the (pre_verdict, post_verdict) pair on every invocation - that pair IS the measurement. If harm >= help you have shipped a random-answer-perturber, and an accuracy-only dashboard hides it because the effects partly cancel.

flashcards.q: Why would asking a model to critique its own answer ever make it worse?
flashcards.a: Sycophancy - the FlipFlop result: challenge a model on a correct answer and it frequently flips to a wrong one, so 'are you sure?' is not a neutral operation. Plus correlated errors: generator and evaluator are the same model with the same training distribution, so 'this looks right' carries very little evidence about correctness.

flashcards.q: Rank verdict sources for a critique loop, best to worst.
flashcards.a: compiler / unit tests / type checker / schema validation / SQL EXPLAIN > assertions on known invariants, checksums, row-count sanity bounds > a second DIFFERENT model as judge (decorrelated errors, some value) > the same model asked 'are you sure?' (~worthless, measurable harm). If you cannot name the source in one word you do not have a reflection loop.

flashcards.q: Degeneration of thought: what is it and how do you detect it?
flashcards.a: The reflection repeats the same flawed diagnosis across attempts. Detect: cosine similarity between reflection k and k-1 above ~0.9, near-zero diff between successive attempts' outputs, pass rate flat while token spend grows linearly. Response: abort at 2-3 attempts, escalate to a human or a different tool.

flashcards.q: When is Tree-of-Thought worth it? Three conditions.
flashcards.a: All three required: (1) single-pass accuracy demonstrably well below ceiling on your task, (2) intermediate states cheaply and OBJECTIVELY scoreable (test, arithmetic, schema, solver - not an LLM judge), (3) you genuinely need the branches, e.g. enumerating alternatives a human will compare. Game of 24 hits all three: 74% with GPT-4 + ToT vs 4% with CoT.

flashcards.q: What does ToT cost, and what is the bottleneck?
flashcards.a: 10-100x tokens of a single pass, O(k^d) evaluations worst case for breadth k depth d. The bottleneck is the per-node SCORER: if it is an LLM judge, the scorer is the whole algorithm and you are paying 100x for a random walk with correlated errors. A deterministic checker per node drops cost by roughly an order of magnitude. Cut breadth before depth.

flashcards.q: Current (2026) numbers on self-consistency with strong models.
flashcards.a: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite on HotpotQA: +0.4% across 20 sampled paths at ~20x token cost, curve fluctuating not rising. Gemini-2.5-Pro on MATH-500: 98% single-pass -> 99.6% at 15 paths, i.e. +1.6% for ~15x compute. Flash-Lite on MATH-500 PEAKED around 10 paths and DECLINED beyond 15 - negative returns, not just diminishing, because extra samples inject spurious paths the aggregator cannot suppress.

flashcards.q: How much can you cut self-consistency sampling without losing accuracy?
flashcards.a: Adaptive-consistency (early stop on convergence) cut sample usage 7.9x for under 0.1% accuracy loss; criteria-based early stopping cut ~70% with negligible loss. Both say the useful sampling threshold is per-item and is dropping as models improve - so use difficulty-aware routing, not a blanket k.

flashcards.q: The decision rule for picking a reasoning pattern.
flashcards.a: 1) Do later steps depend on what earlier steps RETURN? Yes -> ReAct. No AND decomposition stable up front -> Plan-Execute/ReWOO plus a gate. 2) Cheap external verdict? Yes -> retry-with-critique, cap 2-3, track help/harm/cost-per-net-correct. No -> do NOT add self-critique. 3) Single-pass accuracy below ceiling AND nodes cheaply scoreable? -> self-consistency k=3-5 first; ToT only if you need the tree. 4) Default for a new agent: plain ReAct loop, no reflection, no ToT. Add one pattern at a time and eval each.

flashcards.q: Where does the boundary sit now that reasoning models do internal deliberation?
flashcards.a: The line is 'does it touch the world'.
