Absorbed by the model: single-turn deliberation, branching over candidates, verifying arithmetic/logic within one answer, short self-correction inside one response - so external ToT and self-consistency mostly no longer beat native extended thinking on math and code. Not absorbed: side effects (a real tool call producing a real observation), durable state across a boundary, any REAL verifier (a test suite is not a thought), and all control machinery. Reasoning models ate the Thought half of ReAct and left the Act/Observe half untouched.

flashcards.q: Rank the four patterns by how much reasoning models eroded them.
flashcards.a: Most eroded: ToT / self-consistency (largely subsumed for math and code; external gains now sub-2% at 15-20x cost). Then Reflexion (split: introspection half absorbed, verifier-driven retry half untouched and never absorbable - a compiler is not a thought). Then Plan-Execute (models plan natively, but the ARTIFACT survives for cost, parallelism and human review - reasons orthogonal to model capability). Least eroded: ReAct, because Act/Observe is a statement about the world, not about the model.

flashcards.q: Is LangGraph's create_react_agent the ReAct paper?
flashcards.a: No. It is a tool-calling loop inspired by ReAct: model call, if the response has tool_calls run the tool node, append ToolMessages, repeat until no tool calls. There is no mandatory Thought step and no text parsing. As of 2026 it is deprecated in favour of create_agent in the langchain package with a middleware system.

flashcards.q: Why was 'always plan before every action' (literal ReAct prompting) shown to be wrong?
flashcards.a: arXiv 2509.03581 (Crafter environment): always planning is computationally expensive and DEGRADES performance on long-horizon tasks, while never planning limits performance. Neither pole wins - the allocation is the thing. Practically: set thinking budget per turn, high on branch points, zero on mechanical steps.

flashcards.q: Your ReAct reasoning traces are blowing the context but later steps genuinely depend on earlier ones. What do you do?
flashcards.a: Keep ReAct and attack the trace. (1) Truncate observations at the TOOL boundary - 40KB JSON becomes 2KB plus a pointer. (2) Drop or summarise OLD thoughts while keeping recent ones verbatim: thoughts are locally useful, facts are globally useful, so compact thoughts before facts. (3) Set the thinking budget per turn. Never drop the current turn's reasoning block, and promote any thought recording a decision or open obligation into an explicit open-items list.

flashcards.q: Three things wrong with the 2022 text-parsed ReAct implementation.
flashcards.a: (1) stop=['\nObservation:'] is mandatory and fragile - forget it and the model fabricates the observation and reasons against fiction; symptom is an Observation: line with no matching tool-log entry. (2) The regex is a parser for an unspecified grammar - quotes, nested brackets, markdown fences and newlines all break it, ~2-8% of turns, each costing a full round trip plus the whole scratchpad re-sent. (3) No arity or type checking - search[], search[a, b] and serach[x] are all syntactically fine and semantically garbage.

flashcards.q: The composition that actually ships in production.
flashcards.a: Plan-Execute as the outer orchestration, ReAct sub-agents inside each step, one verifier-gated retry at the boundary. Plan for auditability and cost, loop for adaptivity, retry only where there is a test. And do not stack more than that: four patterns is four multiplicative cost centres and four independent failure modes you cannot attribute a regression to.

flashcards.q: What does Anthropic's Building Effective Agents say that is relevant here?
flashcards.a: The most successful implementations were not using complex frameworks or specialised libraries; find the simplest solution possible and increase complexity only when needed; add complexity ONLY when it demonstrably improves outcomes. Its evaluator-optimizer pattern is Reflexion's honest form: use it when there are clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement gives measurable value. And their SWE-bench work spent more time optimising TOOLS than prompts - better tool descriptions usually beat any reasoning pattern you could bolt on.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: What is the core asymmetry that explains all of tool design?
flashcards.a: A traditional client has cheap memory, perfect recall, and reads docs once. A model has PAID context, no memory, and re-reads your description every single turn. So `list_contacts()` returning 5,000 rows is correct software and a broken tool. Your REST API is not your tool surface; one-to-one wrapping is the default mistake.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: Why is the tool description prompt engineering rather than documentation?
flashcards.a: It is loaded into context every turn and is the primary thing steering tool selection and parameter construction. Anthropic reports that precise description refinements alone took Claude Sonnet 3.5 to state-of-the-art on SWE-bench Verified, and that Claude's web search tool was needlessly appending `2025` to queries until the description was fixed.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: Give three canonical tool consolidations.
flashcards.a: `list_users` + `list_events` + `create_event` -> `schedule_event`. `read_logs` -> `search_logs` (matching lines plus context). `get_customer_by_id` + `list_transactions` + `list_notes` -> `get_customer_context`. Each removes definitions from context AND moves the loop/filter/join out of the model's reasoning into deterministic code.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: What are the two most common tool-use failures, and give the named example.
flashcards.a: Wrong tool selection and wrong parameters — especially with near-identical names. The named example is `notification-send-user` vs `notification-send-channel`. Fix: merge behind one tool with a `target_type` enum, or rename so the names differ structurally.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: Six parameter-design rules that reduce model error.
flashcards.a: `user_id` not `user` (ambiguity). `Literal[...]` enums not free strings. Flat over deeply nested (valid JSON does not imply correct usage). Document formats with an example (`ISO 8601, e.g. 2026-07-26`). Explicit `max_results` with a default. `response_format: Literal["concise","detailed"]` so verbosity is a choice.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: Should tool results return UUIDs?
flashcards.a: Usually not in the default shape. Anthropic found that resolving arbitrary alphanumeric UUIDs to semantically meaningful names (or a 0-indexed scheme) significantly improves retrieval precision by reducing hallucinations. Expose technical ids only in `response_format="detailed"` for chaining calls, or resolve names to ids server-side inside the tool.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: What do `input_examples` buy you that JSON Schema cannot?
flashcards.a: Usage conventions schema can't express: date format (`2024-11-06` vs an ISO timestamp), id conventions (`USR-12345` vs UUID), when to populate nested objects, and which optional parameter groups correlate. Anthropic measured complex parameter handling improving from 72% to 90%. Guidance: 1-5 examples, realistic data, full/partial/minimal variety, only where the schema is genuinely ambiguous.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: Where does tool-result truncation belong and what must the truncation message contain?
flashcards.a: In the TOOL, not the loop — the tool knows what's relevant and doing it in the loop means you already paid to serialise and transport the payload. Claude Code's default cap is 25,000 tokens per response. The message must contain the counts AND the specific corrective action (which parameter to narrow). 'Output truncated' teaches the model nothing and it will re-request with a bigger limit.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: Four mechanisms for keeping tool responses small, and how much a concise format saves.
flashcards.a: Pagination, range selection, filtering, and truncation — all with sensible default parameter values. Drop low-signal fields (`uuid`, `mime_type`, `etag`, `_links`, `256px_image_url`). In Anthropic's Slack example a `"concise"` response was 72 tokens versus 206 for `"detailed"`, roughly one third.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: Which tool failures become observations and which should crash?
flashcards.a: The tool's dependency failing (503, 429, 404, 403) becomes a readable string the model can route around, with the corrective action in it. A bug in YOUR harness (`KeyError` in dispatch) should be logged with the traceback and fail loudly, because the model cannot fix it and swallowing it ships an agent that looks merely stupid. Also: 'no results' is SUCCESS, not an error — misclassifying it produces identical-retry loops.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: Who should generate the idempotency key for a mutating tool, and how?
flashcards.a: The HARNESS, never the model — a model regenerates a different key on retry, producing exactly the duplicates the key was meant to prevent. Derive it deterministically from execution identity: `f"{thread_id}:{checkpoint_id}:{tool}"` in LangGraph, or `f"{run_id}:{step}:{tool}:{hash(args)}"`. Store `(key -> response)` atomically with `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` plus a rowcount check; TTL must exceed the max retry window.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: Name the five risk tiers and the one load-bearing line in the dispatcher.
flashcards.a: `read_only`, `write_reversible`, `write_external`, `financial`, `destructive`. The load-bearing line is `tier = RISK.get(name, "destructive")` — default unclassified tools to the MOST dangerous tier so adding one without classifying it fails closed. Enforce in the dispatcher, not the prompt: 'don't delete without asking' is a suggestion, a dispatcher that refuses without an approval token is a control.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: Name the four MCP tool annotations, their defaults, and their limitation.
flashcards.a: `readOnlyHint` (default false), `destructiveHint` (default TRUE), `idempotentHint` (default false), `openWorldHint` (default TRUE), shipped in the 2025-03-26 spec revision. Defaults are deliberately pessimistic, so an unannotated tool is assumed destructive, non-idempotent, and open-world. Limitation: they are HINTS a server asserts about ITSELF with no enforcement. Use them to reduce friction on trusted tools; never as a security boundary.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: What isolation do you need to run LLM-generated code, and what are the cold-start numbers?
flashcards.a: microVM (Firecracker, Kata), not a container — containers share the host kernel so one kernel bug is a host escape. gVisor (a user-space kernel; Modal runs multi-tenant sandboxes on it) is an acceptable middle. Firecracker boots in ~125ms with under 5 MiB overhead per VM and up to 150 VMs/sec/host; E2B ~150ms, Daytona ~90ms. The latency excuse for weaker isolation is gone.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: Isolation alone is not enough. What else does a sandbox need?
flashcards.a: No credentials inside and no reachable cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254). Network egress DENIED by default then allowlisted — isolation with open egress is still an exfiltration channel. CPU/memory/wall-clock/disk/process caps. Read-only root plus a small tmpfs, no host bind mounts. Non-root with seccomp/AppArmor, no CAP_SYS_ADMIN. And log the code, not just the result.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: Quantify how tool selection degrades with tool count.
flashcards.a: Berkeley Function Calling data: calendar-scheduling accuracy fell from 43% to 2% as the tool set went from 4 to 51 tools. RAG-MCP (arXiv 2505.03275): baseline selection accuracy 13.62% with a large tool set, 43.13% with retrieval-based selection, plus over 50% fewer prompt tokens. Practitioner reports put measurable degradation at 10-15 tools, with 20+ clearly worse than a focused set of 5-8.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: How much context do MCP tool definitions actually consume?
flashcards.a: A five-server setup (GitHub 35 tools ~26K tokens, Slack 11 ~21K, Sentry 5 ~3K, Grafana 5 ~3K, Splunk 2 ~2K) is 58 tools and ~55K tokens BEFORE the conversation starts. Jira alone is ~17K. Anthropic measured 134K tokens of tool definitions internally before optimising.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: List the fixes for too many tools, cheapest first.
flashcards.a: 1) DELETE tools nothing selects (instrument selection frequency). 2) Consolidate around human tasks. 3) Fix names and descriptions, disambiguate confusable pairs. 4) Namespace by service then resource. 5) Gate by state/permission so only valid tools are bound. 6) Retrieval/search over a tool index (`defer_loading: true` + a tool-search tool). 7) Subagents with scoped tool sets — SECOND resort, not first.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: What does a tool-search / deferred-loading approach measure out at?
flashcards.a: ~500 tokens loaded upfront instead of ~72K for 50+ MCP tools; total context ~8.7K versus ~77K, an 85% reduction. MCP eval accuracy improved 49% -> 74% on Opus 4 and 79.5% -> 88.1% on Opus 4.5. It does not break prompt caching, because deferred tools were never in the cached prefix. Use it above ~10 tools or >10K tokens of definitions; skip it below 10 tools or when every tool is used every session.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: Make the case for and against having the model write code that calls your tools.
flashcards.a: For: intermediate results never enter context — 2,000+ expense line items (200KB) collapsed to ~1KB; average tokens 43,588 -> 27,297 (37%); knowledge retrieval 25.6% -> 28.5%; GAIA 46.5% -> 51.2%; 20 calls in one code block eliminates 19 inference round-trips; MCP-as-code reports reach 150K -> 2K tokens (~98.7%). Against: arbitrary code execution is now part of your control flow, so you own the whole microVM/egress/credentials problem, and it hides intermediate results the model may need to reason over.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: How do you test tools in three layers, and which need a model?
flashcards.a: L1 unit tests (no model): happy path, empty result, 404, 429, 403, and a payload big enough to trigger truncation with an assertion the message is ACTIONABLE; property-test that two calls with the same idempotency key produce one side effect and identical responses. L2 contract tests in CI (no model): description length, per-parameter descriptions, enums where needed, examples validate, names unique and not confusable, every mutating tool has a tier and a key. L3 evals (model needed): realistic multi-step tasks that do NOT name the tool, with a held-out test set.

flashcards.topic: Tool Engineering: Schemas, Errors, Idempotency, Sandboxing
flashcards.q: What metrics do you collect in a tool eval, beyond accuracy?
flashcards.a: Tool-call count, total tokens, per-call and per-task latency, tool error rate by error class, and WHICH tools were selected. Redundant calls point at bad pagination defaults; invalid-parameter errors point at thin descriptions or missing examples; selection frequency tells you which tools to delete. Also read raw transcripts, because what agents OMIT from their stated reasoning is often more informative than what they say.

flashcards.q: Formal definition of calibration, and the ECE formula.
flashcards.a: Perfectly calibrated: P(Y_hat = Y | p_hat = p) = p for all p. You cannot evaluate that conditional directly, so bin: ECE = SUM_m (|B_m|/n) · |acc(B_m) − conf(B_m)|, typically M=10 or 15 bins. MCE is the worst bin. Overconfidence = points below the diagonal on a reliability diagram.

flashcards.q: Four things wrong with using ECE alone.
flashcards.a: 1) It is not a proper scoring rule — a constant base-rate predictor has ECE ~0 and zero resolution, so report Brier or NLL too. 2) Bin count is a free parameter with no principled default; always state M. 3) Equal-width bins are meaningless for LLM verbalised confidence because 90%+ of mass lands in the top two bins — use equal-mass/adaptive bins. 4) It is downward-biased at small n, so cross-model comparison needs equal n and equal M.

flashcards.q: Three mechanisms that make LLM verbalised confidence useless.
flashcards.a: 1) No training signal — the tokens '0.9' come from next-token prediction with no loss comparing them to observed outcome frequency. 2) RLHF pushes the wrong way — raters prefer decisive answers, so post-training raises stated confidence independent of correctness (GPT-4 report: near-diagonal pre-training, overconfident after). 3) The scoreboard pays for guessing — binary accuracy gives 0 for abstaining and p(correct)>0 for a guess.

flashcards.q: Measured ECE range for LLM verbalised confidence, and where the mass sits.
flashcards.a: Mass concentrates in the 0.8-1.0 band almost regardless of accuracy. Task-dependent ECE spans roughly 0.05 (constrained JSON) to 0.61 (NQ-Open) in 2026 benchmark work (ConfidenceBench, arXiv:2607.20526). Diagnostic: plot the histogram — if >80% of mass is above 0.8 while eval accuracy is 60%, the field is decorative.

flashcards.q: Where do logprobs work as confidence, and where do they fail?
flashcards.a: Work: multiple choice (softmax over option letters), classification/routing over a fixed label set, extraction (min-token logprob catches one fabricated digit). Fail: free-form generation, because likelihood is over SURFACE FORMS — 'Paris' / 'It's Paris' / 'The capital is Paris' split the mass three ways for a certain model, while a model torn between two facts puts 0.5 on each. Sequence entropy cannot distinguish those.

flashcards.q: Semantic entropy: algorithm, cost, and citation.
flashcards.a: Farquhar et al., Nature 630:625-630 (2024). Sample n≈10 at T≈1, cluster into semantic equivalence classes by BIDIRECTIONAL entailment (a ⊨ b AND b ⊨ a), then SE = −SUM_c p(c) log p(c) over clusters. Cost: n generations plus up to O(n²) NLI pairs, reducible to O(n·|C|) by comparing each sample against one representative per cluster. NLI itself is ~10-40ms per pair.

flashcards.q: The blind spot shared by every self-consistency method.
flashcards.a: Confidently wrong: if the model reliably believes something false, all samples agree, entropy is near zero, and semantic entropy / SelfCheckGPT / sampling variance are all silent. 2026 work states this directly (arXiv:2603.21172, 'Entropy Alone is Insufficient for Safe Selective Prediction'). Only grounding against an external source catches this class.

flashcards.q: Honest AUROC numbers for consistency-family detectors.
flashcards.a: Strongly benchmark-dependent. SelfCheckGPT's best variant reported AUC-PR ~0.53-0.67 on its original benchmark (n=20 samples); on harder 2026 benchmarks both SelfCheckGPT and semantic entropy have been reported near 0.58-0.60 AUROC, while performing much better on the confabulation-heavy sets they were designed for. Quoting one AUROC as if it generalises is overselling.

flashcards.q: Selective prediction vocabulary: coverage, selective risk, AURC, coverage@risk.
flashcards.a: Coverage phi = answered/n. Selective risk R = wrong among answered / answered. AURC = area under the risk-coverage curve (lower is better, threshold-free). coverage@risk<=r = the maximum coverage keeping R <= r, which is the number you put in a product SLO. Need >= ~200 answered items before the risk estimate means anything.

flashcards.q: What does a FLAT risk-coverage curve tell you?
flashcards.a: The confidence signal has no resolution: abstaining discards correct and incorrect answers in the same proportion, so you buy nothing with the coverage you give up. This is the normal outcome when thresholding on verbalised confidence, and plotting the curve is the cheapest way to kill a bad confidence feature before it ships.

flashcards.q: The abstention ladder, in order.
flashcards.a: answer → answer + flag unsupported claims → ASK ONE CLARIFYING QUESTION → escalate (stronger model / human) → decline with a reason and a next step. The clarifying-question tier recovers the most value because much low-confidence traffic is underspecified rather than unanswerable. 'I don't know' with no next step is a dead end.

flashcards.q: Three inputs an abstention policy needs (most people name one).
flashcards.a: 1) A confidence signal. 2) The STAKE of the query — read_only and financial do not share a threshold. 3) What abstention COSTS, i.e. what happens instead: a clarifying question, a stronger model, a retrieval retry, a human, or a documented out-of-scope. Abstention is only a good move when there is a better next step.

flashcards.q: What did AbstentionBench find, and why is it uncomfortable?
flashcards.a: arXiv:2506.09038: 20 datasets, 35k+ unanswerable queries covering unknown answers, underspecification, false premises, subjective interpretation, and stale information. Abstention is unsolved, scaling models barely helps, and REASONING FINE-TUNING DEGRADES the ability to abstain — which breaks the plan of 'just use the reasoning model'.

flashcards.q: Best default confidence signal in production, and why it beats semantic entropy.
flashcards.a: A small logistic regression over 4-6 features you already compute — NLI entailment coverage, retrieval top-1 score, top1−top2 score gap, min-token logprob, answer length, tool-error flag — trained on a few thousand labelled production examples. It is calibrated by construction, free at inference, and trained on YOUR distribution, which is where calibration lives. Semantic entropy is the better unsupervised signal and the worse engineering default.

flashcards.q: Conformal prediction for LLMs: what it guarantees and what it does not.
flashcards.a: Split conformal: compute nonconformity scores on a calibration set, take the ceil((n+1)(1−alpha))/n quantile, and the prediction set has coverage >= 1−alpha assuming EXCHANGEABILITY. The guarantee is MARGINAL, not conditional — 90% overall can be 60% on the slice you care about — and exchangeability breaks under distribution shift. Works for MCQ/label sets; 2026 impossibility results (arXiv:2606.29054) show it degrades for free-form generation.

flashcards.q: Temperature scaling: what, whose paper, and where it applies to LLMs.
flashcards.a: Guo et al., 'On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks' (ICML 2017, arXiv:1706.04599). Rescale logits z -> z/T with a single parameter T fit on a HELD-OUT split by NLL. For LLMs it applies wherever you have logits over a fixed label set: MCQ options, class tokens, p(true). One parameter, near-free, re-fit per model version.

flashcards.q: p(true) — what it is and why it beats verbalised percentages.
flashcards.a: A second call presenting the question and candidate answer, asking for a single True/False token, and reading the logprob of 'True'. It beats verbalised percentages because it moves into the regime where LLM calibration is least bad: a single-token binary decision with logprob access. Still overconfident — temperature-scale it — and use a DIFFERENT model family if possible, since self-evaluation has correlated errors.

flashcards.q: How do you communicate uncertainty without making the product feel broken?
flashcards.a: Change the ACTION, not the adjective — low confidence should produce a different interaction, not the same answer wrapped in hedges. Four discrete states with distinct affordances: verified / unverified+flags / needs-input (one clarifying question) / out-of-scope+route. No raw percentages for lay users. Flag ONLY what failed verification, because constant labelling becomes wallpaper. Budget abstention rate as an SLO with an owner.

flashcards.q: Why must the harness own the abstention decision rather than the model?
flashcards.a: 2026 work (arXiv:2601.07767, 'Are LLM Decisions Faithful to Verbal Confidence?') finds models successfully verbalise uncertainty and then fail to translate it into behaviour. So extract a signal, apply the threshold in code, and gate in the harness. Letting the model decide inside its own prose means the decision is unmeasurable and unenforceable.

flashcards.q: What must you log per response to be able to calibrate at all?
flashcards.a: The confidence signal(s) and their version, the threshold and its version, the decision (answered / flagged / clarified / escalated / declined), the stake tier, and the DOWNSTREAM USER ACTION (accepted, edited, thumbs-down, escalated, abandoned). That last field is your label source; without it every threshold argument is anecdote.

flashcards.q: Why does exposing a raw confidence float in a public API create a future incident?
flashcards.a: Consumers threshold on it, so you can never change its distribution: a model upgrade that improves accuracy but shifts the score silently breaks every consumer. Expose a decision plus a stable tier instead ({status, risk_tier, unsupported_claims, evidence}). If a partner insists on a number, version it (confidence_version: v3) with documented semantics and a commitment to bump on every re-fit.

flashcards.q: Why calibration is per-model-per-prompt-per-distribution.
flashcards.a: A threshold is a property of the (model, prompt, distribution) triple, not a constant. An ECE measured on MMLU or TriviaQA says almost nothing about your domain. Re-sweep the threshold on held-out data at every model or prompt change and treat thresholds as VERSIONED artefacts — unversioned threshold constants are a latent outage.

flashcards.q: State CAP theorem precisely (Gilbert-Lynch 2002).
flashcards.a: Under an actual network partition, a distributed system must choose between Consistency (linearizability) and Availability (every non-failing node responds) -- cannot guarantee both plus Partition tolerance simultaneously during a partition.

flashcards.q: What's wrong with "CAP means pick two of three"?
flashcards.a: Partition tolerance isn't optional in a real multi-node system (partitions will happen), so the only live choice is CP vs AP, and only DURING an actual partition. Outside a partition, a system can be fully consistent and fully available simultaneously.

flashcards.q: How does CAP's "Availability" differ from a 99.99% uptime SLA?
flashcards.a: CAP's A is binary and instantaneous per-request: every request to a non-failing node gets SOME non-error response, with no statement about latency. An SLA is a statistical, time-averaged measure that typically implies a latency bound too.

flashcards.q: How does CAP's "C" differ from ACID's "C"?
flashcards.a: ACID consistency = transactions preserve application-defined invariants (foreign keys, uniqueness). CAP consistency = all nodes agree on the current value of a piece of data (linearizability). Same letter, unrelated concepts.

flashcards.q: State PACELC and explain why it's more useful than CAP alone.
flashcards.a: If Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency; Else (normal operation), choose Latency or Consistency. More useful because real systems spend ~99.99% of time in the 'Else' branch, which CAP is entirely silent about.

flashcards.q: Classify Spanner and DynamoDB/Cassandra in PACELC terms.
flashcards.a: Spanner = PC/EC (always consistent, pays latency cost via TrueTime commit-wait even with no partition). Dynamo/Cassandra = PA/EL by default (available and fast; consistency is a tunable knob usually loosened).

flashcards.q: Rank linearizable, sequential, causal, eventual consistency and state what each permits.
flashcards.a: Linearizable: real-time total order, as if one copy. Sequential: one shared total order respecting each process's own order, but not tied to real time across processes. Causal: only causally-related ops ordered; concurrent ops can differ across replicas. Eventual: only convergence guaranteed given no new writes, no ordering guarantee otherwise.

flashcards.q: What do read-your-writes and monotonic-reads session guarantees fix?
flashcards.a: Read-your-writes: a client sees its own prior writes (or newer) on subsequent reads even if it hits a lagging replica. Monotonic reads: successive reads by the same client never go backward in time across different replicas.

flashcards.q: State the R+W>N quorum arithmetic and what it guarantees vs doesn't.
flashcards.a: If R+W>N, every read quorum and write quorum share at least one replica, guaranteeing a read sees the most recent completed write. It does NOT guarantee real-time recency for concurrent operations -- two racing ops can still need reconciliation (vector clocks, LWW).

flashcards.q: Compare single-leader, multi-leader, and leaderless replication in one line each.
flashcards.a: Single-leader: simple, no write conflicts, leader is bottleneck+SPOF, async replicas can be stale. Multi-leader: better cross-region write latency, needs conflict resolution (LWW/CRDT/app-merge). Leaderless/quorum: no single point of failure, tunable per-op consistency via R/W/N.

flashcards.q: What's the hot-partition failure mode for range partitioning, and for hash partitioning?
flashcards.a: Range: a monotonically increasing key (timestamp, auto-increment ID) concentrates all new writes on the partition owning the tail of the range. Hash: fixes that, but kills range scans (scatter-gather) and doesn't fix a single wildly popular key overloading the one partition that owns it.

flashcards.q: How does Spanner achieve external consistency, and at what latency cost?
flashcards.a: TrueTime exposes clock uncertainty as a bounded interval; the leader waits out that uncertainty (commit-wait) before acknowledging a commit, guaranteeing the timestamp has passed in real time. Measured commit-wait: ~5-8ms single-region, 20ms+ multi-region -- a permanent latency tax on every write.

flashcards.q: What consistency levels does Cassandra expose per query, and what does LOCAL_QUORUM mean?
flashcards.a: ONE, QUORUM (majority across ALL datacenters), LOCAL_QUORUM (majority within the coordinator's own datacenter only, avoiding cross-region latency), ALL. Consistency is tunable per query, not fixed at the system level.

flashcards.q: What does DynamoDB's managed service default to for read consistency, and what's the opt-in alternative?
flashcards.a: Default reads are eventually consistent (effectively R=1). An explicit option for strongly consistent reads exists, reading from the partition's current leader-equivalent copy.

flashcards.q: What did agentic coding actually change about the engineering bottleneck?
flashcards.a: It moved it rather than removing it. On Anthropic's Claude Code team, writing code, writing tests and refactoring rarely slow them down anymore, and verification, code review and security took their place. The consequence for a Principal: the artifacts you author shift from implementations to specs, ADRs and enforcement (lint rules, hooks, CI gates, fitness functions).

flashcards.q: State the three levels of control over an agent, and the rule that follows.
flashcards.a: Level 1 instruction (CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md explains the rule) is a recommendation. Level 2 reminder (a skill re-states it at the moment it matters) raises compliance but stays probabilistic. Level 3 enforcement (hook, lint rule, CI gate, or a type that makes the wrong thing unrepresentable) is a constraint. Rule: anything you would be upset to find violated belongs at Level 3.

flashcards.q: Give the mechanical reason a rule in conversation history will be ignored later.
flashcards.a: Compaction reliably preserves the current task, recent errors and file names, and reliably loses initial instructions, intermediate decisions and style rules. So a style rule stated in conversation is gone by turn 60. A rule in CLAUDE.md lives in the system prompt and survives compaction. A rule in a lint config cannot be lost at all.

flashcards.q: Why is plan mode a control rather than a convention?
flashcards.a: Because the write tools are physically unavailable in plan mode: it is a hard read-only sandbox enforced at the tool level, not a promise the model keeps. That is the difference between Level 1 ('please don't edit yet') and Level 3 applied to the agent's own workflow, and it is why plan mode changes outcomes. Microsoft Agent Framework ships the same idea as a plan/execute mode provider.

flashcards.q: What makes a spec self-contained, and what failure does each clause prevent?
flashcards.a: It names the files and interfaces involved (prevents assumption propagation, where the agent invents a plausible module boundary and builds three PRs on it), states what is out of scope (prevents abstraction bloat and scope creep), and ends with an end-to-end verification step that actually runs (prevents fail-plausible completion, where a green mocked unit test hides the broken thing). Add an 'open questions for the human' section; an empty list on an ambiguous task is suspicious.

flashcards.q: What does Karpathy's catalogue of remaining agent failures say?
flashcards.a: The models make wrong assumptions on your behalf and run with them without checking. They do not manage confusion, do not seek clarifications, do not surface inconsistencies, do not present tradeoffs, and do not push back when they should. They are still a little too sycophantic. Consequence: a wrong architectural premise arrives looking identical to a right one, which is why an explicit 'open questions' slot in the spec is the mitigation.

flashcards.q: Give the five properties of an agent-sized unit of work.
flashcards.a: Bounded blast radius (you can name the files it should touch). A stated contract (interfaces and error semantics fixed in advance). Machine-checkable success (a command whose exit code decides done). Reversibility (one git revert undoes it). Fits the context (relevant code and constraints in one window). Two or more failures means the decomposition is the problem, not the agent.

flashcards.q: Name five categories of work an agent predictably cannot do.
flashcards.a: 1 Under-determined design decisions with long shadows (consistency models, tenancy, service boundaries, data ownership), because the agent lacks the political, organizational and roadmap constraints and returns a plausible answer confidently. 2 Correctness resting on unwritten invariants, which is why mature codebases invert the calculus relative to greenfield. 3 Thinly-represented APIs (internal libraries, recently-changed SDKs), where confident hallucination concentrates. 4 Cross-cutting migrations where 15% of call sites need judgment, because it will make the 15% look like the 85%. 5 Work where the test suite is the thing being fixed.

flashcards.q: What should you write into AGENTS.md, and what should you keep out?
flashcards.a: In: exact copy-pasteable commands for install/test/lint/types/migrate; a map of the tree telling the agent where to look next (including a pointer to docs/adr with 'stop if your plan contradicts an ADR'); hard rules stated AND noted as CI-enforced; a behaviour block (read before modifying, prefer three duplicate lines over a premature abstraction, don't comment unchanged code, don't add error handling the contract doesn't require, diagnose before retrying, report honestly, stop and ask above about 60% uncertainty); an explicit verifiable 'done means'. Out: anything you'd be upset to see violated but haven't enforced, secrets, permission logic, long prose rationale (that's an ADR, link it), and content that will drift from the code.

flashcards.q: AGENTS.md versus CLAUDE.md in 2026: what is the status?
flashcards.a: AGENTS.md became the de facto cross-tool convention (read natively by Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI, Aider, Windsurf, Zed and 20+ others, stewarded by the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation, adopted in 60,000+ repositories). It is a convention, not an ISO/IETF standard. It exists because teams maintained .cursorrules, CLAUDE.md and copilot-instructions.md in parallel. Practical answer for a polyglot shop: AGENTS.md as source of truth, CLAUDE.md as a thin pointer plus Claude-specific additions.

flashcards.q: In what order do you review an agent-authored PR, and why that order?
flashcards.a: Test diff, then file list, then code. Test diff first because the highest-cost catchable failure is 'passes tests while being wrong', typically by mocking out the broken dependency or asserting the implementation rather than the behaviour; the question is 'would this test fail if the feature were absent?'. File list second, against the spec's named files, because that catches scope leakage and dead code cheaply. Code last, grepping for escape hatches and swallowed errors, which compile silently and therefore survive review.

flashcards.q: List the nine failure classes in agent-written code, roughly by descending cost.
flashcards.a: 1 Assumption propagation. 2 Passes tests while being wrong. 3 Silent bypass of language guarantees (type: ignore, Any, casts, unsafe). 4 Swallowed errors (bare except, discarded Result, unawaited coroutine, ignored return code). 5 Confident hallucination on thin APIs. 6 Abstraction bloat. 7 Dead code accumulation. 8 Scope leakage. 9 Fail-plausible reporting (fabricated command output).

flashcards.q: Which agent-code failure class is not catchable at diff-review time, and what catches it?
flashcards.a: Assumption propagation. If the model misunderstood something early and built on a faulty premise, the diff can be locally excellent and globally wrong, and you may not notice until you are five PRs deep with the architecture cemented. What catches it: reviewing the plan rather than the diff, requiring the spec to name interfaces, and architecture-fitness functions in CI (import-linter, dependency rules, boundary tests) that fail mechanically on a wrong premise.

flashcards.q: Give the delivery-data numbers on the review bottleneck.
flashcards.a: DORA 2025: high-AI-adoption teams merged 98% more PRs with review time up 91% and PR size up 154%. 2026: median PR review time up 441% and 31% more PRs merging with no review at all. Agentic PRs wait 5.3x longer for a reviewer and run 2.6x larger. Median batch size roughly doubled between Q1 2025 and Q1 2026, growing about 2.5x faster from October onward. Atlassian: 99% of AI-using developers saved 10+ hours per week and most reported no decrease in overall workload.

flashcards.q: State the METR result and why it is the most important number in this topic.
flashcards.a: METR's July 2025 randomized controlled trial (16 experienced open-source developers, 246 tasks on repositories they regularly contributed to) found early-2025 AI tools made them 19% SLOWER, while they predicted a 24% speedup and, after experiencing the slowdown, still estimated they had been 20% faster. That 39-point perception gap means self-report is not evidence, which invalidates most productivity claims. METR's continuation estimates the slowdown flipping to about +18% faster by early 2026.

flashcards.q: What is comprehension debt?
flashcards.a: Generation and discrimination are different capabilities, so you can review code competently after your ability to write it from scratch has atrophied, and there is a threshold at which review silently becomes rubber-stamping. Mechanism: the agent never tires, the code looks plausible, tests pass or seem to, you are shipping under pressure, so you skim and merge, and three days later cannot explain how it works. Unlike technical debt it appears in no dashboard.

flashcards.q: Give the mitigations for comprehension debt.
flashcards.a: TDD, so the specification stays in your head and you get the machine-checkable success criterion for free. Ask for the justification and evaluate the reasoning, not just the output. Deliberately hand-write some things to keep the capability. Own one subsystem end to end, so depth exists somewhere. Treat 'I don't understand this' as a stop signal rather than a win. None of them are complete.

flashcards.q: Why is the compiler analogy for agentic coding wrong?
flashcards.a: A compiler is deterministic and its output is correct by construction, so you never need to read it. An agent's output is probabilistic and occasionally confidently wrong, so somebody must retain the ability to read and judge it. The evidence: 38% of developers report reviewing AI-generated logic takes MORE effort than reviewing human-written code, while only 48% consistently check AI-assisted code before committing. That gap is an unpriced risk, not nostalgia.

flashcards.q: What did Anthropic's Claude Code team change, before and after?
flashcards.a: Planning: six-month roadmaps to just-in-time planning (prototype, put internal users on it, act on feedback), with rituals moving from design docs to PR and prototype discussions. Context gathering: find the author, to ask Claude first then ask whether the question itself can be automated. Code review: humans review everything, to Claude handling style/lint/bug-catching/tests and humans reviewing where domain expertise matters (legal risk tolerance, trust boundaries and security, product taste). Team makeup: fixed roles to blurred, hiring on creative builders with product sense and engineers with deep systems expertise, explicitly de-indexed on raw throughput.

flashcards.q: What three metrics did Anthropic track to know new norms were sticking, and what warning came with them?
flashcards.a: Onboarding ramp time going down (engineers shipping real code within their first week), PR cycle time going down (which surfaces where CI and build systems fail to scale under the new code volume), and Claude-assisted commit share going up (effectively 100% for four months). The warning: do not confuse throughput with success. Throughput is one metric; the real metric is the thing you were trying to solve.

flashcards.q: Would you adopt just-in-time planning anywhere? State the precondition.
flashcards.a: Only conditionally. It worked for the Claude Code team because coding was the dominant cost, their users were internal, and their surface moved weekly (a six-month roadmap was out of date by month three). It fails where the roadmap exists for coordination with downstream teams, compliance calendars, or contractual commitments, because agentic coding reduces implementation cost and does not reduce coordination cost. Adopt the meta-practice unconditionally: question why a process exists, grant explicit permission to kill obsolete ones, and pick the noisiest workflow first.

flashcards.q: What do you never delegate, and what is the organizing principle?
flashcards.a: Never: architectural decisions and their rationale, trust and security boundaries, data model ownership, error-semantics contracts, dependency additions, anything with legal or compliance exposure, and the ship decision. Principle: reversibility multiplied by shadow length. An implementation mistake is cheap and local; a wrong service boundary or consistency model is paid for over years by people who were not in the conversation. The agent may draft the ADR; the test is whether you can defend the REJECTED alternatives without re-reading it.

flashcards.q: What is the rule for subagent use when review is your bottleneck?
flashcards.a: One subagent per independently reviewable artifact. If two subagents produce work you can only evaluate together, you have parallelized generation and serialized review, which is the wrong direction. Reach for a subagent for context isolation (about 67% fewer tokens than skills in multi-domain scenarios), genuine parallelism across independent files, or a different permission scope. Not because you have a lot of tools.

flashcards.q: What is fresh-context self-review and why does it work?
flashcards.a: Having the model review its own diff in a clean context window. It feels wrong to ask the same model to critique itself, and it works because most of the errors are context artifacts (assumptions made 40 turns ago, dead code from a superseded approach) rather than capability limits. Anthropic ships this as Code Review, used by every internal team, handling style, linting, PR feedback, bug-catching pre-commit and test-adding, which preserves the human review budget for things needing expertise.

flashcards.q: Name the first two CI gates to add for an agent-heavy team.
flashcards.a: 1 Fail the PR if it touched files the linked spec did not name; about twenty lines, and it catches scope leakage, dead-code accumulation and opportunistic refactors in one rule (three of the nine failure classes). 2 A diff-size cap with a split requirement, because it is the only thing that actually addresses the merged-unreviewed problem: a 200-line PR reviewed properly beats a 2,000-line PR skimmed, and the skim is what is really happening in 31% of PRs.

flashcards.q: How is AI fluency actually assessed in 2026 senior interviews?
flashcards.a: New round types: code-review rounds, 'evaluate this LLM-generated solution' rounds, and 'AI delta' assessments where you tackle a real GitHub issue in 2-4 hours and are scored on what you add beyond what the AI produced (exploration strategy, engineering rigour, edge cases, documentation). OpenAI allows AI in coding rounds with screen-share and narration, with the boundary being not dumping the whole problem in. Exponent runs a combined coding-plus-design round using Claude Code where the interviewer scores prompting strategy, verification ability, and whether you let the AI make architectural decisions; their stated top pitfall is 'not understanding what the AI is going to do, relying on AI to make decisions for you'.

flashcards.q: Why does leaning on AI during a live interview often hurt candidates?
flashcards.a: Follow-up questions expose that they cannot explain a subtle bug the model introduced. The reported pattern across multiple HN threads is that candidates using AI in live interviews frequently perform worse for exactly this reason. There is also a documented case of a borderline senior candidate getting a soft thumbs-down for insisting LLMs could help with a regression problem where it did not make technical sense: knowing the tools is table stakes, knowing when not to reach for them is the seniority signal.

flashcards.q: Why does agentic coding work in greenfield and invert in mature codebases?
flashcards.a: In greenfield, personal projects, MVPs and small teams you control the stack, can refactor aggressively, throw code away without political friction, and comprehension debt stays manageable, so the agent's weaknesses matter less. In mature codebases with complex invariants the agent does not know what it does not know, cannot intuit unwritten rules, and its confidence scales inversely with context understanding. Also: the last 10% is not linear, and the economics flip somewhere around 75-85% depending on domain complexity.

flashcards.q: What is the bimodal adoption fact and why does it matter for a team?
flashcards.a: Armin Ronacher's 5,000-developer poll found 44% now write less than 10% of their code manually while another 44% still write over 90% manually. It is a bimodal distribution, not a bell curve. It matters because 'how we build software here' is no longer a shared practice, code review across the two populations is genuinely difficult, and Stack Overflow found only 16% reporting 'great' productivity gains. The fix is standardizing the workflow (spec, plan, gates, review), not the tool: the tool is not the practice.

flashcards.q: Give the one-line summary of what actually worries a senior engineer about agentic coding.
flashcards.a: The danger is not that the agent fails. It is that it succeeds so confidently in the wrong direction that you stop checking the compass. And the corollary: if your ability to read does not scale with the agent's ability to output, you are not engineering, you are hoping.

flashcards.q: Name the three state boundaries that own every hard problem in a production agent system.
flashcards.a: 1) The MODEL boundary is stateless, so context is rebuilt every turn and cost is quadratic in turns. 2) The PROCESS boundary is unreliable, so anything that must survive a pod eviction or a 30-hour human approval lives in Postgres, not in Python. 3) The TRUST boundary is porous, so retrieved content, tool results and other tenants' data carry no authority and must be labelled and bounded by code that never consults the model.

flashcards.q: What six questions must be answered before writing any agent code?
flashcards.a: Unit of work (defines trace, checkpoint thread, eval case, cost unit) · verifiable success signal · blast radius of a wrong action (sets the HITL boundary) · latency contract (bounds the step count) · cost ceiling per unit (becomes an enforced budget) · principal AND tenant as two distinct axes. Then write the NON-GOALS down explicitly.

flashcards.q: What are the only three conditions that justify multi-agent over one agent with good tools?
flashcards.a: 1) Genuine parallelism with independent subtasks that merge cleanly. 2) Context isolation, where one workstream would pollute another (subagents process ~67% fewer tokens than skills in multi-domain scenarios). 3) Different permission scopes, where isolation is a security property. Tool COUNT is not a trigger; measured tool-selection degradation is, and the first fixes are better descriptions and phase-scoped visibility inside one agent.

flashcards.q: Give the tool-call contract in order, and say why the order is load-bearing.
flashcards.a: resolve + phase visibility → strict SCHEMA VALIDATE → PERMISSION (allow|deny|ask) → harness-injected tenant scope → budget precheck → idempotency key if mutating → execute with timeout inside the boundary → shape (persist >50k chars, keep a 2 KB preview + pointer) → observation. Validation must precede permission because you cannot authorize arguments you have not parsed. Every rejection path returns an OBSERVATION with a remediation message, never an exception. No bare `except Exception`: a harness bug must crash loudly.

flashcards.q: List the LangGraph AsyncPostgresSaver production gotchas.
flashcards.a: Hand-built connections need autocommit=True and row_factory=dict_row. Run .setup() in a migration job, not on pod boot (N pods racing DDL is an outage). thread_id is the isolation boundary: make it deterministic, caller-controlled, tenant-scoped (tenant:user:session) and under 255 characters. InMemorySaver in a multi-worker deployment silently corrupts state across workers. Writes are 8-15 ms, so free on latency but not on storage: ~40 KB x 4.2 per session; partition daily and prune. interrupt() re-executes the node from its start on resume, so no side effects before the interrupt point.

flashcards.q: Why is an in-agent cost budget only advisory, and where is the real enforcement boundary?
flashcards.a: A bug, a retry wrapper or a subagent can bypass application-level checks. Real enforcement: the worker holds NO provider credentials, egress is restricted by NetworkPolicy to the LLM gateway, and the gateway does the pre-call per-run/per-tenant/per-day budget check and returns a terminal over_budget error the agent handles as an observation. Then reconcile nightly against the provider usage export; drift above 3% means your token accounting is wrong, because pre-call counts are estimates and only the response has true output tokens.

flashcards.q: Why must an agent canary be scored on quality rather than infra health?
flashcards.a: Because a bad prompt returns 200 OK, at normal latency, with a worse answer. CPU, 5xx and p95 all look fine. So the canary gate is: judge-score delta, guardrail block rate, unresolved-citation rate, escalation rate, cost per session and p95 latency, measured on live canary traffic at n >= 400 before a promote decision.

flashcards.q: Give the five blocking CI eval gates for an agent PR.
flashcards.a: Deterministic pass rate >= 0.95 with no regression vs main (schema validity, citation resolution, tool-order and interrupt assertions, budget adherence) · trajectory F1 vs the reference path >= 0.85 · LLM-as-judge mean >= 4.1 and within 0.15 of main, judge model pinned with a human-labelled calibration set · p95 cost per case under the ceiling · a critical-safety subset (cross-tenant, injection, unapproved write) at 100% with no exceptions. Run at temperature 0 with 3 seeds and take the median.

flashcards.q: Why are outcome-only evals insufficient for agents? Give the number.
flashcards.a: Agents evaluated only on final-output quality pass 20-40% more test cases than trajectory-level evaluation reveals, so outcome-only evals systematically overstate readiness. Trajectory scoring asserts the path: which tools were called, in what order, which were forbidden, whether the HITL interrupt fired, and whether the step and cost budgets held.

flashcards.q: What is the single highest-value OpenTelemetry attribute on an agent run, and why?
flashcards.a: The hash of the fully assembled static prompt prefix. It exposes two expensive bug classes at once: silent prompt drift (the hash changed and nobody meant it to) and prompt-cache destruction (the hash changes every turn, cached_input_tokens collapses to ~0, and you pay 5-10x). It also makes runs reproducible, which is a precondition for everything else. Caveat: gen_ai.* conventions moved to a dedicated repo at v1.42.0 on 2026-06-12 and remain Development status, so pin the instrumentation.

flashcards.q: Describe a HITL approval gate that survives a 30-hour human delay, plus its two failure modes.
flashcards.a: The act node raises, the graph interrupt()s, the checkpoint is written, and the worker returns and releases its slot. An approval row records run_id, tool, args digest, rule_id, requester and expires_at. On decision the run resumes from the checkpoint; rejection is appended as an observation the agent can adapt to, not an error. Failure mode 1: stale approval, fixed by revalidating preconditions in the same transaction as the write plus a 24-hour expiry. Failure mode 2: approval fatigue, detected by approve_rate above ~95% with median review time under 10 seconds, which means the gate is decoration and the rule must be narrowed.

flashcards.q: How do you deploy an agent service on Kubernetes, and why is there no GPU?
flashcards.a: No GPU in the agent tier: the model is an API call, so the workers are I/O-bound Python sitting at 8-15% CPU while saturated on concurrent awaits (2 vCPU / 4 GiB holding ~50 runs). Self-hosted models live in a separate vLLM deployment behind the gateway with its own node pool. Scale with KEDA on queue depth, because an HPA on CPU never fires. terminationGracePeriodSeconds 600 with a preStop drain flag, PDB minAvailable 60%, 300 s scale-down stabilisation. Readiness must NOT probe the LLM provider, or a provider blip rolls your whole fleet out of service.

flashcards.q: What actually stops a prompt injection in a retrieved document, and what only reduces its probability?
flashcards.a: Reduces probability: authority labelling in the context builder, with untrusted content in <untrusted source=...> envelopes and a system prompt stating those instructions are data, not policy. Actually bounds damage: the permission engine, which never consults the model, plus a session-level lethal-trifecta rule (once a run has read private data AND ingested untrusted content, any externally-communicating tool requires approval regardless of its own annotations), plus a NetworkPolicy so the worker cannot reach the internet. A classifier is a filter with a false-negative rate, not a boundary. CaMeL and dual-LLM quarantine are the only patterns with a real security argument and no mainstream harness ships them as of mid-2026.

flashcards.q: State the three phase gates from POC to production, and the structural change at each.
flashcards.a: POC (2 weeks): 1 agent, read-only tools, MemorySaver, 20 cases run by hand. GATE: >= 60% pass AND one real user changed behaviour. MVP (6 weeks): LangGraph + AsyncPostgresSaver, tool contract, budgets, OTel, 1 HITL write, 60 advisory goldens. GATE: p95 latency SLO met, cost/session under target, zero unapproved writes, and the eval gate flips from advisory to BLOCKING. Production (8 weeks): permission engine, provenance, compaction, memory, ledger, prompt registry + canary, 140 blocking goldens, runbooks, SLOs. GATE: two weeks at SLO + security review + signed cost forecast. Structural change: POC to MVP moves state from process to database; MVP to Prod moves enforcement from application code to boundaries the code cannot bypass.

flashcards.q: Two weeks instead of two months: what do you cut and what is non-negotiable?
flashcards.a: CUT: multi-agent, cross-session memory, compaction (cap the run at 8 steps instead), the permission DSL (hardcoded allow-list plus HITL on every write), the semantic cache, the prompt registry and canary, judge-based scorers, the output rail beyond schema and citation checks, autoscaling, per-tenant cost attribution, multi-provider failover. KEEP: the Postgres checkpointer, the tool contract, gateway-enforced budgets with no provider credentials in the worker, OTel traces with prompt hash and pinned model version, 20 blocking goldens including cross-tenant and unapproved-write cases, HITL on writes, harness-injected tenant scope, and one runbook for cost spikes.

flashcards.q: Why does a POC cost estimate typically come in 3x low, and what are the cost levers in order?
flashcards.a: Because the POC measures a single model call and production runs 4-6 turns that re-send retrieval context, a verify step adds another call, and a mutable system prompt (a timestamp, a shuffled tool list) breaks prompt caching. Levers by return: prompt caching on a FROZEN prefix (a ~34% total cost cut when 61% of input tokens hit cache) > model routing (RouteLLM: 95% of GPT-4 quality at 26% strong-model calls, ~48% cheaper than random; production teams report 40-85%) > fewer output tokens via structured output > fewer steps via better tools > semantic cache LAST, because honest production hit rates are 20-45% and a loose threshold returns the answer to a nearby question.

flashcards.q: Give the four agent on-call runbooks and the first move in each.
flashcards.a: Cost spike (cost/hour > 2x 7-day p95 for 10 min): lower the gateway per-run cap to 0.5x, cap the offending tenant or disable the offending intent. Loop storm (steps/run p99 > 2x baseline): reduce max_steps by config; the usual root cause is a tool returning HTTP 200 with an empty body so the model retries forever, and the tool is the bug. Checkpoint lag (write p99 > 150 ms, or approval queue age > 8 h): scale the pool, run the prune job, check partition rotation. Injection/deny spike (deny rate > 3x baseline on a tool): quarantine the source corpus or tenant, then pull the untrusted envelopes from traces. Rule: every mitigation is a config or flag change, never a deploy.

flashcards.q: What is the correct harness build order, and why is the order not arbitrary?
flashcards.a: model adapter → deterministic context builder → narrow tool registry → strict schema validation → runtime permission checks → structured observations → step and cost budgets → OTel traces → compaction only when a real run needs it → a golden eval set. The order is not arbitrary because each later component is undebuggable without the earlier ones: you cannot tell whether compaction hurt you without traces, and you cannot tell whether a permission rule is too tight without structured observations showing the denial.

flashcards.q: Three repository boundaries worth defending out loud in a design interview.
flashcards.a: 1) Graph topology lives ONLY in graph/build.py, so a reviewer sees the whole state machine on one screen. 2) Every tool goes through harness/_contract.py with no exceptions, so safety properties are enforced in one place rather than N. 3) evals/run.py is the same entrypoint locally and in CI, because an eval suite that only runs in CI gets ignored and one that only runs locally never gates anything.

flashcards.q: When is building this whole platform the wrong call?
flashcards.a: When the steps are known in advance (write the pipeline: deterministic, 10-50x lower latency, near-zero cost, real tests). When one prompt suffices. When the blast radius does not justify it: a 40-uses-per-day internal tool needs 20 goldens, a cost cap and traces, not a gateway, a canary pipeline and 140 cases. And when nobody can articulate what 'correct' means for a run, in which case go get the success signal first, even if that costs two weeks of labelling.

flashcards.q: How does compaction launder authority, and what is the fix?
flashcards.a: If untrusted retrieved content and the user's instruction pass through the same summariser with no classification step, an instruction planted in a document survives compaction and emerges indistinguishable from legitimate context. Fix: feed the provenance map into the compactor and drop instruction-like spans from untrusted sources rather than summarising them. Also keep the task and the open-items list as structural state fields that are never in the summarisable region, and re-inject the last 3 read documents plus the tool list after compaction, or the agent re-reads what it just read.

flashcards.q: Which four weekly numbers tell you the agent is actually working in production?
flashcards.a: 1) Task success on a live-sampled eval set (e.g. 30 sessions/week stratified by intent, deterministic scorers plus a calibrated judge). 2) Escalation rate and its trend, the honest inverse of deflection. 3) Unresolved-citation rate as the hallucination proxy, target under 2%. 4) p95 cost per session against the SLO. Plus one count that pages at 1: unapproved writes. Traces tell you what happened on one run; only a sampled eval tells you whether the system is systematically good.

flashcards.q: Three failure classes outcome-only agent eval is blind to.
flashcards.a: 1) Right destination via a wrong/dangerous path (correct amount refunded via the wrong tool, losing state elsewhere). 2) Lucky one-off success that won't repeat under real variance. 3) Agent self-reports success when the actual tool call failed or the action didn't happen.

flashcards.q: The four eval layers for agents, in order.
flashcards.a: 1) Tool-call accuracy (binary, per call: right tool, right args). 2) Trajectory eval (golden fuzzy-match or LLM judge on the full trace, 6 dims scored independently: tool selection, arg extraction, result use, error recovery, plan coherence, task completion). 3) Task completion vs ACTUAL system state, never the agent's own summary. 4) Cost/steps per task, first-class metric alongside accuracy.

flashcards.q: Why must task completion be checked against system state instead of the agent's final message?
flashcards.a: An agent can produce a confident, well-formed success message describing an action that didn't happen or happened wrong. Check the actual DB row, the actual mail-provider send log, the actual side effect - never trust the self-report.

flashcards.q: pass@1 vs pass^k - define both and give the reported gap.
flashcards.a: pass@1 = success in at least one of k tries (optimistic). pass^k = ALL k tries succeed (honest reliability number). On realistic multi-turn tau-bench tasks: pass^1 ~70-80% can drop to pass^8 below 25% even for capable models.

flashcards.q: How do you build a golden trajectory correctly?
flashcards.a: Record a real production or expert-solved run, lightly edit into canonical with a domain expert. Explicitly annotate required calls (must appear), forbidden calls (must never appear), and optional/order-independent calls. This is what enables fuzzy matching instead of brittle exact-match.

flashcards.q: The biggest mistake teams make building golden trajectory sets.
flashcards.a: Building the golden set entirely from easy happy-path traces, so the eval never exercises error recovery or policy-edge-case behavior - a regression there goes completely undetected in the dashboard.

flashcards.q: Why track cost and steps per task as first-class metrics, and why report p95 not just mean?
flashcards.a: An agent gaining 2 points accuracy at 4x cost/steps is a Pareto tradeoff, not a strict win - hidden if not tracked. Mean cost can hide a p95 tail from runs that spiral into long retry chains; that tail is usually where real incidents and budget blowouts live.

flashcards.q: How do you build a CI gate on agent eval that doesn't flake?
flashcards.a: Never gate on a single run - use N>=3-5 repeats, gate on aggregate/pass^k with a pre-registered threshold. Hard-gate deterministic checks (tool-call accuracy, state). Statistically gate judge-based checks (drop across a run-set, not one trace). Pin agent AND judge model versions. Quarantine known-flaky tasks.

flashcards.q: Tool-call accuracy: deterministic verifier vs LLM judge - when to use which?
flashcards.a: Deterministic verification (exact match, regex, range check) wherever the argument space allows - cheaper, faster, no judge bias. Reserve an LLM judge only for genuinely open-ended arguments (free-text search query) with no deterministic 'close enough' check.

flashcards.q: Why score trajectory dimensions (tool selection, arg extraction, error recovery, plan coherence...) independently instead of one aggregate number?
flashcards.a: An aggregate hides which specific capability regressed. If error recovery degrades but tool selection stays perfect, an aggregate score might not move enough to trip an alert, while the per-dimension error-recovery score would.

flashcards.q: tau-bench / tau2-bench: what makes this benchmark shape worth imitating?
flashcards.a: Realistic multi-turn tool-and-simulated-user tasks against a real mutable backend database (not a transcript check), checked against actual state plus a policy document, with pass^k built in specifically to force confronting nondeterminism.

flashcards.q: What biases from LLM-as-judge carry over to trajectory-judge scoring, and what's added?
flashcards.a: Verbosity, self-preference, position bias (if comparing trajectories pairwise) all carry over directly. Added risk: trajectory traces are long, so the judge's own long-context degradation becomes a failure mode a short single-turn judge call doesn't have.

flashcards.q: Trajectory accuracy baseline without memory/context engineering, and typical improvement from fixes.
flashcards.a: Reported baseline as low as 0.12 trajectory accuracy (12% of runs followed a correct reasoning path) without memory. Targeted fixes (better tool descriptions, explicit planning, memory) reported to lift trajectory accuracy 20-47 points and goal completion up to 32 points in comparable setups.

flashcards.q: How do you make a 6-hour full eval suite practical for CI gating?
flashcards.a: Tier it: a fast, small, high-signal subset (highest-risk/frequency tasks, full N-repeat rigor) gates every PR in minutes; the full suite with full repeats runs on a slower cadence (nightly/pre-release) and gates the actual release. Validate periodically that the fast subset actually correlates with the full suite's failure modes.

flashcards.q: Tools used in production agent eval, and what each is best at.
flashcards.a: LangSmith - LangGraph-native, node-by-node state diffs, replay against a new model. Braintrust - dataset+scoring+monitoring+CI gates in one lifecycle. Arize Phoenix - OpenTelemetry-native tracing, trajectory-level spans, production drift detection.

flashcards.q: Three modes of LLM-as-judge and the one weakness each is most vulnerable to.
flashcards.a: Pointwise (absolute score) - score anchor drifts across sessions. Pairwise (A vs B) - position bias, verbosity bias. Reference-based (vs gold answer) - penalizes valid paraphrases that don't textually resemble the reference.

flashcards.q: Position bias: what is it and the measured magnitude?
flashcards.a: Swapping the order of two candidates in a pairwise prompt shifts the win rate 10-15 percentage points independent of quality (Zheng et al., MT-Bench 2023). Mitigation: run both orderings, treat a flipped verdict as a tie.

flashcards.q: Verbosity bias: magnitude and mitigation.
flashcards.a: 15-30 points of inflated preference for longer answers regardless of quality, across GPT-4/Claude/PaLM-2 judges (Wang et al., 2023). Mitigate with an explicit 'do not prefer length' rubric line plus length-bucketed analysis.

flashcards.q: Self-preference bias: magnitude and the correct structural fix.
flashcards.a: A judge scores its own model family's outputs 10-25% higher than equivalent-quality outputs from another family (arXiv:2410.21819). No rubric wording reliably surfaces it - the fix is structural: never use the same model family as both judge and candidate in a decision-driving comparison.

flashcards.q: Judge calibration workflow, in order.
flashcards.a: 1) Sample 100-300 real traces. 2) 2-3 humans label on the exact rubric. 3) Compute inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa for 2 raters, Krippendorff's alpha for 3+). 4) Judge scores the same traces. 5) Compute judge-vs-human kappa. Ship only if >=0.6; re-calibrate on any rubric or judge model change.

flashcards.q: Cohen's kappa vs Krippendorff's alpha - when do you use which?
flashcards.a: Cohen's kappa: exactly 2 raters, nominal/ordinal categories. Krippendorff's alpha: 3+ raters, ordinal/interval scales, tolerates missing observations. Both correct for chance agreement, unlike raw percent agreement.

flashcards.q: Kappa/alpha interpretation thresholds.
flashcards.a: <0.4: rubric ambiguous, fix the rubric first. 0.4-0.6: weak, tune it. >0.6: acceptable for production. >0.8: strong. A judge-vs-human kappa above human-human kappa is a red flag for collusion on a superficial correlate, not a win.

flashcards.q: When is a cheap judge sufficient vs when do you need a frontier model?
flashcards.a: Cheap judge (small/fine-tuned/mini model): near-checklist criteria a human could apply in under 10 seconds without re-reading source material - runs CI gates and 100% of production sampling. Frontier judge: criteria requiring real judgment (nuanced correctness, subtle harm) - runs calibration sets and adjudicates hard/ambiguous cases.

flashcards.q: What is G-Eval and why does it beat naive 'output a number' prompting?
flashcards.a: G-Eval (Liu et al., 2023) has the judge generate its own chain-of-thought evaluation steps from the criterion, fills them in as a form, then takes a probability-weighted score across top logprobs. Externalizing reasoning before scoring reduces anchoring on surface cues; probability-weighting smooths single-token sampling noise.

flashcards.q: The shared-blind-spot failure mode.
flashcards.a: If judge and generator share a training-data blind spot, the judge certifies a fabrication as correct because it matches the judge's own equally-wrong prior. Fix: ground the judge in something external to both models - a retrieved source or verified gold answer, not just the judge's own recall.

flashcards.q: Faithfulness vs factuality when judging RAG answers - why keep them separate?
flashcards.a: Faithfulness = matches the provided context; factuality = matches the world. A response can be faithful to a wrong retrieved chunk (factually wrong) or unfaithful to context but factually correct. Conflating them into one score hides whether retrieval or generation broke.

flashcards.q: Rubric design rules that reduce judge bias.
flashcards.a: Concrete anchor examples per score level, not adjectives. Explicitly exclude dimensions not being scored (length, formatting, judge's own style preference). One criterion per rubric call, not three conflated together. Ask for reasoning before the score.

flashcards.q: A judge-vs-human kappa comes back at 0.95 - is that automatically good news?
flashcards.a: No - audit it. Extremely high agreement can mean the judge and humans are both keying off a superficial correlate (length, style) rather than the true quality signal. Check agreement on an adversarial subset built to break that correlate before trusting the aggregate.

flashcards.q: How do you build a CI gate on an LLM judge that doesn't flake?
flashcards.a: Pin the judge model version explicitly (never 'latest'). Run pairwise comparisons in both orderings, treat a flip as a tie. Gate on the judge's calibrated agreement threshold, not an arbitrary score cutoff. Track judge-vs-human kappa itself as a monitored metric so drift shows before it silently degrades the gate.

flashcards.q: Frontier models on adversarial bias benchmarks - the headline 2026 finding.
flashcards.a: A 2026 study found frontier judge models exceeding 50% error rates on challenging bias-stress-test benchmarks despite strong aggregate correlation scores - meaning a judge can look reliable on average while failing hard on the exact dimension a specific eval is testing.

flashcards.q: Give the 8-phase time budget for a 45-minute system design round.
flashcards.a: 2 restate + scope contract; 5 requirements (FR + NFR table); 5 numbers; 5 API contract; 7 data model; 8 architecture; 6 scale; 5 failure; 2 wrap. Hard constraint: architecture on the board by minute 32.

flashcards.q: What is the NFR checklist mnemonic and what does each letter stand for?
flashcards.a: SCALD-CoM: Scale, Consistency, Availability, Latency, Durability, Cost, Multi-tenancy/compliance. Ask 5-6 of the 7, not all of them, and write the answers in a table you refer back to by name.

flashcards.q: What makes a clarifying question high-value versus low-value?
flashcards.a: A high-value question names two concrete alternatives and states that they lead to different designs (read:write 100:1 vs 2:1; chronological vs ranked; fanout distribution with or without 50M-follower accounts). Low-value questions have answers you cannot act on (how many users, should it be scalable).

flashcards.q: Why write the API contract before drawing the architecture?
flashcards.a: The API is falsifiable and commits you to payload size, read/write split, pagination model, and the sync/async boundary. Once POST /follows returns 202, the async queue in the diagram is justified by the contract instead of being an unexplained box.

flashcards.q: Name the five cheap points to bank in an API-contract phase.
flashcards.a: Versioned path (/v1/); Idempotency-Key header on writes with stored key-to-response and a TTL beyond the retry window; cursor pagination not offset (offset skips and duplicates on insert-heavy lists); 202 to encode async work; explicit error codes including 429.

flashcards.q: What is the one line that matters most in the data-model phase?
flashcards.a: The partition key, plus a statement for each table of which query it serves and whether that query is single-partition. A relationship table like follows needs indexing in BOTH directions (follower_id for reads, followee_id for fanout).

flashcards.q: What is the derivation chain that makes the architecture phase mechanical?
flashcards.a: requirements decide which numbers matter; numbers decide whether one machine suffices; API decides read/write split and payload size; data model decides the partition key; partition key decides which queries are cheap; architecture is then DERIVED and every box traces to a line above it.

flashcards.q: In the scale phase, what must you produce per component?
flashcards.a: The specific limit it hits first, the number, and the fix. Then RANK the bottlenecks (which breaks first at 10x and why it beats the runners-up), and attach a cost figure with the dominant line item named.

flashcards.q: What three things must a failure-mode statement include?
flashcards.a: What the user sees, what the operator sees (the observable symptom in a log, metric, or trace), and the recovery. Volunteering one named non-obvious failure mode with its symptom is the highest-value unprompted sentence in the round.

flashcards.q: What are the three wrap-up sentences at minute 43?
flashcards.a: What you would build first (smallest thing that serves the first million users), the biggest risk you are accepting (usually a guessed tuning parameter you would instrument), and what you would cut under cost pressure.

flashcards.q: How do you handle a blocked clarifying question the interviewer refuses to answer?
flashcards.a: State the assumption, state its consequence, and move: assume 100:1 read:write; if it is closer to 2:1 the precomputed timeline stops paying for itself and I flip to read-time merge. Converting a blocked question into a demonstrated tradeoff scores better than the answer would have.

flashcards.q: You discover at minute 30 that an assumption was wrong. What is the recovery protocol?
flashcards.a: Say it precisely (name the statistical error, not just the number), do NOT restart, identify the one or two decisions it feeds, walk the branch you already named, and state what you would measure to fix the assumption for real. Keep the old number visible and annotated.

flashcards.q: What changed about system design interviews in 2026?
flashcards.a: The passing bar rose; AI/LLM infrastructure prompts moved into general engineering loops (roughly half of loops now include an ML-adjacent question, up from ~1 in 10 in 2024); and interviewers now grade cost, so a design with no dollar figure reads as junior.

flashcards.q: Three extra NFR rows for an LLM-in-the-loop prompt.
flashcards.a: Token/cost budget (enforced in code as a per-user per-day cap, not a hope); non-determinism, meaning an eval/regression suite plus an online quality metric; and blast radius, meaning prompt-injection surface and the scope of actions an agent may take. Plus a deterministic fallback for when budget or model fails.

flashcards.q: How does the method change per company style?
flashcards.a: Meta: 45 min, breadth then interviewer-steered depth, so protect 15 minutes for the deep dive. Google: naming a component invites you to implement it, so name fewer. Amazon: expand failure and rollout phases. Stripe: API and data model scored hardest, so expand phase 3. AI-infra: add token/eval/blast-radius NFRs.

flashcards.q: Two candidates draw the same final diagram; one passes. What separates them?
flashcards.a: Traceability of derivation, which shows up under mutation. Change the read:write ratio or the follower distribution and the candidate who derived adjusts one decision, while the one who recalled has nothing to adjust and must defend or restart. Interviewers mutate prompts specifically to find this out.

flashcards.q: Name the four C4 levels and which one an interview wants.
