flashcards.a: L1 Context (your system plus users and external systems, 5-8 boxes, no internals); L2 Container (separately deployable/runnable things with technology and communication, 8-15 boxes) which IS the interview diagram; L3 Component (major modules inside one container, 5-8 boxes) for the deep dive only; L4 Code (classes) which is effectively dead, never draw it.

flashcards.q: What is a C4 container, precisely?
flashcards.a: Anything separately deployable and runnable: a service, a single-page app, a mobile app, a database, a queue, an object-store bucket, a Lambda. Not the same as a Docker container: a sidecar is not a separate C4 container, and a database schema on a shared cluster is one even though it is not containerised.

flashcards.q: Which of the four diagram types answers which question?
flashcards.a: C4 container: what exists, what technology, where state lives, sync vs async. Sequence: order, latency budget decomposition, failure/degradation in time. Dataflow: transformation, volume, throughput ceiling, replay-safety. Deployment: what it runs on, blast radius per failure domain, RPO/RTO, source of truth vs derived index. None can answer another's question, which is why one big diagram always fails.

flashcards.q: What is the very first mark you make on a blank whiteboard?
flashcards.a: Not a box. Divide the space: ~20% left for requirements, NFR table, and numbers (never erased), ~55% middle for the container diagram, ~25% right kept empty for deep dives. Then place two anchors, client far left and primary datastore far right, so the architecture grows between them and you cannot run out of room.

flashcards.q: State the drawing order that keeps the narrative coherent.
flashcards.a: Two anchors, then the happy-path READ end to end without adding anything else, then the WRITE path below it from the same entry point, then the ASYNC path below a visible horizontal line, then a second pass to annotate numbers, then deep dives in the reserved right column. Narrate every transition out loud.

flashcards.q: Give the edge-label grammar.
flashcards.a: protocol/format, sync or async, payload size, rate or latency. Two are mandatory (protocol and sync/async). Example: HTTPS/JSON, sync, 6 KB, 15k rps. Solid line = sync, dashed = async, never changing within a diagram. Arrow direction means INITIATES, not data flow, and you state which convention you use.

flashcards.q: Why does sync versus async on an edge matter so much?
flashcards.a: Sync edges sum into the latency budget: a 200 ms p99 target across five sync hops gives each ~40 ms before processing. Async edges contribute nothing to the budget but each incurs a durability obligation instead: at-least-once delivery, an idempotent consumer, and a lag metric to alert on. Drawing them identically means the diagram answers neither question.

flashcards.q: List the six steps of the scale-annotation pass.
flashcards.a: 1) Rate on hot edges only. 2) Size on stateful boxes. 3) Replica count as a multiplier with failure-domain spread (x12, 3 AZ) instead of drawing 12 boxes. 4) Bottleneck double-boxed with its binding constraint. 5) Partition key on every sharded store. 6) A 'not drawn' text line listing omissions. Do this as a second pass; annotating while drawing slows you to a crawl.

flashcards.q: What do you leave out of an interview diagram, and how do you avoid looking forgetful?
flashcards.a: Authn/authz boxes (say OIDC at the gateway once), observability, CI/CD, DNS/TLS, secrets and config, internal load balancers, service mesh sidecars, individual replicas, and every cache layer at once. Write a one-line 'not drawn:' list, which converts each omission into a scoping decision. Rule: only draw what you can defend in depth, because every box invites a follow-up.

flashcards.q: Why cap a container diagram at 12-15 boxes?
flashcards.a: Human working memory is about 7 plus or minus 2 chunks, so past ~10 boxes the interviewer spends questions on comprehension instead of design. Recover legibility by grouping into 3-5 labelled regions (edge, read path, write path, async, storage) and collapsing replicas into multipliers.

flashcards.q: What must a sequence diagram include beyond the calls?
flashcards.a: Latency on every arrow, summed, with the dominant hop named (a sequence diagram without timings is a call graph with extra steps); the async escape drawn explicitly as a dashed line; and if there is time, one failure variant showing the degraded path (timeout, breaker opens, keyword-only fallback with a degraded flag).

flashcards.q: Five things a dataflow/pipeline diagram must include.
flashcards.a: Volume on every edge so the narrow stage is visible; the narrow stage marked with its burst policy (queue, shed, or drop); the dead-letter path with its expected failure rate; the idempotency key, because pipelines get replayed and where dedup happens is the most important detail; and the freshness SLO with the stage that owns it (usually the crawler interval, not the pipeline).

flashcards.q: What makes a deployment diagram real rather than decorative?
flashcards.a: Replica counts, instance types, and the anti-affinity guarantee that a shard's replicas land in different AZs (8 pods across 3 AZs can still put both replicas of a shard in one AZ); explicit RPO and RTO numbers; and a statement of which store is the source of truth versus a rebuildable derived index. Also: provision 1.5x so N-1 AZ capacity still sits at the target utilisation.

flashcards.q: What is wrong with a diagram full of cloud vendor icons?
flashcards.a: Icons encode the product name and nothing else: no responsibility, protocol, sync/async, throughput, or partition key, while looking authoritative. They also bias the design toward whatever has an icon, so candidates draw an SQS icon instead of deriving that they need a queue. A labelled box with a bracketed technology plus a labelled edge carries strictly more information in the same space.

flashcards.q: Which diagram do you reach for, given what the interviewer says?
flashcards.a: 'Design X' → C4 container (default). 'Walk me through what happens when...' or 'where does the latency go' → sequence. 'How does data get in / reindexing / freshness' → dataflow. 'What if an AZ dies / multi-region' → deployment. 'Tell me more about component Y' → C4 component in fresh space. 'Show me the schema' → not a diagram, write CREATE TABLE. 'Implement the queue' → not a diagram, write code.

flashcards.q: Why is labelling a forcing function rather than decoration?
flashcards.a: You cannot write 'sync, p99 12 ms' on an edge without having decided that hop's consistency and latency properties, and you cannot write a partition key without having decided the access pattern. Candidates who label discover their own gaps at minute 25 instead of the interviewer discovering them at minute 40. The labelling is where the thinking happens.

flashcards.q: Diagrams-as-code: which tool for what?
flashcards.a: Mermaid is the repo default (rendered natively by GitHub/GitLab/Notion, strong sequence and flowchart support, weak C4). Structurizr DSL is right when C4 accuracy matters, because all levels derive from one model and cannot diverge. D2 has the best auto-layout for docs sites. PlantUML is the dated workhorse. Excalidraw/tldraw for canvas interviews. The real durable artefact is the ADR; the diagram indexes it.

flashcards.q: How do you keep an architecture diagram accurate over two years?
flashcards.a: Not by hand. Put it in the repo as Mermaid or Structurizr DSL so staleness surfaces in code review; generate the deployment view from Terraform or manifests so it derives from truth; and compare the declared container graph against the OpenTelemetry service graph to flag edges present in traffic but absent from the model. The last one is worth waiting for tooling on, because a homegrown version alerts on every health check and gets muted.

flashcards.q: State the estimation procedure in six steps.
flashcards.a: 1) Declare what the number will DECIDE. 2) State the assumption out loud and mark it. 3) Round every input to a power of ten. 4) Compute in one pass. 5) AMPLIFY by fanout if there is any. 6) Sanity-check against a system whose scale you know; if the check fails, the assumption is wrong, not the arithmetic.

flashcards.q: The single most useful conversion in estimation.
flashcards.a: 1 million per day is about 10 per second (and 1 billion/day is about 10,000/s). 86,400 s/day rounds to 1e5, a 14% conservative error. Powers: 2^10 KB, 2^20 MB, 2^30 GB, 2^40 TB, 2^50 PB.

flashcards.q: Give the 2026 latency ladder from L1 to cross-region.
flashcards.a: L1 ~1 ns; L2 ~4 ns; L3 ~12 ns; DDR5 RAM ~50-80 ns; compress 1 KB ~1-3 us; NVMe random 4 KB read ~20-100 us; SATA SSD ~100-200 us; same-DC round trip ~0.5 ms; cross-AZ ~1-2 ms; HDD seek ~5-10 ms; US east-west ~60-70 ms; US-Europe ~75-90 ms; US-APAC ~170-230 ms; LLM first token ~300-800 ms.

flashcards.q: State the three latency ratios worth memorising over absolute values.
flashcards.a: RAM is ~1000x faster than SSD. A same-datacenter round trip is ~1000x slower than RAM. A cross-continent round trip is 100-300x a same-datacenter one. Fibre gives ~5 us/km, so ~1 ms per 100 km one-way after routing, and no engineering changes that.

flashcards.q: Throughput numbers to know cold.
flashcards.a: NVMe Gen4 3-7 GB/s and 500k-1M random 4 KB IOPS; EBS gp3 baseline only 125 MB/s and 3,000 IOPS (about 40x slower than local NVMe); 100 GbE = 12.5 GB/s; Postgres 5-20k write TPS on one primary; Redis ~100k ops/s single-threaded (1M+ pipelined); typical JSON service ~2k rps per core; Cassandra/DynamoDB partition ~1-3k writes/s hard ceiling.

flashcards.q: Bytes per thing: the ones that come up.
flashcards.a: UUID 16 B binary but 36 B as text (2.25x waste); int64 8 B; narrow index row 40-60 B; typical entity row ~500 B; Postgres tuple overhead ~23-28 B; Redis per-key overhead 50-100 B; JSON is 2-4x protobuf; web image 100-500 KB; 1080p ~5 Mbps = 2.25 GB/hour; 1024-dim float32 embedding 4 KB (int8 1 KB, binary 128 B); 1 token ~4 chars.

flashcards.q: Peak-to-average multipliers by workload shape.
flashcards.a: Global consumer web/social 2-3x (timezone-smeared); single-region consumer 3-5x; B2B/enterprise 4-8x (ten business hours carry ~95% of load); cron/batch 10-100x; event-driven launches and ticket sales 10-1000x; notification campaigns 50-500x. Derivation: sustained peak ratio is roughly p/f where fraction f of the day carries fraction p of load, times another 2-3x for the instantaneous peak.

flashcards.q: Which peak sizes which component?
flashcards.a: Peak sustained (hour) sizes the fleet and the database. Peak burst (second) sizes the queue depth, connection pool, and rate limiter. Peak concurrent (Little's Law: throughput x latency) sizes memory, file descriptors, and WebSocket capacity. Using the wrong one gives a correctly-sized fleet behind an undersized connection pool.

flashcards.q: Why size a fleet at 50-60% utilisation?
flashcards.a: M/M/1 queueing: wait = service time x rho/(1-rho). At rho=0.5 the wait equals one service time; at 0.9 it is 9x; at 0.95 it is 19x. Latency goes non-linear above ~70%, so '20% headroom' means 'our p99 is about to triple'.

flashcards.q: State the amplification rule and why it matters more than API-level QPS.
flashcards.a: Amplified writes = logical writes/s x fanout. 500 posts/s x 500 followers = 250,000 timeline inserts/s. 1M notifications/s x 1.6 channels = 1.6M sends/s. 100B messages/day x average group size 5 = 500B deliveries/day. The API-level rate is almost never what breaks; candidates who only compute it conclude the system is easy.

flashcards.q: Give the storage formula and the multipliers people forget.
flashcards.a: records x bytes x retention x replication x (1 + index overhead), then a separate line for WAL and backups. 1M records/day x 1 KB over 5 years is 1.8 TB logical, ~5.5 TB at 3x replication, ~7 TB with 30% index, and 10-14 TB provisioned once WAL and backups are counted.

flashcards.q: Nines to downtime, and the composition rule.
flashcards.a: 99% = 3.65 d/yr; 99.9% = 8.8 h/yr (43 min/month); 99.99% = 53 min/yr (4.3 min/month, so no human in the recovery path); 99.999% = 5.3 min/yr. Serial dependencies MULTIPLY: five components at 99.9% in series gives 0.999^5 = 99.5%, or 43 hours a year. Correlated failure makes the real number worse than the arithmetic.

flashcards.q: The Redis cache-sizing trap.
flashcards.a: Payload bytes are not memory. Redis adds ~50-100 B overhead per key, and a sorted set past zset-max-listpack-entries (default 128) converts from a compact listpack to a skiplist plus hash, costing ~80-120 B per member instead of 40. A naive payload calculation is typically 3x low. Verify with MEMORY USAGE and OBJECT ENCODING, not arithmetic.

flashcards.q: LLM cost arithmetic: 1M conversations/day, 6 turns, 4k input + 300 output tokens per turn at $2/$10 per M.
flashcards.a: Input 1e6 x 6 x 4e3 = 2.4e10 = 24,000 M tokens/day x $2 = $48k/day. Output 1.8e9 = 1,800 M x $10 = $18k/day. Total ~$66k/day, ~$2M/month, unviable. Levers: prompt caching at ~10% of input price (~3.6x if 80% cacheable), rerank to top-3 not top-10 (~2.7x), route 70% to a Flash-class model at ~20x cheaper (~2.5x), Batch API -50%. Composed ~24x to ~$80k/month.

flashcards.q: Vector index sizing: 100M chunks at 1024 dimensions.
flashcards.a: float32 vectors = 1e8 x 1024 x 4 B = 410 GB; HNSW M=32 adds ~300 B/node = 30 GB, so ~440 GB and it must be RAM-resident. int8 quantisation is 4x (~132 GB, one 256 GB node) for 1-2 recall points, recoverable by over-fetching top-50 and reranking. Binary is 32x (~13 GB) with a float32 NVMe rerank. Cost falls ~$5,000 to ~$700/month, so quantisation is a 7x lever. Building the index (~$800 one-time in embeddings) is 40x cheaper than serving it.

flashcards.q: What is the recovery script when you realise an assumption was wrong mid-answer?
flashcards.a: Say it immediately and precisely (name the statistical error, not just the number); do not restart; identify the one or two decisions the number fed; walk the branch you already pre-named; state what you would measure to fix the assumption for real; keep the wrong number visible and annotated. Better: pre-empt by stating every assumption WITH its sensitivity.

flashcards.q: What should you refuse to estimate?
flashcards.a: p99.9 and anything driven by variance rather than volume: queueing under bursty arrival, GC pauses, lock contention, noisy neighbours, retry amplification. Also anything within 2-3x of a hard cliff (memory limit, provider rate limit, SLO boundary). Instead, design for tail-insensitivity: timeout inside the budget, bulkhead, queue, load-shedding rule.

flashcards.q: The most dangerous number in any estimate.
flashcards.a: The average of a heavy-tailed quantity: average followers, file size, tenant size, request cost, prompt length. Power-law means the mean is smaller than the values that determine capacity, so the estimate understates the peak in exactly the case where the peak breaks you. Ask for a percentile and say the mean will mislead.

flashcards.q: What three properties make GenAI system design different, and what stays the same?
flashcards.a: Different: the core component is PROBABILISTIC (correctness is a measured distribution, so eval is a component not a phase), EXPENSIVE per request ($0.01-0.30 vs $0.0001, so the cost model is part of the architecture), and SLOW (1-10 s vs 50 ms, so streaming, caching and step reduction are architecture). Unchanged: capacity planning, queues and backpressure, idempotency, sharding and hot partitions, multi-tenancy and noisy neighbours, versioned schemas and migrations, SLOs. Candidates who treat GenAI as a new discipline forget backpressure, which is how the vector index falls over.

flashcards.q: State the six-slot template and the 45-minute time allocation.
flashcards.a: 1) CLARIFY (6 min): what the number means, read:write, latency contract, who is the tenant, what 'correct' means, blast radius. 2) ARCHITECT (10 min): write path and read path drawn separately. 3) DECIDE (12 min): 3-5 forks each stated as 'X over Y because Z, at the cost of W'. 4) SIZE (6 min): QPS, bytes, tokens, cost/request, cost/month. 5) BREAK (6 min): failure to OBSERVABLE SYMPTOM to mitigation. 6) DEFEND (5 min): the three hardest follow-ups answered before they are asked. The GenAI-specific move: produce cost per request unprompted.

flashcards.q: Name the seven patterns that recur across every GenAI design.
flashcards.a: 1) Write path and read path are asymmetric; draw them separately. 2) Two-stage retrieval is universal: cheap recall over many, expensive precision over few (binary then full precision, vector then reranker, graph then vector, cheap model then strong). 3) The enforcement boundary must be unbypassable (gateway plus network policy, permission engine, index predicates). 4) Version everything behaviour-changing and put it on the trace. 5) Cost per request out loud, then per month, then lever ordering. 6) Every failure mode needs an observable symptom. 7) Distinguish a FILTER (classifier, label, prompt) from a BOUNDARY (permissions, network policy, sandbox).

flashcards.q: '10 million documents' for RAG. What do you convert it to, and what does that change?
flashcards.a: At ~6 pages and ~10 chunks of 400 tokens per document: ~100M chunks and ~40B tokens. That changes the architecture, not just the size. 1024-dim fp16 is 2 KB/vector so 100M vectors is 200 GB before graph overhead, which does not fit reasonable RAM; binary quantization at 1 bit/dim is 128 bytes so ~12.8 GB does, so you retrieve 1,000 candidates on binary, rescore with full-precision vectors from disk, then cross-encoder rerank 150 to 8. A 10M-vector system and a 500M-vector system are different architectures, not the same one scaled.

flashcards.q: Why must ACLs be pushed into the vector index rather than applied after retrieval?
flashcards.a: Post-filtering top-k means a user with narrow permissions gets an empty result set from a system that found 10 perfectly relevant documents they cannot see. Observable symptom: users with narrow scopes see 'no results' at 5-10x the average rate, with results_before_filter=10 and results_after_filter=0 in traces. Cost of doing it right: filtered ANN is slower and filter cardinality distribution now affects your p99.

flashcards.q: Where is the pgvector-versus-dedicated-vector-engine boundary, and what else is a premature-scale trap?
flashcards.a: Roughly 5-10 million vectors: below that pgvector on the Postgres you already operate is the right answer and a new stateful system is pure operational cost. Other premature-scale traps: a multi-tenant LLM gateway below roughly $10-20k/month of spend or a handful of consumers; an agent orchestration platform below 5-10 agents (platforms are amortisation plays); a semantic cache on low-repetition traffic; a router before you have attributed your bill; RAG at all when the corpus fits in a cached prefix (~50-100k tokens of stable content).

flashcards.q: Design a multi-tenant LLM gateway in five sentences.
flashcards.a: It exists to be an enforcement boundary the application cannot bypass: virtual keys carrying tenant/team/env/scopes, per-tenant RPM/TPM and dollar budgets checked BEFORE the provider call, routing with a failover chain and circuit breaker, caching, and a cost ledger. Two-tier rate limiting: a local token bucket against a leased share of a global budget refreshed every ~200 ms, so Redis is not on every request and overshoot is bounded and stateable. Pre-call estimate, post-call reconcile, because only the response carries true output tokens; nightly reconciliation against provider usage with a 3% drift alarm. No worker holds a provider credential, enforced by NetworkPolicy. Budget: p99 added latency under 15 ms, and the gateway costs ~1% of the spend it governs.

flashcards.q: Agent orchestration platform: what does the platform own and what do teams own?
flashcards.a: Platform owns the BOUNDARIES: budgets, permissions, network egress, traces and the trajectory store, the eval gate, durable execution, the sandbox tier. Teams own BEHAVIOUR: prompts, tools, topology. Structure: a control plane (versioned agent manifests, policy, prompt registry, approval service, eval service, quotas) separate from a data plane (queue, CPU runner pool with checkpointer, sandbox pool, gateway). You cannot register an agent without an eval suite. This split is the answer to 'who is on call', which is the question behind the question.

flashcards.q: Agent A calls agent B across team boundaries. What are the two things that break?
flashcards.a: Identity propagation and budget accounting. Permissions: the ORIGINATING principal's permissions intersected with the callee's scopes, never unioned, or you get privilege escalation by composition (a confused deputy, which is the enterprise MCP identity-propagation gap in a different costume). Budget: hierarchical, where the child's spend counts against the parent's ceiling, or a nested call is an unbounded budget hole.

flashcards.q: Design an agent memory service. What is the dominant cost and the dominant risk?
flashcards.a: Typed facts (entity, preference, decision, task) never free-text notes, extracted asynchronously at session end, stored bi-temporally with provenance and confidence, partitioned by user, retrieved synchronously in a 60 ms budget under a hard 1.5k-token injection cap. Dominant COST is extraction, not storage: 40M sessions/month at ~$0.0007 is ~$28k/month, mitigated by gating on session length and using a small model. Dominant RISK is that a wrong persisted fact reproduces across sessions forever and is invisible in single-session tests, so ship without cross-session memory first and add it against a measured re-derivation rate.

flashcards.q: Design an eval platform: architecture and the number that justifies trajectory scoring.
flashcards.a: One versioned dataset store shared by the CI gate and production monitoring, a seeded parallel runner that replays fixtures, and three scorer tiers: deterministic first (schema, citations, tool order, cost), trajectory scoring as a first-class type, pinned LLM-as-judge with a ~40-case human calibration set last. Tiered suites to keep the gate under ~15 minutes, result caching keyed on (dataset_ver, prompt_hash, model, seed, code_sha) for a 60-70% hit rate, and continuous live sampling into the golden set. The justifying number: agents evaluated only on final output pass 20-40% MORE cases than trajectory-level evaluation reveals.

flashcards.q: Design prompt management, and state the canary detection floor.
flashcards.a: Git as source of truth, registry as distribution. Immutable content-addressed versions (prompt@1.14.0 = sha256 of the template), deployment pointers separate from versions so rollback is a pointer flip in seconds, local caching that fails closed to last known good, the same eval gate for UI-authored and git-authored changes, and the RENDERED prefix hash on every trace (not just the template hash). Detection floor arithmetic: detecting a 3 percentage-point judge-score delta needs n ~ 400 scored sessions, so a 5% canary on 8,000 sessions/day gives a ONE-DAY floor regardless of tooling. Faster means a bigger canary and more exposure.

flashcards.q: Semantic cache: what is in the key, what is the honest hit rate, and how do you set the threshold?
flashcards.a: Key = (normalized_query, tenant, corpus_version, model, prompt_hash). Keying on the query alone serves tenant A's answer to tenant B, which is the worst bug in this design and easy to ship. Honest hit rates: 20-45% for most workloads, 30-70% on FAQ-shaped traffic; 90%+ claims come from datasets built with heavy repetition. Threshold is embedding-model specific (~0.83 MPNet, ~0.78 Albert); GPTCache's suggested 0.7 is too loose, so start near 0.92, monitor false positives for 48 hours, and tune down in 0.01 steps. Do exact and prefix caching FIRST because they are correctness-preserving.

flashcards.q: Guardrail service: three design rules and the metric that actually matters.
flashcards.a: 1) Parallel detectors, not a chain, because latency is additive in a chain and the checks are independent. 2) Run the input rail CONCURRENTLY with retrieval, which makes it nearly free on the wall clock. 3) Deterministic checks (secret regexes, citation resolution, schema) before classifiers. The metric that matters is the FALSE POSITIVE rate, not compute: at 900 rps a 1% false-block rate is 780k blocked legitimate requests per day, an outage that looks like a safety feature. Target under 0.2%, ship every policy change in shadow mode, and provide an appeal path. Compute is trivial (~$850/month at 900 rps, ~0.15% of LLM cost).

flashcards.q: Document pipeline at 4M pages/day: what is the first decision and what does it save?
flashcards.a: Adaptive per-page routing, on text-layer density, scan quality and table presence. Fast text-layer path ~$0.0002/page, OCR ~$0.0015, VLM ~$0.006. At a 60/30/10 mix that is ~$4.7k/day versus $24k/day for a uniform VLM pass, a 5x saving, which is why the router is the first decision and not an optimisation. Then layout-aware chunking with tables atomic up to a 1,200-token cap and header propagation, confidence-gated human review whose corrections become routing labels, and stored originals plus versioned intermediate representation so a parser upgrade is a replay rather than a re-crawl.

flashcards.q: Support agent: the escalation design, and why deflection alone is a vanity metric.
flashcards.a: Escalate on EXPLICIT triggers, not when the model gives up: low retrieval confidence, three turns without progress, detected frustration, a hard category (legal, safety, cancellation, VIP), or any action outside the allow-list. Then a STRUCTURED handoff (summary, attempted steps, sentiment, the specific blocker, full transcript), because context loss makes an escalated ticket worse than a cold one. Deflection alone is vanity: 2026 median is 41.2% with a top quartile of 58.7%, but resets deflect >70% and nuanced complaints rarely break 25%, so the headline moves with intent MIX. Pair it with re-contact rate, CSAT delta, and hallucinated-policy rate, because deflection rises when the agent stops escalating what it should.

flashcards.q: Code assistant on a 40M-LOC monorepo: three latency tiers and the reliability story.
flashcards.a: Three request classes with three context strategies. Inline completion p95 200 ms: local buffer context only, NO index round trip, small model. Chat p95 2 s: graph-plus-vector retrieval. Agentic multi-file edit over minutes: iterative tools. Index by tree-sitter symbol graph (defs, refs, callers, tests-for-symbol) plus syntax-chunked vectors, incremental on commit with freshness as an SLO. 40M LOC is only ~1.2M chunks (~0.9 GB), so the graph is the expensive part; reported payoff is ~10x fewer tokens and ~2.1x fewer tool calls across 31 repos. The reliability story is entirely the VERIFIER: run the test suite in the sandbox and gate acceptance on exit code, and for a bug fix require a test that fails before and passes after.

flashcards.q: Cut a $720k/month LLM bill by 70%. Order the levers and give the arithmetic.
flashcards.a: Attribute the bill first (feature, model, tenant) or you are guessing. Then four levers multiplicatively, safest first: 1) prompt caching on a frozen prefix, ~22% off, correctness-preserving, to $562k. 2) rules plus a classifier router sending ~58% to a model at ~1/12 price, to $263k. 3) a cascade on structured-output paths where failure is cheaply detectable, to ~$243k. 4) a semantic cache at ~25% hit, to ~$182k. That is ~75% and it requires all four; any single lever is 20-40%. Anchors: RouteLLM 95% of GPT-4 quality at 26% strong-model calls, ~48% cheaper than random, up to 75% with judge-augmented data; production reports 40-85%, so plan for 40-50%.

flashcards.q: Why must router savings be measured per completed task rather than per token?
flashcards.a: Because a weaker model that malforms tool calls and loops three extra times costs MORE than the frontier model and is slower, so a per-token saving can be a per-task loss. Observable symptom: tool-call malformation rate 8x higher on the cheap route while the token bill looks better. Consequence: route on capability, not only on difficulty; pin tool-heavy paths to a model with a measured low malformation rate; and expect some routes to move UP.

flashcards.q: When does self-hosting a model actually save money?
flashcards.a: It is a utilisation bet, not a price bet. An 8B model on 2xA10G at roughly $1.5k/month serving ~600 tok/s sustained is ~1.5B tok/month at full utilisation, or ~$0.001/1k tok; a commercial small model at $0.25/M input is ~$0.00025/1k. So self-hosting beats a commercial small model only above roughly 40-50% SUSTAINED utilisation, and loses badly below it. Below the breakeven you are paying for idle GPUs and calling it savings. Compute the breakeven; do not assert.

flashcards.q: Give the cross-design failure modes worth memorising, with their observable symptoms.
flashcards.a: Aggregate metrics flat while specific users are furious: you are averaging over intents/tenants, so slice every quality metric and alert on slices. Cost 3x the estimate: the estimate was per model call and production is per session with multi-turn context re-send. cached_input_tokens near zero: a timestamp or non-deterministic ordering mutates the stable prefix. Regression untraceable for a week: multiple versioned things changed together and none are on the trace. Gate green but production worse: golden-set drift or a provider moving a floating alias. Retrieval returns nothing for some users: ACLs applied after retrieval. The system is up and the answers are wrong: you have SLOs on availability and latency and none on quality.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between a filter and a boundary, and why does the distinction fail candidates?
flashcards.a: Filters reduce probability and have false-negative rates: injection classifiers, authority labels, system-prompt instructions, content moderation. Boundaries bound damage regardless of what the model believes: the permission engine (a pure function that never consults the model), network egress policy, the sandbox, index-level ACL predicates. Conflating them is the fastest way to fail a GenAI design round, because a design whose security argument rests on a classifier has no security argument. CaMeL-style provenance interpreters and dual-LLM quarantine are the only patterns with a real security argument and no mainstream harness ships them as of mid-2026.

flashcards.q: Name the twelve designs and each one's single most important decision.
flashcards.a: 1 RAG 10M docs: quantized first stage plus full-precision rescore, ACLs into the index. 2 Multi-tenant gateway: in-path proxy plus network egress denial. 3 Agent orchestration: control/data plane split with eval-gated registration. 4 Agent memory: typed bi-temporal facts written asynchronously. 5 Eval platform: one dataset store for CI and prod, deterministic scorers before judges. 6 Prompt management: immutable content-addressed versions with pointer-flip rollback. 7 Semantic cache: the key is (query, tenant, corpus_ver, model, prompt_hash). 8 Guardrail service: parallel detectors with the input rail concurrent with retrieval. 9 Document pipeline: adaptive per-page routing (5x saving). 10 Support agent: explicit escalation triggers with a structured handoff. 11 Code assistant: code graph plus vector, tests as the verifier. 12 Cost router: tiered L0-L4, measured per completed task.

flashcards.q: You have never seen the system being asked about. What do you do?
flashcards.a: Run the six slots anyway, and lean on the transferable structure: separate write path from read path; assume two-stage retrieval (cheap recall then expensive precision); find the enforcement boundary and put it somewhere the caller cannot bypass; version everything behaviour-changing and trace it; compute cost per request from the dominant token or compute term; give each failure mode an observable symptom. Worked example (multimodal video search): write path decodes, samples keyframes, embeds frames, transcribes audio, aligns on timecode; read path does ANN over frame and transcript embeddings then a VLM rerank on top candidates returning timecoded segments; cost is frames-per-hour times embedding on write and VLM rerank on read; failure is sampling missing a short event, with recall collapsing on brief-action queries.

flashcards.q: What are the nine sections of the design-doc template, in order?
flashcards.a: Context and constraints; requirements (functional / non-functional / NON-GOALS); architecture with diagram plus decomposition criterion; key decisions (chose X over Y because Z, accepted cost C); data model; scale numbers; failure modes (symptom first); what I would change now; the hardest questions with answers.

flashcards.q: Why must a failure-mode table be organised by symptom rather than by cause?
flashcards.a: In an incident you have the symptom, not the cause. A cause-ordered table is a design artifact; a symptom-ordered one is operational. Interviewers who have been on call notice the difference immediately.

flashcards.q: Why is the non-goals section the strongest seniority signal in a design doc?
flashcards.a: It shows you knew where the boundary was and put it somewhere deliberately. A doc with no non-goals reads as written after the fact. It is also the section nobody rehearses.

flashcards.q: Why index vectors in ClickHouse HNSW rather than a dedicated vector store at 1.2M rows?
flashcards.a: Three reasons in order: every query is FILTERED by tenant and locale, so colocation makes the filter a native predicate with granule pruning rather than a metadata filter bolted onto an ANN index; 1.2M x 512 x 4 bytes is about 2.5 GB, which fits in memory on one node; and one fewer system to keep consistent, backfill and page on. Migration trigger: ~10x rows, a second consumer, or a hard hybrid BM25-plus-vector requirement.

flashcards.q: Why does a bi-encoder need a cross-encoder reranker behind it for skill resolution?
flashcards.a: A bi-encoder embeds query and candidate independently, so it cannot condition one on the other, and near-synonyms like 'data analysis' and 'data analytics' sit within noise of each other. A cross-encoder reads both strings in one forward pass with attention across them. The cost: nothing can be precomputed, so it runs per candidate at query time behind a truncating recall stage.

flashcards.q: What is the load-bearing table-definition detail for filtered vector search in ClickHouse?
flashcards.a: tenant_id and locale must be a PREFIX of the ordering key, so the filter prunes granules before the ANN search. If they are not, you either scan the whole index or degrade to post-filtering, which over-fetches by the inverse of the selectivity. This is the most common way filtered vector search gets slow and it is a table-definition problem, not an ANN problem.

flashcards.q: Why does the skill resolution engine need an explicit UNRESOLVED outcome?
flashcards.a: A wrong resolution enters the skills graph and silently biases every downstream recommendation, unattributable later. An unresolved item is a counter you can watch, a queue you can work, and a metric you can target. The unresolved rate becomes the system's most useful operational number.

flashcards.q: State the decomposition criterion for the 8-service platform and the cost it bought.
flashcards.a: Boundaries on independent SCALING and independent FAILURE, not data entities: latency-bound serving, throughput-bound event ingestion, batch profile processing. Cost: eight deploy pipelines, eight dashboard sets, distributed tracing to answer one user question, and network calls where a function call would do. At least two would be merged today.

flashcards.q: Back-of-envelope: derive peak rps for the recommendation platform at 2M+ users.
flashcards.a: 2M users, ~10% DAU = 200K. 5 recommendation-bearing views each = 1M requests/day. 1M / 86,400 = ~12 rps average. Peak factor 5-10x = 60-120 rps. Each request hydrates 100+ content IDs, so uncached that is 6,000-12,000 downstream calls/sec, which is why the Redis layer was not optional.

flashcards.q: Why distributed Redis rather than in-process caching for content hydration?
flashcards.a: With N replicas an in-process cache gives N times the misses and N times the external load, and it evaporates on every deploy exactly when you are already restarting things. Keyed per content ID so hydrating 100+ IDs is a multi-get with a small miss set.

flashcards.q: How do you handle a thundering herd when a hot cache key expires?
flashcards.a: Three measures in order: jittered TTLs so keys do not expire in lockstep; single-flight or a short-lived per-key lock so one fetch populates for all waiters; stale-while-revalidate so waiters get the old value while one request refreshes. Jitter alone is a partial answer, because the herd is a concurrency problem, not just a scheduling one.

flashcards.q: Precisely distinguish MCP from A2A.
flashcards.a: MCP (via FastMCP) is a TOOL-SURFACE CONTRACT: it describes what a capability accepts and returns, making it versionable and reusable by a consumer that does not import your code. A2A is INTER-AGENT MESSAGING: an agent boundary becomes a network boundary with its own retry, timeout and failure semantics. Using one does not imply the other.

flashcards.q: What is the test for whether a multi-agent split is justified?
flashcards.a: Separate agents only when failure modes, scaling profiles, or deploy cadences genuinely differ. Otherwise it is one agent with extra latency and an ambiguous failure mode. A single agent with N tools has an N-way blast radius: a chunking change degrades gap detection with no independent rollback.

flashcards.q: Give the agent reliability arithmetic and what it implies.
flashcards.a: Multiplicative: 0.95^3 = ~86%, 0.95^10 = ~60%, 0.85^10 = ~20%. It implies CHECKPOINTING rather than retry tuning, because retry improves per-step reliability by a bounded amount while checkpointing removes the multiplication entirely by making the failed step the only work redone.

flashcards.q: What actually limits concurrency in a vLLM deployment, and how do you derive it?
flashcards.a: KV cache, not FLOPs. An 8B model at fp16 is ~16 GB of weights; on a 24 GB GPU that leaves ~6-7 GB for cache after overhead. KV per token is roughly 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x 2 bytes, on the order of 100-200 KB/token for an 8B-class model, so ~30,000-60,000 tokens of aggregate context, or roughly 15-30 concurrent sequences at 2,000 tokens each. Size for KV cache, not weights.

flashcards.q: What do continuous batching and PagedAttention each do?
flashcards.a: Continuous batching admits new sequences into an in-flight batch as others finish, instead of forming a batch, running it to completion and forming the next, which leaves the GPU idle on every straggler. PagedAttention allocates KV cache in fixed-size blocks like OS paging, so memory is consumed as sequences grow rather than reserved for the worst case per sequence.

flashcards.q: Why separate queue_time from latency in inference observability?
flashcards.a: Under continuous batching a latency regression is usually queueing rather than slower generation, and the two have completely different fixes: queueing is capacity, generation is model or configuration. A single latency number cannot distinguish 'the GPU got slower' from 'more requests than slots'. Without the split you misdiagnose every capacity problem as a performance problem.

flashcards.q: GPU utilisation is 40% and inference is still slow. What is happening?
flashcards.a: KV cache exhaustion, not spare compute. The GPU is not busy because it cannot admit more sequences; requests are waiting for cache blocks. Fixes: reduce max sequence length, reduce max concurrent sequences so admitted requests progress, or move to more GPU memory. Reading 40% as spare capacity and adding traffic is the common wrong move.

flashcards.q: Why bound concurrency rather than retry for LLM calls from distributed executors, and what is the trap?
flashcards.a: A rate limit is a throughput ceiling, so exceeding it and retrying is amplification. The trap: a PER-EXECUTOR budget multiplies by executor count. Twenty executors each holding ten in flight is two hundred in flight against a limit set for one process. A global budget needs a shared counter, i.e. a distributed rate limiter.

flashcards.q: Why does an NL-to-SQL system always show the generated SQL?
flashcards.a: Because a system that silently returns a wrong number is worse than no system: the number ends up in a deck and gets acted on. Showing the SQL makes a wrong answer inspectable and attributable. The cost is some loss of confidence, which is the correct trade, since trust should track correctness rather than exceed it.

flashcards.q: Why RAG over schema plus prior queries rather than the whole schema in the prompt?
flashcards.a: The schema does not fit, and irrelevant tables actively degrade generation: given fifty tables when three matter, the model finds a plausible join through the wrong ones. Prior SUCCESSFUL queries are the most valuable corpus element because they encode join paths and filter conventions that no schema contains. When retrieval misses the right table, generation cannot recover, and the failure looks like a model error while being a retrieval error.

flashcards.q: What is the box budget for an interview architecture diagram, and what goes in the middle?
flashcards.a: At most nine boxes, drawn left-to-right as data flow, narrated in 90 seconds. Put the likely drill-down target (the retrieval path, the event path) in the middle where there is room to expand it. Never mix deployment topology with data flow on the same picture.

flashcards.q: What is the Bar Raiser and what does that mean for your prep?
flashcards.a: A trained interviewer pulled from a different team than the hiring one, with VETO power over the decision, whose job is keeping the bar consistent by probing past the rehearsed layer of your answer. It means depth per story matters more than story count, and every number you cite gets drilled.

flashcards.q: How is an Amazon loop structured, and how many LP questions should you expect?
flashcards.a: Four to five back-to-back interviews, each interviewer assigned two to three specific Leadership Principles so the panel collectively covers all 16, meaning roughly 12-15 LP questions in a day. Every round also has a technical component. At Principal level, reported at seven to eight rounds.

flashcards.q: Which four LPs cluster heaviest in engineering loops in practice?
flashcards.a: Dive Deep, Deliver Results, Invent and Simplify, Bias for Action. Prepare two stories each for these four rather than one story each for all sixteen.

flashcards.q: What does Amazon's own Principal Engineering tenets material say about Deliver Results, and what does it expect instead?
flashcards.a: Deliver Results is described as a LOW BAR for a Principal Engineer. Expected instead: lasting impact that echoes through the technology, product and company; bringing clarity to complexity and framing problems in customer and business context; staying hands-on and leading by example; educating the organisation about trends and approaches.

flashcards.q: Which two Amazon LPs are gaps in this resume, and what must be done?
flashcards.a: Hire and Develop the Best, and Strive to be Earth's Best Employer. Both are people-facing and neither appears on the resume. At Principal level the first will almost certainly be asked. Write one real story each: onboarding someone, raising the review bar, a runbook that stopped a recurring page, changing the on-call rotation, or running interviews.

flashcards.q: What is Google's decisive hiring mechanism, and its single most actionable consequence?
flashcards.a: A hiring committee of senior Googlers who never interviewed you and do not know the hiring team, scoring the written evidence packet. Consequence: anything that does not survive transcription does not count. '54,486 skills across 22 locales resolved through a tiered cascade' survives; 'large-scale multilingual skill system' does not.

flashcards.q: Name Google's four scored attributes and what GCA actually measures.
flashcards.a: Role-Related Knowledge, General Cognitive Ability, Leadership, Googleyness. GCA measures whether your reasoning is structured and adaptive, not whether you reached the right answer, which is why announcing your reasoning structure out loud is itself evidence.

flashcards.q: What does Googleyness explicitly include, and how must it be demonstrated?
flashcards.a: Intellectual humility, comfort with ambiguity, bias to action, collaboration. It must be shown through described BEHAVIOUR, not stated values: noticing that a disagreement was blocking progress and scheduling one-on-ones counts; 'I value collaboration' does not.

flashcards.q: What is the Meta E6 onsite structure in 2026, and what is new?
flashcards.a: One standard coding round, one AI-ASSISTED coding round, one architecture round, one design round, one behavioural round, plus a Leadership Assessment interview before the onsite that replaces the phone screen at this level and is roughly half behavioural and half coding. The AI-assisted round is the notable change; the stated intent is judging whether you can direct work including machine-generated work.

flashcards.q: What does Meta's behavioural round score, and what is the E6 scope bar?
flashcards.a: The 'Jedi' round scores ownership, collaboration, conflict, execution under ambiguity, and learning from mistakes. E6 bar: a disagreement story must involve TWO OR MORE TEAMS on the direction of a large project, and an impact story must have large impact on the ORG, not the team. Single-team stories read as E5.

flashcards.q: What is Microsoft's 'As Appropriate' round and how do you read it?
flashcards.a: The final round, usually run by a Principal Engineering Manager or Partner-level leader, tailored to how you performed earlier; interviewers sync notes first. Relaxed and mostly pitching the team means sell mode and the earlier rounds went well. Aggressively testing technical gaps means you are borderline. Actionable: track your own weakest answer between rounds and prepare the second pass.

flashcards.q: Why is Microsoft the best rubric fit for this resume?
flashcards.a: Microsoft's world is enterprise realities: multi-tenancy, compliance, global readiness, security, backward compatibility, migration of installed customers. That maps directly onto the 22-locale hardening, the cross-tenant authorization fix, the multi-tenant provisioning ingestion, and the Java-to-Python migration with its cutover strategy. Growth mindset is also a real rubric item, so a calibrated answer is safer than a bold one.

flashcards.q: What is distinctive about a Netflix loop, and what must you practise?
flashcards.a: Conversational, domain-specific, frequently NO shared whiteboard (multiple candidates report completing system design with no diagramming tool), roughly seven interviews, keeper-test framing with the written culture memo as the actual rubric. Practise verbal architecture: number the components, state direction explicitly, name them once and reuse the names.

flashcards.q: How does Netflix's rubric change how you tell a self-critical story?
flashcards.a: Candour is scored positively, including toward the interviewer, so 'eight services was too many and here's what I'd do instead' lands better at Netflix than anywhere else. Expect fewer prompts: silence is the absence of scaffolding, not disapproval. Agreeing with everything reads as low talent density.

flashcards.q: What is the decisive round at OpenAI, and what is the screen format?
flashcards.a: A PAID 48-hour work trial graded on shipping speed, code quality, design choices and how you write tests. The technical screen uses a progressive GATE format where one problem gets harder across roughly four stages and most candidates report needing to clear at least two. Process varies by team, and the AI-tool policy varies by team too (research generally AI-prohibited).

flashcards.q: What is the Anthropic engineering loop and what is the distinctive coding format?
flashcards.a: Five stages over roughly four to six weeks for engineering: recruiter screen, 60-minute technical phone screen with one medium-hard problem, take-home, onsite. The coding round is writing code fast to a spec then REFACTORING quickly as constraints are added per stage, in a four-level assessment. The bar for written reasoning is high; culture fit means taking safety seriously without being a doomer.

flashcards.q: Which stories lead at an AI lab, and which metrics must you swap out?
flashcards.a: Lead with vLLM serving (continuous batching, PagedAttention, KV-cache sizing, instance benchmarking), A2A plus FastMCP with the multi-agent test stated, async LLM rate limiting under distributed concurrency, and the golden baseline for a non-deterministic system. Swap product metrics (~25% engagement) for systems metrics: throughput, cost per million tokens, p99, index size, KV-cache-bound concurrency.

flashcards.q: What are the three weaknesses of this profile at an AI lab?
flashcards.a: 1) The evaluation story is thinner than the systems story: RAGAS and DeepEval are listed but not shown producing a decision. 2) No dollar cost model or break-even for the self-hosting decision, and they will ask. 3) No public artifact: a write-up of the OOM fix or the KV-cache sizing work, or a published MCP server, would materially help and costs a weekend.

flashcards.q: What is the single axis that explains most variation between these six companies?
flashcards.a: Where the hiring decision is made and what protects it from being wrong. Amazon: panel with an outside Bar Raiser holding veto. Google: a committee who never met you reading a written packet. Meta: a calibrated panel where speed is itself signal. Microsoft: hiring manager plus an AA round targeting your gaps. Netflix: manager under keeper-test norms with the culture memo as rubric. AI labs: a graded work trial.

flashcards.q: What is the core reframing principle across companies?
flashcards.a: The same story needs four or five different FRAMINGS, not four or five different stories. Amazon leads with the customer; Google leads with quotable specifics; Meta compresses and ends on self-critique; Microsoft leads into domain depth; Netflix opens with candour; AI labs lead with ship velocity and cost.

flashcards.q: What should you always ask the recruiter, and why?
flashcards.a: What the rounds actually are. Published loop structures vary by team, level, region and recruiter, so the reported process is frequently wrong for your specific loop. Recruiters usually tell you, and asking is a positive signal rather than a neutral one.

flashcards.q: Give the minute-by-minute allocation for a 45-minute design round.
flashcards.a: 0-2 restate and declare the plan; 2-5 requirements; 5-8 estimation; 8-22 high-level breadth end to end; 22 checkpoint; 22-40 deep dives; 40-45 close. Deep-dive weight dominates the rubric while most candidates spend ~60% of the round on the high-level diagram.

flashcards.q: What are the four axes an interviewer scores, and where is the failure asymmetry?
flashcards.a: Scoping (did they define the problem or wait for it), Communication (could I follow it without knowing the answer), Technical depth (did they go below the name of the technology), Tradeoffs and judgment (did they choose or just list). Asymmetry: you can pass with a mediocre architecture and excellent reasoning; you cannot pass with an excellent architecture the interviewer could not follow.

flashcards.q: What is the test for whether a clarifying question is worth asking?
flashcards.a: Would a different answer change your architecture? 'How many users' changes it. 'What is the exact SLA in milliseconds' usually does not, so state your assumption instead. Ask three or four questions, not ten; past about four minutes the interviewer starts wondering whether you can make a decision.

flashcards.q: What must an estimation phase output, beyond a number?
flashcards.a: A design constraint. End with a sentence of the form 'which tells me the design problem is ___'. Estimation whose output is a number is a calculation; estimation whose output is a constraint is engineering.

flashcards.q: Give the seven-step structure of one deep dive.
flashcards.a: 1) Name the problem precisely. 2) State the constraint. 3) Give two or three real options. 4) Choose, with the reason. 5) State the cost you accept. 6) Go one level below the choice. 7) VOLUNTEER the failure mode, unprompted. Step 7 is what separates staff from senior.

flashcards.q: Give the eight-second tradeoff template.
flashcards.a: 'A or B. I'd take A, because [property of THIS problem]. What I'm giving up is C.' Once per deep dive, add: 'the argument for the other side is ___, and it wins if ___.'

flashcards.q: What is the single strongest juniority signal, and the rule that prevents it?
flashcards.a: Jargon density: naming technologies in rapid succession without grounding them in the specific problem, which reads as performing knowledge rather than applying it. Rule: every technology you name gets a 'because [this problem]' in the SAME sentence. No orphan nouns.

flashcards.q: What is wrong with answering 'it depends', and what is the fix?
flashcards.a: It is correct and useless; all the information is in what it depends on. Fix: 'It depends on the read-write ratio. If reads dominate, X; if writes, Y.' Name the variable and both branches.

flashcards.q: Give the four-step answer to 'how would you scale this', and which step nobody does.
flashcards.a: 1) Ask what is scaling: users, data, or requests per user. 2) Name the component that breaks first and why. 3) Name the observable SYMPTOM, not just the cause (p99 up, error rate flat, queue time growing faster than compute). 4) Give the fix, then what breaks next. Step 3 is the one almost nobody does and it proves you have operated a system rather than only designed one.

flashcards.q: Give the six-step recovery script for a wrong turn, and say which step matters most.
flashcards.a: Stop mid-sentence; name it ('let me back up, I don't think that works'); SAY WHY in your own words; give the fix; name the new cost; move on without over-apologising. Step 3 matters most: 'you're right, let me change it' scores as compliance, 'you're right, and the reason it doesn't work is X' scores as understanding.

flashcards.q: How do you tell whether to hold your position or update when the interviewer pushes back?
flashcards.a: If they present NEW INFORMATION ('what if the write rate is 100x the read rate'), update. If they only apply PRESSURE ('are you sure?'), restate your reasoning once and name what would change your mind. On a second push, take it seriously regardless. Defending past the second signal is disqualifying; folding on the first is nearly as bad.

flashcards.q: What are the three signals that you are on a wrong turn?
flashcards.a: 1) The interviewer asks the same question a second time in different words: they are steering, not curious. 2) 'Are you sure that works?' or 'walk me through what happens when...': a hint, not a question. 3) They go quiet and stop writing.

flashcards.q: How do you present architecture with no whiteboard?
flashcards.a: Number the components, state direction explicitly since there are no arrows, and name them once so both of you reuse the same vocabulary. 'There are four components. One, an edge service... The request goes edge, then fans out in parallel to two and three.' Then check in before going deeper. Netflix and some staff loops run with no diagramming tool at all.

flashcards.q: What are the four elements of a close, at minute 40?
flashcards.a: What you built; why the key decision was made; what you know is unfinished; what you would do next. Naming your own gaps at the close demonstrates calibration and interviewers write it down. Never let the round end by running out of clock.

flashcards.q: What is the checkpoint sentence at minute 22, and what four things does it do?
flashcards.a: 'That's the whole system end to end. I think the two most interesting problems are X and Y. I'd start with X because I think it's the actual bottleneck. Would you rather I go there, or somewhere else?' It declares breadth complete, demonstrates prioritisation, makes a recommendation rather than only a menu, and hands over control briefly.

flashcards.q: Why is explaining fundamentals penalised at staff level, and how do you calibrate?
flashcards.a: Your interviewer is a staff-plus engineer who already knows most of what you would explain, so exhaustive coverage reads as failing to calibrate. Watch them: nodding without writing means wrong altitude. The move is to compress the known and expand the specific: 'you know how a cache works, so let me go straight to the invalidation question.'

flashcards.q: 'Could you do this with a single machine?' Why is this a trap and how do you answer?
flashcards.a: It tests whether you over-engineer by default. Often the answer is yes: at 100 rps peak with 2.5 GB of vectors a single well-provisioned instance handles it, and you distribute for availability and deployment independence rather than for capacity. Be explicit about which reason is the real one. Candidates who cannot justify their own distribution are marked down.

flashcards.q: You have not mentioned monitoring. What are the right signals, and what do you alert on versus dashboard?
flashcards.a: Name signals that detect YOUR failure modes: queue time separately from total latency, cache hit rate, the silent-failure counter (fallback or unresolved rate), cost per request. Alert on symptoms users feel (error rate, latency SLO burn) that need human action; dashboard the rest. Cause-based alerts on CPU page you for things that do not matter and miss things that do.

flashcards.q: What is the correct time allocation inside a single STAR answer?
flashcards.a: S 10% (~15s), T 10% (~15s), A 50% (~90s), R 15% (~25s), rejected alternative 10% (~20s), what I'd change 5% (~10s). Candidates invert this by spending 60% on Situation.

flashcards.q: What two parts of a STAR answer separate senior from staff, and are usually omitted?
flashcards.a: The alternative you rejected (and the cost you accepted), and what you would do differently now. Without the first you read as 'found one thing that worked' rather than 'chose'; without the second you read as not learning.

flashcards.q: What distinguishes an assigned story from a claimed story, and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: 'My manager asked me to migrate the batch job' is senior. 'I noticed it was the only JVM service in a Python fleet, costing a second build pipeline and on-call runbook, so I proposed and ran the migration' is staff. Same project, different level. Lead with claimed stories.

flashcards.q: How long should the 60-second version of a story be, structurally?
flashcards.a: Nine sentences: one Situation, one Task, three Action, one Result, one rejected alternative. Then stop and offer a direction. Never give the 3-minute version unprompted.

flashcards.q: Which resume numbers must never be rounded, and why?
flashcards.a: 54,486 skills; 3,447 Java lines removed; 812-line Python service; 307 commits; 178K+ net LOC; 1.2M+ skill rows; 2,000+ golden baseline rows; 22 locales. Odd numbers are credible precisely because they are odd. 'About fifty thousand' destroys the signal.

flashcards.q: What is the weakest link in this resume's story set, and what must be prepared first?
flashcards.a: The ~25% engagement uplift. A metric with no stated measurement method is the single most likely place a Bar Raiser breaks the story. Define the metric, the comparison design (holdout vs pre/post), the window, and the tenant scope before any other prep.

flashcards.q: OOM story: what was the symptom, why was raising the memory limit wrong, and why is gc.collect() a smell?
flashcards.a: Symptom: process killed with no Python traceback (kernel OOM killer, not an exception). Raising the limit was wrong because peak memory scaled with corpus size not batch size, so the failure returns at the next growth step. gc.collect() compensates for CPython allocator behaviour; the structural fix is streaming with generators and bounded batches.

flashcards.q: Why was patching only the endpoints you found the wrong fix for the cross-tenant authorization bypass?
flashcards.a: The class of bug is 'authorization decided per endpoint'. Fixing instances leaves the class. Enforcement belongs on the object-fetch path keyed on the authenticated tenant. Middleware is insufficient because it sees the route and token but not which object IDs the handler is about to load.

flashcards.q: Why is 812 lines of Python a faithful replacement for 3,447 lines of Java, not a feature cut?
flashcards.a: Most of the Java was Spring Batch scaffolding: item readers, writers, processors, job and step configuration. The actual transformation rules were a small fraction. Lead with that when someone assumes functionality was dropped.

flashcards.q: Why choose a contextual bandit over a supervised ranker for recommendations?
flashcards.a: A supervised ranker trained on logged clicks learns the previous policy's preferences, so new content is never shown and therefore never generates data justifying showing it. Offline replay flatters supervised models because it scores against the logged policy. The missing piece was off-policy evaluation via inverse propensity scoring.

flashcards.q: What is the honest framing of the vLLM self-hosting decision?
flashcards.a: Not 'self-host everything' but 'split by workload shape': self-hosted vLLM on SageMaker for the high-volume online path, Bedrock batch for offline generation, hosted frontier API for tasks needing frontier quality. The stated gap: no dollar break-even model was built.

flashcards.q: MongoDB race conditions and event loop errors: what were the causes and the wrong fixes?
flashcards.a: Race: read-modify-write across a network round trip is not atomic. Wrong fix was app-level locking (serialises a hot path). Right fix: atomic update operator with a filter condition, so concurrency control lives with the data. Loop errors: a client created on one event loop used from another, or a module-level client outliving its loop. Wrong fix: broad try/except. Right fix: loop-scoped client lifecycle bound to startup/shutdown.

flashcards.q: Why was the ETL story sold on cycle time rather than runtime?
flashcards.a: 4.5 hours means one marketing optimisation cycle per working day, so the runtime was the constraint on the business process. '9x faster pipeline' is an engineering fact; 'marketing can optimise several times a day instead of once' is why it got funded.

flashcards.q: Which stories must exist before entering any senior loop?
flashcards.a: Disagreed AND was wrong. A real failure with a real COST. Said no and lost. Influenced without authority. Reframed a wrong requirement. Prevented an expensive mistake. Missing any of these leaves a rubric column empty.

flashcards.q: What does the write-up 'could not determine candidate's personal contribution' mean, and what causes it?
flashcards.a: It is the most common cause of a no-hire on an otherwise strong story, and the cause is 'we' throughout the Action section. Fix: first person singular in every Action sentence. 'I decided', 'I benchmarked', 'I rejected'.

flashcards.q: Why do golden-baseline assertions have to be on aggregate behaviour rather than exact string equality?
flashcards.a: A semantic system whose output must be byte-identical cannot be improved. The design decision is separating 'must never change' (locale precedence, tenant scoping, pagination: exact assertions) from 'may drift within tolerance' (rankings, resolutions: aggregate assertions with tolerance bands).

flashcards.q: What is the coverage rule for a story-to-competency matrix?
flashcards.a: No competency column may be empty, and no single story may be the lead for more than about three competencies. Interviewers share written notes, so telling one story all loop is visible in the packet.

flashcards.q: What resume defect must be fixed before an AWS-literate interviewer reads it?
flashcards.a: ml.4xlarge and g4.2xlarge are not valid SageMaker instance identifiers. The real ones are almost certainly ml.g4dn.2xlarge and ml.g5.xlarge. It is a ten-second credibility loss on the strongest technical story.

flashcards.q: Define 'grain' and explain why it's the most consequential dimensional modeling decision.
flashcards.a: Grain is the precise definition of what one fact-table row represents, as a business-process sentence. It's most consequential because you can always aggregate a fine grain up to coarse, but you can never disaggregate a coarse grain back down - a wrong grain choice requires a rebuild, not a migration.

flashcards.q: Star vs snowflake schema - what's the tradeoff and which is the default?
flashcards.a: Star: each dimension flattened/denormalized into one table, fewer joins. Snowflake: dimension hierarchies normalized into sub-tables, more joins, easier single-point hierarchy updates. Star is the default recommendation today since storage is cheap and join count dominates query latency.

flashcards.q: Define additive, semi-additive, and non-additive measures with an example of each.
flashcards.a: Additive: sums safely across any dimension (revenue). Semi-additive: sums across some dimensions not others (account balance - safe across accounts, not across time). Non-additive: never sum directly (ratios, unit price - recompute from components instead).

flashcards.q: Why is summing account balance across time wrong, and what should you do instead?
flashcards.a: Balance is semi-additive - summable across accounts at a fixed point in time, but summing across time produces a meaningless number (balance Monday + balance Tuesday isn't a real quantity). Use the latest value or a proper average instead.

flashcards.q: SCD Type 1 vs Type 2 vs Type 3 - one line each.
flashcards.a: Type 1: overwrite in place, no history. Type 2: insert a new versioned row with a new surrogate key and effective dates, preserving full history (the default choice). Type 3: add a previous_X column, preserving only one prior value.

flashcards.q: What is SCD Type 6 and why use it?
flashcards.a: Hybrid of Type 1 (current column) + Type 2 (versioned rows) + Type 3 (previous column) - 1+2+3=6. Use when downstream reports need both point-in-time-correct joins AND an always-current value in the same row without a second join.

flashcards.q: Why does SCD Type 2 require a surrogate key?
flashcards.a: A natural key alone can't represent one business entity having multiple valid attribute versions over time without breaking key uniqueness. A surrogate key gives each version a unique identity so fact rows unambiguously reference the version that was current at the time.

flashcards.q: What is a conformed dimension and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: A dimension built once with consistent keys/definitions/grain, reused identically across multiple fact tables. Enables drill-across queries comparing metrics across facts using the same dimension definition; without it, two teams' incompatible dim_customer variants make cross-fact comparisons meaningless.

flashcards.q: Name the three fact table types and their use.
flashcards.a: Transaction fact: one row per discrete event (most common, most granular). Periodic snapshot fact: one row per entity per fixed interval regardless of activity (needed for semi-additive measures like balance). Accumulating snapshot fact: one row per process instance, updated in place as it progresses through stages.

flashcards.q: What is a mixed-grain fact table and why is it a correctness bug?
flashcards.a: A fact table with rows at inconsistent grains (e.g. order-level shipping-fee rows mixed with order-line-level rows). Naive SUM() double-counts or miscounts unless every query remembers to filter by row type - a silent correctness bug, not a performance issue.

flashcards.q: What is the one-big-table (OBT) debate in dimensional modeling?
flashcards.a: Modern columnar engines' compression and vectorised execution let some teams flatten facts and all dimension attributes into one wide table, matching or beating star-schema join performance, at the cost of losing conformed-dimension reuse and update locality (a changed attribute must be rewritten everywhere it's embedded).

flashcards.q: What does dbt snapshot automate?
flashcards.a: SCD Type 2 mechanics as declarative config (unique key, strategy timestamp/check, tracked columns) instead of hand-written upsert/versioning ETL logic - the standard modern tool for this.

flashcards.q: What does a semantic layer (dbt MetricFlow, Cube, LookML) provide for measure additivity?
flashcards.a: Lets teams declare a measure's correct aggregation rule once (e.g. 'balance resolves to latest value, never summed across time'), enforced consistently across every downstream query/dashboard rather than relying on each analyst remembering the rule.

flashcards.q: What is Kimball's 'bus matrix' used for?
flashcards.a: A grid of business processes/fact tables against shared candidate dimensions, built and agreed on before teams independently build fact tables, to catch incompatible dimension definitions before they're built rather than reconciling them afterward.

flashcards.q: Rule for composite index column order?
flashcards.a: Equality-filtered columns first (relative order among them barely matters), the single range/inequality-filtered column last. Only a left-anchored prefix ending at the first range predicate can narrow the scan.

flashcards.q: What can columns AFTER the first range predicate in a composite index do?
flashcards.a: Only filter rows already found by the prefix scan - they cannot narrow the scan further, and the cost of reading/checking those rows is already paid.

flashcards.q: What is an index-only scan and what does it require?
flashcards.a: A scan answered entirely from index leaf pages with zero heap fetches. Requires every needed column present in the index (key or INCLUDE) and the visibility map confirming no MVCC check against the heap is needed.

flashcards.q: What does 'Heap Fetches: N' (N>0) under an Index Only Scan in EXPLAIN ANALYZE indicate?
flashcards.a: The visibility map is stale for some rows, degrading toward a normal index scan for those rows. Fix: VACUUM the table and check autovacuum is keeping up.

flashcards.q: When is a partial index the right choice?
flashcards.a: When queries consistently filter on a predicate matching a minority of rows - index only that subset for a much smaller index with write cost only on matching rows.

flashcards.q: When is an expression index required instead of a plain column index?
flashcards.a: Whenever the query filters on a FUNCTION of a column (e.g. lower(email)) - a plain index on the raw column cannot serve that predicate because the planner can't infer the implication.

flashcards.q: GIN vs GiST tradeoff?
flashcards.a: GIN: ~3x faster lookups, ~3x slower build, high write overhead (many inverted entries per row) - best for read-heavy static data. GiST: lossy (rechecks candidates), faster to update - best for write-heavy dynamic data.

flashcards.q: What does BRIN store, and what makes it useless?
flashcards.a: Min/max (or similar summary) per physical block range, not per row - tiny footprint. Useless if data isn't physically correlated with the indexed column (check pg_stats.correlation); provides zero pruning benefit if row order doesn't track logical column order.

flashcards.q: What is Postgres HOT and how does updating an indexed column affect it?
flashcards.a: Heap-Only Tuple optimization avoids updating any index when an UPDATE doesn't touch indexed columns and the new row fits on the same page. Updating ANY indexed column disables HOT for that row's update, forcing ALL indexes on the table to be maintained, not just the one on the changed column.

flashcards.q: How do you check if an existing Postgres index is safe to drop?
flashcards.a: Check pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan over a representative window (a full week, to catch periodic jobs) - zero scans is a strong candidate. Also check redundancy: an index on (a) is often subsumed by one on (a,b).

flashcards.q: Why do low-selectivity indexes (e.g. boolean or 3-value status column) get ignored by the planner?
flashcards.a: Once estimated selectivity crosses roughly single-digit percent of the table, random-access index-then-heap-fetch reads for that many rows cost more than one sequential scan pass, so the planner correctly prefers a seq scan - making the index pure write cost with zero read benefit.

flashcards.q: How do you build an index on a production table without blocking writes?
flashcards.a: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY - avoids the exclusive lock a plain CREATE INDEX takes, at the cost of two full table scans instead of one, and can leave an INVALID index if interrupted (must manually drop and retry).

flashcards.q: What did Postgres 18 add for multicolumn B-tree indexes?
flashcards.a: Skip scan - lets the planner use an index efficiently even when the query omits an equality condition on a leading column, probing each distinct leading value's slice individually. Softens but doesn't eliminate the 'leading column must be constrained' rule.

flashcards.q: Postgres index types - name all five and their primary use.
flashcards.a: B-tree: equality/range/sort (default). GIN: arrays/JSONB/full-text. GiST: geometric/ranges/nearest-neighbor. BRIN: huge physically-ordered tables. Hash: pure equality only, rarely beats B-tree.

flashcards.q: What is fastupdate on a GIN index?
flashcards.a: Buffers new entries in a pending list rather than updating the main index structure immediately, trading some read overhead (checking the pending list too) for much cheaper writes.

flashcards.q: Explain the read-then-write race condition in MongoDB and why findOneAndUpdate fixes it.
flashcards.a: find() followed by a separate update() has an unprotected window where a concurrent request can read the same stale state and act on it too. findOneAndUpdate evaluates the filter condition and applies the mutation as ONE atomic server-side operation, eliminating the separate check step entirely.

flashcards.q: What is the trap that catches people who 'know' findOneAndUpdate exists?
flashcards.a: Performing a separate prior find() to DECIDE whether to call findOneAndUpdate, then building business logic on that separate read - this reintroduces the same race. The condition must be inside the atomic operation's filter, never evaluated in application code beforehand.

flashcards.q: Rank the five approaches to fixing a check-then-write race, cheapest to most expensive.
flashcards.a: 1) Atomic update operator with embedded condition (updateOne with filter condition). 2) findOneAndUpdate with conditional filter (need document back). 3) Optimistic concurrency via version field. 4) Unique/partial index (invariant is uniqueness). 5) Multi-document transaction (genuine cross-document invariant only).

flashcards.q: How does WiredTiger's document-level concurrency differ from MMAPv1?
flashcards.a: WiredTiger uses MVCC plus intent locking down to document level - only writers to the SAME document serialize, different documents proceed with zero contention. MMAPv1 locked at the collection level, blocking unrelated concurrent writes to the same collection.

flashcards.q: What is the unbounded array anti-pattern and why does it hurt before hitting the 16MB limit?
flashcards.a: An array that grows indefinitely inside a document eventually forces the document to exceed its allocated disk space, causing WiredTiger to relocate the WHOLE document on append - progressively worsening write latency well before the 16MB hard limit is reached.

flashcards.q: What is the fix for the unbounded array anti-pattern?
flashcards.a: The bucket pattern - group array elements into bounded sub-documents (e.g. one document per user per day, internally capped) - or move the growing data into its own referenced collection entirely.

flashcards.q: w:1 vs w:majority write concern - what's the durability difference during a primary failover?
flashcards.a: w:1 is acknowledged by the primary alone and can be ROLLED BACK if the primary fails before replicating it and a different secondary (without that write) becomes primary. w:majority requires majority acknowledgment, guaranteeing it survives any subsequent election.

flashcards.q: Read concern local vs majority vs linearizable?
flashcards.a: local: may be rolled back later (not majority-replicated yet). majority: only durable, non-rollback-able data. linearizable: strongest guarantee, confirms with a majority on EVERY read (real latency cost).

flashcards.q: What does a causally consistent session guarantee that plain readConcern:majority doesn't?
flashcards.a: Read-your-own-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes-follow-reads within a session - because different reads across the session could otherwise hit secondaries with different replication lag and appear to go backward in time.

flashcards.q: Why does a monotonically increasing shard key create a hot shard, and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: All new writes have the highest key value, landing on the single shard owning the top range - gets worse as write volume grows. Fix: hashed sharding spreads monotonic values pseudo-randomly across shards, at the cost of losing efficient range scans on that key.

flashcards.q: Three shard key selection criteria to check before committing to one?
flashcards.a: Cardinality (enough distinct values to split into chunks), monotonicity (increasing keys concentrate writes on one shard), skew (one dominant value creates a hot shard regardless of overall cardinality).

flashcards.q: Why is $lookup typically more expensive than a relational join?
flashcards.a: Fast only when the foreign collection has an index on the compared field (~nested loop with index); degrades to a full collection scan per input document without one - a much worse cost curve. Constant $lookup on a hot path signals the data should be embedded instead.

flashcards.q: When should you use multi-document transactions in MongoDB, and what's the schema smell if overused?
flashcards.a: Use for operations genuinely spanning multiple documents no embedding could avoid (e.g. funds transfer between two accounts). If most hot-path writes need transactions, that signals the schema should be redesigned around better embedding, not that transactions are simply 'the MongoDB way.'

flashcards.q: What do retryable writes solve, and how is that different from the application-level race condition problem?
flashcards.a: Retryable writes (default since 4.2) auto-retry on transient network/election failure using an idempotency token, solving 'did my write land exactly once.' This is orthogonal to the read-then-write race, which occurs even with perfect networking, purely from concurrent stale reads.

flashcards.q: What does MongoDB 8.0's sh.shardAndDistributeCollection() do?
flashcards.a: Wraps sharding and an immediate resharding-to-the-same-key into one operation, avoiding the historical pain of waiting on the background balancer to slowly redistribute data after an initial shard operation.
