flashcards.q: What are xmin and xmax, and what's the Postgres tuple visibility rule?
flashcards.a: xmin = transaction ID that created the tuple version, xmax = transaction ID that deleted/superseded it (0/unset = live). Visible to a snapshot if xmin's txn committed before the snapshot AND (xmax unset OR xmax's txn hasn't committed as of the snapshot).

flashcards.q: When is a Postgres transaction's snapshot taken, per isolation level?
flashcards.a: Read Committed: a fresh snapshot at the start of EVERY statement (so two SELECTs in one transaction can see different data - read skew possible). Repeatable Read / Serializable: ONE snapshot at transaction start, reused for the whole transaction.

flashcards.q: 2PL vs MVCC - the core tradeoff.
flashcards.a: 2PL: shared lock on read, exclusive on write, held until commit; readers block writers and vice versa; needs predicate locks (not just row locks) to stop phantoms. MVCC: readers see an older committed version instead of waiting, so readers never block writers or vice versa - at the cost of write-write conflicts needing detection (first-committer-wins) and write skew slipping through.

flashcards.q: Define all six anomalies in one line each.
flashcards.a: Dirty read: see another txn's uncommitted write. Dirty write: overwrite another txn's uncommitted write. Read skew: same row read twice in one txn, different committed values. Phantom read: predicate query's result set changes mid-txn. Lost update: same row read-modify-write, one write clobbers the other. Write skew: DIFFERENT rows, disjoint writes jointly violate an invariant neither write alone broke.

flashcards.q: The doctors-on-call write skew repro, in one sentence.
flashcards.a: Invariant: at least 1 doctor on call. Alice and Bob both on call; each reads count=2 from their own snapshot, each independently concludes it's safe to go off-call, each updates only their own row, both commit -> final count = 0, invariant violated, no write-write conflict ever detected.

flashcards.q: Why does snapshot isolation prevent read skew but NOT write skew?
flashcards.a: Read skew is prevented directly by the fixed snapshot (repeated reads see one consistent point in time). Write skew isn't about the snapshot changing - it's about an invariant relating two transactions' independent decisions, violated by writes to DIFFERENT rows, which SI's same-row conflict detection never checks.

flashcards.q: Level -> anomalies permitted, memorize the table.
flashcards.a: Read Uncommitted: all possible except dirty write. Read Committed: dirty read/write prevented, rest possible. Repeatable Read (ANSI min): + read skew prevented. Snapshot Isolation (Postgres REPEATABLE READ): + phantom + lost update prevented; WRITE SKEW STILL POSSIBLE. Serializable: everything prevented.

flashcards.q: Real default isolation level per database.
flashcards.a: Postgres, Oracle, SQL Server -> READ COMMITTED. MySQL/InnoDB -> REPEATABLE READ (with gap locks that suppress most phantoms beyond the ANSI minimum).

flashcards.q: The Oracle SERIALIZABLE gotcha.
flashcards.a: Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is implemented as snapshot isolation, not true serializability - no SSI, no 2PL predicate locking at that level. Write skew is still possible on Oracle SERIALIZABLE despite the name.

flashcards.q: How does Postgres's SSI detect write skew without blocking readers?
flashcards.a: SERIALIZABLE transactions take SIREAD locks on data they read - bookkeeping only, never blocking. A later write to SIREAD-covered data creates an rw-antidependency edge. If edges form a cycle through a pivot transaction (incoming + outgoing rw-antidependency to concurrent transactions), Postgres aborts one transaction with a serialization failure, forcing a retry.

flashcards.q: Two fixes for write skew besides full SERIALIZABLE, and when each wins.
flashcards.a: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the invariant-backing rows - targeted, cheap, but requires correctly enumerating every dangerous read. Atomic conditional UPDATE ... WHERE cond (e.g. seats_available > 0) - best for simple capacity checks, folds check-then-write into one atomic statement, avoids held-lock time and retry loops.

flashcards.q: Lost update vs write skew - the key structural difference.
flashcards.a: Lost update: SAME row read by both, one write overwrites the other, an update is literally lost. Write skew: DIFFERENT rows written, no write is lost or overwritten - the invariant relating the two rows is the casualty, not any single value.

flashcards.q: Why does snapshot isolation prevent lost update in Postgres specifically?
flashcards.a: First-committer-wins: the second transaction's write to the SAME row triggers a serialization failure (must retry) rather than silently overwriting. This is a real protection SI provides - it's write skew (disjoint rows) that survives, not same-row lost update.

flashcards.q: What does XID wraparound risk mean operationally?
flashcards.a: Postgres XIDs are 32-bit, wrapping every ~4 billion transactions. Autovacuum's 'freeze' rewrites old tuples' xmin to a frozen sentinel to prevent ambiguity. An under-vacuumed high-write table risks Postgres forcing itself into read-only mode to prevent corruption as the counter approaches wraparound.

flashcards.q: Why do predicate locks matter for 2PL, and what happens without them?
flashcards.a: Row locks alone only stop conflicts on rows that already existed when the lock was taken - they don't stop phantoms. Predicate locks lock the range/condition a query scanned, so a NEW row inserted into that range is caught too; without them, phantom reads slip through even under strict 2PL.

flashcards.q: Define a functional dependency.
flashcards.a: X -> Y means every row sharing the same X value must have the same Y value - knowing X determines Y. Every normal form is defined purely in terms of which FDs are/aren't allowed relative to candidate keys.

flashcards.q: What does 1NF require?
flashcards.a: Atomic values and no repeating groups - no comma-separated lists in a column, no col1/col2 repeating-group pairs.

flashcards.q: What does 2NF forbid, and when is it automatically satisfied?
flashcards.a: Forbids partial dependencies - every non-key attribute must depend on the WHOLE key, not just part of it. Automatically satisfied by any table with a single-column primary key; only a real constraint with composite keys.

flashcards.q: What does 3NF forbid?
flashcards.a: Transitive dependencies - a non-key attribute depending on another non-key attribute rather than directly on the key (key -> A -> B is the violation shape).

flashcards.q: What loophole does BCNF close that 3NF leaves open?
flashcards.a: 3NF only forbids non-key attributes transitively depending on the key; BCNF additionally requires every determinant of every non-trivial FD to be a candidate key - closing the case where a determinant is part of one candidate key but not a full candidate key itself, in a table with overlapping candidate keys.

flashcards.q: Give the classic BCNF-violates-but-3NF-satisfies example.
flashcards.a: course_enrollment(student_id, course_id, instructor), key (student_id, course_id), with course_id -> instructor. This is 3NF (instructor isn't reached via a non-key attribute) but violates BCNF since course_id alone doesn't determine student_id, so it isn't a candidate key yet is a determinant.

flashcards.q: Why isn't BCNF decomposition always dependency-preserving?
flashcards.a: Decomposing to BCNF can split a functional dependency across two tables such that checking it requires rejoining them, losing the ability to enforce that constraint with a single-table check - unlike 3NF decomposition, which is guaranteed to preserve dependencies.

flashcards.q: What does 4NF forbid, define a multi-valued dependency.
flashcards.a: X ->> Y: the set of Y values associated with X is independent of any other attribute in the table. 4NF forbids combining two independent multi-valued facts about one entity into a single table, which forces storing their cross product.

flashcards.q: Give an example of a 4NF violation and its fix.
flashcards.a: product_tags_warehouses(product_id, tag, warehouse_id) where tags and warehouses are independent - a product with 3 tags and 2 warehouses needs 6 rows instead of 5. Fix: split into product_tags(product_id, tag) and product_warehouses(product_id, warehouse_id).

flashcards.q: Name the three classic anomalies with one-line definitions.
flashcards.a: Update anomaly: duplicated fact updated in some but not all rows -> inconsistency. Insert anomaly: can't record one entity's fact until an unrelated fact is also available. Delete anomaly: deleting a row to remove one fact accidentally destroys a different, unrelated fact stored in the same row.

flashcards.q: What two things must be true for denormalization to be a sound engineering decision, not a shortcut?
flashcards.a: You must be able to name (1) the exact anomaly being reintroduced, and (2) the specific consistency mechanism keeping the duplicate correct (trigger, write-through, CDC sync, or an explicitly accepted staleness window). No mechanism means it's a scheduled bug, not a decision.

flashcards.q: What's the practical default normal form for OLTP schema design?
flashcards.a: 3NF (or BCNF where they diverge) - eliminates essentially all common anomalies with a manageable number of tables. 4NF/5NF only worth pursuing when a genuine multi-valued-dependency problem is actually identified.

flashcards.q: How do you empirically check whether a candidate functional dependency actually holds in real data?
flashcards.a: Group rows by the candidate determinant's value(s) and check whether every group has a single consistent dependent value - any group with more than one distinct value violates the FD in the sampled data (though absence of violation doesn't logically prove the FD holds universally).

flashcards.q: Why do star schemas/OLAP dimensional models count as a legitimate default case for denormalization?
flashcards.a: The read pattern (few large scans, rare updates to dimension data) makes anomaly risk low and join-avoidance benefit high - this is the clearest case where denormalization is a first-class design tool, not an exception requiring special justification.

flashcards.q: Single diagnostic question to decide OLTP vs OLAP shape for a workload?
flashcards.a: Does a single request touch one entity (a row, a small related set) or millions of rows? One entity -> OLTP shape. Millions -> OLAP shape. Resolves ~80% of cases immediately.

flashcards.q: Where does most of a columnar engine's speedup actually come from?
flashcards.a: Both I/O savings (read only needed columns, 5-20x compression) AND vectorised execution (batches of 1000s of values per CPU op, SIMD-friendly, cache-friendly) - the CPU efficiency piece is a large fraction of the 10-100x speedup, not just less I/O.

flashcards.q: Name three columnar compression techniques and what each exploits.
flashcards.a: Dictionary encoding: replaces repeated values with small integer codes (low-cardinality columns). Run-length encoding: (value,count) pairs for consecutive repeats. Delta encoding: stores difference from previous value (monotonic columns like timestamps/IDs).

flashcards.q: Typical OLTP vs OLAP latency budgets and concurrency?
flashcards.a: OLTP: p99 single-digit to low tens of ms, 1-few hundred rows/query, thousands of concurrent small transactions. OLAP: seconds to minutes acceptable, millions-billions rows/query, tens of concurrent large queries.

flashcards.q: What is chunk skipping / predicate pushdown in a columnar engine?
flashcards.a: Columnar files split into row-group chunks with stored min/max stats; a query's predicate is checked against chunk stats before reading any data, letting the engine skip entire chunks that can't match.

flashcards.q: What breaks chunk skipping even on a partitioned table?
flashcards.a: Filtering on a column that isn't the physical partition/cluster key, or wrapping the filtered column in a function (e.g. DATE(created_at)=X) so the engine can't compare it against stored chunk statistics.

flashcards.q: What is the honest limitation of HTAP systems?
flashcards.a: The same CPU, memory, and I/O bandwidth ultimately serve both workloads - a zero-sum resource contention problem that architecture can manage/bound (dual engines, throughput ceilings) but not eliminate.

flashcards.q: How does TiDB architecturally achieve HTAP, and what is that really similar to?
flashcards.a: Two separate engines: TiKV (row store) and TiFlash (columnar), replicated via Raft in near-real-time, can run on separate nodes. Architecturally closer to 'CDC replication packaged inside one product' than a single engine truly serving both patterns.

flashcards.q: Snowflake Unistore hybrid tables - what's the documented throughput ceiling?
flashcards.a: Roughly 1,000 operations/second with active data around 500GB - far below what a dedicated OLTP engine sustains, a direct consequence of one storage layer satisfying both access patterns.

flashcards.q: What is the pragmatic default architecture for near-real-time analytics over operational data?
flashcards.a: CDC (e.g. Debezium reading the WAL/binlog) streaming into Kafka, landing in a columnar store (ClickHouse/BigQuery/Snowflake). Typical lag: seconds to low tens of seconds - simpler and more mature than adopting full HTAP for most requirements.

flashcards.q: What historical pain caused the classic ETL-into-separate-warehouse pattern to emerge?
flashcards.a: Heavy analytical queries run directly against the same row store serving live transactions held locks and consumed buffer pool/cache the transactional workload needed, degrading OLTP latency unpredictably whenever a report ran.

flashcards.q: What's the classic, entirely predictable production incident in this space?
flashcards.a: A heavy ad hoc analytics report run directly against the OLTP primary (or a shared replica) starves transactional p99 latency for the query's full duration. Fix: dedicated read replica or CDC pipeline, not running it at off-peak hours and hoping.

flashcards.q: Rough I/O reduction for a columnar query needing 2 of 50 columns, before compression?
flashcards.a: Roughly 25x less data read (2/50), before compression is even applied - with typical 5-20x compression on top, total I/O reduction for this query shape is often 100x+.

flashcards.q: As the fraction of columns needed per query approaches all of them, what happens to the columnar advantage?
flashcards.a: It shrinks toward parity and can even lose to row storage, since reassembling a full row from many separate column files adds overhead - the columnar advantage is specific to few-columns/many-rows access patterns.

flashcards.q: Why does every Postgres UPDATE leave a dead tuple, and what reclaims it?
flashcards.a: Postgres never overwrites a row in place - UPDATE marks the old tuple's xmax and inserts a new version. The old version becomes a dead tuple, reclaimed only by VACUUM/autovacuum once no active transaction's snapshot needs it.

flashcards.q: Does plain VACUUM shrink the table file on disk?
flashcards.a: No - it reclaims dead-tuple space for reuse within the existing file. Only VACUUM FULL (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, full rewrite) or pg_repack (online) actually shrink the file.

flashcards.q: Autovacuum trigger formula and why the default is dangerous on huge tables?
flashcards.a: dead_tuples > autovacuum_vacuum_threshold(50) + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor(0.2) x total_rows. On a 500M-row table, 20% = 100M dead tuples before autovacuum even runs - too late for high-churn tables, requiring per-table scale_factor overrides.

flashcards.q: What is transaction ID wraparound and why does it force a full outage?
flashcards.a: 32-bit XIDs wrap every ~4B transactions with an unambiguous comparison window of ~2B either direction. Old unfrozen tuples risk appearing invisible/ambiguous post-wrap (data corruption risk), so Postgres hard-stops new writes as the oldest unfrozen XID approaches the limit - a deliberate safety valve, not a bug.

flashcards.q: What number do you alert on to prevent XID wraparound outages?
flashcards.a: age(datfrozenxid) per database via pg_database - alert well before the ~2 billion hard limit (start around 1 billion). Fully preventable; weeks of log warnings precede any real incident.

flashcards.q: What is a HOT update and what disqualifies a row from it?
flashcards.a: Heap-Only Tuple update: new version written on the SAME page with a forwarding pointer, zero index writes. Requires no indexed column changed AND the new tuple fits on the same page. Breaking either condition forces a full update touching ALL indexes on the table.

flashcards.q: What is TOAST and what's its practical performance implication?
flashcards.a: Values over ~2KB are compressed/moved out of the 8KB page into a side table (pg_toast), chunked, with a pointer left in the row. Detoast cost is paid per row per TOASTed column actually accessed - SELECT * on wide JSONB tables costs more than selecting only needed columns.

flashcards.q: Explain the FIFO lock queue trap with ALTER TABLE.
flashcards.a: A long-running SELECT holds ACCESS SHARE; a queued ALTER TABLE (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE) waits for it; every SUBSEQUENT SELECT also queues behind the ALTER TABLE, even though SELECT-SELECT would normally be compatible - because Postgres's lock queue is FIFO.

flashcards.q: Why is raising max_connections alone not the fix for connection exhaustion?
flashcards.a: Each Postgres connection is a full OS process consuming several MB plus setup cost - practical ceiling is hundreds to low thousands, not tens of thousands. PgBouncer (transaction pooling) multiplexes many clients onto fewer backend connections instead.

flashcards.q: What does PgBouncer's transaction pooling mode break in an application?
flashcards.a: Session-level state that doesn't persist across a shared physical connection: prepared statements, session-level SET variables, and advisory locks held outside an explicit transaction.

flashcards.q: What did Postgres 18 add, and why?
flashcards.a: Asynchronous I/O (AIO) subsystem (up to 3x read improvement), skip scan for multicolumn B-tree indexes, and uuidv7() - a time-ordered UUID built-in fixing the index bloat/cache-locality problem caused by random UUIDv4 primary keys.

flashcards.q: Why does a random UUIDv4 primary key cause worse index bloat than a sequential ID, and what's the uuidv7 tradeoff?
flashcards.a: Random values scatter inserts uniformly across the B-Tree's key range, causing page splits and cache misses instead of appending near the end. uuidv7() embeds a timestamp for monotonic ordering, but this leaks approximate creation time if the ID is exposed externally.

flashcards.q: pgvector: IVFFlat vs HNSW, and when do you still need a dedicated vector database?
flashcards.a: IVFFlat needs a training step, faster build, worse recall/latency. HNSW needs no training, current default recommendation. Choose a dedicated vector DB over pgvector at hundreds of millions of vectors with strict recall/latency SLAs.

flashcards.q: Why sort pg_stat_statements by total_exec_time rather than mean_exec_time?
flashcards.a: A query called 100,000 times at 5ms averages costs far more aggregate database time (500s) than one slow query called once - total_exec_time finds the most actionable target for reducing overall DB load; mean/max_exec_time is for tail-latency/SLO hunting instead.

flashcards.q: What does logical replication depend on, and what's the common production incident related to it?
flashcards.a: A replication slot, which retains WAL segments until its consumer confirms processing them. A disconnected/stuck consumer (e.g. Debezium) is one of the most common causes of WAL directory disk exhaustion in production Postgres.

flashcards.q: The full query pipeline, in order.
flashcards.a: Parse (SQL text -> AST, syntax only) -> Rewrite (expand views, flatten subqueries, apply rules) -> Plan enumeration (candidate access methods, join algorithms, join orders) -> Cost estimation (stats-driven, NOT real data) -> Execute (chosen lowest-estimated-cost plan runs against real data).

flashcards.q: Postgres default cost constants, memorize the numbers.
flashcards.a: seq_page_cost = 1.0, random_page_cost = 4.0 (random I/O modeled as 4x sequential - spinning-disk-era assumption, lower to ~1.1-2.0 on SSD), cpu_tuple_cost = 0.01 per row processed, cpu_operator_cost = 0.0025.

flashcards.q: What statistics does the planner maintain per column, and what do they feed?
flashcards.a: Most-common-values (MCV) list with frequencies, a histogram of the remaining distribution (equal-depth buckets), null fraction, and n_distinct estimate - refreshed by ANALYZE/autovacuum. These feed selectivity estimation for filters and joins, which drives cardinality estimates for every plan node built on top.

flashcards.q: The independence assumption flaw - what breaks it and how do you fix it?
flashcards.a: Cost models estimate combined selectivity of two predicates by multiplying their individual selectivities, assuming independence. Correlated columns (e.g. city and state) violate this, causing estimates too low by an order of magnitude or more. Fix: CREATE STATISTICS ... (dependencies) ON (col1, col2) FROM table - the planner never detects correlation automatically.

flashcards.q: Three join algorithms, complexity, and when each wins.
flashcards.a: Nested loop: O(N*M) naive, O(N log M) with an inner index - wins when one side is tiny/well-indexed. Hash join: O(N+M), builds a hash table on the smaller side - wins on large unsorted equality joins. Merge join: O(N+M) if both sides already sorted on the join key (else + sort cost) - wins when both come from index scans already in join-key order.

flashcards.q: The single most important number in EXPLAIN ANALYZE output.
flashcards.a: Estimated vs actual row count at each plan node. A 10x+ divergence means every plan decision made ABOVE that node in the tree was built on a false premise - the plan SHAPE itself is likely wrong, not just mis-costed.

flashcards.q: EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE - the operational hazard.
flashcards.a: EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan and cost ESTIMATES without running the query. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually EXECUTES the query (real side effects for DML!) and reports actual rows/timing next to the estimates. Test a DML statement's plan inside BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK; to avoid really executing it against production.

flashcards.q: Hash join build vs probe side, and what Batches>1 means.
flashcards.a: Build side (smaller estimated input) loaded into an in-memory hash table; probe side streamed through, looking up matches. If the build side's ACTUAL size exceeds work_mem, Postgres splits into multiple batches and spills to disk - visible as Batches>1 in EXPLAIN ANALYZE, adding I/O cost the original estimate may not have predicted.

flashcards.q: What is GEQO and when does Postgres switch to it?
flashcards.a: For many-table joins, exhaustive dynamic-programming plan enumeration becomes too expensive. Postgres's geqo_threshold (default 12 tables) switches to a genetic algorithm beyond that point, trading a guarantee of optimal join order for tractable planning time.

flashcards.q: The correct fix-order when a query is slow.
flashcards.a: 1) EXPLAIN ANALYZE first, always. 2) If estimate is wrong: ANALYZE / extended stats / raise per-column STATISTICS target - fix stats BEFORE adding indexes. 3) If estimate is right but no good access path exists: THEN add the index. 4) Still slow: check query shape (function-wrapped predicate defeating index use, unnecessary correlated subquery, SELECT *).

flashcards.q: A filtered sequential scan estimates 48 rows, actual is 6104 - what's the mechanical consequence for the join above it?
flashcards.a: The planner chose a Hash Join believing the filtered side was tiny (cheap build side). At the real 127x-larger cardinality, the hash table is much bigger than planned - fine if it still fits in work_mem (Batches:1), but a worse misestimate pushes Batches above 1, spilling to disk with I/O the original estimate never accounted for.

flashcards.q: Why is 'add an index' the wrong first move on a slow query?
flashcards.a: If the root cause is a stale-statistics-driven bad plan SHAPE (wrong join algorithm/order), an index can mask the symptom temporarily or simply not get chosen at all under the current wrong cost estimate - fix statistics first, verify with a second EXPLAIN ANALYZE, then consider indexing.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't adaptive query execution (Spark SQL AQE, cloud warehouses) exist in traditional OLTP planners like Postgres?
flashcards.a: OLTP queries are short and latency-sensitive at the millisecond level, where runtime re-planning overhead is proportionally far more expensive relative to total query cost than for a long analytical query processing terabytes across a cluster - the cost/benefit favors adaptive execution much more for long analytical queries.

flashcards.q: Why can a function wrapped around a column (e.g. WHERE lower(email) = ...) defeat the planner's ability to estimate well, even with good general statistics?
flashcards.a: Normal column statistics are collected on the raw column, not on the result of an arbitrary function applied to it, so the planner can't use the MCV/histogram to estimate selectivity of the wrapped expression accurately - fix with an expression index and/or extended statistics on that exact expression.

flashcards.q: Selinger et al. (1979) - what did System R's cost-based optimizer actually introduce?
flashcards.a: The idea that a query has many valid physical execution plans and the system should pick among them via an estimated cost model, rather than executing a single naive translation or requiring the programmer to hand-specify the physical access path as pre-relational systems did.

flashcards.q: B+Tree vs LSM-Tree: the one-sentence structural difference?
flashcards.a: B+Tree updates in place and stays sorted on disk at all times; LSM-Tree never updates in place, writing to an in-memory memtable then flushing immutable sorted SSTables, deferring reorganization to background compaction.

flashcards.q: B-Tree fanout formula and typical value?
flashcards.a: fanout ≈ page_size / (key_size + pointer_size). For a 16KB InnoDB page, 16-byte key, 8-byte pointer: fanout ≈ 680.

flashcards.q: B-Tree height for 100M rows at fanout ~680?
flashcards.a: log_680(100,000,000) ≈ 3 levels. With upper levels cached, warm lookup is ~1-2 real disk I/Os, not literal log N reads.

flashcards.q: Define write amplification, read amplification, space amplification.
flashcards.a: WA = physical bytes written / logical bytes written. RA = disk reads per logical read. SA = physical bytes on disk / logical live bytes.

flashcards.q: Typical amplification numbers: B-Tree vs LSM (leveled)?
flashcards.a: B-Tree: WA ~3-4x, RA ~1-2x, SA ~1.1-1.5x. LSM leveled: WA ~20-30x+, RA ~1-2x with tuned bloom filters (5-10x+ without), SA ~1.1-1.3x tuned (spikes ~2x mid-compaction).

flashcards.q: Size-tiered vs leveled compaction tradeoff?
flashcards.a: Size-tiered: lower write amplification (~10-15x) but overlapping key ranges raise read amplification and space can spike ~2x. Leveled: higher write amplification (~20-30x+) but non-overlapping levels give lower read amplification and tighter space usage.

flashcards.q: What is Time-Window Compaction Strategy (TWCS) and when do you use it?
flashcards.a: Buckets SSTables by time window, compacts only within a window, and drops whole expired files instead of rewriting them. Right choice for time-series data with uniform TTL expiry.

flashcards.q: What does a bloom filter buy an LSM-Tree, with real numbers?
flashcards.a: Probabilistic 'definitely not present / maybe present' check per SSTable. RocksDB default ~10 bits/key gives ~1% false positive rate, letting reads skip disk I/O on ~99% of files that don't contain the key.

flashcards.q: RUM conjecture — what does it say?
flashcards.a: Read, Update, Memory (space) amplification cannot all be minimized simultaneously — optimizing any two makes the third worse. It's a proven tradeoff, not an engineering habit.

flashcards.q: What causes B-Tree write amplification mechanically?
flashcards.a: A single row update dirties an entire page (8-16KB), and the whole page gets flushed even though only a fraction logically changed; a page split doubles this by dirtying two pages.

flashcards.q: Which real systems use B+Tree vs LSM storage?
flashcards.a: B+Tree family: Postgres, MySQL/InnoDB, SQL Server. LSM family: Cassandra, RocksDB-backed stores (MyRocks, TiKV, CockroachDB's Pebble/RocksDB), ScyllaDB.

flashcards.q: Leading indicator that an LSM store's read latency is about to degrade?
flashcards.a: L0 file count or pending-compaction-bytes climbing — compaction has fallen behind ingest. Instrument and alert on this before it shows up in read p99.

flashcards.q: Workload fit rule of thumb for choosing storage engine family?
flashcards.a: OLTP / read-heavy / mixed workloads -> B+Tree (Postgres, InnoDB). Write-firehose / high-ingest / logs / time-series -> LSM (Cassandra, RocksDB). Large analytical scans -> neither; columnar storage.

flashcards.q: Why can L0 SSTables be more expensive to read from than lower levels?
flashcards.a: L0 files are flushed independently from separate memtable snapshots, so their key ranges can overlap; a point read may need to check every L0 file, unlike lower levels (leveled compaction) where each level has non-overlapping ranges.

flashcards.q: Default page sizes: Postgres vs InnoDB?
flashcards.a: Postgres: 8 KB pages. InnoDB: 16 KB pages by default.

flashcards.q: State the write-ahead logging rule in one sentence.
flashcards.a: The log record for a change must be durable before the corresponding data page is allowed to reach disk, and the commit log record must be durable before the client is told the transaction committed.

flashcards.q: Name ARIES's three recovery phases and what each does.
flashcards.a: Analysis: scan from last checkpoint, build Transaction Table + Dirty Page Table, find where redo must start. Redo: replay ALL changes forward (committed and uncommitted) - 'repeat history'. Undo: roll back uncommitted transactions in reverse order using Compensation Log Records.

flashcards.q: What is a pageLSN and how does it make redo idempotent?
flashcards.a: pageLSN is the LSN of the last log record reflected in a given page. Redo skips any log record whose LSN <= the page's current pageLSN, so already-applied changes are never reapplied - safe to rerun recovery from scratch.

flashcards.q: Why does redo replay changes from uncommitted transactions too?
flashcards.a: At analysis time you can't cheaply/correctly determine what's 'needed' without the state you're reconstructing. Redo is deliberately blind ('repeat history'); undo removes the effects of transactions that never committed afterward.

flashcards.q: What is a Compensation Log Record (CLR) and why does undo need it?
flashcards.a: A CLR logs each undo action itself, so a crash during recovery's undo phase doesn't lose track of progress. It makes undo replayable and idempotent, matching the guarantees of the forward log.

flashcards.q: What is a checkpoint's actual purpose?
flashcards.a: Solely to bound recovery time by giving analysis a recent starting point (the oldest recLSN of any dirty page as of the checkpoint) instead of scanning from the start of the log. Not for saving disk space.

flashcards.q: What is the most common real-world cause of WAL directory filling up disk?
flashcards.a: A disconnected or stuck replication slot (physical or logical) retaining WAL segments because its consumer isn't reading them, preventing log truncation.

flashcards.q: Name two real fsync 'lies' that cause silent data loss.
flashcards.a: A volatile disk write-back cache (no battery backing) can ack a write before it's physically durable. The 2018 Linux kernel fsync-error-handling bug cleared the dirty-page error flag after a failed fsync, letting a later fsync call falsely report success.

flashcards.q: Why do databases PANIC on fsync failure instead of retrying?
flashcards.a: Because of documented kernel behavior where a retried fsync after a failure can report false success, silently discarding data the app believed was durable. PANICing (crashing) is the defensive alternative to that risk.

flashcards.q: What is group commit and what does it optimize?
flashcards.a: Batching multiple transactions' WAL records into one fsync call instead of one fsync per commit, amortizing the fixed fsync latency across many transactions - often an order-of-magnitude throughput gain under concurrency.

flashcards.q: Postgres synchronous_commit on vs off - what's the tradeoff?
flashcards.a: on: fsync WAL before acking commit (full durability, higher latency). off: ack before fsync completes, risking loss of the last fraction-of-a-second of acked commits on an OS/machine crash, in exchange for throughput.

flashcards.q: InnoDB innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit values and their meaning?
flashcards.a: 1 = fsync every commit (full ACID durability). 2 = write to OS cache every commit, fsync ~once/sec (survives mysqld crash, not OS crash). 0 = write+fsync ~once/sec regardless of commits (fastest, can lose ~1s of transactions).

flashcards.q: What does Postgres full_page_writes protect against, and what's its cost?
flashcards.a: Torn pages - a crash mid-write leaving a page partly old/partly new bytes, which normal WAL replay can't repair. Cost: WAL volume spikes right after every checkpoint since the whole page is logged on its first post-checkpoint write.

flashcards.q: Why is kill -9 not a valid test of durability guarantees?
flashcards.a: It doesn't interrupt in-flight disk writes or lose OS page cache the way a real power loss does. A valid test pulls power or fault-injects mid-write and verifies exactly what was acknowledged survived.

flashcards.q: Why did WAL win over shadow paging as the dominant recovery architecture?
flashcards.a: Shadow paging gives crash safety via copy-on-write + atomic root swap but destroys physical locality over time and complicates fine-grained concurrent transactions. WAL keeps pages in place, preserving locality and allowing independent row/page-level locking or MVCC.

flashcards.q: In `curl -v` output, what do the `*`, `>`, and `<` prefixes mean?
flashcards.a: `*` = connection/TLS metadata from curl itself (DNS, TCP connect, negotiated TLS version/cipher, ALPN, cert chain). `>` = literal bytes curl sent (your actual request). `<` = literal response headers the server sent back (ground truth for what came back).

flashcards.q: List the curl -w timing variables in order and what each delta tells you.
flashcards.a: time_namelookup -> time_connect -> time_appconnect -> time_pretransfer -> time_starttransfer (TTFB) -> time_total. connect-namelookup=DNS cost; appconnect-connect=TLS cost; starttransfer-appconnect=server processing time (usual bottleneck); total-starttransfer=body transfer time.

flashcards.q: What Content-Type does `-d`/`--data` send by default, and why does this break JSON APIs?
flashcards.a: application/x-www-form-urlencoded, not application/json. A JSON body sent with just -d will be misparsed as form-encoded by a server expecting JSON unless you explicitly add -H "Content-Type: application/json".

flashcards.q: What happens to a POST body on a 301/302 redirect with `-L`, and what changes with 307/308?
flashcards.a: curl (like browsers) converts POST to GET and drops the body by default on 301/302. Only 307/308 explicitly preserve method and body. You can force `-X POST` to keep POST through a redirect, but that overrides the server's semantic hint.

flashcards.q: Difference between -F and -T for uploads?
flashcards.a: -F "file=@x.pdf" builds a multipart/form-data body (like a browser form, supports multiple fields plus file). -T file.bin sends the raw file bytes as the entire request body via PUT, no multipart framing -- for APIs expecting raw content directly (e.g. S3-style PUT-to-URL).

flashcards.q: Why is -k dangerous outside a debugging session?
flashcards.a: -k disables certificate verification entirely, silently accepting an expired cert, wrong hostname, or an active MITM without error -- exactly what TLS exists to catch. A health check using -k reports 'healthy' even when every real client would fail.

flashcards.q: What do --cacert and --cert/--key do?
flashcards.a: --cacert points curl at a specific CA bundle (for internal/private CAs not in the system trust store). --cert/--key present a client certificate for mutual TLS (mTLS), where the server also verifies the client's identity.

flashcards.q: --connect-timeout vs -m/--max-time?
flashcards.a: --connect-timeout bounds only the TCP/TLS connection-establishment phase. -m/--max-time bounds the entire request lifecycle including waiting for the response and transferring the body. A host that connects instantly but hangs mid-response is only caught by -m.

flashcards.q: Does --retry retry every failed request?
flashcards.a: No -- only transient transport failures (connection refused/reset, timeout) and a defined set of HTTP response codes, with --retry-delay (or exponential backoff by default) between attempts. It doesn't know or care about your endpoint's idempotency, so don't blindly add it to non-idempotent write calls.

flashcards.q: Difference between --resolve and --connect-to?
flashcards.a: --resolve host:port:IP fully overrides DNS resolution for that host (as if DNS itself changed). --connect-to host:port:IP:port only redirects the TCP connection target while keeping the original Host header, SNI, and cert validation against the original hostname -- useful to hit one specific LB backend while still validating its cert against the real name.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between -s and -S, and why pair them?
flashcards.a: -s (silent) suppresses the progress meter AND error messages, needed for clean scripting output. -S keeps error output visible even in silent mode. Pair -s -S so scripts stay quiet on success but still surface real failures.

flashcards.q: What does -I do, and what's the HTTP-semantics expectation for its output vs a full GET?
flashcards.a: -I sends a HEAD request, returning only response headers with no body -- useful for checking existence, size (Content-Length), or cache headers without downloading content. Per HTTP semantics, headers should match what an equivalent GET would return; meaningful divergence (different Content-Type, missing ETag) signals a real server-side inconsistency.

flashcards.q: How many network round trips does a fully cold DNS lookup take, worst case vs common case?
flashcards.a: Worst case up to 3-4 (root, TLD, authoritative), each a separate round trip. Common case is 1 round trip to the authoritative server, since root and TLD delegation are usually already cached (TTLs of days).

flashcards.q: Why is DNS-based failover often much slower than the configured TTL suggests?
flashcards.a: TTL is advisory, not enforced -- OS resolvers, app-runtime caches, and corporate/ISP resolvers routinely cache longer than instructed or override TTL entirely. Real propagation can take minutes to hours despite a 60s TTL.

flashcards.q: Why can't a CNAME sit at a domain's zone apex?
flashcards.a: The apex must also hold NS (and typically SOA) records for zone delegation, and DNS disallows any other record type coexisting at a name that has a CNAME. The workaround is a provider-specific ALIAS/ANAME record that resolves like a CNAME but is flattened to an A record at the edge.

flashcards.q: What's the mechanical difference between L4 and L7 load balancing?
flashcards.a: L4 (e.g. AWS NLB) routes on IP/TCP headers only -- no HTTP parsing, near-zero added latency, can't route on path/host. L7 (e.g. AWS ALB, Envoy) terminates TLS and parses HTTP, enabling path/host/header/cookie routing at the cost of real per-request CPU.

flashcards.q: Why does consistent hashing matter for a distributed cache?
flashcards.a: Naive hash(key) % n remaps nearly every key when n changes (a node joins/leaves), wiping the cache. Consistent hashing places keys and servers on a ring so a node change remaps only ~1/n of keys, leaving the rest warm.

flashcards.q: Why use virtual nodes (~100-200 per physical node) in a consistent hash ring?
flashcards.a: A single ring position per physical node produces uneven arc sizes by chance. Multiple virtual positions per physical node smooth the key distribution close to uniform.

flashcards.q: What's the thundering-herd risk of an aggressive health check interval?
flashcards.a: A short interval with a low failure threshold can eject a large fraction of the fleet simultaneously during a correlated blip (shared dependency hiccup, GC pause across the fleet), dumping all traffic onto survivors and cascading. Fix: require N consecutive failures, stagger checks, cap max-ejection %.

flashcards.q: Why do sticky sessions fight horizontal scaling?
flashcards.a: They pin a client to a specific backend instance, so you can't freely add/remove instances without disrupting pinned sessions, and rolling deploys must drain sticky connections rather than just cycling instances. IP-hash affinity additionally hot-spots when many clients share one NAT IP.

flashcards.q: Does anycast route to the physically nearest server?
flashcards.a: No. The same IP is announced from multiple sites via BGP, and routers pick the path with the best BGP cost (shortest AS-path, policy attributes) -- often correlated with distance but not the same thing. A client can be routed to a farther site with better peering.

flashcards.q: Why is anycast/BGP failover faster than DNS-based failover?
flashcards.a: BGP convergence after withdrawing an announcement is typically seconds. DNS failover depends on clients/resolvers honoring TTL, which they routinely don't -- real propagation can take minutes to hours.

flashcards.q: What is CDN origin shielding and what failure does it prevent?
flashcards.a: Designating one CDN PoP as the sole one allowed to fetch from origin on a miss; other PoPs fetch from the shield. Prevents the thundering herd where a popular object's TTL expires and dozens of edge PoPs simultaneously hit origin at once.

flashcards.q: What CDN cache-key mistake causes a personalization data leak, not just poor hit rate?
flashcards.a: Caching a personalized/auth-dependent response at a shared cache layer without Cache-Control: private -- another user can be served the first user's cached response, which is a security incident, not just a performance bug.

flashcards.q: Why is negative DNS caching (NXDOMAIN) important to know about?
flashcards.a: NXDOMAIN/NODATA answers are cached too, per the zone's SOA negative-cache TTL (commonly minutes to an hour). Querying a name before its record propagates can get you a cached 'doesn't exist' answer that outlives the record's actual creation.

flashcards.q: State the protobuf tag formula and decode tag byte 0x08.
flashcards.a: tag = (field_number << 3) | wire_type. 0x08 = binary 0000 1000 -> wire_type = last 3 bits = 0 (varint), field_number = remaining bits shifted right 3 = 1. So 0x08 is field 1, varint wire type.

flashcards.q: Encode int32 field 1 = 150 in protobuf wire format.
flashcards.a: Tag = (1<<3)|0 = 0x08. Value 150 as varint (7 bits/byte, MSB=continuation, little-endian groups) = 0x96 0x01 (two bytes since 150 needs more than 7 bits). Full encoding: 08 96 01 (3 bytes total).

flashcards.q: List the 4 protobuf wire types and what they encode.
flashcards.a: 0 = varint (int32/int64/bool/enum), 1 = 64-bit fixed, 2 = length-delimited (string/bytes/embedded message/packed repeated), 5 = 32-bit fixed.

flashcards.q: What protobuf schema change silently corrupts data with no error thrown?
flashcards.a: Reusing a field number for a different field after it was previously used and removed. An old message deserialized with the new field's meaning applied to old bytes produces wrong data silently -- nothing crashes because the parser doesn't validate a field number's historical meaning.

flashcards.q: Why does gRPC require HTTP/2 and cannot run on HTTP/1.1?
flashcards.a: gRPC needs trailing headers (HTTP/2 trailers frame) to carry the final grpc-status after the body since the outcome isn't known until the handler finishes, and it needs true independent multiplexed streams for concurrent RPCs plus native bidirectional streaming -- neither reliably exists on HTTP/1.1.

flashcards.q: Name the 4 gRPC RPC types and a use case for each.
flashcards.a: Unary (fetch-a-record). Server-streaming (log tail, live price feed -- 1 request, N responses). Client-streaming (chunked upload, batched telemetry with one final ack -- N requests, 1 response). Bidirectional streaming (chat-like, live audio-to-text -- N and M interleaved, independently paced).

flashcards.q: How does a gRPC deadline differ from a plain per-call timeout?
flashcards.a: A deadline is an absolute timestamp set once by the originating client and auto-propagated through every downstream call derived from that request's context. A per-call timeout is independently set at each hop with no shared knowledge -- so uncoordinated hop timeouts can collectively blow past what the original caller wanted.

flashcards.q: What happens to child RPCs when a parent gRPC context is cancelled?
flashcards.a: Cancelling the parent context cancels every child call derived from it, so downstream services stop doing work nobody's waiting on -- this only works if downstream calls actually derive their context from the inbound one; a fresh/unrelated context silently breaks propagation.

flashcards.q: List gRPC's status code count and 5 key codes with their meaning.
flashcards.a: 17 total codes including OK. Key ones: CANCELLED (client cancelled), DEADLINE_EXCEEDED (ran out of time), INVALID_ARGUMENT (client sent bad request, don't retry), UNAVAILABLE (transient, retry may help), FAILED_PRECONDITION (client must fix state before retrying, don't blindly retry).

flashcards.q: What does google.rpc.Status give you beyond a bare status code?
flashcards.a: Structured, typed error `details` (e.g. a BadRequest message listing which fields violated validation, or RetryInfo suggesting a backoff duration) so a client can programmatically branch on rich error content instead of parsing a human-readable message string.

flashcards.q: What is a gRPC interceptor, and where does auth validation belong?
flashcards.a: Middleware wrapping every RPC -- client-side interceptors wrap outgoing calls (inject auth, tracing), server-side wrap incoming calls (validate auth, rate-limit, metrics), composed in a chain analogous to HTTP middleware. Auth belongs in a server-side interceptor, not duplicated in every service method.

flashcards.q: When does gRPC beat REST, and when does REST win?
flashcards.a: gRPC wins for internal service-to-service calls needing low latency, strict schemas, streaming, and polyglot codegen. REST wins for public/third-party APIs and browser clients: curl-ability, standard HTTP caching (ETag/Cache-Control), and no proxy requirement (gRPC-Web needs Envoy or similar to reach browsers directly).

flashcards.q: What's the operational gotcha with load balancing gRPC traffic?
flashcards.a: gRPC keeps a single long-lived HTTP/2 connection per client-server pair. A plain L4/TCP load balancer only balances new CONNECTIONS, not requests within one -- one backend pod can get all the traffic while others sit idle. Fix: client-side load balancing or an L7-aware proxy (Envoy) that balances individual streams.

flashcards.q: Define safe and idempotent precisely, and list which verbs qualify for each.
flashcards.a: Safe: no intended server-side side effects (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE). Idempotent: N identical requests produce the same server STATE as 1 (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT, DELETE). Safe implies idempotent; idempotent does not imply safe.

flashcards.q: Why is PUT idempotent but POST is not, by definition?
flashcards.a: PUT is defined as 'store this representation AS the entire target resource' -- an end-state statement, so repeating it is a no-op by construction. POST is defined as 'create a new subordinate resource' -- repetition is definitionally the opposite of a no-op, since each call creates something new.

flashcards.q: Is PATCH idempotent?
flashcards.a: Not by default (RFC 5789 deliberately doesn't claim it is). Depends on the specific operation encoded in the patch document: 'set field to X' twice is idempotent in practice; 'increment field' twice is not.

flashcards.q: What's the network-layer retry rule that follows from safety/idempotency?
flashcards.a: Safe/idempotent methods (GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE) are safe to retry blindly on ambiguous failure. POST and non-provably-idempotent PATCH need a client-generated Idempotency-Key so a retry can't cause a duplicate side effect.

flashcards.q: How must an idempotency-key check be implemented to be correct under concurrency?
flashcards.a: Atomically -- reserve the key BEFORE executing the operation (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, checking affected-row count), never read-then-write. Naive read-then-write races when two retries arrive near-simultaneously and both pass the existence check.

flashcards.q: 401 vs 403 -- what's the distinction and why does conflating them break clients?
flashcards.a: 401 = no valid authentication (correct response: authenticate/refresh token). 403 = authenticated but not authorized (re-authenticating won't help). A client treating every 403 as 'token expired' loops refreshing a token that was never the problem.

flashcards.q: Why do 307 and 308 exist when 301/302 already redirect?
flashcards.a: 301/302 predate a strict method-preservation guarantee, and browsers historically rewrote a POST to a GET when following either, dropping the body. 307 (temporary) and 308 (permanent) are explicitly specified to preserve both the original method AND body across the redirect.

flashcards.q: How do ETags enable both caching and optimistic concurrency from one mechanism?
flashcards.a: Caching: If-None-Match on GET, matching ETag -> 304 with no body. Concurrency: If-Match on PUT/PATCH, matching ETag -> write proceeds; mismatch -> 412 Precondition Failed, preventing a silent lost update (compare-and-swap via headers).

flashcards.q: Strong vs weak ETag validators -- which is safe for optimistic concurrency?
flashcards.a: Strong validators guarantee byte-identical representations on a match; weak validators (W/"...") only guarantee semantic equivalence. Only strong validators are safe for compare-and-swap (If-Match) write safety and for range requests.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between Cache-Control: no-cache and no-store?
flashcards.a: no-store: never persist the response anywhere. no-cache: CAN be cached, but must revalidate with the origin before every reuse -- misleadingly named; it doesn't mean 'don't cache', it means 'don't reuse without checking first'.

flashcards.q: What does stale-while-revalidate=N trade off?
flashcards.a: Serves the stale cached copy immediately (zero added latency) while asynchronously revalidating in the background for up to N seconds; the next request gets the fresh copy. Trades a bounded staleness window for consistently low latency.

flashcards.q: Why is 429 retryable when most other 4xx codes aren't?
flashcards.a: Most 4xx mean the request itself is malformed/invalid -- retrying identically fails identically. 429 means the request was valid but rate-limited; it should carry a Retry-After header telling the client exactly when to retry, making it a scheduling instruction rather than a fatal error.

flashcards.q: What does a 304 response actually contain, and why does that matter for server cost?
flashcards.a: No body at all -- just a signal that the client's cached copy is still current. For expensive-to-generate resources, the real savings is the server-side generation work itself, provided the ETag is computed from something cheap (a version column, updated_at) rather than requiring a full render first.

flashcards.q: Idempotency is a property of server state, not of the HTTP response. Give the classic example that trips people up.
flashcards.a: A repeat DELETE on an already-deleted resource may return 404 instead of the first call's 200/204 -- the response differs, but the resource state ('it doesn't exist') is identical either way, so DELETE is still idempotent.

flashcards.q: GET is cacheable by default -- is POST ever cacheable?
flashcards.a: Yes, but only with explicit freshness information in the response, and it's rarely used in practice; GET remains the default cacheable method and the one caches are built to optimize for.

flashcards.q: Why did HTTP/1.1 pipelining fail?
flashcards.a: Responses had to return in request order (spec requirement), so one slow response head-of-line-blocked every faster response behind it, and real-world middlebox/proxy bugs mishandled pipelined traffic. No major browser shipped it enabled; Firefox removed the code entirely in v54 (2017).

flashcards.q: What workaround did browsers use for HTTP/1.1 HOL blocking, and what did it cost?
flashcards.a: 6 parallel TCP connections per origin (some browsers historically 2-8). Cost: 6x TCP handshakes, 6x TLS handshakes, 6x slow-start ramp-up, 6x server-side connection resources -- and each connection is still independently HOL-blocked.

flashcards.q: What are HTTP/2's two HPACK tables and their sizes?
flashcards.a: A static table of 61 predefined common header field name/value pairs, plus a per-connection dynamic table (default max size 4096 bytes) populated as headers are actually sent, so repeated headers (cookies, bearer tokens) are referenced by a 1-2 byte index instead of resent in full.

flashcards.q: What is HTTP/2's transport-layer HOL blocking gotcha?
flashcards.a: TCP delivers one ordered byte stream for the whole connection with no concept of 'stream.' One lost TCP segment stalls ALL multiplexed HTTP/2 streams behind it in the receive buffer, even ones unrelated to the loss -- can make HTTP/2 worse than 6 HTTP/1.1 connections on lossy (cellular) networks.

flashcards.q: Why did HTTP/2 server push die?
flashcards.a: The server can't know what the client already has cached, so naive push implementations re-pushed already-cached assets, wasting bandwidth in practice rather than saving a round trip. Chrome disabled it by default in Chrome 106 (October 2022) after data showed low adoption and no consistent win.

flashcards.q: What replaced HTTP/2 server push, and why is it safer?
flashcards.a: 103 Early Hints (RFC 8297): server sends an informational 103 response with Link/preload headers while still computing the real response, letting the client start fetching based on its OWN cache state -- avoiding push's cache-pollution failure mode.

flashcards.q: What transport does HTTP/3 run on, and why not just patch TCP instead?
flashcards.a: QUIC, built on UDP (RFC 9000/9114). TCP can't be evolved at the transport layer because it's baked into kernels and middleboxes across the whole internet (protocol ossification); QUIC sidesteps this by encrypting almost the entire packet so middleboxes can't meddle with it, and runs in userspace.

flashcards.q: How does QUIC solve transport-layer HOL blocking?
flashcards.a: Each QUIC stream has its own independent sequence space and loss-recovery/ack state (unlike TCP's single ordered byte stream for the whole connection). A lost UDP packet belongs to exactly one stream; only that stream stalls, others keep delivering immediately.

flashcards.q: Compare RTT cost for a fresh connection: TCP+TLS1.2 vs TCP+TLS1.3 vs QUIC.
flashcards.a: TCP+TLS1.2 ~3 RTT before app data flows. TCP+TLS1.3 collapses to ~2 RTT. QUIC integrates the handshake to ~1 RTT for a new connection, with 0-RTT resumption for repeat visits (data at 0 RTT, but restricted to idempotent requests due to replay risk).

flashcards.q: Why is 0-RTT data in QUIC unsafe for a POST/write?
flashcards.a: The first-flight 0-RTT data can be replayed by an attacker who captured it, since there's no fresh handshake proof yet -- safe only for idempotent/safe-to-duplicate operations, not for payments or other writes.

flashcards.q: How does a client discover a server supports HTTP/3, given QUIC has no ALPN-equivalent bootstrap?
flashcards.a: The server advertises `Alt-Svc: h3=":443"` in a response header over an existing HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 (TCP) connection; the client caches this and tries QUIC directly on the next visit, since ALPN itself requires an existing TLS/TCP handshake to negotiate over.

flashcards.q: Why does gRPC require HTTP/2, and is domain sharding still a good idea under HTTP/2/3?
flashcards.a: gRPC needs independent multiplexed streams and true bidirectional streaming, which HTTP/1.1 has no concept of. Domain sharding is now counterproductive: it fragments HPACK's shared dynamic table and forces multiple handshakes/slow-starts that a single multiplexed connection was designed to avoid.

flashcards.q: State the general formula for usable hosts given a prefix length, and the one exception.
flashcards.a: usable hosts = 2^(32-prefix) - 2 (subtract network and broadcast addresses). Exception: /31 (RFC 3021), used for point-to-point links -- both addresses are usable, no broadcast exists.

flashcards.q: Give host counts for /24, /27, and /22.
flashcards.a: /24 = 256 addresses, 254 usable. /27 = 32 addresses, 30 usable, block size 32. /22 = 1024 addresses, 1022 usable, spans four /24s.

flashcards.q: What is the block-size shortcut for fast subnet math?
flashcards.a: 256 minus the mask's last nonzero octet value = block size. E.g. mask 255.255.255.224 -> 256-224=32.

flashcards.q: State the routing rule for resolving multiple matching routes to the same destination.
flashcards.a: Longest prefix match always wins -- the most specific matching route is chosen, regardless of insertion order; ties on equal prefix length are broken by administrative distance then metric.

flashcards.q: What mechanism lets IPv4 avoid in-network fragmentation, and what ICMP message drives it?
flashcards.a: Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD, RFC 1191): sender sets DF; if a router can't forward without fragmenting, it drops the packet and returns ICMP Type 3 Code 4 (Fragmentation Needed and DF Set) with the next-hop MTU.

flashcards.q: Describe the PMTUD black hole failure and its observable symptom.
flashcards.a: A firewall blocks the ICMP 'frag needed' message, so the sender never learns to shrink packets. Symptom: TCP handshake and small requests work fine, but any payload crossing the MTU threshold hangs -- tcpdump shows a large packet leaving with no ACK and no ICMP response, retransmitted repeatedly until timeout.

flashcards.q: Give the four MTU numbers to know cold.
flashcards.a: Standard Ethernet 1500. PPPoE 1492 (8B PPPoE header). Jumbo frames 9000 (sometimes 9216). IPv6 minimum guaranteed 1280.

flashcards.q: Distinguish SNAT, DNAT, and PAT/NAPT.
flashcards.a: SNAT rewrites source address (outbound sharing). DNAT rewrites destination address (port-forward/LB). PAT/NAPT = SNAT + port rewrite, the mechanism that lets many hosts share one public IP, tracked by a state table keyed on the 4-tuple.

flashcards.q: What two categories of things break under NAT, and why?
flashcards.a: 1) Unsolicited inbound connections -- no state-table entry exists for a connection nobody inside initiated. 2) Protocols embedding IPs/ports in their payload (FTP active mode, SIP/SDP) -- NAT only rewrites headers, not application data, unless an ALG or STUN/TURN/ICE fixes the embedded address.

flashcards.q: List the concrete differences between IPv4 and IPv6 that matter in production.
flashcards.a: 32-bit (~4.3B, exhausted 2011) vs 128-bit (~3.4e38). ARP (broadcast) vs NDP (ICMPv6 multicast). Router fragmentation allowed vs never (host-only, ICMPv6 Packet Too Big). 20-60B variable header vs 40B fixed. IPv4 has a header checksum recomputed every hop; IPv6 removed it entirely, relying on L2/L4 checksums.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't IPv6 allow routers to fragment packets?
flashcards.a: Deliberate design: fragmentation cost is pushed entirely to the originating host (via an IPv6 Fragment extension header added only by the sender); routers that get an oversized packet just drop it and send ICMPv6 Packet Too Big -- PMTUD is mandatory, not optional, with no in-network fallback.

flashcards.q: What's the standard mitigation for a PMTUD black hole when you can't guarantee ICMP passes through?
flashcards.a: TCP MSS clamping at the border router/firewall -- rewrite the MSS option in SYN packets so TCP never tries to send a segment that would need fragmentation on that path.

flashcards.q: What does 'connection refused' tell you, and what's your first command to check it?
flashcards.a: Something actively rejected the SYN -- no listener on that port (OS sends RST) or an explicit firewall REJECT rule. First command: ss -tlnp on the target to confirm whether anything is actually listening.

flashcards.q: What does 'connection timed out' tell you, and what doesn't it tell you?
flashcards.a: It tells you no response arrived within your wait window -- silence. It tells you NOTHING about where the failure is: could be a firewall DROP, genuine unreachability, or an overloaded destination. Requires active probing (mtr, nc -zv) to localize.

flashcards.q: What are curl -w's timing fields, and are they cumulative or per-phase?
flashcards.a: time_namelookup (DNS), time_connect (+TCP), time_appconnect (+TLS), time_starttransfer (+server think time/TTFB), time_total (+transfer). They are CUMULATIVE -- subtract the previous phase's value to get that phase's actual duration.

flashcards.q: Why use mtr instead of one-shot traceroute for intermittent packet loss?
flashcards.a: mtr samples loss over time per hop across many packets. One-shot traceroute gives a single sample per hop and can't distinguish a transient blip (e.g. ICMP rate-limiting on a router) from sustained real loss.

flashcards.q: How do you tell if packet loss shown at one traceroute/mtr hop is real?
flashcards.a: Real loss persists from that hop through to the destination. Loss that appears at one hop and clears at the next is usually ICMP deprioritization on that specific router (slow to answer about itself, forwards real traffic fine) -- confirm by testing the actual application protocol end-to-end.

flashcards.q: How do you manually inspect a TLS handshake and certificate chain from the command line?
flashcards.a: openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host -- shows the cert chain, verify return code, negotiated protocol/cipher. curl -v also shows the cert chain in its verbose output.

flashcards.q: What does a large TIME_WAIT count indicate, and what's the real fix?
flashcards.a: A service opening many short-lived outbound connections is exhausting the ephemeral port range (~28,000 ports on Linux default), since each closed connection holds TIME_WAIT for ~2xMSL (~60s). Real fix is connection pooling/reuse in the application, not just tuning sysctls.

flashcards.q: Give the ss command to check if a process is actually listening, and the key gotcha in the output.
flashcards.a: ss -tlnp. Gotcha: 0.0.0.0 means listening on all interfaces, 127.0.0.1 means loopback-only -- a common 'works locally, unreachable from another host' bug is binding to loopback instead of 0.0.0.0 or the actual interface IP.

flashcards.q: Give the dig commands to diagnose a stale/wrong DNS answer.
flashcards.a: dig +trace (full resolution path from root) and dig @8.8.8.8 host (bypass your local cache, query a specific resolver directly) to compare against what your local resolver returns.

flashcards.q: Give the tcpdump filter for new outbound TCP connection attempts (SYN only) and its Wireshark equivalent.
flashcards.a: tcpdump: tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0 and tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-ack == 0. Wireshark: tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0.

flashcards.q: Give the tcpdump filter and Wireshark filter for TCP resets only.
flashcards.a: tcpdump: tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-rst != 0. Wireshark: tcp.flags.reset==1.

flashcards.q: How do you test raw port reachability without curl, and what does a success NOT prove?
flashcards.a: nc -zv host port (zero-I/O scan mode). A successful TCP connection does NOT prove the application protocol behind it is healthy -- a port can accept TCP connections while the service itself is broken at the HTTP/TLS layer.

flashcards.q: How do you manually reproduce an HTTP exchange over raw TCP and over TLS?
flashcards.a: Raw TCP: nc host 80, then type 'GET / HTTP/1.1', 'Host: host', blank line. Over TLS: openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host -quiet, then type the same HTTP request.

flashcards.q: TLS handshake completes but larger payloads hang forever. What's the likely cause, and how do you confirm it?
flashcards.a: MTU blackhole -- a hop drops oversized DF-set packets and the ICMP fragmentation-needed message that would fix it. Confirm with ping -M do -s <size> host to find the failing size threshold, and tcpdump to see repeated retransmissions with no ICMP response.

flashcards.q: Name four real-world causes of network partitions.
flashcards.a: Switch/top-of-rack failure, BGP misconfiguration/route leak, a security-group/NACL rule change, cross-AZ/region link failure. Most real partitions are partial and asymmetric, not clean/total/symmetric.

flashcards.q: Rank timeout, RST, and silent drop by diagnostic information, and explain why.
flashcards.a: RST is most informative (a live device actively answered/rejected). Timeout and silent drop are functionally identical to the client -- both give zero information and require active probing (mtr, checking SG/NACL rules) to localize.

flashcards.q: Why can a client see a timeout while the server's write actually completed?
flashcards.a: The write and its acknowledgment are separate network events -- the server can commit and send success, and that response/ACK can be lost on the way back. The client can't distinguish 'never arrived' from 'completed but confirmation lost.'

flashcards.q: TCP's own retransmission: what's the initial RTO and backoff behavior, and does it usually matter to the application?
flashcards.a: Initial RTO is RTT-derived (often ~1s with no prior sample), doubling (exponential backoff) each retry, giving up after a bounded count (tcp_retries2, often ~15-30min on an established connection). Application timeouts almost always fire first, so this OS-level budget rarely matters in practice.

flashcards.q: What is split brain and why is 'just elect a new leader' insufficient?
flashcards.a: During a partition, both sides can conclude they're the sole leader and both accept writes. Electing a new leader without fencing leaves the old leader able to keep acting if it hasn't detected the partition -- you can end up with two active writers.

flashcards.q: What is STONITH and why is it more reliable than asking a node to step down?
flashcards.a: 'Shoot The Other Node In The Head' -- forcibly power off/reboot a suspected node via an out-of-band channel (IPMI, cloud terminate API) that doesn't depend on the node's cooperation. A partitioned-but-alive node can't defend itself against a power-off command, unlike a graceful step-down request it might never receive or honor.

flashcards.q: Describe the MTU blackhole mechanism precisely.
flashcards.a: Sender sets DF (Don't Fragment); a router that can't forward an oversized packet should send ICMP Type 3 Code 4 (Fragmentation Needed) back, but a firewall drops that ICMP message. The sender never learns to shrink packets and keeps sending the same oversized ones into the void.

flashcards.q: What's the classic MTU blackhole symptom, exactly?
flashcards.a: TCP handshake completes fine (small packets), small HTTP requests work, but a TLS handshake with a large cert chain or any large payload hangs indefinitely -- those are the first packets large enough to hit the MTU ceiling.

flashcards.q: What's the practical fix for an MTU blackhole when you don't control the firewall dropping ICMP?
flashcards.a: MSS clamping at a gateway/tunnel endpoint you DO control -- rewrites the TCP MSS option in SYN/SYN-ACK to force smaller segments from the start, rather than depending on ICMP feedback from a path you don't own. Standard on VPN/tunnel endpoints since tunneling overhead shrinks effective MTU.

flashcards.q: Connection pool exhaustion: how do you distinguish a leak from genuine under-capacity?
flashcards.a: Check the downstream's own connection view (e.g. Postgres pg_stat_activity): connections sitting idle/idle-in-transaction for a long time = leak (missing finally/context manager). Connections genuinely active/busy = capacity problem (pool too small or slow queries).

flashcards.q: NXDOMAIN vs SERVFAIL -- what does each imply?
flashcards.a: NXDOMAIN: authoritative server answered, the name genuinely doesn't exist (or a cached negative answer). SERVFAIL: resolver couldn't get a valid answer at all -- unreachable authoritative server, timeout, or DNSSEC validation failure -- points at the resolution chain being broken, not a missing record.

flashcards.q: What is split-horizon DNS and what bug does it commonly cause?
flashcards.a: A zone returns different answers depending on whether the query originates internally or externally. Misconfigured, it causes 'works from my VPN, fails for external users/CI' bugs, since internal engineers get a different resolution than what real external clients see.

flashcards.q: Why do most real partitions being 'partial and asymmetric' matter for system design?
flashcards.a: A can reach B but B can't reach A (asymmetric routing/one-directional firewall rule), or a link is flaky rather than fully down. Designs/tests that only model a clean, total, symmetric partition miss the failure modes that actually happen in production.

flashcards.q: Why might a security perimeter deliberately choose DROP over REJECT despite REJECT being easier to debug?
flashcards.a: REJECT confirms to a potential attacker that a host exists and a specific rule is blocking them (useful reconnaissance information). DROP gives no information back at all -- the same informativeness that helps you during an incident helps an attacker during reconnaissance.

flashcards.q: Name the 7 OSI layers in order.
flashcards.a: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

flashcards.q: How does TCP/IP's 4-layer model map to OSI's 7?
flashcards.a: Application (collapses Session+Presentation+Application), Transport (=OSI Transport), Internet (=OSI Network), Link (collapses Physical+Data Link; some texts split this back into 5 layers).

flashcards.q: What is the Ethernet header size, and what's added by an 802.1Q VLAN tag?
flashcards.a: 14 bytes (6B dst MAC + 6B src MAC + 2B EtherType), plus a 4-byte FCS trailer. A VLAN tag adds 4 more bytes (max frame goes from 1518 to 1522).

flashcards.q: What are the minimum IPv4, IPv6, TCP, and UDP header sizes?
flashcards.a: IPv4: 20B (up to 60B with options). IPv6: 40B fixed, no options field. TCP: 20B (up to 60B with options). UDP: 8B flat, always.

flashcards.q: Compute total non-payload overhead for a TCP segment on a 1500-byte-MTU Ethernet link with no options, and the resulting usable payload.
flashcards.a: 14 (Eth) + 20 (IP) + 20 (TCP) + 4 (FCS) = 58 bytes overhead. Usable payload = 1500 - 20 - 20 = 1460 bytes, which is the default MSS on a 1500-MTU path.

flashcards.q: Why did TCP/IP win over OSI's own protocol suite (X.25, CLNP)?
flashcards.a: "Rough consensus and running code" beat design-by-committee: TCP/IP was already deployed and iterating on real networks years before OSI's transport/network protocols were finalized.

flashcards.q: Does the OSI model exist as running protocols today?
flashcards.a: No. It survives purely as shared vocabulary ("layer 3 switch", "layer 7 load balancer") describing devices built on a TCP/IP stack, not as deployed protocols.

flashcards.q: What's the correct diagnostic ladder for "the network is slow"?
flashcards.a: ping (L3 reachability) -> traceroute/mtr (L3 path) -> nc -zv/curl -v (L4 reachability) -> tcpdump (raw bytes) -> application logs (L7) LAST.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between getting an RST vs a silent timeout when connecting to a port?
flashcards.a: RST means the destination actively refused (something's up, but nothing listening on that port) -- fast. A silent timeout means the packet was filtered or the host is unreachable -- slow, no information.

flashcards.q: What is duplex mismatch, and what's its observable symptom?
flashcards.a: One end of an Ethernet link auto-negotiates full-duplex while the other is half-duplex. Symptom: throughput collapses to a fraction of link speed while ethtool -S shows climbing rx_crc_errors / late collisions on the half-duplex side; app logs show only vague intermittent slowness.

flashcards.q: Where does TLS fit in the OSI model, mechanically?
flashcards.a: Functionally it does what OSI called Presentation (encryption/formatting), but it's implemented as a library between the application and the transport socket -- there's no standalone OSI Presentation-layer protocol in a real stack.

flashcards.q: Why don't modern technologies like QUIC or eBPF/XDP map cleanly to one OSI layer?
flashcards.a: QUIC moves transport-layer responsibility (reliability, congestion control) into a user-space library riding over UDP; eBPF/XDP processes packets in the kernel driver context before the normal stack runs. Both deliberately span layer boundaries rather than fitting one box.

flashcards.q: What does REST actually buy you that GraphQL and gRPC don't, mechanically?
flashcards.a: Free HTTP-level caching and universal tooling: a GET with a stable URL can be cached by any intermediary (CDN, browser, proxy) with zero extra work. GraphQL's POST-body queries and gRPC's binary framing don't get this for free.

flashcards.q: How much smaller is Protobuf than the equivalent JSON payload, roughly?
flashcards.a: Commonly 2-5x smaller on the wire, plus gRPC gets HTTP/2 multiplexing and native deadline propagation that plain JSON-over-HTTP doesn't have by convention.

flashcards.q: What is the GraphQL N+1 problem and what fixes it?
flashcards.a: A naive resolver for a list field issues one DB query per parent item (N) plus the original list query (1). DataLoader batches all requests for the same field type issued within one event-loop tick into a single WHERE id IN (...) query.

flashcards.q: GraphQL has no default depth or cost limit. What two controls must you add, and what do they each catch?
flashcards.a: Depth limiting (reject queries nested past ~5-10 levels) catches deep nesting attacks. Cost/complexity analysis (assign per-field cost, scaled by list-size arguments, reject over a budget e.g. 1000 points) catches wide queries that depth limiting alone misses.

flashcards.q: What HTTP status code does GraphQL return on a partial resolver failure, and why does that matter?
flashcards.a: 200 OK, with an `errors` array alongside partial `data`. It matters because clients can't rely on status-code checking alone and must inspect the errors array explicitly.

flashcards.q: WebSocket vs SSE: what's the precise deciding question?
flashcards.a: Does the client need to send data on the same low-latency channel mid-stream? If yes, WebSocket (full duplex). If the client only receives (ticker, notifications, LLM token streaming), use SSE -- it's plain HTTP with automatic reconnect built into the EventSource spec.

flashcards.q: Why does SSE pass through corporate proxies and CDNs more easily than WebSocket?
flashcards.a: SSE is a normal long-lived HTTP GET response, so it flows through ordinary HTTP infrastructure. WebSocket requires an `Upgrade: websocket` handshake that many proxies/firewalls don't handle correctly, and needs connection affinity at the load balancer.

flashcards.q: What three things must a webhook receiver implement that the provider does NOT guarantee for you?
flashcards.a: Retry-safe idempotency (dedupe by provider event ID, atomic insert-or-ignore), signature verification (HMAC over the raw body before trusting the payload), and handling of out-of-order delivery (no ordering guarantee across retries).

flashcards.q: Long-polling vs plain polling -- what's the mechanical difference?
flashcards.a: Plain polling: client requests at a fixed interval, gets an immediate (possibly empty) response every time. Long-polling: server holds the request open (commonly 20-30s) until data is ready or a timeout, then the client immediately reissues -- better latency, but ties up a connection per waiting client.

flashcards.q: Name three concrete cases where a message queue beats any request/response protocol.
flashcards.a: 1) Downstream is unreliable/slow -- queue buffers instead of the caller timing out. 2) Need at-least-once delivery with replay (Kafka retains messages for a configurable window, e.g. 7 days). 3) Fan-out to many consumers at different processing speeds without adding to the producer's latency budget.

flashcards.q: When is a message queue the WRONG tool despite decoupling being attractive?
flashcards.a: When the caller needs a synchronous answer right now to proceed (e.g., render a page). A queue just relocates the wait (polling or holding a connection for the eventual result); it doesn't remove it, and it adds queue operational overhead on top.

flashcards.q: What's the single most common real GraphQL production incident?
flashcards.a: Naive resolver N+1 -- a query that looks fine syntactically fires one DB query per item in a list because DataLoader-style batching wasn't implemented, causing p99 spikes on specific queries.

flashcards.q: gRPC deadlines vs plain HTTP timeouts -- what's the mechanical difference?
flashcards.a: gRPC deadlines propagate as wire metadata through the whole call chain, so a downstream service sees the REMAINING time budget, not a fresh timeout. Plain HTTP has no equivalent unless every hop manually threads a deadline header through the chain.

flashcards.q: Walk through the three-way handshake with sequence numbers for client ISN=1000, server ISN=5000.
flashcards.a: SYN(seq=1000) -> SYN-ACK(seq=5000, ack=1001) -> ACK(ack=5001). SYN consumes one sequence number even with zero payload bytes.

flashcards.q: List all 11 TCP states.
flashcards.a: CLOSED, LISTEN, SYN_SENT, SYN_RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN_WAIT_1, FIN_WAIT_2, CLOSE_WAIT, CLOSING, LAST_ACK, TIME_WAIT.

flashcards.q: What does a pileup of sockets in CLOSE_WAIT mean?
flashcards.a: The peer sent a FIN and the kernel acked it, but the local application never called close(). This is an application resource leak, essentially never a network problem.

flashcards.q: Why does TIME_WAIT exist? Give both reasons.
flashcards.a: 1) Absorb any delayed duplicate segment from this exact connection so it can't be misdelivered into a new connection reusing the same 4-tuple. 2) Ensure the final ACK is retransmittable if the peer's LAST_ACK-state FIN retransmission arrives because the original ACK was lost.

flashcards.q: What is TIME_WAIT's duration per RFC 793 theory vs actual Linux implementation?
flashcards.a: RFC 793 assumes MSL=2min so 2xMSL=4min theoretically. Linux hardcodes TIME_WAIT to a flat 60 seconds (TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN), not configurable via sysctl, regardless of MSL assumptions.

flashcards.q: Distinguish tcp_fin_timeout from TIME_WAIT duration.
flashcards.a: tcp_fin_timeout (default 60s) governs how long an orphaned socket sits in FIN_WAIT_2 -- a different, distinct knob. It does not control TIME_WAIT's duration, which is hardcoded separately.
