flashcards.a: Forget gate: decides what fraction of long-term memory to erase. Input gate: decides what fraction of new info to write. Candidate (tanh, signed): the actual content proposed for writing. Output gate: decides how much of the cell state to expose as the hidden state.

flashcards.q: How does GRU differ structurally from LSTM, and what's the practical parameter savings?
flashcards.a: GRU merges the forget and input gates into a single update gate, and merges the cell state and hidden state into one vector, removing LSTM's separate long-term-memory highway. This gives roughly 25% fewer parameters at the same hidden size (3 gate weight sets vs 4).

flashcards.q: State the two structural reasons transformers replaced RNNs/LSTMs for large-scale sequence modeling.
flashcards.a: 1) Path length: O(1) attention hop between any two positions vs O(n) sequential RNN steps, giving far more reliable long-range dependency learning. 2) Parallelism: RNN step t depends on step t-1 finishing, so training can't parallelize across the sequence dimension; self-attention computes the whole sequence's interactions in one batched matmul, fully parallel across positions.

flashcards.q: What does a transformer trade for its O(1) cross-position path length?
flashcards.a: O(n^2) time and memory for the attention score matrix -- at n=8,192 one head's score matrix is on the order of hundreds of MB at fp16, and at n=100,000 it's infeasible to materialize directly without tiling (FlashAttention).

flashcards.q: When is a 1D CNN still the right choice for a sequence task?
flashcards.a: When the pattern being detected is local and roughly position-independent (phoneme boundaries, ECG motifs, genomic local patterns) and/or when low latency and cheap, parallel, fixed-cost-per-position compute matters more than modeling unbounded-range, content-dependent dependencies.

flashcards.q: When is an RNN/LSTM still the right choice over a transformer in production?
flashcards.a: True streaming with unbounded sequence length and a hard fixed memory budget (RNN state is a constant-size vector; a transformer's KV cache grows linearly with context length), and tiny-footprint edge/embedded deployment where a transformer's attention matrix and parameter count don't fit at all.

flashcards.q: What is the core architectural innovation of Mamba versus classical (S4-era) state-space models?
flashcards.a: Mamba makes the step size and transition matrices functions of the current input token (a 'selective' SSM), letting the model dynamically choose what to remember or forget based on content -- classical SSMs had fixed transition parameters regardless of input, so couldn't selectively attend to content.

flashcards.q: What is Mamba's reported complexity advantage over transformer attention, and what is the current (2026) status of SSMs replacing transformers?
flashcards.a: Linear-time and constant-memory-per-step scaling in sequence length versus attention's O(n^2), with demonstrated benefit on sequences up to roughly 1M tokens on some tasks. Status: an active, promising research direction, NOT a confirmed replacement -- pure SSMs haven't displaced transformers as the frontier LLM default, and much current work builds hybrids interleaving attention and SSM layers instead.

flashcards.q: Why can't gradient clipping alone rescue a vanilla RNN's ability to learn long-range dependencies?
flashcards.a: Clipping only bounds gradients that are too large; it does nothing for gradients that have already vanished to near-zero, since there's no meaningful magnitude left to rescale. Long-range learning requires an architectural gradient highway (LSTM/GRU gating, or attention/SSM), not a training-loop adjustment.

flashcards.q: What is the single architectural difference between an encoder (BERT) and a decoder (GPT) Transformer block?
flashcards.a: The attention mask. Decoders use a causal mask so token i only attends to tokens 0..i (needed for autoregressive generation). Encoders use no mask, so every token attends to every other token bidirectionally.

flashcards.q: BERT has two pretraining objectives. Which one turned out not to matter, and what replaced/removed it?
flashcards.a: Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) turned out not to matter — RoBERTa dropped it entirely, trained longer on more data with bigger batches, and matched or beat BERT. MLM (masked language modeling) is the objective that does the real work.

flashcards.q: Why does mean pooling usually beat [CLS] pooling for sentence embeddings on a non-fine-tuned BERT checkpoint?
flashcards.a: [CLS]'s only pretraining signal was NSP, a weak, largely-useless objective, so its raw embedding was never optimized to summarize sentence meaning. Mean pooling aggregates every token's contextual embedding instead of relying on one under-trained token.

flashcards.q: When is [CLS] pooling actually the right choice?
flashcards.a: After fine-tuning a classification head directly on top of [CLS] for a specific task — that fine-tuning is what makes the token's representation meaningful.

flashcards.q: State the bi-encoder vs cross-encoder difference precisely, in terms of what's precomputable.
flashcards.a: A bi-encoder embeds query and document independently, so document vectors are precomputed offline and search is O(1)/query via ANN lookup. A cross-encoder feeds query+document jointly through one model, so the score depends on both together and cannot be precomputed — it costs O(n) full forward passes for n candidates.

flashcards.q: Give the rough latency numbers: ANN search over 10M docs vs cross-encoder reranking 100 candidates vs cross-encoder over the full 10M corpus.
flashcards.a: ANN search over 10M docs: single-digit-to-low-double-digit ms. Cross-encoder reranking 100 candidates: ~50-100ms on GPU. Cross-encoder over the full 10M corpus: on the order of hours per query (10M forward passes) — never done in practice.

flashcards.q: Why can't a cross-encoder's document-side computation be cached across different queries?
flashcards.a: Because attention runs jointly across query and document tokens through every layer, so the document's internal representations are influenced by the specific query tokens attending into them — there's no clean document-only intermediate state to freeze and reuse.

flashcards.q: How does ColBERT's late interaction relate to bi-encoders and cross-encoders?
flashcards.a: ColBERT keeps a per-token embedding for query and document (precomputed independently, like a bi-encoder) and scores with MaxSim (best-matching document token per query token, summed). It recovers token-level precision closer to a cross-encoder while staying precomputable, at the cost of storage scaling with total token count.

flashcards.q: Name four production tasks where a fine-tuned encoder beats a generative LLM, and roughly how much cheaper/faster.
flashcards.a: Classification, NER, retrieval embeddings, and moderation. Encoders run roughly 15-250x faster and 20-200x more cost/energy-efficient than an LLM prompted for the same fixed-label task, at equal or better accuracy.

flashcards.q: What determines whether a task should use an encoder or a decoder-based LLM?
flashcards.a: The shape of the output. Fixed labels, embeddings, or bounded extraction want an encoder (one forward pass, deterministic bounded output space). Open-ended generation, reasoning, or tasks needing natural-language justification want a decoder/LLM.

flashcards.q: What did ModernBERT change relative to the original 2018 BERT architecture?
flashcards.a: Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) instead of learned absolute positions, Flash Attention, alternating local/global attention layers, GeGLU activations, and an 8192-token context window, trained on 2T tokens of text and code — decoder-side advances retrofitted onto the encoder-only architecture.

flashcards.q: Why is BERT structurally unable to generate text the way GPT does?
flashcards.a: Bidirectional attention means every position already has access to the full sequence including future tokens, so there is no well-defined next-token distribution conditioned only on the past — the core mechanism autoregressive generation requires.

flashcards.q: A reranking pipeline's p99 latency blows the budget. What's the highest-leverage fix?
flashcards.a: Shrink the shortlist size fed to the cross-encoder (e.g. rerank top 20-50 instead of top 200-500) — cross-encoder cost is linear in candidate count, so this is almost always more effective than optimizing the model itself.

flashcards.q: What's the architectural difference between BERT (encoder-only) and T5 (encoder-decoder)?
flashcards.a: T5 has a bidirectional encoder that processes input once, plus a causal decoder that autoregressively generates output while cross-attending into the encoder output — built for seq2seq tasks with variable-length output. BERT has no decoder and cannot generate new token sequences; it produces labels, spans, or vectors.

flashcards.q: Why does transfer learning work — what do early vs late layers of a pretrained network actually learn?
flashcards.a: Hierarchical feature reuse: early layers learn general, broadly reusable patterns (edges, subword co-occurrence); late layers compose those into task-specific representations. Reusing general early layers means the target task only needs data to relearn the specific mapping, not the whole hierarchy.

flashcards.q: You have 800 labeled examples for a task close to the base model's pretraining domain. Where on the adaptation spectrum do you start?
flashcards.a: Frozen-feature extraction (freeze the base, train only a new head) or small-rank PEFT. Full fine-tuning on 800 examples risks overfitting and catastrophic forgetting.

flashcards.q: What is the observable symptom of catastrophic forgetting?
flashcards.a: A model fine-tuned on a narrow task suddenly fails at general capabilities it had before fine-tuning — e.g. a support-ticket classifier can no longer answer a general-knowledge question it used to get right. Caught via a held-out general-capability eval run before and after fine-tuning.

flashcards.q: How do discriminative (layer-wise) learning rates reduce catastrophic forgetting?
flashcards.a: They assign smaller learning rates to early (general-feature) layers and larger rates to late (task-specific) layers, typically via multiplicative decay per layer group (~0.9-0.95), so general features move minimally while task-specific layers adapt fully.

flashcards.q: State the 'dark knowledge' argument for why soft targets beat hard labels in distillation.
flashcards.a: A hard label says one class is right and all others are equally wrong. A teacher's full probability distribution encodes real similarity structure between classes (e.g. an ambiguous '2' getting P(2)=0.7, P(7)=0.25) that a one-hot label discards entirely — that structure is extra supervisory signal (Hinton et al., 2015).

flashcards.q: Write the knowledge distillation loss and explain the T^2 term.
flashcards.a: L = alpha * T^2 * KL(softmax_T(teacher) || softmax_T(student)) + (1-alpha) * CE(hard_label, student). T^2 corrects for softmax_T's gradient shrinking roughly as 1/T^2 as temperature rises, so the KL term's contribution isn't numerically drowned out at high T.

flashcards.q: What does temperature do in distillation, and what happens at T=1?
flashcards.a: Temperature softens (flattens) the teacher's output distribution so the useful signal in small probabilities over wrong classes becomes numerically visible instead of being drowned out by an overconfident near-one-hot softmax. At T=1 you're using the raw softmax, which degenerates distillation toward plain supervised learning on the teacher's argmax.

flashcards.q: Give DistilBERT's compression and retention numbers.
flashcards.a: ~97% of BERT-base's GLUE average (77.0 vs 79.5), at 40% smaller (66M vs 110M params) and roughly 60% faster inference on CPU.

flashcards.q: Give TinyBERT-4's compression and retention numbers, and what technique lets it compress harder than DistilBERT.
flashcards.a: 7.5x smaller (14.5M params), 9.4x faster, ~96.8% of BERT-base's GLUE average. It uses two-stage feature-level distillation (matching hidden states and attention matrices, not just final logits), giving a richer per-layer training signal than DistilBERT's response-only distillation.

flashcards.q: Name the three types of knowledge distillation by what's matched between teacher and student.
flashcards.a: Response distillation (final output logits/probabilities only), feature distillation (intermediate hidden states / attention matrices), and relation distillation (relationships between examples, e.g. pairwise similarity, rather than any single example's output).

flashcards.q: What is the licensing constraint that actually threatens real-world distillation projects?
flashcards.a: Most frontier providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, xAI) have anti-competitive-distillation clauses in their terms of service prohibiting use of model outputs to train a competing model. This is not hypothetical — it is the substance of a real, public OpenAI-vs-DeepSeek dispute alleging ToS violation via output extraction at scale.

flashcards.q: When is distillation the wrong call?
flashcards.a: When you already have enough labeled data to fine-tune the small student directly (skip the teacher-management overhead), when the task exceeds the student's capacity regardless of teacher quality (compression has a floor), or when there's no latency/cost pressure justifying the engineering investment (low QPS: just ship the big model).

flashcards.q: How do PEFT (e.g. LoRA) and knowledge distillation differ in what problem they solve?
flashcards.a: PEFT adapts one existing model to a new task by training small additional parameters while freezing the base — it's a fine-tuning technique. Distillation transfers capability from one model into a different, smaller architecture — it's a compression technique. They compose: fine-tune a large model first, then distill it into a small deployed model.

flashcards.q: How do you distill from a hosted frontier LLM you only access via API (no logit access)?
flashcards.a: Sequence-level distillation: generate a large volume of (input, teacher-generation) pairs and supervised-fine-tune the student on the teacher's generated text as the target. This loses the dark-knowledge benefit since you don't have the teacher's token-level probability distribution, and it may violate the provider's ToS if the teacher is a competing service.

flashcards.q: Precisely distinguish tokenization, stemming, and lemmatization.
flashcards.a: Tokenization segments text into units, no information loss. Stemming chops affixes via fixed rules, fast, can produce non-words ('universal' -> 'univers'). Lemmatization maps to a dictionary base form using part-of-speech, slower, always produces a real word.

flashcards.q: Give an example a stemmer cannot handle but a lemmatizer can.
flashcards.a: 'better' -> 'good' (adjective comparative to base form) or 'saw' -> 'see' (irregular past tense). Neither has a shared substring for rule-based stemming to exploit; both need dictionary/POS knowledge.

flashcards.q: Why does removing stopwords break phrase search and semantic search?
flashcards.a: Phrase search: removing a stopword can change query meaning entirely ('The Who' minus 'the' becomes just 'Who'). Semantic search: function words like negations ('not') carry structural signal a transformer's attention relies on; removing them can flip a sentence's meaning.

flashcards.q: Derive TF-IDF and explain why a term appearing in every document scores zero.
flashcards.a: TF-IDF(t,d) = TF(t,d) * IDF(t), where IDF(t) = log(N/df(t)). A term in every document has df(t)=N, so IDF = log(1) = 0, contributing nothing — this is algorithmic stopword removal, arrived at by formula instead of a hand-curated list.

flashcards.q: What two corrections does BM25 add over raw TF-IDF, and what do the parameters k1 and b control?
flashcards.a: Term-frequency saturation (k1, typically 1.2-2.0): score approaches k1+1 asymptotically rather than growing linearly with repeated term occurrences. Length normalization (b, typically 0.75): penalizes documents longer than the corpus average, since length alone increases the chance of containing any query term.

flashcards.q: Write the BM25 scoring formula.
flashcards.a: BM25(D,Q) = sum over t in Q of: IDF(t) * (f(t,D)*(k1+1)) / (f(t,D) + k1*(1-b+b*|D|/avgdl)), where f(t,D) is term frequency in D, |D| is document length, avgdl is corpus average document length.

flashcards.q: Why did subword tokenization (BPE/WordPiece/SentencePiece) replace whole-word tokenization for neural models?
flashcards.a: Whole-word tokenization collapses any out-of-vocabulary word into an unrecoverable <UNK> token, destroying information. Character-level has no OOV problem but produces very long sequences, wasting capacity relearning word structure. Subword tokenization keeps common words as single tokens, decomposes rare words into meaningful pieces, and has no true OOV case.

flashcards.q: What is mojibake and where does it silently break a retrieval pipeline?
flashcards.a: Mojibake is garbled text from decoding with the wrong character encoding (e.g. 'Ã©' instead of 'é'). It shows up as documents that tokenize/embed into meaningless garbage — a garbage lexical index entry, or an embedding vector for noise instead of content — with no thrown error.

flashcards.q: Why does NFC vs NFD Unicode normalization cause silent retrieval failures, and where should normalization happen?
flashcards.a: The same visual character (e.g. 'é') can have multiple valid byte representations (precomposed NFC vs base+combining-mark NFD) — visually identical but byte-different, so exact-match or hashing treats them as different strings. Normalize to NFC (or NFKC) at the ingestion boundary, applied consistently to both the query and document paths, before tokenization or hashing.

flashcards.q: Your team adds lowercase/stem/strip-punctuation preprocessing ahead of a dense embedding model and retrieval quality drops. Why?
flashcards.a: The embedding model was trained on natural, unmodified text. Feeding it stemmed non-words, lowercased text, or punctuation-stripped text produces token sequences and structure patterns it never saw in training, degrading embedding quality silently — the model still returns a vector, just a worse one.

flashcards.q: Why is a classical stem-then-search pipeline a specific risk for a 22-locale product?
flashcards.a: Stemmers/lemmatizers are hand-built per-language resources; high-quality coverage exists for only a few dozen languages, with none at all for many others. A pipeline whose correctness depends on stemming has silently uneven quality per locale, usually undiscovered until a locale-specific bug report.

flashcards.q: Give an example of a term that should NOT be stemmed, and why.
flashcards.a: An exact identifier like a SKU code or 'iOS17' — stemming rules aren't aware of identifier semantics and can mangle the string so it no longer matches the literal text, destroying the exact match that identifier-style lexical search depends on.

flashcards.q: What's the correct amount of preprocessing for a pipeline feeding a dense embedding model?
flashcards.a: Close to none: Unicode-normalize (NFC), strip genuine non-content artifacts (control characters, encoding errors), and otherwise feed text as close to its natural form as possible — no stemming, no stopword removal, no aggressive case folding.

flashcards.q: What does a few-shot example actually teach a model, for tasks it already has strong pretrained competence at?
flashcards.a: Primarily output format and label space (exact label strings, JSON structure, answer length/granularity), not the underlying task capability — the model likely already 'knows' the task and mostly needs disambiguation of expected output shape.

flashcards.q: How many few-shot examples before returns typically flatten, with a concrete number?
flashcards.a: Roughly 4-5 examples for standard classification-style tasks. One measured case: 5 few-shot examples lifted a GPT-4o classification task from 84.5% to 91.5%, a 7-point jump over zero-shot; beyond that, added examples show diminishing or negative returns.

flashcards.q: What is recency bias in few-shot prompting and how do you exploit it deliberately?
flashcards.a: Examples placed closer to the query (typically last) have disproportionate influence on the model's output. Exploit it by placing your highest-quality, most representative example last in a fixed few-shot set.

flashcards.q: State chain-of-thought's original finding (Wei et al. 2022) and its key caveat.
flashcards.a: Prompting a model to produce intermediate reasoning steps substantially improves accuracy on multi-step reasoning tasks. Caveat: this benefit is emergent with model scale/capability — below a threshold, CoT prompting shows flat or negative effects, since the model can produce reasoning-shaped text without the capacity to make it track toward correctness.

flashcards.q: What is zero-shot CoT and who introduced it?
flashcards.a: Kojima et al. (2022) showed that simply appending 'Let's think step by step' to a zero-shot prompt (no worked examples needed) recovers much of few-shot CoT's benefit, since the instruction alone often elicits reasoning-trace behavior in models with the underlying capacity.

flashcards.q: Should you tell a reasoning-native model (o-series, Claude extended thinking, DeepSeek-R1) to 'think step by step'? Why or why not?
flashcards.a: Usually no. These models are trained via RL to produce internal extended reasoning before answering — a trained architectural behavior, not a prompted one. Explicit CoT instructions are often redundant and measured cases show they can actively reduce accuracy by fighting the model's own trained reasoning process.

flashcards.q: Why does self-consistency (sampled majority vote) improve accuracy over single-pass CoT?
flashcards.a: Wrong answers tend to arise from idiosyncratic, uncorrelated reasoning errors, while correct answers tend to be reachable via multiple different valid reasoning paths converging on the same result — majority vote across N samples statistically favors the correct answer as N grows, given each path is better than chance.

flashcards.q: Give the real accuracy numbers for self-consistency on GSM8K with PaLM-540B.
flashcards.a: Standard CoT: 56.5% accuracy. Self-consistency with N=40 samples: 74.4% — an 18-point gain, at N times the token/latency cost.

flashcards.q: Why shouldn't self-consistency be applied uniformly to all production traffic?
flashcards.a: It costs N times the tokens and latency/compute, and its accuracy gains plateau — or even decline on problems already being solved correctly, since extra sampling on easy problems adds noise rather than correcting genuine errors. It should be gated behind a confidence check and applied selectively to genuinely hard problems.

flashcards.q: Rank, in order, what actually moves accuracy most reliably in a production LLM system.
flashcards.a: 1) Eval set quality (can you detect real change at all), 2) retrieval/context quality for RAG systems, 3) structured output constraints, 4) prompt wording — real but smaller in effect than folklore claims; most magic-phrase advice does not survive measurement.

flashcards.q: What is least-to-most prompting and when would you reach for it over standard CoT?
flashcards.a: Decomposing a problem into an explicit ordered sequence of simpler subproblems, solving each and feeding prior answers forward. Use it when a problem has genuine compositional structure (multi-hop questions) that a single continuous CoT trace tends to skip or conflate steps on.

flashcards.q: What is step-back prompting?
flashcards.a: Having the model first answer a more general, abstracted version of the question (e.g. 'what principle governs this?') before answering the specific question, surfacing relevant background knowledge it might otherwise fail to retrieve when jumping straight to the specific case (Zheng et al., 2023).

flashcards.q: What is CoT faithfulness, and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: A reasoning-native model's visible chain-of-thought trace does not always reflect its actual internal decision process. Treating a visible CoT as a reliable explanation of why the model answered as it did, rather than merely a useful scaffold, is a trap — the trace can look plausible without being causally accurate.

flashcards.q: Name the four distinct SageMaker inference products and their core cost/latency profile.
flashcards.a: Real-Time Endpoints: always-on, sub-second, billed per instance-hour regardless of load. Serverless Inference: scale-to-zero, 1-5s cold start, billed per invocation. Async Inference: queued, up to 1GB payload/1hr processing, scales to zero. Batch Transform: offline job, no live endpoint, billed per instance-hour for job duration.

flashcards.q: What is JumpStart, and why isn't it a fifth SageMaker inference product?
flashcards.a: JumpStart is a model zoo/deployment accelerator that pre-packages open models for one-click or one-API deployment onto one of the four actual inference products (Real-Time, Serverless, Async, or Batch Transform) — it's not a distinct serving mode itself.

flashcards.q: Contrast the cost-model shape of Bedrock on-demand versus self-hosted vLLM.
flashcards.a: Bedrock on-demand is linear in actual token usage (pay per token processed). Self-hosting is a step function in provisioned capacity (pay per instance-hour regardless of utilization) — at low/spiky usage Bedrock wins, at high steady utilization self-hosting's effective per-token cost drops below Bedrock's.

flashcards.q: Describe Bedrock's three service tiers.
flashcards.a: Standard: baseline pricing/performance. Priority: premium over Standard for preferential queue treatment, up to ~25% better output-tokens-per-second latency. Flex: discounted vs Standard, for workloads tolerant of being queued behind Standard-tier traffic during high load (batch-like, non-urgent multi-step work).

flashcards.q: What is Bedrock Provisioned Throughput, and where do you find its pricing?
flashcards.a: Reserved dedicated capacity (in 'model units') for a 1- or 6-month commitment, guaranteeing throughput independent of the shared on-demand pool. AWS generally does not publish per-model-unit rates on the standard pricing page; enterprise customers are directed to their account team for a quote.

flashcards.q: What's the directionally-estimated crossover point where self-hosting starts beating Bedrock on cost, and what caveat must accompany it?
flashcards.a: Roughly 10,000-20,000 requests/day or a few thousand dollars/month in API spend, per industry estimates — but this is heavily workload-dependent (token length, latency SLA, traffic steadiness) and should never be quoted as a precise universal number.

flashcards.q: What does the 'fully-loaded' cost of self-hosting include beyond the raw EC2 bill?
flashcards.a: Engineer-hours for capacity planning and on-call, ongoing vLLM/CUDA/driver upgrade maintenance, building autoscaling that reacts as fast as a hosted provider's shared fleet, and the opportunity cost of the team's attention.

flashcards.q: How do Bedrock and SageMaker compare to self-hosting on data residency?
flashcards.a: Bedrock and SageMaker are broadly similar: both AWS-operated within the customer's account/region boundary, with AWS's stated policy of not training on customer data or moving it out of region. Self-hosting is stricter — the literal serving process runs on infrastructure the org directly controls, which some regulated environments require as a hard line.

flashcards.q: Compare lock-in across Bedrock, SageMaker, and self-hosted.
flashcards.a: Bedrock: high — prompts/evals/fine-tuning built against AWS's specific model catalog and API. SageMaker: medium — AWS-infrastructure-specific, but the model artifact/container itself is portable. Self-hosted: low technical lock-in (same container runs anywhere), though the organizational investment in your own ops tooling is real.

flashcards.q: What happens if traffic exceeds your Bedrock on-demand quota during a spike?
flashcards.a: Requests are throttled (fail closed) rather than autoscaled, since quota increases require a support-ticket request subject to AWS capacity and are not instant — proactively request quota increases before a known traffic event.

flashcards.q: A SageMaker Real-Time Endpoint has low, intermittent traffic and a high bill. What's the fix?
flashcards.a: Real-Time Endpoints bill per instance-hour regardless of utilization — switch to Serverless Inference (scale-to-zero, pay per invocation) for intermittent/unpredictable traffic, or Async Inference if payloads/processing time don't fit a synchronous model.

flashcards.q: When is SageMaker the right middle-ground choice over both Bedrock and plain self-hosted EC2/EKS?
flashcards.a: When you need full control over the model artifact/container (custom or fine-tuned open-weight model) but don't want to own infrastructure orchestration (provisioning, health checks, autoscaling wiring) yourself — SageMaker gives you AWS-managed infra around a model you fully control.

flashcards.q: Define covariate shift, prior/label shift, and concept drift precisely.
flashcards.a: Covariate shift: P(X) changes, P(Y|X) fixed. Prior/label shift: P(Y) changes, P(X|Y) fixed. Concept drift: P(Y|X) itself changes — the model's learned relationship is no longer true.

flashcards.q: Which type of shift necessarily degrades accuracy, and why do the others not?
flashcards.a: Only concept drift necessarily degrades accuracy, because it changes the actual relationship the model learned. Covariate and label shift can leave a well-generalizing model just as accurate on the new distribution/class balance.

flashcards.q: State PSI's formula and standard action thresholds.
flashcards.a: PSI = Σ(cur%-ref%)·ln(cur%/ref%) over buckets (typically 10, from reference-distribution deciles). <0.10 no significant shift; 0.10-0.25 investigate; ≥0.25 significant shift, action needed. A banking-industry convention, not derived from first principles.

flashcards.q: Why must PSI buckets be built from the reference distribution's quantiles, not the current distribution's?
flashcards.a: Bucketing on the reference distribution means each bucket starts with an even split (e.g. 10% each) by construction, so any departure in the current distribution is the real drift signal. Bucketing on current data instead makes it always look artificially uniform against itself.

flashcards.q: Why does the KS test's p-value become useless at large sample sizes?
flashcards.a: Statistical power scales with n; at production scale (10^5+ samples), even a trivial, practically meaningless difference produces a near-zero p-value. Fix: threshold the KS statistic (max CDF distance, a real effect size) instead of the p-value, or fix the sample size before testing.

flashcards.q: Contrast KL divergence, JS divergence, and Wasserstein distance.
flashcards.a: KL: asymmetric, undefined where reference has zero probability but current doesn't (breaks on sparse categoricals). JS: symmetrized, bounded [0,1], always finite. Wasserstein: respects actual numeric distance between values, not just bucket-proportion shape — correctly distinguishes 'mass moved a little' from 'mass moved a lot.'

flashcards.q: How does a domain classifier detect multivariate drift that univariate tests miss?
flashcards.a: Label reference-window rows 0 and current-window rows 1, train a classifier to distinguish them on the full feature set. AUC ≈ 0.5 means no detectable joint drift; AUC ≥ ~0.7 means a real, learnable difference exists even if every individual feature's marginal test passed.

flashcards.q: Why does a rolling reference window hide slow, gradual drift?
flashcards.a: If each window is compared only to the window right before it, drift slower than the window length looks like a series of insignificant changes even though cumulative drift from the original training distribution can be enormous — the reference itself drifts along with the data.

flashcards.q: What's the fix for the rolling-reference blind spot to slow drift?
flashcards.a: Keep a frozen training-time reference for long-horizon cumulative drift detection alongside a rolling short window for fast operational alerting — they answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other.

flashcards.q: Name the three retraining trigger types and the failure mode of using each alone.
flashcards.a: Scheduled (wastes compute on stable periods, misses fast drift between runs). Threshold-based (retrains on statistical noise or benign shift that doesn't hurt accuracy). Performance-based (never fires in time without fast labels or a trustworthy estimation method). Mature practice combines all three: scheduled floor, drift gate, performance corroboration.

flashcards.q: What does CBPE-style performance estimation (e.g. NannyML) do and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: Estimates a model's accuracy/AUC on unlabeled production data from its own confidence outputs plus observed drift, calibrated against labeled validation data. It matters because it closes the gap between 'drift detected' and 'did performance actually drop,' the thing drift alone can't answer.

flashcards.q: Distinguish sudden, gradual, incremental, and recurring/seasonal drift.
flashcards.a: Sudden: step function (pipeline/schema change). Gradual: slow monotonic trend (evolving user behavior). Incremental: many small changes accumulating noisily. Recurring/seasonal: cyclical (weekday/weekend, holidays) — often better addressed by a season-aware model than by retraining.

flashcards.q: Why is 'drift detected' not the same claim as 'model broken'?
flashcards.a: Drift only measures that a distribution changed; only concept drift is guaranteed to hurt accuracy. Covariate/label shift can be detected with high PSI while the business metric and accuracy stay completely flat — retraining on that signal alone wastes compute.

flashcards.q: What does each of transformers, datasets, tokenizers, accelerate, peft, and trl actually do?
flashcards.a: transformers = uniform model/tokenizer interface. datasets = Arrow-backed, memory-mapped/streamable data loading. tokenizers = fast Rust tokenization backend. accelerate = topology-agnostic training launch + mixed precision. peft = parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA/QLoRA). trl = post-training trainers (SFT/DPO/GRPO) built on the rest.

flashcards.q: Explain LoRA's parameter math and why it drastically cuts trainable parameters.
flashcards.a: LoRA freezes W and learns ΔW=BA where B is d×r, A is r×k, r≪d,k. Trainable params = r(d+k) instead of d·k. For a 4096×4096 matrix with r=16: ~131K params vs 16.8M full, over 100x fewer.

flashcards.q: What does QLoRA add on top of LoRA, and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: QLoRA loads the frozen base model in 4-bit quantization (NF4, plus double quantization of quant constants) and trains LoRA adapters in higher precision on top. This makes fine-tuning a 70B model feasible on a single 48-80GB GPU instead of needing multiple 80GB GPUs for full-precision fine-tuning.

flashcards.q: Why is a pickle-based .bin checkpoint a security risk that safetensors eliminates?
flashcards.a: Pickle serializes instructions for reconstructing arbitrary Python objects, including calls to arbitrary callables — deserializing can execute code. Safetensors stores only a header (names/shapes/dtypes/offsets) plus raw tensor bytes, with no executable content possible by the format's construction.

flashcards.q: What is the current (as of Dec 2025) status of Hugging Face's TGI, and what does HF recommend instead?
flashcards.a: TGI entered maintenance mode in December 2025 — only minor bug fixes and doc updates accepted. HF's own documentation recommends vLLM and SGLang for new production serving.

flashcards.q: What does device_map="auto" actually do, and which library implements it?
flashcards.a: It's an accelerate feature exposed through transformers: accelerate inspects available GPU/CPU/disk memory, computes a layer-to-device assignment, and inserts hooks so activations move across device boundaries transparently during the forward pass.

flashcards.q: Contrast datasets' memory-mapped mode with streaming mode.
flashcards.a: Memory-mapped (default): backed by a local Arrow file, gives full random access (ds[i], .shuffle(), cached .map()) but needs the file on local disk. Streaming: no local materialization, iterates directly, but only supports buffer-based approximate shuffling, no true random access.

flashcards.q: Why should you always pin an explicit revision hash when loading a model from the Hub in production?
flashcards.a: Without pinning, from_pretrained(..., revision="main") resolves to whatever the repo owner most recently pushed. A production system can silently start loading different weights or tokenizer behavior after a cold start or cache eviction with zero code change on your side.

flashcards.q: Distinguish SFT, DPO, and GRPO.
flashcards.a: SFT: supervised next-token training on instruction/response pairs. DPO: closed-form training directly on preference pairs (chosen vs rejected), no separate reward model or rollouts. GRPO: RL using group-relative advantage from sampled completions, needs a verifiable reward (math/code correctness), underlies DeepSeek-R1-style reasoning post-training.

flashcards.q: Where does LangChain genuinely earn its place versus where senior teams now skip it?
flashcards.a: Earns it: complex multi-provider orchestration, and specifically LangGraph for durable checkpointed multi-agent state. Skipped by seniors: LCEL beyond simple linear chains, LangChain's memory abstractions (teams roll their own), and the vector-store wrapper layer once committed to one DB's native client.

flashcards.q: What's the 2026 pattern for teams with 5+ engineers on LLM features moving off LangChain?
flashcards.a: Provider SDK calls directly, LiteLLM for cross-provider routing, and Pydantic for schema validation — because model providers converged enough by 2026 that the abstraction no longer hides much real complexity, while adding 15-40 frame debugging stack traces.

flashcards.q: Why is saving a PEFT/LoRA adapter so much smaller than the base model, and why does that matter for serving?
flashcards.a: save_pretrained on a PEFT model saves only the adapter weights (tens to low-hundreds of MB), not the frozen base (which can be 100+ GB). This is why serving many fine-tuned variants of one base model is cheap — vLLM's multi-LoRA serving loads the base once and swaps adapters per request.

flashcards.q: What real-world incident illustrates the danger of trust_remote_code=True?
flashcards.a: CVE-2026-6859: InstructLab hardcoded trust_remote_code=True, meaning a specially crafted malicious model uploaded to the Hub could achieve remote code execution on any user who loaded it — independent of whether the checkpoint format itself was safetensors or pickle.

flashcards.q: What are the four layers of ML monitoring and what does each catch?
flashcards.a: Infra (latency, error rate, saturation) catches the system falling over. Data (schema, nulls, range, cardinality) catches upstream pipeline breakage. Model (prediction distribution, confidence, feature-importance shift) catches model degradation before labels exist. Business (the metric that pays) is the final, slowest-moving arbiter.

flashcards.q: Why is ground truth usually unavailable in production, and what do you monitor instead?
flashcards.a: Labels lag (fraud chargebacks 30-90 days, recs conversion weeks, content-mod maybe never). Monitor proxies instead: shadow/challenger agreement, prediction/confidence drift, cheap proxy labels, sampled human review, LLM-as-judge scoring.

flashcards.q: Why do static alert thresholds page you at 3am for nothing?
flashcards.a: A static threshold doesn't account for seasonality (weekday/weekend traffic mix, Monday ramps), so it either pages routinely on benign variation or is set loose enough to miss a real regression during a quiet period. Fix: seasonality-aware baselines, rate-of-change over absolute value, multi-signal correlation before paging.

flashcards.q: Describe the silently-truncated-feature-pipeline failure mode.
flashcards.a: An upstream ETL bug truncates a feature (e.g. history window 500→50 events). Prediction mean steps at the deploy timestamp, null rate stays 0% (field is populated, just shorter), infra stays flat, and accuracy stays flat for the full label-lag window (e.g. 2 weeks) because labels haven't arrived. Only layer-3 prediction-distribution monitoring catches it in real time.

flashcards.q: What's the recommended logging/sampling strategy per request?
flashcards.a: Log 100% of cheap structured metadata (ids, latency breakdown, token counts, confidence, model version) always. Sample 1-10% of full-fidelity payloads (raw features/prompt/completion), but always oversample the tail: errors, low-confidence predictions, flagged outputs.

flashcards.q: What LLM-specific signals go beyond classical model monitoring?
flashcards.a: Token cost per request (and per prompt-template version), hallucination proxies (retrieval-groundedness, self-consistency, judge factuality score), refusal rate, and judge-score drift (including drift from the judge model itself being silently updated).

flashcards.q: Give a concrete numeric example of invisible LLM cost drift.
flashcards.a: Average input tokens creeping from 800 to 1,400 (e.g. a prompt template regression) at $3/1M input tokens and 2M requests/month is roughly $1,800/month in pure cost drift, with zero symptom in latency.

flashcards.q: Why does a refusal rate spike sometimes have nothing to do with your own code?
flashcards.a: On a managed/hosted model pointed at a rolling alias rather than a pinned version, the provider can silently update safety tuning, changing refusal behavior with no deploy on your side.

flashcards.q: What makes a monitoring dashboard actually get looked at during an incident?
flashcards.a: It's linked directly from the alert/runbook (not a separate artifact), shows a comparison baseline (now vs last week, not a bare current value), and is small enough (one 'model health' panel per model) for a human to scan in 30 seconds.

flashcards.q: Why should a circuit-breaker-style multi-signal gate exist before paging on model-layer drift?
flashcards.a: Drift alone (e.g. a data or model layer signal) has a high false-positive rate because benign covariate/label shift can trigger it without hurting accuracy. Requiring two layers to agree (e.g. data AND model) before paging reduces false pages while still catching real incidents.

flashcards.q: What's the tradeoff between semaphore-style full-fidelity LLM logging and cost?
flashcards.a: Full-fidelity prompt/completion logging at scale (e.g. 1M req/day) compounds storage cost, observability platform per-event/GB pricing, and judge-scoring compute cost. Design sampling and retention up front rather than retrofitting after a cost or compliance incident.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT build a full four-layer monitoring stack?
flashcards.a: For a low-stakes, low-traffic model (e.g. a weekly-batch model with 200 predictions/day feeding an internal dashboard) — a spreadsheet someone eyeballs monthly is correctly sized; over-instrumenting wastes engineering time better spent elsewhere.

flashcards.q: Rank the two error types a naive alert threshold produces.
flashcards.a: False positives: pages on routine seasonality/traffic ramps until the channel gets muted. False negatives: a threshold loosened to survive that noise then misses a real regression during a normally-quiet period where the absolute threshold was calibrated wrong.

flashcards.q: What is a domain-classifier-style agreement check used as a drift proxy in monitoring?
flashcards.a: Run a cheap fallback model or older model version alongside the current one; track their disagreement rate. Rising disagreement is a robust drift signal that requires no ground-truth labels at all.

flashcards.q: FastAPI is built on top of what two libraries, and what does each contribute?
flashcards.a: Starlette (ASGI web layer: routing, middleware, WebSockets, BackgroundTasks) and Pydantic (validation, serialization, settings). FastAPI's own contribution is wiring type hints to both plus DI and OpenAPI generation.

flashcards.q: Why is `response_model` a real security control, not just a docs annotation?
flashcards.a: It filters the return value against the declared schema at runtime, dropping any field not on the schema (e.g. a hashed_password on the DB model) before serialization, regardless of what the function actually returns.

flashcards.q: Roughly how much faster is Pydantic v2 than v1, and why?
flashcards.a: Roughly 4x-50x depending on model shape (a commonly cited headline is ~17x on a representative mix of field types, ~20x on complex nested models), because the validation core moved to Rust (pydantic-core).

flashcards.q: What does `model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")` do, and what's the default?
flashcards.a: Rejects requests containing fields not declared on the model (422) instead of silently dropping them. Default is extra="ignore", which silently discards unknown fields.

flashcards.q: Are `Depends()` results cached within a single request? What's the implication for a `get_db` dependency referenced by two other dependencies?
flashcards.a: Yes, cached per request keyed by the callable, so get_db() is called once and the same session/connection is shared across every dependency in that request's graph, unless use_cache=False is passed.

flashcards.q: For a `yield`-based dependency chain A -> B -> C (C depends on B depends on A), what order does teardown run in, and when relative to the response?
flashcards.a: LIFO: C tears down first, then B, then A (reverse of setup order), managed by AsyncExitStack. Teardown runs after the response has already been sent to the client.

flashcards.q: What specific mechanism makes FastAPI considered 'testable', beyond generic good design?
flashcards.a: app.dependency_overrides — a dict keyed by the original dependency callable, letting tests swap in fakes (e.g. a test DB session) with no monkeypatching or import-path mocking.

flashcards.q: A client sends a malformed request body. What status code does FastAPI return by default, and why not 400?
flashcards.a: 422 Unprocessable Entity, raised as RequestValidationError. FastAPI reserves 400 for structurally malformed requests and uses 422 (WebDAV/RFC 4918) for requests that parse fine but fail schema/semantic validation.

flashcards.q: Why must a global exception handler never return `str(exc)` or a traceback to the client?
flashcards.a: It can leak table names, ORM query fragments, internal hostnames, or library versions useful for an attacker fingerprinting the stack. Log the full detail server-side with a correlation id, return a generic body plus that id to the client.

flashcards.q: What is the core trap with `BackgroundTasks`, and what's the observable symptom in production?
flashcards.a: It runs in-process with no broker, persistence, or retry; a SIGTERM (deploy, autoscale-down, OOM) mid-task silently drops the work with no log. Symptom: support tickets like 'never got my confirmation email' with nothing in any log.

flashcards.q: What do sync (`def`) path operations run on, versus `async def` ones?
flashcards.a: async def runs directly on the single event loop. Sync def is dispatched to Starlette's threadpool (default cap commonly cited around 40 threads) and awaited.

flashcards.q: A blocking call sits inside an `async def` endpoint. What's the observable symptom under increasing concurrency, and why does CPU stay low?
flashcards.a: Throughput plateaus then collapses, p99 latency and error rate climb, while CPU stays low/idle -- because the entire single event loop is blocked on I/O, stalling every other concurrent request, not just the one that made the call.

flashcards.q: What's the fix for an unavoidable blocking call inside an async endpoint?
flashcards.a: Use an async-native client (e.g. httpx.AsyncClient) if one exists, or wrap the sync call with `await run_in_threadpool(fn, ...)` to push it off the event loop explicitly.

flashcards.q: What replaced `@app.on_event("startup"/"shutdown")`, and why is it useful?
flashcards.a: The `lifespan` async context manager -- a single place to open resources (DB pool, model warmup) before yield and close them after, replacing two separately-registered, easy-to-desync event handlers.

flashcards.q: Name two scenarios where FastAPI is the wrong framework choice.
flashcards.a: CPU-bound compute-heavy workloads (async buys nothing, need process-based parallelism regardless of web framework); teams already deep in Django wanting async gains not worth losing the ORM/admin/migrations investment for.

flashcards.q: What is the real modelling difference between RDF triples and a labelled property graph?
flashcards.a: RDF (subject-predicate-object) has no native place to hang properties on a relationship -- qualifying a fact requires reification. Property graphs attach arbitrary key-value properties directly to both nodes AND edges.

flashcards.q: Match each to its query language: RDF, property graph (Neo4j), TinkerPop engines.
flashcards.a: RDF -> SPARQL (W3C standard, declarative). Neo4j -> Cypher (declarative, ASCII-art, basis for ISO GQL). TinkerPop (Neptune, JanusGraph) -> Gremlin (imperative, step-based).

flashcards.q: What is index-free adjacency, and what is its complexity claim?
flashcards.a: Each node stores direct pointers to its adjacent relationships, so a single-hop traversal is a pointer dereference -- O(1) regardless of total graph size -- versus a relational JOIN's cost scaling with table size.

flashcards.q: Name three conditions under which index-free adjacency's O(1) guarantee breaks down.
flashcards.a: Global queries needing a conventional index; supernodes (millions of edges on one node); the graph exceeding available RAM (falls to disk I/O); cross-shard traversal in a distributed graph (network hop per edge crossing a shard).

flashcards.q: Does Amazon Neptune offer a self-hosted deployment option?
flashcards.a: No -- Neptune is fully managed only, unlike Neo4j (self-host or AuraDB) and ArangoDB (self-host or ArangoGraph managed).

flashcards.q: What is ArangoDB's core architectural bet, and what does it cost?
flashcards.a: Multi-model: document + graph + full-text/vector search in one engine, one AQL query language -- one operational surface instead of three. Cost: less traversal-specific depth than a specialist graph engine on heavy algorithmic workloads (community detection, centrality at scale).

flashcards.q: Roughly how does Neo4j AuraDB Professional pricing compare to ArangoDB's list pricing?
flashcards.a: AuraDB Professional runs roughly $65/GB/month (Business Critical ~$146/GB/month); ArangoDB is reported roughly 15-25% cheaper list price than Neo4j for comparable deployments.

flashcards.q: What is entity resolution, and why is it consistently under-resourced in knowledge-graph projects?
flashcards.a: Deciding whether records from different sources referring to slightly different representations of the same entity should merge into one node. Under-resourced because teams scope it as a one-time cleanup phase, when it's actually an ongoing pipeline stage that reopens every time a new source system is onboarded.

flashcards.q: What does GraphRAG add over vector-only RAG, and what's the rough indexing cost?
flashcards.a: Extracts entities/relationships into a graph, clusters into communities (Leiden algorithm), pre-summarizes each -- enabling 'global' cross-corpus questions single chunks can't answer. Full Microsoft-style indexing: ~$20-40/million tokens (one-time); LightRAG-style lighter alternative: ~$0.50/million tokens.

flashcards.q: When is GraphRAG NOT worth its indexing cost?
flashcards.a: When real query logs show traffic is dominated by single-document, single-fact lookups -- hybrid search plus reranking captures most of the achievable quality at a fraction of the cost for that majority case.

flashcards.q: What SQL feature replaces most 'we need a graph database' requirements, and what's the tradeoff?
flashcards.a: A recursive CTE (WITH RECURSIVE) on a well-indexed relational schema handles variable-depth traversal with no new infrastructure, no new query language, and no consistency-model split -- but it degrades at high fan-out or truly unbounded depth compared to a native graph engine.

flashcards.q: What standards body governs RDF, and roughly when was it standardized?
flashcards.a: W3C -- RDF standardized in 2008 (updated 2013), alongside RDFS/OWL for formal ontology and reasoning.

flashcards.q: Why do property graphs handle 'Alice placed Order#42 on 2026-01-04' more naturally than RDF?
flashcards.a: The relationship (PLACED) itself carries the date property directly on the edge. In RDF, a triple has no native slot for qualifying a relationship, so representing the date requires reifying the statement into its own node, multiplying triple count.

flashcards.q: Give a concrete example of a supernode problem and its fix.
flashcards.a: A 'Country: USA' node connected to every US-based user; traversing from it fans out to millions of edges, breaking the O(1)-per-hop assumption. Fix: remodel by bucketing (e.g. by state/region) or invert the query to start from a more selective node.

flashcards.q: Name one genuinely strong use case for a dedicated graph database (not solvable well by a relational CTE).
flashcards.a: Fraud-ring detection: entities are accounts/devices/payment instruments, edges are shared attributes, and the query is 'find densely-connected subgraphs' -- a graph algorithm (community detection/connected-components), not a lookup, which native graph-algorithm libraries (e.g. Neo4j GDS) solve directly.

flashcards.q: Why does query-based incremental extraction (WHERE updated_at > watermark) miss hard deletes?
flashcards.a: A deleted row produces zero rows in the query result — there's nothing to diff against. Only log-based CDC, soft deletes, or periodic full reconciliation can detect it.

flashcards.q: What's the observable symptom of a broken/stuck incremental watermark?
flashcards.a: Row counts look normal every run, no errors thrown, but a downstream aggregate (revenue, MAU) quietly drifts from the source of truth over days/weeks.

flashcards.q: What delivery guarantee do Kafka consumer rebalances, Airflow task retries, and webhook redelivery all default to?
flashcards.a: At-least-once. Exactly-once is not given by the delivery layer — it must be built at the write/sink layer via idempotency.

flashcards.q: What does 'at-least-once delivery + non-idempotent load' produce?
flashcards.a: Silent duplication — the same row gets inserted twice on retry/redelivery, inflating aggregates with no error thrown.

flashcards.q: Name the two idempotent-load patterns for handling at-least-once delivery.
flashcards.a: 1) Merge/upsert on a natural key with a monotonic guard column. 2) Idempotency key + INSERT...ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, checked by affected-row count (never read-then-write).

flashcards.q: Why does a merge/upsert need a monotonic guard column (e.g. `updated_at`) in addition to a natural key?
flashcards.a: Without it, an out-of-order redelivery (a stale event replayed after a newer one already landed) overwrites newer data with older data — idempotent against duplicates but not against out-of-order delivery.

flashcards.q: How does log-based CDC (Debezium) capture deletes and un-timestamped updates that query-based incremental misses?
flashcards.a: It tails the database's transaction log (binlog/WAL/redo log) directly, emitting every committed insert/update/delete regardless of whether the application maintained a timestamp column.

flashcards.q: What operational risk does an unconsumed CDC replication slot create?
flashcards.a: It grows unboundedly and can fill the source database's disk — the log can't be purged until the slot's consumer catches up.

flashcards.q: Typical MySQL binlog retention, and why it matters for CDC consumer downtime?
flashcards.a: Commonly 1-7 days by default. If the CDC consumer (e.g. Kafka Connect) is down longer than retention, incremental catch-up is impossible and a full re-snapshot is required.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT build streaming CDC for a table?
flashcards.a: When nothing downstream needs sub-minute freshness (e.g. a daily BI dashboard) — streaming adds always-on infra cost plus an entire correctness surface (ordering, exactly-once sinks, late data) for freshness nobody uses.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between ETL and ELT, and why did the industry shift toward ELT?
flashcards.a: ETL transforms before loading; ELT loads raw then transforms in-warehouse (dbt). The shift happened because cheap columnar compute made in-warehouse transforms fast, and ELT decouples 'did it land' from 'is it correct'.

flashcards.q: What should trigger a dead-letter alert in a nightly batch of millions of rows — and what shouldn't?
flashcards.a: Alert on dead-letter volume crossing a threshold (e.g. >0.1% of batch); never alert per-row, which produces alert fatigue and gets muted within a week.

flashcards.q: What's the safest schema-drift posture at the raw/bronze ingest layer vs. at a contracted silver/gold layer?
flashcards.a: Bronze: permissive/additive, accept new fields without failing. Silver/gold with a data contract: fail loudly on a type change to an existing field.

flashcards.q: Two structural responses to late-arriving event data in a streaming pipeline?
flashcards.a: A grace period / watermark with allowed lateness (Spark/Flink hold the partition open before finalizing), or accept it late and run a targeted backfill once detected.

flashcards.q: Full snapshot extraction is still the right default for what kind of table?
flashcards.a: Small, slowly-changing dimension tables (roughly under 1M rows) with no urgent freshness requirement — the incremental/CDC machinery isn't worth the complexity.

flashcards.q: What is the observable symptom of data skew in the Spark UI?
flashcards.a: 199 tasks in a stage finish in seconds; 1 task runs for tens of minutes at near-100% CPU. That task's shuffle-read size is an outlier versus the median, confirming data volume, not a slow node.

flashcards.q: Which Spark version made AQE default-enabled, and which shuffles does it re-plan?
flashcards.a: Spark 3.2.0. It re-plans only at shuffle boundaries (materialization points where real stats exist), and only for the DataFrame/SQL API, never RDDs.

flashcards.q: Name AQE's three features and their default config values.
flashcards.a: 1) coalescePartitions (default true) merges small post-shuffle partitions toward advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes (64MB default). 2) automatic join-strategy switch to broadcast if runtime size proves it small enough. 3) skewJoin.enabled (default true): splits a sort-merge join partition exceeding skewedPartitionFactor (5x median) AND skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes (256MB).

flashcards.q: AQE's skew-join handling doesn't fix your skewed job. What two cases does it not cover?
flashcards.a: Aggregation skew (a plain groupBy, not a join) and non-equi joins. Those still require manual salting.

flashcards.q: What is spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold's default, and why is it conservative rather than aggressive?
flashcards.a: 10MB. Conservative because a broadcast materializes the whole 'small' side in the driver then pushes a full copy to every executor; a stale/wrong size estimate under an aggressive threshold risks driver or executor OOM, a worse failure than a slow sort-merge join.

flashcards.q: What causes a BroadcastNestedLoopJoin, and why is it usually a red flag?
flashcards.a: No equality condition available for a hash join (a non-equi join predicate, or an accidental cross join). It's O(n*m) per partition; seeing it unintentionally on two large tables usually means the join condition isn't what was intended.

flashcards.q: What speedup do pandas UDFs give over row-at-a-time Python UDFs, and what mechanism produces it?
flashcards.a: 3x to 100x, because data crosses the JVM/Python boundary in Arrow columnar batches instead of per-row, letting the Python function run vectorized over a pandas Series/DataFrame instead of one row at a time.

flashcards.q: How do newer Arrow UDFs improve on pandas UDFs?
flashcards.a: ~10% faster and ~40% less memory, by operating directly on Arrow's columnar format and skipping the pandas/NumPy materialization step pandas UDFs require.

flashcards.q: Name three concrete cases where .cache() makes a job slower.
flashcards.a: 1) The DataFrame is consumed only once (materialization cost for zero reuse). 2) The cache evicts a more valuable cached DataFrame, forcing its recompute. 3) Caching happens before a filter that would have shrunk the data significantly.

flashcards.q: Describe Spark's Unified Memory Manager layout: what do spark.memory.fraction and spark.memory.storageFraction control?
flashcards.a: memory.fraction (default 0.6) is the share of the executor heap given to the Unified Memory region (execution + storage). storageFraction (default 0.5) is the soft boundary inside that region between storage (cached data) and execution (shuffle/sort/hash-table buffers) — execution can evict storage under pressure, not the reverse.

flashcards.q: What is spark.executor.memoryOverhead's default, and why does it matter especially for PySpark?
flashcards.a: 10% of executor memory, minimum 384MB, off-heap. For PySpark, the separate Python worker process(es) run outside the JVM heap and are effectively budgeted against this overhead — undersizing it starves the Python process while JVM heap graphs look fine.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between spill and OOM?
flashcards.a: Spill is a supported fallback: an operator (sort, aggregate) that exceeds execution memory writes intermediate state to disk and merges later, trading time for staying in bounds. OOM is a hard failure with no such fallback (e.g. broadcast build side, which must be fully in memory by design).

flashcards.q: What does bucketBy do at write time, and when does it fail to pay off?
flashcards.a: Pre-shuffles data into a fixed number of hash buckets by column, so a future join on that same column between two identically-bucketed tables can skip the shuffle. Fails to pay off if the join pattern changes or bucket count/column mismatches between tables — that silently falls back to a full shuffle join, wasting the write-time cost.

flashcards.q: You tripled executor count and the job barely sped up. What should you check before concluding Spark 'doesn't scale' for this workload?
flashcards.a: Check for skew first (one oversized task bottlenecks regardless of idle executors), then serial bottlenecks (driver-side collect, a single broadcast build, few output partitions), then whether the stage is UDF/Python-bound (more executors don't fix per-row Python interpreter overhead).

flashcards.q: What triggers a job, and what causes a new stage to be cut within it?
flashcards.a: An action (collect, count, write) triggers a job. The DAGScheduler cuts a new stage at every shuffle dependency (wide transformation like groupBy, join, repartition). Narrow transformations pipeline into one stage.

flashcards.q: What does an RDD actually store?
flashcards.a: Not data — a lineage graph: (parent RDDs, the transformation function, the partitioner). Lazy; nothing executes until an action.

flashcards.q: Why can Catalyst optimize a DataFrame plan but not an RDD lambda?
flashcards.a: A DataFrame's transformations are an expression tree (Column/Expression nodes) that Catalyst can read as data. An RDD lambda is opaque code — Spark cannot see what it does, so it cannot push filters, prune columns, or reorder around it.

flashcards.q: Name Catalyst's four/five plan phases in order.
flashcards.a: Parsed Plan -> Analyzed Plan (resolve names/types) -> Optimized Logical Plan (rule-based rewrites) -> Physical Plan(s) (cost-based join/operator selection) -> whole-stage codegen (Tungsten) -> RDDs.

flashcards.q: What are the two separate mechanisms bundled under 'Tungsten'?
flashcards.a: 1) UnsafeRow: off-heap binary row format, no per-object headers or boxing, less GC pressure. 2) Whole-stage codegen: fuses a stage's operators into one JIT-compiled function, eliminating per-row virtual iterator calls.

flashcards.q: What speedup does whole-stage codegen give over Volcano-style interpreted execution, per Databricks' benchmark?
flashcards.a: Roughly 10x, approaching hand-written loop performance. The same 2016 Databricks post demonstrated ~1 billion rows/sec for a simple aggregation on one laptop core.

flashcards.q: In explain() output, what does PushedFilters:[] on a scan with an obvious WHERE clause tell you?
flashcards.a: The filter did not reach the file reader — often because it references a derived/computed column or sits inside a UDF, so predicate pushdown couldn't apply. Filter on raw source columns before deriving new ones.

flashcards.q: What is the default value of spark.sql.shuffle.partitions and why is it wrong for both small and large jobs?
flashcards.a: 200, applied globally to every shuffle. Too many for a small job (tiny partitions, scheduling overhead dominates); too few for a large job (huge partitions risk spill/OOM). Fixed in practice by AQE's dynamic coalescing.

flashcards.q: Mechanically, what does a shuffle do and why does it force a stage boundary?
flashcards.a: Upstream tasks write output bucketed by a partitioner into per-downstream-partition files on local disk (shuffle write); downstream tasks fetch their bucket over the network (shuffle read). The downstream stage cannot start until the entire upstream shuffle write is complete, so no pipelining is possible across it.

flashcards.q: How does Spark recover a lost RDD partition, and why not replicate like HDFS?
flashcards.a: It recomputes the lost partition by replaying its recorded lineage (parent partition + transformation), trading some recompute cost for avoiding the storage/write cost of replicating every intermediate dataset.

flashcards.q: What does .checkpoint() do and when is it needed?
flashcards.a: Materializes an RDD to reliable storage, truncating its lineage. Needed for iterative algorithms where lineage would otherwise grow unboundedly across iterations, making failure recovery increasingly expensive.

flashcards.q: Why is calling `.rdd.map(...)` in the middle of a DataFrame pipeline expensive?
flashcards.a: It's a full optimization-barrier round trip: UnsafeRows must be materialized back into JVM/Python objects (a full JVM<->Python serialization trip in PySpark), the opaque map runs, then Spark re-infers a schema and reconstructs UnsafeRows to resume DataFrame execution.

flashcards.q: What does explain(mode="cost") add over the default explain(), and what's it used to diagnose?
flashcards.a: Estimated row counts and data sizes per operator, derived from table statistics. Used to catch cases where a bad or stale ANALYZE TABLE statistic caused the optimizer to pick the wrong join strategy.

flashcards.q: When is it still correct to reach for RDDs over DataFrames?
flashcards.a: Custom non-default partitioning logic the DataFrame partitioner API doesn't expose, non-tabular data (arbitrary Python objects, graphs), or library code that must be stable against the DataFrame API's evolving semantics.

flashcards.q: Why is 16 kHz the ASR standard sample rate, and how does it relate to Nyquist's theorem?
flashcards.a: By Nyquist, a sample rate f captures frequencies up to f/2. Speech-intelligibility-critical energy sits below ~8 kHz, so 16 kHz (8 kHz Nyquist limit) captures essentially all speech-relevant information without the extra cost of a higher rate.

flashcards.q: List the six steps of MFCC derivation in order.
flashcards.a: Framing (short overlapping windows) -> Windowing (Hamming, avoid spectral leakage) -> FFT (time to frequency domain) -> Mel filterbank (log-spaced triangular filters) -> Log (matches perceived loudness) -> DCT (decorrelates, keep first ~12-13 coefficients).

flashcards.q: Why does the mel scale use logarithmic spacing above ~1 kHz instead of linear Hz spacing?
flashcards.a: It mirrors human pitch perception: we discriminate pitch differences much more finely at low frequencies than high ones, so mel spacing allocates more filter resolution to the low-frequency range where speech carries the most phonetically distinctive information.

flashcards.q: What are the three independently-trained components Kaldi composes via WFST, and what specific pain killed this architecture?
flashcards.a: Acoustic model (audio->phoneme), pronunciation lexicon (word->phonemes), language model (word-sequence probability), composed via H∘C∘L∘G. Killed by: none of the three transfer between languages, so a new language needed real engineering-months of specialized, non-transferable work per language.

flashcards.q: What loss function does Wav2Vec2 use for fine-tuning, and what problem does it solve?
flashcards.a: CTC (Connectionist Temporal Classification) -- solves the lack of frame-level alignment between many audio frames and fewer target text tokens by summing probability over all valid alignments via a forward-backward dynamic-programming algorithm, using a blank token to distinguish repeated consecutive characters.

flashcards.q: What is the headline low-resource result from the Wav2Vec2 paper?
flashcards.a: Fine-tuning with just 10 minutes of labeled data, on top of pretraining on 53,000 hours of unlabeled audio (Libri-light), achieved 4.8/8.2 WER on clean/other test sets.

flashcards.q: How large is Whisper's training data, and what makes its supervision 'weak'?
flashcards.a: 680,000 hours of audio-transcript pairs scraped from the internet, spanning 96 languages -- weak because the transcripts are noisy web data, not carefully curated labels, unlike Wav2Vec2's small clean labeled fine-tuning set.

flashcards.q: Name Whisper's three characteristic failure modes and what architectural feature causes them.
flashcards.a: Hallucinated text on silence (generative decoder trained to always produce output), timestamp drift (independent 30-second chunk decoding compounds small errors across boundaries), repetition loops (autoregressive decoder stuck with no strong signal to advance) -- all rooted in the fixed 30-second processing window.

flashcards.q: Compare distil-whisper and whisper-large-v3-turbo on speed and accuracy tradeoff versus large-v3.
flashcards.a: distil-large-v3: 756M params (vs 1.54B), ~6x faster, within ~1% WER of full model. large-v3-turbo: 809M params (decoder pruned 32->4 layers), ~6-8x faster, only 0.3-0.7 percentage-point WER increase.

flashcards.q: Define WER precisely, and why is it a poor proxy for downstream task success?
flashcards.a: WER = (Substitutions + Deletions + Insertions) / (reference word count), via edit-distance alignment. Poor proxy because it weighs every word error equally -- a missed negation or wrong entity is one error with severe downstream impact, while a mis-transcribed filler word is one error with near-zero impact.

flashcards.q: What's the standard diarization pipeline, and what makes overlapping speech the hard problem?
flashcards.a: VAD isolates speech regions -> neural embedding model computes a speaker vector per segment -> clustering (commonly agglomerative) groups by similarity. Overlap is hard because classical architectures assign one speaker label per time segment, structurally wrong whenever two people talk simultaneously.

flashcards.q: What does pyannote 3.x's Powerset architecture do differently, and why should you check whether a DER comparison scores overlap?
flashcards.a: It treats overlapping-speaker combinations as their own output classes instead of one-label-per-frame. Old DER definitions often didn't score overlap at all, giving partial credit to systems that just picked the dominant speaker -- comparing an overlap-unaware DER to an overlap-aware one directly is apples-to-oranges.

flashcards.q: State the streaming-vs-batch ASR tradeoff in one sentence, and why Whisper isn't a native streaming model.
flashcards.a: More lookahead context improves accuracy but adds latency directly -- it's a single dial, not separable knobs. Whisper is architecturally batch-oriented (full attention over a fixed 30-second window); 'streaming Whisper' is a sliding-window workaround, not native incremental decoding.

flashcards.q: What's the standard efficient runtime for deploying any Whisper variant on GPU, and what does it use under the hood?
flashcards.a: faster-whisper (SYSTRAN), which reimplements Whisper inference using CTranslate2, a highly optimized C++ inference engine, independent of which specific model weights (large-v3, turbo, distil) you load.

flashcards.q: Give the deciding factor for choosing a managed transcription API vs self-hosting Whisper/faster-whisper.
flashcards.a: Volume and utilization: low/bursty volume favors a managed API's pay-per-use pricing over idle GPU cost; sustained high volume, on-prem/compliance requirements, or need for domain fine-tuning favors self-hosting.

flashcards.q: AWS Glue ETL job pricing?
flashcards.a: $0.44/DPU-hour on-demand, billed per-second with a 1-minute minimum; $0.29/DPU-hour under Flex execution for jobs that can tolerate a delayed start.

flashcards.q: Give three concrete reasons Glue can be worse than EMR for a job.
flashcards.a: Long-running/continuous jobs (Glue's per-job startup overhead repeats each run), need for custom Spark config/libraries/versions, and poorly-optimized Spark code that can burn 10x the DPU-hours a tuned EMR job would.

flashcards.q: Athena pricing model and minimum charge?
flashcards.a: $5 per TB of data scanned, with a 10MB minimum charge per query. It's managed Presto/Trino under the hood.

flashcards.q: What are the three cost levers for Athena, in order of typical impact?
flashcards.a: 1) Columnar format (Parquet/ORC -- read only referenced columns) 2) Compression (Snappy 3-5x, gzip 5-10x) 3) Partitioning on a filtered column (e.g. date). A documented case went from ~15TB/query to ~50GB/query using all three.

flashcards.q: What is partition projection and why use it over registered partitions?
flashcards.a: Athena computes partition S3 locations algorithmically from a configured pattern (date range, enum list) instead of storing every partition in the Glue Catalog -- eliminates crawler/MSCK REPAIR maintenance and per-query metadata lookup overhead for high-cardinality time-series tables.

flashcards.q: What does Redshift RA3 change architecturally?
flashcards.a: Decouples compute from storage via Redshift Managed Storage -- storage scales independently up to 64TB/node, so you size compute for query performance rather than data volume.

flashcards.q: DISTKEY vs SORTKEY in Redshift?
flashcards.a: DISTKEY determines which node a row physically lands on (colocate joined tables to avoid cross-node shuffle). SORTKEY determines on-disk ordering within a node, enabling zone-map block skipping on range-filtered queries.

flashcards.q: What's the fundamental billing-model difference between Redshift and Athena/BigQuery?
flashcards.a: Redshift (outside Serverless) is cluster-billed -- you pay for provisioned compute-time whether idle or not. Athena/BigQuery are query-billed -- you pay per byte scanned, nothing when idle. This flips the cost-optimization approach from 'size the cluster' to 'control the scan'.

flashcards.q: Kinesis Data Streams shard throughput limit?
flashcards.a: 1 MB/s in, 2 MB/s out per shard in provisioned mode. To match a 1GB/s Kafka topic on 10 partitions you'd need on the order of 1,000 provisioned-mode Kinesis shards.

flashcards.q: Kinesis Data Streams vs Firehose vs MSK -- one-line selection rule for each?
flashcards.a: Data Streams: need custom multi-consumer processing or replay. Firehose: lowest-effort delivery pipe into S3/Parquet, no consumer code, but one-way (not replayable). MSK: already have Kafka clients/tooling -- migration cost of rewriting almost never pays off.

flashcards.q: When is OpenSearch the wrong tool for a RAG retrieval backend?
flashcards.a: When the workload is pure vector-similarity search with no lexical/full-text need and the team wants minimal index-tuning ops -- a dedicated vector DB or Bedrock Knowledge Bases with a simpler backend gives comparable retrieval quality with less cluster/shard management. OpenSearch earns its complexity for hybrid BM25+vector search.

flashcards.q: What does Redshift Spectrum do, and what does it NOT do?
flashcards.a: Lets a Redshift cluster query data sitting in S3 directly without loading it. It does NOT add to the cluster's managed storage, since the queried data never actually lands in Redshift.

flashcards.q: What is the Glue Data Catalog's role beyond Glue ETL jobs?
flashcards.a: A shared, Hive-metastore-compatible metadata store used automatically by Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR -- one schema/partition registry serving multiple query engines, which is often the real reason to use Glue even without running a Glue ETL job.

flashcards.q: What are the three phases of a Lambda cold start, in order?
flashcards.a: Download/pull the package or image, then INIT (runtime bootstrap plus any global-scope code, runs once per execution environment), then INVOKE (the handler runs per call). After INVOKE the environment freezes and can be thawed later, skipping INIT.

flashcards.q: Typical cold start p50 for Java without SnapStart vs with SnapStart?
flashcards.a: 5-15+ seconds without SnapStart (JVM boot and class loading dominate) versus 90-140ms with SnapStart, because SnapStart restores a snapshot taken after init already ran once instead of rebooting the JVM from zero.

flashcards.q: Which runtimes have GA SnapStart support as of the 2024-2025 rollout?
flashcards.a: Java 11+, Python 3.12+, and .NET 8+ (which also covers C#, F#, and PowerShell). Regional availability expanded significantly through 2025 -- verify current region coverage before an interview since this keeps changing.

flashcards.q: What is the SnapStart gotcha around randomness and credentials?
flashcards.a: Anything generated during init (random seeds, cached credentials, unique IDs) gets frozen into the snapshot and would be identical across every cold start restored from it, unless you explicitly re-randomize or refresh them in a beforeCheckpoint/afterRestore runtime hook.

flashcards.q: Is Lambda-in-a-VPC still a major cold-start penalty in 2026?
flashcards.a: No. The 2019 Hyperplane networking change replaced per-execution-environment ENI creation (which took 10-15 seconds) with pre-created ENIs shared per subnet+security-group combination. VPC attachment today adds well under 50ms. The remaining VPC cost is a NAT Gateway bill for internet egress, not latency.

flashcards.q: Difference between reserved concurrency and provisioned concurrency?
flashcards.a: Reserved concurrency sets a floor-and-ceiling on how much of the account's concurrency pool one function can consume, guaranteeing isolation but not eliminating cold starts. Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes a fixed number of warm environments, eliminating cold starts for invocations within that count, at a continuous hourly cost.

flashcards.q: What happens when you exceed available Lambda concurrency for a synchronous invoke?
