flashcards.q: Which Spark version added the built-in RocksDB state store, and what problem does it solve versus the default?
flashcards.a: Spark 3.2. The default HDFSBackedStateStore keeps state as JVM heap objects, causing GC pressure as key count grows. RocksDB keeps state off-heap in native, disk-backed storage local to each executor, handling tens of millions of keys without JVM GC pressure.

flashcards.q: What is the observable symptom of state explosion, and its most common cause?
flashcards.a: Symptom: state size in the Streaming UI grows with no plateau, batch time creeps up, eventually OOM or disk fill. Cause: no watermark declared, a watermark set far too generously, or a stream-stream join missing a watermark on one or both sides.

flashcards.q: Why is Trigger.Once() deprecated in favor of Trigger.AvailableNow()?
flashcards.a: Once() forces all currently-available data through a single micro-batch regardless of size, which can create one unmanageably large batch after downtime. AvailableNow() processes the backlog across multiple appropriately-sized batches (respecting rate limits like maxOffsetsPerTrigger) before stopping.

flashcards.q: What does the engine's 'exactly-once processing' guarantee actually cover, and what does it NOT cover?
flashcards.a: It covers offset tracking and operator state, committed atomically with each batch's completion via the checkpoint, so restarts neither reprocess nor skip committed batches. It does NOT cover the sink write itself — writing to the destination and committing the checkpoint are separate steps, and a crash between them can duplicate output unless the sink is idempotent or transactional.

flashcards.q: Is Spark's Kafka sink exactly-once by default? Why or why not?
flashcards.a: No, it is at-least-once by default. Kafka's idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true) only prevents duplicate sends within one producer session/retry — it has no memory across an entirely new attempt at the same logical batch after a restart. True exactly-once against Kafka needs custom foreachBatch logic with transactional writes.

flashcards.q: Why does Structured Streaming track Kafka offsets in its own checkpoint instead of relying on Kafka consumer-group commits?
flashcards.a: Engine-side exactly-once processing requires offset advancement and operator state to commit atomically together. Kafka consumer-group commits are a separate, non-atomic system relative to Spark's checkpoint; relying on them would reopen the race condition the checkpoint exists to close.

flashcards.q: Which sink is commonly cited as exactly-once 'for free', and why?
flashcards.a: The file sink, because Spark's file-sink commit protocol uses an atomic manifest/rename-based commit that avoids partial files on retry, so a retried batch's duplicate whole-file write is safe under standard manifest-based consumption.

flashcards.q: Describe Aurora's storage replication and quorum model.
flashcards.a: Data is replicated 6 ways across 3 Availability Zones (2 copies per AZ). Writes commit on a 4-of-6 quorum; reads are served from a 3-of-6 quorum. Since 4+3 > 6, any read quorum is guaranteed to overlap a write quorum by at least one node, avoiding the need for full consensus on every read.

flashcards.q: Why is Aurora failover typically under 60 seconds while standard RDS Multi-AZ failover takes 1-2 minutes?
flashcards.a: Aurora replicas share the same underlying distributed storage as the writer, so failover is just a role promotion. Standard RDS Multi-AZ promotes a separate synchronously-replicated standby with its own storage volume and redirects DNS, which takes longer.

flashcards.q: How does Aurora Serverless v2 scale, and what changed in November 2024?
flashcards.a: It scales in 0.5 ACU increments, scaling up within seconds but scaling down gradually over several minutes to avoid thrashing. In November 2024 it gained scale-to-zero support: it can pause entirely when idle (only storage charges continue) and resumes in roughly 15 seconds on the next connection.

flashcards.q: Compare typical replica lag for standard RDS async replication vs Aurora replicas.
flashcards.a: Standard RDS replica lag is measured in seconds and can stretch into minutes (or worse) under heavy write load. Aurora replicas read from the same shared storage as the writer, typically producing sub-10ms lag.

flashcards.q: What is the DynamoDB per-partition throughput ceiling, and what's the observable symptom of exceeding it?
flashcards.a: 3,000 read capacity units or 1,000 write capacity units per second, per partition -- a hard ceiling regardless of table-wide provisioned capacity. Symptom: ProvisionedThroughputExceededException throttling on specific items/key ranges while CloudWatch shows healthy aggregate consumed capacity well below the table total.

flashcards.q: Does DynamoDB adaptive capacity eliminate hot-partition throttling?
flashcards.a: No. It absorbs some traffic imbalance automatically by boosting a hot partition's effective throughput, but it cannot exceed the hard per-partition ceiling (3,000 RCU/1,000 WCU). A genuinely too-hot key still throttles and needs a partition-key redesign.

flashcards.q: Give an honest assessment of DynamoDB single-table design.
flashcards.a: Works when access patterns are well-understood, stable, and the team has real DynamoDB expertise, minimizing round trips at high scale. Fails when access patterns evolve, since retrofitting a new query shape onto an already-overloaded PK/SK/GSI schema is harder than adding a table would have been. Most teams should not do it -- even Rick Houlihan, its original advocate, has publicly acknowledged the backlash against treating it as a default.

flashcards.q: Key constraint differences between DynamoDB LSI and GSI?
flashcards.a: LSI: must share the base table's partition key, can only be defined at table creation and never added/removed later, supports strongly consistent reads, up to 5 per table, shares a 10GB-per-partition-key-value size limit with the base table. GSI: independent partition key, addable/removable anytime with automatic backfill, eventually consistent reads only, up to 20 per table (soft limit).

flashcards.q: How much more do DynamoDB transactions cost versus a normal read/write, and when do you actually need them?
flashcards.a: 2x the capacity units of the equivalent non-transactional operation. Needed only for genuine cross-item/cross-table atomicity (up to 100 items, 4MB aggregate cap); for single-item idempotency, a conditional write achieves the same safety at half the cost.

flashcards.q: What happened to ElastiCache's default engine choice, and why?
flashcards.a: The Redis license changed to SSPL/RSALv2 in 2024 and added an AGPLv3 option in 2025, so ElastiCache now defaults new deployments to Valkey, a Linux Foundation-governed, BSD-licensed fork of Redis OSS 7.2. ElastiCache only carries legacy Redis OSS support up to version 7.2. Valkey is also roughly 8% faster, 20% less memory, and about 20% cheaper per hour.

flashcards.q: Name three real MongoDB features DocumentDB does not fully support.
flashcards.a: No retryable writes (app code needs its own retry error-handling), no $graphLookup aggregation stage, and missing or limited support for capped collections, GridFS, text indexes, vector search indexes, partial indexes, and client-side field-level/queryable encryption.

flashcards.q: When is a graph database like Neptune the right choice over a relational database?
flashcards.a: When the dominant query shape is deep, multi-hop traversal (fraud-ring detection, recommendation collaborative filtering, social-graph queries) where relational joins degrade as hop count grows but graph traversal cost per hop stays roughly constant. Wrong choice for workloads that are mostly single-entity lookups with shallow joins -- relational is simpler and cheaper there.

flashcards.q: How did DynamoDB's November 2024 price change shift the on-demand vs provisioned decision?
flashcards.a: On-demand pricing dropped substantially, making it the recommended default for unpredictable or lower-volume workloads (roughly under 10M requests/month). Provisioned capacity with auto-scaling remains meaningfully cheaper -- commonly 3-4x at realistic ~70% utilization -- for sustained, predictable, high-utilization workloads.

flashcards.q: How long do DynamoDB Streams records persist, and what's the operational risk?
flashcards.a: 24 hours. A consumer down for longer than 24 hours permanently loses those change records (unlike Kinesis's configurable longer retention), so consumer recovery SLAs need to stay well under that window, or a periodic reconciliation should back it up.

flashcards.q: Why does the primary in Aurora send redo log records instead of full data pages to storage?
flashcards.a: Redo log records are much smaller (tens to hundreds of bytes) than full pages, which is what makes a 4-of-6 write quorum practical across the network without saturating it -- shipping full pages to 6 storage nodes for every write would be far more bandwidth-intensive.

flashcards.q: How does CloudWatch bill custom metrics, and why is this dangerous?
flashcards.a: Per unique time series -- every distinct combination of metric name, namespace, and dimension VALUES is a separate billable metric ($0.30/mo for first 10,000). Dimensions are multiplicative: one metric name with 10,000 distinct dimension values (e.g. userId) becomes 10,000 billable metrics, roughly $3,000/month.

flashcards.q: How do you avoid the CloudWatch high-cardinality trap?
flashcards.a: Keep metric dimensions to low-cardinality, bounded sets (service, environment, route, status class). Route high-cardinality detail (per-user, per-request) to structured logs (EMF or plain JSON), queried on demand via Logs Insights instead of billed per time series every month.

flashcards.q: X-Ray default sampling rate, and its 2026 status?
flashcards.a: Default: first request per second plus 5% of the rest, tunable per service/route. As of February 2026, X-Ray's SDKs and daemon are in maintenance mode -- AWS recommends OpenTelemetry instrumentation for new work.

flashcards.q: CloudTrail management events vs data events -- default and pricing?
flashcards.a: Management events: logged by default, first copy per region free, extra copies ~$2/100,000 events. Data events: NOT enabled by default, billed at $0.10/100,000 events from the very first event, no free tier.

flashcards.q: What's the classic CloudTrail cost trap?
flashcards.a: Enabling data events account-wide/bucket-wide for a compliance requirement with no scoping ('wide open'), sometimes compounded by overlapping multi-region + single-region trails double-logging the same events (the '2nd-copy trap'). Fix: advanced event selectors scoped to specific resources.

flashcards.q: Name the six Well-Architected Framework pillars.
flashcards.a: Operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, sustainability -- run as a structured review via the Well-Architected Tool, producing a prioritized High-Risk Issue list, not a slogan.

flashcards.q: Name the top 5 line items that dominate a real AI/data-heavy AWS bill.
flashcards.a: 1) NAT gateway data processing 2) Cross-AZ data transfer 3) Idle provisioned capacity (SageMaker endpoints, Bedrock model units, oversized Redshift) 4) Unpartitioned/uncompressed Athena or Redshift scans 5) Unscoped CloudTrail data events + high-cardinality CloudWatch metrics.

flashcards.q: Cost Explorer vs Budgets vs Cost Anomaly Detection -- what does each do?
flashcards.a: Cost Explorer: historical/forecast spend analysis, filterable by tag/service/region. Budgets: proactive threshold alerts (commonly 80%/100% of a target). Cost Anomaly Detection: ML-based alerting on spend deviating from a resource's own historical baseline.

flashcards.q: Why must cost allocation tags be applied at resource creation, not retroactively?
flashcards.a: Cost Explorer/Budgets/Anomaly Detection attribution only works from the point a tag is applied forward -- untagged historical spend has no retroactive attribution, so deferring tagging permanently loses that visibility for the deferred period.

flashcards.q: What is Embedded Metric Format (EMF) and does it avoid the cardinality cost problem?
flashcards.a: EMF lets you emit structured JSON log lines that CloudWatch automatically extracts into metrics -- good for high-volume metric emission because log ingestion is cheaper than PutMetricData and doesn't multiply per dimension the way custom metrics do at the emission layer. But whatever dimensions you configure it to EXTRACT into actual metrics are still subject to the same per-unique-time-series billing -- it doesn't remove the cardinality discipline requirement.

flashcards.q: What is 'idle provisioned capacity' as a cost failure mode, and why is it hard to catch with Cost Anomaly Detection?
flashcards.a: Capacity (SageMaker endpoints, Bedrock provisioned throughput, Redshift clusters) sized for peak and left running at trough. Anomaly Detection is tuned to catch deviations from a resource's OWN historical baseline -- steady idle spend doesn't look anomalous against its own history, so catching it requires a utilization-based review (provisioned vs actual usage), not an anomaly alert.

flashcards.q: What are the six cross-pillar Well-Architected design principles?
flashcards.a: Stop guessing capacity, test systems at production scale, automate with experimentation in mind, build for evolutionary architectures, drive decisions using data, and improve through game days.

flashcards.q: What are the three mandatory follow-ups asked after EVERY story in this round, regardless of how good it sounds?
flashcards.a: 1) 'Give me the number, and how you measured it.' 2) 'What did you consider and not do, and what did that alternative cost you?' 3) 'What would you do differently if you did it again tomorrow?'

flashcards.q: What's the asymmetric time shape of a single STAR answer?
flashcards.a: Situation 10% (~15s), Task 10% (~15s), Action 50% (~90s), Result 15% (~25s), rejected alternative 10% (~20s), redo/retrospective 5% (~10s). Action is where the score lives.

flashcards.q: Why is a story with no number scored at the bottom of the rubric regardless of how well it's told?
flashcards.a: Because the Result section requires a number with a stated measurement method to be verifiable evidence rather than a claim -- a well-told story with no number is indistinguishable from a well-told fabrication.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between 'claimed' and 'assigned' work, and why does it matter for level calibration?
flashcards.a: Assigned: 'my manager asked me to migrate the batch job' (senior work). Claimed: 'I noticed X was costing us Y and proposed and ran the fix' (staff work) -- same project, different level. Mark your own stories A/C and lead with the C ones at staff+.

flashcards.q: What number in this student's own story bank is explicitly flagged as the most attackable claim, and why?
flashcards.a: The ~25% engagement uplift figure -- a Bar Raiser is trained to find exactly this kind of bare percentage with no stated denominator, baseline, comparison design (holdout vs pre/post), or confounders named.

flashcards.q: What's the honest answer if a metric was measured via pre/post comparison with no holdout, and why does admitting it score higher than inventing rigor?
flashcards.a: Say so plainly and name why a holdout wasn't available (tenant contracts, rollout mechanics, no experimentation platform). Fabricated specificity about methodology collapses under one more question; honest limitation does not.

flashcards.q: What's a 'disguised praise' retrospective, and why does it fail the 'what would you do differently' question?
flashcards.a: A restatement of what already went well dressed up as humility ('I'd probably do the exact same thing, it worked out great'). It fails because a real retrospective must cost something to admit -- a specific, non-trivial revision, not affirmation of the original decision.

flashcards.q: Why does inflating a single-team story to cross-team/org-wide scope collapse quickly, and what's the safer move?
flashcards.a: It collapses on 'which teams, and what did they want?' -- an unanswerable follow-up if the scope was invented. Safer: state scope honestly, including admitting a story is single-team, since honest scope survives scrutiny and inflated scope does not.

flashcards.q: How does the interviewer's drilling style change by default company lens (Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Netflix)?
flashcards.a: Amazon: Bar Raiser drills for depth until something breaks. Google: demands quotable, transcribable sentences (a committee reads written notes, never met you). Meta: demands compression + multi-team scope + ends on self-critique. Microsoft: tracks your weakest answer for a second pass (AA round). Netflix: expects peer-level candor with no scaffolding.

flashcards.q: Why is 'we decided to self-host and it worked well' scored lower than 'I benchmarked three instance families against the real request distribution'?
flashcards.a: The first is first-person-plural with no isolable personal contribution ('team narration'); the second is first-person-singular with a specific, verifiable mechanism. Personal ownership vs. team narration is the single most common reason a strong-sounding story scores low.

flashcards.q: What's the required, prepared 2026 answer this round tests, and what does a weak version of it look like?
flashcards.a: How you work with AI coding tools, with a category rule (accept lightly reviewed vs. verify-deeply) and one concrete override instance. Weak: 'I always review AI-generated code carefully' with no category rule and no real instance.

flashcards.q: Why should you never criticize a current or former employer, even when a criticism is factually justified?
flashcards.a: It reads as a risk signal regardless of justification, and it devalues every other story told in the same round that was built on that employer's platform -- criticizing the employer criticizes the evidence base of the whole round.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between the LEAN HIRE band (9-12/20) and the HIRE band (13-16/20) in this round?
flashcards.a: LEAN HIRE: stories are real and personally owned but numbers are frequently bare (no denominator/baseline) and the rejected-alternative/retrospective are thin even after being asked directly. HIRE: STAR shape solid, mandatory follow-ups produce real answers, but 1-2 need the follow-up prompt to surface rather than being volunteered.

flashcards.q: Why is repeating the same headline story unchanged across multiple competency questions a time-management failure?
flashcards.a: It reads as a thin story bank even when the underlying story is strong. Fix: explicit reframing ('I mentioned the platform earlier for ownership; let me take the security angle this time').

flashcards.q: What single red flag is worse than a low score on any individual story?
flashcards.a: Naming a Leadership Principle or competency explicitly while telling the story ('this really shows my ownership') instead of simply exhibiting the behavior -- narrating the rubric instead of meeting it.

flashcards.q: State the 9-phase design-round sequence and its 45-minute timebox.
flashcards.a: Restate(2) -> requirements(5) -> constraints/numbers(5) -> API(5) -> data model(7) -> architecture(8) -> scale(6) -> failure(5) -> wrap(2). Each phase's artefact constrains the next -- skipping or reordering breaks the derivation chain.

flashcards.q: Why must the API contract and data model come BEFORE the architecture diagram?
flashcards.a: An API signature forces the read/write split into the open; a schema commits to an access pattern, which determines the partition key, which determines whether the scaling story is even coherent. Boxes drawn before this exist have nothing to be derived from.

flashcards.q: What's the rule for how many capacity numbers to compute, and how do you decide which ones?
flashcards.a: Compute only the 2-3 numbers you're actually going to USE, and state the use before computing ('I need QPS to decide whether one Postgres primary can take the write path'). Numbers that never feed a decision are theater.

flashcards.q: Give the four interrupt lines a design-round interviewer uses, and when each fires.
flashcards.a: Minute 20, no data model yet: 'We're almost halfway and I don't have a data model.' Minute 30, boxes with no derivation: 'Why does this box exist?' Minute 33, no number stated: 'Give me a QPS number, just estimate it.' Minute 40, no failure modes: 'The primary just went down -- what does the user see, right now?'

flashcards.q: Fan-out-on-write vs fan-out-on-read for a social feed: what's the tradeoff, and what's the real production answer?
flashcards.a: Write: fast reads, breaks on celebrity accounts (millions of writes per post). Read: avoids celebrity write-amplification, but every read is expensive. Real answer: hybrid -- write for normal accounts, read (or special-cased merge) for accounts above a follower threshold.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't 'exactly-once execution' exist across a network, and what do you design for instead?
flashcards.a: True exactly-once cannot be guaranteed in the general case across a network. Design for at-least-once execution plus idempotency at the consumer, or a distributed lock with a lease/fencing token to prevent two owners from both believing they hold a job.

flashcards.q: A distributed lock has a 30-second lease; the job takes 45 seconds under load. What breaks, exactly?
flashcards.a: The lease expires mid-execution, a second worker acquires the lock believing the first is dead, and two instances of the job run concurrently. Fix: heartbeat/lease-renewal from the still-alive worker, or accept the job must be idempotent regardless.

flashcards.q: Why is a metadata post-filter bolted onto an ANN index a common, real bug in multi-tenant vector search?
flashcards.a: If you filter by tenant/locale AFTER retrieving top-k, the top-k can be entirely the wrong tenant, returning zero valid results even though matching vectors exist. Fix: a native filtered index or filtering that's structurally part of retrieval, not applied after.

flashcards.q: What's the 2026-specific NFR that a GenAI/LLM design must include or it reads as junior?
flashcards.a: Cost -- a dollar figure per request or per month, order of magnitude is fine, is now a first-class non-functional requirement alongside latency and availability, especially for anything GPU-adjacent.

flashcards.q: What's the specific real mechanism that turns self-hosted LLM serving efficient, and what does sizing by GPU memory alone miss?
flashcards.a: Continuous batching plus PagedAttention-style KV-cache management turns single-digit GPU utilization into useful throughput for many concurrent short requests. Sizing by GPU memory alone can hide a KV-cache-driven throughput COLLAPSE under load that a memory-fit check wouldn't catch.

flashcards.q: When two services always deploy together and never scale independently, what's the honest architectural conclusion?
flashcards.a: They are one service with a network hop. The decomposition criterion (independent scaling, independent failure) should be tested against real evidence, and the honest answer may be to merge them or to concede more data is needed before defending the split.

flashcards.q: Why should consistency requirements NOT be applied uniformly across one product (e.g. checkout inventory vs. recommendation freshness)?
flashcards.a: Inventory during checkout needs strong consistency or an explicit reservation/lock (oversell is a costly, customer-facing failure). Recommendation freshness can tolerate eventual consistency measured in minutes with no customer-visible harm. Applying one model to both wastes latency/throughput budget or risks real financial loss.

flashcards.q: An agent can take irreversible actions on a user's behalf. Where must the authorization for a privileged action live?
flashcards.a: In code outside the model -- an explicit allowlist, spend limit, or human-in-the-loop confirmation for anything above a risk threshold -- never as a claim the model's stated intent should be trusted to have obeyed under adversarial pressure.

flashcards.q: What's the single most common pacing failure across FAANG-style design rounds?
flashcards.a: Drawing the architecture diagram in the first 3-5 minutes and spending 60%+ of the 45 minutes on the high-level box diagram, leaving almost no time for deep dives and failure modes -- which is where the score weight actually sits.

flashcards.q: What defines the STRONG HIRE band (17-20/20) for the design round?
flashcards.a: Requirements-to-numbers-to-API-to-data-model-to-architecture sequence self-driven with no prompting between phases; every box traces to something said earlier; cost stated with real arithmetic; recovers from an interrupt or 'why not X' challenge within one exchange by updating the design, not defending it.

flashcards.q: What's the deliberate order of the five rounds in the full loop, and why that order?
flashcards.a: Coding -> Design -> AI Depth (ML or GenAI) -> Behavioral -> HM Grill. Coding first (mechanically graded, before fatigue). Design second (fresh for 45min of sustained structure). AI depth third (mid-loop, derivation over recall). Behavioral fourth (deliberately after the technical gauntlet, to surface whether STAR discipline survives fatigue). HM grill last (mirrors how real onsites close).

flashcards.q: What's the single core principle of the committee verdict, stated as a rule?
flashcards.a: A candidate does not get hired by being good on average -- they get hired by not being bad anywhere, plus being excellent somewhere. The verdict is not an arithmetic average of the five round scores.

flashcards.q: What's the operative question the committee asks about the weakest round, instead of computing a mean?
flashcards.a: Does the weakest round, on its own, indicate a gap serious enough to sink the hire regardless of the other four -- weighted by how central that round's skill is to the actual role.

flashcards.q: Why is a pattern of contradiction between a strong round and a weak round worse than uniformly middling performance across all five?
flashcards.a: It suggests the strong round may have been well-rehearsed rather than reflecting real depth -- the committee should re-examine the strong round's evidence more skeptically, not just average around the weak one.

flashcards.q: How is the level read (senior/staff/principal) determined from a full loop, and what's the common mistake?
flashcards.a: From the PATTERN across at least 3 of the 5 rounds, not from the single best round. The common mistake is rounding up to the best data point -- if 4 rounds show senior-level structure and only 1 shows a staff-level unprompted tradeoff, the honest read is senior with staff potential, not staff.

flashcards.q: What are the four required elements of the committee verdict, in order?
flashcards.a: 1) Overall recommendation (not an average). 2) The round that would have sunk it, named specifically even in an overall HIRE. 3) The level read with specific supporting evidence and the specific gap to the next level. 4) One thing to fix -- the single highest-leverage gap across all five rounds, not five separate fixes.

flashcards.q: What's the 'consistency check' in the debrief, and what specifically does it look for?
flashcards.a: Whether the same fact, number, or scope claim stays identical across rounds where the same story recurs (e.g. the same headline metric's measurement method described the same way in the behavioral round and the HM grill), and whether seniority signals (unprompted tradeoffs, honest uncertainty) persist into round 4-5 or only appear early.

flashcards.q: What does 'front-loading' look like as a full-loop failure pattern, and why does it read worse than simple fatigue?
flashcards.a: A visibly strong round 1 followed by a collapse in seniority signals (no more unprompted tradeoffs, no more honest uncertainty) by round 4-5. It reads as rehearsed material running out, not fatigue, because genuine depth doesn't have a fixed supply that runs dry after one round.

flashcards.q: Why is referencing an earlier round's content ('I already covered this in the design round') treated as evasive in the full loop, even though it might be true?
flashcards.a: Real interviewers in a real loop have not seen the other rounds' content -- referencing an earlier round instead of answering the current question directly reads as evasive regardless of the candidate's intent.

flashcards.q: What single round outcome is treated as a serious signal regardless of how strong the other four rounds are?
flashcards.a: Any single round scoring STRONG NO HIRE (0-4/20) -- a real committee treats this as a serious, not automatically overridable, signal even against four strong rounds.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between the STRONG HIRE and HIRE overall bands, in terms of round distribution?
flashcards.a: STRONG HIRE: no round below HIRE (13+), at least one round at STRONG HIRE (17+) in the domain most relevant to the target role, level read supported by 3+ rounds. HIRE: at most one round at LEAN HIRE (and not in a role-central domain), no round at NO HIRE or below, seniority signals persist (even if less frequently) into later rounds.

flashcards.q: Why should the debrief never be skipped, even after a 4-hour loop?
flashcards.a: Roughly half the module's value lives in the debrief's cross-round consistency check and level-read reasoning -- running all five rounds and skipping straight to an overall verdict without it wastes the harder, more diagnostic half of the exercise.

flashcards.q: How should a bad round be handled going into the next round, both by the interviewer and the candidate?
flashcards.a: Each round is judged on its own evidence -- a bad round's score should not bleed into the next round's scoring. The candidate's failure mode to avoid: spending the next round's early minutes mentally re-litigating the previous bad round instead of resetting and being present for the new prompt.

flashcards.q: What's the cross-cutting rubric dimension this module adds on top of the five rounds' own 20-point rubrics?
flashcards.a: Consistency across rounds -- scored separately and reported alongside the five round scores, checking whether facts/numbers/scope claims stay identical across rounds and whether seniority signals persist at the same rate in round 5 as round 1.

flashcards.q: Why is a LEAN HIRE in the role's core skill weighted worse than a STRONG HIRE somewhere less central to the role?
flashcards.a: The committee verdict weights the weakest round by its relevance to the actual job -- a LEAN HIRE on GenAI depth for a GenAI-heavy role is a bigger problem than a LEAN HIRE on coding for a role that's 90% design and stakeholder work, even if the raw scores look similar.

flashcards.q: Name three valid stop conditions for an agent loop, and why you need at least two simultaneously.
flashcards.a: Max-iteration cap, model-emitted 'done' signal, cost/token budget ceiling. Need 2+ because relying solely on the model to say 'I'm done' fails when the model gets stuck reasoning in circles.

flashcards.q: Why does dense-vector-only retrieval fail on exact-match queries, and what fixes it?
flashcards.a: An embedding model can rate a semantically similar but lexically wrong result higher than an exact but less 'fluent' match -- fails on SKUs, error codes, proper nouns, acronyms. Fix: hybrid search, fusing BM25 (lexical) with dense vectors, typically via Reciprocal Rank Fusion: score = sum(1/(k+rank_i)), k~60.

flashcards.q: What do HNSW's M and ef_search parameters each control, and which is the cheaper tuning lever?
flashcards.a: M = max links per node per layer (recall vs. memory/build-time, requires reindex to change). ef_search = query-time candidate list size (recall vs. latency, cheapest lever, no reindex needed). Recall@k is a tunable curve, not a fixed property of 'using HNSW.'

flashcards.q: Recall@10 is 85%, product wants 95%. What are your levers in order of cost?
flashcards.a: 1) Raise ef_search (cheapest, query-time only). 2) Raise M (requires full reindex, more memory). 3) Check if the embedding model itself is the ceiling -- compare ANN recall against brute-force exact search on the same query set; if exact search also fails, the embedding is the problem, not the index.

flashcards.q: Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder: what's the architectural difference, and why can't a cross-encoder replace retrieval entirely?
flashcards.a: Bi-encoder embeds query and doc independently (index-able, cheap, but no query-doc attention). Cross-encoder concatenates query+doc and runs jointly through a transformer (catches token-level interactions, but nothing to precompute -- score depends on the query, unknown until query time). Can't scale to a full corpus per query, so it only reranks a small top-k.

flashcards.q: Give a measurable definition of hallucination, and the two-tier eval pipeline that catches a regression.
flashcards.a: A claim in the output not supported by the retrieved context/source, stated with unwarranted confidence. Pipeline: fast tolerance-based check gating every deploy (aggregate groundedness score against a golden set of real production queries) + slower thorough check (human review or LLM-judge ensemble) running nightly/pre-release.

flashcards.q: Name two concrete failure modes of 'just put everything in the context window' even with a 1M-token model.
flashcards.a: Lost-in-the-middle (models attend more reliably to content near the start/end than content buried mid-context) and cost/latency scaling (attention cost and time-to-first-token both grow with context length -- not free even when it fits).

flashcards.q: What's the real test for whether splitting a monolithic agent into multiple specialized agents is justified?
flashcards.a: Split only when failure modes, scaling profiles, or retry/rollback semantics genuinely differ between responsibilities. Most reported multi-agent failures are 'one agent's worth of logic with extra network hops and an ambiguous failure mode,' not genuine decomposition.

flashcards.q: What does MCP/FastMCP actually add over writing function-calling tools directly, and when should you skip it?
flashcards.a: Protocol-level decoupling: a tool surface becomes a versioned contract a second, unrelated consumer can use without importing the first app's code. Skip it for a single application with no reuse case -- in-process function calling is simpler with one fewer moving part.

flashcards.q: Where does prompt injection actually live, and what's the real architectural mitigation (not the linguistic one)?
flashcards.a: Any content the model reads that originated outside your control can contain text crafted to look like an instruction, and the model can't reliably distinguish system instructions from embedded ones -- both arrive as tokens in the same context. Real mitigation: untrusted content is data the model reasons ABOUT, never instructions it obeys; privileged/irreversible actions are gated by CODE outside the model (allowlist, human confirmation), never by a system-prompt instruction alone.

flashcards.q: Rank structured-output mitigations by reliability, and state what none of them guarantee.
flashcards.a: Constrained/grammar-based decoding (structural guarantee, strongest) > few-shot examples + strict system prompt (behavioral nudge, weak) > regex extraction + retry-on-failure (fallback, non-zero failure rate). None guarantee SEMANTIC correctness -- a syntactically valid JSON can still call the wrong tool with hallucinated arguments.

flashcards.q: Fine-tuning vs. RAG: what's each actually good for, and what's the diagnostic for which one a failure needs?
flashcards.a: Fine-tuning teaches STYLE/format/behavior; poorly suited to FACTS that change (stale the moment data changes, needs retraining). RAG serves facts that update the moment the index refreshes. Diagnostic: wrong/outdated facts -> retrieval problem; wrong tone/format/reasoning style regardless of facts given -> fine-tuning problem.

flashcards.q: Your RAG-as-tool call times out, returns zero results, or returns uniformly low-confidence results. Are these one failure mode or three?
flashcards.a: Three distinct failure modes needing distinct handlers: timeout -> bounded retry + graceful degradation with an explicit caveat; zero results -> bounded query-reformulation retry or honest 'not found,' never a fabricated fill-in; low confidence -> lower stated certainty or surface the uncertainty, never present as solid grounding. Never one generic retry-and-hope.

flashcards.q: Why is fine-tuning on domain Q&A pairs sometimes correlated with a HIGHER hallucination rate, not lower?
flashcards.a: It can teach the model the STYLE of correctness (in-domain vocabulary, plausible structure) without improving factual grounding, and can suppress the base model's calibrated uncertainty -- a model that would have hedged now speaks with unearned fine-tuned confidence.

flashcards.q: This round's calibration rule: what score band should feel harder to earn here than in the ML round, and why?
flashcards.a: HIRE (14-17/20) and above should be harder to earn, because GenAI is the student's strongest domain and a shallow pass here is a meaningful red flag for a principal-level GenAI role, not an acceptable outcome.

flashcards.q: In this round, who picks which resume bullets get drilled, and why does that matter for preparation?
flashcards.a: The interviewer picks, not the candidate. This means every bullet needs to be prepared to real depth, not just the 3 favorite rehearsed stories -- the test is specifically whether depth is uniform across the resume or concentrated in a few spots.

flashcards.q: What resume error must be corrected unprompted the moment the vLLM/SageMaker bullet comes up, and what are the real values?
flashcards.a: 'ml.4xlarge' and 'g4.2xlarge' are not real SageMaker instance identifiers. Real ones are almost certainly ml.g4dn.2xlarge and ml.g5.xlarge. Correcting it cleanly and without defensiveness is the actual signal; the error itself is forgivable.

flashcards.q: For the 8-service platform bullet, what's the strong answer to 'if you had to cut two people and had half the timeline, which of these eight would not exist?'
flashcards.a: A real prioritization with a stated reason -- event and context path first, because a recommender with no context is a popularity list. Not 'we needed all eight,' which reveals no ordering logic behind the scope.

flashcards.q: For the 89% ETL latency reduction bullet, what's the first follow-up a technically literate hiring manager asks, and why is it the weakest part of the story as written?
flashcards.a: 'What was actually consuming the 4.5 hours?' The story as documented gives the before/after numbers but not the root bottleneck (sequential stages, unpartitioned reads, a skewed join, single-node processing) -- repeating the headline number without this is the single most attackable gap on this bullet.

flashcards.q: Why is 'nine times faster' on the ETL story an incomplete answer, and what follow-up exposes it?
flashcards.a: 'Nine times faster sometimes just means nine times more compute spend.' A candidate who hasn't considered the cost side of their own signature performance metric reads as someone who optimized one dimension without checking the other.

flashcards.q: For the OWASP/cross-tenant authorization bullet, what's the strong answer to 'how loudly did you escalate it, and to whom?'
flashcards.a: A concrete reproduction written up (not a vague concern), escalated immediately rather than quietly patched (a silent fix leaves nobody able to assess exposure), fixed at the object-fetch layer as a class fix rather than patching only discovered instances.

flashcards.q: For the ClickHouse OOM bullet, what's the honest answer to 'gc.collect() is a workaround, not the real fix -- why didn't you build it right the first time?'
flashcards.a: Admit it plainly: streaming with generators and bounded batches so no large object graph ever exists is the structural fix; gc.collect() compensates for allocator behavior rather than eliminating memory pressure. Admitting the first fix was expedient is stronger than defending it as ideal.

flashcards.q: For the MongoDB race-conditions bullet, what does 'your test suite passed the whole time this bug existed' actually reveal, and what should change?
flashcards.a: Both bug classes (race conditions, event-loop errors) are invisible at parallelism one, which is the concurrency level most test suites run at by default. The real fix isn't complete without a CI concurrency test that runs the hot path above production peak parallelism.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between the answer 'I built all eight services' and a strong answer to 'which parts specifically did you write'?
flashcards.a: A strong answer differentiates: which services had direct personal code contribution vs. architecture/design ownership with review vs. delegation -- precision about scope of authorship, not a blanket claim of having built everything personally.

flashcards.q: What's the hardest version of the scope-calibration question, and why is it deliberately the hardest?
flashcards.a: 'Name one thing outside your own code that other engineers had to change because of a decision you made.' It's deliberately hard because this is a genuinely thin area on this resume -- the strong answer is an honest one even if it's 'I have one strong example and not a second as strong,' not a manufactured second claim.

flashcards.q: What's the real test behind 'why are you leaving,' and what follow-up checks for coherence?
flashcards.a: Whether the stated reason is forward-looking, specific, and not disparaging the current employer. Coherence check: 'if your current company offered you this exact role and scope, would you stay?' -- an answer revealing pure compensation motivation with nothing structural is legitimate but weaker than one naming something the current employer structurally cannot offer.

flashcards.q: For the manager-disagreement question, what does the follow-up 'would you have escalated further if your manager's manager overruled you?' actually test?
flashcards.a: Whether the disagreement was really about being right or about a safe, low-stakes battle. Strong answer: a stated threshold for when to let a technical disagreement go (low-stakes) vs. escalate further (real correctness/safety consequences) -- not claiming to fight every battle regardless of stakes.

flashcards.q: Why is the order of this round's rounds within a full loop deliberate (coding -> design -> AI depth -> behavioral -> HM grill)?
flashcards.a: HM grill runs last because it's closest to how most real onsites close -- with the person who has to defend the hire internally -- and because it tests whether depth and honesty persist after four rounds of cumulative fatigue, not just at the start of the day.

flashcards.q: What must be true about the STAR bank's [CONFIRM: ...] markers before this round can be run for a real score?
flashcards.a: They must be resolved with real numbers first -- team size, adoption counts, measurement methods. Running the round with placeholder gaps still in the source material means the round can't score correctness/depth meaningfully, since the ground truth itself is incomplete.

flashcards.q: What's the STRONG NO HIRE tell in this round, distinct from just getting facts wrong?
flashcards.a: Not noticing, or getting defensive about, a direct factual correction from the interviewer (e.g. the SageMaker instance names) -- the inability to cleanly absorb a correction is a bigger red flag than the original error.

flashcards.q: What is the central risk of any backfill or replay, stated precisely?
flashcards.a: It runs today's code and today's reference data against a historical date parameter. Code drift and reference-data drift (exchange rates, tax tables) both apply, so the result may reflect the present rather than the past that actually occurred.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between a backfill and a replay, and why is replay riskier?
flashcards.a: A backfill fills a genuine gap (nothing there to corrupt, bounded downside). A replay recomputes existing history already in use downstream, so a bug in the replay actively overwrites and can corrupt data that was previously correct and already relied upon.

flashcards.q: What's the mechanical safety net that makes a backfill/replay survivable?
flashcards.a: Idempotent partition overwrite (INSERT OVERWRITE PARTITION, not append) or merge/upsert on a natural key, combined with deterministic transforms (no NOW()/random ordering in business logic).

flashcards.q: Why does embedding CURRENT_TIMESTAMP/NOW() in business logic break idempotency?
flashcards.a: Every rerun of the same partition produces a superficially different result even when the underlying logic hasn't changed, making it impossible to distinguish a genuine discrepancy from expected non-determinism.

flashcards.q: Why must a naive year-long backfill be concurrency-limited?
flashcards.a: Firing all 365 date-partitions concurrently against the same warehouse compute and source systems is functionally a self-inflicted denial-of-service against your own infrastructure. Use max_active_runs (or equivalent) to bound concurrent partitions.

flashcards.q: Why must a backfill of a cumulative/running-total metric process partitions in strict chronological order?
flashcards.a: Parallelizing it would compute each day's cumulative value against a stale or missing prior-day base. Independent, non-cumulative daily aggregates can safely parallelize, but dependent ones cannot.

flashcards.q: What's the observable symptom of a partially-applied backfill?
flashcards.a: A time-series chart of the metric shows a sudden step-change/discontinuity exactly at the boundary between reprocessed and not-yet-reprocessed partitions, with no underlying business reason for the jump.

flashcards.q: What operational feature turns diagnosing a partial backfill failure from chart-staring into a log query?
flashcards.a: Resumable, partition-level tracking — an audit log recording success/failure per partition, so a restarted backfill resumes from the last successful partition instead of restarting from scratch or silently leaving the remainder unprocessed.

flashcards.q: Name three concrete cases where you should NOT backfill.
flashcards.a: 1) The source data needed no longer exists (don't fabricate an approximation). 2) The cost/risk exceeds the value of a rarely-queried historical gap. 3) The 'bug' is actually a legitimate historical fact — old logic was correct then, so applying today's logic retroactively misrepresents history.

flashcards.q: Why is a naive currency-conversion backfill dangerous, and what's the correct approach?
flashcards.a: Joining historical transactions to a 'current' exchange-rate table applies today's rate to old transactions, producing plausible but factually wrong revenue. The correct approach uses an SCD Type 2 exchange-rate dimension with an as-of filter matching each transaction's actual date.

flashcards.q: What does a backfill audit trail need to record, and what does lakehouse time-travel add on top?
flashcards.a: The audit trail records what range was rerun, when, by whom, and with what code version, per partition. Lakehouse time-travel (Delta/Iceberg snapshots) complements this by letting you diff the table's exact state immediately before and after the operation as a query, not a backup restore.

flashcards.q: What is a reprocessing window, and how does it differ operationally from an ad hoc backfill?
flashcards.a: A reprocessing window is a planned, small-scope, automatic replay built into normal pipeline operation (e.g. 'final after 3 days' to catch late data). It's bounded and expected by design, unlike an unplanned, manually-triggered backfill, so it doesn't need the same case-by-case risk review.

flashcards.q: Why should backfill risk review not be a full committee process for every request?
flashcards.a: Mechanical safety nets (idempotent overwrite, bounded concurrency, mandatory audit logging) can be enforced automatically by tooling, letting review focus on the judgment calls that actually matter: whether a discrepancy is a bug or legitimate history, and what the concurrency/compute plan is.

flashcards.q: Why can't prompt injection be fixed the way SQL injection was fixed?
flashcards.a: SQL has a real grammar; parameterization compiles query structure before user data is bound, so the parser can't reinterpret data as syntax. Natural language has no equivalent grammar — there's no placeholder to bind around, so instructions and data always share one channel.

flashcards.q: Direct vs indirect prompt injection — define both.
flashcards.a: Direct: the user themselves types the attack into their own input. Indirect: the attack arrives embedded in content the model reads later — a web page, a RAG document, a tool's error string, even a filename.

flashcards.q: Indirect vs direct injection success rate from the 2026 Gray Swan/NIST red-team analysis?
flashcards.a: Indirect attacks succeeded 27.1% of the time vs 5.7% for direct attacks, across 1.8M submitted attacks against 22 frontier agents.

flashcards.q: What are the three legs of Simon Willison's lethal trifecta?
flashcards.a: Access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally. All three present means an attacker who controls any untrusted content the agent reads can potentially exfiltrate the private data.

flashcards.q: What's the primary fix once you identify a lethal trifecta in an agent design?
flashcards.a: Remove one leg (make browsing read-only with no rendering, scope away private-data access from the session, or gate external communication behind approval) rather than relying on detecting the injection harder.

flashcards.q: What is LLM01 in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, and how many consecutive editions has it held that spot?
flashcards.a: Prompt Injection — LLM01 for the third consecutive edition. Found in 87% of enterprise-pentested LLM apps in 2025-2026.

flashcards.q: What are the three new/changed categories in the OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 edition vs the prior list?
flashcards.a: System Prompt Leakage (LLM07) and Vector and Embedding Weaknesses (LLM08) are new; Unbounded Consumption (LLM10) expanded from Model Denial of Service; Misinformation (LLM09) absorbed the old Overreliance category.

flashcards.q: What does LLM06 Excessive Agency mean concretely for an agent?
flashcards.a: The agent has more functionality, permissions, or autonomy than its task requires — e.g. a calendar assistant given a generic delete-any-event tool when it only ever needs to create events on the requesting user's own calendar.

flashcards.q: Name two risk categories from the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (Dec 2025) not covered by the original LLM Top 10.
flashcards.a: Agent behavior hijacking and tool misuse/exploitation (also: identity and privilege abuse, and memory/context poisoning).

flashcards.q: Why is a system-prompt rule like 'never delete records without confirmation' not a security control?
flashcards.a: It's advisory text in the same channel an attacker's injected content can also write to, so it competes with the attack on equal footing instead of from a privileged position. A permission engine evaluated as code, which the model cannot influence, is the actual control.

flashcards.q: Are MCP tool annotation hints (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint) an enforcement mechanism?
flashcards.a: No. They're self-asserted by the tool server and unenforced — useful as inputs to a permission engine's decision, not a substitute for one.

flashcards.q: What's the observable trace symptom of a successful prompt injection?
flashcards.a: A tool call to a target, recipient, or destination that was never present in the user's own request, appearing immediately downstream of a step that ingested untrusted content (a document read or a web fetch).

flashcards.q: Name two indirect-injection benchmarks used to measure agent injection resistance, with their scale.
flashcards.a: AgentDojo (97 realistic tasks, 629 security test cases, NeurIPS 2024) and AgentHarm (110 malicious tasks, 440 with augmentations, 11 harm categories).

flashcards.q: Does a more capable/larger model resist prompt injection better?
flashcards.a: No clear correlation was found between model capability or size and injection robustness in NIST's 2026 red-team analysis. Model upgrades don't fix this; harness and architecture changes do.

flashcards.q: What made the GitLab Duo Chatbot exploit a textbook lethal trifecta?
flashcards.a: It could ingest a public project's text containing rogue instructions (untrusted content), had access to private repository information (private data), and could render attacker-supplied content/links (external communication) — all three legs simultaneously live.

flashcards.q: What are the four things that actually change between a demo agent loop and a production one?
flashcards.a: Budgets move from a for-loop bound to enforced, shared, server-side limits. Failure recovery moves from restart-from-scratch to resume-from-checkpoint. Cancellation moves from Ctrl-C to a cooperative flag checked at safe boundaries. Output moves from one blocking response to a multi-granularity event stream (token, step, event). The forty-line loop core barely changes; these four wrappers are the actual work.

flashcards.q: Why is a client-side (in-process) budget check insufficient in production, and what fixes it?
flashcards.a: It is per-process. If a run scales across multiple workers or gets retried onto a different worker, each process independently believes it holds the authoritative remaining budget, and N processes can each spend up to the cap, overspending by up to Nx. The fix is a shared, atomically-updated ledger (Redis counter, Postgres row with a conditional update) as the actual enforcement point; the client-side check remains a legitimate fast-fail optimization on top of it.

flashcards.q: Describe the budget reservation pattern and why plain check-then-spend fails under concurrency.
flashcards.a: Reservation debits the maximum possible cost of the next operation BEFORE it runs, then credits back the unspent difference after. Check-then-spend asks 'do I have headroom right now' and spends optimistically, which is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race: two processes can both check, both see headroom, and both spend, jointly overshooting the cap by up to Nx under N concurrent workers.

flashcards.q: At 85% per-step reliability, a 10-step agent completes end-to-end about 20% of the time. What does checkpointing actually fix about this, and what does it NOT fix?
flashcards.a: 0.85^10 ~= 20% is the compounding-failure math and checkpointing does not change it -- it does not raise per-step reliability. What it fixes is the COST of a failure: without checkpointing, every failure discards all prior correct work and forces a restart from step zero; with checkpointing, a transient failure resumes from the last durably-saved state, so a failure at step 7 loses one step's work, not seven. Raising the actual 85% requires errors-as-observations, better tools, or a better model -- orthogonal fixes that compose with checkpointing.

flashcards.q: Where must checkpoint boundaries sit relative to tool calls, and why?
flashcards.a: After a tool result is durably recorded, before the next model call. A crash mid-model-call then resumes by re-issuing a request that hasn't happened yet, which is safe. A crash mid-tool-execution is the genuinely hard case, since the side effect may have already occurred with no recorded result -- this is exactly why every mutating tool needs an idempotency key regardless of checkpoint placement.

flashcards.q: Why is a kill switch for an agent loop cooperative rather than preemptive, and what is the hard-kill escalation path?
flashcards.a: You cannot forcibly interrupt an in-flight tool call without risking a half-completed side effect (e.g. an SMTP call that returns after the kill signal but before your code records 'sent'). So the kill flag is checked at safe boundaries -- between the model call and tool execution, never mid-call -- and a slow tool must accept its own cancellation token and check it internally, since the harness can't reach inside a black-box call. If soft kill doesn't resolve within a grace period (mirroring SIGTERM then SIGKILL, ~30s typical), escalate to a hard kill (terminate the worker process), which is not correctness-safe and requires idempotency on every mutating tool to recover from.

flashcards.q: What is the observable symptom that a kill switch isn't actually stopping spend, and what causes it?
flashcards.a: The run's status flips to 'cancelled' in your database, but API spend or tool side effects continue for tens of seconds afterward -- visible as billing activity or tool-side log entries timestamped after the recorded cancellation. That gap is the time between 'flag set' and 'worker checks flag'; if it's large, the check interval is too coarse, e.g. checking only once per full loop iteration when a single tool call inside that iteration runs for 90 seconds.

flashcards.q: Name the three streaming granularities a production agent UI needs, and what each one fixes.
flashcards.a: Token-level (raw SSE deltas, e.g. Anthropic's content_block_delta) fixes perceived latency during generation. Step-level (harness-synthesized events like 'using tool: search') fixes the silence problem during tool execution, which produces no text tokens and otherwise looks identical to a hang. Event-level (budget state, checkpoints, compaction) fixes transparency and debuggability. Token-only streaming misses tool-execution silence; step-only misses generation latency; neither gives operational visibility.

flashcards.q: Why does a 5-tool-call turn get reported by users as 'the agent hung', and what's the zero-cost fix?
flashcards.a: Tool execution produces no text tokens, so a client watching only token-level deltas sees pure silence for the full duration of the tool calls (commonly 15-40 seconds across several calls), and users interpret silence as broken well before any real timeout fires. The fix is emitting step-level events ('using tool: X') during exactly that gap -- it costs nothing at the model layer since it's entirely harness-emitted, not part of the raw model stream.

flashcards.q: One tool call in a parallel batch fails. What must you send back, and what breaks if you don't?
flashcards.a: A tool_result for EVERY tool_use block in that turn, including an error result (is_error: true) for the one that failed -- never silently omit it. The API pairs tool_use and tool_result by id; a turn with an unpaired tool_use produces an invalid next request (API 400). This also applies after a crash mid-batch: the resumed run must synthesize an error/cancelled tool_result for any tool_use left unfinished before the next model call.

flashcards.q: Your fleet's retries against a recovering upstream are making the outage worse, not better. Diagnose and fix.
flashcards.a: Classic retry amplification without a fleet-level budget: every worker independently backs off and retries, and without jitter the retries synchronize into waves that hit the recovering service exactly as it comes back up. Respecting retry-after alone doesn't fix it, because if 500 workers all honor the same retry-after value they all retry at the same moment. Fix: add jitter on top of provider guidance, plus a fleet-level retry budget (cap retries at some fraction of total request volume) so aggregate behavior is bounded regardless of individual worker count.

flashcards.q: How should you detect a runaway agent loop before the bill does?
flashcards.a: Alert on p99 step count and p99 cost per run, not the mean -- step-count distributions are commonly bimodal (most runs finish fast, a tail hits the step cap), and a mean hides the runaway tail entirely. Also watch time-to-first-token per step: a step that used to take 2s and now takes 40s signals upstream degradation or context bloat before a customer reports it.

flashcards.q: What are the two settled directions and one unsettled direction in where production agent loop architecture is heading?
flashcards.a: Settled (high confidence): event-sourced agent state as an append-only log of typed events, rather than a mutable message array, that both resume and audit replay from -- this is how major managed platforms already work internally. Also settled: durable execution generally, i.e. state belongs in a database/log, not process memory. Unsettled: standardized cancellation semantics -- there is no cross-framework convention yet for what 'kill this run' guarantees (wait for the in-flight call? roll back? just stop scheduling?), and frameworks differ today.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT build the full production-loop apparatus (budgets, resume, kill switch, streaming)?
flashcards.a: For short, synchronous, single-user tasks finishing in a few seconds with a handful of tool calls -- a step cap and a deadline suffice, and the full apparatus is pure overhead relative to the risk. Also skip building it yourself if the org already runs a workflow engine (Temporal, Step Functions), since checkpointing and durable retries are exactly what those already provide and reimplementing them on a raw loop produces a worse version of something you have. And if a managed agent platform already runs the loop server-side with sessions, streaming, and cancellation, paying for that is a legitimate choice over building it.

flashcards.q: Why must the kill switch's shared state live outside the worker process rather than as an in-process boolean?
flashcards.a: The request to kill a run almost always originates from a different process than the one running the loop -- an API call, an admin action, a control-plane decision. An in-process flag has no way to receive that signal. The kill state has to live in something both sides can reach: a Redis key, a database row, or a control-plane API the worker polls or subscribes to between steps.

flashcards.q: Why is 'the clustered index IS the table' the key fact for SQL Server index design?
flashcards.a: The clustered index's leaf level stores the actual row data in key order (no separate heap). Every nonclustered index leaf stores the clustering key as its row locator, so a wide/volatile clustering key bloats every nonclustered index on the table, not just itself.

flashcards.q: What is a key lookup and when does the optimizer stop using the index because of it?
flashcards.a: A second seek into the clustered index to fetch columns a nonclustered index doesn't carry. Past an estimated row count where per-row lookup cost exceeds a scan's cost, the optimizer flips the plan to a scan. Fix: INCLUDE the needed columns to make it a covering index.

flashcards.q: Define parameter sniffing precisely.
flashcards.a: The first execution of a parameterized query/procedure compiles a plan using that call's actual parameter values via the column histogram; every later call reuses the cached plan by query text regardless of its own parameter values. Correct when data is uniform, wrong when skewed.

flashcards.q: What is the observable symptom of bad parameter sniffing in production?
flashcards.a: A stored procedure fast for months suddenly runs slow for one specific parameter value with no code change. sys.dm_exec_query_stats + sys.dm_exec_query_plan shows a large gap between estimated and actual rows on the current call.

flashcards.q: Compare OPTION(RECOMPILE), OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN, and PSP optimization as parameter-sniffing fixes.
flashcards.a: RECOMPILE: fresh correct plan every call, pays compile cost every call - fine for rare/expensive queries. OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN: one average-case plan, cheap but mediocre for both extremes. PSP optimization (SQL Server 2022, compat 160+): multiple plans bucketed by sniffed value's cardinality range, for EQUALITY predicates only.

flashcards.q: How do you distinguish parameter sniffing from stale statistics as root cause?
flashcards.a: Stale statistics produce bad row estimates uniformly across all parameter values (recent bulk load/delete not yet reflected). Sniffing produces good estimates for the sniffed value and bad estimates specifically for differently-distributed values. Check sys.dm_db_stats_properties for staleness first - UPDATE STATISTICS is cheaper to try.

flashcards.q: How is SQL Server's default READ COMMITTED different from Postgres's?
flashcards.a: SQL Server's default READ COMMITTED is LOCK-based: shared locks on reads (released as the scan moves on), exclusive locks on writes held until commit - readers and writers DO block each other. Postgres's READ COMMITTED is MVCC-based from the start; readers never block writers by default.

flashcards.q: What does RCSI fix and what does it cost?
flashcards.a: READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON switches READ COMMITTED to row versioning: readers see the last-committed version as of statement start, no reader/writer blocking. Cost: every old row version touched gets copied to the TEMPDB version store - size and stripe tempdb before enabling on a high-write database.

flashcards.q: Legacy CE vs new CE - what changed and why is it risky to upgrade?
flashcards.a: SQL Server 2014 shipped a new cardinality estimator (compat level >=120) with different cross-predicate correlation assumptions than legacy CE (compat <=110, or forced via trace flag 9481). Upgrading compat level can silently reshape plans across the WHOLE workload at once - test against real production queries first.

flashcards.q: What makes columnstore indexes fast for aggregation?
flashcards.a: Column-wise compressed storage means a query touching 3 of 40 columns only reads those 3 columns' compressed segments (vs rowstore reading every column of every row). Batch mode execution processes ~900 rows per operator call instead of 1, amortizing CPU overhead - typically cited as another 2-4x on top of storage/compression wins.

flashcards.q: What is segment elimination and what condition does it require?
flashcards.a: Each columnstore segment carries min/max metadata per column; a filtering query can skip segments whose range can't satisfy the predicate, without decompressing them. Requires the data be physically ordered/correlated relative to the filtered column - a randomly-inserted timestamp gives every segment a similar min/max spread, eliminating nothing.

flashcards.q: CCI vs NCCI - what's the difference and when do you use each?
flashcards.a: Clustered Columnstore Index (CCI) replaces the table's row storage entirely. Nonclustered Columnstore Index (NCCI) adds columnar storage alongside an existing rowstore clustered index. NCCI is the 'operational analytics' pattern: OLTP point lookups keep using the B-tree, analytics hit the columnstore, on the same table.

flashcards.q: When is a clustered columnstore index the wrong choice?
flashcards.a: For tables needing frequent singleton point lookups or small, frequent updates. Columnstore's unit of work is the rowgroup/segment, and the delta-store mechanism absorbing small inserts before compression adds its own overhead under high-frequency small writes.

flashcards.q: Why does a plan guide count as a real operational risk even though it 'fixes' a query?
flashcards.a: It's invisible in the source code - the next engineer debugging the same procedure has no way to discover it without knowing to check sys.plan_guides. Prefer an in-code query hint or PSP optimization wherever the source is modifiable.

flashcards.q: What causes columnstore insert-rate degradation over time and what's the SQL Server operational fix?
flashcards.a: Background compression (the tuple mover) falling behind insert volume, leaving too many delta-store rowgroups uncompressed - the SQL Server analogue of ClickHouse's 'too many parts'. Fix: batch inserts into larger, less frequent operations, or manually run ALTER INDEX ... REORGANIZE to force the tuple mover to catch up.

flashcards.q: Give the prompt caching write/read cost multipliers and the break-even hit count for each TTL.
flashcards.a: Write: 1.25x standard input price at the 5-minute TTL, 2x at the 1-hour TTL. Read: roughly 0.1x (90% discount). Break-even: 5-min TTL breaks even after ONE hit (1.25+0.1=1.35 vs 2x uncached for two requests); 1-hour TTL needs THREE hits (2+0.2=2.2 vs 3x uncached).

flashcards.q: Why does caching invalidate 'forward' from the first differing byte, and what's the practical rule this implies?
flashcards.a: The cache key is a prefix hash over the rendered request (tools -> system -> messages render order); any byte difference at position N invalidates the cache for everything at or after N, regardless of how stable the rest is. The practical rule: put stable content first, volatile content (timestamps, per-request IDs, varying questions) last, after the cache_control breakpoint.

flashcards.q: Name five things that silently invalidate a prompt cache.
flashcards.a: A timestamp or request UUID in the system prompt, non-deterministic JSON serialization (unsorted keys, iterating a set), per-user content injected into the system prompt, tools added/removed/reordered mid-conversation (tools render at position 0), and switching models mid-conversation (caches are model-scoped, no cross-model reuse).

flashcards.q: Minimum cacheable prefix length is not monotonic across model generations. What does this mean in practice, and how do you detect it silently failing?
flashcards.a: Minimums range roughly 512 to 4,096 tokens depending on model generation (e.g. 512 on the newest models, up to 4,096 on some older ones), so a prompt sized for one model's minimum can fail to cache on a different model with NO error -- just usage.cache_creation_input_tokens showing 0. Always check the usage fields rather than assuming a cache_control marker placement bug.

flashcards.q: How do you set the difficulty boundary for model routing, and what is the RouteLLM published result?
flashcards.a: Empirically: collect a labeled sample of real production traffic, get quality judgments for both models on that sample (LLM-as-judge or human labels), fit a classifier/threshold predicting whether the cheap model matches the expensive one, and validate on a held-out set. RouteLLM (UC Berkeley, ICLR 2025) achieved over 85% cost reduction on MT-Bench while retaining 95% of the stronger model's judged quality, routing only 14% of queries to the expensive model in its best configuration.

flashcards.q: Why must a routing threshold be recalibrated after either model in the pair changes?
flashcards.a: The threshold was fit against the QUALITY GAP between the two specific models, not an absolute difficulty scale. Upgrading either model shifts that gap, so a stale threshold either overspends (routing traffic to a now-unnecessarily-strong model) or underspends on quality (routing traffic that now needs the stronger model to the cheap one). There is no shortcut -- re-run the calibration process.

flashcards.q: Distinguish model routing from fallback chains, and explain why people conflate them.
flashcards.a: Routing decides where a request SHOULD go based on predicted difficulty, validated empirically ahead of time. Fallback decides where a request goes AFTER something went wrong (429, 5xx, safety refusal) -- reactive, not predictive. People conflate them because 'try cheap, escalate on low confidence' looks like fallback but is functionally a router with a bad calibration method, and it inherits fallback's latency cost (two sequential round trips) without the empirical validation a real router gets.

flashcards.q: Why are fallback chains categorized as an availability tool, not a cost-optimization tool?
flashcards.a: Every fallback firing costs the latency of the failed attempt plus the latency of the successful one on the substitute model -- a chain of three targets pays up to three sequential round trips in the worst case. This latency cost is why fallback exists to preserve availability through outages/refusals, and using it as a cost-routing mechanism ('try cheap first, escalate on any hiccup') means paying an availability mechanism's latency price to get a cost-routing outcome, which should instead be evaluated and priced as a router.

flashcards.q: What is the Batch API discount, its latency tradeoff, and how does it compound with caching?
flashcards.a: 50% off both input and output tokens on every model, with up to 24-hour turnaround (making it unsuitable for anything latency-sensitive). It composes with prompt caching as an independent discount: a batch job over a shared, cached corpus can combine the 50% batch discount with the ~90% cache-read discount to land the cached-and-batched portion near 5% of the naive uncached, unbatched rate.

flashcards.q: Why is 'the tenant is within budget' an insufficient cost-governance signal, and what fixes it?
flashcards.a: A cumulative-spend-only dashboard misses trajectory: a tenant whose spend has doubled week-over-week but hasn't yet crossed the absolute cap looks fine until it suddenly doesn't. Fix: alert on RATE of spend change, not just cumulative spend against the budget -- rate-of-change is the leading indicator that catches the trend before the cap is blown.

flashcards.q: How should cost be attributed to a feature or tenant, and why does the timing of tagging matter?
flashcards.a: Tag every request with a feature/workflow identifier AT REQUEST TIME, not reconstructed after the fact from logs. Reconstruction-after-the-fact is exactly the exercise that fails during an actual incident when someone asks 'which feature caused the spike' and speed matters -- request-time tagging makes attribution a query, not an investigation.

flashcards.q: Why is 'swap to a cheaper model' often not the highest-leverage cost fix, with a worked number?
flashcards.a: Token volume, not per-token price, is frequently the dominant cost driver, and a model swap doesn't touch volume at all. Worked example: truncating a chatty tool result from 4K to 1K tokens per turn across a 40-turn run with a 6K stable prefix drops total tokens from roughly 1.16M to about 0.30M -- larger than most single-tier model downgrades, and it stacks with caching and routing rather than competing with them.

flashcards.q: Quota and budget are both cost-governance controls but catch different failures. What's the distinction?
flashcards.a: A budget caps DOLLARS spent. A quota caps request or token VOLUME independent of price. They catch different risks: a runaway loop making many cheap requests can blow a quota while staying under a dollar budget, and a single expensive request can blow a budget while staying well under a request-count quota. Use both.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT build a learned router (RouteLLM-style) and reach for a rule-based one instead?
flashcards.a: When a rule-based router (route by explicit task type, or by a user-selected quality tier) already captures most of the achievable savings, since it's often ~80% of the win for a fraction of the engineering. A learned classifier needs labeled preference data on YOUR traffic, ongoing recalibration on every model change, and drift detection -- if that infrastructure doesn't exist yet, the marginal gain may not justify building and maintaining it.

flashcards.q: What can an input guardrail catch that an output guardrail cannot, and vice versa?
flashcards.a: Input rails see the request before generation and block known-bad patterns before the model runs, but can't see what would have been generated. Output rails see the actual response but only after generation, so a tool-call side effect has already happened by the time they check.

flashcards.q: Name the six guardrail layers and one thing each catches.
flashcards.a: Schema validation (malformed structured output), PII detection/redaction (named-entity PII), toxicity classifiers (overtly harmful language), topical restriction (off-domain requests), jailbreak detection (known attack patterns), groundedness checks (claims not traceable to RAG sources).

flashcards.q: What's the industry latency budget target for input and output rails, and where does the stack become the bottleneck?
flashcards.a: Sub-100ms p50 for input, sub-150ms p50 for output. 200ms p50 is the threshold where the guardrail stack becomes the product's latency bottleneck.

flashcards.q: Give the latency range for an LLM-based guardrail validator, and its cost impact.
flashcards.a: 200-800ms added latency, plus roughly 15-40% added to the provider bill per turn.

flashcards.q: What's Llama Guard 4's measured p95 latency on typical GPU hardware?
flashcards.a: Around 459ms.

flashcards.q: What are the industry-typical catch rate and false-positive rate ranges for guardrail frameworks?
flashcards.a: 60-85% catch rate on problems a human would classify as serious, and 5-15% false positives on legitimate turns.

flashcards.q: Why is false-positive rate the metric that decides whether a guardrail survives in production, not catch rate?
flashcards.a: Catch rate is what you tune in a demo; a high false-positive rate generates daily user friction and support load, which leads teams to loosen thresholds under pressure and often forget to re-tighten, silently eroding protection.

flashcards.q: When should a guardrail fail-closed vs fail-open on its own error?
flashcards.a: Fail-closed for regulated/high-stakes domains (healthcare, finance, legal exposure) where an unfiltered response is unacceptable even at the cost of availability. Fail-open for low-stakes paths, especially where a stronger downstream control already covers the real risk.

flashcards.q: Why do most open-source guardrail libraries default to fail-open, and why is that dangerous?
flashcards.a: Fail-open avoids paging anyone when the classifier goes down. It's dangerous because teams inherit this default without realizing they made a compliance decision by not making one explicitly for their domain.

flashcards.q: Describe the canonical 'guardrails as theatre' failure.
flashcards.a: An agent leaks data via a tool call (email, API write, log line), then produces an innocuous text summary like 'data exported successfully.' An output filter scanning only the chat response reports clean because it never saw the tool call where the leak actually happened.

flashcards.q: Contrast NeMo Guardrails, Guardrails AI, and Llama Guard architecturally.
flashcards.a: NeMo Guardrails: programmable Colang rails (input/output/dialog/retrieval/execution) running in-process, under 50ms on GPU. Guardrails AI: Pydantic-based Guard + validator Hub (50+ validators), 50-200ms per validator. Llama Guard: a standalone classifier model returning safe/unsafe plus a category, not a framework.

flashcards.q: What does a groundedness check verify, and what can't it catch?
flashcards.a: It verifies that response claims trace back to the retrieved source documents — the core defense against RAG hallucination. It can't catch hallucination with nothing to ground against, and can't catch a claim that's technically traceable to a source that is itself wrong.

flashcards.q: Name three cloud-managed guardrail products and one distinguishing feature each.
