flashcards.a: AWS Bedrock Guardrails (model-agnostic policy layer via ApplyGuardrail API); Azure AI Content Safety (Prompt Shields for jailbreak/indirect-injection detection, plus groundedness detection); Google Model Armor (prompt/response inspection and safety filtering).

flashcards.q: Why does a jailbreak detector's effectiveness decay over time even without any code changes?
flashcards.a: Jailbreak/injection classifiers are adversarial targets; attackers iterate against known detectors the way they iterate against WAF rules, so a static classifier's real-world catch rate drops as new phrasings are discovered and shared.

flashcards.q: Give a case where adding an available, cheap guardrail layer is still the wrong call.
flashcards.a: When it duplicates coverage a stronger control already provides (e.g. a text PII filter behind a system with no tool that could leak PII), since every added layer compounds false-positive odds across the stack for no matching threat.

flashcards.q: What wire format does MCP use, and what are the three message shapes?
flashcards.a: JSON-RPC 2.0. Request (has id, expects a response), response (id + result or error), notification (no id, no reply expected).

flashcards.q: Name the three MCP primitives and who decides to invoke each.
flashcards.a: Tools (model-controlled), resources (application-controlled, URI-addressed), prompts (user-controlled templates).

flashcards.q: Which MCP spec revision does this module describe, and what is its headline change?
flashcards.a: 2026-07-28. It makes the protocol stateless: removes the initialize handshake and Mcp-Session-Id sessions.

flashcards.q: List the MCP spec revisions in order.
flashcards.a: 2024-11-05 (initial) -> 2025-03-26 (Streamable HTTP, OAuth) -> 2025-06-18 (elicitation, RFC 8707) -> 2025-11-25 (URL-mode elicit) -> 2026-07-28 (stateless).

flashcards.q: Why is HTTP+SSE deprecated as an MCP transport?
flashcards.a: It required sticky sessions (POST had to reach the instance holding the SSE stream), broke horizontal scaling, and had no clean resume after a dropped connection.

flashcards.q: A tool fails inside an MCP server. How should the failure be returned, and why?
flashcards.a: As a normal tools/call result with isError:true and content describing the failure, not a JSON-RPC error -- the model must see it as an observation to react to, not have the run killed by an exception.

flashcards.q: What is the confused-deputy problem as it applies to an MCP server?
flashcards.a: The server holds its own elevated credentials and acts on behalf of a caller (the model) that can be manipulated by injected content it reads, so it can be tricked into misusing its own authority.

flashcards.q: What is token passthrough and why does the MCP spec forbid it?
flashcards.a: Forwarding the client's bearer token straight to a downstream API. It breaks the audit trail, bypasses the server's own access policy, and leaks every forwarded user token if the server is compromised. Spec: MUST NOT.

flashcards.q: What replaces token passthrough as the correct pattern?
flashcards.a: Validate the incoming token's audience against the server's own identity, then use a separately held, narrowly scoped credential for the downstream call.

flashcards.q: What is sampling in MCP, and what happened to it in 2026-07-28?
flashcards.a: sampling/createMessage lets a server without model access ask the connected client to run a completion. Deprecated 2026-07-28; migration is to call a provider directly with your own key.

flashcards.q: How does elicitation work under the new stateless (2026-07-28) Multi Round-Trip Request pattern?
flashcards.a: The server returns an InputRequiredResult naming what it needs; the client retries the ORIGINAL request with inputResponses filled in, instead of the server pushing a new request mid-flight.

flashcards.q: Why are Roots being deprecated, and does that weaken sandboxing?
flashcards.a: Most implementations already pass paths as tool arguments or bake scope into config. Roots was always advisory (unenforced), so removing it doesn't remove any real control -- server-side authorization was always the actual boundary.

flashcards.q: What does resource indicators (RFC 8707) add to MCP auth, and when was it introduced?
flashcards.a: Introduced 2025-06-18. Scopes an issued OAuth token to one specific MCP server so it can't be replayed against a different server the client also holds a token for.

flashcards.q: When is MCP the wrong abstraction?
flashcards.a: One agent calling one in-process function -- MCP adds schema validation, serialization, and a subprocess spawn or network round trip to reach code that's already right there, with no portability benefit if nothing else will ever call it.

flashcards.q: State the one-paragraph distinction between MCP and A2A.
flashcards.a: MCP connects an agent to tools/context (client-to-server, resource-shaped). A2A connects agents to each other as peers (task-shaped, agent-card discovery, stateful task lifecycle). They compose, not compete.

flashcards.q: Why does wide-column schema design start from queries, not entities?
flashcards.a: No cheap join and no free secondary access path by default. A query needing differently-shaped data requires a second round trip or write-time denormalization. Design order: enumerate access patterns first, build one table per pattern.

flashcards.q: What is a hot partition and what's the observable symptom?
flashcards.a: A partition key whose cardinality or traffic distribution concentrates rows/requests on one replica set, since all rows sharing a key live together forever. Symptom: one node/replica set at ~100% CPU/IO while the rest of the cluster looks idle; p99 degrades cluster-wide via coordinator overhead.

flashcards.q: Does adding nodes fix a hot partition?
flashcards.a: No, if the cause is key cardinality (not raw capacity) - the hot key still hashes to the same replica set regardless of cluster size. Fix is architectural: salt/shard the partition key and fan out reads.

flashcards.q: State the R+W>N rule and give a strong-consistency and an eventual-consistency example (RF=3).
flashcards.a: R+W>N guarantees every read/write replica set overlaps by >=1 node, so a read sees the latest write. RF=3, W=QUORUM(2), R=QUORUM(2): 2+2=4>3, strong, survives 1 node down. RF=3, W=1, R=1: 1+1=2, not >3, eventual consistency only, fastest.

flashcards.q: Compare STCS, LCS, and TWCS compaction strategies.
flashcards.a: STCS (default): merges similar-size SSTables, can need ~2x disk during large compactions, read amp grows with SSTable count. LCS: fixed-size levels, low read amp but HIGH write amp (repeated rewrites through levels). TWCS: groups SSTables by time window - best for TTL-heavy time-series, expired windows drop predictably.

flashcards.q: What is the tombstone read-latency trap?
flashcards.a: DELETE writes a tombstone, retained until gc_grace_seconds (default 10 days) for replica-repair safety, not removed immediately. A hot-read partition with heavy delete/TTL churn accumulates tombstones the read path scans past, causing timeouts / tombstone_warn/failure_threshold errors - looks like a slow query, is actually scanning graves.

flashcards.q: What is DynamoDB's per-partition physical cap, and what can adaptive capacity NOT do?
flashcards.a: 3,000 RCU/s or 1,000 WCU/s per partition, hard cap. Adaptive capacity smooths moderate/temporary skew up to that cap but cannot raise the physical ceiling - severe sustained skew still throttles.

flashcards.q: LSI vs GSI - the sharpest constraint difference.
flashcards.a: LSI: shares base table partition key, must be declared at table CREATION (can't add later), item collection (base + all LSIs, per partition key) capped at 10GB - hard write failure if exceeded. GSI: own partition key, addable after creation, eventually consistent, own throughput.

flashcards.q: Why can a throttled GSI block writes to a healthy base table?
flashcards.a: DynamoDB propagates writes to GSIs synchronously as part of accepting the base table write, not fully decoupled async - if the GSI's own capacity throttles, the base table write is rejected too, even with spare base table capacity.

flashcards.q: On-demand vs provisioned DynamoDB capacity - when to choose each.
flashcards.a: On-demand: per-request billing, instant elasticity, higher cost/request - safer default for new/unpredictable workloads. Provisioned: pre-declared RCU/WCU (optional auto-scaling with lag), cheaper at steady predictable volume - move here once traffic patterns stabilize.

flashcards.q: Single-table design: what does it buy and what does it cost?
flashcards.a: Buys: fewer round trips per logical op, and under provisioned capacity, one over-provisioning buffer instead of N. Costs: unreadable overloaded generic keys, cross-team schema fragility, hard ad hoc analytics, expensive migrations for unanticipated access patterns.

flashcards.q: When should a team NOT default to single-table design?
flashcards.a: When access patterns are still evolving, when multiple uncoordinated teams share the table, or when ad hoc analytical queries are needed. It assumes fully-enumerated, stable access patterns - most teams should start with simpler per-entity tables.

flashcards.q: How do you fix a hot partition for a time-series IoT table naively keyed by device_id?
flashcards.a: Compound the partition key with a coarser time bucket and/or an entropy suffix, e.g. device_id#2026-08-01#03 (hourly bucket) or device_id#shard_N. Trades a fan-out read (query all shards, merge client-side) for spreading storage and request load across more physical partitions.

flashcards.q: Are DynamoDB and Cassandra interchangeable because both trace to the Dynamo paper?
flashcards.a: No. They have materially different consistency models (Cassandra's per-request tunable R/W consistency vs DynamoDB's simpler eventually-consistent/strongly-consistent read toggle) and different secondary index mechanics (LSI/GSI vs Cassandra secondary indexes/materialized views) and operational models.

flashcards.q: Why is denormalization the default in wide-column modeling, not an optimization applied later?
flashcards.a: Because there's no cheap join, a query needing data shaped differently from storage requires either an extra round trip or duplicating data at write time into a table shaped for that query - you accept write-time duplication and app-managed consistency in exchange for every read being a single-partition operation.

flashcards.q: Write the formula for Recall@k and Precision@k, and what question each answers.
flashcards.a: Recall@k = |relevant ∩ top-k| / |relevant| -- of everything relevant, how much did you find. Precision@k = |relevant ∩ top-k| / k -- of what you returned, how much was relevant.

flashcards.q: Write the formula for MRR and explain its key limitation.
flashcards.a: RR(query) = 1/rank_of_first_relevant_result; MRR = mean(RR). It only cares about the FIRST correct answer's position -- blind to whether more relevant documents exist further down or how many exist at all.

flashcards.q: Write the formula for MAP and explain how it differs from MRR.
flashcards.a: AP(query) = (1/|relevant docs|) * sum of Precision@k at each rank where a relevant doc appears; MAP = mean(AP). Unlike MRR, it credits finding MULTIPLE relevant documents and rewards finding them early.

flashcards.q: Write the nDCG formula and explain what the log2(i+1) discount represents.
flashcards.a: DCG@k = sum(rel_i / log2(i+1)); nDCG@k = DCG@k / IDCG@k (IDCG = DCG of the ideal ranking). log2(i+1) discounts by rank position: rank 1 contributes rel/log2(2)=rel, rank 10 contributes only rel/log2(11)~=rel/3.46 -- position matters, with diminishing sensitivity further down.

flashcards.q: Which retrieval metric should a RAG system optimize for when the generator reads the whole top-k context regardless of order?
flashcards.a: Recall@k primarily (Precision@k secondarily for noise/cost) -- getting the answer INTO the context matters more than its exact position when the LLM reads all of the top-k anyway.

flashcards.q: What size floor makes a golden set usable for gating decisions, and what happens below it?
flashcards.a: Fewer than 30 labeled queries is mostly noise -- a single query flipping swings the aggregate by several percentage points. Practical floor: 50+ queries, growing to 100-200+ as the product matures, stratified by query type and locale.

flashcards.q: State the four steps of the error-analysis loop.
flashcards.a: 1) Sample real failures. 2) Classify each by root cause (retrieval miss / ranking miss / chunking miss / generation miss). 3) Fix the DOMINANT class, not the loudest individual failure. 4) Re-measure and repeat.

flashcards.q: State the "ceiling argument" precisely.
flashcards.a: A reranker only reorders candidates first-stage retrieval already surfaced; if the answer-bearing chunk never entered the candidate set, no downstream stage can recover it. You cannot rerank your way out of a recall miss -- each stage bounds what every stage after it can achieve.

flashcards.q: Why is a chunking miss easy to misdiagnose as a retrieval miss?
flashcards.a: Both produce the same downstream symptom (LLM lacks the answer or hallucinates), but a retrieval miss means the document was never found, while a chunking miss means it was found and ranked well but the chunk boundary cut the answer. Fixes are completely different (retrieval architecture vs. chunk strategy).

flashcards.q: What is ablation discipline and why does it matter when multiple pipeline changes ship together?
flashcards.a: When several changes (chunk size, embedding model, reranker) ship in one bundle, an aggregate metric improvement tells you the bundle helped, not which component did -- some could even be hurting while others mask it. Ablation isolates and measures each change independently before attributing credit.

flashcards.q: What is the typical correlation between offline retrieval metrics and online outcomes, and what does that imply?
flashcards.a: Published Pearson correlations are typically around 0.3, not 0.8+. An offline metric win is a hypothesis worth an online A/B test, not a conclusion -- ship behind experimentation where the product supports it.

flashcards.q: What golden-set annotation practice guards against a single annotator's unreliable judgment?
flashcards.a: Reconcile every case with at least two independent annotators before resolving disagreements, and give annotators worked explanations of WHY each example is relevant, not just the label, to keep future annotators consistent.

flashcards.q: Which metric fits a multi-document synthesis product (a report citing several sources), and why?
flashcards.a: MAP, or Recall@k at a higher k -- product value scales with finding multiple good sources, not just the first relevant one, which is exactly what MAP credits and MRR does not.

flashcards.q: Why is multi-column PDF text extraction a 'silent' failure?
flashcards.a: Text extraction that ignores layout reads content in the PDF's internal object order, which for two columns is often interleaved line-by-line across columns. The result is fluent, grammatically plausible but semantically scrambled text -- no exception thrown, nothing looks obviously broken.

flashcards.q: Name the three table-handling strategies and when to use each.
flashcards.a: Markdown serialization (default, small-medium tables, repeat header row). Per-row records (large tables exceeding chunk budget, header carried per row group, row index as metadata). Summary + reference (very large/wide tables where per-row produces too many near-duplicate chunks -- summarize for retrieval, keep full table as reference).

flashcards.q: Which PDF parsers have documented strengths/weaknesses on multi-column layouts?
flashcards.a: LlamaParse's 'accurate' mode has a documented reading-order weakness on multi-column layouts. Docling and Marker-PDF are more commonly recommended for documents with complex multi-column layouts (academic papers, dense reports). Validate against your own corpus rather than assuming one tool generalizes.

flashcards.q: Why must code be split on AST boundaries rather than character/line counts?
flashcards.a: Character/line splitting routinely cuts a function mid-body or discards its enclosing class/import context, producing a fragment that's frequently unusable for code generation/review. AST-aware splitting (tree-sitter) guarantees chunks are syntactically complete units except for the rare oversized-function case.

flashcards.q: What paper formalizes AST-based code chunking as a measurable retrieval-quality improvement?
flashcards.a: cAST (arXiv:2506.15655) -- shows AST-based structural chunking improves code-RAG retrieval quality over naive line-based splitting, not just as an intuitive best practice.

flashcards.q: What is parent-child hierarchical retrieval and what problem does it solve?
flashcards.a: Index small leaf chunks for precise embedding similarity search, but substitute the parent chunk at retrieval time when enough of its children are retrieved together (LlamaIndex AutoMergingRetriever). Solves the case where a document's sections vary widely in natural density -- no single flat chunk size serves both a short definition and a dense multi-page procedure well.

flashcards.q: Why is a captioned image a lossy representation, and what's the practical consequence?
flashcards.a: A caption compresses the image's full information content into text, so retrieval only succeeds for queries the caption's text actually captures. A vague caption ('a chart showing data') gives retrieval nothing to match a specific query against, even though the answer is visible in the image.

flashcards.q: What can knowledge-graph-augmented RAG do that flat chunk retrieval structurally cannot?
flashcards.a: Answer multi-hop questions requiring connections across many documents (e.g. 'which vendors does our largest customer's parent company also do business with') and 'global' whole-corpus-summary questions, since similarity search has no notion of relationship structure across entities.

flashcards.q: Give the real cost numbers for GraphRAG's original cost profile.
flashcards.a: Entity/relation extraction inflates token usage ~3-5x over plain chunking. Early indexing runs for a large corpus were reported around $33,000 (2024). Query-time graph traversal/community summarization adds a measured 2-3x higher end-to-end latency versus flat retrieval.

flashcards.q: How much has GraphRAG indexing cost dropped, and what techniques drove it?
flashcards.a: Microsoft reports indexing cost falling to roughly 0.1% of its original 2024 figure within about 18 months via better extraction prompting and caching. LightRAG cuts indexing token cost ~60% and roughly halves median query latency. KET-RAG limits expensive LLM extraction to a PageRank-selected subset of chunks combined with a cheap keyword-bipartite graph.

flashcards.q: Why do PDF headers and footers need special handling instead of being chunked as body text?
flashcards.a: Running titles, page numbers, and repeated boilerplate appear identically on nearly every page; chunking them as body content pollutes the corpus with dozens/hundreds of near-duplicate, low-information chunks competing for top-k slots against genuinely useful content.

flashcards.q: What triggers OCR fallback in a PDF ingestion pipeline, and why is it needed?
flashcards.a: Per-page text-density detection: born-digital pages extract directly via the text layer, but scanned pages have no text layer and a text-only pipeline silently returns empty/near-empty content for them. OCR (EasyOCR/Tesseract) is triggered specifically for low-text-density pages.

flashcards.q: Why is provenance metadata a first-class requirement for every structured unit produced during ingestion?
flashcards.a: Without source_id, page/section, and extraction-method metadata, a wrong answer traced to a scrambled multi-column extraction or a bad OCR read looks identical to any other retrieval failure, and the error-analysis loop (T06-accuracy-tuning) has nothing to classify against.

flashcards.q: Why does applying a metadata filter to an ANN index break both naive strategies?
flashcards.a: Every ANN index (HNSW, IVF) is built assuming any indexed vector is a valid target. Pre-filtering restricts to a subset with no ANN index built over it, degenerating toward brute force. Post-filtering discards non-matches after search, which can silently under-return since the greedy search never routed toward the filter-valid region.

flashcards.q: Give the concrete arithmetic of post-filter under-return.
flashcards.a: A filter matching ~10% of the corpus with a default beam width like ef_search=40 retrieves on average only ~4 filter-valid candidates by chance -- well short of a k=10 request, even though far more valid matches exist elsewhere in the graph.

flashcards.q: Define cardinality and selectivity, and explain why high-cardinality filters are the expensive case.
flashcards.a: Cardinality = number of distinct values a field can take. Selectivity = fraction of corpus a specific value matches. High-cardinality fields (tenant_id, millions of values) produce high selectivity per value, which is worst for both strategies: pre-filter scans a small unindexed subset, post-filter suffers the most severe under-return.

flashcards.q: State the non-negotiable rule for ACL-aware filtering.
flashcards.a: The ACL filter must be applied IN the retrieval query itself, never as a post-retrieval check. Retrieve-then-discard means unauthorized data may already be logged, cached, briefly in a response payload, or exposed via a timing/count side-channel before the discard runs.

flashcards.q: What does Weaviate's ACORN do to fix filtered search?
flashcards.a: Multi-hop graph expansion so the search radius covers enough of the graph to find filter-valid neighbors regardless of selectivity. As of v1.34 it automatically chooses between multi-hop exploration (selective filters), relaxed broader traversal (broad filters), or flat brute-force scan (tiny result sets).

flashcards.q: What does Pinecone do by default for filtered search, and what's the risk?
flashcards.a: Merges metadata and vector index into one structure and defaults to post-filtering -- fast on average but carries the classic under-return risk on highly selective filters unless the caller oversamples.

flashcards.q: What is oversampling as a post-filter mitigation, and why is it not a fix?
flashcards.a: Request k*factor candidates (e.g. k=10 as k1=50-100), then filter down. Reduces but doesn't eliminate under-return since the search still isn't routing toward the filter-valid region deliberately -- a selective enough filter can still under-return, and it costs proportionally more compute.

flashcards.q: Compare shared index with a tenant_id metadata field vs. separate collection per tenant.
flashcards.a: Shared index: simplest to operate, one schema, but inherits all pre/post-filter tradeoffs scaled by tenant-size skew. Separate collection: isolates performance/data completely, no filter-vs-graph reconciliation, at the cost of N indexes to build/monitor/reindex.

flashcards.q: For a tenant-size distribution from 100 to 5 million documents, what's the right multi-tenancy strategy?
flashcards.a: Tiered: smallest tenants use brute-force/in-memory search (trivially fast, sidesteps the filtered-ANN problem); mid-size tenants share a filtered index with a filter-aware strategy; largest tenants get dedicated physical index isolation for both performance and blast-radius isolation.

flashcards.q: Compare RBAC and ABAC for retrieval filtering.
flashcards.a: RBAC: permissions on roles -- simple, coarse-grained. ABAC: permissions computed from user+resource+context attributes (e.g. department match AND clearance >= sensitivity) -- finer-grained, more complex to evaluate. Production systems typically layer both rather than choosing either/or.

flashcards.q: Why is denormalizing metadata onto chunk records the right call, and what risk does it carry?
flashcards.a: Vector databases generally don't support efficient joins, and a per-query round-trip to a separate permissions store adds latency to every retrieval call. Risk: the denormalized copy can drift out of sync with the source of truth (e.g. an ACL change) until the next sync/backfill -- requires explicit staleness monitoring, especially for ACLs.

flashcards.q: When does schema evolution require a full reindex, and when doesn't it?
flashcards.a: Adding a new filterable field is typically a metadata backfill only -- the vector is unaffected, no re-embedding needed. Changing an existing field's type/semantics (boolean to enum) requires auditing every dependent code path and a transitional sentinel state during rollout, since partial migration can produce inconsistent filtering.

flashcards.q: What does pgvector's hnsw.iterative_scan do?
flashcards.a: Continues traversing further into the graph (deeper beam, more candidates) until enough filter-valid results are found or a scan-depth limit is hit -- a filter-aware mitigation for moderate-selectivity filters.

flashcards.q: Mechanically, why does cross-lingual retrieval work with no translation step at query time?
flashcards.a: Multilingual embedding models train with a contrastive objective over cross-lingual pairs known/inferred to share meaning, pulling translation-equivalent text together in vector space regardless of language. The model never distinguished "similar because same language" from "similar because same meaning" -- it only optimized for the latter.

flashcards.q: What is tokenizer fertility, and why is it an operational cost, not just a linguistic footnote?
flashcards.a: Fertility is tokens produced per word (or per character for non-whitespace scripts). Non-English, especially morphologically rich or non-Latin-script languages, routinely need 1.5-2x+ the tokens for equivalent content -- a direct cost/latency tax on embedding, chunking, and generation, not merely a quality nuance.

flashcards.q: Does lower tokenizer fertility always predict better model performance for that language?
flashcards.a: No. A 2025 70-language study found fertility alone explains relatively little of the variance in downstream performance -- it's a real cost signal but not a complete quality proxy.

flashcards.q: Why is a single blended recall@k metric dangerous for a 22-locale product?
flashcards.a: One language's retrieval can collapse to near-zero while being mathematically absorbed by 21 other healthy languages, leaving the blended number flat. The failure typically surfaces via support tickets weeks later, not monitoring.

flashcards.q: What is the structural fix for the silent per-locale degradation failure?
flashcards.a: Report and alert on recall@k/nDCG PER LOCALE as a hard requirement, not only blended -- a golden set stratified by language with independent alerting thresholds per locale.

flashcards.q: Compare shared multilingual index vs. per-language index, with the real cost of each.
flashcards.a: Shared index: simpler (one index, one model) but risks cross-lingual leakage that a blended metric hides. Per-language index: isolates quality, allows language-specific models, but costs N indexes to build/monitor/reindex, multiplying every ops task by locale count.

flashcards.q: What's the practical default for shared vs. per-language indexing at scale?
flashcards.a: Shared index with language-aware routing/metadata filtering as the default, moving to per-language handling only for specific locales where per-locale evaluation shows the shared model measurably underperforms.

flashcards.q: Why does a whitespace tokenizer fail on Japanese or Chinese text for lexical retrieval?
flashcards.a: CJK scripts have no whitespace between words. A whitespace tokenizer either treats each character as its own token (destroying multi-character word meaning BM25 depends on) or fails to segment at all. A dedicated segmenter (Jieba for Chinese, MeCab for Japanese) is required.

flashcards.q: What happens by default when a user types a romanized query for a non-Latin-script language, and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: Nothing matches -- the index holds native-script content and the romanized query shares no tokens or embedding proximity unless the model incidentally learned transliteration robustness. Fix: normalize via transliteration at index or query time, or select/fine-tune a model with demonstrated transliteration robustness.

flashcards.q: How should mixed-language (code-switched) queries be handled by language detection and routing?
flashcards.a: Use top-k language predictions, not top-1. On low-confidence or closely-contested top-2, either run retrieval across both candidate languages and fuse, or fall back to the shared multilingual embedding space directly, since it doesn't require a language label to function.

flashcards.q: What is fastText lid.176 and what are its performance characteristics?
flashcards.a: A language identification model trained on Wikipedia/Tatoeba/SETimes data covering 176 languages. Compressed .ftz variant is under 1MB, reports F1 in the high-0.9s on clean single-language text, fast enough to run per-query with negligible latency.

flashcards.q: Why might a language advertised inside a "100+ languages supported" embedding model still underperform?
flashcards.a: Aggregate language-count claims say nothing about per-language training data volume; low-resource languages sit in the weaker tail of the same model's coverage by construction. Validate per-locale against your own golden set rather than trusting the vendor's headline claim.

flashcards.q: When does translate-then-retrieve still beat a multilingual embedding model in 2026?
flashcards.a: For a genuinely low-resource language where the multilingual embedding's cross-lingual alignment is weak due to insufficient training data -- the translation model may have more effective signal for that language pair than the embedding does.

flashcards.q: Name the three caching layers in a production LLM stack, in fallthrough order.
flashcards.a: 1) Exact-match (hash full normalized request, zero correctness risk). 2) Prefix/prompt caching (KV cache reuse for a byte-identical shared prefix, zero correctness risk, NOT semantic). 3) True semantic caching (embedding similarity above a threshold, the only layer that generalizes across paraphrasing, and the only one with real correctness risk).

flashcards.q: What are Anthropic's prompt-caching write and read cost multipliers?
flashcards.a: Cache write: 1.25x base input rate for a 5-minute TTL, 2.0x for a 1-hour TTL. Cache read: 0.1x base input rate (90% discount). Accessing a cached block resets its TTL.

flashcards.q: What is OpenAI's minimum prompt length for automatic prefix caching, and the default retention?
flashcards.a: At least 1,024 tokens minimum for a prefix to be cached; default retention is 24 hours. Current-generation models get up to a 90% discount on cache reads.

flashcards.q: What similarity threshold range is a conservative first deployment, and what does it buy you?
flashcards.a: 0.97 -- low hit rate (~5-10%) but false-positive rate under 0.5%. Typical FAQ deployments run 0.92-0.95; start at 0.92 and monitor false-positive rate for 48 hours before adjusting.

flashcards.q: Give a concrete example of a semantic-cache false hit.
flashcards.a: "Refund policy for annual plans" vs "...for monthly plans" can embed above 0.95 cosine similarity (differ by one word) despite potentially opposite correct answers -- the dangerous zone (~0.88-0.94) is topically close pairs differing in exactly the token that changes the answer (date/tier/polarity swaps).

flashcards.q: What is vCache and what does it improve over static thresholds?
flashcards.a: vCache (arXiv:2502.03771, Feb 2025) learns a per-cached-entry similarity threshold online with a formal, user-specified error-rate guarantee, instead of one global cutoff. Reports up to 12.5x higher cache hit rate and 26x lower error rate than static-threshold/fine-tuned-embedding baselines at a matched error budget.

flashcards.q: Why are static global similarity thresholds fragile?
flashcards.a: The right cutoff genuinely differs by query cluster -- some clusters (rigid FAQ phrasing) tolerate loose matching safely, others (queries with an embedded date/tier/quantity) need tight matching because the embedding space doesn't cleanly separate same-intent from same-intent-different-parameter. One global threshold is a compromise that's wrong somewhere.

flashcards.q: What two metrics must always be reported together for a semantic cache, and why?
flashcards.a: Hit rate (% served from cache) AND positive-hit-rate/false-positive rate (% of those hits that were actually correct). A high hit rate with unmeasured false-positive rate tells you nothing -- it can be built partly on wrong answers.

flashcards.q: In the worked example (1M queries/day, 40% hit rate, $0.003/query LLM cost, $0.0001/hit cost), what's the daily cost with and without caching?
flashcards.a: Without cache: $3,000/day. With cache: ~$1,840/day (~39% reduction), tracking the hit rate closely since cache-hit cost/latency is near-negligible relative to a full LLM call.

flashcards.q: Rank the three invalidation strategies for a semantic cache from simplest to most precise.
flashcards.a: TTL-only (simplest, serves stale during the window, evicts fresh entries early) < event-driven invalidation (tag entries with source doc/chunk IDs, invalidate on reindex, most precise) < versioned cache namespaces (reindex = fresh namespace, simple correctness but cold-starts on every reindex).

flashcards.q: Why is a shared semantic cache across tenants a security risk, not just a correctness risk?
flashcards.a: If tenant A's query embeds close enough to a cached response built from tenant B's data, tenant A can receive an answer derived from tenant B's private content -- a genuine cross-tenant data leak. Fix: tenant_id must be a hard filter in the cache lookup query itself, never a post-hoc check.

flashcards.q: Name three categories of queries where semantic caching is the wrong tool.
flashcards.a: Personalized answers (same phrasing, different correct answer per user), time-sensitive information (stock prices, live inventory), and high-stakes domains (medical/legal/financial advice) where any residual false-hit rate carries real consequences.

flashcards.q: What components make up GPTCache's architecture?
flashcards.a: An embedding generator, a vector store for ANN lookup, a similarity evaluator (exact-match, embedding-distance, or an ONNX model -- swappable), and an eviction policy (LRU or FIFO by cache count, plus TTL).

flashcards.q: What is the four-era lineage of search ranking, and what specific failure motivated each transition?
flashcards.a: Boolean (no ranking, match/no-match) -> TF-IDF/BM25 (fixes ranking, but vocabulary mismatch: "car" never matches "automobile") -> dense bi-encoder (fixes vocabulary mismatch, but blurs rare/exact tokens like SKUs) -> hybrid (fuses both, complementary failure modes) -> learned ranking (adds business signals no text-similarity method can see).

flashcards.q: What are typical recall@10 numbers comparing hybrid, dense-only, and sparse-only retrieval?
flashcards.a: Roughly 91% recall@10 for hybrid vs. 78% dense-only vs. 65% sparse-only in typical production benchmarks.

flashcards.q: Name three concrete cases where BM25 still beats embeddings, and the mechanism in each.
flashcards.a: (1) Exact identifiers (SKUs, error codes) -- rare tokens an embedding model never anchored well; BM25's IDF finds the literal string. (2) Rare technical/domain jargon, same reason. (3) Code search -- identifiers are precise structured tokens; users want exact symbol matches, not "semantically similar" code.

flashcards.q: How does learned-to-rank (LTR) differ from a cross-encoder reranker?
flashcards.a: A cross-encoder reranker scores query-document text relevance only. LTR takes a feature vector per query-candidate pair (which can include the cross-encoder's score as one input) plus business signals -- CTR, recency, price, personalization, inventory -- that no text-similarity model can see, and trains a model to optimize a ranking metric like nDCG over the combined set.

flashcards.q: What is LambdaMART and why has it remained a production standard?
flashcards.a: A gradient-boosted decision tree ranker (building on RankNet/LambdaRank, formalized ~2010) trained to directly optimize a ranking metric like nDCG rather than pointwise regression. Won the 2010 Yahoo! LTR Challenge; remains standard because GBDTs handle nonlinear feature interactions well, train fast, and are cheap/predictable to serve versus a neural ranker.

flashcards.q: Describe the four-stage cascade architecture used in large-scale search/ads ranking.
flashcards.a: Matching (cheap, corpus-scale candidate generation via inverted index/ANN) -> pre-ranking (lightweight model narrows millions to thousands) -> ranking (full LTR/neural model scores thousands down to tens) -> mix-ranking (business rules: diversity, ad interleaving, dedup) before serving.

flashcards.q: What is position bias in LTR training data, and how do you correct for it?
flashcards.a: Users click higher-ranked results more often regardless of true relevance because they rarely scroll to fairly evaluate lower results. Training on raw click logs teaches the model to reinforce the existing ranking, not true relevance. Fix: inverse propensity scoring (weight clicks by inverse probability of being seen at that position) or randomized result interleaving.

flashcards.q: What is the observable symptom that an LTR model is suffering from position bias?
flashcards.a: Offline ranking metrics (e.g. nDCG on click-derived labels) improve steadily while online engagement metrics stay flat or regress -- that divergence is the signature symptom.

flashcards.q: Why can query rewriting (HyDE, keyword expansion) hurt retrieval instead of helping it?
flashcards.a: It can distort the original query's intent or overamplify rare terms the user never cared about, shifting retrieval toward a subtly different question. This is a documented failure mode, not hypothetical -- it needs per-query-type eval, not blanket application.

flashcards.q: When is a full LTR layer the wrong investment?
flashcards.a: When there isn't enough real interaction/click data -- small catalogs, low traffic, cold-start. A GBDT trained on sparse/synthetic labels overfits noise; hand-tuned boosting (weighted BM25 + recency + popularity, e.g. Elasticsearch function scoring) is more transparent and just as effective at that scale.

flashcards.q: What is the honest default answer to "which retrieval architecture should we ship first"?
flashcards.a: Hybrid retrieval (BM25 + dense, RRF-fused) plus a cross-encoder reranker over the fused shortlist, validated against a recall@k/nDCG eval. A full learned-ranking layer with business features is additional investment justified only when there's a business objective beyond relevance AND enough interaction data to train on.

flashcards.q: Why can't reranking or LTR fully compensate for weak retrieval or reranking below them?
flashcards.a: Each layer in the stack can only reorder what the layer below already surfaced. A business-aware LTR model cannot promote a genuinely relevant item that hybrid retrieval never put in the candidate set to begin with.

flashcards.q: In marketplace search with sponsored listings, should sponsored placement be blended into the LTR score or kept separate?
flashcards.a: Keep sponsored listings as a distinct mix-ranking step interleaved after organic ranking, not blended into the same LTR score, so ranking transparency and auditability (e.g. proving sponsored placement doesn't bias organic relevance) are preserved.

flashcards.q: What are the two mandatory nodes create_react_agent wires into a StateGraph?
flashcards.a: `agent` (calls the model with tools bound, returns an AIMessage) and `tools` (a ToolNode that dispatches every tool_call on the last message and returns matched ToolMessages).

flashcards.q: What reducer does AgentState's `messages` key use, and what does it do differently from operator.add?
flashcards.a: add_messages. It merges by message id, replacing an existing message when the incoming one shares an id, instead of blindly concatenating like operator.add.

flashcards.q: Distinguish should_continue from tools_condition.
flashcards.a: should_continue is the private, three-way routing function create_react_agent wires internally (tools / structured response / end). tools_condition is the public, two-way standalone utility in langgraph.prebuilt for people building their own StateGraph who want the same tool-calls check.

flashcards.q: What happens when remaining_steps < 2 and the model's response has tool calls?
flashcards.a: The graph short-circuits without raising and returns a synthetic final AIMessage: "Sorry, need more steps to process this request." This is a soft, graceful-degradation path, distinct from GraphRecursionError.

flashcards.q: How does remaining_steps differ from recursion_limit?
flashcards.a: recursion_limit is a hard cap on super-steps (default 1000 since langgraph 1.0.6) set as a top-level config key; exceeding it raises GraphRecursionError. remaining_steps is a soft, auto-decremented managed value specific to create_react_agent that degrades gracefully to a canned message instead of raising.

flashcards.q: A pre_model_hook returns {"messages": [...]}. What's the effect versus returning {"llm_input_messages": [...]}?
flashcards.a: "messages" writes through the add_messages reducer into permanent graph state (a real edit). "llm_input_messages" feeds a different list to this one model call only, without persisting the change.

flashcards.q: What does pre_model_hook's return dict require at minimum?
flashcards.a: At least one of `messages` or `llm_input_messages` must be present.

flashcards.q: What is the documented bug pattern with post_model_hook and tool routing?
flashcards.a: With post_model_hook present, routing goes through post_model_hook_router, which determines pending tool calls by diffing tool_call ids on the last AIMessage against existing ToolMessages, not the plain tool_calls check. A hook that mutates or drops messages can break that diff and silently skip tool dispatch.

flashcards.q: What's the behavioral difference between version="v1" and version="v2" tool dispatch?
flashcards.a: v1: all tool calls in one AIMessage execute inside a single ToolNode invocation as one graph step; a per-node policy applies to the whole batch. v2 (default): each tool call becomes its own Send targeting its own ToolNode task, so retry/timeout policies apply per individual call.

flashcards.q: What does the tools node do by default when a tool raises an exception?
flashcards.a: ToolNode catches it and returns it as a ToolMessage containing the error text rather than propagating it, the framework-level version of 'errors are observations, not exceptions.'

flashcards.q: What does response_format actually add to the graph, and when does it run?
flashcards.a: A terminal generate_structured_response node, reached only when the loop would otherwise exit to END (no pending tool calls). It makes one additional schema-constrained model call and writes state["structured_response"]; messages are untouched.

flashcards.q: What constraint applies to interrupt_before/interrupt_after with create_react_agent that doesn't apply to a hand-rolled StateGraph?
flashcards.a: Breakpoints can only target nodes that actually exist in the prebuilt's fixed topology: "agent", "tools", and whichever hook/structured-response nodes were configured, because you didn't build the graph yourself.

flashcards.q: What is create_react_agent's deprecation status as of LangGraph 1.0?
flashcards.a: Deprecated in favor of create_agent from the langchain package (same LangGraph runtime, but with a composable 6-hook AgentMiddleware system instead of two fixed hook slots). Still functional with no published removal date.

flashcards.q: Name a concrete reason to drop create_react_agent for a hand-rolled StateGraph.
flashcards.a: Needing more than one tool-execution phase, branching beyond a simple tool-calls-yes/no check, fan-out beyond per-call Send dispatch, or per-tool (rather than global) approval gating — the prebuilt has exactly one tools node and two fixed hook seams.

flashcards.q: What invariant does ToolNode's 1:1 tool_call_id matching enforce, and what breaks if it's violated?
flashcards.a: Every tool_use call gets exactly one matching ToolMessage before the next model call. Violating it (e.g. a hook dropping a ToolMessage) produces an API 400 on malformed conversation, the same failure mode T07-loop-engineering names for cancelled or partially-failed turns.

flashcards.q: Quorum size formula and fault tolerance for N=3, 5, 7 in Raft.
flashcards.a: Quorum = floor(N/2)+1. N=3 -> quorum 2, tolerates 1 failure. N=5 -> quorum 3, tolerates 2 failures. N=7 -> quorum 4, tolerates 3 failures. 4 nodes tolerates only 1 failure, same as 3, which is why production clusters use odd N.

flashcards.q: Raft election timeout and heartbeat interval, from the original paper.
flashcards.a: Election timeout: randomized 150-300ms. Heartbeat interval: ~50ms (roughly 10x margin below the timeout). Production rule: election timeout should be >= 10x the measured inter-node RTT.

flashcards.q: Why is election timeout randomized rather than fixed?
flashcards.a: A fixed timeout means every follower times out simultaneously, causing repeated split votes. Randomizing (e.g. 150-300ms) means one node almost always fires first and wins the election before others become candidates.

flashcards.q: What is a Raft "term" and what role does it play?
flashcards.a: A monotonically increasing integer acting as a logical clock over leadership epochs. Every election bumps it. Any message carrying a lower term is rejected immediately, which is what makes it safe for a stale, isolated leader's heartbeats to be ignored once everyone else has moved to a higher term.

flashcards.q: Difference between "replicated" and "committed" in Raft's log.
flashcards.a: Replicated = appended to a follower's log (can be a minority). Committed = replicated to a MAJORITY, at which point it's safe to apply to the state machine and ack the client, because majority-replication guarantees survival across future leader elections.

flashcards.q: What is the Raft "election restriction" and why does it matter for safety?
flashcards.a: A candidate can only win a vote if its log is at least as up-to-date (by last-entry term, then index) as the voter's. This guarantees any future leader's log is a superset of all previously committed entries, preventing committed data loss across leader changes.

flashcards.q: Did Raft beat Paxos on power or on comprehensibility? What's the evidence?
flashcards.a: Comprehensibility, not power -- they are proven equivalent in the failure conditions under which they can make progress. Evidence: the 2014 user study of 43 students found most scored better on Raft comprehension questions than Paxos questions after learning both.

flashcards.q: What is a fencing token and where must it be enforced?
flashcards.a: A monotonically increasing number issued on every lease/leadership acquisition. Must be enforced at the STORAGE/WRITE layer (reject any write with a token lower than the last seen), not just at the lock service, or a stale paused holder can still corrupt state after waking up.

flashcards.q: What did Kleppmann's 2016 Redlock critique actually identify as missing?
flashcards.a: Redlock provides mutual exclusion under a timing assumption but produces no fencing token -- no monotonically increasing number guaranteed on each acquisition -- so nothing stops a stale, paused holder's write from landing at the storage layer even if the locking algorithm itself is otherwise sound.

flashcards.q: Lamport clock: what does C(a) < C(b) actually prove?
flashcards.a: Almost nothing on its own. If a causally precedes b, C(a) < C(b) is guaranteed, but the converse is false -- two unrelated concurrent events can get any relative counter values via arbitrary tie-breaking. Lamport gives total order, not causality detection.

flashcards.q: Why do vector clocks not scale, concretely?
flashcards.a: A vector clock carries one counter per participating node (O(n) space per event/version), and n grows with every node/client that has ever contributed and doesn't shrink without active pruning -- in high-churn systems this becomes real bandwidth/storage overhead (Dynamo's sibling version-vector bloat).

flashcards.q: How does a Hybrid Logical Clock (HLC) compute its next value?
flashcards.a: Keeps a pair (physical_time, logical_counter). If wall-clock time exceeds the max of last-seen HLC values, adopt it and reset the counter to 0; otherwise keep the higher physical component and increment the counter to break ties. Gives causal ordering plus a value that stays close to real wall-clock time, at O(1) space.

flashcards.q: Which production systems use HLC and for what?
flashcards.a: CockroachDB uses HLC for transaction timestamp ordering, with an uncertainty interval equal to the configured max clock offset (default 500ms) to resolve ambiguous reads. MongoDB exposes it as ClusterTime/operationTime for causal consistency across replica sets.

flashcards.q: Why must lease/timeout code use a monotonic clock rather than wall-clock time?
flashcards.a: NTP step corrections can jump wall-clock time backward or forward discontinuously, breaking any elapsed-time calculation. A monotonic clock (e.g. CLOCK_MONOTONIC) only ever moves forward at a steady rate, which is what elapsed-duration checks (like lease expiry) actually need.

flashcards.q: Does "we use Raft" mean a system is fully split-brain proof? Why or why not?
flashcards.a: No. Raft prevents split-brain within the consensus log itself (two leaders both getting entries committed in one term). It says nothing about a stale leader's side effects issued OUTSIDE the log (e.g. calling an external API before it has stepped down), which aren't protected by term/quorum checks at all.

flashcards.q: Why is every single Redis command atomic with no locking code?
flashcards.a: Redis executes commands on a single thread with no interleaving between commands. Since Redis 6 the socket I/O layer is multi-threaded, but command execution itself is still single-threaded.

flashcards.q: What is the KEYS incident and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: KEYS * walks the entire keyspace on the single command thread, blocking every other client for the whole scan (can spike p99 from ~1ms to seconds). Fix: SCAN with a cursor does bounded work per call and interleaves with other commands.

flashcards.q: RDB vs AOF: what does each guarantee on crash?
flashcards.a: RDB is a periodic point-in-time snapshot; you lose everything since the last snapshot (commonly minutes). AOF logs every write; durability depends on appendfsync: always loses <=1 command (disk-fsync speed throughput), everysec (default) loses ~1s, no defers to OS flush (~30s on Linux).

flashcards.q: How many hash slots does Redis Cluster use and how is a key mapped to one?
flashcards.a: 16,384 slots. slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384. Each slot is owned by exactly one primary node.

flashcards.q: What causes a CROSSSLOT error and how do you fix it?
flashcards.a: A multi-key command (MGET, transactions, multi-key Lua) references keys that hash to different slots. Fix: hash tags -- wrap the shared part of the key in {} (e.g. {user:42}:profile) so only that substring is hashed, co-locating related keys on one slot.

flashcards.q: What's the default maxmemory-policy and why is it usually wrong for a cache?
flashcards.a: noeviction -- once maxmemory is hit, writes fail with an OOM error while reads keep working. A cache workload usually wants allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu so cold data is evicted instead of writes failing.

flashcards.q: What's the correctness hole in a naive SET key val NX EX ttl distributed lock?
flashcards.a: The TTL is a guess at critical-section duration. If the holder pauses (GC, VM stall, network partition) longer than the TTL, the lock expires and a second process can acquire it -- two processes can believe they hold the lock simultaneously with nothing detecting it.

flashcards.q: What is Kleppmann's specific critique of Redlock?
flashcards.a: Redlock has no fencing token. A process that acquires the lock and then pauses (GC, VM migration) past the TTL can resume believing it still holds the lock and write to the protected resource after a different process has legitimately acquired the lock -- nothing stops the stale write because the resource itself can't tell the writer is stale.

flashcards.q: What actually fixes the Redlock fencing gap, and where does the fix live?
flashcards.a: A fencing token: a monotonically increasing number issued with each lock acquisition, checked and rejected by the PROTECTED RESOURCE if it's lower than the last accepted token. The fix must live at the resource, not the lock service, since the lock service can't know the writer has gone stale after it resumes from a pause.

flashcards.q: What's the honest conclusion about Redis distributed locks?
flashcards.a: They are a performance optimization to reduce duplicate work (e.g. preventing two cron instances from both running an expensive job), not a correctness mechanism for anything where two processes concurrently holding the lock would be a real safety violation.

flashcards.q: Sentinel vs Cluster: what problem does each solve?
flashcards.a: Sentinel provides automatic failover for a primary/replica set where the whole dataset fits on one node -- it solves availability. Cluster shards the keyspace across multiple primaries via hash slots -- it solves capacity, with each shard optionally having its own replicas for HA.

flashcards.q: Why does a Redis Stream keep growing even after every consumer has processed and acked every message?
flashcards.a: Streams are append-only; XACK just marks a message as no longer pending, it doesn't delete it. Without XTRIM (MAXLEN/MINID), every message ever added stays in memory forever.

flashcards.q: When is Redis Streams the right choice over Kafka, and when is Kafka better?
flashcards.a: Streams fit single-region workloads under roughly 200k events/sec per stream, already-on-Redis teams, and bounded in-memory retention. Kafka fits durable disk-backed retention independent of memory, throughput beyond that range, multiple independent uncoordinated consumers, or strict exactly-once semantics.

flashcards.q: Which Redis structure would you use for a leaderboard and why?
flashcards.a: A sorted set (ZSet): O(log N) insert/update via its internal skip list plus hash table, and O(log N + M) range queries for top-N or range-by-score lookups.

flashcards.q: What does HyperLogLog trade away to count distinct elements in fixed space?
flashcards.a: Exactness -- it gives an approximate cardinality estimate (~0.81% standard error) using a fixed ~12KB regardless of element count, and cannot enumerate which elements were seen, only estimate how many there were.

flashcards.q: How many bytes per parameter does full fine-tuning with Adam need, and what's the 7B/70B memory cost?
flashcards.a: ~16-18 bytes/param (bf16 weight + bf16 grad + fp32 master weight + fp32 momentum + fp32 variance), before activations. 7B ~112-140GB, 70B ~1.1-1.4TB.

flashcards.q: What is the LoRA forward-pass formula and why is B initialized to zero?
flashcards.a: h = Wx + (alpha/r) * B A x. B starts at zero (A is small random) so delta W = 0 at step 0 -- the model is numerically identical to the frozen base at the start of training, which keeps training stable.

flashcards.q: Worked example: LoRA parameter count vs full FT for a 4096x4096 matrix at rank 8.
flashcards.a: Full FT: 4096x4096 = 16.8M params. LoRA r=8: 4096x8 + 8x4096 = 65,536 params -- about a 256x reduction for that matrix.

flashcards.q: What are the three specific tricks QLoRA adds beyond plain LoRA?
flashcards.a: 1) NF4: 4-bit quantization with bins at normal-distribution quantiles (fits pretrained weight stats). 2) Double quantization: quantizes the per-block scaling constants to 8-bit, saving ~0.37 bits/param (~3GB on a 65B model). 3) Paged optimizers: page Adam state to CPU RAM on gradient-checkpointing memory spikes instead of OOMing.

flashcards.q: QLoRA memory: 7B and 70B model sizes, roughly?
flashcards.a: 7B QLoRA ~12GB. 70B QLoRA ~35-48GB -- fits on a single 80GB GPU, versus ~1.1-1.4TB for full FT of the 70B model.

flashcards.q: How does DoRA decompose a weight matrix, and why does it add zero inference latency?
flashcards.a: W = m * (V / ||V||): a learned per-column magnitude m times a unit-norm direction V. LoRA is applied only to the direction; magnitude is learned separately. Because both are linear compositions on the frozen base, DoRA merges into a single weight matrix at inference exactly like plain LoRA -- no extra runtime compute.

flashcards.q: Why does DoRA outperform LoRA at matched rank?
flashcards.a: Full fine-tuning changes a weight's magnitude and direction somewhat independently; a single additive low-rank LoRA update tends to change both together in a way that doesn't match that pattern. DoRA's explicit magnitude/direction split tracks full-FT's update pattern more closely, closing most of the remaining quality gap.

flashcards.q: What is the 2026 practical default LoRA configuration, and when should rank go higher?
flashcards.a: r=16, alpha=16, DoRA enabled, target_modules=all-linear. Raise to r=32-64 for complex multi-turn, code, or math tasks -- 2025 research found intermediate ranks give a better capacity/stability tradeoff than the smaller 8-16 range from the original paper.

flashcards.q: Why does targeting all linear layers (not just attention Q/V) matter more than rank in some cases?
flashcards.a: The original LoRA paper only adapted attention query/value projections. Adapting all linear layers including MLP up/down/gate projections closes more of the gap to full FT, especially on tasks stressing MLP capacity like code and math.

flashcards.q: What is catastrophic forgetting and how does LoRA compare to full FT on it?
flashcards.a: Fine-tuning on a narrow distribution degrades capability the training data didn't reinforce (e.g. general instruction-following regresses after narrow-domain FT). LoRA forgets measurably less than full FT at matched task performance because frozen base weights preserve most general capability -- but LoRA also 'learns less,' so low rank can underfit tasks needing real new capability.

flashcards.q: How do serving stacks like vLLM run thousands of LoRA adapters on one GPU?
flashcards.a: One base model stays resident; each adapter is applied per-request via small batched matmuls rather than merged into a separate full model copy. Because the adapter matmuls are tiny relative to the base forward pass, throughput stays close to serving the base model alone.

flashcards.q: State the RAG-vs-fine-tuning decision rule in one sentence.
flashcards.a: If the failure looks like 'the model doesn't know a fact,' use retrieval; if it looks like 'the model knows it but does the wrong thing with it' (format, tone, behavior), try a better prompt first, then fine-tune.

flashcards.q: Why does fine-tuning to inject knowledge fail in production, specifically?
flashcards.a: Facts baked into weights are frozen at training time -- the model recites them correctly right after training, then gives stale or fabricated answers as the underlying facts change, and every update requires a full retrain. Retrieval updates immediately when the index changes and provides provenance fine-tuning can't.

flashcards.q: What data quality rule of thumb should guide whether to attempt fine-tuning?
flashcards.a: 1,000 hand-curated, diverse examples routinely beat 100,000 noisy ones. Below a few hundred genuinely high-quality examples, the model overfits to incidental patterns rather than the intended general behavior, often invisible until tested out-of-domain.

flashcards.q: Give a legitimate (non-knowledge-injection) reason to fine-tune.
flashcards.a: Distilling a long system prompt / few-shot pattern into weights to cut per-call token cost at volume -- this is teaching form/behavior, not facts, as long as the examples don't themselves embed facts that would get memorized.

flashcards.q: Give bytes-per-parameter for fp32, fp16/bf16, fp8, int8, int4/nf4.
flashcards.a: fp32=4, fp16/bf16=2, fp8=1, int8=1, int4/nf4=0.5 bytes per parameter.

flashcards.q: Why does quantization speed up decode more than prefill?
flashcards.a: Decode at low batch size is memory-bandwidth-bound (~1 FLOP per byte read, ~100-200x below the compute/bandwidth ridge point on H100-class GPUs) so shrinking weight bytes speeds it up roughly proportionally. Prefill reuses weights across many tokens in parallel and is compute-bound, so it needs real INT8/FP8 tensor-core throughput (weight+activation quant), not just smaller weight bytes.

flashcards.q: PTQ vs QAT: what's the difference and when is QAT worth it?
flashcards.a: PTQ quantizes an already-trained model using a small calibration set (128-512 samples), cheap, no retraining -- the default. QAT simulates quantization noise during training so weights adapt to tolerate it; worth it only for sub-4-bit targets when already running a fine-tuning pipeline.

flashcards.q: GPTQ vs AWQ: mechanism difference and 2026 default.
flashcards.a: GPTQ uses layer-wise Hessian-based error correction (quantize a weight, adjust the rest of the layer to compensate). AWQ identifies salient weight channels via ACTIVATION magnitude and protects them with per-channel scaling. AWQ is the 2026 GPU-serving default -- better quality at 4-bit, especially on instruction-tuned models.

flashcards.q: Measured HumanEval degradation at 4-bit: fp16 baseline vs AWQ/GGUF vs GPTQ.
flashcards.a: fp16 baseline 56.1%. AWQ and GGUF both ~51.8% (~4pt loss). GPTQ trails at ~46% (~10pt loss).

flashcards.q: Why are activations harder to quantize than weights in LLMs?
flashcards.a: Weight distributions are uniform and well-behaved. Activations develop systematic outlier channels, 20-100x larger than the rest, in fixed feature dimensions across nearly every token, once models exceed ~6-7B params. A max-based INT8 scale either clips the outliers (losing signal) or wastes precision accommodating them.

flashcards.q: State SmoothQuant's rescaling identity and why it's exact, not approximate.
flashcards.a: (X/s)(sW) = XW for any per-channel scale s. Dividing activations by s and multiplying the corresponding weight channel by s leaves the matmul output unchanged -- it migrates quantization difficulty from activations to weights via an exact algebraic identity, not a lossy approximation.

flashcards.q: What does GGUF add beyond being another 4-bit format?
flashcards.a: A self-contained file format for llama.cpp with multiple quant levels per tensor (Q2_K-Q8_0); k-quants mix precision within a block, keeping a minority of important values at higher precision. Dominant for CPU/edge/consumer-GPU inference, not GPU-cluster serving.

flashcards.q: Rank task categories by how much they degrade under aggressive quantization, easiest to hardest.
flashcards.a: Chat/summarization (most tolerant) < long-context retrieval / multilingual (especially low-resource languages) < math/code (degrades first and hardest, because compounding multi-step errors invalidate the whole output).

flashcards.q: KV cache quantization: give the rough quality cost of INT8, FP8, and INT4.
flashcards.a: INT8: holds accuracy well across most tasks. FP8: typically under 0.5 percentage points on long-context retrieval benchmarks. INT4: real, growing degradation with context length and reasoning depth, because per-step error compounds across every subsequent attention read of the cache.

flashcards.q: Why does calibration data choice matter for GPTQ/AWQ?
flashcards.a: Both derive quantization parameters (Hessian stats or salient channels) from a calibration set of ~128-512 samples. Calibrating on a generic corpus when production traffic is domain-specific (code, a non-English language) means the wrong channels get protected, causing degradation invisible on general benchmarks.

flashcards.q: Weight-only vs weight-and-activation quantization: when does each matter?
flashcards.a: Weight-only (GPTQ/AWQ/GGUF/NF4) shrinks bytes read from HBM -- helps memory-bound decode, but the matmul still runs at higher precision after dequant, so it doesn't unlock faster compute. Weight-and-activation (SmoothQuant W8A8, FP8) engages real INT8/FP8 tensor-core throughput, needed for compute-bound regimes like large-batch prefill.

flashcards.q: What is the LLM.int8() mixed-precision decomposition?
flashcards.a: Identify the small set of outlier activation feature dimensions per forward pass, compute those specific columns in fp16 and everything else in INT8, then recombine -- correct but adds overhead proportional to how many outlier dimensions appear.

flashcards.q: Why is decode's arithmetic intensity roughly 1 FLOP/byte at batch size 1?
flashcards.a: Each decode step reads the entire weight matrix from HBM once and performs on the order of one FLOP of matmul work per byte read (e.g. a 70B fp16 model reads 140GB and does ~140 GFLOPs per token) -- far below the ridge point where GPU compute would become the bottleneck.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT quantize at all?
flashcards.a: When you have ample GPU memory headroom, the workload is latency-insensitive at your actual batch sizes, or reproducibility against a known fp16 baseline matters more than memory savings -- the validation cost (calibration, task-specific eval, KV-cache-specific testing) of doing it correctly is real.

flashcards.q: What is AutoGen's status as of 2026, and what replaced it?
flashcards.a: Maintenance mode — Microsoft redirected its roadmap to Microsoft Agent Framework, which merges AutoGen's multi-agent orchestration with Semantic Kernel's enterprise features and reached GA 1.0 on 2026-04-03 for Python and .NET.

flashcards.q: Where is Google ADK's durability story strong, and where is it a trap?
flashcards.a: Strong in production via VertexAiSessionService backed by Vertex AI Agent Engine. Trap: InMemorySessionService (used in dev) doesn't survive a restart, and the whole durability/memory story is coupled to Google Cloud deployment.

flashcards.q: Does OpenAI's Agents SDK have native cross-process checkpointing?
flashcards.a: No. Sessions give persistent conversational memory within a live run, not resumability across a crash. Durable execution across restarts has to be built separately or delegated to an orchestrator like Temporal.

flashcards.q: What is CrewAI's core process-model limitation?
flashcards.a: Its Process is sequential or hierarchical, which can't express genuine conditional branching — a workflow needing 'if X route to A else B, then converge' doesn't map cleanly onto either process type.

flashcards.q: How much token overhead does CrewAI carry versus LangGraph on simple workflows?
flashcards.a: Up to 3x the token overhead, the measured cost of its higher-ceremony role/backstory-based prompting style.

flashcards.q: What does it mean that framework choice can move agent benchmark scores by up to 30 percentage points on the identical model?
flashcards.a: The graph design and tool set dominate the framework's brand — a bad implementation on a 'good' framework loses to a good implementation on a 'weaker' one, so benchmark leaderboard numbers don't transfer to your specific workload.

flashcards.q: Contrast LangGraph's and OpenAI Agents SDK's approach to multi-agent.
flashcards.a: Both treat multi-agent as composition on top of a single-agent primitive rather than a core abstraction: LangGraph via subgraphs and Send fan-out, OpenAI's SDK via handoffs (an agent calling another agent as a tool). You don't pay a multi-agent tax unless you use it.

flashcards.q: Which two frameworks treat multi-agent orchestration as the core abstraction from the start?
flashcards.a: Google ADK (composable agent trees: Sequential/Parallel/Loop agents) and CrewAI (named crews coordinated by a Process). AutoGen's conversational turn-taking is also multi-agent-first but the project is frozen.

flashcards.q: What is LangGraph's streaming churn risk?
flashcards.a: Three different wire formats in fifteen months (v1 tuples, v2 unified StreamPart, v3 typed projections). Code written against the streaming surface has already had to migrate twice; pin the version explicitly.

flashcards.q: What is the most composable human-in-the-loop primitive across these frameworks, and why?
flashcards.a: LangGraph's interrupt() plus a durable checkpointer, because it suspends to storage at an arbitrary point and Command(resume=...) continues — a genuinely durable, arbitrary-point pause, unlike OpenAI's guardrails (fail-fast validation, not a durable pause) or ADK's session-based pause (GCP-coupled).

flashcards.q: When is hand-rolled usually the right choice among all these options?
flashcards.a: When you don't simultaneously need durable resume across a crash, a real multi-day approval gate, multi-format streaming to a UI, and branching/fan-out topology — below that bar, every framework here is negative value relative to a straightforward loop.

flashcards.q: Why does heavier framework structure age worse as models improve, per the Bitter Lesson framing?
flashcards.a: Every structural component encodes an assumption that the model can't do something, and those assumptions expire as models improve. A fixed multi-agent topology or heavy scaffolding built for an older model can be actively worse than a newer model given fewer tools and a shorter loop.

flashcards.q: What's the practical migration risk of a codebase built on AutoGen?
flashcards.a: Not vendor lock-in but time lock-in: the codebase is written against a frozen project, so debugging and community support only shrink from here. Maintenance-mode bug/security fixes still flow, but new feature investment should go toward migrating to Microsoft Agent Framework.

flashcards.q: Give a concrete cost/latency comparison across LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen from a comparative benchmark harness.
flashcards.a: LangGraph reported roughly $0.08/task on cost and latency; CrewAI won time-to-a-working-prototype; AutoGen won open-ended reasoning quality but at 5-6x the cost of the cheaper options — a Pareto tradeoff, not a strict win for any one.

flashcards.q: What is Google ADK's native streaming differentiator versus the other frameworks?
flashcards.a: Native bidirectional (Bidi) multimodal streaming — text, audio, and video — built as a production-ready feature, which is a genuine advantage if the product is voice or live video rather than request-response chat.

flashcards.q: What is Kafka's ordering guarantee, exactly?
flashcards.a: Ordering is guaranteed only WITHIN a partition, never across partitions of the same topic. Same-key messages land on the same partition via hashing, which is how per-entity ordering is actually achieved -- it's a routing side effect, not a topic-wide property.

flashcards.q: What breaks ordering when you increase a topic's partition count?
flashcards.a: The key-to-partition hash mapping changes for a percentage of keys, so messages for the same key produced before vs after the resize can land on different partitions, breaking per-key ordering across that boundary.

flashcards.q: What exactly does Kafka's exactly-once semantics (EOS) guarantee, and where does it stop?
flashcards.a: Idempotent producer (dedup by producer-id + sequence number) + transactions (atomic multi-partition writes and offset commits) give effectively-once processing INSIDE Kafka. It does not cover side effects outside Kafka (DB writes, API calls) -- those need their own idempotency (unique constraint/upsert/dedup key).

flashcards.q: Eager vs cooperative consumer group rebalance.
flashcards.a: Eager: stop-the-world -- every consumer revokes all partitions and the whole group pauses until reassignment finishes. Cooperative (KIP-429, CooperativeStickyAssignor, Kafka 2.4+): incremental, two-phase -- only partitions actually moving are revoked, unaffected consumers keep processing.

flashcards.q: How do you avoid a rebalance on a brief planned consumer restart?
flashcards.a: Configure static group membership via group.instance.id -- the coordinator recognizes a returning consumer within a grace period and skips triggering a rebalance.

flashcards.q: Define consumer lag and its diagnostic symptoms.
flashcards.a: Lag = latest_offset - committed_offset. Lag climbing linearly = sustained under-capacity (slow processing or too few consumers). One partition's lag far above group average = key skew -- adding consumers doesn't fix it since one partition still serves only one consumer.

flashcards.q: Kafka default retention period and what cleanup.policy=delete does.
flashcards.a: Default log.retention.hours is 168 hours (7 days). cleanup.policy=delete discards whole log segments once they age past retention or exceed a size limit -- appropriate for event streams where old data loses relevance.

flashcards.q: What does log compaction (cleanup.policy=compact) do, and what is a tombstone?
flashcards.a: Compaction retains only the latest value per key regardless of age, turning the topic into a durable snapshot of current state per key. A tombstone is a record with a null value signaling deletion, retained for delete.retention.ms (default 24h) before being physically removed.

flashcards.q: What problem does the transactional outbox pattern solve, and how does Debezium fit in?
flashcards.a: It solves the dual-write problem (DB commit and broker publish aren't atomic with each other). The app writes an outbox row in the SAME DB transaction as business data; Debezium reads the DB's transaction log (not polling) and relays outbox changes to Kafka, converting a cross-system problem into one ACID transaction plus a reliable relay.

flashcards.q: Tumbling vs hopping vs session windows.
flashcards.a: Tumbling: fixed-size, non-overlapping, each record in exactly one window. Hopping: fixed-size but overlapping (advance step < window size), a record can fall in multiple windows. Session: dynamic, bounded by a gap of inactivity rather than a fixed clock.

flashcards.q: Why does stream processing need watermarks when batch processing doesn't?
flashcards.a: A batch job's dataset is complete by definition. A streaming job's data never definitively ends and can arrive late (event time vs arrival time), so a watermark is an explicit policy for how long to wait for stragglers before closing a window -- an accuracy-vs-latency tradeoff with no batch equivalent.

flashcards.q: Kafka Streams state stores: what backs them and how do they survive a crash?
flashcards.a: Backed locally by RocksDB (default for production). They're also backed by a compacted Kafka changelog topic, so state can be rebuilt after a crash by replaying the changelog without re-processing the entire original input stream.

flashcards.q: Kafka partition throughput vs a single Kinesis shard.
flashcards.a: A single Kafka partition on decent NVMe hardware routinely sustains 10-100+ MB/s. A single Kinesis shard caps at 1 MB/s write / 2 MB/s read -- roughly two orders of magnitude lower ceiling per unit.

flashcards.q: When is SQS a better default than Kafka?
flashcards.a: When throughput is well under ~500-1,000 msg/s sustained, there's a single consumer type, and no replay is needed. SQS is fully managed and zero-ops for that shape of workload; Kafka's differentiators (multi-consumer replay, high per-partition throughput, long retention) go unused.

flashcards.q: How does Pulsar's architecture differ from Kafka's at the storage layer?
flashcards.a: Kafka couples compute (broker) and storage (local disk) in the same process. Pulsar separates them: stateless brokers handle routing while BookKeeper, a separate distributed log layer, holds the data, enabling independent scaling and native tiered storage -- at the cost of operating two distributed systems instead of one.

flashcards.q: Name the four mechanical reasons ClickHouse is fast.
flashcards.a: Columnar storage (scan only needed columns), sparse primary index (binary search over per-granule entries), compression on sorted columnar data (5-20x+), and vectorized execution (SIMD, block-at-a-time operators).

flashcards.q: What is the default index_granularity and what does it mean?
flashcards.a: 8192 rows per granule (adaptive since 19.x, targeting ~10MB uncompressed for wide rows). The sparse primary index stores one entry per granule, not per row.

flashcards.q: Is the MergeTree primary index unique or a B-tree?
flashcards.a: Neither. It's a sparse, sorted array of per-granule starting key values, binary-searched to find candidate granule ranges -- not a per-row structure and not a tree.

flashcards.q: What causes the 'Too many parts' error and what's the primary fix?
flashcards.a: Frequent small inserts create parts faster than background merges can absorb, hitting a protective ceiling (default ~3000 active parts/partition). Primary fix: batch inserts client-side (10K-500K rows per insert, every 1-2s) rather than raising the limit.

flashcards.q: Why does ClickHouse never merge parts across partitions, and what's the practical consequence?
flashcards.a: Partitions are physically separate directories of parts by design. Over-partitioning (e.g. per-minute or high-cardinality keys) multiplies independent small-part pools, each accumulating unmerged parts -- coarser partitioning (monthly vs daily) is a common fix for too-many-parts.

flashcards.q: Which three operations are memory-bound in ClickHouse (not streaming), and why?
flashcards.a: High-cardinality GROUP BY (hash table sized to distinct groups, not rows scanned), JOIN (right-hand table loaded fully into memory for the hash join), and unbounded ORDER BY (must hold or spill the whole result set).

flashcards.q: What's the difference in outcome between a query hitting max_memory_usage vs the server hitting the Linux OOM killer?
flashcards.a: max_memory_usage kills only the offending query with a clean exception. The Linux OOM killer (triggered if max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio, default 0.9, is exceeded) can kill the whole clickhouse-server process, taking down every other running query too.

flashcards.q: How do you diagnose which query caused an OOM after the fact?
flashcards.a: Query system.query_log WHERE type = 'QueryFinish' ordered by memory_usage descending to find the actual offending query pattern rather than guessing from the OOM alert.

flashcards.q: How do you prevent a GROUP BY or ORDER BY from OOMing instead of failing outright?
flashcards.a: Enable max_bytes_before_external_group_by (or external_sort for ORDER BY) so the operation spills partial state to disk past a memory threshold, trading latency for not needing unbounded memory.

flashcards.q: Why are JOINs expensive in ClickHouse mechanically?
flashcards.a: The default hash join loads the entire right-hand table into an in-memory hash table before probing with the left side, so the right table's size (not overall query row count) drives memory pressure, and probing is row-level random access that breaks columnar-scan locality.

flashcards.q: What are the three recommended ways to avoid expensive live JOINs in ClickHouse?
