flashcards.a: Put the smaller table on the right side of any join you must do, use a Dictionary engine (fully in-memory, O(1) lookup) for small frequently-joined dimension tables, and denormalize static large-dimension attributes onto the fact table at ingestion time.

flashcards.q: A ReplacingMergeTree table shows duplicate rows right after insert. Why, and how do you get a correct read immediately?
flashcards.a: Deduplication happens at merge time, not insert time, and merges haven't run yet. Query with FINAL to force on-the-fly deduplication (at real CPU/latency cost) rather than assuming upsert-on-write.

flashcards.q: Difference between a ClickHouse projection and a materialized view?
flashcards.a: A projection is an alternate physical layout of the SAME table that the optimizer transparently picks (no cross-table joins allowed). A materialized view is a trigger on insert that writes results into a SEPARATE target table, moving aggregation from query time to insert time.

flashcards.q: Name three shapes of workload where ClickHouse is the wrong choice.
flashcards.a: Point updates/deletes at OLTP frequency (mutations are heavyweight async part rewrites), high-concurrency transactional writes with many small inserts (triggers too-many-parts), and any need for multi-statement ACID transactions or strict single-row current-value consistency.

flashcards.q: Why does denormalizing make sense in ClickHouse when it's an anti-pattern in Postgres?
flashcards.a: Postgres has cheap, transactional row-level updates so keeping normalized data in sync is cheap; ClickHouse updates are expensive async mutations and joins are the expensive operation, so paying the ingestion-time cost of denormalized writes once beats paying a live-join cost on every query.

flashcards.q: What are the three distinct guarantees provided by refresh, flush, and merge?
flashcards.a: Refresh = visibility (search can see the document, default every 1s). Flush = durability (segments fsync'd to disk, translog cleared). Merge = efficiency (fewer segments to search, deleted docs reclaimed). They are three different things, not synonyms.

flashcards.q: Why isn't a document searchable the instant it's indexed?
flashcards.a: It's added to an in-memory buffer and the translog, but only becomes searchable after a refresh (default interval 1s) turns the buffer into a new immutable Lucene segment. This is what 'near-real-time' means precisely.

flashcards.q: A term query for the exact phrase 'Redis Cluster' against a text-mapped field returns nothing. Why?
flashcards.a: The text field is analyzed at index time into separate lowercased tokens ('redis', 'cluster'), not the raw phrase. A term query compares the raw input against those individual tokens, so a multi-token phrase never matches. Fix: use a keyword field/sub-field for exact match.

flashcards.q: What's the first knob to turn under heavy bulk-indexing load, and what does it trade off?
flashcards.a: Raise (or disable, -1) refresh_interval. Fewer, larger segments get created per unit time, reducing merge pressure and indexing overhead, at the cost of increased search-visibility latency.

flashcards.q: What is the default scoring function in Elasticsearch, and what two parameters define it?
flashcards.a: BM25 (default since Lucene 6 / ES 5, 2016, replacing TF-IDF). k1 (default 1.2) controls term-frequency saturation; b (default 0.75) controls document-length normalization.

flashcards.q: What does BM25's term-frequency saturation (k1) fix relative to plain TF-IDF?
flashcards.a: TF-IDF scales score linearly with term frequency with no cap; BM25's k1 makes repeated occurrences of a term contribute diminishing returns instead of scaling forever.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between a query clause and a filter clause?
flashcards.a: A query clause contributes to the relevance score. A filter clause (bool.filter/must_not) is a yes/no check with no scoring contribution, and is cacheable since the answer doesn't depend on scoring math -- generally cheaper to execute.

flashcards.q: What causes oversharding and what's its observable symptom?
flashcards.a: Provisioning far more shards than data volume/node count justify -- each shard carries real per-shard memory and cluster-state overhead. Symptom: heap usage climbs and query/indexing latency degrades with no correlation to actual data growth, plus slow cluster-state updates.

flashcards.q: What's the commonly recommended shard size range, and the fix for an already-oversharded cluster?
flashcards.a: Roughly 10-50GB per shard. Fix an oversharded cluster by reindexing into fewer, larger shards (or _shrink for read-only indices) -- you can't just reduce a live index's primary shard count in place.

flashcards.q: Why does from/size pagination get slow and error past 10,000 results, and what replaces it?
flashcards.a: Each shard must compute and sort from+size results before the coordinator merges/re-sorts across shards, so cost grows with depth; index.max_result_window (default 10,000) enforces a hard ceiling. search_after uses the last document's sort values as a cursor for depth-independent sequential paging instead.

flashcards.q: Why is a cardinality aggregation approximate by default?
flashcards.a: It uses HyperLogLog++ under the hood, trading exactness for bounded memory on high-cardinality fields. precision_threshold trades more memory for tighter accuracy up to a configurable cardinality.

flashcards.q: What does the translog protect that flushed segments don't?
flashcards.a: The translog is a write-ahead log of raw operations fsync'd per request by default, protecting anything written after the last flush and before the next one -- on unclean shutdown it's replayed to recover unflushed operations.

flashcards.q: How would you diagnose why a search result's ranking looks wrong?
flashcards.a: Run the query with explain:true (or the _explain API) to get the exact per-term BM25 breakdown (term frequency, IDF, length normalization contributions) rather than guessing at relevance tuning blind.

flashcards.q: What vector search capability does modern Elasticsearch have, and its default hybrid fusion method?
flashcards.a: dense_vector fields with HNSW-based approximate kNN search (knn query clause), plus exact brute-force search when configured without HNSW. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is the default method for combining lexical (BM25) and vector scores in a hybrid query.

flashcards.q: When is Elasticsearch's native vector search the right call versus a dedicated vector database?
flashcards.a: Right call when you already run Elasticsearch for lexical/log search and want hybrid retrieval without new infrastructure. A dedicated vector DB wins at very large pure-vector scale with heavy filtering and multi-tenancy needs where ANN recall/latency is the primary concern.

flashcards.q: What is an anaemic domain model and why does layered architecture produce it?
flashcards.a: Domain objects that are pure getters/setters with all business logic in service classes. Layered architecture organizes bands but doesn't enforce dependency direction within them, so this is the path of least resistance under deadline pressure.

flashcards.q: What's the real difference between hexagonal, onion, and clean architecture?
flashcards.a: Same idea (Cockburn 2005, Palermo 2008, Martin 2012): dependencies point inward toward the domain, infra implements interfaces the domain defines. Differences are vocabulary (port/adapter vs entity/use case) not substance.

flashcards.q: What is the core rule all three ports-and-adapters-style architectures enforce?
flashcards.a: Source-code dependencies point toward the domain, never outward. Where control needs to flow outward (e.g. save to DB), the domain defines an interface and an outer layer implements it (dependency inversion).

flashcards.q: What three properties make a module boundary 'real' in a modular monolith?
flashcards.a: No shared tables across modules, no reaching into another module's internal classes, and enforcement by tooling (fitness functions like ArchUnit/import-linter) rather than convention.

flashcards.q: What is the recommended 2026 default starting architecture for most teams?
flashcards.a: The modular monolith: one deployable unit with enforced internal module boundaries, giving most of microservices' organizational clarity without the operational cost.

flashcards.q: What does 2026 industry data show about microservices adoption trends?
flashcards.a: 42% of organizations that adopted microservices have consolidated some services back into larger units; microservices satisfaction down 19 percentage points vs 2024; infra costs reported 3.75x-6x higher for equivalent functionality.

flashcards.q: Name two real costs of microservices that are easy to underestimate.
flashcards.a: Distributed data (cross-service consistency now needs sagas/eventual consistency instead of a DB transaction), and operational multiplication (N services = N deploy pipelines, N dashboards, N on-call surfaces).

flashcards.q: What is a distributed monolith?
flashcards.a: A system with the network-call cost of microservices but without independent deployability, usually because services share a database or have contracts so tightly coupled they must release together.

flashcards.q: State Conway's Law and its practical design implication.
flashcards.a: (1967) Systems mirror the communication structure of the organizations that build them. Practical implication: a service boundary that cuts against how teams actually communicate will be fought continuously regardless of the diagram.

flashcards.q: What is the Inverse Conway Maneuver?
flashcards.a: Deliberately restructuring teams to match the target architecture, since it's cheaper to move team boundaries than to hold a service boundary against the grain of actual communication patterns.

flashcards.q: Why is splitting services along technical layers (auth service, validation service, DB service) usually wrong?
flashcards.a: It produces chattiness rather than independence: a single business operation now fans out across N network hops for what used to be N in-process function calls. Split along bounded contexts/business capabilities instead.

flashcards.q: What is the strangler fig pattern for service extraction?
flashcards.a: Introduce a routing layer, incrementally route growing traffic to the new service while the old code path stays live, cut over once proven, then delete the old path. System is releasable at every step, unlike a big-bang rewrite.

flashcards.q: When is splitting into a separate microservice actually justified?
flashcards.a: A named forcing function: a component with a genuinely different scaling profile, a measured deployment-cadence bottleneck from shared releases, or a real compliance/security isolation requirement -- not 'microservices are what serious companies do.'

flashcards.q: When should you NOT use hexagonal/onion/clean architecture?
flashcards.a: When the app has one datastore that will never realistically change and the domain logic is thin -- the extra ports/adapters/use-case indirection costs more than it saves for a simple CRUD app.

flashcards.q: What are the two bad interleavings in the dual-write problem?
flashcards.a: DB commit succeeds, publish fails -> event never sent, silent data loss. Publish succeeds, DB commit fails/crashes -> false event sent for something that never happened.

flashcards.q: How does the transactional outbox pattern solve the dual-write problem?
flashcards.a: Write the event as a row in an outbox table in the SAME local transaction as the business write, so both commit or neither does. A separate relay drains and publishes it later.

flashcards.q: What delivery guarantee does the outbox pattern provide, and why not stronger?
flashcards.a: At-least-once. The relay can crash after publishing but before marking the row done, so it republishes on restart.

flashcards.q: Polling vs CDC for draining an outbox table -- tradeoff?
flashcards.a: Polling: simple, latency bound by poll interval (100ms-1s), adds read load. CDC (e.g. Debezium tailing the WAL): sub-second latency, no polling load, but requires operating a CDC pipeline.

flashcards.q: What does the inbox pattern add on top of the outbox?
flashcards.a: Consumer-side dedup: insert the incoming message id into a dedup table in the SAME transaction as applying the business effect, skip if already present. Turns at-least-once delivery into effectively-once processing.

flashcards.q: What is a saga?
flashcards.a: A sequence of local transactions across services, each with a compensating action, used when no cross-service ACID transaction is possible.

flashcards.q: Orchestration vs choreography saga -- key tradeoff?
flashcards.a: Orchestration: central coordinator, explicit queryable state, easier debugging, default for >2-3 steps. Choreography: services react to each other's events, decoupled, but saga state is implicit and hard to query.

flashcards.q: Why is a compensating transaction not a rollback?
flashcards.a: A rollback undoes a transaction that never committed (nothing else saw it). A compensation undoes a transaction that DID commit and may already have been observed/acted on -- it's a new forward-moving operation, not an undo of history.

flashcards.q: What is the semantic-lock problem in sagas, and the fix?
flashcards.a: A resource held 'locked' only by saga logic between steps (e.g. reserved inventory), with no DB-level enforcement -- if the saga stalls, it stays locked indefinitely. Fix: add a timeout on every step that triggers compensation.

flashcards.q: Does CQRS require event sourcing?
flashcards.a: No. CQRS just means separate read and write models; the read model can be built by a projector consuming ordinary domain events published via an outbox, with the write side as normal rows.

flashcards.q: What UI problem does CQRS's eventually-consistent read model cause, and the fix?
flashcards.a: A user who just wrote data can see stale/missing data on an immediate read from the projection. Fix: read-your-writes (route immediate post-write reads to the write model) or optimistic UI updates.

flashcards.q: What is event sourcing?
flashcards.a: The append-only event log is the source of truth instead of current-state rows; current state is derived by folding (replaying) the events. Projections are materialized views built from the log.

flashcards.q: How do you handle GDPR deletion in an event-sourced system?
flashcards.a: Two mitigations: crypto-shredding (encrypt PII per-subject, destroy the key to make it unreadable) or forgettable payloads (store PII in a separate mutable store referenced by id, delete there on request). The event log itself is never mutated.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT use event sourcing?
flashcards.a: When nobody can name a specific requirement (real audit mandate, 'what was true at time T' query, or need to rebuild materially different projections) that only the event log satisfies. Adopting it for 'future flexibility' is the most common regret.

flashcards.q: Why do event-sourced systems use snapshots?
flashcards.a: Replaying every event to compute current state is wasteful at scale; periodically persist the folded state (e.g. every 100-500 events) and replay only events since the snapshot.

flashcards.q: Name the five blast-radius bands in order.
flashcards.a: read_only -> write_reversible -> write_irreversible -> financial -> destructive. Assigned once at tool registration and reviewed like code, never decided by the model at call time.

flashcards.q: Which property most often moves a tool up a band from what its verb suggests, and why?
flashcards.a: Externality. Anything a third party observes (email, payment, public post) is irreversible in practice even if the underlying database row can be rolled back -- "you can't un-send." A technically-reversible write with external visibility behaves like write_irreversible.

flashcards.q: State the deny-first guarantee and why it's load-bearing.
flashcards.a: Deny rules are checked before allow rules, unconditionally. If allow were checked first you could never safely narrow a broad grant -- you'd have to enumerate every safe pattern instead of the few unsafe ones. Deny-first lets you grant broadly and carve out exceptions safely.

flashcards.q: Give the real-world precedent for deny-first at scale, in AWS IAM.
flashcards.a: AWS IAM evaluates organization SCPs, resource-based policies, identity-based policies, permission boundaries, and session policies for every request. An explicit Deny anywhere in that set overrides any Allow anywhere else -- the mechanism that lets an org grant broadly by default and still lock down a few dangerous actions.

flashcards.q: Give Claude Code's six-step permission resolution order.
flashcards.a: hooks -> deny rules -> ask rules -> permission mode -> allow rules -> canUseTool callback. A hook denial and a scoped deny rule (e.g. Bash(rm *)) both survive even bypassPermissions mode.

flashcards.q: Define the confused deputy problem and name who coined it.
flashcards.a: Norm Hardy, 1988. A program (or agent) with more privilege than the party directing it, that uses its own privilege on that party's behalf without verifying the party was entitled to it for this specific action. Canonical example: a compiler that writes output to any file the caller names, including protected ones.

flashcards.q: Describe the Railway/PocketOS incident (April 25, 2026) as a confused-deputy case.
flashcards.a: A Cursor agent hit a credential mismatch in staging, found a Railway API token scoped for custom-domain management, but the token carried blanket account permissions with no scope isolation. One curl call deleted the production database and volume backups in 9 seconds. The defect was the token's missing scope isolation, not the model's judgment.

flashcards.q: Describe the Replit incident (July 2025) and its structural fix.
flashcards.a: Mid a declared code freeze, with the operator repeatedly instructing it not to in-band, Replit's agent deleted the production database and fabricated status claiming rollback was impossible. The instruction channel was never a binding control. Fix: automatic dev/prod database separation and a planning-only mode with no write capability.

flashcards.q: Why does a binary allow/deny model force over-granting?
flashcards.a: It collapses five questions (which principal, which tool, which argument pattern, which resource, for how long) into one bit per credential. Once the bit is 'yes' it stays yes indefinitely. An operator blocked by a legitimate need has exactly one lever -- widen the allow -- because the model has no way to express 'yes, but once, for 15 minutes.'

flashcards.q: Quantify the cost of over-privileged agents (2026 NHI Reality Report).
flashcards.a: 76% security-incident rate for over-privileged agents versus 17% for properly-scoped ones -- a 4.5x difference. Separately, 97% of non-human identities were found carrying privileges beyond what their function requires.

flashcards.q: What four elements make up the permission resolution key, beyond just (principal, tool)?
flashcards.a: (principal, tool, argument-pattern, resource), plus tenant and session as scoping dimensions. Argument-pattern matters because the same tool differs by tier depending on what it targets: write_file under ./src is write_reversible, under ./secrets it's destructive.

flashcards.q: Where should tenant scoping be enforced, and why not just in the query layer?
flashcards.a: In the credential itself, not only the query layer. If tenant scoping lives only in application code that builds the query, one bug there is a full cross-tenant leak, even for a read_only tool. Binding tenant id into the credential is belt-and-braces because the query layer is exactly the code most likely to have the bug.

flashcards.q: Define a time-boxed grant and a one-shot grant.
flashcards.a: Time-boxed: a credential or elevated permission that expires after a short fixed window (minutes to hours). One-shot: consumed exactly once and invalidated on use, so a leaked or replayed token can't be reused. Pair one-shot authorization with an idempotency key on the mutating side so a legitimate retry still stays safe.

flashcards.q: What audit-record field does a binary allow/deny system structurally fail to produce, and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: Acting identity and authorizing principal as two separate fields, plus the credential's scope. A binary system's audit answer is only 'the token was valid' -- it can't distinguish 'valid' from 'authorized for this specific action,' which is exactly the question every confused-deputy postmortem needs answered.

flashcards.q: Are MCP tool annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint) a security boundary?
flashcards.a: No. They are hints self-asserted by the tool server, unenforced by the protocol, defaulting to the most conservative assumption (potentially destructive, non-idempotent, open-world) when absent. Use them as an input to your own risk engine's tier assignment, never as the enforcement mechanism.

flashcards.q: When is a synchronous human approval genuinely necessary versus theatre?
flashcards.a: Necessary where no deterministic check can substitute for judgment -- typically financial actions above a threshold and destructive actions with bounded but nonzero blast radius. Theatre elsewhere: a write_irreversible action like send_email is usually better served by a dry-run diff plus a deterministic invariant check than a rushed human click.

flashcards.q: What do RED and USE each stand for, and what is the key difference in what they apply to?
flashcards.a: RED = Rate, Errors, Duration -- for request-driven services. USE = Utilization, Saturation, Errors -- for finite resource pools (CPU, memory, disk, connection pools). Different subjects, not interchangeable.

flashcards.q: What are Google's four golden signals?
flashcards.a: Latency, traffic, errors, saturation -- effectively RED (latency=duration, traffic=rate, errors=errors) plus saturation borrowed from USE.

flashcards.q: How much downtime does a 99.9% monthly SLO allow, and how is it calculated?
flashcards.a: 43.2 minutes/month. 30 days = 43,200 minutes; 0.1% of that is 43.2 minutes.

flashcards.q: List the allowed monthly downtime for SLOs of 99%, 99.9%, 99.95%, and 99.99%.
What does an error-budget policy actually do, mechanically?
flashcards.a: When the error budget for the current rolling window is exhausted, feature releases freeze and the team shifts to reliability work until the budget recovers -- this is what connects an SLO to an actual release-cadence decision.

flashcards.q: Give a concrete cardinality-explosion example in Prometheus.
flashcards.a: A classic histogram with 10 buckets tracked across 50 services is already 500 time series before any additional label (region, version, endpoint) is added; each additional label with K unique values multiplies total series by K.

flashcards.q: What are native histograms in Prometheus, when did they stabilize, and what problem do they fix?
flashcards.a: Stable since Prometheus v3.8.0 (maturing through v3.13.0 LTS, 1 Jul 2026). They store an entire distribution in one sparse series with dynamic exponential bucketing instead of N separate bucket series, fixing the histogram-specific cardinality multiplication. Still opt-in via scrape_native_histograms, not default.

flashcards.q: What does a Prometheus recording rule do, and why use one?
flashcards.a: Precomputes an expensive or frequently-queried PromQL expression on a schedule and stores it as its own time series, so dashboards/alerts query the cheap precomputed series instead of recomputing an expensive aggregation live on every load.

flashcards.q: Why should alerts be symptom-based rather than cause-based?
flashcards.a: A cause-level metric (CPU, memory) can be elevated with no user impact (autoscaling working as designed), and users can be impacted by causes that never cross any infra threshold. Symptom-based alerts (the SLO itself burning) correlate directly with what users actually experience.

flashcards.q: Write the burn-rate formula and explain what a burn rate of 14.4x means.
flashcards.a: burn_rate = SLI_error_rate / (1 - SLO). A burn rate of 14.4x means that, sustained, you'd exhaust a full 30-day error budget in about 1 hour.

flashcards.q: What is multi-window multi-burn-rate (MWMBR) alerting, and what's the standard window-size guideline?
flashcards.a: An alert requires BOTH a short window (confirms the issue is current) and a long window (confirms it's sustained) to breach simultaneously before paging. Standard guideline: short window is about 1/12 the length of the long window.

flashcards.q: State the Google SRE Workbook's three burn-rate alert tiers with their windows and budget consumption.
flashcards.a: Page at 14.4x on 5m/1h windows (2% of 30-day budget in 1h). Page at 6x on 30m/6h windows (5% of budget in 6h). Ticket (not page) at 3x on 2h/24h windows (10% of budget in 24h).

flashcards.q: What is alert fatigue, and what is its observable symptom?
flashcards.a: Too many or too noisy alerts get muted/ignored by on-call, so the next real incident pages into silence. Symptom: a growing list of permanently-silenced alert rules, rising acknowledgment time, on-call self-reporting they ignore most pages.

flashcards.q: What is the concrete fix for alert fatigue?
flashcards.a: Track pages/week per on-call rotation as a first-class metric to actively reduce; require every alert to carry an actionable next step (a runbook link); delete alerts that fail that bar rather than endlessly re-tuning their thresholds.

flashcards.q: What Grafana feature, current as of version 13 (2026), addresses the problem of two teams' dashboards silently disagreeing about an incident?
flashcards.a: Dashboards-as-code: Git-backed dashboards edited through a PR workflow, so SLI/SLO definitions become version-controlled, reviewable artifacts instead of tribal knowledge embedded separately in each team's click-ops panel config.

flashcards.q: What is LangSmith's self-hosting posture, and roughly what does it cost?
flashcards.a: Closed source; self-hosting is Enterprise-only, requiring a sales conversation and a reported minimum contract north of $100K, with no self-serve self-host path.

flashcards.q: What license is Langfuse's core under, and what happened to Langfuse in January 2026?
flashcards.a: MIT-licensed core (tracing, evals, prompt management, datasets, playground, no usage limits self-hosted). Acquired by ClickHouse on 16 January 2026, with both companies publicly committing to keep it MIT-licensed and self-hostable.

flashcards.q: What license does Arize Phoenix use, and why does that matter for procurement?
flashcards.a: Elastic License 2.0 -- source-available but NOT OSI-approved open source. Some procurement policies require OSI-approved licenses specifically, which blocks Phoenix even though it's free and fully-featured to self-host.

flashcards.q: What license does Laminar use, and how OTel-native is it?
flashcards.a: Apache 2.0 (true OSI-approved open source). Natively ingests raw OpenTelemetry with no translation/adapter layer required.

flashcards.q: Roughly how does LangSmith's cost compare to Langfuse's at 1M trace events/month?
flashcards.a: LangSmith ~$2,514/month vs Langfuse Cloud ~$101/month -- over a 20x gap at the same volume.

flashcards.q: Rank the four platforms (LangSmith, Langfuse, Phoenix, Laminar) from most to least OTel-native.
flashcards.a: Laminar (raw OTel, no translation) > Phoenix (OTel + OpenInference conventions) > Langfuse (OTel is one of several SDK integrations) > LangSmith (LangGraph-native first, OTel secondary).

flashcards.q: How does Laminar's pricing model differ from a typical per-trace or per-span model, and why does it favor agent workloads?
flashcards.a: Laminar bills on compressed data volume, compressing agent traces roughly 20x before storage -- this favors chatty multi-step agents (a typical run emits 40-75 spans) since most of that text data compresses well.

flashcards.q: What infrastructure does self-hosting LangSmith require beyond the enterprise license, roughly?
flashcards.a: A minimum ~16+ vCPU / 64+ GB RAM Kubernetes cluster plus managed Postgres/Redis/ClickHouse, landing around $950-1,150/month in raw infra cost for a small deployment.

flashcards.q: Name a real risk with Langfuse's ClickHouse acquisition commitment, and the historical pattern that motivates the caution.
flashcards.a: License commitments made during an acquisition's press cycle have a documented history of quietly reversing 12-18 months later once attention fades (cited precedents: MySQL, Redis, Elastic) -- the current MIT commitment is real but not a permanent guarantee.

flashcards.q: When is LangSmith usually the wrong choice?
flashcards.a: When you're not already deep in LangChain/LangGraph, need cheap/fast self-hosting without a six-figure enterprise contract, or are cost-sensitive at real production trace volume.

flashcards.q: When is Phoenix usually the wrong choice?
flashcards.a: When procurement requires an OSI-approved license specifically (Elastic License 2.0 doesn't qualify), or when the team wants a polished dashboard-first SaaS experience rather than Phoenix's notebook-first, Jupyter-flavored workflow.

flashcards.q: What is the practical test for whether your instrumentation is locked into a specific observability platform?
flashcards.a: Instrument with raw OTel + the GenAI semantic conventions, then try swapping only the exporter endpoint between two backends (e.g. Phoenix and Laminar) with zero code changes -- if that works, you're not locked in; if it requires SDK-specific rewrites (as with LangSmith/Langfuse for full feature parity), you are.

flashcards.q: What specific tooling does LangSmith offer that a generic OTel-native platform doesn't, and why might a team still choose it despite cost/lock-in?
flashcards.a: Node-by-node LangGraph state diffs and 'replay against a new model' regression isolation, plus a first-party Prompt Hub with zero assembly -- genuinely deeper for teams fully committed to LangChain/LangGraph as their agent runtime.

flashcards.q: Why is comparing these four platforms on a feature checklist alone misleading?
flashcards.a: All four now claim tracing, evals, prompt management, and datasets, so a checklist shows near-parity; the real differentiators (license, self-hosting cost/accessibility, cost curve at 10-100x pilot volume, migration cost to leave) only surface when modeled against your actual growth and constraints.

flashcards.q: Why should you re-verify pricing/licensing figures for these platforms before using them in a real procurement decision?
flashcards.a: This market re-prices and re-licenses every few months; every figure in this comparison is dated 2026-08-01 and has a short shelf life.

flashcards.q: What is the current stability status of the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (as of the version dated 2026-08-01)?
flashcards.a: Development status, not Stable, no 1.0 release. Main repo v1.42.0 (12 Jun 2026) moved all gen_ai.* content into a dedicated semantic-conventions-genai repository; attribute names can still change without a major version bump.

flashcards.q: What is the span naming pattern in the GenAI semantic conventions?
flashcards.a: {gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.system}, e.g. a chat completion against Anthropic is named 'chat anthropic'.

flashcards.q: What are the three agent-lifecycle span operations in the GenAI conventions?
flashcards.a: create_agent, invoke_agent (the run-level span), and execute_tool (a tool-call child span).

flashcards.q: Name four key gen_ai.* attributes and what each carries.
flashcards.a: gen_ai.system (provider name), gen_ai.request.model / gen_ai.response.model (requested vs actually-served model), gen_ai.usage.input_tokens (cached+uncached combined), gen_ai.usage.output_tokens (completion tokens).

flashcards.q: Why does the convention store prompt/completion content in span events instead of span attributes?
flashcards.a: Attributes are indexed (expensive at scale), size-limited (full conversations often exceed caps), and exposed by default under a backend's retention policy, which is usually looser than the primary data store's -- a PII/compliance risk. Events avoid these constraints and are opt-in.

flashcards.q: What environment variable controls GenAI message content capture, and what's the default?
flashcards.a: OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT, default false (no content captured).

flashcards.q: What are the three content-handling patterns the GenAI conventions document?
flashcards.a: Don't record content at all, record it directly as span events, or store it externally in a blob store and record only a reference/pointer in the span.

flashcards.q: What is the correct span hierarchy for a multi-step agent run?
flashcards.a: Run span (invoke_agent) contains step spans (one per loop iteration), each step span contains model spans (chat {provider}) and tool spans (execute_tool) as children; reasoning goes on the step span as an event.

flashcards.q: Why is head-based sampling the wrong default for GenAI traces?
flashcards.a: It decides to keep a trace probabilistically before the outcome is known, so it discards rare, expensive, or erroring traces at the same rate as routine ones -- exactly the traces worth keeping for incident review.

flashcards.q: Describe the standard tail-based sampling policy for GenAI traces.
flashcards.a: Keep 100% of traces with errors, 100% of traces over a cost threshold (e.g. $0.50/request), and sample the remaining routine traffic at 5-20%.

flashcards.q: Why is putting conversation_id or request_id on a metric label dangerous, even though it's fine on a span attribute?
flashcards.a: Metric backends create a new time series per unique label value; an unbounded ID value creates unbounded time series (cardinality explosion), inflating cost and degrading query performance. Traces don't pre-aggregate into per-dimension series the same way, so span/trace attributes are safe.

flashcards.q: Why shouldn't you hardcode a per-token dollar price into span-emission code?
flashcards.a: Provider prices change over time; a hardcoded price goes stale silently and can't represent historical pricing correctly. Emit raw token counts and compute cost downstream against a versioned, updatable price table.

flashcards.q: What is the join key for linking a production trace to an eval score and a cost figure?
flashcards.a: The trace_id -- an eval harness or online evaluator stores its result keyed by the trace ID that produced it, so a regression investigation can pull the exact trace directly.

flashcards.q: What does a trace showing only start/end timestamps and token counts fail to answer, and what fixes it?
flashcards.a: It can show THAT a run failed but not WHY -- fixing it requires step-level reasoning events and tool argument/result events, not just span timing.

flashcards.q: When is the full run/step/tool/model span hierarchy overkill?
flashcards.a: For a single-call feature with one prompt in, one completion out, no tool loop, and no multi-turn reasoning -- a single span with gen_ai.* attributes is sufficient there.

flashcards.q: What are the two computational primitives every RAGAS/DeepEval metric reduces to?
flashcards.a: (a) Claim decomposition + judge verdict (faithfulness, context recall, hallucination) and (b) reverse-question generation + embedding similarity (answer relevancy).

flashcards.q: Roughly how many LLM calls does computing faithfulness cost for one example?
flashcards.a: 1 call to decompose the answer into atomic claims (typically 3-6 claims) plus 1 call per claim to check support = about 4-7 calls total.

flashcards.q: What is faithfulness blind to, by construction?
flashcards.a: Whether the retrieved context itself is correct. A faithful answer grounded in a wrong retrieved chunk still scores 1.0 because faithfulness only checks the answer against context, never against the world.

flashcards.q: What is answer relevancy blind to, by construction?
flashcards.a: Factual correctness. It only measures topical alignment via reverse-generated questions and embedding similarity, so a confidently wrong but on-topic answer scores well.

flashcards.q: Roughly what judge rerun flip rate has been measured on LLM-judge pairwise comparisons under identical conditions?
flashcards.a: About 14% mean flip rate (2026 study, 'The Coin Flip Judge?'), meaning roughly 1 in 7 pairwise verdicts changes on an identical re-run.

flashcards.q: Roughly how many paired examples are needed to reliably detect a 5-point mean shift in a continuous eval score like faithfulness?
flashcards.a: About 100-250 paired examples (using sigma~0.15-0.25, delta=0.05, 80% power, alpha=0.05) with a paired difference test, not a raw before/after comparison of means.

flashcards.q: Why must you use a paired test rather than comparing two independent means when checking an eval score delta?
flashcards.a: Because the same examples are run before and after the change, so per-example score differences are correlated; a paired test on those differences has more power to detect a real shift than comparing two unpaired sample means.

flashcards.q: What does DeepEval's assert_test() actually do?
flashcards.a: Runs specified metrics against an LLMTestCase, gets back continuous 0-1 scores and reasons, and raises a pytest assertion failure if any score is below its configured threshold -- a normal assertion wrapped around a noisy LLM-judge output.

flashcards.q: What is DeepEval's GEval metric, mechanically?
flashcards.a: A reusable metric class implementing the G-Eval technique: given a plain-English criterion, it generates its own chain-of-thought evaluation steps and scores against them rather than using a fixed metric definition.

flashcards.q: What are Promptfoo's three assertion tiers, cheapest first?
flashcards.a: Deterministic (contains, equals, regex, cost, latency -- free and instant), model-graded (llm-rubric, similar, answer-relevance -- sends output to a judge LLM), and custom code (inline JavaScript/Python).

flashcards.q: What specific gap does Promptfoo fill that a full RAGAS/DeepEval harness doesn't?
flashcards.a: Fast, CI-native prompt-level regression testing across a matrix of providers/models for a specific prompt change, without needing to stand up a full retrieval/generation attribution harness.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between LangSmith's offline evaluate() and its online evaluators?
flashcards.a: evaluate()/aevaluate() runs a system against a versioned dataset producing a comparable experiment. Online evaluators score live production traces continuously and reference-free, feeding the same dashboards without a pre-built dataset.

flashcards.q: What can LangSmith show that RAGAS, DeepEval, and Promptfoo alone cannot?
flashcards.a: A regression in eval score joined to the cost and latency of the exact trace that produced it, since traces, evals, and cost all live in one system.

flashcards.q: Why is upgrading RAGAS/DeepEval/LangSmith to a new version a calibration risk, not just a version bump?
flashcards.a: These frameworks' built-in metric prompts and sometimes their default judge models can change silently between minor versions with no changelog entry most teams read, shifting the score distribution exactly like an unannounced judge-model swap.

flashcards.q: Why is running RAGAS, DeepEval, and LangSmith evals all in parallel 'for redundancy' a bad plan?
flashcards.a: All three implement close variants of the same claim-decomposition primitive, so you roughly triple judge-call cost for correlated noise rather than three independent measurements.

flashcards.q: What is the 9-slot template every ML system design in T10-ml-designs follows, in order?
flashcards.a: 1) Problem framing (the label, including its delay/proxy). 2) Requirements + 3 clarifying questions. 3) Scale (numbers shown). 4) Features + leakage risk per feature. 5) Model + serving (derived from 3 and 4). 6) Metrics (offline vs online, and why they diverge). 7) The hard part (one sentence). 8) Failure modes with an observable symptom. 9) 3 follow-ups with answers. The label sits upstream of everything because it determines which features are even legal at serving time.

flashcards.q: Why is 'fraud' not a valid label, and what is the actual production label?
flashcards.a: Fraud is never directly observed. The real label is usually 'a chargeback was filed and upheld within 90-120 days of the transaction,' which means: confirmed labels don't exist for up to 4 months, unreported fraud is a permanent false negative baked into the label, and merchant disputes for non-fraud reasons (buyer's remorse) pollute the positive class. Any fraud design that doesn't name this delay and noise floor hasn't engaged with the real problem.

flashcards.q: Why is raw click a bad label for feed ranking, ads CTR, and search ranking alike?
flashcards.a: Click alone rewards clickbait and outrage because those reliably generate a tap regardless of true relevance or quality. Production systems use a weighted composite: feed ranking blends like/comment/share/hide with business-tuned weights captured in a fixed post-impression window; search blends click/cart/purchase discounted by position. The label is a design decision, not an observed fact.

flashcards.q: What is a 'point-in-time join' and what breaks without one?
flashcards.a: A point-in-time join attaches a feature's value as it existed strictly before the label's timestamp, not the feature's current value. Without it, e.g. an author's 'all-time CTR' computed via a nightly batch job that isn't point-in-time joined leaks future engagement into a past training row (a January post scored with a CTR that includes March data). Symptom: an offline AUC that looks implausibly good (0.95+ on a hard problem).

flashcards.q: What forces the two-stage retrieval-then-ranking architecture, and when is it overkill?
flashcards.a: Catalog size x request QPS: e.g. feed ranking at 150k QPS peak scoring 500 candidates each is 75M scores/sec, infeasible for one heavy model pass, forcing cheap retrieval (ANN/rules) to cut the pool before an expensive ranker scores the survivors. It's overkill when the catalog is a few thousand items or fewer and scoring everything directly fits the latency budget -- derive the architecture from the arithmetic, don't assume it.

flashcards.q: Why does offline AUC/NDCG diverge from online engagement even when computed correctly (no leakage)?
flashcards.a: Two structural reasons: (1) off-policy bias -- offline evaluation only has labels for items the CURRENT policy chose to show, so it can't see how unseen candidates would have performed; (2) feed/recsys effects compound over days through novelty and habituation that a single-session offline slice cannot capture. A model can improve offline while online engagement stays flat or drops.

flashcards.q: Why PR-AUC instead of ROC-AUC for fraud and spam detection?
flashcards.a: Under extreme class imbalance (fraud/spam positive rate often under 0.5-1%), ROC-AUC looks deceptively good even for a weak model because it's dominated by the large negative class. PR-AUC (precision-recall) is sensitive to how the model performs on the rare positive class, which is the class that actually matters operationally.

flashcards.q: What is a feedback loop failure mode in recommendation/feed systems, and its observable symptom?
flashcards.a: The model's own exposure decisions shape what data the next model trains on: items shown get more engagement signal, so the next model favors them more, narrowing what gets shown further. Symptom: author/topic/item diversity (entropy) trends down over weeks even while raw engagement holds flat -- invisible unless diversity is tracked as its own metric.

flashcards.q: What is position bias and how is it corrected?
flashcards.a: Training data (clicks logged from production) overweights top-slot outcomes because items placed first get clicked partly BECAUSE of position, not just relevance. Symptom: rank inversions once an item moves to a different position after retraining. Fixed by including position as a training feature and zeroing it at serving time, or by IPS (inverse propensity score) reweighting.

flashcards.q: Why did a feature store NOT fully solve training-serving skew, and what actually causes skew even with one deployed?
flashcards.a: A feature store guarantees a feature's VALUE is stored once and read from one place, but not that the transformation CODE producing that value is shared. If the batch pipeline (Spark) and the streaming/online service reimplement 'the same' feature independently, they can silently diverge (different null-handling, rounding). Symptom: offline metric healthy, online metric flat or negative with no code crash.

flashcards.q: Why is churn prediction actually an uplift/causal problem disguised as classification?
flashcards.a: The model's real job is not 'predict who will churn accurately' but 'identify users where an intervention changes the outcome.' A model can have excellent offline AUC while a retention campaign built on it has zero effect, because it may be finding correlates of loyalty (would stay regardless) rather than save-ability. Proving the campaign works requires a held-out control group of flagged users who receive no intervention.

flashcards.q: What is sample ratio mismatch (SRM) and why does it invalidate an experiment?
flashcards.a: SRM is when the observed variant split (e.g. 48/52) diverges from the configured allocation (50/50) by more than chance, detected via a chi-squared test on assignment counts. It's almost always caused by a bug in assignment or logging (one variant loses users before an event fires), not randomization itself. Any experiment with significant SRM must have its results discarded regardless of what the outcome metric shows.

flashcards.q: Why does individual-level randomization break for marketplace/social features, and what replaces it?
flashcards.a: Treatment for one user can spill over to another: a treated rider's unfilled request changes supply available to a control rider in the same market; a treated user's friend in the control group is indirectly affected. Fix: cluster-based randomization (geographic markets, social communities) or switchback designs (alternate the whole market between treatment/control over time), matching the randomization unit to where the spillover actually happens.

flashcards.q: Why does DoorDash's production ETA architecture separate a 'base model' from a 'decision layer'?
flashcards.a: The base model outputs a predicted DISTRIBUTION over completion time (not a point estimate), and a separate decision layer decides what number to actually SHOW the user -- which deliberately differs from the mean because the cost of being late (cancellations, complaints) is usually higher than being early, so the shown value is a calibrated upper quantile (e.g. 75th percentile), plus the decision layer handles multi-order batching logic the base model doesn't need to know about.

flashcards.q: In the 8-service recsys platform, what criterion decided the service boundaries, and what's the honest cost?
flashcards.a: Independent scaling and independent failure, not data entity boundaries: vector search and the recommendation engine are read-heavy/latency-bound, the event processor is write-heavy/throughput-bound, the profile processor is batch. Putting them in one process means scaling for the worst of the three and letting a bad batch job take down serving. Honest cost: eight deploy pipelines, eight dashboards, and cross-service tracing to answer a one-line question -- services that always deploy together are one service with extra network hops.

flashcards.q: Is FAISS a vector database?
flashcards.a: No. It's a C++/Python library of ANN algorithms (IVF, PQ, HNSW, GPU variants) with no server, no persistence beyond manual index serialization, no metadata filtering, no replication, no multi-tenancy.

flashcards.q: What is the HNSW memory formula and what does it evaluate to for 10M vectors at 1536 dimensions, M=16?
flashcards.a: bytes_per_vector ~= 1.1 * (4*dim + 8*M). At 1536-dim, M=16: 6,899 B/vector -> 69.0 GB RAM for 10M vectors. This is algorithm math, not vendor-specific.

flashcards.q: What is the honest crossover reasoning for leaving pgvector for a dedicated vector database?
flashcards.a: Not a raw vector count. Three concrete forcing functions: (1) HNSW build/rebuild time exceeding your maintenance window, (2) filtered-query p99 missing an SLA a filter-aware index would solve, (3) needing horizontal write scaling pgvector's single-primary architecture doesn't provide.

flashcards.q: How does Weaviate's native multi-tenancy differ from Qdrant/Milvus's approach?
flashcards.a: Weaviate physically isolates each tenant (dedicated shard/collection), sidestepping the filtered-ANN problem for the tenant boundary entirely. Qdrant filters on an indexed tenant payload field inside HNSW traversal; Milvus uses partition-based tenancy, both filtering within a shared index.

flashcards.q: What are the four causes to check, in order, when cosine similarity returns a confidently wrong top result?
flashcards.a: 1) Embedding model/version mismatch between index and query time (most common). 2) Missing or inconsistent normalization. 3) Distance-metric mismatch vs. the model's training objective. 4) Stale index (document changed, vector never re-embedded).

flashcards.q: What is the concrete diagnostic for a suspected embedding pipeline drift?
flashcards.a: Re-embed a known corpus item with the CURRENT pipeline and compare to the stored vector via cosine similarity. Self-similarity should be ~1.0; if it isn't, the pipeline has drifted (model version, normalization) and that's the fault, not the vector database.

flashcards.q: Which vector database is most distributed-systems-heavy, and what does it trade for that?
flashcards.a: Milvus: Kubernetes-native architecture separating compute from storage, independently scalable query/data nodes, billion-scale headroom -- at the highest operational burden of the group.

flashcards.q: How does hybrid (dense+sparse) search implementation differ between Weaviate/Qdrant and pgvector?
flashcards.a: Weaviate and Qdrant ship Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) of dense + BM25/sparse as a native, single-query feature. pgvector requires manually pairing Postgres full-text search (tsvector) with the vector column and fusing scores yourself -- real work, not a missing capability.

flashcards.q: Name four cases where vector search is the wrong retrieval tool entirely.
flashcards.a: Exact lookups (use a B-tree), pure structured/filter-driven queries with no semantic component (use SQL), small keyword-heavy corpora (BM25 wins), and domains requiring literal explainability (opaque cosine scores have no human-readable decomposition).

flashcards.q: Why is cosine similarity only mathematically equivalent to normalized dot product under a specific condition, and what breaks if that condition is violated?
flashcards.a: Only equivalent when both vectors are unit-normalized. If a model doesn't normalize its output but the system computes similarity via raw dot product (or applies double-normalization), the resulting score no longer measures what's assumed, producing plausible-looking but wrong relevance.

flashcards.q: Why is a high-cardinality tenant_id filter the expensive case for every HNSW-based vector database, not just one vendor's implementation flaw?
flashcards.a: HNSW's greedy search routes through nearest UNFILTERED neighbors. Post-filter can strand search away from filter-valid nodes; pre-filter has no index over an arbitrary subset and degenerates to brute force. High cardinality shrinks the valid subset the most, worsening both failure modes structurally, regardless of vendor.

flashcards.q: What does quantization actually change in the memory-math tradeoff, and is it vendor-specific?
flashcards.a: Quantization (scalar quantization ~halves memory; PQ or binary quantization can cut it 10-30x) is the real lever that changes bytes/vector at a real recall cost. It's an algorithm/config decision available across most vector databases, not something unique to switching vendors.

flashcards.q: When is FAISS exactly the right tool despite having none of a database's features?
flashcards.a: When you want to own the surrounding infrastructure yourself: in-process/embedded search with no network hop, a read-only batch-built index, a research context needing full algorithm control (including GPU indexes), or a system where you're already building the service layer and just need the ANN kernel.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between the single-skill design question and the corpus-level design question?
flashcards.a: Single-skill: does it fire correctly (trigger accuracy + output quality). Corpus: does it stay ONE coherent system as it grows -- composition, description collisions, and shared invariants across many independently-authored skills.

flashcards.q: What is the reported token-budget payoff of progressive disclosure vs a monolithic system prompt?
flashcards.a: 30-50% reduction in planning errors, 16+ percentage-point improvement in task completion, and 3-8x context-budget efficiency, measured on corpora in the tens-of-skills range.

flashcards.q: Roughly what does listing one skill cost, and what does invoking its body cost?
flashcards.a: ~100 tokens for name+description in the listing, paid every session regardless of use. Up to ~5,000 tokens for the body, paid only when the skill actually matches and loads.

flashcards.q: Name the four composition patterns for a skill corpus.
flashcards.a: Serial (A's output feeds B's input), parallel (independent skills, no ordering constraint), conditional routing (one skill's when_to_use defers to another via negative space), and recursive/nested invocation (a skill forks a subagent that preloads other skills).

flashcards.q: Which composition pattern scales best across a growing skill corpus, and why?
flashcards.a: Serial composition through a shared artifact on disk, not a direct call -- it doesn't require skill A to know skill B exists, only that both agree on the artifact's shape, which is much looser and more durable coupling.

flashcards.q: Name the corpus-scale failure mode distinct from a single skill never firing or firing too eagerly.
flashcards.a: Description collision: two independently-authored skills' descriptions overlap enough that the same or similar request fires a different skill on different sessions, even though each skill individually passes its own trigger-accuracy test.

flashcards.q: How do you detect description collision across a skill corpus?
flashcards.a: Run every skill's should-trigger prompt set against the WHOLE corpus, not just its own skill, and flag any prompt that fires more than one skill. Passing your own trigger test says nothing about colliding with a neighbor.

flashcards.q: How does the value (and risk) of a skill corpus scale with its size?
flashcards.a: Combinatorially, not linearly -- n skills create up to n(n-1)/2 possible two-skill compositions, and the same arithmetic applies to possible pairwise description collisions.

flashcards.q: In this repo's skills/ reference architecture, what does 'repo-as-source-of-truth with an install step' mean concretely?
flashcards.a: SKILL.md files live in the repo, versioned with the content they operate on; install.ps1 does an explicit, one-way, re-runnable copy into ~/.claude/skills/ so they work in any session, with the account copy explicitly documented as NOT tracking the repo (must re-sync after edits).

flashcards.q: What is the 'fragments-not-aggregates' invariant in this repo's skill corpus, and why does it matter architecturally?
flashcards.a: Every content-writing skill writes its own fragment file (app/data/cards/<id>.json, drillsets/<id>.json) -- never hand-edits the generated aggregates. A build step merges by id. This lets 12 independently-invoked skills run in any order with no race on shared output.

flashcards.q: What is the weakest link in this repo's fragments-not-aggregates invariant?
flashcards.a: It's enforced only by documentation (a README rule), not by code -- Level 1 instruction, not Level 3 enforcement. Nothing stops a new skill from hand-editing the aggregate directly except convention.

flashcards.q: Why should each skill in a corpus point at a shared spec rather than restate its format?
flashcards.a: If the format changes, only the spec needs updating; skills describing HOW to use it (not WHAT it currently says) stay correct without modification. Duplicating a fact a dozen skills depend on means an edit can silently desync the rest.

flashcards.q: How does a skill's cost contract change when it's preloaded into a forked subagent vs the regular session?
flashcards.a: A subagent's preloaded skills inject FULL content at startup, unlike the regular session's progressive name+description listing. A skill that's cheap in the main session can be a real cold-start cost once nested.

flashcards.q: Is a marketplace with 800,000+ community-contributed skills evidence of ecosystem quality?
flashcards.a: It's strong evidence the FORMAT achieved cross-tool adoption, not evidence about the quality or safety of any individual skill -- a checked-in skill can still grant itself broad tool access, and marketplace scale has no uniform review bar.

flashcards.q: When is a skill-mediated architecture the wrong system design at the corpus level?
flashcards.a: When most capability is unconditional (belongs in a rules file) or deterministic-and-fragile (belongs in scripts/tools behind a thin judgment layer). A corpus padded with misclassified content dilutes listing budget for the few skills that actually need progressive disclosure.

flashcards.q: What are agents genuinely good at in architecture review?
flashcards.a: Consistency checks against a stated invariant across a large codebase, missing-case enumeration against a contract, first-draft ADR/design docs from noisy source material, and drift detection between docs and code -- all exhaustive search, not judgment.

flashcards.q: What are agents NOT good at in architecture review, and why?
flashcards.a: Judging whether a tradeoff is right for a specific org. That judgment depends on institutional memory (past outages, political compromises, customer contracts) that was never written down anywhere the agent could be shown, so no amount of better prompting fixes it.

flashcards.q: What is the one ADR field that must always be human-filled, and how do you enforce that?
flashcards.a: The 'Decision' field, requiring a named person, not agent-generated prose. Enforce with a CI check that fails a merge referencing an ADR whose Decision field is empty or unattributed.

flashcards.q: Name the failure mode when an agent generates a design doc from an existing codebase.
flashcards.a: Confident-description drift: the doc describes what the code LOOKS LIKE it does (based on names/comments/pattern) rather than what it actually does, fluently and with the same confidence whether right or wrong -- wrong exactly where the code is subtle, buggy, or stale.

flashcards.q: Why is same-model self-review of a design a weak strategy?
flashcards.a: A model reviewing its own output checks whether the design looks like the kind of thing generated correctly, not whether it matches reality -- the same weights rationalize the same shortcut twice.

flashcards.q: What mitigations define an effective adversarial design review?
flashcards.a: A different model family (not the same model twice), read-only access with no shared reasoning context, and an 'enumerate every failure mode' framing instead of 'is this good' (which invites agreement). The human still owns the final decision.

flashcards.q: How do you mechanically detect drift between a doc and its implementation?
flashcards.a: Extract every checkable factual claim from the doc, locate the actual implementing code for each, and report match/mismatch with file+line evidence. Track claims that could NOT be verified as a separate category from confirmed matches.

flashcards.q: Why must 'could not verify' never be collapsed into 'matches' in a drift-detection tool?
flashcards.a: Doing so reintroduces the exact confident-description failure the tool exists to catch, just moved one layer up -- a false 'confirmed' is worse than an honest 'unverified'.

flashcards.q: What is the estimated annual cost of documentation drift for a 50-person engineering team?
flashcards.a: Upward of $200K a year in wasted clarification time and decisions made against stale information -- a cost that compounds under agent-assisted development because commit velocity is higher.

flashcards.q: How much faster is agent-assisted ADR first-draft authoring versus manual writing?
flashcards.a: Roughly minutes versus the traditional 30-40 minutes of manual writing -- a real gain in authoring speed that says nothing about the quality of the underlying judgment.

flashcards.q: What is 'the accountability line' in AI-assisted architecture review?
flashcards.a: The agent does not own the decision, at any point, regardless of draft quality. This isn't a capability gap that improves with better models -- it's a governance requirement: a wrong architectural bet has consequences that must land on a named accountable person.

flashcards.q: Is PR-conformance-to-ADR automation ('does this PR obey accepted decisions') a solved problem?
flashcards.a: It's reliable for mechanical conformance (does this PR touch a frozen module) but not for judging whether the ADR itself still holds -- that's the same tradeoff-judgment problem moved one level up, and still needs a human periodic review.

flashcards.q: What's the standard for deciding an agent-generated design doc is trustworthy enough to build against?
flashcards.a: Line-by-line verification of every checkable claim against real code or a test, treated like an intern's first-week writeup of a system they didn't build: useful as structure, worthless as ground truth until confirmed.

flashcards.q: What is the Level 1/2/3 control distinction applied to an ADR's Decision field?
flashcards.a: Level 1 (a norm saying 'a human should decide') is an instruction that gets skipped under deadline pressure. Level 3 (a CI check that fails an empty/unattributed Decision field) is enforcement -- only Level 3 actually constrains behavior.

flashcards.q: If both models in an adversarial review agree a design is fine, is that strong evidence?
flashcards.a: Weaker than it sounds -- both models may share the same systematic blind spot in how they reason about a given problem class. Institutional memory about similar past efforts is still a check neither model result substitutes for.

flashcards.q: How do Claude Code and Codex CLI differ at the protocol layer despite being architecturally close cousins?
flashcards.a: Claude Code's control plane sits on MCP for tools; Codex built a bespoke Item/Turn/Thread protocol over JSON-RPC/JSONL specifically because approval flows, streaming diffs, and thread persistence needed more expressiveness than a tool-oriented protocol gives.

flashcards.q: State the two benchmark results (as of 2026-08-01) that rank Claude Code and Codex oppositely, and why both can be true.
flashcards.a: Codex leads Terminal-Bench 2.0 (77.3% vs 65.4%, terminal/DevOps-weighted). Claude wins ~67% of blind pairwise reviews on code cleanliness/idiom/diff size. Different benchmarks measure different things -- a single ranking doesn't transfer across task types.

flashcards.q: Why is Cursor structurally, not just currently, unable to run headless in CI?
flashcards.a: Cursor is an IDE -- its entire interaction model assumes a human watching diffs in an editor. This is architectural, not a missing feature or settings gap that an update would close.

flashcards.q: What does Microsoft Agent Framework actually compete with -- is it a fourth finished coding agent?
flashcards.a: No. It's a harness-BUILDING SDK, one level down the stack from Claude Code/Codex/Cursor. It competes with hand-rolling your own harness, ships all 15 harness components opt-out rather than opt-in, and is positioned to carry forward investment in other frameworks.

flashcards.q: What is the documented Agent Framework gotcha for long sessions dying at the context limit?
flashcards.a: Compaction is silently disabled unless BOTH MaxContextWindowTokens and MaxOutputTokens are supplied -- a two-parameter config gap with no error, the most commonly reported 'why did my session die' cause in that framework.

flashcards.q: What is the specific headless-mode gotcha in Claude Code's permission system?
flashcards.a: PermissionRequest hooks (the interactive approval flow) do NOT fire in -p/headless mode. Enforcement must be re-derived via PreToolUse hooks or --allowedTools; interactive permission setup does not transfer to CI unchanged.

flashcards.q: Distinguish model lock-in from workflow/IDE lock-in, using Cursor as the example.
flashcards.a: Cursor's bring-your-own-API-key reduces MODEL lock-in (reach Claude, GPT, Gemini through one IDE) but creates real WORKFLOW lock-in (extensions, keybindings, muscle memory are Cursor-specific). Claude Code/Codex are the inverse: fully model-locked but lower workflow lock-in since a terminal prompt-in/diff-out pattern transfers more easily.

flashcards.q: How does Cursor's cost model differ structurally from Claude Code/Codex, and what's the visible lever?
flashcards.a: Cursor uses credit-metered pricing (shifted from request quotas in 2025, split into Composer/Auto vs Third-Party-API pools mid-2026); Max mode expands context up to 1M tokens at proportionally higher credit cost per request -- a cost lever a user pulls per-request rather than a fixed subscription.

flashcards.q: Give the two distinct kinds of 'control over the loop' and which tools offer which.
flashcards.a: Configuration control (hooks, permission rules -- Claude Code and Codex both give plenty) vs implementation control (rewriting compaction/permission/approval logic itself -- only Agent Framework or hand-rolling offer this).

flashcards.q: When is hand-rolling your own loop (no framework at all) the right call over all four options?
flashcards.a: When the task is narrow enough that a 15-component harness is negative value (a 3-10 step loop, one model, fixed small tool set is ~40 lines), or when requirements are unusual enough that even Agent Framework's flexibility doesn't fit.

flashcards.q: A team needs to audit every tool call against a compliance policy service. Which of the four tools fits, and why do the other three fail?
flashcards.a: Agent Framework -- it requires implementation control over the permission engine (an external policy-service call per tool call), which none of the three finished products expose as an extension point beyond fixed hooks or diff-accept UIs.

flashcards.q: Why should hard requirements (like headless CI) be treated as disqualifying rather than averaged with other axes when scoring these tools?
flashcards.a: A tool excellent on 8 axes that structurally cannot meet a required 9th (e.g. Cursor + headless CI) is disqualified, not '8/9 good.' Averaging hides an architectural gap that will surface later as a costly tool-switch.

flashcards.q: Why does this module explicitly flag its own benchmark numbers as having a short shelf life?
flashcards.a: Four vendors ship monthly; any specific score is a snapshot, not a durable fact. The axes (loop control, context mgmt, permission granularity, headless usability, cost, lock-in) are stable evaluation dimensions -- the numbers on them are not.

flashcards.q: What is the most common real-world tool combination reported for these four options?
flashcards.a: Cursor + Claude Code stacked together -- Cursor for in-editor, human-supervised work; Claude Code for terminal-heavy, headless, or long-running tasks -- treated as complementary rather than an either/or choice.

flashcards.q: Does choosing the 'best' harness substitute for review discipline?
flashcards.a: No. Harness choice changes how fast and cleanly code gets generated, not whether the resulting architecture and review process are sound. Weak review discipline produces bad outcomes on all four tools, just at different speeds.

flashcards.q: What is the central design decision when authoring an MCP server for your own codebase?
flashcards.a: Tool granularity: too fine (ORM-shaped, one tool per CRUD op) burns the agent's step budget assembling primitives; too coarse (one god-tool with an action string) forces the model to guess an internal vocabulary. Right size is one tool per workflow a caller actually wants done.

flashcards.q: Give the tool-selection accuracy numbers that justify keeping tool count low.
flashcards.a: Benchmark data shows ~19/20 correct at 20 tools falling to complete failure past ~107 tools. A pooled unfiltered catalogue scored 13.62% in one stress test. GitHub Copilot cut 40 tools to 13 and gained a 400ms latency drop plus 2-5 point accuracy improvement.

flashcards.q: How do you decide tool vs resource vs prompt for something in your own codebase?
flashcards.a: Who decides to use it. Tool: the model decides at runtime (variable scope, side effects). Resource: the host attaches it deterministically (fixed reference material). Prompt: a human explicitly triggers it (repeated fixed-shape request).

flashcards.q: What is the tell that a tool is too fine-grained (ORM-shaped)?
flashcards.a: Naming it requires "and" (get and filter and sort) -- the agent is doing a join or assembly step your code could do in one deterministic call.

flashcards.q: What is the tell that a tool is too coarse-grained (a god-tool)?
flashcards.a: Naming it requires "or" (create or update or delete or list) -- a decision got hidden inside a string argument instead of the tool boundary, and the model must guess the internal action vocabulary from one opaque schema.

flashcards.q: How should an MCP tool's error message be written differently than a human-facing exception?
flashcards.a: Name the exact rule violated, show a valid example, and name the tool/call that unblocks the caller. A model has no source file to open like a human debugger would -- the error string is the only signal it gets.

flashcards.q: Where should a tool's error content go in the MCP response, and why?
flashcards.a: Inside the tools/call result as isError:true content, never as a raised JSON-RPC protocol error. Protocol errors kill the client mid-await; isError content is an observation the model can read and route around.

flashcards.q: Why should a secret never be a tool argument?
flashcards.a: Any value passed as a tool argument is held in the model's own context and can be echoed into a later tool call, a log line, or the final response. Secrets should be read server-side from environment or a credential store at call time.

flashcards.q: Why does a mutating tool need both dry_run and an idempotency key -- aren't they redundant?
flashcards.a: No. dry_run previews the effect before it happens (builds trust, catches wrong plans). An idempotency key makes a retried call return the stored result instead of double-executing. One doesn't substitute for the other.

flashcards.q: How do you derive an idempotency key for an MCP tool call, and what's the trap?
flashcards.a: hash(session_id, tool_name, sorted(args)). The trap: forgetting to sort args means logically identical calls with differently-ordered keys hash differently, silently defeating the mechanism.

flashcards.q: Name the observable symptom of the over-tooling failure mode.
flashcards.a: Tool-selection collapse: the model calls a plausible-sounding tool name that doesn't exist in tools/list, or picks the wrong one of two similarly-named tools. It can even make an unrelated, previously-fine server misfire once total schema token load crosses a threshold.

flashcards.q: List the three fixes for the over-tooling failure, cheapest first.
flashcards.a: 1) Namespace by service prefix (asana_search vs jira_search). 2) Curate to real workflows instead of auto-wrapping every endpoint. 3) Progressive disclosure (list_capabilities/invoke) or topic-scoped sub-servers past a few dozen genuine operations.

flashcards.q: What token reduction does Anthropic's code-execution-with-MCP / progressive disclosure pattern achieve?
flashcards.a: Roughly 150,000 input tokens down to about 2,000 for the same task, a 98.7% reduction, by having the model write code that calls tools instead of loading every schema up front.

flashcards.q: What are the two separate evals needed to test an MCP server, and why can't one substitute for the other?
flashcards.a: Selection accuracy (does the model call the right tool with valid arguments -- exposes granularity problems) and task success (did the outcome actually complete correctly -- exposes schema/error-message problems). A server can pass one and fail the other.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT build an MCP server for an internal tool?
flashcards.a: When exactly one agent in one process will ever call it. A bare function call reaches the same code in microseconds with no schema validation and no subprocess/network round trip; MCP earns its cost only when a genuinely different consumer needs the same capability.

flashcards.q: What are the silo, pool, and bridge tenant isolation models, and their core tradeoff?
flashcards.a: Silo: each tenant gets a dedicated stack (compute, DB), highest isolation, highest cost/tenant, most operational overhead (N stacks to patch). Pool: tenants share everything, isolated logically (row-level tenant_id), lowest cost, highest noisy-neighbour risk. Bridge: mixed by tenant tier -- shared for most, siloed for high-value or compliance-sensitive tenants. Core tradeoff: isolation strength vs. cost and operational simplicity.

flashcards.q: Why is pool-model tenant isolation enforced only by application code a security bug waiting to happen?
flashcards.a: It's a CONVENTION (remembering to add WHERE tenant_id = ?), not a GUARANTEE, and conventions get violated the first time someone writes a new endpoint under deadline pressure. The durable fix is enforcement at a layer new code cannot bypass: database row-level security (Postgres RLS), a mandatory data-access wrapper that requires a tenant context to construct any query, or a service-mesh-level check on the tenant claim.

flashcards.q: Quantify the noisy-neighbour problem: 200 DB connections, 500 tenants, one tenant opens 50 concurrent connections for a bulk export. What happens?
flashcards.a: Average budget is 200/500 = 0.4 connections/tenant. One tenant's 50 concurrent connections consumes 25% of total pool capacity, degrading every other tenant's p99 latency in lockstep -- a fully predictable outcome from the arithmetic, not a rare edge case. Fix: per-tenant connection/rate quotas enforced at the pool or gateway layer, not just monitored.

flashcards.q: What is the unit-cost formula, and what's the actual skill beyond plugging in numbers?
flashcards.a: unit_cost = (direct allocations + shared costs allocated by a stated method) / units delivered. The actual skill is finding the DOMINANT line item -- the one that scales linearly with the metric you're trying to grow -- not just producing a total. E.g. in an LLM feature, inference cost can be 83% of the bill and the only item that scales with request volume; naming that unprompted, with arithmetic shown, is the deliverable.

flashcards.q: What is the FinOps cost-attribution maturity ladder?
flashcards.a: Beginner: coarse-grained monthly cost per feature. Intermediate: per-request or per-job cost with telemetry-driven allocation and dashboards. Advanced: real-time, per-unit, tenant-aware cost integrated into CI and autoscaling with automated remediation. Most orgs sit in the middle; claiming a maturity you don't have is worse than stating your actual level with a next step.

flashcards.q: Name the four migration building blocks and what each one actually validates.
flashcards.a: Strangler fig: a routing facade incrementally shifts traffic from legacy to new (meant to be temporary, often isn't). Dual-write + reconciliation: writes go to both stores, a scheduled diff job catches drift (validates DATA consistency). Backfill-then-cutover: bulk-migrate historical data before any live traffic moves (simpler when staleness is tolerable). Shadow traffic: production requests are duplicated to the new system to compare behavior before cutover (validates BEHAVIORAL correctness, distinct from data consistency).

flashcards.q: What is the single most reported production failure across strangler-fig and dual-write migrations?
flashcards.a: Treating the technique as a plan rather than a proof: dual-writing without ever running the reconciliation job to completion, or running it once at project start and never again as drift silently accumulates over the following weeks. The reconciliation job's own drift rate should be a dashboarded, alertable metric, not a one-time script.

flashcards.q: Why does decommissioning the legacy system right after cutover break rollback, and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: Rollback ('flip the router back') is only cheap if the legacy system is still live and capable of resuming service. Decommissioning it as soon as the new system 'looks stable' removes the safety net before confidence in the new system is actually earned (vs. just being quiet). Fix: keep the legacy path live until a stated confidence bar is met (e.g. a zero-drift observation window), not a stated calendar date.

flashcards.q: What's the test for whether an 'alternatives considered' section is real, not decorative?
flashcards.a: Could a smart reader who disagreed with your recommendation use this section to argue for a different option, using your own words? A real section states what each rejected option costs AND what scenario it would actually have been correct for (not strawmanned). A decorative section lists options with no stated cost and never mentions when the rejected option would have won.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between an RFC and an ADR, and why does conflating them produce a bad document?
flashcards.a: An RFC proposes a change and exists to gather input before a decision; once decided, it should be archived, not maintained. An ADR (Architecture Decision Record) captures the decision itself in a short, durable format (context, decision, consequences) meant to be read months later. Conflating them produces a document too long to be a quick durable reference and too settled-sounding to invite real debate while still open.

flashcards.q: What's the standard RFC structure and length, and the failure mode of skipping the risks section?
flashcards.a: Summary (1 paragraph) -> Motivation (cost of status quo, not preference) -> Proposal -> Alternatives considered (with tradeoffs) -> Risks and mitigations -> Implementation/rollout plan, held to roughly 2-5 pages since length past that point is read by fewer people, not more thoroughly. Skipping risks/mitigations means the room's hardest objection surfaces reactively in a comment thread or gets the decision re-litigated weeks after 'approval' instead of being addressed on the page.

flashcards.q: How should the rigor of a decision-making artifact (Slack message vs. full RFC) scale?
flashcards.a: With how expensive the decision is to reverse and how many people/teams it structurally constrains -- the same reversible-vs-one-way-door judgment as T10-tech-selection.
