A cheap, reversible config default doesn't need a 5-page RFC. A data-model or public-API choice other teams will build on for years does, because under-processing a one-way door silently constrains everyone downstream, while over-processing a two-way door just wastes an afternoon.

flashcards.q: State Bayes' rule and what each term means for A/B testing.
flashcards.a: P(theta|D) = P(D|theta)P(theta)/P(D). theta = true conversion rate, P(theta) = prior, P(D|theta) = likelihood, P(theta|D) = posterior, P(D) = normalizing constant (often intractable, why MCMC exists).

flashcards.q: Beta-Binomial conjugate update rule?
flashcards.a: posterior alpha = prior alpha + successes; posterior beta = prior beta + failures. Beta(alpha,beta) prior + Binomial likelihood gives closed-form Beta(alpha+k, beta+n-k) posterior.

flashcards.q: What is partial pooling and why does it beat no-pooling / complete-pooling?
flashcards.a: Hierarchical model: each group's parameter is shrunk toward a shared population estimate by an amount inversely proportional to the group's own sample size. Minimizes total MSE across all groups (Stein's paradox result) -- small groups borrow strength, large groups barely shrink.

flashcards.q: What causes 'funnel' geometry in hierarchical models and how do you fix it?
flashcards.a: Small population-level variance (tau_pop) forces group parameters tightly together, creating a narrowing funnel that breaks HMC's fixed step size. Fix: non-centered parameterization -- sample z~Normal(0,1) and set theta = mu + tau*z instead of sampling theta directly.

flashcards.q: What are the two MCMC convergence diagnostics to check before trusting results?
flashcards.a: R-hat (Gelman-Rubin statistic) < 1.01 across multiple chains, and effective sample size (ESS) > ~400 per parameter. Also check for divergent transitions in HMC/NUTS -- even a few indicate posterior curvature the sampler couldn't integrate through.

flashcards.q: Why does HMC/NUTS outperform plain Metropolis-Hastings?
flashcards.a: HMC uses the log-posterior's gradient to simulate informed trajectories (Hamiltonian dynamics) instead of a random walk, giving low-autocorrelation proposals -- 10-100x fewer iterations needed for the same effective sample size. NUTS automates step size and trajectory length.

flashcards.q: Is Bayesian A/B testing truly immune to the peeking problem?
flashcards.a: Not unconditionally. Immunity requires a pre-registered, fixed decision rule (posterior probability + expected-loss threshold). Staring at a live dashboard and stopping 'whenever it looks good' is still a data-dependent stopping rule and can bias results, just usually less severely than naive frequentist peeking.

flashcards.q: Credible interval vs confidence interval -- the precise difference?
flashcards.a: Credible interval: direct probability statement -- 95% probability the true parameter is in this range, given the model/data. Confidence interval: statement about the procedure -- 95% of intervals built this way (across repeated experiments) would contain the true value; says nothing about this one interval.

flashcards.q: Why shouldn't you ship a launch decision off posterior probability alone?
flashcards.a: A high P(B>A) can coexist with a tiny or highly uncertain effect size. Pair the probability with expected loss (E[max(theta_A-theta_B,0)] etc.) and a pre-agreed threshold tied to the real cost of being wrong, not a live-dashboard gut call.

flashcards.q: When is frequentist testing the honest choice over Bayesian for an experimentation platform?
flashcards.a: When you need one auditable convention (alpha=0.05) applied uniformly across hundreds of simultaneous tests run by teams that won't individually reason about priors, or when anytime-valid frequentist sequential testing already solves the 'I want to peek' problem without requiring a prior.

flashcards.q: What's the practical fix when a colleague's informative prior happens to favor the launch they already wanted?
flashcards.a: Ask for the prior's derivation (pre-specified reference class vs. fit after seeing this campaign's data -- the latter is prior-hacking). Run a sensitivity check by refitting with a flat prior; if the conclusion reverses, the prior is load-bearing and must be surfaced explicitly.

flashcards.q: Why does a plain conversion-probability model make a bad marketing targeting policy?
flashcards.a: It predicts P(Y=1|X), which is high for both 'sure things' (convert regardless) and 'persuadables' (convert because of treatment) -- it has no signal to tell them apart, so targeting off it wastes spend on sure things and can miss persuadables.

flashcards.q: Define CATE and why it can never be observed for a single individual.
flashcards.a: tau(x) = E[Y(1)-Y(0)|X=x]. Any unit is either treated or not, so only one of Y(1)/Y(0) is ever observed for it -- the fundamental problem of causal inference. CATE is estimated by comparing groups, never measured directly per-unit.

flashcards.q: Two-model (T-learner) uplift approach and its main weakness?
flashcards.a: Fit mu_1(x) on treated, mu_0(x) on control independently; tau_hat = mu_1-mu_0. Weakness: independently-fit models can have different bias/variance, so subtracting them amplifies noise instead of canceling it, especially with imbalanced arm sizes.

flashcards.q: What does class-transformation uplift modeling require that the two-model approach doesn't?
flashcards.a: Roughly balanced treatment assignment (P(W=1)~=0.5), since Z = Y*W+(1-Y)*(1-W) only maps cleanly to tau(x) = 2P(Z=1|X)-1 under that balance. Unbalanced assignment needs an explicit correction.

flashcards.q: What do causal forests optimize for that standard random forests don't?
flashcards.a: Splits are chosen to maximize heterogeneity in the estimated TREATMENT EFFECT across leaves (not outcome-prediction variance), using 'honest' splitting (disjoint samples for splits vs. effect estimation) to get asymptotically valid confidence intervals on tau(x).

flashcards.q: Difference-in-differences formula and its key untestable assumption?
flashcards.a: DiD = (Y_treat,post - Y_treat,pre) - (Y_control,post - Y_control,pre). Assumption: parallel trends -- absent treatment, both groups would have moved together. Untestable post-hoc; supported only via pre-treatment trend evidence and placebo tests.

flashcards.q: Propensity score matching's identifying assumption, and why has it lost credibility?
flashcards.a: Unconfoundedness/ignorability -- conditional on measured X, treatment is as good as random (no unmeasured confounders), which is unfalsifiable. King & Nielsen (2019) showed matching on a single scalar propensity score can increase covariate imbalance vs. full/exact matching in some regimes.

flashcards.q: What is the exclusion restriction in instrumental variables, and what breaks it?
flashcards.a: The instrument Z must affect the outcome ONLY through its effect on treatment W, and be independent of confounders. It breaks if Z has any other pathway to affect Y -- e.g. an ad-outage instrument also correlating with a site-wide issue that independently affects purchasing.

flashcards.q: When do you use synthetic control instead of plain difference-in-differences?
flashcards.a: When you have one or very few treated units and no single obviously comparable control -- synthetic control builds a data-driven weighted blend of many donor units matching the treated unit's pre-treatment trajectory, rather than relying on one arbitrary control group.

flashcards.q: How do you evaluate an uplift model when you can't observe both potential outcomes per user?
flashcards.a: Qini curve / uplift AUC on a randomized holdout: rank users by predicted uplift, measure cumulative incremental conversions (treated minus control conversion rate) within top-k ranked slices vs random targeting -- classification AUC doesn't work because there's no per-individual uplift ground truth.

flashcards.q: What is a 'sleeping dog' in uplift modeling and why do only uplift models find them?
flashcards.a: A user for whom treatment actively HURTS the outcome (e.g. a retention email that reminds an inattentive customer to cancel). A plain propensity model has no mechanism to detect negative treatment effects; only a model estimating tau(x) directly can surface this quadrant.

flashcards.q: Why are factual grounding and brand voice conditioning treated as separate mechanisms in a production content pipeline?
flashcards.a: They're orthogonal properties of generated text controlled by different mechanisms -- a model can be perfectly on-brand in tone while stating a fabricated fact. RAG constrained to verified data handles grounding; fine-tuning/few-shot handles voice. Conflating them is a common naive-implementation mistake.

flashcards.q: What happened in the Air Canada chatbot case and what's the architectural lesson?
flashcards.a: The airline's support chatbot invented a bereavement-fare policy that didn't exist; a tribunal held Air Canada contractually bound by it, rejecting the 'separate legal entity' defense. Lesson: claims a customer could rely on (price, policy, availability) must be grounded in retrieved verified data with no open-generation path, not just disclaimed after the fact.

flashcards.q: Few-shot/prompt-based voice conditioning vs. fine-tuning -- tradeoffs?
flashcards.a: Few-shot: cheap, fast to iterate, weak under distribution shift/unusual inputs. Fine-tuning (typically LoRA/QLoRA): more robust and consistent at scale, slower/costlier to update, risks baking in errors present in the curated training corpus.

flashcards.q: What does a production quality gate score, and what's its job?
flashcards.a: A lightweight classifier (not another LLM call) scoring brand-voice adherence, factual-risk flags (price/date/superlative/health/financial claims), compliance flags, and fluency. Its job is TRIAGE -- routing by risk to auto-publish, spot-check, or mandatory human review -- not final judgment.

flashcards.q: How should a quality gate be calibrated, and what's commonly skipped?
flashcards.a: Against real downstream outcomes (precision/recall on published-vs-caught content), not just offline validation accuracy. Skipping this leads to either risky content slipping through or reviewers buried in false-positive flags.

flashcards.q: What is the rubber-stamping failure mode in human-in-the-loop review, and how do you detect it?
flashcards.a: When review volume exceeds capacity or the gate produces mostly false-positive flags, reviewers stop meaningfully scrutinizing content and approve by default -- 'human in the loop' becomes theater. Detect via secondary sampled independent review; a near-zero disagreement rate with high throughput signals rubber-stamping.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't an English-calibrated quality gate transfer to other locales?
flashcards.a: Hallucination rates, fluency, and what counts as on-brand tone vary by language/culture. Lower-resource languages typically show higher error rates due to less training representation, so an English-tuned threshold is usually too permissive elsewhere -- needs per-locale recalibration, not just prompt translation.

flashcards.q: Why is an audit trail (source fact to generated claim) treated as a compliance requirement in 2026?
flashcards.a: Given FTC enforcement priorities targeting deceptive AI marketing claims, EU AI Act content-labeling requirements, and legal precedent (Air Canada) holding companies liable for AI-generated claims, being able to show exactly which verified source grounded a published claim is the difference between a defensible and indefensible position if challenged.

flashcards.q: What content categories should almost never be fully automated with zero human review?
flashcards.a: Anything touching price commitments, availability guarantees, legal/regulatory claims, health/safety statements, or flagship brand messaging -- the cost of a single bad instance vastly outweighs the throughput cost of a human check.

flashcards.q: What FTC 2026 enforcement priorities are relevant to AI-generated marketing content?
flashcards.a: Deceptive AI marketing claims, AI systems overstating their own accuracy/objectivity/neutrality, and AI content not properly disclosed as AI-generated where that distinction affects consumer trust.

flashcards.q: Why is DCO better framed as a bandit problem than a sequence of A/B tests?
flashcards.a: Creative performance isn't stationary -- it fatigues. A fixed-horizon A/B test can't reallocate traffic mid-test as a 'winner' starts declining; a bandit continuously shifts allocation and can pull back from a decaying arm in near-real time.

flashcards.q: Why does full-combination DCO (e.g. 4 headlines x 5 images x 3 CTAs) hit a traffic wall?
flashcards.a: 60 combinations each need roughly the per-arm sample size a single test would -- the same L^k-style cost as full-factorial MVT. Fix: feature-level/component bandits modeling each component's marginal contribution instead of each full combination.

flashcards.q: What assumption do component-level (feature-level) DCO bandits make, and when does it fail?
flashcards.a: They assume components combine roughly additively (limited interaction effects) -- the same bet fractional-factorial designs make. Fails when a specific pairing (e.g. one headline with one image) has a real interaction the additive model can't capture; that pairing should be tested as its own arm.

flashcards.q: Define creative fatigue and its common heuristic thresholds.
flashcards.a: Decline in engagement (CTR, hook rate) as the same audience sees a creative repeatedly. Heuristic flags: CTR decline ~10%+, CPA rise ~15%+, frequency exceeding ~3 impressions/user in prospecting campaigns -- category/context-dependent, not universal constants.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't a plain bandit automatically handle creative fatigue?
flashcards.a: A standard bandit's reward estimate is an un-decayed average/posterior over all history, implicitly assuming stationary reward. It keeps believing a fatiguing creative is as good as its historical average for a while after true performance starts declining, over-allocating traffic to it.

flashcards.q: Name two fixes for fatigue-unaware bandits.
flashcards.a: Exponential decay / sliding window on the reward estimate (weights recent observations more, tracks decline), and explicit per-user frequency capping (hard limit independent of the reward signal, addressing the frequency-driven fatigue mechanism directly).

flashcards.q: Reactive vs proactive fatigue detection -- what's the difference and why does the gap matter?
flashcards.a: Reactive fires once an aggregate metric (CTR/CPA) crosses a threshold, by definition after meaningful decline already happened. Proactive uses early engagement-curve shape to predict decay before the aggregate metric visibly crosses a threshold, catching fatigue earlier and reducing wasted spend.

flashcards.q: What reported real-world magnitudes exist for bandit-based creative allocation vs static rotation?
flashcards.a: Thompson Sampling: ~8% customer acquisition lift at no added cost (retail banking display case study). Bandit-based selection: ~10% CTR lift vs static baseline (online retail case study). Context-specific, not universal guarantees.

flashcards.q: How does frequency capping interact with a bandit's exploration logic, and why isn't reward decay a substitute for it?
flashcards.a: Frequency capping is a hard per-user constraint applied independently of reward-driven allocation, removing an arm from eligibility for that user once hit. Decay handles population-level average fatigue over time but doesn't guarantee any single user avoids excessive repeat exposure -- the two mechanisms are complementary, not substitutes.

flashcards.q: What creative-specific bug commonly causes sample ratio mismatch in creative tests?
flashcards.a: A broken image asset or truncated headline that fails to render on a specific device/browser combination for one variant, silently dropping impressions/clicks from that variant in a way that isn't randomly distributed across the audience.

flashcards.q: Full factorial cell count formula and its traffic implication?
flashcards.a: L^k cells for k factors at L levels each (e.g., 4 factors x 3 levels = 81 cells). Each cell needs roughly a standalone test's per-arm sample size, so total traffic scales with cell count, not linearly with factor count.

flashcards.q: What does fractional factorial design sacrifice to save traffic?
flashcards.a: It runs a chosen subset of cells, confounding (aliasing) specific higher-order interactions with each other or with main effects. It's a bet that those confounded interactions are negligible -- a real design choice, not a free lunch.

flashcards.q: What can MVT (multivariate testing) detect that sequential single-factor A/B tests cannot?
flashcards.a: Interaction effects -- whether one factor's effect depends on another factor's level (e.g., headline lift depends on which image it's paired with). Sequential tests hold other factors fixed and never observe the crossed condition.

flashcards.q: Two-proportion sample size formula, and worked value for p1=5%, 10% relative MDE, 80% power?
What happens to required sample size when you halve the MDE you want to detect?
flashcards.a: It roughly quadruples, because (p2-p1) is squared in the denominator of the sample size formula.

flashcards.q: What is sample ratio mismatch (SRM) and how is it detected?
flashcards.a: Observed traffic split between arms deviates from the intended allocation by more than chance. Detected via chi-squared goodness-of-fit test, commonly triggered at p<0.001. It's the #1 real-world bug that invalidates an experiment until root-caused.

flashcards.q: Name the four pipeline stages where SRM can originate.
flashcards.a: Assignment (bucketing bugs, ID collisions), execution (variant bug breaking tracking, e.g. a JS error), logging (asymmetric join dropping rows by arm), analysis (asymmetric post-hoc filtering).

flashcards.q: CUPED formula and variance reduction expression?
flashcards.a: Y_cuped = Y - theta*(X - E[X]), theta = Cov(X,Y)/Var(X), X measured strictly pre-experiment. Var(Y_cuped) = Var(Y)*(1-rho^2) where rho is the X-Y correlation -- e.g. rho=0.7 gives ~51% variance reduction.

flashcards.q: Blocking vs stratified/post-stratified sampling -- what's the operational difference?
flashcards.a: Blocking randomizes treatment independently within known strata AT assignment time, guaranteeing balance but requiring the randomization service to track the variable live. Post-stratification reweights/adjusts by strata AFTER the fact -- Netflix prefers this + CUPED over at-assignment stratification at scale.

flashcards.q: Why does a session-level randomization unit bias results for a per-user effect?
flashcards.a: The same user can land in both arms across different sessions, diluting the observed treatment effect toward zero because they experience a blend of both conditions rather than one clean assignment.

flashcards.q: Why is multi-touch attribution described as 'mostly wrong' even with sophisticated Shapley-based models?
flashcards.a: MTA only allocates credit across OBSERVED touchpoints and credit is not causation -- a touchpoint can receive credit while contributing zero incremental conversion if the user would have converted regardless. Sophistication in the allocation math doesn't fix either limitation.

flashcards.q: Give the concrete measured example of last-click attribution's bias.
flashcards.a: Last-click undervalues upper-funnel channels like SEO by roughly 2-3x their actual pipeline contribution, while overvaluing bottom-funnel channels like branded paid search by roughly 40-60% relative to actual incremental contribution -- branded search captures users already searching for the brand by name.

flashcards.q: What are adstock and saturation in marketing mix modeling (MMM)?
flashcards.a: Adstock: a channel's effect decays as carryover across subsequent time periods (this week's spend still influences next week's outcome). Saturation: diminishing marginal returns per channel as spend increases, captured via a concave (log/Hill-function) response curve.

flashcards.q: Why has MMM adoption grown substantially (roughly tripling) in recent years?
flashcards.a: MMM needs no individual-level identity -- built entirely from aggregate spend and outcome data -- making it structurally immune to cookie deprecation, iOS ATT opt-outs, and walled-garden restrictions that have degraded MTA's foundational identity-resolution requirement.

flashcards.q: What is a geo holdout and why is it closer to ground truth than MMM or MTA?
flashcards.a: Withhold a marketing treatment from a subset of geographic markets, compare outcomes vs exposed geos via DiD/synthetic control. It's an actual controlled comparison, not an allocation heuristic (MTA) or a regression with estimated specification assumptions (MMM), making it the natural validation layer for both.

flashcards.q: What's the reported benchmark from published geo holdout experiments?
flashcards.a: A dataset of 225 geo/holdout experiments reports a median incremental ROAS (iROAS) of 2.31, with 88.4% reaching statistical significance -- a plausibility benchmark, not a target for any specific channel.

flashcards.q: What practitioner thresholds suggest MTA over MMM for a given measurement question?
flashcards.a: Sales cycle under ~7 days, monthly conversions over ~1,000, identity resolution above ~70%. Outside that regime (long cycles, low volume, degraded identity, offline spend over ~30%), MMM is the better default.

flashcards.q: What is the 2026 industry consensus on MMM vs MTA vs incrementality testing?
flashcards.a: Triangulation, not one method: MMM for strategic channel-level budget allocation, MTA for tactical in-channel optimization within its supported regime, and incrementality testing (geo holdouts) as the causal validation layer both other methods get calibrated against.

flashcards.q: Why shouldn't a geo holdout result from over a year ago still justify current budget decisions?
flashcards.a: Incrementality results are point-in-time -- market conditions, competition, and creative shift, so a stale result risks the same error as never testing, with false confidence attached. Move toward rolling/continuous re-testing rather than treating one legacy result as permanent.

flashcards.q: Why can't MMM fully replace MTA even in a fully post-identity world?
flashcards.a: MMM's aggregate, channel-level granularity structurally can't answer tactical, sub-channel questions (which specific creative, which specific audience segment) that businesses still need answered -- MMM has a granularity ceiling just as MTA has an identity ceiling.

flashcards.q: What is the CRF partition function Z(x) and why does global normalization fix the label bias problem?
flashcards.a: Z(x) = Σ_y' exp(score(x,y')), summing over every possible tag sequence. Because normalization happens once over the whole sequence (not per-transition like an MEMM), no state is penalized just for having fewer outgoing transitions -- this is what fixes MEMM's label bias problem.

flashcards.q: How is Z(x) computed efficiently, and what's the complexity?
flashcards.a: Naive summation is O(T^n) (exponential). The forward algorithm computes it via dynamic programming in O(n*T^2), exploiting that the score decomposes into a sum of terms depending only on adjacent tag pairs.

flashcards.q: What does the Viterbi algorithm do in a CRF, and what's its complexity?
flashcards.a: Finds the single best-scoring legal tag sequence (not the full distribution) via dynamic programming, O(n*T^2). This is where a CRF's learned transition weights prevent illegal sequences like O directly followed by I-PER.

flashcards.q: What are the two halves of BiLSTM-CRF and what does each replace?
flashcards.a: BiLSTM (+ char-CNN/LSTM) is a learned feature extractor replacing hand-engineered features (word shape, gazetteers, suffixes). The CRF layer on top is unchanged from the classical formulation -- same global scoring and Viterbi decoding, just fed learned emissions.

flashcards.q: Why do many transformer NER systems drop the CRF layer, and when should you keep it?
flashcards.a: A strong pretrained encoder rarely produces illegal tag transitions on its own, so many systems use a simple per-token softmax. Keep the CRF layer when downstream logic needs a hard structural guarantee against illegal output (e.g. a booking pipeline that can't tolerate a malformed date span).

flashcards.q: What is the subword-to-word label alignment problem in transformer NER, and how is it handled?
flashcards.a: BPE/WordPiece splits one word into multiple subword tokens, but labels are defined per word. Standard fix: assign the label to the first subword token, mask the rest from the loss (or relabel with I- prefix). Getting this wrong silently corrupts training and shows up as inconsistent multi-subword entity extraction.

flashcards.q: BIO vs BIOES tagging: tag count and tradeoff?
flashcards.a: BIO: 2k+1 tags (Begin/Inside/Outside), compact, universal default. BIOES: 4k+1 tags, adds explicit End/Single tags -- measurably helps boundary detection on longer/adjacent entities, but larger and more confusable label space. Only switch if measured on your own data.

flashcards.q: Why is token-level F1 a misleading NER metric, and what's the correct alternative?
flashcards.a: Real corpora are 80-95%+ 'O' tokens, so a model predicting O for everything scores high token accuracy while extracting zero entities. Entity-level (span-exact-match) F1, computed via seqeval, requires exact start/end/type match with no partial credit.

flashcards.q: How much annotation cost does uncertainty sampling save versus random sampling for NER, per published clinical results?
flashcards.a: Roughly 66% fewer annotated sentences to reach the same target F-measure (clinical NER active learning studies). Uncertainty is measured via margin between top-1/top-2 Viterbi scores (CRF) or aggregated token entropy (softmax models).

flashcards.q: Why can't standard BIO/BIOES tagging represent nested entities (e.g. 'Seattle' inside 'Seattle-Tacoma International Airport')?
flashcards.a: BIO/BIOES assumes flat, non-overlapping spans by construction. Nested entities need schema redesign to avoid nesting, a layered extraction pass, or a nested-NER-specific architecture (span-based/hypergraph models).

flashcards.q: When does fine-tuned transformer NER beat zero-shot LLM extraction in production, and vice versa?
flashcards.a: Fine-tuned NER wins at high document volume (thousands/sec) where per-document cost/latency matters -- its cost per document is a small fraction of an LLM call's. Zero-shot LLM wins for new, rapidly-changing, or low-volume entity schemas where fine-tuning's engineering cost isn't justified.

flashcards.q: What is the TF-IDF formula, log-scaled TF and smoothed IDF (sklearn default)?
flashcards.a: tf(t,d) = 1 + log(count(t,d)). idf(t,D) = log((1+N)/(1+df(t))) + 1. tfidf = tf * idf.

flashcards.q: Why does IDF use a log transform?
flashcards.a: Without it, IDF grows linearly with rarity and a term appearing in 1 of 10,000 docs would dominate a term in 100 of 10,000 by a factor of 100, swamping TF signal; the log compresses that range.

flashcards.q: What does BM25 add over raw TF-IDF, and what do k1 and b control?
flashcards.a: Term-frequency saturation (k1, ~1.2-2.0: diminishing returns for repeated terms, score approaches k1+1 as tf->infinity) and document-length normalization (b, ~0.75). Default similarity in Elasticsearch/OpenSearch/Lucene.

flashcards.q: Stemming vs lemmatization: mechanism and failure mode of each?
flashcards.a: Stemming: rule-based suffix stripping (Porter 1980/Snowball), no dictionary, fast, can produce non-words and over-stem (organization~organ). Lemmatization: dictionary + POS-dependent, correct but 10-50x slower; wrong without POS context (meeting->meet only as a verb).

flashcards.q: How does BPE tokenization work and why did it replace whitespace tokenization for neural models?
flashcards.a: Starts from characters, greedily merges the most frequent adjacent symbol pair until hitting a target vocab size (30k-50k typical for BERT-era). Unlike whitespace tokenization it never produces true OOV -- any string decomposes to known subwords or bytes.

flashcards.q: HMM vs CRF for POS tagging: what's the core difference?
flashcards.a: HMM is generative: P(tag|prev_tag)*P(word|tag), decoded via Viterbi in O(n*T^2), assumes word depends only on its own tag. CRF is discriminative: models P(tags|words) directly with arbitrary overlapping features (shape, affixes, context), no independence assumption -- beats HMM on the same task.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between UAS and LAS in dependency parsing, and which is always >= the other?
flashcards.a: UAS = percent of tokens with the correct head (structural attachment only). LAS = correct head AND correct relation label. LAS <= UAS always, since labeling the relation is strictly harder than attaching the head.

flashcards.q: Transition-based vs graph-based dependency parsing: complexity and production default?
flashcards.a: Transition-based (arc-eager/arc-standard, spaCy's approach): greedy stack/buffer decisions, O(n), production default. Graph-based (MST/Eisner): scores all possible arcs, O(n^2-n^3), better long-range accuracy but slower.

flashcards.q: What's the vocabulary-explosion problem with n-grams and how do production systems bound it?
flashcards.a: Bigrams/trigrams multiply vocabulary combinatorially past unigrams; most occur once. Bound with min_df/max_features cutoffs, or the hashing trick (fixed hash buckets, small collision rate, loses interpretability -- can't recover which term landed in a bucket).

flashcards.q: When should you still choose TF-IDF + linear model over a fine-tuned transformer for text classification?
flashcards.a: As the default first baseline always -- trains in seconds, gives an accuracy floor, fully inspectable via feature weights. Ship it over the transformer unless the accuracy gap sits on a business-critical decision boundary or the task genuinely needs context (negation, long-range dependency) bag-of-words can't capture.

flashcards.q: What's the observable symptom of a stemmer over-stemming in a production search index?
flashcards.a: A spike in zero-click/low-relevance-click search sessions with no code change, traced to a stemmer library upgrade that changed rule aggressiveness and started merging distinct words to the same stem (e.g. organic/organization).

flashcards.q: What determines whether segmentation or 1:1 personalization is the right choice?
flashcards.a: How much (context, action) interaction data actually exists per cell, not engineering sophistication. Segmentation = high bias/low variance (stable, pooled data). 1:1 = low bias/high variance (needs massive per-user data to converge).

flashcards.q: LinUCB's action-selection formula and what each term controls?
flashcards.a: Pick a maximizing x^T theta_a_hat + alpha*sqrt(x^T A_a^-1 x). First term = exploitation (predicted reward). Second term = UCB exploration bonus, large under high uncertainty, shrinks with more data. alpha scales exploration aggressiveness; alpha=0 = pure greedy.

flashcards.q: How does Thompson Sampling balance exploration and exploitation?
flashcards.a: Maintains a posterior over each action's reward, samples one plausible value per action per round, picks the highest sample. Wide posteriors (uncertain) get explored more automatically; no explicit tuning parameter needed -- but the prior is still a real choice.

flashcards.q: Why does epsilon-greedy underperform LinUCB/Thompson Sampling in production?
flashcards.a: It explores every action at the same fixed rate regardless of how well-characterized it already is -- no context-sensitivity, wasting traffic exploring well-understood actions as much as poorly-understood ones.

flashcards.q: What is the cold-start starvation loop in bandits, and name two fixes.
flashcards.a: A new action starts with an uninformative estimate that's rarely competitive with converged actions, so a greedy policy never selects it and it never accumulates data to prove itself. Fixes: mandatory minimum exploration allocation, feature-based priors (initialize from similar item features), hierarchical pooling from category/cluster estimates.

flashcards.q: Define regret in the bandit literature.
flashcards.a: The cumulative gap between the reward actually achieved and what an oracle that always knew the best action would have achieved -- the formal cost of exploring instead of always exploiting the current best guess.

flashcards.q: Why does comparing personalization against an arbitrary baseline overstate its value?
flashcards.a: The honest counterfactual is the BEST SINGLE non-personalized variant (what you'd serve everyone if you picked the single best option), not whatever weak baseline happened to be running. Comparing against a weak baseline credits personalization with gains that actually came from picking a better default.

flashcards.q: How does inverse propensity scoring (IPS) work for off-policy evaluation, and what's its main failure mode?
flashcards.a: Reweights logged rewards by (new policy's action probability / logging policy's action probability). Fails under support mismatch: when the new policy favors actions the logging policy rarely took, dividing by a near-zero logging probability explodes the importance weight, producing an extremely high-variance estimate.

flashcards.q: How do you check whether an IPS off-policy estimate is trustworthy?
flashcards.a: Compute effective sample size, roughly 1/mean(weights^2). If it's far smaller than the raw logged sample size, the estimate is driven by a handful of extreme importance weights and shouldn't be trusted at face value.

flashcards.q: Can off-policy evaluation replace live A/B testing for validating a new personalization policy?
flashcards.a: No -- OPE is a screening tool for filtering obviously bad candidates cheaply, but structurally can't produce reliable estimates for policies meaningfully different from the logging policy (support mismatch), which is exactly the case of interest for a genuinely new policy.

flashcards.q: Derive Naive Bayes' MAP decision rule and state the independence assumption.
flashcards.a: P(c|d) = P(d|c)P(c)/P(d); since P(d) is constant across classes, pick class maximizing P(d|c)P(c). Naive assumption: P(d|c) = Π P(w_i|c) -- every word conditionally independent given class. False for language, but only the RANKING between classes needs to be right, not the individual probabilities.

flashcards.q: What is the Laplace smoothing formula for Naive Bayes and why is it needed?
flashcards.a: P(w|c) = (count(w,c) + α) / (Σcount(w',c) + α*V). Without it, any word absent from a class's training data gets P(w|c)=0, zeroing the entire product-based likelihood for any test document containing that word.

flashcards.q: Multinomial vs Bernoulli Naive Bayes: what does each model and when does Bernoulli win?
flashcards.a: Multinomial models word frequency (counts); standard for most text classification. Bernoulli models only presence/absence, discarding frequency; can outperform Multinomial on short documents where mere presence carries most of the signal and counts are sparse/noisy.

flashcards.q: Logistic regression vs linear SVM for text classification: what do they optimize and what's the calibration difference?
flashcards.a: LogReg minimizes cross-entropy on a sigmoid output, natively producing P(c|d). Linear SVM minimizes hinge loss, maximizing margin, and does NOT natively produce a calibrated probability -- needs Platt scaling as an extra step.

flashcards.q: Why should multi-label classification use independent sigmoids instead of softmax?
flashcards.a: An item can belong to zero, one, or many labels simultaneously. Softmax forces outputs to sum to 1, enforcing mutual exclusivity that doesn't exist and actively fighting the training signal whenever multiple labels are simultaneously true. Use K independent sigmoids with per-label binary cross-entropy instead.

flashcards.q: What is focal loss and how does it differ from class weighting?
flashcards.a: FL(p_t) = -(1-p_t)^γ * log(p_t), γ≈2. Down-weights easy/confidently-correct examples (p_t→1 shrinks the loss toward 0) regardless of class frequency -- reweights by DIFFICULTY. Class weighting reweights by FREQUENCY (weight_c = N/(K*n_c)), a static, different mechanism; often combined with focal loss.

flashcards.q: Why is accuracy a misleading metric under severe class imbalance, and what replaces it?
flashcards.a: A model predicting the majority class for everything can score 95%+ accuracy on a 95/5 split while catching zero minority-class examples. PR-AUC and per-class precision/recall/F1 replace it; ROC-AUC is also misleading since its FPR axis stays deceptively good against a huge negative class.

flashcards.q: What does it mean for a classifier to be calibrated, and are accuracy and calibration the same property?
flashcards.a: Calibration means predicted probability matches empirical correctness frequency -- among 0.9-confidence predictions, roughly 90% should actually be correct. They are independent properties: a highly accurate model can still be badly overconfident (Guo et al. 2017 showed modern neural nets typically are).

flashcards.q: What is temperature scaling and what does it NOT fix?
flashcards.a: Divides pre-softmax logits by a single learned scalar T>1 before softmax, smoothing the output distribution to counteract overconfidence; T is fit by minimizing NLL on a held-out set. It does NOT change accuracy or ranking, and can't fix non-uniform miscalibration (overconfident at high confidence, underconfident at low) since it's a single global parameter -- isotonic regression handles that case instead.

flashcards.q: What does a fine-tuned transformer buy over a linear TF-IDF classifier, mechanically, and at what cost?
flashcards.a: Contextual representation via attention -- captures negation scope, long-range dependency, sarcasm-adjacent context that bag-of-words structurally discards. Cost: single-digit to tens of ms/doc on GPU vs sub-ms to few-ms for linear models on CPU -- a real infrastructure cost at scale, worth paying only when the task has genuine contextual ambiguity and the gap is measured, not assumed.

flashcards.q: What's a cascade architecture for balancing classification cost and accuracy at scale?
flashcards.a: Run the cheap linear model on all traffic, route only low-confidence or specifically-hard-category items to a more expensive fine-tuned transformer for a second pass -- captures most of the accuracy gain at a fraction of the full-transformer infrastructure cost.

flashcards.q: What is LDA's generative story?
flashcards.a: For each topic k, draw word-distribution φ_k ~ Dirichlet(β). For each document d, draw topic-mixture θ_d ~ Dirichlet(α). For each word position: draw topic z ~ Multinomial(θ_d), then word w ~ Multinomial(φ_z).

flashcards.q: What do the α and β Dirichlet priors each control in LDA?
flashcards.a: α controls document-topic sparsity: low α means documents are dominated by a few topics, not a smooth blend. β controls topic-word sparsity: low β means topics concentrate on a distinctive vocabulary rather than the corpus-wide word frequency baseline.

flashcards.q: Why is exact LDA posterior inference intractable, and what does collapsed Gibbs sampling do about it?
flashcards.a: The posterior's normalizing constant sums over every possible topic-assignment configuration across the corpus -- combinatorially intractable. Collapsed Gibbs sampling exploits Dirichlet-multinomial conjugacy to analytically integrate out θ and φ, leaving only the discrete z assignments to sample via a closed-form conditional.

flashcards.q: What is the collapsed Gibbs sampling update rule for LDA, and what does each factor mean?
flashcards.a: P(z=k|rest) ∝ (n_dk^-i + α_k) * (n_kw^-i + β_w) / (n_k^-i + Σβ_v). First factor: how much this document already leans toward topic k. Second factor: how often this word type is assigned to topic k elsewhere in the corpus. Denominator normalizes by topic popularity.

flashcards.q: What is the ELBO in variational inference for LDA, and why does maximizing it make sense?
flashcards.a: The gap between the ELBO and the true log-likelihood equals the KL divergence between the variational approximation q and the true posterior. Since KL divergence is non-negative, the ELBO is a genuine lower bound; maximizing it minimizes that KL divergence without ever computing the intractable true posterior.

flashcards.q: Gibbs sampling vs variational inference for LDA: what does each trade away?
flashcards.a: Gibbs sampling is asymptotically exact but slower per iteration and convergence is harder to diagnose. Variational inference is biased (factorized approximation never exactly equals the true posterior) but faster, and its online/mini-batch variant scales to corpora too large for repeated full passes.

flashcards.q: Why shouldn't you use perplexity alone to choose K in topic modeling?
flashcards.a: Chang et al. (2009) showed perplexity can be negatively correlated with human judgments of topic interpretability -- a model with better held-out likelihood can produce topics humans rate as less coherent. This is why coherence metrics (C_v, UMass) became the standard instead.

flashcards.q: UMass vs C_v coherence: what does each measure and what's the tradeoff?
flashcards.a: UMass: intrinsic, log-conditional co-occurrence probability computed on the training corpus itself -- fast but can overfit to the training corpus's idiosyncrasies. C_v: NPMI + sliding window (often external reference corpus) + cosine similarity -- more expensive but correlates best with human judgment.

flashcards.q: How does NMF factor the document-term matrix, and what does it give up versus LDA?
flashcards.a: X ≈ WH via multiplicative updates minimizing Frobenius/KL loss, both W and H constrained non-negative, no generative/probabilistic story. Gives up: no principled way to infer topic mixtures for new documents under a prior, and W's weights aren't calibrated probabilities unless explicitly renormalized.

flashcards.q: Walk through BERTopic's pipeline.
flashcards.a: Embed documents with a sentence-transformer (semantic representation) → UMAP reduces dimensionality (commonly to 5-10 dims) → HDBSCAN clusters (density-based, can mark documents as noise, min_cluster_size ~10-15) → class-based TF-IDF (c-TF-IDF) extracts representative words per cluster by treating each cluster as one concatenated document.

flashcards.q: Give three concrete reasons a topic model still beats asking an LLM at scale.
flashcards.a: Cost/throughput (one batch fit vs millions of recurring API calls), temporal/cross-document consistency (fixed topic space enables trend tracking; independent LLM calls have no guaranteed consistent categories), and reproducibility/auditability (versioned deterministic model artifacts vs run-to-run LLM output variance).

flashcards.q: What's the standard hybrid pattern combining topic models and LLMs?
flashcards.a: Fit the topic model (LDA/NMF/BERTopic) for cost, consistency, and unsupervised discovery at corpus scale, then make one LLM call per discovered topic (not per document) to turn its top words into a human-readable label -- captures the topic model's scale advantages while using the LLM for what it's actually better at.

flashcards.q: What is the skip-gram negative sampling objective, and why replace the full softmax?
flashcards.a: log σ(v'_wO · v_wI) + Σ_{i=1}^k E[log σ(−v'_wi · v_wI)]. Full softmax needs O(V) dot products per example (infeasible at vocab scale); negative sampling turns it into O(k) binary classification between real and k sampled fake pairs.

flashcards.q: What noise distribution does Word2Vec's negative sampling use, and why?
flashcards.a: P_n(w) ∝ count(w)^0.75 (the 3/4 power). Dampens the dominance of extremely frequent words among negative samples while still oversampling frequent words relative to uniform -- an empirical finding, not derived from first principles.

flashcards.q: CBOW vs skip-gram: mechanism and when each wins?
flashcards.a: CBOW predicts center word from averaged context (faster, one prediction/window, better on frequent words). Skip-gram predicts each context word from center individually (slower, better on rare words and small datasets since it doesn't dilute rare words into an average).

flashcards.q: What did Levy & Goldberg (2014) prove about SGNS, and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: Skip-gram with negative sampling implicitly factorizes a word-context PMI matrix shifted by -log(k): v_wI · v'_wO ≈ PMI(wI,wO) − log(k). It's the theoretical bridge showing Word2Vec (implicit, prediction-based) and GloVe (explicit, count-based) solve structurally related problems.

flashcards.q: What is GloVe's objective function and weighting function f(x)?
flashcards.a: J = Σ f(X_ij)(w_i·w̃_j + b_i + b̃_j − log X_ij)². f(x) = (x/x_max)^α if x<x_max else 1, with x_max=100, α=0.75 -- prevents very frequent co-occurrences dominating the loss while giving zero weight to co-occurrences that never happened.

flashcards.q: How does fastText compute a word vector, and why does that fix OOV words?
flashcards.a: A word's vector is the SUM of its character n-gram vectors (n=3-6) plus a whole-word token. An unseen word decomposes into n-grams likely seen in training, so summing their vectors gives a usable representation -- Word2Vec/GloVe have no vector at all for unseen words.

flashcards.q: Why can a static embedding not represent polysemy, structurally?
flashcards.a: Training assigns exactly one vector per word type, aggregating evidence from every context seen during training into a single point -- there's no mechanism to condition the output on the current sentence, since the vector is computed once offline and looked up, not computed at inference time.

flashcards.q: What broke static embeddings' dominance, and which models did it?
flashcards.a: ELMo (2018, BiLSTM hidden states per token) then BERT (2018, transformer + masked LM) computed a different vector per token occurrence conditioned on the sentence, fixing polysemy structurally and beating static embeddings on nearly every downstream benchmark.

flashcards.q: Name four concrete reasons static embeddings still make sense in production.
flashcards.a: Latency (microsecond lookup vs ms forward pass), cost (precompute once vs pay per request), interpretability (fixed, auditable nearest neighbors), and edge/on-device or high-QPS real-time systems where a transformer forward pass doesn't fit the budget.

flashcards.q: What is item2vec/prod2vec and what's its limitation for true cold start?
flashcards.a: Applying skip-gram with negative sampling to sequences of user-item interactions (browsing/booking) instead of text sentences -- co-occurring items get similar vectors. It doesn't solve true cold start: an item with zero interactions gets no vector, same as Word2Vec's OOV problem for text.

flashcards.q: Why is mixing embedding vectors from two separate training runs in the same similarity index a bug?
flashcards.a: Embedding spaces from separate training runs have arbitrary orientation -- only relative geometry within a single run is meaningful. Mixing runs produces nonsensical nearest neighbors even though each individual run is internally valid.

flashcards.q: What's the core distinction between a model eval and a harness eval?
flashcards.a: Model evals score the LLM's raw capability (task completion, reasoning); harness evals score the scaffolding around it — timeout/budget enforcement, permission scoping, injection resistance, tool-catalog degradation.

flashcards.q: What is AgentDojo and what did it find about base-task completion?
flashcards.a: A tool-use robustness benchmark: 97 tasks, 70 tools, 629 injected-attack variants. Frontier models solve fewer than 66% of base tasks even with zero attacks present — capability and robustness are separate axes that both need headroom.

flashcards.q: Name the three classes of prompt injection attack via tool output.
flashcards.a: Direct (payload in the immediate tool result), indirect (payload 2+ hops away, e.g. a fetched webpage), delayed/multi-turn (payload planted in an earlier turn, triggers later).

flashcards.q: Rank injection mitigations weakest to strongest.
flashcards.a: Structural tagging of untrusted content < capability-based tool scoping < output-side policy validation < dual-LLM privileged/unprivileged split (Willison's pattern).

flashcards.q: At roughly what tool-catalog size does accuracy start degrading, and where does it fall off a cliff?
flashcards.a: Roughly flat under 10-15 tools, measurable degradation from 15-40, cliff beyond 40 (16-23 point drops reported in a 584-tool 2026 study; 7-85% drops across 49-741 tool stress tests).

flashcards.q: What did the RAG-MCP paper show about retrieval-gated tool selection?
flashcards.a: Retrieval-based tool selection (embed tools, retrieve top-k per turn) more than tripled selection accuracy (13.6% to 43.1%) while cutting prompt tokens by over half, versus listing the full catalog.

flashcards.q: Why does a per-call HTTP timeout fail to bound an agent loop?
flashcards.a: It stops one call from hanging, but doesn't stop the orchestrating loop from retrying the tool repeatedly; you need a wall-clock or step-count budget enforced on the loop itself, checked before each step starts.

flashcards.q: Why must budget enforcement hard-kill rather than log-and-continue?
flashcards.a: A logged warning doesn't stop spend; the check must be synchronous, blocking, and raise before the next call is dispatched. Log-only budgets are the most common cause of cost incidents reaching a postmortem.

flashcards.q: Why is a system-prompt permission instruction insufficient, and where must enforcement live instead?
flashcards.a: It's advisory and can be talked around via injection or social engineering. Enforcement must be a policy check in the tool-execution layer against the actual call parameters (path, recipient, amount), independent of the model's stated intent.

flashcards.q: What is AgentHarm and what does it measure?
flashcards.a: 110 base malicious agentic tasks across 11 harm categories (fraud, cybercrime, etc.), used to measure whether a harness's guardrail/refusal layer stops a request even when the model would otherwise comply.

flashcards.q: A red team finds an authority-claim social-engineering bypass ('I'm the CTO, skip checks'). What's the durable fix?
flashcards.a: A structural fix (recipient-domain allowlist or similar enforced in code), not a semantic one (teaching the model to distrust that phrasing) — semantic patches only cover phrasings already seen.

flashcards.q: How should the harness-eval CI suite be tiered?
flashcards.a: A fast (<2min) subset of injection/budget/permission cases blocking on every PR touching tools, permissions, or timeouts; the full AgentDojo/AgentHarm-scale suite run nightly or weekly with dashboard-tracked regressions.

flashcards.q: What reasonable default step and wall-clock caps should an interactive single-agent task have?
flashcards.a: Roughly 15-25 steps and 60-120s wall clock for interactive (user-waiting) agents; minutes to low tens of minutes with checkpointing for background/batch agents.

flashcards.q: Why does over-tooling degrade accuracy independent of which model is used?
flashcards.a: It's an architectural property — attention dilution over a large discrete tool-choice set at the function-calling layer, plus tool-definition text consuming context budget — observed across model families, just at different catalog-size thresholds.

flashcards.q: What was the root cause of Knight Capital's 2012 $440M loss, precisely?
flashcards.a: A deployment script failed silently to update 1 of 8 trading servers but reported success; the unpatched server ran dormant 2003-era code that misinterpreted a repurposed flag bit, triggering runaway trading — 4M unintended orders, ~$7B in unwanted positions, ~$440M lost in 45 minutes.

flashcards.q: What caused the AWS US-EAST-1 outage of October 20, 2025?
flashcards.a: A latent race condition in DynamoDB's internal DNS management system corrupted DNS records for critical endpoints, cascading into failures across dozens of AWS services for 14-15 hours.

flashcards.q: What caused the Cloudflare global outage of November 18, 2025?
flashcards.a: A Bot Management configuration change doubled the size of a 'feature file' used by the traffic-proxy software, exceeding a hard-coded size limit and crashing proxy processes globally and near-simultaneously since config propagated worldwide without staged rollout.

flashcards.q: What's the common structural pattern across the AWS Oct 2025 and Cloudflare Nov 2025 outages?
flashcards.a: Both were control-plane bugs/misconfigurations (DNS record management; a bot-mgmt feature file) that propagated globally rather than being contained by region/scope, because the control plane prioritized fast global consistency over blast-radius containment.

flashcards.q: Describe GitHub's October 2018 incident in CAP-theorem terms.
flashcards.a: A 43-second network partition made the failover orchestrator believe the primary was down (from a single node's local view) and promoted a second primary, choosing availability over consistency. Two primaries both accepted writes; reconciliation took 24+ hours.

flashcards.q: What's the fix for GitHub's split-brain failure mode, precisely?
flashcards.a: Quorum-based failover requiring agreement from multiple independent observers before promoting a new primary, rather than a single node's local 'I can't reach the primary' view — reduces but doesn't eliminate the risk of promoting during a transient partition.

flashcards.q: What did Prime Video's 2023 monolith move actually apply to, and what result did it produce?
flashcards.a: One internal service (Video Quality Analysis monitoring), not the whole platform — moved from Step Functions/Lambda/S3-hop orchestration to a single ECS task with in-memory data passing, cutting infrastructure cost over 90% and increasing scaling capacity. Rest of Prime Video stayed microservices.

flashcards.q: Why is 'Prime Video proves microservices are bad' a misreading of the case study?
flashcards.a: The change was scoped to one service whose workload was a tight, sequentially-dependent processing pipeline — exactly the shape where orchestration/inter-hop overhead dominates. The lesson is matching granularity to workload coordination pattern, not a blanket verdict against microservices.

flashcards.q: What did Segment's 2020 'Goodbye Microservices' consolidation keep, and what did it give up?
flashcards.a: Kept clear internal module boundaries per integration (still modular); gave up full process-level separation (hundreds of per-integration services), since most needed failure isolation was achievable in-process via timeouts/circuit breakers per destination.

flashcards.q: When is full process-level service separation actually worth its operational cost, per the Segment lesson?
flashcards.a: When components genuinely need independent scaling or independent team ownership — not merely fault isolation, which is often achievable in-process at lower operational cost (fewer deploy pipelines, less on-call surface).

flashcards.q: What remediation did both AWS and Cloudflare publicly commit to after their 2025 incidents?
flashcards.a: Staged/canary rollout discipline for control-plane and configuration changes (not just code deploys), with health-check gates before wider propagation, rather than instantaneous global broadcast.

flashcards.q: What single question does each of the four gates answer?
flashcards.a: POC: can this be built at all? Prototype: is this the right thing to build? MVP: will real users adopt this at small scale? Production: will it hold up under real load/failure/cost/ops indefinitely?

flashcards.q: What did RAND's 2025 analysis find about AI project failure, broken down?
flashcards.a: 80.3% of AI projects fail to deliver intended business value: 33.8% abandoned before reaching production, 28.4% complete but underdeliver, 18.1% deliver some value but can't justify cost.

flashcards.q: What did the March 2026 survey of 650 enterprise tech leaders find about AI agent pilots?
flashcards.a: 78% of enterprises have AI agent pilots running, but only 14% have successfully scaled an agent to organization-wide operational use.

flashcards.q: Per multiple 2026 analyses, what's the primary cause of AI pilots failing to reach production — model capability or something else?
flashcards.a: Organizational/operational causes: data readiness gaps, unclear ownership, missing evaluation infrastructure, and change management debt — not model capability.

flashcards.q: What is a 'Wizard of Oz' prototype and what's its biggest planning risk?
flashcards.a: A prototype where a human manually performs the function the system would eventually automate, behind a real-looking interface. Risk: the human can silently handle edge cases/quality the real automated system can't match, so a successful test validates the concept, not the real system's achievable quality.

flashcards.q: What is the AI-specific addition to the classic MVP-to-production gate that traditional CRUD features don't need?
flashcards.a: An automated evaluation harness (golden set with known-good outputs or a graded rubric) gating every model/prompt/retrieval-config change, plus drift monitoring on live traffic — because output quality can silently degrade in ways a binary-correctness test suite wouldn't catch.

flashcards.q: Name five concrete dimensions that structurally change between MVP and production (not just 'more polish').
flashcards.a: Scale (load-tested vs. informal), failure handling (full resilience catalogue vs. errors surface), observability (traces/alerts/on-call vs. basic logs), cost (modeled and owned vs. tracked roughly), rollback (automated/staged vs. manual ad hoc).

flashcards.q: What's the single most expensive mistake in the POC-to-prod pipeline?
flashcards.a: Skipping a gate's QUESTION while reusing its CODE — e.g. taking POC code straight to production because 'it already works,' inheriting all the risk the POC deliberately never tested.

flashcards.q: What makes a valid gate exit criterion versus an invalid one?
flashcards.a: Valid: specific, measured, observed outcome ('6/8 users completed the task unaided'). Invalid: a vague impression or internal approval ('the demo went well').

flashcards.q: Why can an MVP pilot succeed on its cohort but fail at full production rollout?
flashcards.a: Pilot cohorts are often self-selected (early adopters, more tolerant, sometimes internal/friendly users) and don't represent the full population's needs or usage patterns — MVP exit criteria measured on a non-representative cohort can mask a mismatch that only appears at real scale.

flashcards.q: What did MIT-associated research find about the P&L impact of enterprise AI pilots?
flashcards.a: Roughly 95% of enterprise AI pilots deliver zero measurable P&L impact.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between a one-way door and two-way door decision, and who coined the terms in this context?
flashcards.a: Two-way door: cheap to reverse, decide fast at the lowest competent level. One-way door: expensive/impossible to reverse, decide slowly with more input. Popularized by Jeff Bezos's 2015 shareholder letter.

flashcards.q: Name the three checks for whether a decision is actually reversible, beyond API compatibility.
flashcards.a: Data/state lock-in (schemas, fine-tuned artifacts, eval harnesses), organizational lock-in (retraining, new pipelines/on-call shape), and blast radius (how many systems/teams depend on it being stable).

flashcards.q: What is the weighted scorecard formula and where should criteria come from?
flashcards.a: weighted_total = sum(weight * score) per candidate. Criteria must be derived from THIS decision's actual constraints (query pattern, team depth, scale, consistency need) — not a generic reusable checklist every option scores 'fine' on.

flashcards.q: What's the tell that a scorecard's weights were reverse-engineered to justify a pre-made decision?
flashcards.a: The chosen option wins on every single criterion. A real tradeoff produces a mixed picture where the winner loses on 1-2 criteria but wins on the ones weighted most important.

flashcards.q: What single question decides build vs. buy?
flashcards.a: Does this capability touch revenue, retention, margin, or a defensible moat (differentiation)? If yes, lean build; if it's undifferentiated plumbing everyone needs the same version of, lean buy.

flashcards.q: Why is 'build or buy' considered the wrong framing for an entire AI system in 2026?
flashcards.a: Most real systems are a blend across layers (infrastructure, model, orchestration, UX) — the actual question is which layers to own vs. delegate, not a single binary verdict for 'the AI system.'

flashcards.q: Why is an LLM/model vendor swap often more of a one-way door than the API surface suggests?
flashcards.a: Fine-tuning data, prompt engineering tuned to one provider's quirks, and evaluation harnesses built around one provider's output distribution don't transfer cleanly, even though the REST API interface looks interchangeable.

flashcards.q: Who introduced Architecture Decision Records and when, and what problem were they solving?
flashcards.a: Michael Nygard, 2011 blog post — solving 'we don't remember why we did this,' where decisions got re-litigated by people who weren't in the original room because reasoning lived only in someone's head.

flashcards.q: What section of an ADR do most teams skip, and why shouldn't they?
flashcards.a: Alternatives considered (with why each was rejected) — skipping it means the ADR only records the winner, not the reasoning that would let someone evaluate whether the tradeoff still holds later.

flashcards.q: When should a team NOT write an ADR for a technology decision?
flashcards.a: When it's low blast radius and reversible within a single team's effort (a routine dependency bump, an internal linter choice) — writing an ADR for everything drowns the signal of the ones that actually matter.

flashcards.q: What are the three steps to defending a technology choice under adversarial pushback?
flashcards.a: 1) Restate the constraint that drove the decision, not the decision itself. 2) Name concretely what would change your mind. 3) Concede the real tradeoff explicitly rather than defending every dimension as flawless.

flashcards.q: What ADR section prevents the same build-vs-buy debate from being re-litigated from scratch every 6 months?
flashcards.a: The 'what would change this decision' section — stating the concrete trigger/threshold for revisiting, so re-litigation only happens when that trigger actually fires.

flashcards.q: What determines a Docker build layer's cache key?
flashcards.a: Hash of the instruction text plus the upstream layer's cache key, plus (for COPY/ADD) a content hash of the copied files. Any upstream change cascades and invalidates everything downstream.

flashcards.q: Why put dependency-manifest COPY + install before COPY of the full source tree?
flashcards.a: So a source-only change doesn't invalidate and rerun the (slow) dependency install layer — cache keys chain from upstream, so ordering least-to-most-volatile maximizes reuse.

flashcards.q: What does BuildKit's --mount=type=cache do, and does its content end up in the final image?
flashcards.a: Mounts a persistent directory (e.g. pip/npm/go-mod cache) into a RUN step across builds on the same builder. Never becomes part of any image layer — it's excluded from the layer diff entirely.

flashcards.q: Why is ARG/ENV wrong for passing secrets into a Docker build?
flashcards.a: The value gets written into that layer permanently; even deleting it in a later layer only masks it in the merged view (via an overlay2 whiteout) — the earlier layer with the secret is still retrievable via docker history or by extracting the layer tarball.

flashcards.q: What's the fix for secrets during Docker build instead of ARG/ENV?
flashcards.a: BuildKit --mount=type=secret,id=<id> — mounts the secret file only for the duration of that RUN step, never written to any layer.

flashcards.q: Roughly how much does distroless cut CVE surface versus a full-distro base, and why?
flashcards.a: ~90% (Google's figure) — because most flagged CVEs live in OS packages (shell, package manager, coreutils) the application never touches, and distroless removes all of them.

flashcards.q: Distroless container is misbehaving in prod and has no shell. How do you debug it?
flashcards.a: kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container> — attaches an ephemeral debug container sharing the target's process namespace, without modifying the running image.

flashcards.q: Alpine vs distroless/glibc-slim for a Python service with native C-extension dependencies — which risk does Alpine carry?
flashcards.a: Alpine uses musl libc; wheels built against glibc (numpy, cryptography, many ML libs) can fail to install or silently fall back to a slow source compile. Use a glibc-based distroless/slim base instead.

flashcards.q: Difference between image scanning and image signing?
flashcards.a: Scanning answers 'what known-vulnerable software is in this image' (content). Signing (cosign/Sigstore) answers 'was this built by the trusted process and untampered since' (provenance/integrity). Neither substitutes for the other.

flashcards.q: Why does registry re-scanning matter even if build-time scanning already passed?
flashcards.a: CVE databases update independently of your build cadence — an image clean on Monday can have a critical finding by Friday with zero code changes, because a new CVE was published against an already-baked-in package version.

flashcards.q: When did BuildKit become Docker's default builder, and what changed mechanically?
flashcards.a: Docker 23.0, May 2023. Changed from a strictly sequential instruction-by-instruction builder to a DAG scheduler that runs independent stages in parallel and supports --mount=type=cache/secret as first-class primitives.

flashcards.q: Multi-arch image built on an arm64 laptop deployed to amd64 nodes without --platform — what happens?
flashcards.a: "exec format error" — the kernel can't execute a binary compiled for a different instruction set. Fix: docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push to produce a multi-arch manifest.

flashcards.q: Why must etcd clusters be sized odd (3 or 5), and what does a 4-node cluster actually get you?
flashcards.a: Quorum = floor(n/2)+1. 3 nodes need 2 (tolerate 1 failure), 5 need 3 (tolerate 2). A 4-node cluster also needs 3, giving the exact same fault tolerance as 3 nodes for extra replication/storage cost — never size even.

flashcards.q: What single component is the only one allowed to write to etcd, and how does it enforce write safety under concurrent updates?
flashcards.a: The API server. It uses optimistic concurrency via resourceVersion — a stale write (based on an outdated version) is rejected with HTTP 409 Conflict, forcing the client to re-fetch and retry.

flashcards.q: What does 'mvcc: database space exceeded' mean in etcd, and what's the correct two-step fix?
flashcards.a: etcd hit its backend size quota (default 2GB) and entered an alarm state rejecting all writes. Fix: compact old MVCC revisions (logical space) THEN defragment (reclaims disk space at the storage engine level) — compaction alone doesn't shrink the on-disk file.

flashcards.q: What are the scheduler's two sequential phases per pod, and what happens to a node that fails a Filter check?
flashcards.a: Filter (~14 in-tree plugins, e.g. NodeResourcesFit, taints/tolerations, PodTopologySpread) then Score (~9 in-tree plugins, 0-100 weighted sum, e.g. ImageLocality). A node failing ANY Filter check is dropped entirely and never reaches Score.

flashcards.q: What happens when no node passes Filter for a pending pod?
flashcards.a: PostFilter runs preemption: the scheduler looks for lower-priorityClassValue pods on some node whose eviction would free enough room, and if found, evicts them and retries scheduling that node for the pending pod.

flashcards.q: What does a Kubernetes controller's workqueue actually hold — full objects or something else — and why does that matter?
flashcards.a: Object keys (namespace/name), not full objects. This lets a rapid burst of updates to the same object collapse into a single dequeued key, and forces Reconcile to always re-fetch current state rather than trust potentially-stale event payload data.

flashcards.q: Why must a Reconcile function be idempotent?
flashcards.a: The same object key can be dequeued and reconciled multiple times for one logical change — at-least-once delivery, periodic resyncs, and restarts all cause repeat calls with no new information. Non-idempotent side effects (e.g. an external API call with no idempotency key) will double-fire.

flashcards.q: What's a common self-triggering infinite reconcile loop bug, and the fix?
flashcards.a: Calling Status().Update() unconditionally every Reconcile call — a status write is itself an object change that generates a new watch event, re-enqueueing the object and calling Reconcile again forever. Fix: deep-equal check current vs computed status before writing.

flashcards.q: Difference between a 'controller' and an 'operator'?
flashcards.a: Controller is the general term for any reconcile loop (built-in controllers reconcile built-in types like Deployment/ReplicaSet). Operator specifically means a controller paired with a Custom Resource Definition, encoding domain-specific operational knowledge no built-in controller has.

flashcards.q: Why is leader election mandatory for a multi-replica custom controller?
flashcards.a: Without it, every replica's informer and reconcile loop runs independently and concurrently against the same objects, causing duplicate work and conflicting writes as replicas race each other. Leader election (via a Lease object) ensures only one replica actively reconciles at a time.

flashcards.q: What's a finalizer, and why doesn't kubectl delete always remove an object from etcd immediately?
flashcards.a: A string in metadata.finalizers. Deleting an object with finalizers present only sets deletionTimestamp; the object stays visible (terminating) until every finalizer is removed by its owning controller after it finishes cleanup (e.g. deprovisioning an external resource).

flashcards.q: Why must .status be recomputed from observation rather than tracked as remembered controller state?
flashcards.a: The controller process has no durability guarantee and can restart at any time with no memory of prior state; recomputing status from live observation on every Reconcile makes a restart invisible to correctness, since the next reconcile just derives true current state from scratch.

flashcards.q: What is the NodePort default port range, and what does externalTrafficPolicy: Local trade away?
flashcards.a: 30000-32767. Local avoids the extra cross-node hop by only forwarding to same-node pods, but a node with no local pod for that Service simply drops traffic that lands there — trading even load distribution for hop-avoidance and real source IP preservation.

flashcards.q: kube-proxy modes: what's the current default, what replaced it for scale, and what's now deprecated?
flashcards.a: iptables is still the default (O(n) chain walk, slow at scale). IPVS (O(1) hash table) was added to fix that but is deprecated as of Kubernetes 1.35. nftables (stable since 1.33, atomic rule replacement) is the intended long-term replacement but is NOT yet the default, for compatibility reasons.

flashcards.q: What's the default NetworkPolicy posture with zero policy objects, and what changes the moment one policy selects a pod?
flashcards.a: Default is allow-all in both directions. The moment any NetworkPolicy selects a pod for a given direction (ingress or egress), that direction flips to default-deny for that pod except what's explicitly allowed — but only that direction, not both.

flashcards.q: Most common real NetworkPolicy mistake?
flashcards.a: Writing an ingress-only policy and assuming egress is now also restricted — it isn't. Egress stays fully open until a separate policy explicitly selects that pod for the egress direction too.

flashcards.q: Does the Kubernetes API server enforce NetworkPolicy objects?
flashcards.a: No. NetworkPolicy objects are just stored, schema-validated data unless the cluster's CNI implements a policy controller. Plain Flannel enforces nothing by default — policies can look correctly applied via kubectl while having zero actual effect on traffic.

flashcards.q: What is ndots:5 and why does it slow down external API calls from pods?
flashcards.a: Default resolv.conf setting: any hostname with fewer than 5 dots gets every in-cluster search suffix tried in order before an absolute lookup. A call like api.stripe.com (2 dots) triggers up to 4 failed internal lookups before the correct 5th (bare) lookup succeeds — up to ~5x latency on cold external DNS lookups.

flashcards.q: Two fixes for the ndots DNS latency problem?
flashcards.a: Trailing-dot known-external hostnames in code (fully-qualifies them, skips the search list), or tune ndots down via pod.spec.dnsConfig for latency-sensitive workloads; NodeLocal DNSCache also helps by absorbing repeat lookups per node.

flashcards.q: Why is ingress-nginx's retirement significant, and is the Ingress API itself dying?
flashcards.a: No — SIG-Network says the core Ingress API will be maintained indefinitely. What's retiring is the specific ingress-nginx controller implementation: best-effort maintenance only through March 2026, then read-only archival with no further fixes.

flashcards.q: What's the core structural fix Gateway API provides over Ingress?
flashcards.a: Role-oriented separation: GatewayClass/Gateway are infra-team-owned, HTTPRoute is app-team-owned, with native traffic splitting and header-based routing as first-class fields — versus Ingress's thin spec (host/path/TLS only) that pushes everything else into non-portable, controller-specific annotations.

flashcards.q: Why did EndpointSlices replace the single Endpoints object?
flashcards.a: A Service with thousands of pods meant any single pod IP change required rewriting/re-propagating one giant Endpoints object. EndpointSlices shard endpoints (~100 per slice by default) so a single change only updates and propagates the one small slice containing it.

flashcards.q: How does a headless Service's DNS answer differ from a normal ClusterIP Service's?
flashcards.a: ClusterIP returns one A record for the virtual IP (backing pod opaque to client). Headless (clusterIP: None) returns individual pod IPs directly plus SRV records for IP+port discovery per pod — no load balancing at all, client chooses which address to use.

flashcards.q: Why does Cilium's eBPF dataplane scale differently than iptables, not just 'faster'?
flashcards.a: iptables cost grows roughly linearly (O(n)) with rule count via sequential chain walks. eBPF compiles policies into in-kernel maps with near-constant/logarithmic lookup cost — a different growth curve, so the gap becomes dramatic specifically at high Service/policy counts (often cited around 1,000+) rather than being a fixed multiplier at every scale.

flashcards.q: Can you change a Deployment's spec.selector.matchLabels after creation?
flashcards.a: No — it's immutable. kubectl apply rejects the change. You must delete/recreate the Deployment (losing rollout history) or get the selector right from the start.

flashcards.q: Deployment RollingUpdate defaults for maxSurge and maxUnavailable?
flashcards.a: Both default to 25%. A 3-replica Deployment can transiently run up to 4 pods (surge) or as few as 2 Ready (unavailable) during rollout.

flashcards.q: Why is a headless Service (clusterIP: None) required for StatefulSet?
flashcards.a: It gives each pod a stable, individually resolvable DNS name (<pod>.<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local) instead of just load-balancing to any pod — required for clients that need to address a specific ordinal (e.g. the primary at ordinal 0).

flashcards.q: Does scaling a StatefulSet down delete the PVCs of removed pods?
flashcards.a: No, by default — persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy.whenScaled defaults to Retain (as does whenDeleted). This is a deliberate data-safety default, not a bug; set whenScaled: Delete explicitly if that's actually wanted.

flashcards.q: What restartPolicy values are valid for a Job, and what happens if you set Always?
flashcards.a: Only OnFailure or Never. Always is rejected by API validation, because Always is incompatible with a Job ever reaching a terminal 'completed' state.

flashcards.q: What does CronJob's concurrencyPolicy default to, and why does that matter?
flashcards.a: Allow — overlapping runs are permitted if a job takes longer than the schedule interval. For anything touching shared state this causes duplicate writes/races; Forbid or Replace is usually what's actually wanted.

flashcards.q: What happens if a CronJob controller detects 100+ missed schedule times since it last checked (e.g. after a long outage)?
flashcards.a: It stops scheduling further runs for that CronJob entirely rather than firing 100+ overlapping catch-up Jobs at once. Not configurable; requires manual intervention.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't a DaemonSet have a `replicas` field?
flashcards.a: The pod count is implicitly determined by the cluster's node set — one pod per node matching the pod's node selector/affinity and tolerating its taints, not a number you set.

flashcards.q: DaemonSet pods aren't running on GPU/control-plane nodes — most common cause?
flashcards.a: Missing toleration for the taint on those nodes. DaemonSet doesn't bypass taints; it schedules on every node that would accept the pod, same as any workload.

flashcards.q: podManagementPolicy OrderedReady vs Parallel on StatefulSet — difference and when to use Parallel?
flashcards.a: OrderedReady (default) starts pods sequentially, each waiting for the previous to be Ready. Parallel starts/stops all pods simultaneously. Use Parallel when replicas have no real startup ordering dependency (e.g. many Cassandra deployments) to cut sequential startup latency.

flashcards.q: What's a native sidecar container (1.29+) and how does it differ from a plain initContainer?
flashcards.a: An initContainers entry with restartPolicy: Always — starts before app containers like a normal init container, but keeps running alongside them and is guaranteed to terminate AFTER app containers on shutdown, unlike a plain initContainer which just runs once and exits.

flashcards.q: terminationGracePeriodSeconds default, and the shutdown sequence it governs?
flashcards.a: 30 seconds default. Sequence: SIGTERM sent to containers, preStop hook runs concurrently, wait up to the grace period, then SIGKILL anything still alive.

flashcards.q: What's wrong with volumeBindingMode: Immediate for zonal block storage, and what's the default value of this field?
flashcards.a: Immediate IS the default. It binds/provisions the volume before the pod is scheduled, so the provisioner can pick a zone the scheduler later can't place the pod into, causing a permanently unschedulable pod. Use WaitForFirstConsumer for zonal storage.

flashcards.q: reclaimPolicy Delete vs Retain — default, and when to choose Retain?
