flashcards.a: No eviction can ever succeed without violating the budget — kubectl drain or automated node upgrades hang indefinitely, since dropping even one replica violates minAvailable.

flashcards.q: RollingUpdate default maxSurge and maxUnavailable if unset?
flashcards.a: Both default to 25% if unset. maxUnavailable:0 guarantees full capacity but relies entirely on maxSurge, temporarily running above steady-state resource consumption.

flashcards.q: Does Deployment's built-in RollingUpdate do traffic-percentage canary rollouts?
flashcards.a: No. It only replaces pods based on replica count, no traffic weighting or metric-gated progression. Genuine canary/progressive delivery needs Argo Rollouts or Flagger layered on top.

flashcards.q: What changes once a ResourceQuota covering compute resources exists in a namespace?
flashcards.a: Every pod created in that namespace must explicitly specify requests/limits for the covered resources, or pod creation is rejected outright by the API server.

flashcards.q: Why do you need both ResourceQuota and LimitRange, not just one?
flashcards.a: ResourceQuota caps aggregate namespace consumption but doesn't stop one oversized pod spec. LimitRange sets per-container default/min/max but doesn't cap the aggregate — many small compliant containers can still sum unbounded.

flashcards.q: Roughly what CPU utilization vs requested capacity do unoptimized Kubernetes clusters typically run at, and what tool attributes this cost?
flashcards.a: Commonly cited in the 10-30% range for actual CPU utilization vs requested capacity. Kubecost/OpenCost (OpenCost is the CNCF open spec Kubecost is built on) attribute cost per namespace/label/workload, ~97% accuracy cited for on-demand allocation.

flashcards.q: Does NetworkPolicy solve the noisy-neighbor CPU/resource contention problem between multi-tenant namespaces sharing nodes?
flashcards.a: No — NetworkPolicy only controls which pods can talk to which over the network. It says nothing about CPU/memory/disk I/O contention on a shared node, which requires ResourceQuota/LimitRange or dedicated node pools instead.

flashcards.q: How does a CPU limit actually get enforced, and what's the default CFS period?
flashcards.a: Via the cgroup's CFS quota/period. Default period is 100ms; quota = limit x period (0.5 CPU limit = 50ms quota per 100ms period). Exceed the quota within one period and the container is throttled (paused) for the rest of that period.

flashcards.q: Why can a container show a healthy 60s average CPU graph while being badly throttled?
flashcards.a: CFS throttling happens per 100ms period, not per minute. Dozens of brief per-period throttle events can occur within a minute that looks fine on a smoothed average. Check container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total / container_cpu_cfs_periods_total instead.

flashcards.q: How does memory limit enforcement differ mechanically from CPU limit enforcement?
flashcards.a: Memory limits are a hard ceiling enforced by the kernel's cgroup OOM killer — exceed it and the container is killed immediately (exit 137), no throttling or grace period. CPU limits throttle (pause) instead of killing.

flashcards.q: What are the three Kubernetes QoS classes and their node-pressure eviction order?
flashcards.a: Guaranteed (requests==limits, both CPU+mem) evicted last; Burstable (requests set, differ from limits) evicted next; BestEffort (neither set) evicted first.

flashcards.q: Why is running HPA and VPA against the same metric an anti-pattern?
flashcards.a: VPA changing a pod's CPU request changes the denominator HPA computes utilization against, which can trigger HPA replica changes, which changes VPA's own usage observations — an oscillating feedback loop. Split responsibility instead (VPA on memory or Off mode, HPA on an independent metric).

flashcards.q: What can KEDA do that plain HPA structurally cannot, and why?
flashcards.a: Scale to zero replicas (minReplicaCount: 0). HPA's ratio-based algorithm needs at least one running replica to compute a metric against; KEDA adds a separate polling mechanism watching the external event source directly while the Deployment sits at zero.

flashcards.q: HPA defaults: sync interval and scaleDown stabilization window?
flashcards.a: Sync interval 15s by default. scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds commonly defaults to 300s to prevent flapping; scaleUp is near-immediate by default.

flashcards.q: What's the single most common reason Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter never scale up despite Pending pods?
flashcards.a: The pods have no resources.requests set. Both tools ignore zero-request pods entirely because they can't determine resource shortage is the actual blocker.

flashcards.q: Cluster Autoscaler vs Karpenter — provisioning time and mechanism?
flashcards.a: Cluster Autoscaler scales pre-defined node groups (ASG/MIG), ~4-8 min to Ready. Karpenter calls cloud provisioning APIs directly for the best-fit instance type, ~45-60s, plus continuous consolidation for bin-packing.

flashcards.q: How are GPUs requested in Kubernetes by default, and are they fractionally shareable?
flashcards.a: Via the device plugin framework as an extended resource (nvidia.com/gpu) expressed only as a limit, in whole non-fractional units. No built-in fractional allocation — sharing requires MIG (hardware partition, isolated) or time-slicing (software, no isolation).

flashcards.q: A GPU pod is Pending despite a GPU node showing free capacity. Most likely cause?
flashcards.a: Missing toleration for the GPU node pool's taint (e.g. nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule) — GPU nodes are near-universally tainted to keep ordinary workloads off them.

flashcards.q: Why does a service mesh sidecar complicate HPA/VPA sizing?
flashcards.a: HPA computes CPU utilization against total pod CPU (app + sidecar), so sidecar overhead shifts scale-out triggers; VPA recommendations for the app container alone can undercount real pod-level needs if sidecar footprint isn't accounted for separately.

flashcards.q: What's the correct diagnostic order: kubectl logs or kubectl describe pod first?
flashcards.a: describe pod first — its Events and Last State tell you which failure bucket you're in (pull failure, crash, scheduling, eviction). logs is only useful once a container has actually run, and is structurally useless for ImagePullBackOff and most Pending cases.

flashcards.q: CrashLoopBackOff exponential backoff schedule and reset condition?
flashcards.a: 10s, 20s, 40s, 80s, 160s, capped at 300s (5 min). Resets after the container stays up 10 minutes straight.

flashcards.q: What does exit code 137 mean, and is it always OOMKilled?
flashcards.a: 137 = 128+9 = killed by SIGKILL. Often OOMKilled but not always (any external SIGKILL produces it) — confirm via 'Reason: OOMKilled' in describe pod's Last State block, not the exit code alone.

flashcards.q: Why does kubectl logs show nothing for an ImagePullBackOff pod?
flashcards.a: No container has ever started — the failure happens entirely during image pull, before the runtime creates any container. Diagnose from kubectl describe pod's Events instead.

flashcards.q: OOMKilled vs Evicted — what's the mechanical difference?
flashcards.a: OOMKilled: kernel's cgroup OOM killer defends that container's own memory cgroup, immediate SIGKILL, exit 137. Evicted: kubelet proactively kills pods to defend the whole NODE under memory/disk/PID pressure, in QoS order (BestEffort first).

flashcards.q: Default kubelet hard eviction thresholds?
flashcards.a: memory.available: 100Mi, nodefs.available: 10%, imagefs.available: 15%, nodefs.inodesFree: 5%, imagefs.inodesFree: 5%. Hard thresholds evict immediately, no grace period.

flashcards.q: A JVM service keeps getting OOMKilled even though heap usage looks fine. Likely cause?
flashcards.a: -Xmx set too close to the container's memory limit, leaving no headroom for off-heap usage (metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers) which still counts against the cgroup limit.

flashcards.q: What's the real mechanism behind the well-known '5 second Kubernetes DNS delay'?
flashcards.a: A kernel-level conntrack race when two UDP DNS queries (typically simultaneous A/AAAA) go out from the same source port near-simultaneously, causing one to be dropped; the resolver waits out its full timeout (~5s). Restarting CoreDNS does not fix it — it's not a CoreDNS bug.

flashcards.q: What does ndots:5 (Kubernetes pod DNS default) actually cause?
flashcards.a: Any queried name with fewer than 5 dots gets the cluster's search domains tried first, so external calls like api.stripe.com pay for up to 4-5 wasted NXDOMAIN queries before the absolute name finally succeeds — a steady latency tax, distinct from the conntrack race.

flashcards.q: What does kubectl debug --target=<container> actually do, and since when is it GA?
flashcards.a: Injects a temporary ephemeral container into a running pod, sharing its network namespace and (with --target) the target container's process namespace, without modifying the pod spec or restarting. GA since Kubernetes 1.25; works against distroless/shell-less images.

flashcards.q: A wave of Evicted pods appears on a node but the evicted pods' own memory usage is unremarkable. What's the likely cause?
flashcards.a: Disk pressure (nodefs/imagefs), often from an unrelated high-volume logger filling node disk — the 'innocent bystander' pattern. Eviction removes pods in QoS order regardless of whether they caused the disk usage.

flashcards.q: A pod is Pending with '0/12 nodes are available: 12 Insufficient memory' and Cluster Autoscaler is healthy. First move?
flashcards.a: Check kube-system events for an autoscaler scale-up event referencing the pod — if present, it's just provisioning latency (4-8 min for classic Cluster Autoscaler); if absent, the request likely exceeds any available node group's instance type and needs resizing, not patience.

flashcards.q: What is the Terraform state file, mechanically?
flashcards.a: A JSON mapping from each resource's configuration address to its provider-reported attributes as of the last refresh/apply — a cache of believed reality, not a live query.

flashcards.q: Why does terraform plan show unexpected changes even with no .tf edits made?
flashcards.a: Drift — plan refreshes tracked resources against real provider APIs before diffing (unless -refresh=false); the refresh caught a real-world change made outside Terraform, and the plan proposes reverting it to match config.

flashcards.q: What does state locking actually protect against, and what does it not?
flashcards.a: Protects against two concurrent applies writing state at the same time and corrupting it (S3 backend: separate DynamoDB lock table). Does NOT detect or prevent drift — a completely separate mechanism (the refresh step).

flashcards.q: A resource is renamed in config with no moved block. What does terraform plan show?
flashcards.a: The old address as destroy and the new address as create, even though it's conceptually the same resource with no real attribute changes — catastrophic for stateful resources.

flashcards.q: What does a moved block do, and how is it better than the old terraform state mv approach?
flashcards.a: Declares two addresses as the same underlying resource; plan then shows no destroy/create for it. Unlike state mv (an imperative CLI command run out-of-band, invisible in code review), moved blocks are declarative and reviewable in the same PR as the config change.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between built-in Terraform workspaces and separate dev/staging/prod environments?
flashcards.a: Built-in workspaces create multiple named state files from the SAME configuration, isolated only by state — good for identical parallel envs. Real environments with genuinely different config typically use separate backend configs per environment (or Terragrunt), not built-in workspaces.

flashcards.q: What's the over-abstraction trap with Terraform modules?
flashcards.a: A module built to cover every consumer's hypothetical use case upfront accumulates enough conditional logic and flags that using it correctly requires reading its internals — worse than extracting a smaller module from proven, real duplication across 2-3 teams.

flashcards.q: terraform test: difference between command=plan and command=apply modes?
flashcards.a: command=plan is fast, plan-only assertions with no real infrastructure created. command=apply genuinely provisions real infrastructure, asserts against real provider-returned attributes, then tears down — real cost and time per run.

flashcards.q: What is OpenTofu and why does it exist?
flashcards.a: A Linux Foundation-hosted, genuinely open-source fork of Terraform created after HashiCorp's 2023 BSL license change, drop-in compatible through roughly the 1.5.x line and diverging since. Real, live, production-used, not a footnote.

flashcards.q: Where does Terraform/HCL genuinely lose to Pulumi/CDK, and where does it genuinely win?
flashcards.a: Loses on complex, loop/conditional-heavy infra logic and native unit testing (Pulumi/CDK use real programming languages). Wins on provider/module ecosystem breadth and a simple, shared declarative vocabulary across a whole team.

flashcards.q: Why should CI apply the exact saved .tfplan artifact rather than re-running plan+apply fresh after merge?
flashcards.a: Re-running plan fresh after merge can compute a different plan than what was reviewed (a TOCTOU gap) if anything changed in the interim. Applying the saved artifact guarantees what's applied is exactly what a human approved.

flashcards.q: Why does terraform plan get slow on a monolithic 400-resource root module even for a one-line change?
flashcards.a: Plan refreshes ALL tracked resources against real provider APIs before diffing, regardless of the change's size. Fix: split state along logical/lifecycle boundaries (networking, data, app tier) into separate root modules/backends.

flashcards.q: Name the first four integer argument registers in System V x86-64 and AAPCS64.
flashcards.a: System V x86-64: rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx (then r8, r9 for args 5-6). AAPCS64: x0, x1, x2, x3 (through x7 for args 5-8).

flashcards.q: Where do floating-point arguments go relative to integer arguments on x86-64/ARM64?
flashcards.a: A separate register file, numbered independently: xmm0-xmm7 on x86-64, v0-v7 on ARM64. A mixed int/float function's registers are not interleaved into one combined sequence.

flashcards.q: Distinguish caller-saved from callee-saved registers on x86-64 System V.
flashcards.a: Caller-saved (rax,rcx,rdx,rsi,rdi,r8-r11): callee may freely clobber, caller must save what it needs across the call. Callee-saved (rbx,rbp,r12-r15): callee must restore to original value before returning.

flashcards.q: Why can an ARM64 leaf function skip stack frame setup entirely, unlike x86-64?
flashcards.a: ARM64's bl instruction stores the return address in a dedicated register (x30/lr), so a leaf function can work entirely in registers and ret directly. x86-64's call always pushes the return address to the stack, so even the leanest function needs ret to pop it back off.

flashcards.q: What does -fomit-frame-pointer (default at -O2+) do, and what production capability does it break?
flashcards.a: Repurposes rbp as a general register instead of a frame pointer, saving one register but breaking naive rbp-chain-walking backtraces/profilers -- fixed with -fno-omit-frame-pointer or DWARF CFI (.eh_frame)-based unwinding.

flashcards.q: A function crashes only at -O2, not -O0. First hypothesis and how to confirm?
flashcards.a: Undefined behavior (signed overflow, uninitialized read, strict-aliasing violation) that -O0's minimal transformation happened to hide but -O2's aggressive optimization exposes. Confirm with -fsanitize=undefined,address, not by blaming the compiler.

flashcards.q: List the four stacked costs that make a naive CPython arithmetic loop ~50-100x slower than C.
flashcards.a: Bytecode dispatch overhead, boxed PyObject allocation per result, reference counting on every object touch, and dynamic __add__ method dispatch -- none of which exist in a compiled C loop.

flashcards.q: Is 'Python is 100x slower than C' true for all Python code?
flashcards.a: No -- it's true for the interpreter loop's per-element overhead in pure-Python numeric loops. Code whose hot path runs inside a C extension (NumPy, most stdlib internals) pays essentially none of that per-element cost.

flashcards.q: How does the Windows x64 calling convention differ materially from System V x86-64?
flashcards.a: Only 4 register arguments (rcx,rdx,r8,r9 vs System V's 6), a caller-allocated 32-byte shadow space even when args fit in registers, and a different caller/callee-saved split -- making Windows and Linux/macOS x86-64 object code ABI-incompatible on identical hardware.

flashcards.q: What does it look like in objdump when a function call was fully inlined and optimized away?
flashcards.a: No call instruction to the target's label -- its logic appears directly inline in the caller's instruction stream, and if inputs are compile-time-constant, the whole computation can collapse to a single mov of a precomputed value.

flashcards.q: Why might a summing loop compile at -O2 to code with no loop at all?
flashcards.a: The optimizer recognizes a closed-form arithmetic series (e.g. n*(n-1)/2) via strength reduction and induction-variable analysis and replaces the loop with a direct formula computation -- only possible when the loop body is provably side-effect-free.

flashcards.q: What's the cost-benefit case for enabling -fno-omit-frame-pointer fleet-wide?
flashcards.a: Cost: small, typically low-single-digit percent throughput regression from dedicating rbp to frame bookkeeping. Benefit: reliable perf-based production profiling/stack unwinding across the fleet -- worth it when continuous production profiling is a core operational capability.

flashcards.q: List the five stages of the classic compiler pipeline and their output artifacts.
flashcards.a: Lexer: source -> tokens. Parser: tokens -> AST. Lowering: AST -> IR (often SSA, explicit basic-block CFG). Optimization: IR -> optimized IR. Codegen: IR -> machine code (via instruction selection + register allocation).

flashcards.q: What is SSA and why do nearly all modern optimizing compilers use it?
flashcards.a: Static Single Assignment: every variable assigned exactly once textually, with phi nodes merging values at control-flow join points. It turns data-flow analysis (constant prop, DCE, CSE) into a local problem answered by looking at one definition site instead of tracing backward through reassignments.

flashcards.q: Does SSA mean a loop variable is only assigned once at runtime?
flashcards.a: No -- SSA is about one textual definition site per name, not runtime assignment count. A loop variable's phi node at the loop header merges the initial and updated values and can correspond to many runtime assignments across iterations.

flashcards.q: Why is inlining considered the most impactful optimization, beyond removing call overhead?
flashcards.a: It exposes the callee's internals to the caller's optimization context, unlocking constant propagation, DCE, and better register allocation to operate across what used to be an opaque function boundary -- a cascading unlock effect beyond the call/ret savings.

flashcards.q: Why does `restrict` matter for vectorization but not correctness when true?
flashcards.a: restrict promises a pointer doesn't alias certain others; without it the compiler must conservatively assume aliasing and can't safely reorder memory accesses across iterations. With a TRUE restrict promise, it can prove reordering safe and vectorize. Lying about it is undefined behavior.

flashcards.q: Give an example of a genuinely non-vectorizable loop vs a vectorizable reduction.
flashcards.a: a[i] = a[i-1] * 2 is non-vectorizable (true loop-carried dependency on the prior result). sum += a[i] IS vectorizable via multiple partial-sum lanes since addition is approximately associative -- but this changes floating-point rounding order.

flashcards.q: What diagnostic flags reveal why a loop failed to vectorize?
flashcards.a: GCC: -fopt-info-vec-missed. Clang: -Rpass-missed=loop-vectorize. Check these before reaching for hand-written SIMD intrinsics.

flashcards.q: What is register spilling and what does it look like in disassembly?
flashcards.a: When more values are simultaneously live than physical registers available, the allocator stores some to a stack slot and reloads on demand. Visible as [rbp-N]-style stack loads/stores in code that would otherwise be pure register-to-register ops.

flashcards.q: What architectural bet makes LLVM easy to retarget to new backends, and what's the practical gotcha?
flashcards.a: A stable SSA-form IR that frontends and backends target independently, described via TableGen machine descriptions -- new backends need only instruction selection + register allocation against that IR. Gotcha: LLVM IR is NOT guaranteed stable across LLVM versions, so frontends/backends must track compatible versions.

flashcards.q: Compare what PGO and a JIT compiler are both trying to achieve, and where their tradeoffs diverge.
flashcards.a: Both use real observed program behavior instead of static heuristics to guide optimization. PGO does this ahead-of-time (needs a representative training run, zero runtime warmup). A JIT does it continuously at runtime (pays warmup cost, adapts live, can deoptimize when assumptions break).

flashcards.q: Why can a vectorized floating-point reduction produce a slightly different result than the scalar version, and is it a bug?
flashcards.a: Floating-point addition isn't associative, so summing via multiple SIMD-lane partial accumulators computes a different order than strict sequential accumulation, producing a different (close) rounded result. Not a bug -- both orderings are valid under IEEE-754, and compilers only do this under relaxed floating-point flags, not strict default compliance.

flashcards.q: What's the cost side of enabling LTO and PGO for a release pipeline?
flashcards.a: LTO can substantially increase link time and peak memory usage for large codebases. PGO requires maintaining a training/profiling step and re-profiling periodically -- a stale profile can guide optimization toward code paths no longer actually hot.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between pipelining and out-of-order execution?
flashcards.a: Pipelining overlaps the stages of successive instructions but executes them in program order. OoO additionally lets independent instructions execute in a different order than written, retiring results in original order via a reorder buffer.

flashcards.q: Why can't forwarding eliminate a load-use hazard?
flashcards.a: Forwarding routes an already-computed value; a load's result doesn't exist until MEM stage completes (L1 hit latency ~4-5 cycles), so an instruction consuming it immediately has nothing to forward yet and must stall or be scheduled around.

flashcards.q: What is a reorder buffer (ROB) and roughly how large is it on modern cores?
flashcards.a: Tracks in-flight instructions in original program order so results retire in order despite OoO execution. Golden Cove ~512 entries, Zen4 ~320 entries -- larger ROB = bigger instruction window to find independent work past a stall.

flashcards.q: What does register renaming eliminate that forwarding cannot?
flashcards.a: WAW and WAR false dependencies caused by reusing the same architectural register name, by mapping architectural registers onto a much larger physical register file. Forwarding handles true (read-after-write) data dependencies instead.

flashcards.q: What's the misprediction penalty on a modern deep pipeline, and why does it scale with pipeline depth?
flashcards.a: ~15-20 cycles typical -- everything speculatively fetched down the wrong path must be squashed and refetched, and a deeper pipeline means more in-flight speculative instructions to discard per misprediction.

flashcards.q: What branch predictor accuracy do modern cores achieve, and what family of predictor is used?
flashcards.a: 95-99%+ on typical code, using TAGE (Tagged Geometric history length) or perceptron-based predictors trained continuously on runtime branch history.

flashcards.q: Give SIMD register widths and their fp32 lane counts for SSE, AVX2, AVX-512.
flashcards.a: SSE: 128-bit = 4x fp32. AVX2: 256-bit = 8x fp32. AVX-512: 512-bit = 16x fp32.

flashcards.q: Mechanically, how does Spectre leak data through speculative execution?
flashcards.a: A mistrained branch predictor causes speculative execution down a wrong path that reads memory using attacker-influenced data; the read's cache-timing footprint (which line got pulled in) persists even after architectural squash, and the attacker measures cache access timing afterward to infer the leaked value.

flashcards.q: Why does a single running accumulator cap IPC near 1 regardless of core width?
flashcards.a: It creates a strict serial dependency chain -- each add must wait for the previous add's result, so only one addition is ever in flight no matter how many ALU ports exist. Fix: multiple independent partial-sum accumulators.

flashcards.q: What's the reported performance cost range of Spectre/Meltdown mitigations, and where is it worst?
flashcards.a: Commonly single digits up to 20-30%+ depending on workload, worst for syscall-heavy or virtualization-heavy code because page-table isolation taxes privilege-transition TLB behavior specifically.

flashcards.q: Name the three classic hazard types and one fix for each.
flashcards.a: Structural (dup resource, e.g. separate I/D caches or multiple ALU ports), data (forwarding for close deps, OoO scheduling for longer-latency ones like loads), control (branch prediction + speculative execution, squash-and-refetch on miss).

flashcards.q: Why does branch-heavy code over sorted data run faster than over unsorted data at identical algorithmic complexity?
flashcards.a: Sorted data makes the branch outcome sequence highly patterned and learnable by the predictor, driving misprediction near zero; unsorted data makes outcomes effectively random, causing repeated full pipeline-flush penalties -- commonly a 2-6x observed slowdown with no cache effects involved.

flashcards.q: What does the GIL actually protect?
flashcards.a: CPython's internal data structures, most importantly the reference count field on every PyObject, from concurrent unsynchronized modification by multiple threads executing bytecode simultaneously.

flashcards.q: Does the GIL protect against all Python-level race conditions like x += 1 on shared state?
flashcards.a: No -- the GIL guarantees individual bytecode instructions are atomic relative to other threads, but a multi-instruction sequence like load-modify-store can still be interrupted between instructions. It protects CPython internals, not application logic.

flashcards.q: Why can't reference counting alone reclaim reference cycles, and what supplements it?
flashcards.a: Two objects referencing each other (directly or transitively) never reach refcount zero through ordinary dereferencing even with no external references. CPython's generational cyclic garbage collector (gc module) periodically scans for and breaks unreachable cycles.

flashcards.q: Explain the 3.11+ specializing adaptive interpreter with an example.
flashcards.a: A generic bytecode instruction (e.g. BINARY_OP) that observes stable operand types at a call site is rewritten in-place to a specialized, faster variant (BINARY_OP_ADD_INT) with an inline guard. If the guard later fails (a different type arrives), it de-specializes back to the generic path.

flashcards.q: Is the specializing adaptive interpreter the same as a JIT compiler?
flashcards.a: No -- it specializes bytecode instructions executed by the interpreter loop itself, with no native machine code generation. CPython only began shipping an experimental true JIT (copy-and-patch, built on this specialization data) starting in 3.13.

flashcards.q: Why does I/O-bound multi-threaded Python get real concurrency but CPU-bound doesn't?
flashcards.a: The GIL is explicitly released around blocking I/O calls, so another thread can run bytecode while one thread blocks. CPU-bound code never blocks, so the GIL stays continuously held, serializing execution with no parallelism.

flashcards.q: How does NumPy achieve real multi-threaded parallelism despite the GIL for CPU-bound work?
flashcards.a: Its C-level hot loops explicitly release the GIL during long-running native computation since they're not touching Python objects/CPython internals during that time, letting other Python threads run concurrently.

flashcards.q: What are the concrete performance and memory costs of the free-threaded build as of Python 3.14?
flashcards.a: Roughly 5-10% single-threaded slowdown (down from ~40% in 3.13's experimental phase) and roughly 15-20% higher memory usage, from biased reference counting overhead and per-object lock metadata.

flashcards.q: What mechanism does the free-threaded build use to make reference counting thread-safe without the GIL?
flashcards.a: Biased reference counting: a fast path for the common case where an object is touched only by its owning thread, falling back to a slower atomic/shared path for genuine cross-thread references.

flashcards.q: What is CPython's free-threading rollout plan (PEP 703/779)?
flashcards.a: 3.14: officially supported but optional (build tag 't'). ~2026-27: GIL becomes runtime-flag-controllable. ~2028-30: free-threading becomes the DEFAULT, with GIL still available as an opt-in fallback.

flashcards.q: Why does the CPython team's free-threading rollout span multiple years instead of switching immediately?
flashcards.a: The C-extension ecosystem has relied implicitly on the GIL for thread safety for decades without extension authors needing explicit synchronization; an abrupt switch would silently introduce data races and crashes fleet-wide. The phased plan gives maintainers years to audit and update.

flashcards.q: What's the minimum common header every PyObject carries?
flashcards.a: At minimum ob_refcnt (reference count) and ob_type (pointer to the type object). Variable-length container types (PyVarObject: list, tuple, str, int) additionally carry ob_size.

flashcards.q: Define G, M, and P in Go's scheduler, and state what actually bounds parallel Go-code execution.
flashcards.a: G=goroutine (lightweight user-space work unit), M=OS thread (kernel-scheduled), P=logical processor context (exactly GOMAXPROCS of them, each with a local run queue). An M must hold a P to run Go code, so P count -- not M count -- bounds true parallelism.

flashcards.q: Can the number of live OS threads (Ms) exceed GOMAXPROCS?
flashcards.a: Yes -- when a goroutine makes a blocking syscall, its M's P is detached and handed to another M so other goroutines keep running, so live M count can temporarily exceed GOMAXPROCS under blocking-syscall load.

flashcards.q: Describe Go's goroutine stack growth mechanism and why it requires precise compiler support.
flashcards.a: Starts at 2KB; a function-entry check detects insufficient room and triggers allocating a bigger stack, copying old contents over, and rewriting every pointer that referenced the old stack's addresses to point into the new one. Only safe because compiler-generated stack maps tell the runtime precisely which stack words are pointers -- unavailable to a naive C runtime.

flashcards.q: What changed in Go 1.14's scheduler and what bug class did it fix?
flashcards.a: Introduced asynchronous preemption via OS signals, interrupting a goroutine at arbitrary points instead of only at function-call safe points -- fixed tight loops with no calls starving peer goroutines on the same P indefinitely (a real pre-1.14 bug class).

flashcards.q: What was the container-aware GOMAXPROCS problem fixed in Go 1.25?
flashcards.a: Pre-1.25, GOMAXPROCS defaulted to the HOST's total core count even inside a CPU-limited container/cgroup, causing scheduler oversubscription and cgroup CFS throttling-induced tail latency. Go 1.25 made the default container-aware.

flashcards.q: What is a V8 hidden class (Map) and why does property-addition ORDER matter, not just the final property set?
flashcards.a: A hidden class encodes an object's property set and storage offsets, shared by objects built via the same addition sequence. Two objects with identical final properties but different addition orders can end up with DIFFERENT hidden classes, defeating fast fixed-offset access -- consistent construction order (e.g. via a shared constructor) is what actually matters.

flashcards.q: Distinguish monomorphic, polymorphic, and megamorphic inline cache states.
flashcards.a: Monomorphic: one hidden class ever seen, fastest fixed-offset access. Polymorphic: a small bounded number of shapes (commonly up to ~4), still fast via a small dispatch table. Megamorphic: too many shapes, fast path abandoned entirely, generic slow lookup, and TurboFan won't type-specialize that site.

flashcards.q: What are Ignition and TurboFan in V8?
flashcards.a: Ignition: bytecode interpreter that runs all JS initially and records type feedback per call/access site into a per-function FeedbackVector. TurboFan: the optimizing JIT that compiles hot functions using that feedback into speculative, type-specialized machine code.

flashcards.q: What happens when a TurboFan-optimized function's speculative shape/type assumption breaks at runtime?
flashcards.a: V8 deoptimizes: discards the optimized machine code, reconstructs an equivalent interpreter-level stack frame, and resumes execution in Ignition -- architecturally the same pattern as JVM C2 deoptimization and CPython's adaptive-interpreter de-specialization.

flashcards.q: Why is spawning 100,000 goroutines routine in Go but spawning 100,000 OS threads is not?
flashcards.a: Memory: 100,000 goroutines at 2KB starting stack each is roughly 200MB; 100,000 OS threads at a typical 1-8MB default stack each is roughly 200GB-800GB. Goroutine stacks also start tiny and grow on demand rather than reserving a large fixed size upfront.

flashcards.q: How do you diagnose a V8/Node.js function that suddenly got slower with no code change?
flashcards.a: Suspect a shift to megamorphic inline caches or a deoptimization triggered by a change in the data flowing through the function (new object shapes, type changes). Diagnose with --trace-deopt (deopt events/reasons) and --trace-ic (IC state transitions) rather than guessing.

flashcards.q: What is Go's work-stealing scheduling behavior, and what happens when it fails?
flashcards.a: An idle P steals roughly half of another P's local run queue rather than sitting idle, keeping all GOMAXPROCS logical processors busy under uneven load. A global run queue exists only as a fallback/overflow, not the common scheduling path.

flashcards.q: Describe the classloader delegation model and why it exists.
flashcards.a: Bootstrap -> platform -> application, each delegating to its parent first before loading itself. Exists to guarantee core JDK classes always resolve to the trusted bootstrap-loaded version regardless of what an application defines with the same name -- a security/correctness boundary.

flashcards.q: Walk through tiered compilation: interpreter, C1, C2. Why not always use C2?
flashcards.a: Interpreter: zero compile latency, slow dispatch. C1: fast compile, light opt, gathers profiling data once a method warms. C2: slow compile, aggressive opt (inlining, escape analysis) once truly hot. Always using C2 would give best eventual throughput but terrible warmup latency since C2 compilation is comparatively slow.

flashcards.q: What happens when a C2-compiled method's speculative assumption breaks?
flashcards.a: Deoptimization: the JVM discards the compiled code, falls back to interpreting, and may eventually re-profile and recompile with corrected assumptions. Can thrash ('deopt storm') if the pattern is genuinely unstable, e.g. a call site alternating types.

flashcards.q: What is escape analysis and what two optimizations does it enable?
flashcards.a: C2-tier analysis proving an object never escapes its allocating method/thread. Non-escape past the method -> scalar replacement (fields become locals/registers, zero heap allocation, zero GC cost). Non-escape past the thread -> lock elision (synchronized removed since no contention is possible).

flashcards.q: Why is escape analysis only available at the C2 tier, not the interpreter or C1?
flashcards.a: It requires expensive whole-method (often cross-call, with inlining) data-flow analysis to prove non-escape -- exactly the kind of slow, deep analysis reserved for C2's optimization budget once a method has proven itself hot; C1 prioritizes fast compile time instead.

flashcards.q: Compare G1 and generational ZGC on pause time, throughput, and memory.
flashcards.a: G1: region-based, collects highest-garbage regions first, configurable pause goal (commonly tens of ms), still has real stop-the-world phases. ZGC (generational, Java 25 LTS default/only form): sub-ms pauses (~0.1-0.5ms) independent of heap size, but no compressed oops (~15-30% more memory) and ~5-15% lower throughput than G1.

flashcards.q: How does ZGC achieve sub-millisecond pauses regardless of heap size?
flashcards.a: Does marking, relocation, and remapping almost entirely concurrently with running application threads, using colored pointers (GC metadata embedded in unused reference bits) and load barriers (transparently redirect access to mid-relocation objects).

flashcards.q: What is a humongous object in G1 and why is it a real gotcha?
flashcards.a: An object larger than 50% of a region size, allocated specially across contiguous regions instead of a normal region. Frequent large allocations (big arrays, big collections) cause additional GC pressure and fragmentation from this special-cased handling.

flashcards.q: What's the 2026 default guidance for choosing G1 vs generational ZGC?
flashcards.a: G1 for most general-purpose services (predictable, well-understood, resource-efficient). Generational ZGC specifically for large-heap, latency-SLO-bound services where sub-millisecond pause consistency matters more than the memory/throughput cost.

flashcards.q: Why does a JVM microbenchmark appear to 'get faster' over its first several thousand calls?
flashcards.a: JIT warmup -- early calls run interpreted or C1-compiled (slower), and once the method crosses C2's invocation threshold and gets recompiled with aggressive optimization, it stabilizes at steady-state C2-optimized performance. Use JMH, not a naive hand-rolled timing loop, to measure this correctly.

flashcards.q: How does JMH avoid the measurement pitfalls of a hand-rolled timing loop?
flashcards.a: It explicitly separates warmup iterations (discarded, let the JIT reach steady state) from measurement iterations, and guards against dead-code elimination and constant-folding of benchmark inputs via blackholes -- none of which a raw System.nanoTime() loop protects against.

flashcards.q: What causes a classloader leak in a service that dynamically loads/reloads classes?
flashcards.a: Something (a static field, a ThreadLocal, a lingering thread) still references an instance or class from an old classloader after redeploy, keeping the entire loaded-class graph alive indefinitely and eventually causing OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace.

flashcards.q: Give latency numbers for L1, L2, L3, and DRAM.
flashcards.a: L1 ~4-5 cycles (~1ns), L2 ~12-14 cycles (~3-4ns), L3 ~40-75 cycles (~10-20ns), DRAM ~200-300 cycles (~70-100ns). L1-to-DRAM ratio is roughly 100x.

flashcards.q: What is a cache line, and what size is it on x86-64/ARM64?
flashcards.a: The fixed-size unit caches move data in: 64 bytes on both x86-64 and ARM64. Touching one byte pulls the whole line into every cache level.

flashcards.q: What is false sharing, mechanically?
flashcards.a: Two threads write to logically independent variables that happen to share a 64-byte cache line; each write invalidates the whole line for the other core per MESI, forcing repeated cross-core cache-to-cache transfers with no real data contention -- commonly 2-10x slower than padded.

flashcards.q: How do you detect false sharing in a running Linux service?
flashcards.a: perf c2c record / perf c2c report, looking for high HITM (hit-modified) counts -- the signature of cache-to-cache coherence traffic caused by (false or true) sharing.

flashcards.q: What's the correct fix for false sharing, and why is a mutex the wrong fix?
flashcards.a: Pad the contended fields to 64-byte boundaries (alignas(64), @Contended, manual padding). A mutex is wrong because there's no actual data race to synchronize -- only accidental cache-line co-location.

flashcards.q: What is a TLB miss and roughly how expensive is it?
flashcards.a: A miss in the translation lookaside buffer requiring a page-table walk (4 levels on x86-64 for 4KB pages), costing ~100+ cycles -- comparable to or worse than an L2 miss, paid in addition to the actual data access cost.

flashcards.q: How do huge pages reduce TLB pressure, and what's the operational risk of transparent huge pages?
flashcards.a: A 2MB huge page covers what would be 512 separate 4KB TLB entries, cutting miss rate for large working sets. Risk: Linux's transparent huge pages use background compaction (khugepaged) that has caused documented latency spikes (notably in Redis) -- explicit hugetlbfs avoids that.

flashcards.q: What is NUMA, and what's the typical remote-vs-local memory latency penalty?
flashcards.a: Non-Uniform Memory Access: DRAM is physically attached per-socket on multi-socket servers; a core accessing memory on another socket pays roughly 1.3-2x the local latency, with lower bandwidth, traversing the inter-socket interconnect (UPI/Infinity Fabric).

flashcards.q: List the four MESI states and what each means.
flashcards.a: Modified: sole dirty owner. Exclusive: sole clean owner, can silently upgrade to Modified with no bus traffic. Shared: multiple clean readers, a write requires invalidating all others. Invalid: stale, must refetch.

flashcards.q: What happens, state by state, when one of three cores holding a Shared cache line writes to it?
flashcards.a: The writer broadcasts an invalidation; the writer's copy goes Shared->Modified, the other two cores' copies go Shared->Invalid. Either of those cores accessing the address again is a miss requiring a cache-to-cache transfer of the Modified copy.

flashcards.q: Why is sequential array access dramatically faster than pointer-chasing a linked list of equal total size?
flashcards.a: Sequential access amortizes each 64-byte line fetch across many useful bytes and benefits from stride-based hardware prefetching. Pointer-chasing wastes most of each fetched line, is data-dependent so prefetching can't predict the next address, and each hop can be a full latency-bound miss.

flashcards.q: Design a per-CPU counter array for a highly concurrent service. What layout avoids coherence traffic?
flashcards.a: One counter per logical CPU, each padded to its own 64-byte cache line so no two CPUs' counters share a coherence unit -- each CPU writes its own line with zero cross-core invalidation; aggregation reads sum across slots, accepting eventual (not immediately exact) consistency.

flashcards.q: Why does a neural network Q-function reintroduce the deadly triad in a way tabular Q-learning avoids?
flashcards.a: A neural net's weight update generalizes across states -- fitting a target at state s also shifts Q at similar states s', including the state the next TD target depends on. Tabular updates only touch a single (s,a) entry, so only two of the triad's three legs are present in the tabular case.

flashcards.q: Why is a target network necessary for stable DQN training?
flashcards.a: Without it, the regression target is computed from the same weights being updated -- every gradient step moves the target too, so there's no fixed point to converge to. Freezing a copy for C steps converts this into a sequence of ordinary stationary-target regression problems.

flashcards.q: Name the two distinct benefits of a replay buffer.
flashcards.a: (1) Breaking temporal correlation between consecutive transitions, restoring something closer to the i.i.d. minibatch assumption SGD relies on. (2) Sample reuse -- each expensive environment transition can be trained on many times, enabled by Q-learning's off-policy property.

flashcards.q: Derive vanilla DQN's overestimation bias in one line.
flashcards.a: E[max_a' Q(s',a')] >= max_a' E[Q(s',a')] by Jensen's inequality (max is convex) -- taking the max over noisy estimates preferentially selects whichever happens to be overestimated, biasing the target upward.

flashcards.q: State the Double DQN target and explain the fix.
flashcards.a: y = r + gamma*Q_theta-(s', argmax_a' Q_theta(s',a')) -- select the best action with the ONLINE network, evaluate it with the TARGET network. Decoupling selection from evaluation breaks the overestimation mechanism since the two networks have largely independent noise.

flashcards.q: Why is mean-subtraction required in Dueling DQN's Q(s,a)=V(s)+A(s,a) recombination?
flashcards.a: Without it, V and A aren't uniquely identifiable from Q alone (add k to V, subtract k from every A, same Q) -- ill-posed gradients. Subtracting the mean advantage pins down a unique decomposition.

flashcards.q: What does Prioritized Experience Replay change, and why is an importance-sampling correction needed?
flashcards.a: Samples transitions with probability proportional to TD error magnitude instead of uniformly. Non-uniform sampling biases the gradient estimate, so an importance-sampling weight inversely proportional to sampling probability corrects it.

flashcards.q: What are Rainbow's six components?
flashcards.a: Double DQN, Dueling networks, Prioritized Experience Replay, multi-step returns, distributional RL (C51), and Noisy Nets.

flashcards.q: Why can't vanilla DQN be applied directly to continuous action spaces?
flashcards.a: The target and action selection both require max_a' Q(s',a'), which requires enumerating actions -- intractable for a continuous (infinite) action space.

flashcards.q: Why can a stable, low training loss coexist with a stagnant, poorly-performing agent?
flashcards.a: Loss only measures how well Q_theta fits its own bootstrapped target, which may itself be wrong (e.g. from a target network never syncing, or a terminal-bootstrap bug) -- a stable loss doesn't imply the value estimates are close to the true Q*.

flashcards.q: What does policy evaluation compute, and what update rule does it iterate?
flashcards.a: V^pi for a fixed policy pi, by iterating the Bellman expectation backup V_{k+1}(s) = sum_a pi(a|s) sum_s' P(s'|s,a)[R + gamma V_k(s')] until it stops changing.

flashcards.q: State the policy improvement theorem's conclusion.
flashcards.a: If pi' is greedy w.r.t. V^pi, then V^pi'(s) >= V^pi(s) for all states, proven by chaining the one-step inequality Q^pi(s,pi'(s)) >= V^pi(s) forward across all future timesteps.

flashcards.q: Why does policy iteration terminate in a finite number of outer iterations?
flashcards.a: There are only |A|^|S| deterministic policies; each iteration either strictly improves the policy or leaves it unchanged (already optimal) -- a strictly-improving sequence over a finite set must terminate. This is a combinatorial argument, distinct from value iteration's contraction proof.

flashcards.q: What is value iteration's update rule, and when is the policy extracted?
flashcards.a: V_{k+1}(s) = max_a sum_s' P(s'|s,a)[R + gamma V_k(s')]; the policy is extracted only once, after convergence, not mid-loop.

flashcards.q: Is value iteration a special case of policy iteration?
flashcards.a: Yes -- it's generalized policy iteration with the inner evaluation loop truncated to exactly one sweep before every improvement step.

flashcards.q: How many sweeps does value iteration need to halve its error, in terms of gamma?
flashcards.a: n = log(0.5)/log(gamma). At gamma=0.9, about 7 sweeps; at gamma=0.99, about 69; at gamma=0.999, about 693.

flashcards.q: What is the per-sweep computational complexity of value iteration with dense transitions?
flashcards.a: O(|S|^2 |A|) -- for each state, for each action, sum over up to |S| possible next states.

flashcards.q: What is prioritized sweeping and why does it still converge to the exact V*?
flashcards.a: It updates states in order of largest pending Bellman error, pushing predecessors back onto the priority queue after each update. It still applies the same exact Bellman backup, just in a smarter order, so it converges to the same V* with far less wasted computation.

flashcards.q: What hard requirement does dynamic programming have that model-free methods don't?
flashcards.a: P(s'|s,a) and R must be known in advance, and the state space must be small enough to enumerate.

flashcards.q: If ||V - V*||_inf <= eps, how far from optimal is the greedy policy w.r.t. V?
flashcards.a: Within 2*gamma*eps/(1-gamma) of optimal -- errors are amplified more as gamma approaches 1.

flashcards.q: What is the cumulative regret order for fixed-epsilon epsilon-greedy, and why?
flashcards.a: O(epsilon*T), linear in T -- a constant fraction of steps go to random (often bad) actions forever, regardless of how much evidence has accumulated against them.

flashcards.q: What is GLIE and why does it matter for Q-learning?
flashcards.a: Greedy in the Limit with Infinite Exploration -- an epsilon schedule that decays to 0 while still visiting every (s,a) infinitely often. Q-learning's convergence proof requires infinite visitation of every state-action pair.

flashcards.q: Write the UCB1 action-selection rule and name the source of the bonus term.
flashcards.a: a_t = argmax_a [Q_hat(a) + c*sqrt(ln(t)/N(a))]. The bonus is derived from a Hoeffding concentration inequality bounding how far a sample mean can deviate from the true mean given N(a) draws.

flashcards.q: What regret does UCB1 achieve, and how does it compare to fixed-epsilon greedy?
flashcards.a: O(log T), near the Lai-Robbins lower bound -- qualitatively better (sublinear) than fixed-epsilon's O(epsilon*T) linear regret.

flashcards.q: How does Thompson sampling choose an action?
flashcards.a: Sample a value theta_a from each action's posterior distribution, then act greedily on the sampled values (argmax over samples), not the posterior means.

flashcards.q: Why does Thompson sampling explore 'automatically' without a hand-designed bonus term?
flashcards.a: An action with a wide (uncertain) posterior occasionally samples a high value by chance, causing it to be selected -- exploration probability is exactly the probability that a sample from its posterior exceeds all others, automatically proportional to genuine uncertainty.

flashcards.q: What is the noisy TV problem and which method fixes it?
flashcards.a: A forward-dynamics prediction-error curiosity signal stays permanently high on irreducibly stochastic environment elements (visual noise), trapping the agent. Random Network Distillation (RND) fixes it by using a fixed, deterministic random network as the prediction target instead of a stochastic environment outcome.

flashcards.q: Why don't UCB and Thompson sampling transfer cleanly to deep RL with neural network value functions?
flashcards.a: Both need tractable per-arm statistics (a closed-form confidence bound or an exact posterior); neither is naturally available for a huge/continuous action space or a neural network's weights, where an exact Bayesian posterior is computationally intractable.

flashcards.q: What's the risk of setting the intrinsic motivation weight beta too high?
flashcards.a: The agent starts optimizing for novelty over actual task success -- a form of reward hacking sometimes called curiosity-chasing or curiosity addiction.

flashcards.q: Do UCB, Thompson sampling, and epsilon-greedy handle non-stationary reward distributions by default?
flashcards.a: No -- all standard regret guarantees assume a stationary bandit. Non-stationarity requires explicit handling: windowed/discounted statistics, periodic resets, or change-point detection.

flashcards.q: What are the five elements of an MDP tuple?
flashcards.a: (S, A, P, R, gamma) — states, actions, transition kernel P(s'|s,a), reward function R, discount factor.

flashcards.q: What is the one-line algebraic recursion that the entire Bellman equation derivation follows from?
flashcards.a: G_t = r_{t+1} + gamma * G_{t+1}, obtained by factoring gamma out of the tail of the return sum.

flashcards.q: What does the discount factor gamma equal in terms of episode termination probability?
flashcards.a: gamma is equivalent to a (1-gamma) probability of the episode terminating at each step; effective planning horizon is about 1/(1-gamma) steps.

flashcards.q: Why must gamma < 1 for a continuing (non-episodic) task?
flashcards.a: The return sum is a geometric series that only converges for gamma < 1; at gamma=1 the sum can diverge for any policy earning nonzero average reward.

flashcards.q: State the Bellman expectation equation for V^pi.
flashcards.a: V^pi(s) = sum_a pi(a|s) sum_s' P(s'|s,a) [R(s,a,s') + gamma V^pi(s')].

flashcards.q: State the Bellman optimality equation for V*.
flashcards.a: V*(s) = max_a sum_s' P(s'|s,a) [R(s,a,s') + gamma V*(s')].

flashcards.q: Why is the Bellman expectation equation linear but the optimality equation nonlinear?
flashcards.a: The expectation equation has fixed weights (pi and P); the optimality equation has a max_a operator, which is nonlinear, so it needs iterative algorithms instead of a closed-form matrix solve.

flashcards.q: What closed-form solution exists for V^pi under a fixed policy?
flashcards.a: V^pi = (I - gamma P^pi)^-1 R^pi, valid because P^pi is a stochastic matrix with spectral radius <= 1, so gamma*P^pi has spectral radius < 1 and I - gamma*P^pi is invertible.

flashcards.q: Why does value iteration provably converge to a unique V*?
flashcards.a: The Bellman optimality operator T is a gamma-contraction in the max-norm; by the Banach fixed-point theorem a contraction on a complete metric space has a unique fixed point, reached from any starting V0 at geometric rate gamma^n.

flashcards.q: In Q*(s,a) = sum_s' P(s'|s,a)[R + gamma max_a' Q*(s',a')], why is max_a' inside the sum over s' rather than outside?
flashcards.a: The next action a' is chosen after observing s', which is stochastic; taking max outside would incorrectly assume the action is chosen before the transition is known.

flashcards.q: What is the Monte Carlo update target for V(s_t)?
flashcards.a: G_t, the actual observed return from the whole episode -- unbiased but high variance.

flashcards.q: What is the TD(0) update target for V(s_t)?
flashcards.a: r_{t+1} + gamma*V(s_{t+1}) -- bootstrapped off the current value estimate, biased while V is still wrong but low variance.

flashcards.q: Why is TD(0) lower variance than Monte Carlo, mechanically?
flashcards.a: TD's target depends on only one transition's randomness (immediate reward + one bootstrapped value); MC's target sums rewards across the entire remaining trajectory, accumulating variance from every stochastic step until termination.

flashcards.q: Do TD and MC converge to the same fixed point under linear function approximation?
flashcards.a: No -- MC minimizes squared error to observed returns (least-squares fit); TD converges to the fixed point of the projected Bellman equation, a generally different solution.

flashcards.q: Write the n-step return formula and state what n=1 and n=T-t reduce to.
flashcards.a: G_t^(n) = r_{t+1}+...+gamma^(n-1)r_{t+n}+gamma^n V(s_{t+n}). n=1 reduces to TD(0); n=T-t (to terminal) reduces to Monte Carlo.

flashcards.q: Write the TD(lambda) forward-view return and state lambda=0 and lambda=1 special cases.
flashcards.a: G_t^lambda = (1-lambda) * sum_{n=1}^inf lambda^(n-1) G_t^(n). lambda=0 recovers TD(0); lambda=1 recovers Monte Carlo.

flashcards.q: Write the eligibility trace update (backward view of TD(lambda)).
flashcards.a: e_t(s) = gamma*lambda*e_{t-1}(s) + 1[s_t=s]; then update all states V(s) += alpha*delta_t*e_t(s).

flashcards.q: Why can't literal eligibility traces be used with a replay buffer in deep RL?
flashcards.a: Traces assume sequential online updates along one continuous trajectory; replay buffers sample transitions in random order, breaking that assumption. Systems like Rainbow/Ape-X use precomputed fixed n-step returns instead.

flashcards.q: What is GAE's relationship to TD(lambda)?
flashcards.a: GAE (Generalized Advantage Estimation) applies the identical exponentially-weighted lambda blend of n-step estimates, but to the advantage A(s,a)=Q(s,a)-V(s) instead of directly to the value function.

flashcards.q: Can pure Monte Carlo be used in continuing (non-episodic) tasks?
flashcards.a: No -- it requires an episode to terminate before any update can be computed. TD works online and is the only option for continuing tasks.

flashcards.q: State the SARSA update rule and identify its target.
flashcards.a: Q(s,a) += alpha*[r + gamma*Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)], where a' is the action actually sampled from the behavior policy at s'.

flashcards.q: State the Q-learning update rule and identify its target.
flashcards.a: Q(s,a) += alpha*[r + gamma*max_a' Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)] -- uses the best possible next action regardless of what the behavior policy will actually do.

flashcards.q: Define on-policy and off-policy precisely.
flashcards.a: On-policy: the behavior policy generating data and the target policy being evaluated/improved are the same. Off-policy: they differ. SARSA is on-policy; Q-learning is off-policy.

flashcards.q: On cliff walking, which algorithm has higher average reward DURING training, and why?
flashcards.a: SARSA -- because its target already accounts for the epsilon-chance of an exploratory step off the cliff, so it learns a safer route; Q-learning's target assumes optimal play from the next state onward, so it keeps walking the risky cliff-edge path during training.

flashcards.q: Why does Q-learning's off-policy property make experience replay valid?
flashcards.a: Q-learning's target depends only on (s,a,r,s'), not on which policy generated the transition or would act next, so old transitions from an old policy remain valid training data for the current greedy target.

flashcards.q: What condition must hold for Q-learning's convergence proof (Watkins & Dayan, 1992) to apply?
flashcards.a: Every state-action pair must be visited infinitely often, under standard stochastic approximation step-size conditions.

flashcards.q: What is Expected SARSA's target, and why is it still on-policy?
flashcards.a: r + gamma * sum_a' pi(a'|s') Q(s',a') -- the exact expectation over the behavior policy's action distribution. Still on-policy because the policy in the target is the same policy generating the data, just computed exactly instead of via one sample.

flashcards.q: When do SARSA and Q-learning produce identical updates?
flashcards.a: When the behavior policy is fully greedy (eps=0): the sampled a' equals argmax_a' Q(s',a'), so Q(s',a') = max_a' Q(s',a') and the two updates coincide.

flashcards.q: Why does naively replaying transitions break vanilla SARSA?
flashcards.a: SARSA's target needs a', the action the CURRENT behavior policy would take; a replayed transition's recorded a' came from an old, possibly very different policy, violating the on-policy assumption.

flashcards.q: Why is 'deep SARSA' much rarer in practice than DQN?
flashcards.a: On-policy learning can't freely reuse a large diverse replay buffer, a severe sample-efficiency cost in deep RL where environment interaction is expensive -- so on-policy deep RL usually takes the policy-gradient/actor-critic path instead.

flashcards.q: What quantity does an RL agent actually optimize — reward or return?
flashcards.a: Return G_t = sum of discounted future rewards from time t onward, not the immediate reward r_t.

flashcards.q: Name the three things that make RL fundamentally different from supervised learning.
flashcards.a: No labels (only scalar reward), non-stationary self-generated data distribution, and delayed/sparse credit assignment.

flashcards.q: Why is RL's training data called 'non-stationary'?
flashcards.a: Every policy update changes which states the agent visits next, since visitation is caused by the agent's own actions — the data distribution shifts as learning happens.

flashcards.q: What is the deadly triad?
flashcards.a: Function approximation + bootstrapping + off-policy learning combined together can cause training to diverge; any two of the three alone are provably safe.

flashcards.q: What distinguishes a contextual bandit from a full MDP?
flashcards.a: In a contextual bandit the agent's action does not affect the distribution of the next context/state; in a full MDP it does, reintroducing delayed credit assignment.

flashcards.q: Is reward hacking an algorithm bug or a specification bug?
flashcards.a: A specification bug — the policy optimized the reward exactly as written; the reward was an imperfect proxy for the true goal.

flashcards.q: What is the Markov property and why does it matter for TD/Q-learning?
flashcards.a: P(s_t+1 | s_t, a_t) = P(s_t+1 | full history) — the current state must be a sufficient statistic for the future. TD/Q-learning bootstrap off Q(s,a), which is only valid if s carries all relevant information.

flashcards.q: How do deep RL systems typically approximate a belief state in a POMDP without exact Bayesian filtering?
flashcards.a: Frame-stacking or a recurrent/attention layer over recent observation history, so the network implicitly infers hidden state like velocity.

flashcards.q: Roughly how much less sample-efficient is RL than supervised learning for comparable task performance?
flashcards.a: Often 100-1000x more environment interactions needed, which is why you should prefer supervised learning whenever labels genuinely exist.

flashcards.q: Why must RL reward be a single scalar?
flashcards.a: The Bellman equations and value-function machinery require a total order over outcomes so returns can be summed and compared; multi-objective goals must be scalarized (weighted sum, Lagrangian) before RL can optimize them.

flashcards.q: What are the two independent kernel mechanisms containers are built from?
flashcards.a: Namespaces (visibility isolation — what a process can see) and cgroups (resource isolation — what a process can use). No container-specific kernel object exists.

flashcards.q: Name the 8 Linux namespace types.
flashcards.a: pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user, cgroup, time (time is newest, kernel 5.6, 2020).

flashcards.q: Why does the user namespace matter most for container-escape severity?
flashcards.a: It maps UID 0 inside the container to an unprivileged UID on the host, so even an escape doesn't automatically grant host root — not mapping host root into the container blocks the most severe escape class.

flashcards.q: Why do CPU limits throttle but memory limits kill?
flashcards.a: CPU is compressible (kernel just stops scheduling for the rest of the cfs_quota_us period, default period 100ms). Memory is incompressible — crossing memory.max triggers immediate SIGKILL via the OOM killer.

flashcards.q: What does container exit code 137 mean?
flashcards.a: 128 + 9 (SIGKILL) — the signature of an OOM kill from exceeding memory.max, not an application-level crash.

flashcards.q: What CPU-throttling ratio in production signals a limit set too tight?
flashcards.a: container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total / container_cpu_cfs_periods_total above roughly 25% on a normal traffic day.

flashcards.q: What is the process chain from `docker run` to a running container?
flashcards.a: docker CLI -> dockerd -> containerd (lifecycle mgmt) -> containerd-shim (1 per container, survives containerd restarts, holds stdio) -> runc (OCI runtime, does clone()/unshare() + cgroup writes, execs, then exits).

flashcards.q: Why does runc exit right after starting the container instead of staying resident?
flashcards.a: So restarting/upgrading a long-lived daemon (containerd/dockerd) doesn't require killing running containers — the shim, not runc, is the container's real parent process.

flashcards.q: What causes the OverlayFS 'slow first write' surprise?
flashcards.a: Modifying a file that exists only in a read-only lower image layer triggers a full copy-up of the entire file into the writable upper layer before the write proceeds.

flashcards.q: Why is a container escape generally more severe than a VM escape?
flashcards.a: A container shares the host kernel with no hypervisor boundary, so escaping the namespace/cgroup jail lands directly in host kernel context; a VM escape must additionally defeat a hardware-enforced hypervisor boundary.

flashcards.q: Name a real recent runc container-escape CVE and its mechanism.
flashcards.a: CVE-2024-21626 (runc <=1.1.11): an internal file descriptor leak could give a newly-spawned container process a working directory in the host filesystem namespace, granting full host filesystem access.

flashcards.q: What does pids.max protect against?
flashcards.a: A fork bomb inside one container exhausting the host's entire PID table, which would affect every other process on the host, not just the offending container.

flashcards.q: What changed between cgroups v1 and v2?
flashcards.a: v1 had separate per-controller hierarchies with unreliable buffered-I/O accounting; v2 (kernel 4.5, 2016) unifies everything into one hierarchy with more consistent accounting. Migration across production is still ongoing.

flashcards.q: What's the production alternative to plain containers for running untrusted, multi-tenant code?
flashcards.a: gVisor (userspace syscall interception) or Kata Containers (per-job lightweight VM with its own guest kernel) — both trade overhead for a stronger isolation boundary than shared-kernel namespaces/cgroups.

flashcards.q: What is a warp and how does SIMT execution work?
flashcards.a: A fixed group of 32 threads on an SM that execute the same instruction in lockstep, sharing one instruction fetch/decode unit -- threads not on the active path are masked off, not truly parallel.

flashcards.q: Why does warp divergence cost real cycles?
flashcards.a: When threads in a warp take different branches, the hardware serializes: runs the if-path with else-taking threads masked off, then the else-path with if-taking threads masked off -- a 2-way divergence costs roughly 2x the cycles of no divergence.

flashcards.q: What is occupancy and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: The ratio of resident warps to the max an SM can host (64/SM on H100). High occupancy lets the scheduler switch to a different ready warp at ~0 cost when one stalls on memory, hiding HBM latency instead of leaving the SM idle.

flashcards.q: Why is a GPU warp switch essentially free, unlike a CPU thread context switch?
flashcards.a: Every resident warp's full register state lives permanently and simultaneously in the SM's register file -- there's nothing to save or restore, just a scheduling decision about which resident warp's registers to read next.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't nvidia-smi utilization percentage indicate compute efficiency?
flashcards.a: It reports whether any kernel is running during the sampling window, not how efficiently it uses compute -- a memory-bandwidth-bound kernel can show 100% utilization while compute units sit substantially idle waiting on HBM.

flashcards.q: What is arithmetic intensity and what does it determine?
flashcards.a: FLOPs performed per byte of data moved from memory. Compared against the GPU's compute-to-bandwidth ridge point, it determines whether a kernel is compute-bound or memory-bandwidth-bound.

flashcards.q: Why is LLM inference at batch size 1 memory-bandwidth-bound?
flashcards.a: Generating one token requires loading the entire model's weights from HBM but performs relatively few FLOPs per token relative to that data volume -- low arithmetic intensity leaves compute units mostly idle.

flashcards.q: How does batching fix the memory-bandwidth-bound problem in LLM inference?
flashcards.a: The same weight-loading cost from HBM is amortized across many requests' compute in one kernel launch, raising arithmetic intensity and pushing the workload toward compute-bound, extracting more useful tokens per GPU-hour.

flashcards.q: What is continuous batching and why does it beat static batching?
flashcards.a: Static batching waits for every request in a fixed group to finish, wasting slots on early-finishing short requests. Continuous batching swaps finished requests out and new ones in at every decode step, keeping the batch continuously full of active work.

flashcards.q: What throughput gains are reported for continuous batching?
flashcards.a: vLLM reports up to ~23x throughput with reduced p50 latency vs naive serving; the Orca paper reported up to ~36.9x vs static batching in its benchmarks.

flashcards.q: What does PagedAttention solve, distinct from continuous batching?
flashcards.a: It manages the KV cache in fixed-size, non-contiguous pages (like OS virtual memory) instead of one large contiguous block sized for max sequence length, reducing fragmentation so more requests' KV caches fit simultaneously, enabling bigger effective batch sizes.

flashcards.q: What is kernel launch overhead and why does it matter for real workloads?
flashcards.a: Roughly 3-10 microseconds fixed cost per launch even for a minimal kernel; a workload issuing thousands of small sequential kernels pays this repeatedly, and it dominates total cost when it exceeds per-kernel compute time -- fixed by kernel fusion.

flashcards.q: What are Tensor Cores and why do they matter for mixed-precision ML?
flashcards.a: Dedicated matrix-multiply-accumulate hardware (introduced Volta, 2017) optimized for fp16/bf16/fp8, far more efficient per cycle than composing matmul from general CUDA cores -- the actual mechanism delivering reduced-precision throughput gains.

flashcards.q: Why does thread-per-connection I/O hit a wall around a few thousand connections (C10K)?
flashcards.a: Each thread needs its own stack (commonly 1-8MB reserved) and the kernel scheduler degrades juggling thousands of runnable/blocked threads; named by Dan Kegel's 1999 C10K essay.

flashcards.q: Why are select() and poll() O(n) per call?
flashcards.a: They are stateless across calls: the kernel re-scans the entire watched-fd list every call regardless of how many descriptors actually changed state.

flashcards.q: What is select()'s hard descriptor limit and why can't it just be raised?
flashcards.a: FD_SETSIZE, typically 1024 — a compile-time bitmap size baked into the ABI; raising it isn't portable and doesn't fix the underlying O(n)-per-call scan cost anyway.

flashcards.q: Why is epoll's epoll_wait O(1) per ready event instead of O(n)?
flashcards.a: The interest list lives in the kernel (a red-black tree via epoll_ctl) and driver callbacks push state changes onto a separate ready-list; epoll_wait only drains that ready-list.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between level-triggered and edge-triggered epoll?
flashcards.a: LT re-fires every call while the fd stays ready (forgiving). ET fires only on the ready-state transition, so a handler must read-loop until EAGAIN or it silently stalls.

flashcards.q: What does io_uring's SQ/CQ model avoid that epoll+read() doesn't?
flashcards.a: Submission entries are written into a shared-memory ring with no syscall; only io_uring_enter() is a syscall, and it can batch many operations at once instead of a syscall per operation.

flashcards.q: What does IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL do and what does it cost?
flashcards.a: A dedicated kernel thread polls the submission queue so steady-state submission needs zero syscalls — at the cost of that thread burning a full CPU core continuously.

flashcards.q: Is io_uring always faster than epoll?
flashcards.a: No — unbatched, one-operation-at-a-time io_uring can be slower than epoll because its setup/bookkeeping overhead isn't amortized; the win requires batching.

flashcards.q: Why has Google disabled io_uring by default in ChromeOS, Android, and production servers?
flashcards.a: Roughly 60% of Google's kCTF kernel bug-bounty submissions have targeted io_uring (~$1M paid), including CVE-2024-0582, a use-after-free giving read/write access to freed kernel pages.

flashcards.q: What does sendfile() save versus read()+write(), concretely?
flashcards.a: A measured 2.5GiB transfer took 2,972 syscalls with sendfile() versus 131,093 syscalls with read+write — about 44x fewer syscalls and zero userspace copies.

flashcards.q: When does zero-copy (sendfile/splice) provide no benefit?
flashcards.a: When the data must be transformed in userspace, e.g. on-the-fly gzip compression or encryption — the bytes must pass through userspace to be transformed, so the kernel-only copy path doesn't apply.

flashcards.q: When is mmap the wrong choice for reading a large file?
flashcards.a: For a one-pass sequential scan — mmap loses kernel readahead and pays a minor-fault cost (~1-10us) per first-touched page, often losing to a plain buffered read(); mmap wins for repeated random-access workloads.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between sendfile() and splice()?
flashcards.a: sendfile() is specifically file-to-socket (or similar); splice() is the general primitive moving data between a pipe and any other fd, which is how socket-to-socket proxying (nginx, HAProxy) stays zero-copy.

flashcards.q: What is NAPI and why does it exist?
flashcards.a: New API: after the first hardIRQ on packet arrival, the driver switches to polling mode (softirq context, default budget 64 packets/pass) instead of interrupting per-packet, preventing a receive livelock under high packet rates.

flashcards.q: What does interrupt coalescing trade off?
flashcards.a: ethtool -c settings (rx-usecs/rx-frames) delay the hardware interrupt to batch more packets per interrupt, reducing CPU overhead under sustained load at the cost of added per-packet latency and jitter.

flashcards.q: What is GRO?
flashcards.a: Generic Receive Offload: coalesces multiple physically-received TCP segments of the same stream into one larger skb before IP/TCP processing, amortizing per-segment processing cost.

flashcards.q: How many round trips does a TLS 1.3 handshake need versus TLS 1.2?
flashcards.a: TLS 1.3: 1 RTT (client sends key share speculatively in the first flight). TLS 1.2: 2 RTT. 0-RTT resumption can send app data in the first flight but with no replay protection.

flashcards.q: What is the catch with TLS 0-RTT resumption?
flashcards.a: The first flight of 0-RTT application data has no replay protection -- an attacker can capture and resend it, so production restricts 0-RTT to idempotent requests (GET) or disables it for side-effecting endpoints.

flashcards.q: Why do browsers open 6-8 parallel connections per origin under HTTP/1.1?
flashcards.a: HTTP/1.1 allows only one request in flight per connection in practice (pipelining is unused due to HOL blocking and broken proxies), so browsers parallelize connections instead -- each paying its own TCP+TLS handshake.

flashcards.q: What causes TCP-level head-of-line blocking in HTTP/2?
flashcards.a: TCP guarantees strict in-order delivery for the whole connection as one byte stream; a lost packet for one multiplexed stream blocks delivery of all later-arrived bytes, including unrelated streams, until it's retransmitted.

flashcards.q: How does QUIC/HTTP-3 fix TCP head-of-line blocking?
flashcards.a: QUIC implements its own reliability with independent per-stream loss recovery over UDP, so a lost packet only stalls its own stream; other streams' already-arrived data is delivered immediately.

flashcards.q: Why can QUIC survive a client IP change (WiFi to cellular) but TCP can't?
flashcards.a: TCP identifies a connection by the 4-tuple (src/dst IP:port), which breaks on an IP change. QUIC identifies a connection by a connection ID independent of IP address.

flashcards.q: What is the real tradeoff of QUIC/HTTP-3 versus TCP that keeps it from being a strict upgrade?
flashcards.a: QUIC's userspace reliability implementation currently costs more server-side CPU per byte than TCP's decades-optimized, often hardware-offloaded kernel path -- a real, unresolved cost for CPU-bound, low-loss internal services.

flashcards.q: How does HPACK header compression differ from gzipping headers?
flashcards.a: HPACK maintains a stateful shared dynamic table across the connection's lifetime so repeated headers are referenced by a short index instead of resent; stateless per-message gzip can't exploit that cross-request redundancy and was avoided partly because it enabled CRIME/BREACH-style compression side-channel attacks.

flashcards.q: What does curl -w's per-phase timing let you attribute latency to?
flashcards.a: DNS resolution (time_namelookup), TCP connect (time_connect), TLS handshake (time_appconnect), and time-to-first-byte (time_starttransfer) -- pinpointing which layer actually added latency instead of guessing.

flashcards.q: What does a cold DNS resolution cost versus a cached one?
flashcards.a: Cached: effectively 0 extra RTT. Cold recursive resolution (root -> TLD -> authoritative) commonly adds tens of milliseconds.

flashcards.q: What are the sign/exponent/mantissa bit widths for IEEE-754 fp32?
flashcards.a: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, 23 mantissa bits. value = (-1)^sign x 1.mantissa x 2^(exponent-bias).

flashcards.q: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in every IEEE-754 language?
flashcards.a: 0.1 and 0.2 are repeating fractions in binary (like 1/3 in decimal) and are already rounded before addition happens; the sum rounds again, landing on 0.30000000000000004. Not a language bug, not fixable with more bits.

flashcards.q: What is catastrophic cancellation and does it depend on the magnitude of the numbers?
flashcards.a: Subtracting two nearly-equal floats destroys the leading significant digits, amplifying existing input rounding error. It depends only on how close the operands are, not on whether the numbers are large or small.

flashcards.q: What's the tell you're looking at catastrophic cancellation?
flashcards.a: A suspiciously small, clean/near-integer result from a computation involving much larger input magnitudes.

flashcards.q: What does Kahan summation fix and what's its error bound?
flashcards.a: It tracks a compensation term for low-order bits lost each addition. Naive summation error grows ~O(n*epsilon); Kahan keeps error near O(epsilon) for n < 1/epsilon.

flashcards.q: bf16 bit layout and why it became the ML training default?
flashcards.a: 1 sign, 8 exponent, 7 mantissa bits -- same exponent range as fp32 (no overflow at typical training magnitudes), so it usually needs no loss scaling, despite coarser precision (~2-3 decimal digits) than fp16.

flashcards.q: fp16 bit layout and its production problem?
flashcards.a: 1 sign, 5 exponent, 10 mantissa bits. Max representable magnitude ~65,504 -- gradients in large models routinely overflow this, causing inf/NaN, which is why fp16 training requires loss scaling.

flashcards.q: What is loss scaling and why does bf16 usually not need it?
flashcards.a: Multiply the loss by a large constant before backprop so gradients land in fp16's representable range, then divide back before the optimizer step. bf16 doesn't need it because its exponent range already matches fp32's.

flashcards.q: What are the two fp8 variants and their use cases?
