flashcards.a: E4M3 (4 exp/3 mantissa bits): more precision, less range, used for weights/activations. E5M2 (5 exp/2 mantissa bits): more range, less precision, used for gradients.

flashcards.q: Why does fp8 need per-tensor/per-block scaling instead of one global loss scale?
flashcards.a: With only 2-3 mantissa bits there's almost no margin for representation error; one global scale tuned for one tensor's distribution is likely wrong for another tensor at a different magnitude.

flashcards.q: When should you use Decimal/BigDecimal instead of float/double?
flashcards.a: For currency and any value requiring exact decimal arithmetic under addition -- accumulated float rounding error is a real correctness bug there, at the cost of meaningfully slower arithmetic (no native FPU support).

flashcards.q: Why is comparing floats with == unreliable?
flashcards.a: Values reaching the same mathematical answer via different computation paths can carry different accumulated rounding error; use a tolerance-based comparison (abs(a-b) < epsilon, scaled to magnitude) instead.

flashcards.q: Map the four 2026 API protocol choices to their non-overlapping niches: REST, GraphQL, gRPC, tRPC.
flashcards.a: REST = public APIs (CDN caching, debuggability). GraphQL = aggregation layer serving diverse client shapes from one backend. gRPC = internal service-to-service (binary, HTTP/2, auto deadline propagation). tRPC = TypeScript full-stack, same team owns both ends, eliminates the API boundary's type gap entirely.

flashcards.q: List the four Richardson Maturity Model levels, and where most production APIs deliberately stop.
flashcards.a: L0 swamp of POX (one endpoint, everything's POST), L1 real resource URLs, L2 correct HTTP verbs + status codes, L3 HATEOAS (hypermedia links). Most production APIs deliberately stop at L2 -- L3's dynamic-discovery benefit rarely justifies its cost for a typical hardcoded-client population.

flashcards.q: Mechanically, why does offset pagination degrade at scale while cursor pagination doesn't?
flashcards.a: OFFSET N forces the database to scan and discard N rows every time -- not index-friendly, cost grows linearly with depth. Cursor pagination (WHERE col > :last ORDER BY col LIMIT N) is a real indexable predicate -- the database seeks directly via the index, cost stays roughly constant at any depth.

flashcards.q: What does cursor pagination give up that offset pagination provides?
flashcards.a: The ability to jump to an arbitrary page number, or cheaply show a total page count -- cursor pagination is inherently sequential, only movable forward/backward from a known position.

flashcards.q: What are RFC 9457's five standard Problem Details members, and what RFC did it supersede?
flashcards.a: type, title, status, detail, instance (plus arbitrary extension fields). Supersedes RFC 7807 (2016) as of August 2023 -- both describe compatible shapes, tooling generally targets either interchangeably.

flashcards.q: What percentage of real-time use cases does SSE cover, and what's SSE's built-in reconnection mechanism?
flashcards.a: ~95%. Built-in reconnection via the Last-Event-ID header -- the browser's EventSource automatically reconnects on disconnect and sends the last event id it received, letting the server resume the stream rather than replay from the start.

flashcards.q: Name the genuine 5% use cases that justify WebSocket over SSE.
flashcards.a: Cases needing genuine bidirectional, low-latency, binary-capable communication: voice/video signaling, collaborative multi-cursor editing, gaming input streams -- not general 'real-time' needs, which SSE covers.

flashcards.q: What's the specific caching bug header-based API versioning is prone to, and how is it avoided?
flashcards.a: A CDN/cache keying purely on URL serves a cached v1 response to a v2 request hitting the same URL, unless the server correctly sets Vary: Accept (or equivalent) at EVERY layer in the caching chain. URL-path versioning avoids this class of bug entirely by construction, since each version has a genuinely distinct URL.

flashcards.q: Which real companies use date-based API versioning, and what workload does it suit?
flashcards.a: Stripe and GitHub. Suits platforms shipping frequent, fine-grained breaking changes -- clients pin to a specific date/snapshot rather than forcing every small change through a new major URL-path version.

flashcards.q: What GraphQL mechanism lets a partial response succeed even when one underlying service fails, and why is this a genuine advantage over a typical REST aggregation endpoint?
flashcards.a: GraphQL returns successfully-resolved fields alongside a structured error entry (in the errors array, associated with the failed field's path) for the fields that failed, rather than failing the entire query -- a REST aggregation endpoint more commonly succeeds or fails as one atomic unit.

flashcards.q: What's tRPC's core value proposition, and what's its real limitation?
flashcards.a: Eliminates the API contract boundary for a TypeScript full-stack app -- backend function signatures ARE the contract, imported directly with full type inference, no schema/codegen, no contract-drift bugs. Limitation: requires both ends to be TypeScript in the same monorepo/type-sharing pipeline -- no benefit for external partners or non-TypeScript consumers.

flashcards.q: Should every POST endpoint accept an idempotency key?
flashcards.a: No -- only endpoints with real, costly-to-duplicate side effects (payments, provisioning, notifications). A naturally-idempotent-by-construction endpoint (e.g. an upsert keyed on a client-provided ID) or a purely read-adjacent one doesn't need the extra mechanism.

flashcards.q: Cite the cited 2026 benchmark numbers for Go vs FastAPI vs Express on a JSON CRUD workload.
flashcards.a: Go (Fiber/Gin-class) ~142,000 RPS vs FastAPI ~38,000 RPS vs Express 5 ~19,000 RPS, with up to 7x better Go tail latency under high stress (gap narrows under moderate load).

flashcards.q: What's the single biggest caveat about the Go-vs-FastAPI benchmark numbers?
flashcards.a: They measure pure framework/runtime overhead with no real database or downstream calls -- exactly the condition where framework choice is the entire cost, which almost never describes a real production service where I/O dominates total latency regardless of language.

flashcards.q: Why does adding more async/await points to a CPU-bound Python handler not improve its throughput?
flashcards.a: Async restructures HOW a process waits on I/O; it adds concurrency, not CPU parallelism. The GIL still serializes actual bytecode execution regardless of whether code is inside async def -- a CPU-bound handler gets zero benefit from being async.

flashcards.q: What's Python's standard fix for CPU-bound scaling within one machine, and what does it cost?
flashcards.a: More OS worker processes (uvicorn --workers N) -- each is a full separate process with its own GIL and its own duplicated memory (loaded modules, models), with no shared in-process cache between them unless externalized (e.g. Redis).

flashcards.q: What are the four steps in the profiling checklist before proposing a Go rewrite, in order?
flashcards.a: 1) Is a blocking call stalling the event loop? 2) N+1 queries/missing indexes/missing caching? 3) Is it genuinely CPU-bound (not I/O-wait) via py-spy/cProfile? 4) Only then: is an already-tuned endpoint still hitting ~50K+ RPS or a hard latency wall more workers can't clear cost-effectively?

flashcards.q: What is a strangler-fig migration, and why is it preferred over a big-bang full rewrite?
flashcards.a: Migrating one proven-bottlenecked endpoint/service at a time behind a stable gateway contract: shadow real traffic first, gradually cut over while monitoring, decommission only that path. Bounds risk to one endpoint, preserves cheap rollback, and matches how real case studies (Reddit's service-by-service migration) actually happened.

flashcards.q: What specific wire-contract risk is often underestimated when scoping a FastAPI-to-Go rewrite?
flashcards.a: Preserving FastAPI's exact validation error shape ({"detail":[{"loc","msg","type"}]}), field naming convention, and status code semantics -- a rewrite that changes these breaks existing clients silently even if the underlying behavior is functionally equivalent.

flashcards.q: What RPS threshold is cited as roughly where language choice starts to matter for a peak traffic load?
flashcards.a: ~8,000 RPS peak runs equally well on FastAPI or Go; ~80,000 RPS peak does not -- the order of magnitude, not a language-is-faster reflex, is the actual decision criterion.

flashcards.q: What alternative to a full rewrite captures a CPU-bound performance win while minimizing migration risk?
flashcards.a: Offload just the genuinely CPU-bound computational component to Go (or Rust/a C extension), calling it from the rest of the service which stays in Python -- captures the real win while minimizing wire-contract-preservation risk and ongoing polyglot maintenance cost.

flashcards.q: What is Python's free-threaded build (PEP 703), and is it production-default in 2026?
flashcards.a: An experimental, opt-in CPython mode removing the GIL, under active multi-year development. Not yet production-default in mainstream Python as of 2026 -- a real 'where it's heading' direction, not current reality.

flashcards.q: What makes a goroutine cheaper than an OS thread, mechanically?
flashcards.a: Small starting stack (~2KB, dynamically grown/shrunk) vs a thread's fixed 1-8MB, plus M:N scheduling onto a small GOMAXPROCS-bounded pool of OS threads -- blocking on a channel/mutex parks the goroutine with no OS context switch.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't Go's garbage collector clean up a leaked goroutine?
flashcards.a: A blocked goroutine's stack and captured variables are still live and referenced by the runtime's scheduler bookkeeping -- nothing about a parked goroutine looks unreachable to the GC.

flashcards.q: What's the observable production symptom of a goroutine leak, and how do you diagnose it?
flashcards.a: Goroutine count and memory climb steadily under sustained traffic, no crash, no error log. Diagnose via pprof's goroutine profile: a large number of goroutines sharing an IDENTICAL blocked stack trace.

flashcards.q: What's wrong with calling time.After() inside a select in a loop, and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: Allocates a new *time.Timer every iteration, not GC'd until it fires -- steady memory/GC pressure in a hot loop. Fix: create one time.NewTimer outside the loop and call .Reset() instead.

flashcards.q: Why must you defer cancel() even when a context.WithTimeout's deadline is expected to fire on its own?
flashcards.a: The context's internal timer/goroutine stays alive until the PARENT context ends if cancel() is never called, not just until this function returns -- a real, cumulative leak even on the common timeout-fires-naturally path. cancel() is idempotent, safe to call unconditionally.

flashcards.q: State the Go memory model's happens-before guarantee for a channel send and its corresponding receive.
flashcards.a: A send on a channel happens-before the corresponding receive COMPLETES (not just starts) -- true for both unbuffered and buffered channels, matched send/receive in FIFO order.

flashcards.q: Does a clean `go test -race` run prove a codebase has no data races?
flashcards.a: No -- it only proves the specific concurrent paths actually exercised during that run were race-free during that run. It cannot detect races in untested paths or rare interleavings the run didn't hit.

flashcards.q: What does the `~` prefix mean in a Go generic constraint, e.g. `~int`?
flashcards.a: Matches any type whose UNDERLYING type is int, including named/derived types (type Meters int). Plain `int` in a constraint matches only the exact type, rejecting named types built on it.

flashcards.q: Who is allowed to close a channel, and what happens if you get it wrong?
flashcards.a: Only the sender, and only when certain no further sends will happen. Sending on a closed channel panics; closing twice panics; two goroutines racing to close the same channel is a real production bug.

flashcards.q: What is escape analysis, and how do you diagnose a hot path unexpectedly heap-allocating?
flashcards.a: Compile-time determination of whether a variable's lifetime is provably local (stack-allocatable) or could outlive its function (heap-allocated). Diagnose with `go build -gcflags="-m"` for per-variable escape decisions; a pprof CPU profile showing high runtime.mallocgc time on a hot path points back to this.

flashcards.q: What changed about GOMAXPROCS in Go 1.25, and why did it matter for Kubernetes pods?
flashcards.a: GOMAXPROCS became container-aware by default, reading the cgroup CPU limit instead of the host's full logical CPU count. Before 1.25, a pod capped at 2 CPUs on a large host could over-schedule parallelism, causing CPU throttling despite metrics showing moderate usage.

flashcards.q: What's current in Go as of 2026, and what did Go 1.26 (Feb 2026) ship?
flashcards.a: Go 1.26 is current stable: Green Tea GC now default (~10-40% GC overhead reduction), cgo overhead down ~30%, and a built-in goroutine leak detector integrated with testing/synctest.

flashcards.q: What's the defining property that makes a set of goroutines a 'worker pool' rather than unbounded fan-out?
flashcards.a: A fixed, bounded number of goroutines reading from a bounded input channel, which provides real backpressure by blocking the producer once workers are saturated -- versus spawning one goroutine per item with no cap, which grows without limit under a traffic spike.

flashcards.q: How does gRPC propagate deadlines across a service call automatically?
flashcards.a: A client's context.WithTimeout/WithDeadline is serialized into the RPC's HTTP/2 metadata as a grpc-timeout header; the server-side library deserializes it into a real context.Context deadline on receipt -- no application-level convention needed, works identically across languages.

flashcards.q: Why can a gRPC service with multiple healthy backend pods still see wildly uneven traffic distribution?
flashcards.a: gRPC multiplexes many RPCs over ONE long-lived HTTP/2 TCP connection. An L4 (connection-level) load balancer routes once, when the connection is established -- every subsequent RPC on it goes to the same backend, pinning a client's entire traffic to one pod.

flashcards.q: What are the two real fixes for the gRPC connection-pinning load-balancing trap?
flashcards.a: Client-side RPC-level load balancing (gRPC's round_robin service config resolving multiple backend addresses), or an L7-aware proxy (Envoy) that balances individual HTTP/2 streams rather than whole connections.

flashcards.q: Name the three main HNSW parameters and what each controls.
flashcards.a: M = max neighbor connections per node (graph connectivity, fixed at build, drives memory/build cost, 12-48 typical). efConstruction = build-time search breadth (higher = better graph, much slower build, fixed once built). efSearch = query-time search breadth, the ONLY one tunable live per-request, trades recall for latency.

flashcards.q: If vector search recall drops after a re-index and raising efSearch doesn't fully fix it, what should you check?
flashcards.a: efConstruction -- it may have been reduced, producing a lower-quality graph at build time. No amount of query-time efSearch tuning can fully compensate for a structurally worse graph built with a low efConstruction.

flashcards.q: When is building a custom Go vector-search microservice the right call over using a managed vector database?
flashcards.a: Only after profiling proves the managed DB's network hop and abstraction overhead is the actual bottleneck against a genuinely tight latency budget (e.g. sub-10ms p99), or when per-traffic-class efSearch control the managed API doesn't expose is genuinely needed -- not as a default choice.

flashcards.q: What does errgroup.WithContext provide over a hand-rolled sync.WaitGroup plus manual error channel?
flashcards.a: A derived context automatically canceled the moment any goroutine returns a non-nil error (so siblings get a ctx.Done() signal to exit cleanly), and Wait() returns the first error while guaranteeing all goroutines have finished -- coordination that's otherwise hand-wired and error-prone.

flashcards.q: How should you size a CPU-bound worker pool vs an I/O-bound one?
flashcards.a: CPU-bound: cap near GOMAXPROCS -- more workers than logical CPUs adds scheduling overhead with no throughput gain. I/O-bound: size via Little's Law (concurrency ~ downstream throughput x latency) against the downstream's actual capacity, not core count.

flashcards.q: Why isn't gRPC generally the default choice for public/browser-facing APIs despite its wire-level efficiency advantages?
flashcards.a: Browsers can't natively speak gRPC's HTTP/2-trailers-based framing without a proxy translation layer (grpc-web), and REST/JSON's tooling ubiquity, human-readability, and standard HTTP caching semantics matter more for external, partner-facing, debugging-heavy contexts than raw binary efficiency.

flashcards.q: What problem do virtual threads solve, and what do they not solve?
flashcards.a: Thread-per-request scalability for I/O-bound work (unmount from carrier while blocked). They do nothing for CPU-bound work -- a CPU-bound virtual thread occupies its carrier for its full duration just like a platform thread.

flashcards.q: What causes a virtual thread to be pinned to its carrier, and which case did JDK 24 fix?
flashcards.a: synchronized blocks/methods (FIXED in JDK 24 via JEP 491) and native/JNI calls (still pins on JDK 25, unfixed).

flashcards.q: What does `sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square` guarantee that pre-sealed-types Java could not?
flashcards.a: Compiler-enforced closed set of implementors, checked at compile time -- a switch over it can be verified exhaustive (no default needed, missing case = build failure). Before, this was convention-only (private constructor + comment), unverifiable by the compiler.

flashcards.q: What are records implicitly, and what can you NOT add to one?
flashcards.a: All fields implicit private final, canonical constructor, auto equals/hashCode/toString from ALL components. Cannot add a mutable field, cannot extend a class, implicitly final (no subclassing).

flashcards.q: How does ScopedValue differ from ThreadLocal, and why does it matter at virtual-thread scale?
flashcards.a: ScopedValue is immutable and auto-unbinds when the bound scope exits (no leak risk); ThreadLocal needs manual remove(). At millions of short-lived virtual threads, ThreadLocal's per-thread allocation cost becomes real; ScopedValue avoids it. Finalized in Java 25 (JEP 506).

flashcards.q: Is Structured Concurrency stable in Java 25?
flashcards.a: No -- still a preview API (JEP 505, sixth preview round in JDK 25). Claiming it's finalized/stable is a checkable interview mistake.

flashcards.q: Roughly how does throughput compare: pure reactive Netty vs virtual threads vs a traditional bounded platform-thread pool?
flashcards.a: Cited 2025-2026 benchmarks: pure reactive Netty ~200K RPS > VT-on-Netty ~150K RPS ~= VT-on-Tomcat ~140K RPS >> bounded platform-thread pool ~5K RPS (workload-dependent).

flashcards.q: What does `case Triangle(double base, double height) ->` do in a switch, and what JEP finalized it?
flashcards.a: Record deconstruction pattern -- binds the record's components directly as local variables in that branch, no accessor calls needed. Finalized as part of JEP 440 (record patterns) in Java 21.

flashcards.q: What is a carrier thread, and what happens on mount/unmount?
flashcards.a: A platform thread that runs virtual threads. MOUNT: virtual thread executes on a carrier. UNMOUNT: on a recognized blocking call (I/O), the virtual thread detaches, freeing the carrier to run a different virtual thread.

flashcards.q: When is Java 21 the right LTS target over Java 25?
flashcards.a: When the ecosystem (app server, legacy framework, vendor support matrix) hasn't certified 25 yet, or code accidentally relies on old synchronized-pinning-as-implicit-lock behavior. Otherwise 25 is the better default: extra JIT/GC years, Scoped Values finalized, pinning fix baked in.

flashcards.q: Why does creating a fixed platform-thread pool of 200 for I/O calls cap throughput regardless of downstream speed?
flashcards.a: Each in-flight call occupies a pooled OS thread (with its ~1MB reserved stack) for the whole blocking wait; with 200 threads and a 100ms call, max throughput is 200/0.1s = 2,000 req/s no matter how fast the downstream actually responds.

flashcards.q: Does virtual threads eliminate the need for concurrency limiting (semaphores/bulkheads)?
flashcards.a: No -- thread count is no longer the natural throttle it was with small platform-thread pools. A downstream's real capacity (DB pool size, API rate limit) still needs explicit backpressure even with virtual threads.

flashcards.q: What is the weak generational hypothesis and why does it make young GC cheap?
flashcards.a: Most objects die shortly after allocation. A young GC only scans the young generation plus a remembered set of old->young references, not the whole heap, so cost scales with live young-gen data, not total heap size.

flashcards.q: What is a G1 humongous object and why does it cause more Full GCs than the live data size suggests?
flashcards.a: Any object larger than 50% of the region size. It's allocated directly into contiguous regions, bypassing the cheap young-gen lifecycle -- behaves as old-gen data from allocation, reclaimable only via old/mixed collection, fragmenting the heap.

flashcards.q: What does -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis actually control, and what's its default?
flashcards.a: A soft TARGET (not a guarantee), default 200ms. G1 sizes young-gen and mixed-GC work to try to hit it; setting it unrealistically low increases GC frequency sharply rather than guaranteeing shorter pauses.

flashcards.q: What specific failure mode killed CMS, and what's its G1 analog?
flashcards.a: CMS never compacted concurrently, so old gen fragmented until a large allocation had no contiguous space, forcing a full stop-the-world compaction ('concurrent mode failure'). G1's analog: allocation outpacing concurrent marking triggers a Full GC fallback -- same lineage, concurrent collector falling behind.

flashcards.q: Mechanically, how does ZGC achieve sub-millisecond pauses regardless of heap size?
flashcards.a: Colored pointers encode object state in unused pointer bits; every reference read goes through a load barrier that transparently fixes a stale reference if the object moved. Relocation happens concurrently with the app running, so the stop-the-world component shrinks to small, heap-size-independent bookkeeping.

flashcards.q: What's ZGC's real, permanent cost versus G1?
flashcards.a: 15-30% more memory, 5-10% more CPU for equivalent workloads -- the structural price of concurrent relocation, not a tuning artifact.

flashcards.q: When did Generational ZGC become the default, and what happened to non-generational ZGC?
flashcards.a: Default since JDK 23 (JEP 474). Non-generational mode was later removed entirely (JEP 490) because generational mode won essentially every benchmark, cutting CPU overhead ~30-40% on allocation-heavy workloads.

flashcards.q: List the JIT tiers from cold to hot.
flashcards.a: Tier 0 interpreter -> Tier 1 C1 no profiling -> Tier 2/3 C1 with increasing profiling -> Tier 4 C2 full optimization (inlining, loop unrolling, escape analysis).

flashcards.q: Why is a naive 'time it in a loop' Java microbenchmark unreliable?
flashcards.a: It includes interpreter and C1 warm-up phases in the measurement, so for anything but very large N it measures compilation behavior, not steady-state C2-optimized throughput. Use JMH with a discarded warm-up phase.

flashcards.q: What causes JIT deoptimization, and what's the observable symptom of a method thrashing on it?
flashcards.a: C2 compiled code based on an optimistic assumption (e.g. monomorphic call site) that later proves wrong when a second implementation appears; the JVM falls back to the interpreter and recompiles. Symptom: the same method repeatedly compiled/discarded/recompiled, visible via JFR jdk.Deoptimization events or -XX:+PrintCompilation.

flashcards.q: In a G1 GC log line, what does a shrinking before->after heap-used gap over many collections (with flat traffic) indicate?
flashcards.a: A slow memory leak -- less garbage is reclaimed each cycle because more objects stay permanently live. Fix with a heap dump and retained-size analysis, not GC flag tuning.

flashcards.q: What does async-profiler see that JFR misses, and vice versa?
flashcards.a: async-profiler samples via perf_events/AsyncGetCallTrace outside JVM instrumentation, so it sees native frames (JNI, native libs) JFR misses. JFR is always-on-capable at <1% overhead and correlates GC/allocation/deopt/thread events on one shared timeline in a single recording -- complementary tools, not either/or.

flashcards.q: What are the three current (2026), specific statistics showing the correction away from microservices-by-default?
flashcards.a: CNCF 2025: 42% of orgs actively consolidating microservices back. Gartner: 60% of teams regret microservices adoption for small-to-medium apps (monoliths cut costs ~25% on average). DZone 2024: teams spend 35% more time debugging microservices vs modular monoliths.

flashcards.q: What makes a modular monolith different from an ordinary monolith with a nice folder structure?
flashcards.a: ENFORCED, checkable module boundaries -- a violation is a build/CI failure, not a code-review nit. Mechanisms: language-level privacy (Go unexported, Java JPMS), architecture-test tools (import-linter/ArchUnit), or per-module DB schema separation with no cross-schema joins.

flashcards.q: Name the four defensible reasons to split a monolith into real microservices.
flashcards.a: 1) Independent deployment cadence (a team genuinely blocked by another's unrelated releases). 2) Independent scaling profile. 3) Fault isolation (genuinely different failure modes). 4) Forced polyglot (a proven need for a different language/runtime).

flashcards.q: Mechanically, why does splitting into microservices cost ~35% more debugging time?
flashcards.a: A monolith's request execution is one call stack in one process (grep logs, set a breakpoint). Microservices scatter execution across processes connected by network calls, requiring distributed tracing with correctly-propagated trace context at every hop -- any hop that fails to propagate it leaves a gap exactly where the bug likely is.

flashcards.q: What did Segment's real case study show about consolidating 140+ services back to one application?
flashcards.a: A shared library change required deploying all 140+ services together, defeating the entire purpose of independent deployability -- the services were never truly independent, recreating a 'distributed monolith' with all the operational cost and none of the benefit.

flashcards.q: What did Amazon Prime Video's 2023 case study actually show, and what's the common overstatement?
flashcards.a: One specific monitoring tool moved from serverless/microservices to a monolith, cutting infra cost 90%. Overstatement: treating this as 'Amazon abandoned microservices platform-wide' -- it was scoped to one tool, not the whole Prime Video platform.

flashcards.q: Is monorepo vs polyrepo the same decision as monolith vs microservices? Give the real counter-examples.
flashcards.a: No, orthogonal decisions. Shopify: monorepo + modular monolith. Amazon: polyrepo + microservices. Google: monorepo + many independently-deployed services. The repo-layout choice is about cross-cutting refactor ease (monorepo) vs per-team CI/deploy autonomy (polyrepo).

flashcards.q: How does splitting a monolith's single database into per-service databases change data consistency handling?
flashcards.a: A single-DB transaction (BEGIN/UPDATE/UPDATE/COMMIT, atomic) becomes a saga or outbox pattern across separate databases with eventual consistency -- introducing new failure modes (a lost message between steps causing silent data drift) that literally couldn't occur inside one transactional boundary.

flashcards.q: How does Conway's Law inform where to draw service boundaries, and what happens on a mismatch?
flashcards.a: Architecture tends to mirror organizational communication structure whether designed that way or not -- deliberately draw service boundaries to match team boundaries. A mismatch produces a 'distributed monolith' (teams still coordinating across nominally-independent services) or unnecessary split overhead for coordination that didn't need a network boundary.

flashcards.q: What's the most common mistake teams make when extracting a microservice from a monolith?
flashcards.a: Extracting the code before resolving data ownership -- the new 'service' still reads/writes the monolith's shared database directly, recreating tight coupling through the schema while paying the full network/deployment overhead of separation (the distributed-monolith failure mode).

flashcards.q: List libuv's 6 event loop phases in order.
flashcards.a: Timers, pending callbacks, idle/prepare, poll, check (setImmediate), close callbacks.

flashcards.q: After every single callback returns, what two queues drain, in what priority order, before the loop proceeds?
flashcards.a: 1) process.nextTick queue fully (Node-specific, highest priority). 2) V8 microtask queue fully (Promise .then/.catch/.finally). Only then does the loop proceed to the next callback or phase.

flashcards.q: Is setTimeout(fn,0) vs setImmediate ordering deterministic? In what context is it guaranteed?
flashcards.a: Non-deterministic at a script's top level (depends on process startup timing). Guaranteed deterministic -- setImmediate always fires first -- when both are scheduled from inside an I/O callback, because CHECK (setImmediate) directly follows POLL, while TIMERS is the next loop iteration's first phase.

flashcards.q: What's the observable CPU signature of a synchronous CPU-heavy operation blocking Node's event loop, versus a blocking I/O call in FastAPI/WebFlux?
flashcards.a: Node CPU-blocking: CPU PEGGED near 100% on one core (genuinely computing). FastAPI/WebFlux blocking-I/O-call: CPU stays IDLE/low (blocked waiting on I/O, not computing) -- opposite signatures despite both collapsing throughput.

flashcards.q: What is libuv's thread pool for, and what's its default size?
flashcards.a: A small, fixed-size (default 4) pool of real background threads faking asynchrony for operations with no non-blocking OS syscall equivalent -- some fs operations, dns.lookup (not dns.resolve), some crypto (pbkdf2/scrypt). Must set UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE before any thread-pool-using module first loads.

flashcards.q: Why is Node stream backpressure called 'cooperative, not enforced'?
flashcards.a: writable.write() returning false is only a REQUEST to pause -- nothing in the runtime forces the producer to stop. A producer ignoring it keeps succeeding (data keeps being buffered) until memory pressure becomes an incident -- the real Walmart production memory leak was exactly a missing backpressure check in Node core's own C++.

flashcards.q: What's the safe default for wiring a Node stream pipeline, and why?
flashcards.a: stream.pipeline() (from node:stream/promises) or .pipe() -- both respect backpressure automatically and handle error propagation/cleanup correctly by default, unlike hand-rolled 'data'/'drain' event wiring which is a well-documented source of real production memory leaks.

flashcards.q: What does @nestjs/platform-fastify solve, and what's NestJS's default adapter as of v11?
flashcards.a: NestJS v11 defaults to Express v5, whose overhead is real and measurable; the Fastify adapter swaps in Fastify's faster routing while keeping NestJS's decorator-based DI/module structure, recovering most of the throughput gap for teams that want both structure and performance.

flashcards.q: What did Node's 2026 release schedule change to?
flashcards.a: Moved from odd/even major-version LTS pattern to one major release per year, landing every April with LTS promotion every October, removing the odd/even distinction entirely starting with Node 27.

flashcards.q: What does 'Node is single-threaded' actually constrain, and what does it not constrain?
flashcards.a: Constrains CPU-bound parallelism within one process (genuinely simultaneous computation needs worker_threads or a separate process). Does NOT constrain I/O-bound concurrency -- libuv's event loop lets one thread juggle thousands of concurrent I/O-waiting connections cheaply, which is the entire reason Node was designed this way.

flashcards.q: What is ArC, and what does it resolve at build time instead of runtime?
flashcards.a: Quarkus's build-time implementation of Jakarta CDI Lite. It resolves the entire DI graph and generates wiring bytecode during compilation, so runtime startup skips classpath scanning and reflection-based bean instantiation entirely.

flashcards.q: Roughly how much faster and lighter is a Quarkus native image vs the same app on the JVM, per cited benchmarks?
flashcards.a: ~29x faster startup (0.079s vs 2.292s) and ~86% less memory at startup (16.27 MiB vs 113.5 MiB).

flashcards.q: What is GraalVM's 'closed-world assumption' and what does it break?
flashcards.a: Static reachability analysis at build time determines every reachable class/method/field from the app's entry points and compiles ONLY that set. Breaks dynamic reflection (Class.forName with a computed string), runtime proxy/bytecode generation, and dynamic classloading unless explicitly configured via reflect-config.json or a Quarkus extension.

flashcards.q: Why can a warmed-up JVM outperform a native image on sustained peak throughput despite native's faster startup?
flashcards.a: Native image is AOT-compiled with optimization decisions FIXED at build time and no runtime adaptation. The JVM's JIT (C2) profiles actual live traffic and progressively specializes hot paths, which can out-optimize AOT's build-time-only guesses at true long-running steady state.

flashcards.q: What are Uni<T> and Multi<T> in Mutiny, and what are their Reactor equivalents?
flashcards.a: Uni<T> = zero-or-one eventual result or failure (~ Mono/CompletableFuture, richer composable operators). Multi<T> = a reactive stream of 0..N items (~ Flux).

flashcards.q: What does @Blocking do in a Quarkus REST route, and why is it needed?
flashcards.a: Routes the method to a worker thread instead of Quarkus's default Vert.x event loop. Without it, a blocking call inside a route stalls an event-loop thread -- the same hazard as an unmarked blocking call inside a WebFlux Mono chain or a FastAPI async def handler.

flashcards.q: Does Panache eliminate the N+1 lazy-loading query risk from JPA/Hibernate?
flashcards.a: No. Panache is a syntax layer (active-record via PanacheEntity, or repository via PanacheRepository<T>) over the same Hibernate lazy-loading mechanics -- a lazy association accessed in a loop is exactly as N+1-prone as under Spring Data.

flashcards.q: When is Quarkus the right default over Spring Boot, and when is it not?
flashcards.a: Right for serverless/Lambda (cold-start latency billed and user-visible), CLI-as-native-binary, and high-pod-count Kubernetes where per-pod memory is the actual budget constraint. Not the default for a long-running, steady-traffic service where the process runs hours/days between restarts and Spring's ecosystem depth outweighs a startup win nobody's waiting on.

flashcards.q: Why is a native-image build a genuinely different CI cost than a JVM compile?
flashcards.a: Native compilation is minutes, not seconds, with real peak memory pressure during the build itself (can need several GB), requiring dedicated, larger CI build resources rather than being a drop-in step in a lightweight pipeline.

flashcards.q: Why can code that runs fine in `quarkus:dev` fail only when compiled to native image?
flashcards.a: Dev mode runs on the JVM with full reflection capability; native-image applies closed-world static reachability analysis, which can fail to prove a reflective call site reachable even though it's valid on any JVM. The two modes have genuinely different execution semantics, not just different startup speed.

flashcards.q: What's fixed at build time in ArC's dependency graph, and what can still resolve at runtime?
flashcards.a: The EXISTENCE and wiring of beans (which implementation gets injected where, whether an extension's beans are in the final artifact) is fixed at build time. Individual configuration VALUES (via @ConfigProperty/MicroProfile Config) can still come from runtime environment variables, config maps, or secrets.

flashcards.q: Why is a Next.js Server Action functionally identical to a public REST API endpoint?
flashcards.a: A function marked "use server" compiles to a real HTTP POST endpoint callable directly (e.g. via curl) by anyone, regardless of whether the associated UI even renders for that user. TypeScript types and client-side validation only constrain your own app's happy path, not an attacker bypassing the UI.

flashcards.q: What's the specific 2026 Server Action vulnerability pattern where a UI redirect fails to protect a mutation?
flashcards.a: A page redirects unauthorized users away before a mutation button renders (correctly hiding the UI), but the Server Action itself is a separately-callable endpoint with no independent authorization check -- the redirect controls what's rendered, not what's callable, so an attacker can call the Action directly.

flashcards.q: Name Next.js's four caching layers, from most ephemeral to most persistent-and-shared.
flashcards.a: Router Cache (client-side nav polish) and Request Memoization (in-process, one request's lifetime, auto-dedupes fetch calls) are ephemeral. Data Cache (persistent, on-disk, survives restarts, shared across users) and Full Route Cache (build-time static HTML, zero server/DB hit) are the persistent, shared layers.

flashcards.q: What's the most common Next.js caching production bug, and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: Forgetting to call revalidateTag/revalidatePath after a mutation, leaving the persistent Data Cache serving stale data to every subsequent user until an explicit invalidation or full rebuild -- mechanically identical to forgetting to invalidate a Redis key after a database write.

flashcards.q: Why is the Edge runtime a poor fit for holding a traditional database connection pool?
flashcards.a: Edge executes in short-lived, geographically distributed V8 isolates rather than a long-running process -- many ephemeral, scattered invocations each opening (or exhausting a small shared limit of) raw connections is a structural mismatch with a traditional pool's assumption of a small number of stable, long-lived processes.

flashcards.q: What are the two fixes for a Next.js edge route hitting database connection errors under load, from smaller to larger architectural change?
flashcards.a: Smaller: introduce a serverless/edge-aware connection-pooling proxy between edge invocations and the database. Larger: route data access through a real backend service (on a traditional runtime with its own managed pool) instead of connecting from the edge directly -- converting Next.js's role to BFF.

flashcards.q: What was the key remediation guidance from Next.js's July 2026 security release regarding middleware-based authorization?
flashcards.a: Move real authorization checks into Server Actions and Route Handlers themselves; never rely on middleware.ts/proxy.ts alone as the sole enforcement point, since middleware-only checks can be bypassed or misconfigured in ways an endpoint's own check cannot.

flashcards.q: When is direct database access from a Next.js Server Action architecturally defensible, and when should it call a separate backend service instead?
flashcards.a: Defensible: small application, single-frontend product, early prototype. Call a real backend service instead once: multiple consumers (mobile app, partner API) need the same data, inline-DB-access review discipline is weaker than for a dedicated API, or edge connection-pooling risk is real at scale.

flashcards.q: Are Server Action identifiers a viable security-through-obscurity mitigation?
flashcards.a: No -- Server Action identifiers are discoverable in the shipped client JavaScript bundle (needed to enable the client-to-server call), so 'the attacker won't guess the function name' is not a real mitigation.

flashcards.q: When would you choose a Route Handler over a Server Action for a new server-side endpoint?
flashcards.a: When the caller isn't your own React tree -- a webhook receiver, a mobile app, a third-party integration, or any consumer not going through Next.js's client-to-server Action-calling convention needs a stable, documented URL (a Route Handler), not a Server Action.

flashcards.q: What is Resilience4j's fixed AOP decorator order for stacked annotations, and does annotation position on the method affect it?
flashcards.a: Retry(CircuitBreaker(RateLimiter(TimeLimiter(Bulkhead(Method))))) -- hardcoded by the library. Annotation declaration order on the method has no effect; override only via resilience4j.<module>.<module>AspectOrder properties.

flashcards.q: Is Resilience4j's RateLimiter a token bucket? What's the actual algorithm and its consequence?
flashcards.a: No -- fixed window. limitForPeriod permissions reset at the START of each limitRefreshPeriod cycle (tracked via lock-free AtomicReference CAS in AtomicRateLimiter). Consequence: a full burst at the end of one cycle plus a full burst at the start of the next can produce up to ~2x the nominal rate in a short boundary window.

flashcards.q: What are the two Resilience4j Bulkhead implementations, and when is each the right choice?
flashcards.a: SemaphoreBulkhead (default): counting semaphore, caller's own thread, cheap, CANNOT interrupt an in-flight call -- use for async/reactive code. ThreadPoolBulkhead: dedicated ThreadPoolExecutor + bounded queue, true isolation, CAN enforce a timeout on a blocking client -- use for legacy blocking SDKs you don't control.

flashcards.q: A @CircuitBreaker fallbackMethod is configured but never gets called -- the original exception propagates. What's the likely cause?
flashcards.a: fallbackMethod is resolved by reflection at startup against the exact original method signature plus a trailing Throwable/exception parameter. A signature mismatch fails registration silently -- no compile error, just a startup-log warning to check.

flashcards.q: Why does a SemaphoreBulkhead fail to protect against a stuck blocking downstream call with no timeout of its own?
flashcards.a: A semaphore can only block NEW calls from starting once permits run out -- it cannot interrupt a call already in flight. A stuck call holds its permit forever, so the bulkhead degrades slower than with no protection but doesn't actually stop the exhaustion.

flashcards.q: What specific gap in Hystrix does Resilience4j's slowCallRateThreshold/slowCallDurationThreshold close?
flashcards.a: Hystrix's failure-rate-only breaker never tripped on a downstream returning 200s slowly (e.g. 10s response times) -- 'slow success' exhausted threads exactly like failure but was invisible to the breaker. Leaving slowCallRateThreshold unconfigured in Resilience4j reproduces that same blind spot.

flashcards.q: Why did Hystrix's thread-pool-per-command default become a liability at scale, and how does Resilience4j fix it?
flashcards.a: Every dependency got its own dedicated thread pool by default -- real memory and context-switch cost multiplying with dependency count, with no opt-out. Resilience4j defaults to the cheap SemaphoreBulkhead and makes ThreadPoolBulkhead opt-in per dependency instead of mandatory for all.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't a synchronized-based rate limiter risk virtual thread pinning matter for Resilience4j's default RateLimiter?
flashcards.a: AtomicRateLimiter uses a lock-free AtomicReference compare-and-swap, not a synchronized block -- there's no monitor to pin a virtual thread on, regardless of JDK version.

flashcards.q: If both a service mesh and Resilience4j's @Retry are configured to retry the same call 3 times each, what happens?
flashcards.a: Amplification multiplies: up to 3x3=9 total attempts for one logical call. Pick one layer to own retry for a given call path and explicitly disable it at the other.

flashcards.q: Does Resilience4j's TimeLimiter guarantee the downstream work actually stops when it cancels a call?
flashcards.a: No -- it cancels the Future/reactive chain your code is waiting on, but the underlying downstream work only actually stops if the client itself honors thread interruption/cancellation propagation. Same server-work-continues-after-client-gives-up gap as the general resilience catalogue.

flashcards.q: Why does calling an @Transactional method via this.method() from inside the same class not start a transaction?
flashcards.a: AOP annotations work via a runtime proxy (CGLIB subclass or JDK dynamic proxy) wrapping the bean. Only calls arriving from OUTSIDE the bean go through the proxy; this.method() calls the real object directly, bypassing interception silently -- no error, just wrong behavior.

flashcards.q: In the Spring bean lifecycle, where does the AOP proxy typically get swapped in?
flashcards.a: During BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization, after @PostConstruct/InitializingBean callbacks have run on the real bean -- the reference handed to other beans from that point on is the proxy, not the raw object.

flashcards.q: Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?
flashcards.a: Makes dependencies final and required at construction (plain new()-able in unit tests, no half-wired state); field injection compiles with missing beans until runtime and can mask genuine circular dependencies via Spring's three-level singleton cache instead of failing fast at startup.

flashcards.q: What has narrowed WebFlux's differentiated use case since 2023, and what's left?
flashcards.a: Java 21+ virtual threads (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true, matured in Boot 4) now solve WebFlux's original 'handle more concurrent I/O' case with plain MVC and simpler code. What's left: true streaming/long-lived-connection APIs and genuine backpressure requirements.

flashcards.q: Why is a half-migrated WebFlux service (reactive controller, blocking JDBC repository) worse than plain MVC?
flashcards.a: It pays reactive's programming-model complexity while still blocking one of the small, fixed pool of Netty event-loop threads per blocking call -- stalling a disproportionate share of total capacity, same failure mode as a blocking call inside an async handler.

flashcards.q: What's the N+1 query problem in Spring Data JPA, and why does it survive code review?
flashcards.a: A repository method returns entities via one query, but each lazy-loaded association accessed afterward (often in a loop) triggers its own query -- 1+N round trips. Survives review because the code looks like an ordinary getter call and is invisible at small N in tests.

flashcards.q: What replaced WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter, and when was it removed?
flashcards.a: SecurityFilterChain @Bean-based configuration. WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter was deprecated in Spring Security 5.7 and removed entirely by Spring Security 6/7.

flashcards.q: When is disabling CSRF a defensible default vs a real security hole?
flashcards.a: Defensible for stateless, token-authenticated (JWT/OAuth2 bearer) APIs with no cookie session. A real hole for session-cookie-based auth, where CSRF protection is still needed.

flashcards.q: What does Testcontainers @ServiceConnection solve that H2-in-Postgres-mode didn't?
flashcards.a: H2 compatibility mode doesn't faithfully implement Postgres's real SQL dialect/JSON/locking behavior, causing works-in-CI-breaks-in-prod bugs. @ServiceConnection (Boot 3.1+) auto-wires a real database in Docker, with the actual engine's behavior.

flashcards.q: What's the fix for a blocking call left inside a WebFlux reactive pipeline, and which Scheduler?
flashcards.a: Mono.fromCallable(() -> blockingCall()).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) -- NOT Schedulers.parallel(), which is sized for CPU-bound work and would itself become a bottleneck under blocking I/O.

flashcards.q: What is the current Spring Boot / Spring Framework generation as of mid-2026, and what does Spring AI 2.0 require?
flashcards.a: Spring Boot 4.0 (GA Nov 20 2025) on Spring Framework 7.0. Spring AI 2.0 (GA June 2026) hard-requires Boot 4 -- teams on Boot 3.x must migrate first before adopting it. Boot 3.5/Framework 6.2 reached EOL June 30 2026.

flashcards.q: What's the fix for N+1 in a JPA repository method?
flashcards.a: JOIN FETCH in a custom JPQL query, or @EntityGraph to declare eager fetch for that specific method without changing the entity's global fetch type, or a projection interface selecting only needed fields.

flashcards.q: Why does a CNN need far fewer parameters than an MLP for the same image?
flashcards.a: Parameter sharing: a Conv2d(3->64, k=3) layer has only 3*3*3*64+64=1792 params regardless of image size, because the same kernel convolves at every position. A dense layer on a flattened 32x32x3 image to 64 units needs 196,672 params -- over 100x more.

flashcards.q: What is the CNN output-size formula, and what does 3x3/stride1/padding1 give for a 32x32 input?
flashcards.a: H' = floor((H-K+2P)/S)+1. For H=32,K=3,P=1,S=1: floor(31)+1=32 -- spatial size preserved, hence 'same' padding.

flashcards.q: What is receptive field, and how much does one 3x3 stride-1 conv layer add to it?
flashcards.a: How much of the input a feature-map location depends on. Each 3x3 stride-1 layer adds 2: RF(L)=1+2L, so 5 layers give RF=11, 10 layers give RF=21.

flashcards.q: Why is BPTT not a separate algorithm from ordinary backpropagation?
flashcards.a: Unrolling an RNN across T timesteps produces an ordinary computation graph with the same weights (W_h, W_x) reused (tied) at every step. BPTT is reverse-mode AD applied to this weight-tied graph, with the shared weight's gradient accumulated across all T timesteps -- the same rule any reused parameter gets.

flashcards.q: Why does a vanilla RNN suffer vanishing gradients across long sequences?
flashcards.a: The unrolled graph is structurally a T-layer deep network with tanh activations (derivative ceiling <1) repeated at every timestep -- the identical product-of-derivatives argument from backprop-derivation, with T (sequence length) playing the role of L (depth).

flashcards.q: Write the four LSTM gate equations.
flashcards.a: f_t=sigmoid(Wf.[h,x]+bf) forget; i_t=sigmoid(Wi.[h,x]+bi) input; g_t=tanh(Wg.[h,x]+bg) candidate; o_t=sigmoid(Wo.[h,x]+bo) output. c_t=f_t*c_{t-1}+i_t*g_t; h_t=o_t*tanh(c_t).

flashcards.q: Why does the LSTM's additive cell-state update fix vanishing gradients?
flashcards.a: d(c_t)/d(c_{t-1}) = f_t, a single learned factor per timestep the network can keep near 1, rather than a forced product of a weight Jacobian and a saturating activation derivative -- the 'constant error carousel', structurally the same idea as a residual connection's I+Jf Jacobian.

flashcards.q: Are LSTMs immune to vanishing/exploding gradients?
flashcards.a: No -- the additive cell-state path resists vanishing when the forget gate stays open, but the gates' own weight matrices and readout layers can still vanish/explode through the ordinary multiplicative mechanism. Gradient clipping remains standard practice for RNN/LSTM training regardless.

flashcards.q: Why might you still choose an LSTM over a Transformer in 2026?
flashcards.a: LSTM per-step inference cost is constant regardless of history length, unlike attention's cost growing with context length (quadratic full attention, or a growing KV cache). LSTMs can also generalize better in genuinely low-data regimes due to a stronger sequential inductive bias.

flashcards.q: Why does GlobalAveragePooling2D->Dense use far fewer parameters than Flatten->Dense, and what's the tradeoff?
flashcards.a: GAP averages each channel over its full spatial extent, giving a C-length vector regardless of H,W, so the dense layer scales with channel count not spatial size. Tradeoff: it discards spatial position information, which matters for detection/segmentation but not whole-image classification.

flashcards.q: What is Keras 3's key architectural difference from pre-3.0 Keras, and what breaks its portability?
flashcards.a: Keras 3 is multi-backend (TensorFlow, JAX, PyTorch, OpenVINO for inference), selected via KERAS_BACKEND. Using a raw backend-specific op (e.g. tf.*) instead of keras.ops.* inside a model breaks that portability.

flashcards.q: In the worked LSTM example (h_prev=0.1, c_prev=0.2, x=0.5), what are the resulting c_new and h_new?
What four things does an autograd computation-graph node store?
flashcards.a: Its data, its grad (accumulator starting at 0), its parent nodes, and a local backward closure created during the forward pass that computes its operation's contribution to each parent's gradient.

flashcards.q: Why does an autograd engine accumulate (+=) gradients instead of overwriting?
flashcards.a: The multivariable chain rule sums contributions over every path a value is used in: dL/dx = sum_over_paths (dL/dpath)(dpath/dx). Overwriting would let the last-run path clobber earlier contributions.

flashcards.q: For L=a*a+a with a=3.0, what is dL/da and how is it verified?
flashcards.a: dL/da = 2a+1 = 7.0, verified by central finite differences (f(a+h)-f(a-h))/(2h) at h=1e-6, giving ~7.0000000019.

flashcards.q: What does topological sorting guarantee for the backward pass?
flashcards.a: Every node appears before all nodes that depend on it; reversing that order guarantees each node's backward runs only after every downstream consumer has already contributed its gradient.

flashcards.q: Why does reverse-mode AD dominate deep learning training over forward-mode?
flashcards.a: Reverse-mode computes a vector-Jacobian product: one output (the scalar loss), all inputs, in one pass. Forward-mode computes a Jacobian-vector product: one input direction, all outputs, needing one pass PER parameter. With millions of params and one scalar loss, reverse-mode wins by millions-to-one.

flashcards.q: When is forward-mode AD actually the better choice?
flashcards.a: The opposite shape from training: few inputs, many outputs -- e.g. certain scientific-computing/PDE workloads, or per-sample gradients combined with vmap.

flashcards.q: What must a tensor engine's backward pass do for a broadcasted operation, e.g. z=x+y with x:(3,1), y:(1,4)?
flashcards.a: Sum the incoming gradient dL/dz (shape 3,4) over exactly the broadcast dimensions to restore each input's original shape: dL/dx = sum over axis 1 -> (3,1); dL/dy = sum over axis 0 -> (1,4).

flashcards.q: Why does PyTorch raise an error on in-place modification of an autograd-tracked tensor instead of computing a slightly-off gradient?
flashcards.a: A cached tensor (ctx.save_for_backward) mutated in place would silently produce the gradient of a different function than what actually ran forward. PyTorch uses a per-tensor version counter to fail loudly instead of silently returning a wrong gradient.

flashcards.q: What are the two bugs behind 'forgot zero_grad()' vs 'in-place modification error', and how do they differ?
flashcards.a: Forgetting zero_grad(): gradients from a PREVIOUS training step accumulate onto the new step's gradients (accumulation across unrelated graphs). In-place modification error: a cached tensor's value changed before backward ran, corrupting a SINGLE graph's computation -- different causes, different fixes.

flashcards.q: What does create_graph=True do, and why is it needed for a WGAN-GP style gradient penalty?
flashcards.a: It makes the backward pass's own operations autograd-tracked, so the resulting gradient can itself be differentiated again (double backward). A gradient penalty term needs the gradient itself to be part of the loss being optimized, requiring this.

flashcards.q: What does a custom torch.autograd.Function's forward/backward pair need to implement?
flashcards.a: forward(ctx, x): compute the output and ctx.save_for_backward(x) whatever is needed later. backward(ctx, grad_output): retrieve saved tensors and return grad_output times the operation's local derivative (forgetting to multiply by grad_output is a common bug).

flashcards.q: In the worked scalar graph a=2.0,b=-3.0,c=10.0,d=a*b,e=d+c,L=e*e, what are dL/da and dL/db?
State the multivariable chain rule connecting a layer's Jacobian to backprop.
flashcards.a: For L(h(x)), grad_x L = J_h^T grad_h L, where J_h is h's Jacobian. Backprop applies this once per layer, walking from the loss back to the inputs.

flashcards.q: What is the Jacobian of a linear layer z=Wx+b with respect to x?
flashcards.a: Exactly W itself (an m x n matrix). Backward pass through a linear layer left-multiplies the incoming gradient by W^T.

flashcards.q: Why is the Jacobian of an elementwise activation diagonal, and what does that simplify?
flashcards.a: Each output depends on exactly one input coordinate, so off-diagonal entries are zero and the diagonal is f'(z). Left-multiplying by a diagonal matrix is elementwise multiply, so backward through an activation is dL/dz = dL/da (elementwise*) f'(z).

flashcards.q: What is the formula for a layer's weight gradient, and why must the layer cache its input?
flashcards.a: dL/dW = (dL/dz) outer x^T. The input x is needed again during the backward pass to form this outer product, so it must be cached from the forward pass -- the core memory cost gradient checkpointing trades away.

flashcards.q: In the worked network, what are delta_o1 and delta_o2 (output layer error signals)?
In the worked network, what are dE/dw5 through dE/dw8?
flashcards.a: dE/dw5=0.082167, dE/dw6=0.082668, dE/dw7=-0.022603, dE/dw8=-0.022740 (each = delta_o times the corresponding hidden output).

flashcards.q: When propagating gradient back into the hidden layer, which weight values must be used -- original or already-updated?
flashcards.a: The ORIGINAL forward-pass weights (e.g. w5, w7), not weights already updated by that step's gradient descent -- using updated weights computes a gradient for a different function and silently produces incorrect numbers.

flashcards.q: Mechanically, why do gradients vanish in deep sigmoid networks?
flashcards.a: Sigmoid's derivative sigma(z)(1-sigma(z)) has a hard ceiling of 0.25. The gradient reaching early layers is a product of L such factors; 0.25^10 = 9.5e-7, 0.25^50 = 7.9e-31 -- geometric shrinkage, not a mysterious effect.

flashcards.q: Mechanically, why and how do gradients explode, and how does that relate to vanishing?
flashcards.a: Same product-of-L-factors equation, but with typical per-layer factor above 1 (e.g. weight amplification): 1.5^20=3325, 1.5^50=6.4e8. Vanishing and exploding are the same equation in opposite numeric regimes, not unrelated phenomena.

flashcards.q: How do residual connections structurally fix vanishing gradients?
flashcards.a: a=x+f(x) has Jacobian I+J_f instead of J_f. Backprop adds an unimpeded identity term to the learned path's contribution, giving a gradient path independent of how small J_f has shrunk to.

flashcards.q: Does gradient clipping fix vanishing gradients?
flashcards.a: No. Clipping only ever reduces a gradient's magnitude when it exceeds a threshold -- it is purely a ceiling, never a floor, so it cannot address a gradient that's already too small.

flashcards.q: After one gradient update to the worked network, what happens to the loss, and why does this matter?
flashcards.a: E_total goes from 0.298371 to 0.291028 -- the loss decreased, which is the sanity check that every sign and magnitude in the hand-derived backward pass was correct, not just plausible-looking.

flashcards.q: What does Dynamo do mechanically, and how does that differ from torch.jit.script?
flashcards.a: Dynamo hooks CPython's frame evaluation API to trace real, unmodified eager code as it runs, capturing an FX graph plus runtime guards. torch.jit.script required rewriting code into a restricted, statically-analyzable subset ahead of time, which broke on dynamic control flow Dynamo handles via graceful graph breaks.

flashcards.q: What is a guard, and what happens when one fails?
flashcards.a: A cheap runtime check (shape, dtype, device, certain Python values) that must hold for a captured graph to be safely reused. A guard failure triggers recompilation for the new condition, with graphs cached per distinct guard combination.

flashcards.q: What is a graph break, and is it a failure?
flashcards.a: When Dynamo hits code it can't trace (data-dependent control flow on a tensor value, an untraceable library call), it falls back to eager execution for that piece and resumes tracing after -- not a crash, but Inductor can't fuse/optimize across the break, reducing compilation's benefit.

flashcards.q: What is a recompilation storm, and how is it mitigated?
flashcards.a: Highly variable input shapes trigger a new guard failure (and full recompilation) on nearly every call, so compilation cost dominates instead of amortizing. Mitigated by marking dimensions dynamic, compiling once for a range of shapes instead of one exact shape per call.

flashcards.q: What does AOTAutograd add on top of Dynamo's graph capture?
flashcards.a: It runs the forward pass once under tracing specifically to also derive the backward pass's graph ahead of time, producing a joint forward+backward representation so Inductor can apply fusion/scheduling to the backward pass with the same graph-level knowledge as the forward.

flashcards.q: What does Inductor do, and why does operator fusion matter (connect to GPU architecture)?
flashcards.a: Inductor lowers the joint graph into generated code -- fused Triton kernels for GPU, C++/OpenMP for CPU. Fusion combines a chain of ops into one kernel, paying the ~3-10us launch overhead once instead of per-op and keeping intermediates in registers/shared memory instead of redundant HBM round-trips.

flashcards.q: What is torch._dynamo.error_on_graph_break() used for?
flashcards.a: It forces an explicit error at a graph break instead of a silent eager fallback, letting developers find exactly where and why performance-costing breaks occur during development rather than only inferring it from disappointing benchmarks.

flashcards.q: What does a Triton kernel let you describe, versus raw CUDA C++?
flashcards.a: Computation over a BLOCK of data (via program_id-based offsets), with the compiler handling the mapping to individual GPU threads/warps -- no manual thread indexing, shared memory management, or warp-level synchronization required, unlike raw CUDA.

flashcards.q: In a Triton kernel, why is the mask a correctness requirement, not just an optimization?
flashcards.a: Without it, tl.load/tl.store for the final partially-filled block would read/write memory past the array's actual allocated end, since blocks are launched uniformly regardless of whether n_elements divides evenly by BLOCK_SIZE -- an out-of-bounds access, not a performance issue.

flashcards.q: For n_elements=10000 and BLOCK_SIZE=1024, how many Triton grid blocks are launched, and how many trailing lanes are masked in the last block?
flashcards.a: ceil(10000/1024)=10 blocks. The 10th block covers offsets 9216-10239; only 9216-9999 (784 elements) are valid, so 240 trailing lanes are masked off.

flashcards.q: A teammate finds torch.compile makes their benchmark slower. What's the first thing to check?
flashcards.a: Whether the benchmark includes the first (compiling) call's cost -- the initial invocation pays tracing and codegen time on top of execution, which can dominate if the model only runs a handful of times.

flashcards.q: Why does Inductor generate Triton kernels rather than raw CUDA C++ for GPU targets?
flashcards.a: Triton's block-level abstraction is a smaller, more tractable code-generation target for a compiler than hand-tuned CUDA C++, while still producing kernels competitive with hand-written CUDA for most real workloads, and the output remains inspectable Python-embedded code.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't DDP's ring all-reduce communication cost grow proportionally with GPU count?
flashcards.a: Total data moved per GPU is 2*(N-1)/N * S. As N grows, (N-1)/N approaches 1, so bandwidth cost per GPU approaches a constant (~2S), independent of GPU count -- only the smaller per-step latency term scales with N.

flashcards.q: What is DDP's actual ceiling if not communication cost?
flashcards.a: The full model, gradients, and optimizer state must fit on EVERY GPU (DDP replicates, doesn't shard, model state) -- adding more GPUs doesn't reduce any single GPU's memory footprint.

flashcards.q: What does each ZeRO stage shard, and what are the memory figures for Psi=7.5B params, Nd=64 GPUs?
flashcards.a: Baseline (16*Psi bytes, all replicated) = 120GB. Stage1 (shard optimizer state, 12*Psi): 31.4GB. Stage2 (+shard gradients): 16.6GB. Stage3 (+shard params): 1.9GB -- a 64x reduction, matching the original ZeRO paper.

flashcards.q: Why does ZeRO Stage 3 need roughly 1.5x DDP's communication volume?
flashcards.a: Parameters are never held in full on any GPU, so each layer's shard must be all-gathered into a full copy immediately before both the forward AND backward compute for that layer, then freed -- adding roughly a full parameter all-gather twice on top of DDP's existing gradient all-reduce.

flashcards.q: What does FSDP2 change relative to FSDP1, and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: FSDP2 shards at per-parameter granularity instead of FSDP1's flattened/concatenated sharding -- composes more cleanly with mixed per-layer dtypes, freezing individual parameters (LoRA-style fine-tuning), and torch.compile. Reported up to ~5x ZeRO-3's per-iteration throughput where both fit memory.

flashcards.q: Why is tensor parallelism kept within a single node rather than spread across nodes?
flashcards.a: Tensor parallelism requires a communication operation (all-reduce/all-gather) at EVERY split layer -- high frequency, acutely sensitive to interconnect bandwidth/latency. Keeping it within one NVLink-connected node avoids paying that cost at slower inter-node speeds.

flashcards.q: What is the pipeline-parallel bubble fraction formula, and what is it for 4 stages with 8 vs 32 microbatches?
flashcards.a: Bubble fraction ~= (P-1)/M. P=4,M=8: (4-1)/8=37.5% idle. P=4,M=32: (4-1)/32=9.4% idle -- more microbatches amortizes the fixed pipeline fill/drain cost over more useful work.

flashcards.q: A model doesn't fit even after applying ZeRO-3/FSDP2 at max affordable GPU count. What's the next lever, and why doesn't more data-parallel sharding help?
flashcards.a: Tensor parallelism (split the oversized layer's matrices) and/or pipeline parallelism (split model depth). ZeRO/FSDP shards across data-parallel replicas, but at compute time a full layer's parameters must still be materialized on one GPU -- more replicas doesn't shrink that per-layer peak requirement.

flashcards.q: Why do the largest production training runs combine data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism simultaneously?
flashcards.a: Each solves a different ceiling: data parallelism (with ZeRO/FSDP) scales throughput and reduces aggregate per-GPU memory; tensor parallelism handles one layer too large for one GPU; pipeline parallelism handles a model whose total depth doesn't fit. No single axis addresses every possible ceiling alone.

flashcards.q: What's the practical difference between ZeRO/FSDP and tensor parallelism, given both reduce memory per GPU?
flashcards.a: ZeRO/FSDP reduce aggregate memory across a data-parallel group, but a layer's full parameters must still be materialized on one GPU when it computes. Tensor parallelism genuinely splits that layer's computation so no single GPU ever needs its full parameters -- relevant specifically when one layer alone is too large for one GPU.

flashcards.q: If a model already fits comfortably on a single GPU but training is too slow, which distributed strategy should you reach for first?
flashcards.a: Plain DDP -- simplest failure modes, near-N-independent communication cost, no sharding/all-gather overhead you don't need since memory was never the constraint. ZeRO/FSDP sharding is only worth adding once memory pressure genuinely emerges.

flashcards.q: What is the mixed-precision Adam per-parameter memory breakdown that gives ZeRO's 16*Psi bytes total?
flashcards.a: 2*Psi fp16 params + 2*Psi fp16 gradients + 4*Psi fp32 master params + 4*Psi fp32 momentum + 4*Psi fp32 variance = 16*Psi bytes, of which optimizer state (12*Psi) is 75% of total memory.

flashcards.q: What is an ONNX opset, and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: A specific, versioned set of operation definitions a graph is allowed to use. A model exported at opset N can only use ops defined by opset N or earlier, and the consuming runtime must support that opset -- current is opset 27 (ONNX 1.22, mid-2026).

flashcards.q: Why does PyTorch 2.9 default torch.onnx.export to the Dynamo-based exporter for opset>=18?
flashcards.a: It reuses Dynamo's robust real-Python-control-flow tracing (same machinery as torch.compile) instead of the older tracing/scripting-based exporter, which struggled with genuinely dynamic control flow.

flashcards.q: Compute the quantization error for w=1.3, range [-2,2], at INT8 vs INT4.
flashcards.a: INT8: scale=2/127=0.01575, q=83, dequant=1.307, error=0.0071. INT4: scale=2/7=0.2857, q=5, dequant=1.429, error=0.1286 -- roughly 18x larger error at INT4.

flashcards.q: Distinguish PTQ from QAT.
flashcards.a: PTQ quantizes an already-trained model using calibration data to pick scales, with no retraining -- cheap but accuracy drops more at aggressive bit-widths. QAT simulates quantization during training/fine-tuning with a straight-through estimator, letting weights adapt to be robust -- costs retraining compute, better accuracy at aggressive bit-widths.

flashcards.q: Why can't you train through a fake-quantization round() operation with ordinary backprop, and what fixes it?
flashcards.a: round() is a step function with true derivative zero almost everywhere, so ordinary backprop reports zero gradient. The straight-through estimator (STE) uses a custom backward pass that passes the incoming gradient through unchanged (masking clipped regions) instead of round's true near-zero gradient.

flashcards.q: Why does unstructured pruning often deliver no inference speedup despite high nominal sparsity?
flashcards.a: Zeroed weights scattered arbitrarily still occupy full memory layout and get multiplied (wastefully) in ordinary dense matmul without specialized sparse-matmul hardware/kernels -- no speedup without hardware support.

flashcards.q: What is semi-structured N:M sparsity, and what hardware accelerates it?
flashcards.a: A regular pattern (e.g. exactly 2 of every 4 contiguous weights zeroed) natively accelerated by NVIDIA Ampere-and-newer sparse Tensor Cores, giving roughly 2x throughput for a correctly-configured 2:4 sparse matmul vs dense -- the practical middle ground between structured and unstructured pruning.

flashcards.q: What is 'dark knowledge' in distillation, and how does temperature reveal it?
flashcards.a: A confident teacher's raw output (T=1) is sharply peaked, e.g. [0.858,0.116,0.026]. Applying temperature T=4 inside softmax(z/T) softens it to [0.494,0.300,0.206], revealing relative confidence across wrong classes that hard labels discard.

flashcards.q: What is the empirically-best compression ordering, and why prune before quantize?
flashcards.a: Prune, then distill/retrain, then quantize (P-KD-Q). Pruning first removes unnecessary capacity while the model can still fully recover via distillation retraining; quantizing before that forces the model to jointly absorb structural loss and quantization noise at once, a harder combined problem.

flashcards.q: What problem does SmoothQuant address in LLM INT8 quantization?
flashcards.a: LLM activations have outlier values concentrated in specific channels that force a wide quantization scale, wasting resolution on typical values. SmoothQuant migrates quantization difficulty from activations to weights via an algebraic identity (x*s)(w/s)=x*w, leaving the result unchanged but easier to quantize accurately.

flashcards.q: Why is a TensorRT-compiled engine not portable across GPU generations, unlike an ONNX graph?
flashcards.a: TensorRT's fusion and kernel auto-tuning decisions target the specific hardware's Tensor Core generation, memory bandwidth, and known-good kernel implementations -- that specificity is what buys the performance gain but means engines must be recompiled per target GPU generation.

flashcards.q: What does AWQ do differently from naive uniform PTQ?
flashcards.a: AWQ (activation-aware weight quantization) identifies and preserves the small fraction of weights most sensitive to quantization error based on their corresponding activation magnitudes, rather than quantizing every weight identically -- used for INT4 in TensorRT-LLM.

flashcards.q: What does a single artificial neuron compute?
flashcards.a: a = f(w.x + b) -- a weighted sum of inputs plus bias (z, the pre-activation/logit), passed through a nonlinear activation f.

flashcards.q: Why does stacking linear layers with no activation add zero representational power?
flashcards.a: Composing affine maps stays affine: W2(W1x+b1)+b2 = (W2W1)x + (W2b1+b2), one effective linear layer regardless of depth. Inserting a nonlinearity between layers breaks this collapse.

flashcards.q: What is the vectorized form of a layer, and its batched form?
flashcards.a: z = Wx + b for one example (W is out_features x in_features). Batched: Z = XW^T + b where X is B x n, giving Z shape B x m, with b broadcast.

flashcards.q: In the worked 2-2-2 sigmoid network (x=[0.05,0.10]), what are out_h1 and out_h2?
In that same worked network, what is the final total loss (SSE)?
What loss function is the mathematically correct choice for regression, binary classification, and multi-class classification respectively?
flashcards.a: Regression (Gaussian noise): MSE. Binary classification (Bernoulli): BCE. Multi-class (categorical): cross-entropy. Each is the negative log-likelihood under that distribution.

flashcards.q: What is d(CrossEntropy)/d(logits) when softmax feeds directly into cross-entropy?
flashcards.a: p_hat - y_onehot -- the softmax output minus the one-hot true label, elementwise. This is why frameworks require raw logits, not post-softmax probabilities, as input to CrossEntropyLoss.

flashcards.q: What silently breaks if you apply softmax manually before nn.CrossEntropyLoss?
flashcards.a: Softmax gets applied twice. It doesn't crash and gradient direction is roughly preserved, but magnitude is distorted, capping achievable accuracy with no visible error -- a classic silent bug.

flashcards.q: Why must you subtract max(z) before exponentiating in softmax?
flashcards.a: It's an algebraic identity that doesn't change the result but keeps every exponent <= 0, preventing exp() overflow to inf (and inf/inf = nan) for large logits.

flashcards.q: What does the bias term do geometrically, and what happens if you omit it?
flashcards.a: w.x alone defines a hyperplane through the origin; b shifts it off the origin. Omitting b restricts every neuron's decision boundary to pass through the origin -- a real capacity limit, not a harmless simplification.

flashcards.q: Why is MSE a poor loss choice for classification even though it's simpler?
flashcards.a: MSE's gradient through a saturated sigmoid/softmax vanishes exactly where predictions are most confidently wrong, whereas cross-entropy's gradient (p_hat - y) stays proportional to the error.

flashcards.q: softmax([2.0, 1.0, 0.1]) -- what are the resulting probabilities and the cross-entropy loss against true class 0?
What is the sigmoid derivative formula, and its maximum value?
flashcards.a: sigma'(z) = sigma(z)(1 - sigma(z)); maximum value 0.25, occurring at z=0 where sigma(0)=0.5.

flashcards.q: What are the Xavier and He initialization variance formulas, and why does He use double Xavier's variance?
flashcards.a: Xavier: Var(W)=2/(fan_in+fan_out). He: Var(W)=2/fan_in. He doubles it because ReLU zeroes ~half its inputs, halving variance unless compensated.

flashcards.q: For a 784->256 linear layer, what are the Xavier and He initialization stds?
What dimension does BatchNorm normalize across vs LayerNorm, and why do transformers default to LayerNorm/RMSNorm?
flashcards.a: BatchNorm normalizes across the batch, per feature (batch-size-dependent, needs running stats at inference). LayerNorm normalizes across features, per example (batch-independent) -- essential for transformers' variable-length sequences and small/streaming batch sizes.

flashcards.q: What does RMSNorm change relative to LayerNorm?
flashcards.a: It skips mean-centering entirely, normalizing only by root-mean-square: x_hat = x/sqrt(mean(x^2)+eps). Cheaper, and empirically matches LayerNorm quality in large transformer stacks (e.g. LLaMA-family).

flashcards.q: Why does Adam need bias correction, illustrated with a constant gradient?
flashcards.a: With g=1.0, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999: bias-corrected m_hat/v_hat equal exactly 1.0 at every step, but the UNcorrected ratio drifts from 3.16x too large at t=1 upward, since beta2=0.999 needs ~1000 steps to warm up vs beta1's ~10 steps -- an uncontrolled early step-size artifact without correction.

flashcards.q: What bug does AdamW fix relative to Adam-with-L2-regularization?
flashcards.a: Folding weight decay into the gradient couples it to Adam's adaptive scaling: params with large v_hat get proportionally LESS effective decay. AdamW applies wd directly (theta -= lr*(...+wd*theta)), giving every parameter the same proportional shrinkage -- measurably improves generalization, not just speed.

flashcards.q: What does Lion trade away relative to Adam/AdamW?
flashcards.a: Lion updates by sign(momentum) with no second moment at all -- roughly halves optimizer-state memory, but every update has the same magnitude regardless of gradient scale, typically needing smaller lr and larger weight decay than AdamW.

flashcards.q: What structural idea does Muon exploit that Adam/AdamW/Lion miss?
flashcards.a: It treats weight matrices as genuinely 2D structure rather than independent scalars: after a momentum update, it applies Newton-Schulz iterations to orthogonalize the update matrix (flattening its singular value spectrum). Applied only to 2D matrices; embeddings/biases still use AdamW.

flashcards.q: What production adoption does Muon have as of 2026?
flashcards.a: Reported ~2x compute efficiency vs AdamW at compute-optimal scale; used in training Kimi K2/2.5, GLM-4.5/4.7, and DeepSeek-V4 (1.6T-param DeepSeek-V4-Pro); NVIDIA integrated Muon into Megatron Core in April 2026.

flashcards.q: Why does learning-rate warmup matter specifically for adaptive optimizers like Adam/AdamW?
flashcards.a: Even with exact bias correction, m and v are estimated from very few gradient samples early in training, giving them high variance as estimators. A large lr applied to a high-variance, still-settling estimate risks a badly-calibrated early step -- warmup addresses this variance issue, distinct from bias correction's mean-bias fix.

flashcards.q: Why does learning rate decay (cosine/step) improve final loss over a constant learning rate?
