flashcards.topic: SageMaker, Bedrock, Vertex, KServe, Ray Serve, BentoML
flashcards.q: State the Knative Pod Autoscaler's control-loop constants.
flashcards.a: 60-second stable window for average concurrency, 6-second panic window, panic mode entered when the panic window reaches 2x target concurrency, and exit from panic mode after 60 seconds of the panic condition not holding.

flashcards.topic: SageMaker, Bedrock, Vertex, KServe, Ray Serve, BentoML
flashcards.q: What is the current status of ModelMesh?
flashcards.a: Dead. Both kserve/modelmesh and kserve/modelmesh-serving were archived on 2026-04-14, the last release was v0.12.0 in July 2024, and the admin-guide/modelmesh docs page exists for KServe docs 0.16 and 0.17 but 404s on 0.18 and 0.19. The KServe landing page still advertises it, which is stale copy.

flashcards.topic: SageMaker, Bedrock, Vertex, KServe, Ray Serve, BentoML
flashcards.q: How much does prefix-cache-aware routing buy over round-robin, with the measured configuration?
flashcards.a: 3x output tokens/s and 2x lower TTFT, reported by Tesla and Red Hat serving Llama 3.1 70B on 4x MI300X with tensor-parallel-size=4, gpu-memory-utilization=0.90, --max-model-len=65536, using KServe's InferencePool plus the Gateway API Inference Extension endpoint picker.

flashcards.topic: SageMaker, Bedrock, Vertex, KServe, Ray Serve, BentoML
flashcards.q: How is model composition expressed in current Ray Serve, and what API is gone?
flashcards.a: .bind() deployments into each other's constructors; Ray converts the arguments into DeploymentHandle objects, you call methods with .remote() and await the DeploymentResponse. DAGDriver, InputNode, and serve.build are gone. Describing the old DAG DSL dates you to roughly Ray 2.5.

flashcards.topic: SageMaker, Bedrock, Vertex, KServe, Ray Serve, BentoML
flashcards.q: Which two Ray Serve defaults changed in Ray 2.32.0 and what breaks on upgrade?
flashcards.a: max_ongoing_requests dropped from 100 to 5 (a 20x cut in per-replica admission) and target_ongoing_requests moved from 1.0 to 2.0. The symptom on upgrade is BackPressureError on handles or HTTP 503 on the proxy with GPUs at low utilization, because the bottleneck is admission control rather than compute.

flashcards.topic: SageMaker, Bedrock, Vertex, KServe, Ray Serve, BentoML
flashcards.q: List the key Ray Serve autoscaling defaults.
flashcards.a: num_replicas 1; target_ongoing_requests 2; max_ongoing_requests 5; min_replicas 1 and max_replicas 1; upscale_delay_s 30; downscale_delay_s 600 (also governs 1 to 0); metrics_interval_s 10; look_back_period_s 30; max_queued_requests -1 (unbounded); health check 10s period / 30s timeout; graceful shutdown 2s wait / 20s timeout.

flashcards.topic: SageMaker, Bedrock, Vertex, KServe, Ray Serve, BentoML
flashcards.q: When is Ray Serve the right choice, and when is it a mistake?
flashcards.a: Right when one logical request fans out across models on different hardware with different scaling curves (CPU retriever, GPU reranker, GPU generator) as independently scaled deployments in one app. A mistake for a single model behind a single endpoint: you inherit a Ray head node as a new coordination failure domain and a second scheduler that disagrees with Kubernetes, for nothing a Deployment plus vLLM's OpenAI server does not give you.

flashcards.topic: SageMaker, Bedrock, Vertex, KServe, Ray Serve, BentoML
flashcards.q: What layer does BentoML occupy, and what is its 2026 governance status?
flashcards.a: Layer 3, packaging: @bentoml.service / @bentoml.api(batchable=True), bentoml build produces a Bento, bentoml containerize produces an OCI image, serves on port 3000. It competes with your Dockerfile, not with KServe, and still needs a scheduler. It was acquired by Modular (forum.modular.com hosts an acquisition roundup thread dated 2026-03-01) and the last OSS release is v1.4.39 from 2026-05-07.

flashcards.topic: SageMaker, Bedrock, Vertex, KServe, Ray Serve, BentoML
flashcards.q: Why is GPU utilization the wrong autoscaling signal for a vLLM replica, and what is right?
flashcards.a: A replica at 95% GPU with an empty waiting queue is healthy and must not scale; one at 40% GPU with 200 requests waiting is saturated on KV cache and must. Request count is also bad because output lengths vary by two orders of magnitude. Scale on vllm:num_requests_waiting or KV-cache pool occupancy (vllm:gpu_cache_usage_perc), which requires the KEDA/Prometheus path.

flashcards.topic: SageMaker, Bedrock, Vertex, KServe, Ray Serve, BentoML
flashcards.q: Break down the cold-start chain for a scaled-to-zero GPU endpoint and name the biggest lever.
flashcards.a: Detect, schedule a GPU node (90-180s if the autoscaler must launch one), pull an 8-15 GB CUDA image (60-200s cold), fetch weights (16 GB for an 8B is ~20s, 140 GB for a 70B is ~140s at 1 GB/s), then CUDA graph capture and KV pool allocation (20-90s). Roughly 30-60s for an 8B on a warm node, 8-15 minutes for a 70B cold. Biggest lever is weight pre-staging on node-local NVMe (KServe LocalModelCache / LocalModelNamespaceCache) plus image pre-pull.

flashcards.topic: SageMaker, Bedrock, Vertex, KServe, Ray Serve, BentoML
flashcards.q: Why do multi-model endpoints work for small models but not LLMs, and what replaces them?
flashcards.a: MME assumes a model load is cheap relative to a request: a 50 MB tree ensemble loads in ~100ms against a ~5ms invocation. An 8B fp16 model is 16 GB and loads in tens of seconds, and density packing fights the KV cache for the same VRAM (vLLM claims gpu_memory_utilization=0.90 deliberately). For LLMs you keep one base model resident and vary the LoRA adapter per request.

flashcards.topic: SageMaker, Bedrock, Vertex, KServe, Ray Serve, BentoML
flashcards.q: What changed in KServe v0.18 regarding multi-node inference and Ray?
flashcards.a: Multi-node inference no longer requires a Ray head node: vLLM's mp (multiprocessing) distributed executor backend can be selected via a multinode/executor-backend annotation on the ServingRuntime, with node count derived from pipeline parallelism and GPUs-per-node from tensor parallelism. v0.18 also added LeaderWorkerSet as an autoscaling target so a multi-node replica scales as one unit.

flashcards.topic: SageMaker, Bedrock, Vertex, KServe, Ray Serve, BentoML
flashcards.q: What is the status of TorchServe?
flashcards.a: Archived. The pytorch/serve README states the project is no longer actively maintained, with no planned updates, bug fixes, new features, or security patches, and warns that vulnerabilities may not be addressed. Last push was 2025-08-06. Proposing it for new work in 2026 is disqualifying.

flashcards.topic: SageMaker, Bedrock, Vertex, KServe, Ray Serve, BentoML
flashcards.q: Why is round-robin routing in front of vLLM actively harmful?
flashcards.a: It splits the prefix cache. With a shared system prompt, one replica holds the prefilled prefix and the others do not, so a fraction of requests pay full prefill, which is the compute-bound half of inference. The observable symptom is p99 doubling when you add a replica while p50 stays flat. Check vllm:prefix_cache_hit_rate.

flashcards.q: What question does each of RBAC, ABAC, and ReBAC answer, and what is each one's failure mode?
flashcards.a: RBAC: 'what may this JOB FUNCTION do' -- cheapest and trivially auditable, fails by role explosion. ABAC: 'under what CONDITIONS' -- kills role explosion, fails because access is computed not stored so 'who can see X?' is O(all subjects). ReBAC: 'what RELATIONSHIP does this user have to this OBJECT' -- native cheap reverse query, fails on time-of-day / IP / MFA-level which are not relationships. They compose; they do not compete.

flashcards.q: Why is role explosion arithmetic rather than sloppiness, and what is the real fix?
flashcards.a: Role count is the PRODUCT of every dimension you encode into roles: 3 job functions x 4 regions x 3 environments x 2 data classifications = 72 roles for one conceptual job. The observable symptom is roles growing faster than headcount. The fix is not consolidation -- it is moving the exploding dimension out of the role into an attribute condition or a relationship, keeping RBAC only for the genuinely static coarse function.

flashcards.q: Give Zanzibar's production numbers from the USENIX ATC 2019 paper.
flashcards.a: More than 2 trillion relation tuples occupying ~100 TB. More than 10 million client QPS aggregate: Check peaking ~4.2M, Read 8.2M, Expand 760K, Write 25K. p95 latency under 10 ms. Availability above 99.999% over 3 years. More than 10,000 servers in several dozen clusters, median ~500 per cluster, fully replicated to more than 30 locations.

flashcards.q: What is Zanzibar's data model and its two userset rewrite rules?
flashcards.a: One tuple type: object#relation@subject, where the subject may itself be a userset like group:eng#member. Rewrites: computed_userset means a relation includes members of another relation on the SAME object (owners are editors, editors are viewers); tuple_to_userset means follow a relation to a parent object and check a relation there (a doc's viewers include its parent folder's viewers). Check is a graph traversal over that.

flashcards.q: State both flavors of the new enemy problem.
flashcards.a: 1) ACL updates applied OUT OF ORDER: Alice removes Bob from a folder, then adds a secret doc to it; a replica applying the second write first lets Bob read the doc. 2) OLD ACL applied to NEW CONTENT: Alice removes Bob from a doc, then adds sensitive content; if the content read is authorized against a pre-removal ACL snapshot, Bob reads the new content under the old permission.

flashcards.q: How does the zookie solve the new enemy problem, and why not just use strong consistency everywhere?
flashcards.a: A zookie is an opaque consistency token carrying a Spanner timestamp. The content store records it when content is written; subsequent Check calls pass it, and Zanzibar guarantees evaluation at a snapshot no earlier than that timestamp. Causal order between content and ACL updates is preserved while Zanzibar remains free to pick any LATER timestamp, which is what keeps caches hot. Strong consistency everywhere would destroy the cache and couple every check to global commit latency at 4.2M Check QPS -- so the freshness requirement was pushed into the request instead.

flashcards.q: Name the five rungs of the tenant-isolation enforcement ladder, weakest to strongest.
flashcards.a: 1) Hand-written WHERE tenant_id = ? (dies at the first background job). 2) ORM global scope (dies at raw SQL and admin tools). 3) Postgres RLS with FORCE plus SET LOCAL in an explicit transaction (the realistic target). 4) Per-tenant credentials or STS session tags (enforcement OUTSIDE the buggy process). 5) Silo, separate DB or account (dies at your ops budget, roughly 50 tenants). Every real cross-tenant leak is a path that skipped the rung the rest of the system stands on.

flashcards.q: You enabled RLS and wrote a policy, but it filters nothing. What is the #1 cause?
flashcards.a: The application connects as the role that OWNS the tables, and table owners bypass RLS by default. It is silent: the policy exists, ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is on, and every row comes back. Fix with ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and separate the migration role (owner) from the runtime role. Other candidates: the role is superuser or has BYPASSRLS (the built-in postgres role has it and it cannot be removed).

flashcards.q: Tenant A intermittently sees tenant B's rows, only under load. Diagnose.
flashcards.a: SET app.tenant_id (session-scoped) combined with a pooler in transaction pooling mode. The setting survives on the backend connection past the transaction, so the next request borrowing that connection inherits the previous tenant's context. It only shows under load because that is when connection reuse actually happens. Fix: SET LOCAL / set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true) inside an EXPLICIT transaction, plus a fail-closed assertion when no tenant context is set.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between USING and WITH CHECK in an RLS policy, and what breaks if you omit WITH CHECK?
flashcards.a: USING filters reads and the PRE-image of a write. WITH CHECK validates the POST-image of INSERT/UPDATE. Omit WITH CHECK and a tenant can run UPDATE ... SET tenant_id = <other tenant>, because the row was visible before the change and nothing validates it afterward. That is a write-side cross-tenant leak that read-side testing looks clean on.

flashcards.q: Name the two PostgreSQL CVEs that show RLS is not a complete boundary.
flashcards.a: CVE-2024-10976: incomplete tracking of tables with row security meant a reused query plan referenced below a subquery, WITH query, security-invoker view, or SQL-language function could view or change different rows than intended when the user ID changed. CVE-2025-8713 (disclosed 14-Aug-2025, fixed in 17.6/16.10/15.14/14.19/13.22): optimizer statistics -- histograms and most-common-values lists -- let a user read sampled data RLS intended to hide, via a crafted leaky operator. RLS constrains query RESULTS, not everything the planner will tell you about the data.

flashcards.q: List the cross-tenant leak surfaces that RLS does not cover.
flashcards.a: Cache keys without a tenant prefix; background workers running outside tenant context with an admin connection; search indexes filtered AFTER top-K instead of inside the index; object storage prefixes without a per-tenant IAM boundary; sequential IDs plus a missing object-level check (BOLA); 404-vs-403 differences acting as an existence oracle; and in multi-tenant LLM serving, a shared prefix/KV cache acting as a timing side channel across tenants.

flashcards.q: What is BOLA, why is it #1 in the API Top 10, and do UUIDs fix it?
flashcards.a: API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization: an endpoint takes an object id, fetches the object, and never checks the authenticated caller is entitled to THAT object. It is the API framing of A01 Broken Access Control (#1 in the web Top 10, 40 CWEs, 3.73% avg incidence). It is #1 because it is the default outcome of the most natural handler shape. UUIDs do NOT fix it: they raise enumeration cost and change nothing about authorization; a leaked, logged, or referrer-exposed id is still a working key.

flashcards.q: Describe NIST SP 800-207's architectural decomposition.
flashcards.a: A Policy Engine makes the decision and a Policy Administrator establishes or tears down the session credential; together they form the PDP. A Policy Enforcement Point sits in the data path in front of EVERY resource. The PE reads from identity management, device posture/CDM, PKI, activity logs, threat intel, and data access policy. Published August 2020. Every product a vendor sells you is one of those three boxes.

flashcards.q: What Zero Trust is actually deployed at scale in 2026 versus what SP 800-207 describes?
flashcards.a: Deployed: identity-aware proxies replacing VPN for internal apps (the BeyondCorp pattern), mTLS with SPIFFE/SPIRE workload identity in service meshes, device posture as a factor at authentication, and short-lived scoped credentials. Described but largely NOT deployed: continuous per-request policy re-evaluation against live risk telemetry. Most deployments evaluate richly at session establishment and then coast on a token for its lifetime.

flashcards.q: Does a completed Zero Trust rollout close your Broken Access Control risk?
flashcards.a: No, and this is the key point. Zero trust is about the NETWORK and the SESSION; object-level authorization is about the ROW. Full mTLS, device posture, identity-aware proxies, and per-session credentials do not stop GET /api/documents/8123 from returning another tenant's document when the handler fetches by id and forgets the ownership check. The PEP authorizes access to the SERVICE; A01 and BOLA live entirely behind it.

flashcards.q: Compare centralized PDP, sidecar, and in-query authorization.
flashcards.a: In-query (RLS, predicate pushdown): strongest guarantee because a code path that does not know the check exists still gets it; limited to what a SQL predicate can express. Sidecar (the OPA pattern): sub-millisecond decisions, no availability coupling, at the cost of policy distribution and N possibly-divergent copies. Centralized PDP: one auditable place to change policy, costs ~1-5 ms per decision plus a hard availability dependency. Large systems run all three at different layers; the skill is deciding which CLASS of decision goes where.

flashcards.q: Your PDP adds 4 ms p50 and you make 12 authorization calls per request. Fix it in order.
flashcards.a: 1) Batch -- every Zanzibar-derived system exposes a bulk check, so 12 calls become one. 2) Invert the query -- if you are checking 12 objects to render a list you wanted ListObjects (what can this user see), which also fixes the pagination bug where post-filtering returns short pages. 3) Cache with a bounded staleness and a real invalidation signal (SpiceDB's Watch API exists for this). Only after those three consider moving to a sidecar.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT deploy a Zanzibar-style ReBAC system?
flashcards.a: When the product has no user-to-user sharing. If permissions are 'your org's members see your org's data' and nothing else, you needed RBAC plus a tenant predicate, and you have added a distributed database, a consistency model, and an on-call rotation to solve a WHERE clause. The honest trigger for ReBAC is per-object grants with inheritance, or a genuine need for the reverse query.

flashcards.q: What is the AWS dynamically-scoped credential pattern, and what does Lambda tenant isolation mode add?
flashcards.a: Call sts:AssumeRole with a session tag carrying the tenant id, then condition the IAM policy on aws:PrincipalTag/tenant (for example against dynamodb:LeadingKeys), so the credential the code holds physically cannot reach another tenant's data even when the query is wrong -- rung 4 implemented in IAM, outside the buggy process. Lambda tenant isolation mode (announced Nov-2025, all regions except ap-southeast New Zealand, GovCloud, and China): pass a tenant identifier at invoke and Lambda guarantees an execution environment is never reused across tenants. Cost: cold starts multiply by active tenant count, so it fits high-value low-cardinality tenants and not a long tail.

flashcards.q: How does authorization change when an AI agent acts on a user's behalf?
flashcards.a: The request no longer has one principal. The decision becomes an intersection: the agent may do X only if the USER may do X, AND the agent's own delegated grant permits X, AND context conditions hold. The working pieces: per-agent identity rather than sharing the user's credential, a delegated short-TTL credential scoped to a subset of the user's permissions (OAuth token exchange, RFC 8693, is the closest standard), tool allowlisting at the gateway rather than in the prompt, and human confirmation on irreversible actions. Re-delegation to sub-agents has no standard answer: mint sub-agent credentials from the original user grant with strictly smaller scope, never pass the parent's credential down.

flashcards.q: What are the two NEW categories and the one consolidation in OWASP Top 10:2025?
flashcards.a: New: A03 Software Supply Chain Failures (expanded from 2021's A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components) and A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions (24 CWEs, fail-open and improper error handling). Consolidation: SSRF, which was its own A10:2021 category, folded into A01 Broken Access Control.

flashcards.q: Injection fell from #3 to #5 in 2025. Why, and does it mean SQLi got less dangerous?
flashcards.a: No. Injection has 62,445 CVEs, the most of any category, and 100% max coverage (everyone tests for it). Its average weighted impact of 4.32 is dragged down because 30,000+ high-frequency/low-impact XSS CVEs share the category with 14,000+ low-frequency/high-impact SQLi CVEs. The rank moved on category composition, not on real-world danger. Avg weighted exploit is still 7.15.

flashcards.q: What is the OWASP Top 10:2025 methodology, in numbers?
flashcards.a: 8th edition. Data on 2.8M applications from 13 named contributors, 589 CWEs analyzed (vs ~400 in 2021, ~30 in 2017), 248 CWEs inside the 10 categories out of 968 in MITRE's dictionary, ~175k CVE-to-CWE records for exploit/impact. Cap of 40 CWEs per category, average 25. Eight categories come from the data; two are voted in by a community survey. CVSS v4 was excluded because it no longer exposes separable exploit and impact subscores.

flashcards.q: What is 'incidence rate' in the OWASP ranking, and why does it ignore frequency?
flashcards.a: The percentage of tested applications with at least one instance of a CWE. Frequency is deliberately ignored because manual testers report a finding once while automated scanners report every instance, so counting instances would measure tooling rather than prevalence.

flashcards.q: What can a bind parameter never replace, and why?
flashcards.a: Identifiers and keywords: table names, column names, ORDER BY direction. The query is parsed and planned at Parse time, before Bind, and the planner needs those tokens to build the plan. Anything you cannot bind must come from a set the server controls (an allowlist), not from a regex.

flashcards.q: What does cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM docs ORDER BY %s', ('created_at',)) actually produce?
flashcards.a: ORDER BY 'created_at' -- sorting by a constant string. It is not injectable and it raises no error; it silently returns an unsorted result set. That silence is why the next commit is usually an f-string. Fix with a server-controlled allowlist plus sql.Identifier().

flashcards.q: Describe what a bind parameter physically does on the wire in PostgreSQL.
flashcards.a: Client sends Parse with SQL text containing $1 placeholders; the server lexes, parses, and plans it once. Client sends Bind with parameter values as a length-prefixed array, then Execute. Parameter bytes never reach the SQL lexer, so no byte sequence can terminate a literal and start a statement. That is why parameterization is a structural guarantee and escaping is best-effort.

flashcards.q: What is second-order SQL injection and why does input sanitization not stop it?
flashcards.a: The payload is stored through a safe parameterized path as literal text, then concatenated into a query later by a different code path (report job, admin tool, migration). Sanitization fails because the value was never malformed on input; it is only dangerous at the second sink. The correct model is parameterize on OUTPUT at every interpreter boundary. Data from your own database is attacker data with higher latency.

flashcards.q: How fast can boolean-blind vs time-based SQLi extract a 60-character bcrypt hash?
flashcards.a: Boolean-blind binary-searches printable ASCII at roughly 7 requests per character: ~420 requests, about 21 seconds at 20 rps. Time-based costs ~7 sleeps x 5s = ~35s per character, so ~35 minutes. That is why time-based is used to CONFIRM the vulnerability and boolean or UNION is used to EXTRACT.

flashcards.q: What does blind SQL injection look like in production logs?
flashcards.a: Time-based: p50 latency on one route quantized to multiples of the sleep interval (pg_sleep(5), SLEEP(5), WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5') with all responses HTTP 200. Boolean-blind: thousands of 200s on one route where the response body alternates between exactly two byte lengths. UNION probing: a run of ORDER BY 1, 2, 3... then UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,... with increasing NULL counts. Out-of-band: DNS queries leaving the DB subnet to a domain you do not own.

flashcards.q: What does CVE-2025-1094 prove about escaping as a SQLi defense?
flashcards.a: PostgreSQL's own escaping APIs (PQescapeLiteral, PQescapeIdentifier, PQescapeString, PQescapeStringConn) failed to neutralize quoting syntax on text that fails UTF-8 validation. CVSS 8.1, fixed 13-Feb-2025 in 17.3/16.7/15.11/14.16/13.19, then the FIX REGRESSED and needed 17.4/16.8/15.12/14.17/13.20 on 20-Feb-2025. Rapid7 found it because exploiting CVE-2024-12356 (BeyondTrust) to RCE required it; that chain reached the US Treasury. If your defense is 'we escape correctly,' your defense is a dependency on someone else's parser edge cases.

flashcards.q: Name the three ways an ORM still gets you SQL injection.
flashcards.a: 1) Escape hatches: .raw(), .extra(), RawSQL(), session.execute(text(f'...')), and Hibernate HQL concatenation which has its own CWE-564. 2) Identifier positions the ORM emits from user input -- CVE-2024-42005 was Django's QuerySet.values()/values_list() on a JSONField using a crafted JSON key unescaped as a COLUMN ALIAS (fixed 4.2.15 / 5.0.8). 3) Dynamic field names passed as **kwargs filters, which is authorization bypass landing in the same incident review.

flashcards.q: How do you handle an IN clause and a LIKE pattern safely?
flashcards.a: IN: never build '(1,2,3)' with str.join. Use '= ANY(%s)' with a real Python list (Postgres), or one placeholder per element. LIKE: the value binds safely, but % and _ in user input become wildcards -- escape them. That is not injection, it is a logic bug and a wildcard-scan DoS (a leading % prevents index use).

flashcards.q: What is the correct SQLi remediation ORDER, and where does a WAF sit?
flashcards.a: 1) Parameterize values, allowlist identifiers, enforce with a CI rule not review. 2) Drop the app DB role to least privilege (converts every finding from 'read everything' to 'read what this service owns'). 3) Suppress DB errors to clients (kills error-based extraction). 4) Authorization at the data-access layer. 5) Pin and scan dependencies. 6) Only then a WAF. A WAF is mitigation, never remediation: comment insertion, case shifting, encodings, and MySQL versioned comments all bypass signatures.

flashcards.q: Why is LLM01 Prompt Injection unsolved, mechanically?
flashcards.a: Every injection defense that works uses TWO transport channels so the interpreter cannot re-parse data as grammar: Parse/Bind for SQL, argv for shells, DOM APIs for HTML. A transformer has ONE token stream -- system prompt, user turn, retrieved chunk, and tool output are all attended to by the same mechanism. There is no Bind message for attention, so there is no way to mark a span as data-not-instructions that the model cannot be argued out of.

flashcards.q: What does EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) prove about prompt-injection classifiers?
flashcards.a: CVSS 9.3, June 2025, zero-click against Microsoft 365 Copilot: a single crafted email bypassed Microsoft's purpose-built XPIA (Cross-Prompt Injection Attempt) classifier, evaded link redaction using reference-style Markdown, exfiltrated via an auto-fetched image, and routed the callback through a Teams proxy already allowlisted in the CSP. The vendor with the most at stake shipped the classifier and it fell to four chained ordinary web bugs. Classifiers are a layer, not a boundary.

flashcards.q: What was CVE-2026-42208 and what does it teach about the AI stack?
flashcards.a: Pre-authentication SQL injection in LiteLLM, CVSS 9.3, versions 1.81.16 through 1.83.6, patched 1.83.7-stable. The raw Authorization: Bearer header value was concatenated into SQL on the key-verification path, so every LLM route was an entry point and none required credentials. Exploited within 36 hours of GitHub advisory indexing, 17 UNION payloads, targeting LiteLLM_VerificationToken / litellm_credentials / litellm_config. CISA KEV 8-May-2026, FCEB deadline 11-May-2026. Patching is not done: rotate every upstream provider key.

flashcards.q: List the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 (ASI01-ASI10).
flashcards.a: ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack, ASI02 Tool Misuse and Exploitation, ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse, ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities, ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution (RCE), ASI06 Memory and Context Poisoning, ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication, ASI08 Cascading Failures, ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation, ASI10 Rogue Agents. Published 9-Dec-2025 with 100+ contributors.

flashcards.q: What is the agent security posture, ordered by value per unit of effort?
flashcards.a: Gateway-enforced tool allowlist (not a prompt instruction -- the prompt is the thing under attack); step + token + wall-clock budget; no high-risk tool available in the same turn as a read of untrusted external content; human confirmation on irreversible actions; per-agent identity with short-lived scoped credentials (highest value, slowest to ship); full prompt-to-action traces. If you can only do two in a week: gateway allowlist and the budget.

flashcards.q: How do you ship text-to-SQL without building an RCE service?
flashcards.a: Dedicated read-only DB role scoped to specific views, no base tables; parse the generated SQL and reject anything that is not a single SELECT (no semicolon-separated statements, no filesystem/network functions); a tenant predicate injected by your code, not requested in the prompt; statement_timeout and a row cap; results rendered as escaped text. 'The prompt says only generate SELECT' is a hint to the model, not a control. If the product needs writes, the model proposes a diff and a human approves it.

flashcards.q: Why does the Incident Commander never touch a terminal?
flashcards.a: Coordination and diagnosis each consume full attention, and the coordinator's failure is silent. The IC tracks who is doing what, what has been ruled out, when the next comms update is due, and whether a mitigation is safe. The moment they debug, all of that halts and nobody notices for ~20 minutes. Observable symptom: the incident channel goes quiet for 6+ minutes, then resumes as a deep technical thread with no status line.

flashcards.q: Name the four ICS-derived incident roles and the specific failure each prevents.
flashcards.a: Incident Commander (prevents parallel uncoordinated remediation: three people changing three things, nobody knows which fixed or broke it). Operations Lead, the only person making prod changes (prevents the untracked change). Communications Lead (prevents a status page 55 minutes stale while the channel has 300 messages). Scribe (prevents an unreconstructable timeline). Scale DOWN to one person at Sev3; never double up at Sev1, because the role that silently drops is always Scribe.

flashcards.q: State mitigate-before-diagnose and the three cases where it is wrong.
flashcards.a: Default: stop impact, don't understand it. Menu executable without knowing the cause: roll back, flag off, fail over, shed load, scale, restart; most reversible in under 60s. Inverts when (a) the mitigation is irreversible or data-destructive (failover with unknown replication lag loses unreplicated writes), (b) you cannot state the mitigation's own blast radius, which is a diagnosis problem in disguise, (c) the suspect is a stateful in-flight operation such as a half-applied schema migration.

flashcards.q: What are the four parts of a status update written at minute 6 with no known cause?
flashcards.a: What users see, when it started, what we are doing, and when the next update will come. No cause until confirmed, no ETA to resolution, no speculation. The next-update-by promise is the load-bearing element: it is what stops the 'any update?' traffic that otherwise consumes the IC. Example: 'Since 14:12 UTC, a portion of requests to /v1/search are returning HTTP 500. Other endpoints are unaffected. We are investigating. Next update by 14:45 UTC.'

flashcards.q: Symptom alert vs cause alert: which pages, and what is the one legitimate exception?
flashcards.a: Symptoms page; causes go to dashboards or tickets. A cause alert ('CPU on host-7 at 92%') both fires when nobody is harmed and misses breakage whose cause you never instrumented. A symptom alert ('fraction of /v1/search under 400ms dropped below SLO burn threshold') catches causes you have never seen. Exception: slow, predictable resource saturation, where you alert on the projection ('reaches 100% in under 4 hours at current rate') and route to a ticket, not the pager.

flashcards.q: Error budget arithmetic: what does 99.9% over 30 days give you, and what is burn rate?
flashcards.a: Error budget = 1 - SLO. 99.9% over 30 days = 0.1% of requests, about 43.2 minutes of full unavailability. Burn rate N is the multiple of nominal consumption: at burn rate 1 you exhaust the budget exactly at the window's end; at 14.4 you exhaust it in 1/14.4 of the window.

flashcards.q: Give the Google SRE Workbook's three multiwindow multi-burn-rate alert tiers.
flashcards.a: 14.4x burn over a 1-hour long window with a 5-minute short window, 2% of budget consumed, PAGE. 6x over 6 hours with a 30-minute short window, 5% consumed, PAGE. 1x over 3 days with a 6-hour short window, 10% consumed, TICKET. Both windows must breach for the alert to fire; the short window exists so a recovered incident clears the page in minutes rather than leaving it lit for hours.

flashcards.q: What is the target pager load, and what is the metric almost nobody tracks?
flashcards.a: At most about 2 paging events per 8-to-12-hour shift (Google SRE Book), and the stated reason is operational: above that, incidents stop being investigated properly and postmortems stop happening. The untracked metric is actionability rate: of pages in the last 90 days, what fraction produced a corrective human action. Under ~50% the pager is training people to ignore it, and the symptom is median ack drifting from ~2 minutes to ~11 minutes.

flashcards.q: Why is 'human error' never a root cause, and what is the replacement question?
flashcards.a: It terminates the investigation where it should start. Three defects: not actionable (no code change corresponds to 'be more careful'), counterfactual (it describes a world where the alert was not the fortieth firing that hour), and predicts nothing, since the next person with the same tool and information makes the same choice. Replacement question (Allspaw): what made the wrong path look like the right path from where they stood, with what they actually knew?

flashcards.q: How did AWS write up the February 2017 S3 outage without blaming the engineer?
flashcards.a: At 09:37 PST an authorised engineer following an established playbook mistyped an input and removed more capacity than intended, taking down the index and placement subsystems; GET/LIST/DELETE returned 13:18, PUT 13:54 (~4 hours). AWS wrote that the tool allowed too much capacity to be removed too quickly, then modified it to remove capacity more slowly, added a safeguard preventing removal below any subsystem's minimum required capacity, and audited every other operational tool for the same missing check. The finding is a property of the tool: testable, and it generalises to tools nobody has mistyped yet.

flashcards.q: Cloudflare, 18 November 2025: what was the causal chain and the key timeline numbers?
flashcards.a: 11:05 a ClickHouse grant change made previously implicit access to the r0 database explicit. A Bot Management feature-file generator queried system.columns without filtering on database name, so it started returning r0's columns too, more than doubling rows. The file exceeded the bot module's hard limit of 200 features (normal usage ~60), hitting an unhandled Rust Result and panicking with 'thread fl2_worker_thread panicked: called Result::unwrap() on an Err value'. 11:28 impact starts, 11:31 automated detection, 11:35 incident call, 11:32-13:05 chasing the wrong hypothesis (Workers KV), 14:30 main impact resolved, 17:06 all clear.

flashcards.q: What is the 'saw-tooth' lesson from the Cloudflare November 2025 outage?
flashcards.a: The feature file regenerated every 5 minutes while the ClickHouse cluster was updated node by node, so the file was sometimes good and sometimes bad and the system repeatedly recovered and failed. That oscillation read as an attack, and the team believed they might be facing a hyper-scale DDoS. The generalisable rule: when a system oscillates between healthy and broken on a fixed period, look for a periodic job, not an adversary. A five-minute oscillation is a five-minute cron.

flashcards.q: GitHub, 21 October 2018: what is the number that carries the whole lesson?
flashcards.a: 43 seconds of network partition produced 24 hours 11 minutes of degraded service. During planned optical-equipment maintenance the East Coast primary accepted writes that had not replicated West; Orchestrator promoted the West Coast cluster, creating a split write set. The overwhelming majority of the incident was not fixing a broken system but safely reconciling data, a deliberate choice of consistency over availability. The technical fault self-healed in 43 seconds; the decision cost 24 hours.

flashcards.q: What are the two structural problems with Five Whys, and what replaces it?
flashcards.a: It walks a single chain backwards, forcing a single-cause model onto a multi-factor event, and because each step narrows it converges reliably on either a person or a platitude. Allspaw's 2014 critique (drawing on Dekker, Conklin, Leveson) is that the danger is the confident sensation of having found THE cause. Replacement: a causal graph. Draw the failure, draw every condition that had to hold, recurse, stop at conditions you can change, then rank nodes by how many downstream paths a fix cuts. Chain is still fine for a Sev3; graph for Sev1.

flashcards.q: What does 'blameless' actually mean, and where does it legitimately break down?
flashcards.a: The account you give in the postmortem carries no punitive consequence. The reason is epistemic, not emotional: the person who took the triggering action is the only one who knows what their screen showed and what they believed, and if that account is dangerous to give you get a sanitised timeline and every downstream conclusion is built on corrupted data. It breaks down in security incidents with a possible insider component, regulated environments with legal reporting duties, and deliberate policy circumvention. The workable split: the technical postmortem stays blameless, any accountability process runs separately and is not fed by it, and everyone is told this up front.

flashcards.q: Why do postmortem action items fail to get done, and what is the fix?
flashcards.a: Four consistent causes: owned by a team rather than a named individual; living only in the postmortem doc and never entering the backlog where they compete with feature work; phrased so they cannot be completed ('improve monitoring'); and too many, since a postmortem with 14 items completes about 3. Fix: cap Sev1 at 5 ranked items, each with a named person, a real ticket, and a date, plus an explicit 'considered and not doing' list. Health metric: fraction of incidents in the last 12 months whose contributing factors recur from an earlier one; above ~20% the action items are not landing.

flashcards.q: Probability-of-recurrence vs cost-of-recurrence action items: which is under-prioritised and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: Probability items reduce the chance of the same bug (the validation, the test, the type change). Cost items reduce the damage next time (the alert, the runbook, the kill switch, the canary, the graceful-degradation path). Cost items are systematically under-prioritised because they feel less like fixing the bug, yet they are usually cheaper and generalise to failures nobody has imagined. Cloudflare's highest-value fix was not the query filter, it was making the bot module fall back to last-known-good instead of panicking, which converts an entire class of bad-config events from a global outage into a stale-config degradation.

flashcards.q: How do you size an on-call rotation, and what makes follow-the-sun fail?
flashcards.a: Primary rotation of 6-8: below 5 the shift frequency drives attrition, above 10 people lose tooling familiarity and spend the first 40 minutes of each incident relearning it. Secondary covers missed acks and escalation only; routine secondary engagement means pager load is too high. The team that owns the code carries its pager, always. Follow-the-sun needs about 3 regions with genuinely duplicated expertise; with 2 you get all the handoff cost and none of the sleep benefit, and an in-flight incident crossing a boundary with no state transfer restarts diagnosis from zero.

flashcards.q: What does a proper on-call handoff contain?
flashcards.a: A 10-minute overlapping synchronous conversation, not an async end-of-shift message, plus a written note covering: open incidents and the current hypothesis for each, anything degraded but not incident-worthy, alerts that fired and were dismissed along with the reason, deploys in flight or frozen, and anything expected to fire in the next shift.

flashcards.q: Why does 'tell me about your worst outage' fail most staff candidates?
flashcards.a: They narrate the debugging (the metric, the log line, the config change, the recovery) instead of the decisions. That demonstrates only that you can debug, which the interviewer already assumed, so it caps you at senior. The staff-level answer leads with quantified impact, then the decision points: when you declared and on what evidence, what you chose not to investigate, what you told customers at minute 12 while still not knowing the cause, and what system change made the failure class cheaper afterwards.

flashcards.q: What are the five sections of a Nygard ADR?
flashcards.a: Title (short noun phrase), Context (value-neutral facts, forces in tension), Decision ("We will...", active voice), Status (proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded by ADR-NNN), Consequences (all of them, positive and negative). One to two pages, kept in-repo at doc/arch/adr-NNN.md. Original post: Michael Nygard, 15 November 2011.

flashcards.q: ADR vs design doc: what is the actual difference?
flashcards.a: Timing and mutability. A design doc is a mutable, pre-decision proposal that argues among options to build consensus, and its reader can still change the outcome. An ADR is an immutable post-decision record whose reader is an engineer years later asking "what were they thinking". A large design doc typically produces two or three ADRs as output.

flashcards.q: Why are ADRs superseded rather than edited?
flashcards.a: The value of the archive is a faithful record of what the team believed at the time, with the information it had. Editing in place produces a corpus in which the team was always right, teaches nothing about how decisions get made, and destroys the constraint set that no longer exists. Write a new ADR, flip the old one's Status to "superseded by ADR-NNN", never renumber and never reuse a number.

flashcards.q: Where do rejected alternatives go in an ADR?
flashcards.a: Inside Context, as forces in tension. An ADR has no alternatives section because it is recording, not arguing. The rival appears as a force ("Weaviate's HNSW is faster on our query shape: p99 45ms against 70ms") and the Decision explains what outweighed it. If you need a comparison table, you are writing a design doc.

flashcards.q: What is a non-goal, and what is the classic wrong example?
flashcards.a: A non-goal is something that could reasonably have been a goal and was deliberately excluded, with the reason and ideally the condition to revisit. Malte Ubl's canonical example: ACID compliance in a database design. The classic wrong example is a negated goal such as "the system shouldn't crash", which is the tell that the author filled in the template without understanding it.

flashcards.q: Why is the non-goals section the highest-leverage part of a design doc?
flashcards.a: Mechanically: every reviewer arrives with a mental list of what a system like yours might do, and anything on their list not on your goals list becomes a comment thread costing 4 to 48 hours of round trip. Naming the six most likely items converts six threads into zero. On a doc with 12 reviewers that is converging in three days instead of three weeks.

flashcards.q: How do you tell an abused non-goal from a legitimate one?
flashcards.a: Would a competent reviewer accept it as a legitimate v1 boundary, or does excluding it mean the system does not actually work? "Multi-region replication is out of scope for v1, we accept a 15-minute RPO" is scoping. "Correctness under concurrent writes is a non-goal" is abdication dressed as scoping.

flashcards.q: What are the three rules for writing up an option you rejected?
flashcards.a: 1) State it at its strongest, in its advocate's words, ideally after asking them to review that paragraph. 2) Name the deciding criterion explicitly and admit it is a weighting, not a law ("we weighted operational surface above p99 because we have 4 on-call engineers and 8 services"). 3) Say what would flip the decision ("beyond ~60M vectors the answer changes"), which makes it falsifiable and tells a future team whether it has expired.

flashcards.q: What is the design-doc section order that actually gets read, and why is the order load-bearing?
flashcards.a: TL;DR, context and scope, goals, non-goals, the design (one diagram), options considered, decision, consequences, rollout, open questions, cross-cutting concerns. Order matters because a reader who hits your design before your goals evaluates it against their own goals, which produces comments that look like design objections but are actually unsurfaced goal disagreements.

flashcards.q: What length should a design doc be, per Google's stated guidance?
flashcards.a: Sweet spot 10-20 pages for a large project; an explicitly blessed 1-3 page mini design doc for incremental work, doing all the same steps more tersely. Past ~20 pages the correct move is to split the problem, not keep writing, because the marginal page is read by nobody and every unread page hides an unreviewed mistake.

flashcards.q: When is a design doc the wrong tool?
flashcards.a: When the solution is not ambiguous (Google: it becomes an implementation manual, write the code instead); when prototyping, since the prototype is how you produce the doc; when the real problem is two people who have not talked, since a doc makes positions public and harder to abandon; when it is one decision with obvious consequences (that is an ADR); when the door is cheap and two-way; and when the audience is one person.

flashcards.q: Which sections does the Rust RFC template require that most corporate templates omit?
flashcards.a: Drawbacks (framed as what the proposal forecloses, i.e. what becomes impossible later because this exists), Rationale and alternatives ("why is this design the best in the space of possible designs"), Prior art, Unresolved questions, and Future possibilities. Splitting drawbacks from alternatives forces two different kinds of honesty instead of one hedged paragraph.

flashcards.q: What operational sections does a Kubernetes KEP require that most design docs skip?
flashcards.a: Test plan, graduation criteria (alpha/beta/stable), upgrade/downgrade strategy, version skew strategy, and a Production Readiness Review questionnaire covering feature enablement and rollback, rollout planning, monitoring requirements, dependencies and scalability. This is why a KEP reads as a plan someone will be on call for rather than an architecture exercise.

flashcards.q: What does the Amazon 6-pager solve that comment-thread review does not?
flashcards.a: The participation problem. Async review lets the reviewers whose objections matter most (the busiest) skim, so approvals become social rather than technical. Twenty to twenty-five minutes of enforced silent reading at the start of the meeting guarantees they actually read it. Bezos banned PowerPoint for these reviews in 2004; the memo started at 4 pages and became 6.

flashcards.q: A doc has 60 comments and no decision after three weeks. What is the triage?
flashcards.a: Three buckets, publicly, in the doc. Blocking (correctness, security, a cost that compounds) get addressed. Non-blocking-but-worth-fixing get fixed silently. Preference with no stated cost gets one reply ("noted, going with the current approach because X") and no re-litigation. Then set a comment close date, and buy 25 minutes of synchronous time for the two or three genuinely contentious items.

flashcards.q: What is the "Yes, if" review norm and what problem does it solve?
flashcards.a: Reviewers frame objections as conditions for approval rather than rejections (Squarespace's published change to their RFC process). It changes the author's job from defending to satisfying a list, and it forces the objector to name what would actually satisfy them, which reveals how many objections have no such condition. Those were preferences.

flashcards.q: Why does Nygard insist on prose rather than bullet fragments in an ADR?
flashcards.a: Fragments let you skip the connective reasoning. "Latency concerns" hides whether you mean p50, p99, ingest or query, and a reader years later cannot recover which you meant. His guidance: bullets are acceptable for visual style, not as an excuse for sentence fragments. Write each ADR as a conversation with a future developer.

flashcards.q: You inherit a legacy platform with no decision records. What do you do?
flashcards.a: Do not backfill the archive. Backfill selectively and pain-driven: write a retroactive ADR only when someone is about to change that decision or is blocked by not understanding it, marked clearly as reconstructed. Then enforce at review: any PR reversing an architectural decision must add an ADR and flip the old Status, like a schema change requires a migration.

flashcards.q: Is a half-abandoned ADR directory better or worse than none?
flashcards.a: Worse. A directory that looks authoritative and is 80% stale actively misleads new engineers, who trust it and build on something that stopped being true. If a team cannot commit to flipping Status at review time, an append-only dated DECISIONS.md of one-paragraph entries is better, because its format does not promise currency.

flashcards.q: How does AI-assisted development change what you write down?
flashcards.a: High confidence: in-repo ADRs become agent context alongside AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md, carrying the "why" that code cannot express, which raises the value of hygiene (stable numbering, accurate Status, superseded-not-deleted) because an agent is worse than a human at inferring staleness. MADR's YAML variant (YADR, March 2026) signals machine consumption as a design constraint. Speculative: mechanical sections draft well from a prompt while goals, non-goals and the honest rejected-option argument do not, so the median doc gets longer and less informative.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: Why is CLAUDE.md length a correctness issue, not a tidiness issue?
flashcards.a: The file loads in full at every session start and is paid again on every turn, competing with the task for attention. Adherence measurably degrades as it grows, so past some length adding a rule reduces compliance with every rule. Documented target: under 200 lines.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: What belongs in CLAUDE.md and what is wasted tokens?
flashcards.a: IN: non-guessable commands, conventions that differ from tool defaults, ownership boundaries, the 3-5 mistakes the agent repeats here. OUT: directory layouts and dependency lists (derivable, and stale is worse than absent), multi-step procedures (make them skills), unenforceable aspirations, anything a linter already enforces. Trigger for adding a line: the agent got it wrong twice.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: Where does a rule go if violating it would be an incident?
flashcards.a: A hook (PreToolUse), a permissions.deny rule, or CI. CLAUDE.md is context delivered as a message with no compliance guarantee; hooks run as shell commands at lifecycle events regardless of what the model decides. CLAUDE.md is advice, hooks are law.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: Do @path imports in CLAUDE.md reduce context cost?
flashcards.a: No. Imports expand and load at launch (max 4 hops deep), so they help organization and change nothing about tokens. Only paths:-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ and nested subdirectory CLAUDE.md files are genuinely lazy.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: What is the relationship between AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md?
flashcards.a: AGENTS.md is the cross-tool convention (open spec Aug 2025, donated to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation Dec 2025, 60k+ public repos, 30+ tools, nearest file in the tree wins). Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md and not AGENTS.md, so use a CLAUDE.md containing `@AGENTS.md` plus Claude-specific additions, or a symlink. Maintaining two drifting copies is the actual failure mode.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: What survives compaction and what is lost?
flashcards.a: Survives (re-injected from disk): system prompt, project-root CLAUDE.md, unscoped rules, auto memory. Lost until a matching file is read again: rules with paths: frontmatter and nested subdirectory CLAUDE.md. Skills are re-injected but capped at 5,000 tokens per skill and 25,000 total, oldest dropped first.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: Why put the load-bearing instructions at the TOP of a SKILL.md?
flashcards.a: Post-compaction re-injection truncates skills to fit the 5,000-token-per-skill cap and truncation keeps the start of the file. Anything in a trailing 'Notes' section is the first thing dropped in a long session.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: What is the economic argument for a skill over CLAUDE.md content?
flashcards.a: Only the description (plus when_to_use, combined and truncated at 1,536 characters in the listing) sits in context at startup; the body loads on invocation. A 3,000-word runbook costs about 30 tokens until the day you use it. The trigger to extract one: a CLAUDE.md section has grown into steps with an outcome.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: What does a non-fork subagent get at startup, and what does it never get?
flashcards.a: Gets: its own system prompt, the parent's delegation message, the full CLAUDE.md hierarchy, a git-status snapshot, and any preloaded skills. Never gets: your conversation history, your file reads, your output style, your auto memory. Built-in Explore and Plan additionally skip CLAUDE.md and git status, so rules meant for them must be restated in the delegation prompt.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: When does subagent parallelism pay, and when does it fragment?
flashcards.a: Pays for independent, high-volume-in / low-volume-out work: test runs, greps, doc fetching, unrelated module reads. Fragments on shared invariants (each agent makes a locally reasonable, mutually incompatible contract decision because only lossy summaries return), on iterative work needing steering, and when many detailed returns leave the parent fuller than inline work would. Rule: delegate reads, keep writes.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: Default subagent limits worth knowing.
flashcards.a: 200 subagents per session (CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENTS_PER_SESSION), 20 concurrent (CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS), nesting 3 layers deep (CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH; was 5 before v2.1.217, 1 in v2.1.217-218, 3 from v2.1.219). Transcripts persist under ~/.claude/projects/{project}/{sessionId}/subagents/ for cleanupPeriodDays, default 30.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: Why is MCP tool search on by default, and what does ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=auto do?
flashcards.a: Tool schemas are the hidden startup cost. With tool search on, only tool names and server instructions load at startup and full schemas are fetched on demand, so adding servers is near-free. ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=auto switches to threshold loading: schemas upfront while they fit within 10% of the context window, overflow deferred.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: What are the MCP output limits and why do they matter for correctness?
flashcards.a: A warning fires above 10,000 tokens of MCP tool output and the default hard cap is 25,000 (MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS; per-tool override via anthropic/maxResultSizeChars). An unpaginated query silently becomes a partial result that the agent then reasons over as if complete.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: What changed in the MCP 2026-07-28 specification?
flashcards.a: Largest revision since launch: stateless core (initialize/notifications-initialized handshake removed; protocol version and client capabilities ride in _meta per request), ttlMs and cacheScope on list and resources/read responses, list endpoints no longer varying per connection, deterministic tool ordering for prompt-cache hits, required Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers on Streamable HTTP, and a formal deprecation policy.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: State the core principle of spec-driven development in one sentence.
flashcards.a: Whoever writes the verification signal controls the outcome, and it cannot be the thing being verified. Tests the agent writes after seeing its own implementation describe what it built; tests written from the spec before implementation are the only ones with independent evidentiary value.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: What did SpecBench measure, and what is the headline number?
flashcards.a: arXiv 2605.21384 (May 2026): 30 systems-level tasks decomposed into spec, visible validation tests, and held-out composition tests; the pass-rate gap quantifies reward hacking. Every frontier agent saturated the visible suite, and the gap grows about 28 percentage points per tenfold increase in code size. Most memorable failure: a 2,900-line hash table that memorized test inputs.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: How do you turn 'did the agent weaken the tests' from a judgment call into a check?
flashcards.a: Commit specs/ and tests/ before the agent runs, then `git diff HEAD -- tests/` inside the single verify script (not as a review habit). Enforce with a PreToolUse hook matching Edit|Write that exits non-zero for paths under tests/. A CLAUDE.md line saying 'never modify tests' is a request, not a control.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: How should a verification gate be ordered, and why one command?
flashcards.a: One command, because a multi-command gate lets the agent report partial success as success. Inside, order by signal quality per token: types (kills fabricated APIs in seconds), then lint, then tests, then the test-tamper check. Route large test output through a subagent so a 40k-token run does not permanently occupy the main window.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: What did the METR randomized trial find, and what is its scope?
flashcards.a: arXiv 2507.09089: 16 experienced open-source developers, 246 tasks, repos they averaged 5 years on. Allowing early-2025 AI tooling increased completion time 19%, against a pre-task forecast of 24% faster and a post-task self-report of 20% faster. Scope is narrow (that population, that tooling generation; METR revised its design Feb 2026), but the perception gap is the durable finding: felt speedup is not evidence of speedup.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: Why is a 1M-token context window not a solution to context management?
flashcards.a: Capacity is not attention. NoLiMa tested 12 models claiming 128K+ support: 11 of 12 fell below 50% of their short-context performance by 32K tokens on non-literal retrieval. Chroma's context-rot work adds that irrelevant context is not neutral, since focused prompts beat full prompts containing the same relevant information plus distractors.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: Where does agentic coding structurally not work?
flashcards.a: Novel algorithms (the verification loop cannot close: your tests only cover cases you already understood). Deep concurrency debugging (the signal lies: a race that fires once per 10,000 interleavings passes every run, so the loop reports success on a broken fix). Anything where writing the spec is the hard part. Small changes you already have in your head. Coupled work split across parallel subagents.

flashcards.topic: AI-Assisted Coding: CLAUDE.md, Skills, Subagents, Spec-Driven Dev
flashcards.q: What is the graded axis in a 2026 AI-assisted coding interview round?
flashcards.a: Judgment under delegation, not prompt cleverness. Google's pilot scores 'AI fluency: prompt engineering, output validation, debugging' in a human-led, AI-assisted code-comprehension round; Meta's since Oct 2025 is a 60-minute three-panel CoderPad scored on problem solving, code quality, verification, and communication. Candidates get dinged for relying on the assistant without demonstrating independent understanding, and equally for conspicuously under-using it.

flashcards.q: Write the `Future` trait signature from memory.
flashcards.a: `trait Future { type Output; fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Self::Output>; }` with `enum Poll<T> { Ready(T), Pending }`. Stabilized in Rust 1.36.0 (July 2019); async/await syntax followed in 1.39.0 (November 2019).

flashcards.q: What is the poll contract, and what happens if you break it?
flashcards.a: If poll returns Pending it MUST first register cx.waker().clone() somewhere that will call wake() when progress is possible. Break it and the task is silently lost forever: no panic, no log, it is never polled again. The subtler bug is storing the waker only on the first poll; work-stealing may migrate the task between polls, so a stale waker wakes the wrong slot and the task hangs only under load. Re-store on every Pending, or gate with Waker::will_wake.

flashcards.q: How does Rust's laziness differ from asyncio and Go, and what is the one exception?
flashcards.a: Calling `async fn foo()` runs zero lines of the body; it constructs an inert state machine value. asyncio's create_task and Go's `go f()` both start immediately. The exception is tokio::spawn, which hands the future to the scheduler and starts it right away. Dropping the returned JoinHandle DETACHES the task, it does not cancel it; use handle.abort() or a JoinSet.

flashcards.q: Why does Pin exist? Derive it from the desugaring.
flashcards.a:
async fn compiles to a generated enum whose fields are exactly the locals live across .await points. If one of those locals borrows another (`let s = &buf[..]` held across an await), the enum contains a pointer into itself. Rust assumes values are freely movable via memcpy, so moving it would dangle that pointer. Pin

withholds &mut Target unless Target: Unpin, and the compiler-generated coroutines are precisely the !Unpin types. Since poll takes self: Pin<&mut Self>, an executor structurally cannot move a half-run state machine.

flashcards.q: Box::pin vs std::pin::pin! vs neither.
flashcards.a: Box::pin: one heap allocation, gives a stable heap address, and the Pin<Box<F>> handle is itself movable. pin! (std, stable 1.68.0, March 2023): zero allocation, pins to the current stack frame by shadowing the binding. Neither is needed for a plain .await, because the enclosing async block pins the future structurally. Reach for them when polling by hand, storing dyn Future, holding a future across loop iterations for select!, or breaking a recursive async fn.

flashcards.q: Tokio's multi-threaded scheduler: state the six defaults.
flashcards.a: Workers = CPU core count (TOKIO_WORKER_THREADS overrides). Local queue holds at most 256 tasks; overflow moves half (128) to the global queue. global_queue_interval is 31 on current_thread, dynamically computed targeting ~10ms on multi-thread. event_interval is 61 polls before parking in epoll for I/O and timers. Idle workers steal half a random peer's local queue. The LIFO slot polls a just-woken task next, is disabled after 3 consecutive uses, and is not stealable.

flashcards.q: What is Tokio's cooperative budget and why does it exist?
flashcards.a: 128 operations per task poll (Budget(Some(128)) in tokio::task::coop). Tokio's own resource futures (channel recv, socket read, mutex lock) decrement it and, at zero, return Pending while self-waking, forcing a yield. It stops `while let Some(x) = rx.recv().await {}` on an always-ready channel from monopolizing a worker. It only works for futures that participate; pure compute loops and hand-written futures are invisible to it. Opt out with task::coop::unconstrained; yield manually with task::yield_now().await.

flashcards.q: Name the observable symptoms of a blocked Tokio executor.
flashcards.a: p99 rises in clean quantized steps (5ms, 250ms, 500ms) rather than a smooth curve. Load average equals worker count while CPU utilization is near zero, if the blocker is I/O. YOUR OWN timers fire late: sleep(10ms) returns after 260ms, which is the tell that separates a blocked executor from a slow downstream. /healthz times out and the orchestrator kills a healthy pod. tokio-console shows high worker_mean_poll_time. A stack dump shows tokio-runtime-worker threads inside a syscall rather than epoll_wait.

flashcards.q: spawn_blocking defaults and limitations.
flashcards.a: max_blocking_threads defaults to 512 (a cap, not a preallocation); thread_keep_alive is 10 seconds of idleness; the pool is separate from and excludes async worker threads; calls beyond the cap queue. Blocking tasks CANNOT be aborted once started, so abort() is a no-op and runtime shutdown waits indefinitely unless you use Runtime::shutdown_timeout. The 512 default is sized for I/O blocking, not CPU work: gate CPU work behind a Semaphore sized to core count.

flashcards.q: spawn_blocking vs block_in_place vs std::thread::spawn.
flashcards.a: spawn_blocking moves the closure to another thread from the blocking pool; use it for short, bounded blocking work. block_in_place runs on the current worker after handing that worker's local queue and LIFO slot to another thread; use it when the work needs borrowed or !Send data from the current task. It panics on a current_thread runtime, does not help a join! sibling in the same task, and cannot be cancelled. std::thread::spawn is correct for long-lived or infinite blocking loops, which would otherwise permanently occupy a pool slot.

flashcards.q: What does `Send` mean for a future, and why does a RefCell guard break it?
flashcards.a: The compiler computes Send structurally: the generated future is Send only if every field is Send, and the fields are exactly the locals held across .await points. RefMut is !Send because RefCell's borrow counter is a plain Cell<isize> with no atomics, so two threads decrementing it would be a data race rather than a panic. Since a work-stealing scheduler may migrate the task at exactly that suspension point, the compiler rejects it.

flashcards.q: Why is holding a std::sync::Mutex guard across an .await dangerous even though it compiles?
flashcards.a: MutexGuard<T> is Send when T: Send, so the future is Send and spawn accepts it. But a blocking mutex held across an await can deadlock the entire runtime: worker A holds the lock and suspends, workers B..H all block on the lock, and no thread is left to poll the task that would release it. Symptom is zero CPU and zero progress under load. Fixes in order: drop the guard before the await, use tokio::sync::Mutex (async lock, Send guard, ~10x slower uncontended), or restructure to an actor behind an mpsc.

flashcards.q: Why is an unbounded channel a memory leak waiting to happen? Give the arithmetic.
flashcards.a: unbounded_channel().send() is synchronous and cannot fail while open, so it cannot apply backpressure. At 1,000 msg/sec in and 333/sec out (3ms of work each) at 4 KiB per message, the queue grows 2.7 MiB/sec and a 4 GiB container OOMs in about 25 minutes. Worse, latency degrades first: by Little's Law a 100,000-deep queue draining at 333/sec means every emerging message is 300 seconds stale, and the OOM kill is attributed to the consumer, so the postmortem chases the wrong service.

flashcards.q: mpsc vs oneshot vs broadcast vs watch: one line each plus the gotcha.
flashcards.a: mpsc: many producers, one consumer, bounded for backpressure; channel(0) panics and the true high-water mark is n plus the number of senders. oneshot: a single value; send is not async and returns your value in the Err if the receiver is gone. broadcast: every receiver sees every value; capacity is rounded UP to the next power of two, so channel(3) allocates 4, and RecvError::Lagged is recoverable, not fatal. watch: latest value only; the initial value counts as SEEN so changed() waits for a subsequent send, and holding borrow() across an .await blocks all senders.

flashcards.q: What does cancellation mean in async Rust, and what does it mean for in-flight I/O?
flashcards.a: Cancellation is dropping the future. There is no CancelledError, no unwinding through async frames, and no async Drop (still unstable in Rust 1.97.1). A dropped read loses at most a partial buffer in the future's state; the socket is untouched. A dropped write_all that already issued 3 of 5 write syscalls has ALREADY put those bytes on the wire, so the protocol is desynchronized and the connection must be closed. A cancelled POST /charge may still have charged the card. Cancellation is not rollback.

flashcards.q: Define cancellation safety and list what is NOT cancel-safe in tokio::select!.
flashcards.a: A future is cancellation-safe if dropping it before completion and recreating it loses no progress. select! drops every losing branch, and in a loop the losers are rebuilt each iteration. Data-lossy (partial progress in the future's own state): read_exact, read_to_end, read_to_string, write_all. Unsafe for a different reason (they use a fair FIFO wait queue, so you lose your place): Mutex::lock, RwLock::read, RwLock::write, Semaphore::acquire, Notify::notified. Safe: mpsc/broadcast recv, watch changed, TcpListener::accept, AsyncReadExt::read, StreamExt::next.

flashcards.q: Two facts about tokio::select! branch behaviour beyond cancellation safety.
flashcards.a: Branch polling order is RANDOMIZED by default for fairness across always-ready branches, and the RNG has a non-zero CPU cost; `biased;` polls top to bottom, which you want when a shutdown branch must not be starved by a saturated stream, but then fairness becomes your responsibility. And select! PANICS if every branch is disabled by an `if` precondition or a non-matching pattern and there is no `else` branch.

flashcards.q: JoinSet vs Vec<JoinHandle>, and what CancellationToken adds.
flashcards.a: Dropping a JoinSet aborts every task in it, so you cannot leak a task by dropping the handle, which bare tokio::spawn does not guarantee (dropping a JoinHandle detaches). join_next() yields results in completion order. Both still require 'static, so this is not std::thread::scope. CancellationToken (tokio-util) inverts drop-cancellation: the task selects on token.cancelled() and runs its own cleanup before returning. Tokens form a tree via child_token(); drop_guard() propagates a supervisor's death; pair with TaskTracker and always bound the wait with timeout().

flashcards.q: Status of async fn in traits as of August 2026.
flashcards.a: Stable since Rust 1.75.0 (December 2023) via RPITIT: async fn get(&self) desugars to fn get(&self) -> impl Future + '_, monomorphized per impl with zero allocation and static dispatch. Two gaps remain: it is NOT dyn-compatible (async_fn_in_dyn_trait is still an incomplete nightly feature), and you cannot bound the returned future as Send from the trait definition. Workarounds: #[async_trait] (Pin<Box<dyn Future + Send>>, one allocation per call) when you need dyn, and the trait-variant crate when you need Send across a generic boundary. Return-type notation is the long-term fix and is unstable.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT use async Rust?
flashcards.a: CPU-bound workloads: async solves waiting, not computing; use a thread pool or rayon. CLIs and batch jobs: #[tokio::main] adds ~25-30 crates and runtime startup for sequential calls that gain nothing. Below a few thousand concurrent connections: thread-per-connection is simpler, has better tail latency because the kernel preempts, and debugs with an ordinary stack trace; the empirical crossover is roughly 10k-50k connections. Also budget for the debugging cost, since an async stack trace shows executor frames, not your logical call chain.

flashcards.q: What is the one repeating pattern that makes a component get rewritten in Rust in the AI stack?
flashcards.a: A hot loop that is NOT a matmul, called millions of times, with small per-item work, that cannot be batched onto a GPU and cannot be handed to BLAS/cuBLAS. In that shape CPython bytecode dispatch IS the runtime and the GIL caps you at one core. Rust owns the band where the unit of work is a byte/token/AST-node; Python keeps the band where it is a tensor, because a tensor op already spends ~99.9% of its time in someone else's C.

flashcards.q: What does an empty PyO3 function call cost, and what is the practical break-even for writing a binding?
flashcards.a: Measured on PyO3 0.29.2 / CPython 3.10.12: an empty #[pyfunction] costs 54.56 ns/call against 50.71 ns for an empty Python def, with a floor of 34.31 ns for the attribute lookup alone. So crossing the boundary costs roughly one Python call. Practical break-even is about 1 microsecond of Rust work per call; below that the crossing is a double-digit percentage of the call.

flashcards.q: Is a Rust `add(a: i64, b: i64) -> i64` faster than Python's `a + b` across a PyO3 binding?
flashcards.a: No, it is measurably SLOWER: 79.16 ns vs 70.85 ns, a 12% regression. Two PyLong_AsLongLong conversions plus boxing the i64 result back into a PyLong cost more than an add instruction saves, and CPython's small-int cache makes the Python-side allocation free. If a Rust function does less work than its own argument conversion, the binding is a pessimisation.

flashcards.q: Why does binding a function that takes `Vec<i64>` (a Python list) fail to beat the builtin `sum()`?
flashcards.a: Because a Python container argument makes the boundary O(n), not O(1). Extracting Vec<i64> is a per-element PyLong_AsLongLong plus a Vec push, measured at 7.6-12.3 ns/element, which is exactly the work sum()'s C loop was already doing. Measured 0.40x-0.68x of sum() at EVERY size from N=1 to N=1,048,576. There is no crossover point.

flashcards.q: What does zero-copy via the buffer protocol buy, and where does it stop winning?
flashcards.a: PyBuffer::get is O(1) regardless of array size: it fills a Py_buffer with a pointer/length/itemsize/format and takes a reference on the exporter. No bytes move. Measured vs np.sum on f64: 12.41x at N=1, 6.53x at N=256, 1.08x at N=4,096, then 0.42x at N=65,536. Rust wins on numpy's ~3 microsecond per-call DISPATCH, not on the loop, and loses at large N because iter().sum() on f64 does not autovectorise (IEEE non-associativity) while numpy uses pairwise SIMD.

flashcards.q: What is `py.detach()` in PyO3 0.29, what does it cost, and when should you use it?
flashcards.a: It is the renamed `Python::allow_threads`: it releases the GIL for the duration of a closure (Python::with_gil was likewise renamed to Python::attach). Safety is enforced by the type system since Python<'py> is not Send, so no Python object can be dereferenced inside. Measured cost of a detach/attach round trip: ~30-40 ns (48.5% overhead at zero work, 5.1% at 100 iterations, 0.9% at 10,000). Rule: detach when the closure does more than roughly 1 microsecond of work.

flashcards.q: Why is BPE tokenization the canonical example of the Rust-in-AI pattern?
flashcards.a: GPT-2's table is 50,000 merges over a 50,257-token vocabulary. Encoding is a regex pre-tokenization (my corpus: 166,702 pre-tokens, mean length 4.37 chars, p99 12, max 70) followed by a data-dependent merge loop per pre-token. That loop is O(L^2) Python operations, has no vectorisable inner kernel, no GPU path, and is called on every document in a pretraining corpus and every request in a serving path. Under the GIL it also cannot use a second core.

flashcards.q: How much faster is a Rust BPE tokenizer than pure Python, measured on byte-identical output?
flashcards.a: Range, not a single number. On a 101,723-byte slice (30,697 tokens, verified id-identical): pure Python cold cache 103.7 ms (0.98 MB/s), pure Python WARM cache 33.8 ms (3.01 MB/s), HuggingFace tokenizers 0.23.1 43.2 ms (2.36 MB/s), tiktoken 7.2 ms (14.08 MB/s). So tiktoken is 14.4x over cold Python, but HF tokenizers is only 2.4x over cold and actually LOSES to warm pure Python. Never quote a single multiplier.

flashcards.q: Why does a warm-cache pure-Python BPE beat HuggingFace `tokenizers`?
flashcards.a: Two reasons. (1) Natural text is Zipf-distributed and both implementations memoise per pre-token: 30,697 tokens produced only 3,682 distinct cache entries, so the expensive merge loop mostly does not run. The hot loop everyone rewrites is largely memoised away. (2) HF's encode() returns an Encoding with eight parallel vectors (ids, type_ids, tokens, offsets, attention_mask, special_tokens_mask, word_ids, overflowing), including a heap String PER TOKEN. That construction costs more than the merge loop it saved.

flashcards.q: tiktoken is 7.8x faster than HuggingFace `tokenizers` on identical output. Both are Rust. Why?
flashcards.a: The return type, not the language. On 738,046 bytes producing an identical 191,673 ids: hf.encode() 400.1 ms (1.84 MB/s) vs tiktoken.encode_ordinary() 51.5 ms (14.33 MB/s). HF materialises 8 parallel vectors plus a String per token plus char-to-byte offset bookkeeping; tiktoken returns a Vec<u32>. Proof of mechanism: encode_batch_fast, which skips offsets, recovers 1.19x (132.9 -> 111.8 ms), so offsets alone were ~16% and the per-token String is the rest.

flashcards.q: What does `TOKENIZERS_PARALLELISM` control, and what is it worth?
flashcards.a: It enables the rayon thread pool inside encode_batch, which releases the GIL and fans out across cores. Measured on 2,511 documents on 2 vCPUs: true = 142.7 ms (5.17 MB/s), false = 324.6 ms (2.27 MB/s), a 2.27x that is essentially linear. This is the categorical win Rust bindings give that pure Python cannot reach in one process. People set it to false to silence the fork-safety warning and silently halve their throughput.

flashcards.q: Why does wrapping `tokenizers.encode_batch` in a ThreadPoolExecutor give no speedup?
