flashcards.a: Because encode_batch already releases the GIL and saturates the cores via its internal rayon pool. Measured over 2,511 docs: 1 thread 147.0 ms, 2 threads 147.3 ms, 4 threads 152.3 ms. Flat, then slightly worse from oversubscription. Fix: delete the pool and control parallelism where it actually lives, with RAYON_NUM_THREADS.

flashcards.q: What does the GIL cost on a CPU-bound Rust loop across Python threads, and what is Rust's raw constant factor?
flashcards.a: On a 30,000,000-iteration hash loop: GIL held gave 0.049 s at 1 thread and 0.507 s at 8, which is 10.3x, worse than perfectly serial because of GIL handoff contention (default sys.setswitchinterval is 5 ms). With py.detach() the same work went 0.065 s to 0.198 s, saturating at 2.19x on 2 vCPUs. The separate constant-factor term: 104.00 ns per interpreted iteration vs 1.81 ns in Rust, a 57.5x gap that no GIL change touches.

flashcards.q: What is the status of free-threaded Python as of 2026, and what does it do to the case for Rust?
flashcards.a: PEP 779 was accepted for Python 3.14, moving free-threading to phase two: officially supported, no longer experimental, but still opt-in as the separate 3.14t binary. Single-threaded overhead is down to ~5-10% from ~40% in the 3.13 experimental build; phase three (default) has criteria but no committed version. It kills the PARALLELISM argument for Rust on a multi-year horizon, kills none of the 57.5x CONSTANT-FACTOR argument, and strengthens the thread-safety argument because latent races the GIL was accidentally serialising now surface.

flashcards.q: What silently breaks when a PyO3 extension is imported under free-threaded Python 3.14t?
flashcards.a: If the module has not declared `gil_used = false` in its #[pymodule], CPython re-enables the GIL at import. You get no parallelism, no error, and only a RuntimeWarning most people have filtered. PyO3 has supported the free-threaded build since 0.23; from 0.23 through 0.27 the default was gil_used = true so opting in was explicit. Separately, shared mutable #[pyclass] state that was implicitly GIL-protected becomes genuinely concurrent, so PyRefMut borrow panics appear under load, and GILOnceCell (deprecated in 0.29 for PyOnceLock) or static mut become bugs.

flashcards.q: What is abi3 and why does it dominate PyO3 packaging decisions?
flashcards.a: Building with `pyo3 = { features = ["abi3-py310"] }` links only against CPython's stable ABI, so ONE wheel per platform serves 3.10 and every later version. Without it the wheel is tagged cp310-cp310 and the CI matrix is versions x platforms (5x5 = 25 jobs vs 5). tokenizers ships tokenizers-0.23.1-cp310-abi3-manylinux_2_17_x86_64...whl (3,346,235 bytes). Cost: no access to non-stable C-API functions, some PyO3 struct-internals optimisations disabled, and slightly slower calls through function pointers rather than macros.

flashcards.q: Why must you NOT set `panic = "abort"` in a PyO3 extension's release profile?
flashcards.a: Unwinding a Rust panic across the FFI boundary is undefined behaviour, so PyO3 catches panics at the #[pyfunction] boundary and converts them into a Python PanicException that kills only that request. `panic = "abort"` disables that catch, so any panic (out-of-bounds index, unwrap on None, PyRefMut borrow violation) becomes an immediate SIGABRT that kills the interpreter and every concurrent in-flight request, with no Python traceback. The 5-10% binary-size saving is not worth an availability incident.

flashcards.q: When are candle and burn genuinely the right choice over PyTorch, and when are they not?
flashcards.a: Right when the deployment ARTIFACT is the constraint, not throughput: no-Python deployment (a static binary vs a 4+ GB PyTorch container), edge/embedded/WASM (burn compiles to wasm32 on WebGPU via CubeCL, which also targets CUDA/ROCm/Metal/Vulkan/SIMD CPU), small CPU models like MiniLM embedding endpoints, and embedding a model in an existing Rust service to remove a 1-3 ms sidecar hop. Wrong on a GPU fleet at scale: reported results range from 35-47% faster than PyTorch to 8.5x SLOWER (candle issue #2877: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 at 122.30 ms/batch vs ~14.34 ms), depending entirely on whether your ops have tuned kernels.

flashcards.q: Name the production systems where Rust won in the AI stack, and what is conspicuously NOT Rust.
flashcards.a: Won: tokenizers and tiktoken (BPE), safetensors (mmap-able, and pickle is arbitrary code execution), ruff and uv (uv measured 8.7x over pip cold cache, 145x warm: 14.54 s -> 1.68 s -> 0.10 s), Polars, Qdrant and LanceDB, and SGLang's sgl-router plus vLLM's router (a fork of it) which run Rust tokenizers/reasoning-parsers/tool-parsers for cache-aware routing. NOT Rust, on both sides: PyTorch/JAX/vLLM/SGLang above (the loop body is a cuBLAS call), and CUDA/Triton/CUTLASS/cuDNN below (Rust has no story there). Rust took the band defined by the absence of a tensor.

flashcards.q: An interviewer says 'our LLM serving p99 is 4 seconds, let's rewrite it in Rust.' What is the numerate answer?
flashcards.a: Ask what fraction of the 4,000 ms is CPU-bound Python bytecode; on a generation request it is under 2% because the GPU is doing prefill and decode. Measured tokenization of a real 30-char prompt was 11.02 microseconds = 0.00028% of a 4-second request. So the ceiling on a full rewrite is single-digit ms out of 4,000, at a cost of two quarters plus losing ML-engineer iteration. The real levers are continuous-batching config, KV-cache hit rate and eviction, prefill/decode interference, queueing, speculative decoding and cold model loads. Threshold rule: >40% CPU-bound Python bind it, 10-40% profile first, <10% no.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: What are the three cases that genuinely force you to use Box<T>?
flashcards.a: 1) Recursive types: `struct Node { next: Node }` has infinite size, rustc emits E0072; boxing makes the field a fixed 8 bytes. 2) Trait objects: `dyn Trait` is unsized so it only exists behind a pointer; size_of::<Box<dyn Debug>>() == 16 (data ptr + vtable ptr). 3) Large moves: a move is a memcpy of the stack representation, so moving a [u8; 1<<20] costs 1 MiB per move. Outside these three, Box is usually unnecessary.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: Measured cost of Rc::clone vs Arc::clone, and where does the difference come from?
flashcards.a: Measured on rustc 1.97.1 -O, x86_64, i5-12450H, 50M iterations of clone-then-drop: Rc = 1.53 ns/op, Arc = 14.44 ns/op, a 9.4x ratio. Rc uses a plain load-add-store on a usize; Arc uses fetch_add(1, Relaxed) which lowers to `lock xadd` and requires exclusive ownership of the cache line. A bare AtomicUsize::fetch_add(Relaxed) measured 6.04 ns, and Arc clone+drop is two of those plus a branch. Both types are 8 bytes on the stack with a 16-byte header (strong + weak).

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: Which memory orderings does Arc use for clone and drop, and why?
flashcards.a: Clone is fetch_add(1, Relaxed): incrementing publishes nothing, since you already had a valid Arc so the value already exists. Drop is fetch_sub(1, Release): writes made through this Arc must become visible to whichever thread runs the destructor. The last dropper, seeing the old count was 1, executes atomic::fence(Acquire) before touching the data; that fence pairs with every other thread's Release decrement to establish exclusive access. Overflow is checked against MAX_REFCOUNT = isize::MAX as usize and calls abort(), not panic!, because a caught panic would leave the count corrupt.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: Why does an Rc/Arc reference cycle leak, and what is the observable symptom in production?
flashcards.a: Rust has no cycle collector, because that would require a tracing runtime. Two nodes holding strong references to each other never reach strong count 0, so their Drop impls never run. Leaking is safe in Rust: mem::forget and Box::leak are both safe functions, and leak-freedom is explicitly NOT part of the memory-safety guarantee. Symptom: RSS climbs monotonically under steady load and never returns to baseline, no crash, nothing in logs, and a heap profiler shows live allocations with no live root. Fix: owning edges are Rc/Arc, back-edges are Weak.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: What is the strong-count / weak-count invariant in Rc and Arc?
flashcards.a: The header is 16 bytes on 64-bit: strong (usize, or AtomicUsize for Arc) and weak. The VALUE is dropped when strong hits 0. The ALLOCATION is freed when weak hits 0. All the strong references collectively hold one implicit weak count, which is why an Rc with no Weaks frees its allocation immediately at strong 0. Weak::upgrade() returns Option<Rc<T>> and yields None once the value is gone; for Arc it is a compare-exchange loop that refuses to increment from 0, making it race-free against a concurrent last drop.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: Cell<T> vs RefCell<T>: mechanism, size, and failure mode.
flashcards.a: Cell never hands out a reference: get() copies out (needs T: Copy), set() copies in, replace()/take() move. Nothing to invalidate means no bookkeeping, so size_of::<Cell<u64>>() == 8 (zero overhead) and it CANNOT panic. RefCell hands out real Ref/RefMut guards that deref to &T/&mut T, so it tracks live borrows in an extra isize flag: size_of::<RefCell<u64>>() == 16, size_of::<RefCell<()>>() == 8. Both cost ~0.25 ns/op measured. If the data is small and Copy, Cell is strictly better and removes a class of runtime failure.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: What is the exact RefCell panic message on current stable Rust, and why is it hard to debug?
flashcards.a: Verified on rustc 1.97.1: borrow_mut() while a Ref is live panics with `RefCell already borrowed` (error type BorrowMutError); borrow() while a RefMut is live panics with `RefCell already mutably borrowed` (error type BorrowError). Older releases and most blog posts phrase these as `already borrowed: BorrowMutError`. Hard to debug because (a) the line number is the SECOND borrow, not the still-live first one, and (b) it is a re-entrancy bug, so it is rare and load-dependent. Use try_borrow_mut() to get an Err you can log with your own context.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: What is the encoding of RefCell's borrow flag?
flashcards.a: One isize (std::cell::BorrowFlag) held in a Cell: 0 means unborrowed; n > 0 means n live shared borrows (Ref); n < 0 means mutably borrowed. Normally exactly -1, but it can go further negative because RefMut::map_split splits one RefMut into two disjoint ones over non-overlapping parts of the value. borrow() fails if flag < 0; borrow_mut() fails if flag != 0.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: How does Rust's Mutex<T> differ structurally from Java's synchronized and Go's sync.Mutex?
flashcards.a: Rust's Mutex OWNS the T. The only way to reach the data is lock(), which returns a MutexGuard that derefs to &mut T, so `forgot to take the lock` is not expressible. Java's synchronized/ReentrantLock guard a BLOCK; the lock-to-fields mapping lives in a @GuardedBy annotation checked only by optional tools. Go's sync.Mutex is a bare field with no type-level link to what it protects, which is why Go shipped a ThreadSanitizer-based race detector in Go 1.1 (2013) that its docs peg at 2x-20x execution time and 5x-10x memory, and which only reports races that actually occurred on the executed interleaving.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: Two ways Rust's std Mutex is WORSE than Java's, for someone porting from Java.
flashcards.a: 1) Non-reentrant. std documents locking a Mutex on a thread that already holds it as unspecified behaviour that will not return; Java's synchronized and ReentrantLock are reentrant. A recursive helper that is fine in Java hangs in Rust, symptom being a thread parked in futex_wait at 0% CPU with no log output. 2) Poisoning. A panic while holding the guard marks the mutex poisoned permanently, so every subsequent lock() returns Err(PoisonError), which is why real code is full of .unwrap(). PoisonError::into_inner() recovers the guard; parking_lot::Mutex drops poisoning entirely and is 1 byte instead of 8.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: Measured uncontended costs of Mutex vs RwLock, and when does RwLock actually win?
flashcards.a: Measured on rustc 1.97.1 -O, 30M iterations: Mutex lock+unlock 13.19 ns, RwLock read+unlock 15.12 ns, RwLock write+unlock 13.34 ns, AtomicUsize fetch_add 6.04 ns, RefCell borrow_mut 0.25 ns. RwLock::read was SLOWER than Mutex::lock, because a read lock still performs an atomic RMW to register the reader, so N readers still contend on the same cache line. RwLock only wins when critical sections are long enough (roughly hundreds of ns and up) that parallel reader execution dominates acquisition cost. For read-mostly data replaced wholesale, use arc-swap instead.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: Define Send and Sync precisely, and explain the auto-trait mechanism.
flashcards.a: Send: the value can be moved to another thread. Sync: &T can be shared with another thread, formally T: Sync iff &T: Send. Both are AUTO TRAITS: you do not implement them, the compiler derives them structurally, so a struct is Send if all its fields are Send and Sync if all its fields are Sync. The recursion bottoms out at a handful of hand-written positive and negative impls in std. Consequence: adding one Rc field deep inside a struct silently makes the whole aggregate !Send, and the error surfaces hundreds of lines away at a thread::spawn or tokio::spawn.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: Why is Rc neither Send nor Sync, and why is MutexGuard Sync but not Send?
flashcards.a: Rc is !Send because its strong count is a plain usize; two threads incrementing it would interleave and lose an update, the count would read low, the value would drop while a live Rc still points at it, and you get use-after-free. !Sync follows because any thread with &Rc<T> can call clone(). MutexGuard is !Send because unlocking must happen on the locking thread (POSIX makes pthread_mutex_unlock from a non-owner UB) and the guard's Drop is what unlocks. MutexGuard IS Sync when T: Sync, because &MutexGuard<T> only yields &T, and sharing a reference to the guard never moves the guard, so the unlock stays put.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: Send/Sync status of the common types, with the exact compiler errors.
flashcards.a: Rc<T>: !Send, !Sync. Arc<T> where T: Send + Sync: Send + Sync. Cell<T>/RefCell<T> where T: Send: Send YES, Sync NO. Mutex<T> where T: Send: Send + Sync. MutexGuard<'_, T> where T: Sync: Sync YES, Send NO. &T where T: Sync: Send. *const T / *mut T: !Send, !Sync by fiat, forcing an explicit unsafe impl. Errors: `error[E0277]: Rc<i32> cannot be sent between threads safely`, `error[E0277]: RefCell<i32> cannot be shared between threads safely`, `error[E0277]: std::sync::MutexGuard<'static, i32> cannot be sent between threads safely`.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: What are the five superpowers of unsafe, and what does unsafe NOT turn off?
flashcards.a: Five: 1) dereference a raw pointer, 2) call an unsafe fn or method, 3) access or modify a mutable static, 4) implement an unsafe trait, 5) access union fields. It turns off NOTHING else. The borrow checker still runs inside an unsafe block, lifetimes are still checked, move semantics and type checking are unchanged, Drop still fires. The only change is that rustc stops asking you to prove those five are safe and starts ASSUMING you were right, then optimizes on that assumption. unsafe is silent mode, not permissive mode.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: What is the difference between an `unsafe fn` and an `unsafe {}` block, and what did edition 2024 change?
flashcards.a: Opposite directions. An unsafe BLOCK discharges an obligation: `I checked the preconditions`. An unsafe FN imposes one on callers: `read my # Safety doc`. Rust 2024 edition (shipped in 1.85.0, 2025-02-20) made this explicit by turning unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn on by default, so the body of an unsafe fn is no longer implicitly an unsafe block and you must write the inner unsafe {}. Edition 2024 also requires `unsafe extern "C"` blocks and unsafe attributes such as #[unsafe(no_mangle)], and promotes static_mut_refs from warn to deny.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: Why is UnsafeCell<T> the only legal way to mutate through a &T?
flashcards.a: rustc tells LLVM that a &T points at memory that will not change for the reference's lifetime (noalias, plus readonly where applicable). UnsafeCell is the marker that suppresses that annotation. Mutating through a &T not inside an UnsafeCell is undefined behaviour EVEN IF you observe the right answer, because LLVM has already been licensed to cache the load, hoist it out of a loop, or reorder around it. A raw-pointer cast is not a workaround: the UB is a property of the &T existing over that memory, not of the syntax used to write. UnsafeCell is repr(transparent) so it costs 0 bytes, and it is !Sync, which is where Cell's and RefCell's !Sync comes from.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: What does soundness mean for an unsafe abstraction, and why is Vec sound despite being full of unsafe?
flashcards.a: Sound iff NO safe caller, using ANY combination of the public API in ANY order, can cause undefined behaviour. Vec is sound because its public API makes its internal invariants (len <= cap, first len elements initialized, pointer valid for cap elements) unbreakable from outside. The proof this is load-bearing is set_len: if it were safe, a caller could set len past the initialized region and index, reading uninitialized memory, so it is correctly an unsafe fn. Three teeth people miss: two individually safe methods can be jointly unsound; your type must stay sound composed with any other sound crate; and panics count, because unwinding runs Drop on a temporarily invalid object.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: Why does undefined behaviour usually only manifest under --release, with a verified example?
flashcards.a: At -O0 the optimizer does almost nothing, so a broken assumption often has no visible consequence. At -O the optimizer USES the assumption, and when it is false it can emit ud2, delete a branch it proved unreachable, or produce a value that is neither true nor false. Verified on rustc 1.97.1: reading an uninitialized bool via MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init() prints `saw-false` and exits 0 in debug, and dies with `Illegal instruction (core dumped)`, exit status 132, at -O, from identical source on the same machine. Note integer overflow is NOT UB: it is defined to panic with debug_assertions and to wrap without, controlled by -C overflow-checks.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: What does Miri catch, what are its defaults, and what can it fundamentally not do?
flashcards.a: Nightly only (cargo +nightly miri test). Catches out-of-bounds, use-after-free, uninitialized reads, misaligned accesses, invalid values, violated intrinsic preconditions, DATA RACES with weak-memory emulation, LEAKS (anything live at exit not reachable from a static), and aliasing violations. Defaults: seed 0; -Zmiri-many-seeds explores 0..64; preemption 1% per basic block; compare_exchange_weak fails 80%; num-cpus reported as 1; provenance GC every 10,000 basic blocks. Cannot: prove soundness (it tests executions, not all safe callers), do networking, run most FFI, or explore all interleavings. Miri-clean is not sound.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: Stacked Borrows vs Tree Borrows: what is the live disagreement and how should you handle it in CI?
flashcards.a: Rust has NOT stabilized a definition of UB for references. Stacked Borrows (Jung et al., POPL 2020) models each location as a stack of borrow tags; a reborrow pops the tags above it and using a popped tag is UB. Strict, justifies aggressive noalias, and is Miri's default. Tree Borrows (Villani, Hostert, Dreyer, Jung; PLDI 2025, Distinguished Paper, 6 of 89 accepted) replaces the stack with a tree mirroring the reborrow structure; over the 30,000 most-downloaded crates it rejects 54% fewer test cases and its Rocq proofs show it keeps most SB optimizations plus read-read reordering. CI procedure: gate on Stacked Borrows; use -Zmiri-tree-borrows as a DIAGNOSTIC. Miri's README warns the eventual official model is likely STRICTER than Tree Borrows, so TB-accepted code may be declared UB later.

flashcards.topic: Box/Rc/Arc/RefCell, Interior Mutability, Send + Sync, Unsafe
flashcards.q: What does Rust's concurrency guarantee actually cover, and what does it not?
flashcards.a: It prevents DATA RACES for safe code: two threads accessing the same memory without synchronization where at least one writes. It does NOT prevent deadlocks (two mutexes in inconsistent order deadlock exactly as in C), logical race conditions (memory-safe but wrong-order operations), memory leaks (mem::forget and Box::leak are safe; Rc/Arc cycles leak), priority inversion, lock convoying, or unbounded queue growth. Making that narrow claim unprompted, instead of saying `Rust prevents concurrency bugs`, is the clearest staff-level signal in this topic.

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: What does "zero-cost abstraction" actually claim, and how do you verify it?
flashcards.a: It claims the abstraction costs nothing beyond what the hand-written equivalent with the same semantics costs, and that you don't pay for what you don't use. Verify by reading generated assembly in a --release build: `cargo asm --lib 'crate::f' --rust`, Compiler Explorer, or `objdump -d` on the rlib. Measured on rustc 1.97.1: `v.iter().copied().fold(0, wrapping_add)` = 35 instructions vs the index loop's 34, identical SSE2 `paddq` core (2x unrolled, 4 u64/iter); the only diff was label names and the order of two register-zeroing `xor`s.

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: Name the four places the zero-cost claim reliably breaks.
flashcards.a: 1) `dyn Trait`: an inlining barrier. A fold over `&[Add1]` compiled to 2 instructions (`lea (%rsi,%rdx,1),%rax; ret`); the same fold over `&[Box<dyn Op>]` was 24 instructions with `call *0x18(%rcx)` per element. 2) FP reductions: IEEE non-associativity blocks reassociation, so `sum::<f32>()` stayed scalar `addss` even with `-C target-cpu=native` on AVX2+FMA. 3) Data-dependent indexing `out[i] = src[idx[i]]`: 2 live bounds checks/iteration, zero vectorisation. 4) Large cross-crate functions without `#[inline]` and without LTO (weaker than folklore now, see MIR inliner).

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: What is the measured cost of monomorphisation?
flashcards.a: One small generic function instantiated over 200 concrete types vs the same function taking `&[&dyn Shape]` once: clean release rebuild 536 ms vs 169 ms (3.17x), .rlib 494,904 vs 387,256 bytes (+107,648 B, 1.28x), LLVM IR 10,847 vs 5,690 lines (1.91x). Find offenders with `cargo llvm-lines --release | head -30`. Fix with a thin generic wrapper: `fn load<P: AsRef<Path>>(p: P) { load_inner(p.as_ref()) }` duplicates one line per P instead of the whole body.

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: Do bounds checks cost a fixed percentage?
flashcards.a: No, the outcome is bimodal. `v[i]` with `i` from `0..v.len()`: check not emitted. `v[i]` with an unrelated `n`: LLVM HOISTED it to a single `cmp; jbe` before the loop, then vectorised the body (which is why `assert!(n <= v.len())` often measures as no change). Data-dependent `src[idx[i]]`: two checks survive per iteration and vectorisation is blocked entirely. Measured over 1M elements: random indirect 1.896 ms, sequential indirect 0.714 ms, iterator zip 0.179 ms (10.6x and 4.0x faster respectively).

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: How do you help LLVM eliminate bounds checks, in order of preference?
flashcards.a: 1) Use iterators (`zip`, `chunks_exact`, `windows`) so the length is a loop invariant the compiler owns. Measured: `out.iter_mut().zip(a).zip(b)` = 37 instructions with 0 panic edges vs the hand-written index loop's 63 instructions with 2 panic call sites. 2) Slice once up front: `let (a, b) = (&a[..n], &b[..n]);` collapses three length facts into one. 3) `chunks_exact(8)` gives a compile-time-known inner trip count, the strongest safe vectorisation hint. 4) `assert!` before the loop (often a no-op, the hoist already happened). 5) `get_unchecked`, unsafe, only after the profile shows `panic_bounds_check` executing, with a `// SAFETY:` proof.

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: Why does `v.iter().sum::<f32>()` not vectorise when `sum::<i32>()` does?
flashcards.a: IEEE-754 addition is not associative: `(a+b)+c` can differ from `a+(b+c)`. Vectorising a reduction means splitting one serial sum into 4/8 partial sums, which is a reassociation, so LLVM refuses rather than change your output. Integer wrapping addition IS associative, so `sum_i32` vectorised to 8 `ymm` registers in the same build. `sum_f32` was 39 instructions of 8x-unrolled scalar `addss` all into `%xmm0`, so the unroll bought nothing (every add depends on the previous, ~4 cycles latency each). Stable Rust has no `-ffast-math` equivalent.

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: How do you get the speedup on an f32 reduction anyway, and what does it cost?
flashcards.a: Split the accumulator yourself into 8 independent partial sums in a `[f32; 8]`, combined at the end. Measured on 4096-element f32 dot product with Criterion 0.8.2: scalar 1.9323 us vs 8-way unroll 289.69 ns = 6.67x (471.7 ps vs 70.7 ps per element). The cost is a CORRECTNESS change: you are choosing to reassociate, so last-bit results differ. Unacceptable if the output feeds a financial aggregate or must be bit-reproducible across machines or lane counts. Say that out loud.

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: What do `#[inline]`, `#[inline(always)]` and `#[inline(never)]` actually do?
flashcards.a: `#[inline]` is a hint PLUS a guarantee the function's MIR is exported so downstream crates can inline it. `#[inline(always)]` overrides LLVM's cost model and is almost always wrong: it inflates code size and evicts other code from the ~32 KB L1 instruction cache. Its two legitimate uses are `#[target_feature]` wrappers and functions smaller than their call sequence. `#[inline(never)]` is a PROFILING tool: add it temporarily so a function appears as its own flamegraph frame instead of being smeared into callers. Generic functions are implicitly inlinable cross-crate (their MIR must be exported to monomorphise at all).

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: What does LTO actually buy in 2026, and what is the old folklore that is now wrong?
flashcards.a: The folklore "cross-crate inlining requires #[inline] or LTO" is now only partly true: rustc's MIR inliner does cross-crate inlining of small-to-medium functions on stable without either. Tested with a two-crate workspace, no `#[inline]`, `lto = false`: zero `call` instructions to the dependency's function, and it still inlined when made bulky. What LTO reliably bought: binary 4,426,416 -> 2,221,304 bytes (49.8% reduction) at 0.14 s -> 2.48 s build (17.7x), with a 3.6% runtime delta that was noise. LTO is primarily a SIZE and devirtualisation tool. `lto = "thin"` is the sane default.

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: Is `Vec::with_capacity` always worth it?
flashcards.a: No. 1M `u64` pushes: `Vec::new()` 0.677 ms vs `with_capacity` 0.674 ms, no win (amortised doubling means ~20 reallocs, and glibc `realloc` often extends large mappings in place). 200k `String` pushes: 10.491 vs 6.619 ms = 1.58x, a real win, because each realloc must memcpy 24-byte String headers and the heap is already fragmented. Beating both: `(0..1M).collect::<Vec<u64>>()` at 0.203 ms = 3.33x, using `size_hint` to allocate exactly once and write through a raw pointer with no per-push capacity check. For `HashMap`, growth means rehashing every key, so `with_capacity` matters more there.

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: What is the measured cost of `String` where `&str` would do, and what is the allocation toolkit?
flashcards.a: Over 200k words: `w.clone() + "!"` took 3.899 ms; `w.len() + 1` took 0.068 ms. 57x. In order of how often it is right: take `&str`/`&[T]` in signatures and own only at storage boundaries; `Cow<'a, str>` when you usually borrow and occasionally modify; `with_capacity` at boundaries; `SmallVec<[T; N]>` with N from the measured p95 (check `size_of` first, a 512-byte SmallVec is a pessimisation); arena/bumpalo (alloc = pointer increment, ~2-3 instructions vs ~100+ for malloc); swap in `mimalloc`/`jemallocator` as `#[global_allocator]` for 10-30% on threaded allocation-heavy workloads; reuse buffers with `clear()`.

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: Array-of-structs vs struct-of-arrays: give the number and the counter-case.
flashcards.a: 1M particles, `size_of::<Particle>() == 32` bytes (8 x f32), summing just `p.x`: AoS touches 32,000,000 bytes at 1.394 ms; SoA (`Vec<f32>` of just x) touches 4,000,000 bytes at 0.456 ms. 3.06x, sublinear in the 8x traffic reduction because at 32 MB you are DRAM-bandwidth-bound. SoA is WRONG when the hot loop touches all fields of one object at a time: you get 8 independent memory streams competing for prefetcher slots and TLB entries, plus harder-to-read code. Hot/cold splitting (3 hot fields in one struct, the other 20 boxed) is usually the better cost/benefit point.

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: What is false sharing, what does it cost, and how do you diagnose it?
flashcards.a: Cache coherence operates on 64-byte lines, not variables, so 4 logically-independent `AtomicU64` counters (8 B each) share one line and every core's write invalidates it in the other three cores' L1. Measured: 4 threads x 50,000,000 relaxed `fetch_add` took 1768.298 ms packed vs 481.023 ms with `#[repr(align(64))]`. 3.68x from one attribute. Symptom: throughput DROPS as you add threads, high CPU, huge cache-miss count on a tiny working set. Diagnose with `perf c2c record`/`report` (HITM events name the line and the two contending instructions). Use `crossbeam_utils::CachePadded`, which pads to 128 B on aarch64/Apple silicon where hand-rolled `align(64)` is subtly wrong.

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: What is the status of `std::simd`, and what ships on stable?
flashcards.a: As of rustc 1.97.1 (2026-07-14) `std::simd` is STILL nightly-only, gated behind `#![feature(portable_simd)]`, tracking issue rust-lang/rust#86656. It provides `Simd<T, N>` for lane counts 1 through 64, `Mask<T, N>`, `simd_swizzle!`, and now `f16xN` types; it degrades to scalar code on targets without SIMD rather than failing to compile. On stable: make autovectorisation fire first (`chunks_exact(8)`, iterators, split FP accumulators), then the `wide` crate for portable vector types, then hand-written `std::arch` intrinsics. Never claim it is stable in an interview.

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: How do you ship AVX2 code to a fleet where some hosts lack AVX2?
flashcards.a: Not with `-C target-cpu=native`, which produces a binary that SIGILLs on any host missing an instruction it used, silently until it isn't. Set a floor in `.cargo/config.toml`: `x86-64-v2` (SSE4.2, POPCNT, ~2009+) or `x86-64-v3` (AVX2, FMA, BMI2, Haswell 2013+ / Zen 1+), verified against your actual instance families. Above the floor use `#[target_feature(enable = "avx2")] unsafe fn` guarded by `is_x86_feature_detected!("avx2")`, resolved ONCE into a fn pointer in a `OnceLock` rather than checked inside the hot loop. Calling a `#[target_feature]` fn from a non-AVX2 context blocks inlining across that boundary, so the idiom is one big `#[inline(always)] #[target_feature]` region. The `multiversion` crate generates this.

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: Criterion: current status, what it does that a timing loop doesn't, and the forgotten config line.
flashcards.a: Criterion moved to the `criterion-rs` GitHub org (the original `bheisler` repo is unmaintained); latest is 0.8.2 released 2026-02-04, MSRV is the last three stable minors = Rust 1.88+. It gives 3 s warmup, ~100 samples over ~5 s, bootstrap resampling for a median with 95% CI, Tukey outlier classification, and automatic comparison against the previous run in `target/criterion/` with a change estimate and p-value. `#[bench]` from libtest is now a hard error on stable. THE FORGOTTEN LINE is `harness = false` under `[[bench]]`; without it libtest eats the CLI args and Criterion never runs. `black_box` is `std::hint::black_box`, stable since 1.66.

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: How do you spot a benchmark that is measuring nothing?
flashcards.a: Measured case: `(0..n).fold(0u64, wrapping_add)` with n = 10,000,000 benchmarked at 975.34 ps, and STILL 958.84 ps with `black_box` on the input, because LLVM recognised the triangular sum and used the closed form. Criterion's own line gave it away: "Collecting 100 samples in estimated 5.0000 s (5.2B iterations)". Checks in order of speed: (1) sanity-check against physics, a loop over N elements can't beat ~N/8 cycles; (2) run at N and 2N and confirm the time roughly doubles for an O(n) function, the single most reliable 30-second test; (3) read the bench binary's assembly with `cargo asm --bench`; (4) a CI narrower than 1% on a sub-ns measurement means you're measuring harness overhead (~1-2 ns/iter).

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: How do you use `black_box` correctly, and what is its actual guarantee?
flashcards.a: Block the optimiser on BOTH ends: `b.iter(|| black_box(my_fn(black_box(&input))))`. The inner call stops constant propagation into the function; the outer stops dead-code elimination of the result. But if the body is analytically foldable (as `(0..n).fold(+)` was), no amount of call-site `black_box` helps and you must make the body opaque or benchmark something the compiler can't solve in closed form. Its documented guarantee is best-effort with no formal promise, which is worth stating precisely because interviewers value the honesty.

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: What is the correct profiling order for a Rust service pinned at 100% CPU?
flashcards.a: 1) `perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-misses,branch-misses` for 30 s. IPC below ~1.0 with high cache misses = memory-bound, stop micro-optimising instructions. IPC above ~2.5 with high branch-misses = branch-bound. That one number decides the next hour. 2) `samply record -p <pid>` for a flamegraph PLUS a time axis (an aggregate flamegraph hides a 200 ms stall inside a 20 s run). 3) Aggregate `__rust_alloc`/`__rust_dealloc`/`malloc`/`free`/`memcpy`: over ~15% means allocation-bound and everything else is premature. 4) Look for wide `drop_in_place` (bulk destruction on the request path) and any `panic_bounds_check` at all. Requires `debug = 1` in `[profile.release]`.

flashcards.topic: Zero-Cost Abstractions, SIMD, Benchmarking with Criterion, Profiling
flashcards.q: Why is a Rust flamegraph often one giant frame, and why are async flamegraphs useless?
flashcards.a: Inlining destroys frames: an inlined function doesn't appear, its samples are attributed to the caller, so you get a fat `main` or `poll`. Two fixes: `debug = 1` in the release profile for line tables (nearly free at runtime), and temporarily add `#[inline(never)]` to the specific functions you want as distinct frames, rebuilt just for the profiling run. Never profile a debug build, it is a different program (no inlining, no vectorisation, all checks live). For async, a stack sampler is the wrong tool entirely: every sample lands under `tokio::runtime::...::poll` and the logical call chain is lost across `.await` points because each poll is a separate stack. Use `tokio-console` for task state and `tracing` spans with `tracing-flame` for the logical picture.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: What trait does an axum `Router` implement, and what is its `Error` type?
flashcards.a: `tower::Service<Request<Body>, Response = Response<Body>, Error = Infallible>`. Because the error type is uninhabited, axum has no error channel: every failure must already be a `Response`. That is why raw `tower::timeout::Timeout` (Error = `Box<dyn Error>`) needs `HandleErrorLayer`, and why `tower_http::timeout::TimeoutLayer` (returns 408 as a response) is the one you actually use.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: Why can a body extractor like `Json<T>` only appear as the last handler argument?
flashcards.a: Arguments 1..15 are bound by `FromRequestParts` (takes `&mut http::request::Parts`, head only, so many can run in sequence); the last is bound by `FromRequest` (takes `Request` by value because a body is a stream consumable once). axum's `Handler` impl is macro-generated for arities 1 through 16 exactly. Misplacing it fails the whole `Handler` bound, hence `#[axum::debug_handler]`.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: `State<S>` vs `Extension<T>`: how does each fail when you forget to provide it?
flashcards.a: `State` fails at compile time: `Router<S>` carries the required state in its type and `axum::serve` requires `Router<()>`, so a missing `with_state` will not build. `Extension` fails at runtime with a 500 and `Missing request extension: Extension of type 'T' was not found`. Use `State` for startup-known data, `Extension` only for per-request data injected by middleware. Note `State` is cloned per request, so every field must be `Arc`-shaped.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: Why can `.layer(RequireAuth)` silently protect nothing?
flashcards.a: `Router::layer` wraps only routes that exist on the router at the moment it is called. `Router::new().layer(auth).route("/admin", get(h))` wraps an empty router, so `/admin` is unauthenticated with no compile error and no warning. Add all `.route()`/`.nest()` calls first, then `.layer()` last. `route_layer` panics if no routes have been declared, which is the guard `layer` deliberately lacks.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: `Router::layer` vs `Router::route_layer` for an auth middleware?
flashcards.a: `layer` also wraps the fallback, so an auth layer added with it turns every 404 into a 401. `route_layer` runs only when the request matched a route, which is exactly what authorization wants. axum's docs say this explicitly: `route_layer` is 'useful for middleware that returns early (such as authorization) which might otherwise convert a 404 Not Found into a 401 Unauthorized'.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: Which direction does middleware ordering run in `ServiceBuilder` vs chained `Router::layer`?
flashcards.a: Opposite directions. `ServiceBuilder::new().layer(A).layer(B).service(s)` builds `A(B(s))`, so A sees the request first (tower's docs: 'layers added first will be called with the request first'). Chained `Router::layer(A).layer(B)` builds `B(A(router))`, so B sees it first. The convention that avoids the whole class of bug is one `ServiceBuilder` passed to one `.layer()` call.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: List the sqlx `PoolOptions::new()` defaults that matter, and which one you change first.
flashcards.a: `max_connections = 10`, `min_connections = 0`, `acquire_timeout = 30 s`, `idle_timeout = 600 s`, `max_lifetime = 1800 s`, `test_before_acquire = true`, `acquire_slow_threshold = 2 s`, `fair = true`, statement cache 100. Change `acquire_timeout` to ~3 s first: the 30 s default turns pool exhaustion into a stall the client has already timed out on, instead of a fast 503 you can see in your own metrics.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: How do you size a sqlx connection pool, and what is the binding constraint?
flashcards.a: Little's Law: `L = rps x seconds_of_connection_time_per_request`. At 2,000 rps holding a connection 3 ms, L = 6; divide by target utilisation 0.7 for ~9, since queueing delay grows as 1/(1-rho). The binding constraint is the database: `(replicas + maxSurge) x max_connections <= Postgres max_connections (default 100) - 3 reserved`. Beyond that, use PgBouncer transaction pooling, not a bigger Postgres limit.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: Why do you get intermittent `prepared statement "sqlx_s_7" does not exist` behind PgBouncer?
flashcards.a: sqlx uses named prepared statements cached per connection (`statement_cache_capacity` default 100). PgBouncer in transaction mode reuses server connections across clients, so the cached name may not exist on the connection you get. Fix: PgBouncer 1.21+ with `max_prepared_statements > 0`, or `PgConnectOptions::statement_cache_capacity(0)` (costs a parse per query). Same root cause breaks sqlx's session-scoped migration advisory lock, so use `Migrator::set_locking(false)`.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: What does `cargo sqlx prepare` produce, and how do you keep it honest in CI?
flashcards.a: It runs every `query!` macro against a live database and writes one JSON file per unique query into `.sqlx/`, named by the SHA-256 of the SQL. Commit it and build with `SQLX_OFFLINE=true`. Gate it with `cargo sqlx prepare --check --workspace` in CI plus a Postgres service container, or a stale cache fails the build with 'set DATABASE_URL to use query macros online, or run cargo sqlx prepare'.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: sqlx `query!` column-annotation syntax: what do `!`, `?` and `: Type` mean?
flashcards.a: `as "x!"` forces non-null (`T` not `Option<T>`), `as "x?"` forces nullable, `as "x: MyType"` overrides the Rust type, `as "x!: MyType"` does both. You need them because Postgres reports nullability conservatively for aggregates, expressions, and the nullable side of a LEFT JOIN. sqlx 0.9.0 changed this inference ('force generic plan'), a listed breaking change that can produce a wave of type errors on upgrade.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: Inside a sqlx transaction, what is the silent data-integrity bug?
flashcards.a: Executing against `&pool` instead of `&mut *tx`. `&pool` checks out a different connection, so those statements run outside the transaction and commit independently. No compiler error. Grep for `&pool`/`&state.db` in any function that also calls `begin()`. Related: `Drop` on a `Transaction` issues a ROLLBACK (queued, since Drop cannot be async), and `tx.begin()` on an existing transaction issues a SAVEPOINT.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: Why does `log` fail for async Rust services, and what does `tracing` do instead?
flashcards.a: `log` correlates by (timestamp, thread id, module). On a Tokio multi-thread runtime one worker interleaves polls from thousands of tasks and work-stealing migrates a task across workers, so thread id partitions nothing and one request's lines are non-contiguous. `tracing` attaches a span to the *future*: `.instrument(span)` / `#[instrument]` enters at the start of every poll and exits at every return, so context follows the task. Spans nest, so a deep `error!` carries all ancestor fields.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: Why must you never hold a `span.enter()` guard across an `.await`?
flashcards.a: `Span::enter()` sets a thread-local current span. At the `.await` the task yields and the worker immediately polls a different task, whose events are then attributed to your span. Result: traces where unrelated requests nest inside each other, only reproducible under concurrency. Use `#[tracing::instrument]` or `.instrument(span)`, which enter and exit around each individual `poll`.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: Give the measured cargo-chef numbers and the caveat.
flashcards.a: Reference service (axum + sqlx + tracing, 179 crates, rustc 1.97.1, 2 vCPU): cold build 117 s, warm build with dependencies cached 24 s, a 4.9x win. Consistent with ~5x reported on a ~500-dependency commercial codebase and ~9x on ExpressVPN's repo. Caveat: with no persistent Docker layer cache, cargo-chef adds a planner stage and a dummy-source build on top of the real one and can make builds slower (a documented 5 min to 25 min case).

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: Base image sizes (compressed amd64, Aug 2026) and which one you ship.
flashcards.a: `rust:latest` 569.3 MiB, `rust:1.97-slim` 308.1 MiB (builders only). `debian:bookworm-slim` 26.9 MiB, `alpine:3.22` 3.6 MiB, `gcr.io/distroless/cc-debian12` 8.75 MiB, `distroless/static-debian12` 0.67 MiB. Ship `distroless/cc-debian12:nonroot`: glibc, no shell, no package manager, UID 65532. With a 3.38 MiB stripped binary the final image is ~12 MiB compressed / ~26 MB on disk.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: What is the musl trap, and what is the symptom?
flashcards.a: musl's `malloc` serialises multithreaded allocation far harder than glibc's ptmalloc (which uses up to 8 x ncores arenas). Rust allocates constantly, so it lands on the hot path; reported slowdowns reach 7x, worsening with thread count. Symptom: throughput scales to 2 threads then flattens or regresses as cores are added, with `perf` showing cycles in musl's malloc lock path. Fix: build glibc and use distroless/cc, or if static is mandatory set `#[global_allocator]` to mimalloc or jemalloc.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: Why is `panic = "abort"` wrong for a service?
flashcards.a: It removes unwind tables, which makes `std::panic::catch_unwind` a no-op. `tower_http::catch_panic::CatchPanicLayer` stops working and Tokio's per-task panic isolation (`JoinError::is_panic`) stops working, so one malformed request that trips an `unwrap()` kills the whole process and every in-flight request with it. Ship `panic = "unwind"` (the default) plus `CatchPanicLayer` and `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: Design rule for liveness vs readiness probes, and the Kubernetes defaults that matter.
flashcards.a: Liveness must depend on nothing external (a constant handler), or one database blip restarts every replica at once and the recovery is a reconnect storm. Readiness may ping the database, with an internal 300-500 ms timeout because `timeoutSeconds` defaults to 1. Defaults: `periodSeconds 10`, `timeoutSeconds 1`, `failureThreshold 3`, so a default liveness config SIGKILLs 30 s after the first failure. Add a `startupProbe` to cover migrations and pool warm-up.

flashcards.topic: Building a Service: axum, sqlx, tracing, Docker, and Deploying It
flashcards.q: Measured memory profile of an axum+sqlx service, and the two ways Rust still uses too much.
flashcards.a: Measured on 2 vCPU with rustc 1.97.1: 3,140 KiB RSS idle, 3,540 KiB after 3,000 requests, 3 OS threads, single-digit-ms startup. Spring Boot equivalents typically sit at 150-400 MB with 25-60 threads and 2-8 s startup. Rust's failure modes: glibc arena growth (up to 8 x ncores arenas retaining freed memory; fix with `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2` or jemalloc/mimalloc), and OOM as SIGKILL with exit code 137 and no stack trace, since there is no `OutOfMemoryError`.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: What is the machine-level difference between a generic parameter and a `dyn Trait` argument?
flashcards.a: Generics monomorphise: the compiler emits one specialised machine-code copy per concrete type, called directly and inlinable, with a thin 8-byte pointer. `dyn Trait` emits exactly one copy of the function; the value is a fat 16-byte pointer (data pointer + vtable pointer) and each method call loads a function pointer from the vtable and calls indirectly. Static is Rust's default; you opt into dynamic.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: What does a Rust vtable actually contain, and how many are generated?
flashcards.a: One vtable per (concrete type, trait) pair, emitted into read-only data. It holds a `drop_in_place` pointer, the value's size, its alignment, then one slot per dispatchable method. The layout is an implementation detail and is explicitly not guaranteed, so transmuting a trait object to inspect it is unspecified behaviour.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: Why is `Clone` not dyn compatible? Derive it rather than recite it.
flashcards.a: `fn clone(&self) -> Self` returns `Self`. A caller holding `&dyn Clone` has erased the concrete type, so it does not know the returned value's size or alignment and cannot allocate a slot for it; the calling convention cannot express that vtable slot. The same reason disqualifies `Copy`, `Default`, `From`, and `Into`.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: State the dyn-compatibility (formerly object-safety) rules that trigger error[E0038].
flashcards.a:
Trait level: no `Self: Sized` supertrait, all supertraits dyn compatible, no associated constants, no associated types with their own generic parameters (so no GATs). Method level, to be dispatchable: no generic type parameters (lifetimes are fine), `Self` appears nowhere except as the receiver, the receiver is one of `&self`/`&mut self`/`Box`/`Rc`/`Arc`/`Pin

`, and no `where Self: Sized`.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: How does `Iterator` stay dyn compatible with roughly 70 methods, many of them generic?
flashcards.a: Every generic provided method (`map`, `filter`, `collect`, `fold`, ...) carries `where Self: Sized`, which excludes it from the vtable while keeping it callable on concrete types. Only `next` is required and it is dispatchable, so `Box<dyn Iterator<Item = u32>>` works. You can still call `.map()` on that `Box` because `Box<I>` itself implements `Iterator` and is `Sized`.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: Associated type or generic parameter on a trait: what is the deciding rule?
flashcards.a: A generic parameter is an input, so one type can implement the trait many times with different arguments (`String: From<&str>`, `From<char>`, `From<Box<str>>`). An associated type is an output determined by the impl, so a type implements the trait exactly once (`Iterator::Item`), which is what keeps `.next()` inferable without a turbofish. Ask: can one type sensibly implement this more than once? Yes means generic parameter.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: State the orphan rule and the standard workaround.
flashcards.a: `impl ForeignTrait<T1..Tn> for T0` is allowed only if at least one of `T0..Tn` is a local type and no uncovered type parameter precedes the first local type. Practically: your trait for anyone's type, yes; anyone's trait for your type, yes; someone else's trait for someone else's type, no (error[E0117]). Workaround is the newtype, `struct Hex(Vec<u8>)`, which is zero-cost because a single-field tuple struct has identical layout to its field. RFC 2451 loosened the rule in 2018.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: Is adding a blanket impl to an already-published trait a breaking change?
flashcards.a: Yes, in the general case, even though it adds no method to any signature. `impl<T: Display> MyTrait for T` produces error[E0119] in any downstream crate that already wrote `impl MyTrait for TheirType` where `TheirType: Display`. There is no way to opt out and no `specialization` on stable (RFC 1210 has been unstable since 2015) to break the tie.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: Write out the exact desugaring of the `?` operator.
flashcards.a: `let n = f()?;` becomes `let n = match f() { Ok(v) => v, Err(e) => return Err(From::from(e)) };`. The `From::from` is the entire design: write `impl From<E> for MyError` once and every `?` in the crate converts for free. Runtime cost is one branch: no unwinding, no stack capture, no allocation, no dynamic dispatch.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: In what sense are `Option` and `Result` not special-cased by the compiler, and what are the three honest exceptions?
flashcards.a: Both are ordinary library enums in `core::option` and `core::result`, about ten lines each, using no syntax you cannot use yourself. The exceptions: they are in the prelude so `Some`/`None`/`Ok`/`Err` are always in scope; both are `#[must_use]`, which is what makes error handling compiler-enforced rather than conventional; and `?` works via the `Try` trait, which is still unstable (`try_trait_v2`) as of Rust 1.97, so you cannot make `?` work on your own type on stable.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: Give the niche-optimisation sizes you should be able to state cold (64-bit).
flashcards.a: `size_of::<Option<&T>>() == 8` (null is the niche), `size_of::<Option<Box<T>>>() == 8`, `size_of::<Option<NonZeroU32>>() == 4` (zero is the niche), `size_of::<Option<bool>>() == 1`, but `size_of::<Option<u32>>() == 8` because `u32` has no spare bit pattern so a real tag plus padding is needed. Also `size_of::<std::io::Error>() == 8`, a tagged pointer packing errno, a static message, or a boxed custom error.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: How is match exhaustiveness a refactoring tool, and how do people throw it away?
flashcards.a: Adding an enum variant makes every `match` on that enum stop compiling with error[E0004], naming the uncovered pattern at each site, so the compiler generates the to-do list for you. Writing `_ => {}` on an enum you own permanently opts that site out of the check. Use explicit variants for enums you control, reserve `_` for genuinely open sets (integers, strings, foreign `#[non_exhaustive]` enums); `clippy::wildcard_enum_match_arm` enforces it. Match guards also defeat exhaustiveness checking, so guarded arms still need a catch-all.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: What does `#[non_exhaustive]` do, and when do you add it?
flashcards.a: On a public enum it forces downstream crates to include a wildcard arm, so you can add variants in a minor release without breaking them; your own crate keeps full exhaustiveness checking. On a struct it blocks downstream literal construction and functional update. Add it to public error and event enums from day one: it is semver-major exactly once and buys unlimited future variants.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: thiserror or anyhow, and why?
flashcards.a: thiserror (2.0.19) in libraries, because the caller must be able to `match` to distinguish 'file missing, use a default' from 'file corrupt, fail loudly' from 'timeout, retry with backoff'; it is a pure proc macro generating the Display/Error/From impls with zero runtime cost. anyhow (1.0.104) in applications, binaries, tests, and glue, where handling is almost always 'log with context, return 500'. anyhow::Error is 8 bytes on 64-bit (vtable stored inside the allocation) versus 16 for `Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>`. Converting thiserror into anyhow is one `?`; the reverse is impossible.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: Why is `unwrap()` in a library a bug, and when is panicking correct?
flashcards.a: It converts a condition the caller could handle into a process-level event they never opted into. Under `panic = "unwind"` in a Tokio service it surfaces as `JoinError::is_panic`, silently killing one task and producing a bare 500; under `panic = "abort"` it kills the whole process; across an `extern "C"` boundary it is a guaranteed abort. Panic is correct only for your own broken invariants (indexing a slice you just sized, a poisoned lock, `unreachable!()` after an exhaustive check). Test: could a well-behaved caller with valid arguments trigger this? If yes, it must be a `Result`.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: How do you diagnose a compile time that jumped from 40 seconds to 9 minutes, or a binary that grew several MB?
flashcards.a: `cargo build --timings` to confirm codegen (not the frontend) dominates, then `cargo llvm-lines --release | head -30` for LLVM IR lines and copy counts per generic function, then `cargo bloat --release --crates` and `-n 20` to attribute the binary. Fix with the de-monomorphisation trick std uses on itself: keep the generic wrapper two lines and move the body into a non-generic inner function, `fn read<P: AsRef<Path>>(p: P) { fn inner(p: &Path) { /* body */ } inner(p.as_ref()) }`.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: Why does `#[async_trait]` still exist when `async fn` in traits stabilised in Rust 1.75?
flashcards.a: The built-in version desugars to `-> impl Future`, an anonymous associated type of unknown size, which makes the trait not dyn compatible. Services need `Arc<dyn Repository + Send + Sync>`, so the macro rewrites each method to return `Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = T> + Send + '_>>`, costing one heap allocation per call. If the trait is only ever used with static dispatch, skip the macro: native `async fn` in traits is free and gives better errors.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: You need a collection of mixed types implementing one trait. What are the options?
flashcards.a: Generics do not solve it: `Vec<T>` holds one concrete `T`. Either `Vec<Box<dyn Draw>>` for an open set (16 bytes per element, one heap allocation each, indirect calls, trait must be dyn compatible so no Clone/PartialEq/generic methods), or an enum with one variant per implementation for a closed set (static dispatch through an exhaustive match, derives Clone/PartialEq freely, no allocation, but every value is sized to the largest variant and all impls must live in one crate). The `enum_dispatch` crate generates the delegating match. Closed set means enum; open or plugin-shaped means dyn.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: Distinguish error[E0282], error[E0207], and error[E0119].
flashcards.a: E0282 'type annotations needed' is inference having no information, typically on `.parse()` or `.collect()` which are generic over their return type; fix with a turbofish (`.collect::<Vec<_>>()`) or a binding annotation. E0207 'the type parameter T is not constrained' is an `impl` block declaring a parameter that appears nowhere in the trait or self type; fix with a `PhantomData<T>` field, by moving `T` down to the methods, or by making it an associated type. E0119 'conflicting implementations' is the coherence overlap check, usually a blanket impl covering a type that already has its own impl.

flashcards.topic: Traits, Generics, Enums, Pattern Matching, Error Handling (Result/?)
flashcards.q: How does Rust's approach differ from Java generics and Go interfaces?
flashcards.a: Java erases, so `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are one class with inserted casts, primitives are boxed (1,000,000 `Integer` objects versus a contiguous 4 MB `Vec<i32>` buffer), and you cannot implement your interface for a type you do not own. Rust monomorphises and the orphan rule permits `impl MyTrait for String`; bounds are checked at definition time, not instantiation time. Go interfaces are structural and implicit (accidental conformance is possible) and always dynamically dispatched through a 2-word fat pointer; Rust traits are nominal and explicit with static dispatch by default. Go generics since 1.18 use GC shape stenciling plus dictionaries, a middle ground that avoids bloat but does not get Rust's full inlining.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: Where does each of Rust, Go and Python make you pay its cost?
flashcards.a: Rust pays at authoring and build time (55% of devs wait >10s per incremental rebuild; 45% of people who quit Rust cited compile times). Go pays at runtime in GC (25% CPU budget, ~2x live heap, mark assist in the request path) and at scale in expressiveness. Python pays at runtime (GIL, ~40 MB/s json.loads, 10-100x slower on pure-Python CPU work) and in operational risk from dynamic typing. Total cost is roughly constant; you choose which column your org can absorb.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: What is Go's stop-the-world pause history and its stated SLO?
flashcards.a: 300-400 ms pre-1.5, 30-40 ms in 1.5 (Aug 2015), 4-5 ms in 1.6, sub-millisecond in 1.8 (Mar 2017, after removing STW stack re-scanning), with a 'whisper number' of 100-200 microseconds by 1.9. Go's stated 2018 SLO: 500 microseconds STW per GC cycle, heap at 2x live, GC CPU capped at 25% of GOMAXPROCS. Source: Rick Hudson's ISMM 2018 keynote.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: If Go's STW pauses are sub-millisecond, why did Discord's Read States service spike every 2 minutes?
flashcards.a: The cost is proportional to the LIVE heap scanned, not the garbage freed. Their LRU cache held tens of millions of Read States, so every cycle traced the whole cache. Go's runtime forces a GC at least every 2 minutes regardless of allocation rate (forcegcperiod). SetGCPercent tuning did nothing because they were not allocating fast enough. The cost lands as mark assist charged to allocating goroutines, so it shows up as a p99.9 regression, not a pause in the trace.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: What is the 'tyranny of the nines' and why does it kill a p99 GC argument?
flashcards.a: From Go's own ISMM keynote: if 99% of GC cycles are under 10 ms and a user session makes 100 server requests, only 0.99^100 = 37% of users get a consistently sub-10ms session. To get 99% of USERS under the bar you need the 99.99th percentile, not the 99th. Any latency argument that stops at p99 has not engaged with the problem.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: Measured: what happens when you run two CPU-bound Python threads on two cores?
flashcards.a: It gets SLOWER. Two loops of 6,000,000 iterations: 898 ms serial in one thread, 1,062 ms across two threading.Thread. That is 0.85x, an 18% regression, purely from GIL handoff and eval-breaker overhead. Threads help in Python only when the work releases the GIL (I/O or a C extension).

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: What is the current status of free-threaded Python, precisely?
flashcards.a: PEP 703 designed it; PEP 779 made the free-threaded build officially supported in Python 3.14, shipping as a separate 3.14t binary. Single-thread overhead is ~1% on macOS aarch64 and ~8% on x86-64 Linux (down from ~40% in 3.13). Memory is higher: None is 32 B vs 16 B, interned strings are immortal, mimalloc replaces pymalloc, QSBR defers frees. Importing a C extension not marked free-threading-compatible silently RE-ENABLES the GIL. GIL default-off is not planned before the 2028-2030 window.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: Compare the three concurrency units: goroutine, Rust future, asyncio task.
flashcards.a: Goroutine: 2 KB initial stack grown by copying, GMP work-stealing scheduler with 256-slot local run queues, GOMAXPROCS OS threads, signal-based async preemption since Go 1.14 (~10 ms), no function colouring. Rust future: a compile-time state machine, inert until polled, size equals the largest live state across await points, NO preemption at all. Asyncio task: measured 2,185 bytes per task (100k tasks), 161 ns per await of a ready coroutine, no preemption, and no parallelism on the GIL build.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: What happens when you make a blocking call inside a handler, in each language?
flashcards.a: Go: the runtime parks the goroutine and other goroutines keep running, so a blocking syscall is fine (a tight CPU loop was a hang before 1.14's async preemption). Rust: it stalls one Tokio worker thread for the whole duration, because nothing preempts poll. Python asyncio: it stalls the ENTIRE event loop and therefore every concurrent request. Tools: tokio-console, asyncio debug mode with loop.slow_callback_duration, and Go's runtime/trace plus the new 1.26 /sched/goroutines metrics.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: What did the Rust project's own 2025 compiler performance survey find?
flashcards.a: 3,700+ responses. Average build satisfaction 6/10. 55% wait more than 10 seconds for an incremental rebuild. ~45% of respondents who had STOPPED using Rust cited compile times. ~20% blocked by clean builds; ~25% of the 1,495 CI users blocked by CI build time, and ~36% of those use no CI cache at all. ~33% blocked by IDE annotation latency; >35% by Rust Analyzer and Cargo fighting over the build lock. ~42% have tried no mitigation whatsoever.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: Why is Rust slow to compile, and what actually helps?
flashcards.a: Monomorphisation plus LLVM plus linking, not the borrow checker (which is single-digit percent of build time). Measured: 200 instantiations of one 8-line generic function produce 10,847 lines of LLVM IR and a 536 ms rebuild versus 5,690 lines and 169 ms for the single dyn version, a 3.17x difference. Fixes: LLD (default on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu since Rust 1.90) or mold, sccache, debug = 'line-tables-only' (2-30% cycles), cargo llvm-lines then the thin-generic-wrapper refactor, splitting the workspace, cutting default features.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: What are the PostHog Django-to-Rust numbers, and what is the honest reading?
flashcards.a: p50 21.7 -> 11.8 ms (1.8x), p90 160 -> 31.2 ms (5.1x), p95 381 -> 42.9 ms (8.9x), p99 904 -> 85.4 ms (10.6x). Same ~500k req/min went from ~300 pods at ~$8.8k/month to ~90 pods at ~$2.8k/month, a 68% cost cut. Their synthetic benchmark was 21x (axum ~32k rps vs Django ~1.5k) and did not materialise. Honest reading: the median barely moved while the tail collapsed, and in the same change they moved evaluation out of SQL, added cohort caching, and deleted PgBouncer. Much of the win is architectural.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: Name five specific cases where Rust is the wrong choice.
flashcards.a: 1) I/O-dominated services: 20x faster on 15% of latency buys 3%. 2) Requirements still moving: Rust's cost is front-loaded onto getting ownership right and is repaid only when the code stops changing. 3) Fewer than ~40% of the team can review it, so the review queue becomes one person. 4) Anything Kubernetes-adjacent, because the ecosystem gravity is Go and you will reimplement client-go badly. 5) ML training and the model layer of inference, because the kernels are CUDA with Python bindings.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: What did Google's Rust productivity study actually say, including the clause people omit?
flashcards.a: Lars Bergstrom at Rust Nation UK 2024: rewriting C++ services in Rust cut effort to build and maintain by more than 2x in every measured case, and retraining C++ to Rust took time comparable to Java to Kotlin. The omitted clause: Go and Rust teams finished the same rewrite task at the SAME speed, while the C++ team took twice as long. The study supports Rust over C++, not Rust over Go.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: What are the hiring-pool numbers, and why do they cut both ways?
flashcards.a: Stack Overflow 2025 (89k+ respondents), used in the past year: Python 57.9%, Java 29.4%, Go 16.4%, Rust 14.8%, JavaScript 66%+. Rust has been most admired for ten consecutive years (72% in 2025). Admiration measures desire, not supply: many want to write Rust, roughly one in seven has written any, and far fewer have shipped and operated a production Rust service. Time to first useful PR is roughly day one for Python, 3-7 days for Go, 4-8 weeks for Rust.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: Why is Python's memory footprint structurally worse, and by how much?
flashcards.a: Not per-object overhead, but process multiplication: a GIL-bound service that needs 8 cores runs 8 processes, each paying the full interpreter plus every preloaded artefact. Measured: a bare Python 3.10 interpreter is 17.3 MB RSS, +10.7 MB after a modest stdlib import set. If each worker also holds a 400 MB model, that is 3.2 GB for one pod to use 8 cores. For comparison, a Rust axum service is ~10-30 MB and a Go net/http service ~20-60 MB, with Go typically 2-4x Rust because the collector keeps roughly 2x live heap resident.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: What are GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT, and what is the trap with GOMEMLIMIT?
flashcards.a: GOGC defaults to 100: collect when the heap reaches (1 + GOGC/100) x live, i.e. 2x. Raising it to 200-400 is a cheap win for allocation-heavy services with RAM to spare. GOMEMLIMIT (Go 1.19+) is a SOFT limit that makes the collector work harder as you approach it; the idiomatic container config is GOGC=off plus GOMEMLIMIT at ~90% of the container limit. The trap: soft means that if live heap genuinely exceeds it you get a GC death spiral (100% GC CPU, no forward progress) instead of a clean OOM. Keep a real container limit too, and alert on GC cycle rate, not RSS.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: What is the polyglot boundary rule, and why is Rust uniquely good at FFI?
flashcards.a: Cross language over a NETWORK boundary (gRPC/HTTP) by default; cross via FFI only when the call is hot enough that a network hop dominates, and then make the boundary COARSE (once per request over 10k rows, never 10k calls). Rust is uniquely good at FFI because it has no runtime to initialise: no GC to start, no interpreter to embed, no scheduler assuming it owns the process. PyO3 with py.allow_threads() releases the GIL, which is how pydantic-core, tokenizers, polars, orjson, ruff and uv give Python real parallelism. Go is the weak one: cgo crosses goroutine to system stack (Go 1.26 cut that overhead ~30%) and c-shared drags the whole Go runtime into the host.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: What changed in Go 1.26's garbage collector?
flashcards.a: The Green Tea collector, an experiment in 1.25, became the default. Its design improves marking and scanning of small objects through better locality and CPU scalability. Expected 10-40% reduction in GC overhead on programs that use the GC heavily, plus a further ~10% on Intel Ice Lake / AMD Zen 4 and newer where it uses vector instructions for small-object scanning. Opt out with GOEXPERIMENT=nogreenteagc, which is expected to be removed in Go 1.27. It narrows the Rust gap; it does not close it, because the mechanism (scan the live heap) is unchanged.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: State the seven-step language decision procedure.
flashcards.a: 1) Write the constraint as a number, or admit there is none. 2) Check hard disqualifiers (no GC allowed -> Rust/C; native extension -> Rust; p99.9 <5 ms with GB live heap -> Rust; model training -> Python; k8s operator -> Go). 3) Estimate the runtime gap, then multiply by the fraction of wall time actually spent in your code. 4) Price the team cost: below 40% fluent, add a quarter of ramp and name it. 5) Price the iteration cost: above ~60 s edit-compile-test, engineers stop running tests locally. 6) If nothing fires, use what the team already runs. 7) Write down the falsification condition.

flashcards.topic: Rust vs Go vs Python: The Honest Selection Criteria
flashcards.q: What is the correct language stack for a multi-tenant LLM inference product?
flashcards.a: Python for the model tier, because vLLM, TGI and TensorRT-LLM are where continuous batching and paged attention live. Rust for the tier AROUND the model: router, admission control, KV-cache-aware load balancing, tokenisation (tokenizers is already Rust), request/response streaming. That tier is CPU-bound, latency-sensitive, memory-per-pod sensitive and has a stable spec, which is exactly Rust's profile. Go for the control plane and anything talking to Kubernetes. Cross over gRPC, not FFI, except where PyO3 already does it. Do NOT propose replacing the CUDA kernels with candle or burn.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: Write CLIP's training objective and say what the labels are.
flashcards.a: Symmetric InfoNCE. L2-normalise both encoder outputs, compute the B x B cosine matrix S, scale by 1/tau, apply cross-entropy in both directions with labels = arange(B). It is a B-way classification problem where the correct class for row i is column i. There is NO target similarity value: ranks are trained, magnitudes are not calibrated.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: CLIP's key training numbers: data, batch, temperature, headline result.
flashcards.a: 400M web image-text pairs; global batch 32,768; tau initialised to 0.07 (logit_scale = log(1/tau) = 14.29 at init), learned, clamped so 1/tau <= 100 i.e. tau >= 0.01; 76.2% zero-shot ImageNet top-1 with ViT-L/14@336px; largest run RN50x64 took 18 days on 592 V100s.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: Why is contrastive batch size a capability parameter rather than a memory knob?
flashcards.a: Negatives come exclusively from the batch: B-1 per example. Chance-level top-1 is 1/B (0.39% at B=256, 0.003% at B=32,768), so the task literally gets harder with B. And InfoNCE is a variational lower bound on mutual information capped at log B nats: 5.55 nats (8.0 bits) at B=256, 10.40 nats (15.0 bits) at B=32,768. A small-batch run is bound-limited, not optimisation-limited.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: Does gradient accumulation give you a larger contrastive batch?
flashcards.a: No. Accumulation gives you 128 separate 256-way softmaxes summed, not one 32,768-way softmax; the negatives never meet in the same denominator. The only real options are a gradient-propagating all-gather across devices, a memory bank / MoCo-style queue, or a loss that avoids the global softmax entirely (SigLIP's pairwise sigmoid loss, strong at batch 4,096-8,192 and saturating around 32k).

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: What does temperature do to the InfoNCE gradient, and why is it clipped?
flashcards.a: dL/dS_ij = (1/tau) * p_ij for negatives, where p_ij is that negative's softmax weight. As tau -> 0 the softmax concentrates on the single hardest negative, so the update becomes hard-negative mining with an effective batch near 2; as tau grows the gradient spreads uniformly and learns nothing discriminative. CLIP clamps 1/tau <= 100 because gradient magnitude scales as 1/tau, so the model reduces loss faster by shrinking tau than by improving alignment, until fp16 logits overflow. The learned logit_scale saturates AT the clamp.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: ImageBind's contribution in one sentence, and the combinatorial argument for it.
flashcards.a: You do not need N(N-1)/2 modality pairs, because images are the natural hub of the world's already-paired data, so binding all N modalities to images gets you every other pair for free. Six modalities would need 15 pair-specific models and about 13 of those pairs (audio-thermal, IMU-depth) have essentially no naturally-paired data at any price, whereas image pairing falls out of the sensor stack for free.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
