flashcards.q: ImageBind's six modalities, joint dimensionality, and the hub design decision.
flashcards.a: Image/video, text, audio, depth, thermal, IMU. Joint space d = 1024. The image and text encoders are a FROZEN pretrained OpenCLIP ViT-H/14 (roughly 630M vision, roughly 302M text). Each spoke is trained independently against the frozen hub with symmetric InfoNCE; the spokes never see each other. There is no joint training run.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: Why must the ImageBind hub be frozen?
flashcards.a: Data asymmetry of three to four orders of magnitude. The hub was pretrained on hundreds of millions of image-text pairs; the thermal spoke sees roughly 15k LLVIP pairs and the depth spoke roughly 10k SUN RGB-D images. Fine-tuning a 630M-parameter ViT-H against 15k examples destroys it. The signature of getting this wrong is catastrophic forgetting: previously-good text-image retrieval regresses while the new pair improves.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: Derive emergent cross-modal alignment in three lines.
flashcards.a: Train (I,A): f_A(a) ~ f_I(i) for paired (i,a). Train (I,T): f_T(t) ~ f_I(i) for paired (i,t). Therefore f_A(a) ~ f_T(t) whenever both describe the same image. The hub is a shared basis and each spoke was fitted to express itself in that basis, so any two spokes already share a coordinate system. Nothing about audio-text was ever in a loss, which is why it is emergent and also why it is weaker than a directly-trained pair.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: How strong is emergent alignment versus a directly-trained or supervised model? Give numbers.
flashcards.a: ESC-50 audio classification: ImageBind emergent roughly 66.9% top-1, AudioCLIP (text-audio supervised) roughly 68.6%, fully supervised audio specialist 95%+. Harder spokes are worse: NYU-v2 depth roughly 54.0%, SUN RGB-D roughly 35.1%, LLVIP thermal roughly 63.4%, Ego4D IMU roughly 25.0%; AudioCaps text-to-audio R@1 roughly 9.3, Clotho roughly 6.0. Rule of thumb: 60-70% of the way to a specialist on easy modalities, 25-35% on hard ones.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: What bounds emergent alignment quality besides the two-hop path?
flashcards.a: The hub's coverage of your domain. Emergent performance tracks image-encoder strength: moving the frozen hub from ViT-B to ViT-H lifted emergent audio classification by roughly 12 points. If the hub never saw your domain (medical imaging, factory-floor audio), the spokes are projected into coordinates that do not describe your data and the emergent pair can be near-useless while a directly-trained pair is fine.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: What does LanguageBind show about the choice of hub?
flashcards.a: That images are not uniquely correct, only conveniently paired. LanguageBind (ICLR 2024) froze a VL-pretrained language encoder, trained spokes against it on VIDAL-10M (10M five-modality tuples), and beat ImageBind by roughly 5.8 R@1 on MSR-VTT zero-shot video-text with roughly 15% of the parameters. Pick the hub with the densest semantics AND adequate natural pairing; for anything ending in a text query that is usually language. The tradeoff is that language pairing for infrared and depth had to be built, whereas image pairing was free.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: What is the modality gap and what causes it?
flashcards.a: Embeddings from different modalities occupy separate narrow cones rather than interleaving. Cause chain: the cone effect means a deep net's outputs occupy a narrow cone at random initialisation, so two independently initialised encoders occupy two different cones; contrastive loss only constrains relative ordering within a row, which is preserved under any rigid separation, so it has no incentive to merge them; and a low learned temperature actively rewards separation because separating cones is a cheap way to make the softmax confident. The gap survives training all the way into your production index.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: Measured modality gap numbers on two untrained encoders, and what they prove.
flashcards.a: Two independently initialised 4-layer 512-d ReLU MLPs fed the same 512 inputs, outputs L2-normalised, zero training: within-A mean cos 0.6794, within-B 0.6863, cross-modality 0.3091, matched pair 0.3095, centroid distance 0.8653, gap 0.3738, median rank of the true match 257 of 512 (chance). Proves the gap is an initialisation artefact, not something contrastive training creates, and that geometry and semantics are independent.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: Does per-modality mean-centring fix the modality gap?
flashcards.a: It erases the gap and buys nothing for retrieval. Measured: centring drove cross-modal mean cosine from 0.3091 to 0.0000 and the matched pair to 0.0015, while the median rank of the true match stayed at 260 of 512, i.e. unchanged. Centring changes score DISTRIBUTIONS, not RANKINGS. Use it for threshold hygiene (making score ranges comparable), never as a quality fix.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: Why does a single HNSW index over mixed modalities return only same-modality results?
flashcards.a: Modality gap meeting greedy graph traversal. With within-modality cosine around 0.68 and cross-modality around 0.31, a text node's M = 32 neighbours are with high probability all text nodes, so the graph is effectively two components joined by a few low-quality bridge edges. Greedy descent from a text entry point never crosses. The tell: within-modality recall@10 stays at 0.95 while cross-modal hit rate is under 5%, and raising ef from 64 to 512 changes nothing because the problem is topology, not search effort. Diagnostic: if brute-force search finds the matches and HNSW does not, the diagnosis is confirmed.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: What is the 'separation' metric and what is a healthy value?
flashcards.a: separation = mean(cosine of matched cross-modal pairs) - mean(cosine of all cross-modal pairs). It is the only quantity that predicts cross-modal retrieval quality, because it is invariant to the gap. A healthy trained CLIP-family model on in-domain data shows roughly 0.05 to 0.15. Below 0.02 the model is not aligned on your data regardless of what the raw cosines or the gap look like. Report it alongside gap and centroid distance, which predict threshold and index misbehaviour rather than quality.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: Production recommendation for multimodal RAG: joint space or separate indices?
flashcards.a: Never one joint index over mixed modalities. Default to captioning/OCR/ASR into ONE TEXT INDEX with BM25 hybrid and your existing reranker; that handles most queries and gives one calibrated score space. Add per-modality native indices with RRF fusion at k = 60 only when the query modality genuinely differs from the corpus modality or captioning is provably lossy. Add ColPali-style late interaction for layout-sensitive documents under a few million pages. Always rerank the top 50, because a good second stage absorbs first-stage geometry problems.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: Why fuse by rank (RRF) rather than by score across modalities?
flashcards.a: Score distributions are per (query_modality, corpus_modality) pair: text-to-text scores live around 0.7-0.9, text-to-image around 0.25-0.35. Any score-weighted fusion across those compares incommensurable quantities, and any single global threshold measures the gap rather than relevance. RRF (score = sum_i 1/(60 + rank_i), k = 60) needs no calibration and is the same tool you already use for BM25-plus-dense hybrid. If you insist on scores, you must calibrate one threshold per modality pair on a held-out labelled set.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: Storage cost per asset for each multimodal retrieval option at 10M assets.
flashcards.a: 1024-d fp32 single vector = 4 KB, so 10M = 40 GB (fits in RAM on one r6i.4xlarge, plus roughly 2.5 GB of HNSW neighbour lists at M = 32). int8 = 1 KB (10 GB). Binary = 128 B (1.28 GB) with fp32 rescoring over the top 200. ColPali-style late interaction = roughly 1,030 patches x 128 dims x 2 bytes = roughly 264 KB per page, so 10M pages is roughly 2.6 TB, a 130x multiplier that changes the class of system you build. Query: roughly 2-5 ms per HNSW index at ef = 128, roughly 6-10 ms p50 for a 4-way concurrent fan-out plus RRF.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: A contrastive run plateaus at loss 4.85 with a reported global batch of 32,768. Diagnosis?
flashcards.a: log(128) = 4.85 and 128 is the per-device batch, so the loss is sitting at the uniform-softmax floor for the LOCAL batch. Cause: dist.all_gather used without a gradient-propagating autograd wrapper, so the forward pass sees 32,768 embeddings but the backward pass drops everything outside the local shard. Fix: a custom autograd.Function that all-reduces the incoming gradient and slices out this rank's shard. Prevention: assert at step 0 that loss is approximately log(global_batch), i.e. 10.40 for 32,768.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: When should you NOT use a joint embedding space?
flashcards.a: Four cases. (1) Query and corpus are the same modality, which is most retrieval: a specialist text embedder beats a multimodal joint model on text-text because the joint model spent capacity on an alignment you are not using. (2) A caption is lossless enough, which is true for most documents, charts and product photos. (3) The asset carries more information than one vector can hold (a 40-page PDF, a 30-minute recording); the signature is good recall on 'what is this about' and zero recall on 'which page has the Q3 EMEA number'. (4) A directly-trained pair is affordable, since 10k-100k real pairs is usually enough and beats the emergent path substantially.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: In 2026, would you build a new multimodal retrieval system on ImageBind?
flashcards.a: For text-image, no: ImageBind's hub is a frozen 2023 OpenCLIP ViT-H, and current MMEB / MMEB-V2 / MIEB leaders are VLM-derived embedders (VLM2Vec-V2) plus commercial models from Cohere Embed v4, Voyage Multimodal 3.5, Gemini Embed and Jina CLIP v2. For layout-sensitive documents, late-interaction ColPali/ColQwen models lead. Use ImageBind for exactly one thing: binding an exotic modality with no paired text data into an existing space, fast. And never pick from a leaderboard: build a 300-500 query eval set from your own traffic and measure nDCG@10 and recall@50 against the boring caption-to-text baseline.

flashcards.topic: ImageBind & Joint Embedding Spaces Across 6 Modalities
flashcards.q: How is audio encoded in ImageBind, and why does an image-pretrained ViT transfer to it?
flashcards.a: 2-second clips at 16 kHz converted to a log-mel spectrogram with 128 mel bins, giving roughly a 128 x 204 single-channel image, patched with 16 x 16 patches at stride 10 (overlapping) and fed to a ViT-B. The trick is that a spectrogram is literally an image with time on one axis and frequency on the other, so the ViT's local patch statistics and 2D inductive bias apply. IMU by contrast is 6 channels (3-axis accelerometer plus 3-axis gyro) over a 5-second window, projected with a kernel-8 1D convolution into a 6-layer transformer.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: In one sentence, what is a JEPA and what makes it different from a masked autoencoder?
flashcards.a: A JEPA predicts the EMBEDDING of a masked target from the EMBEDDING of the visible context, with no decoder; MAE predicts raw PIXELS against an externally fixed ground truth. Consequence: JEPA's target is learned, so the encoder can decline to represent unpredictable detail, and a degenerate constant-encoder solution with exactly zero loss exists.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: Write the JEPA energy function and say what collapse looks like in that language.
flashcards.a: E(x,y) = D( Pred(Enc_ctx(x), z), Enc_tgt(y) ), i.e. the prediction error in representation space, with no normalisation over y (no partition function). Collapse is a FLAT energy surface: E low for all y, not just on the data manifold.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: Name the four components of a JEPA and which one is trained by SGD.
flashcards.a: Context encoder (ViT, trained by SGD, this is what you keep); target encoder (architecturally identical, updated ONLY by EMA, stop-gradient, sees the FULL unmasked input); narrow predictor (ViT at dim 384 vs the encoder's 1280); L2 or smooth-L1 loss on embeddings. Only the context encoder and predictor receive gradients.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: What is the EMA momentum schedule in I-JEPA and what is the implied averaging window at the start?
flashcards.a: Linear from 0.996 to 1.0 over training. At m = 0.996 the effective window is 1/(1-m) = 250 steps, so the context encoder optimises against a target computed by a version of itself roughly 250 steps ago. Ramping to 1.0 freezes the target completely as an endgame stability measure.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: State the I-JEPA multi-block masking parameters exactly.
flashcards.a: 4 target blocks, area scale ~ U(0.15, 0.20), aspect ratio ~ U(0.75, 1.5), allowed to overlap each other. 1 context block, area scale ~ U(0.85, 1.0), aspect ratio 1.0, with every patch overlapping any target block REMOVED. Targets are sliced from the target encoder's output over the full unmasked image.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: Why must the target encoder run on the full image rather than only on the target patches?
flashcards.a: So each target embedding is computed WITH global context available, which makes it a semantically rich target rather than a patch-level appearance descriptor. Running it on target patches alone silently produces a weaker representation with no error message.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: What is the single most common I-JEPA reimplementation bug and what is its signature?
flashcards.a: Overlap leakage: failing to remove target-overlapping patches from the context block. The prediction becomes partly a copy operation. Signature: the loss curve drops FASTER than the reference run while the linear probe stays flat. No assertion fires.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: I-JEPA's compute-efficiency numbers: what does it cost to pretrain a ViT-H/14, and how does that compare to MAE and iBOT?
flashcards.a: Under 1,200 GPU-hours (16 A100s in under 72 hours wall-clock). Reported as over 10x more compute-efficient than a ViT-H/14 pretrained with MAE, and over 2.5x faster than a much smaller ViT-S/16 pretrained with iBOT, while giving better frozen-probe representations than MAE.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: How do you detect representation collapse, and why can't you use the training loss?
flashcards.a: The loss cannot detect it because collapse LOWERS the loss. Use: (1) per-dimension std of L2-normalised embeddings, healthy near 1/sqrt(D) = 0.028 at D=1280, alert below 0.3/sqrt(D); (2) RankMe (exp of the entropy of normalised singular values of the embedding covariance), healthy 0.2-0.8 x D, 1 when fully collapsed, 20-60 when partially collapsed; (3) pairwise cosine similarity distribution, healthy broad around 0.0-0.3, collapsed spikes above 0.95; (4) a detail-sensitive probe such as depth or object counting.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: Why is a linear probe on ImageNet insufficient evidence that a JEPA representation is healthy?
flashcards.a: Coarse classification survives enormous information loss: a representation that has partially collapsed onto a few dozen semantic clusters still probes well. That is dimensional collapse, and it shows up only on detail-sensitive probes (depth, object counting, keypoints, segmentation mIoU) and on RankMe, which would read ~20-60 out of 1280 while every headline metric looks fine.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: Name the three mechanisms proposed to prevent collapse, and say whether any of them is a proof.
flashcards.a: Stop-gradient on the target branch (removes the gradient path that would pull the target toward the prediction); EMA lag (the target is a low-pass-filtered copy, so shrinking is opposed step by step); narrow predictor (dim 384 vs 1280 is too under-parameterised to absorb a degenerate encoder). None is a proof. Collapse remains a global minimum of the objective throughout. SimSiam showed stop-gradient alone suffices without a momentum encoder, so EMA is not the sole mechanism.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: What is LeJEPA and why is it significant for the collapse debate?
flashcards.a: Balestriero and LeCun, arXiv 2511.08544, 11 November 2025. Proves the isotropic Gaussian is the unique embedding distribution minimising worst-case downstream prediction risk, and enforces it with SIGReg: project embeddings onto random 1D directions, match characteristic functions per projection, resample directions each iteration. Linear time and memory, roughly one trade-off hyperparameter. Significant because LeCun co-authoring a paper that calls his own prior anti-collapse stack 'heuristics' confirms that criticism was correct.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: Give the V-JEPA (2024) headline numbers with the qualifier that makes them meaningful.
flashcards.a: arXiv 2404.08471, February 2024, trained on VideoMix2M (2 million videos). ViT-H/16 with a FROZEN backbone and attentive probe: 81.9% on Kinetics-400, 72.2% on Something-Something-v2, 77.9% on ImageNet-1K. Frozen-backbone is the qualifier: the numbers measure the representation, not a fine-tuning budget.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: Describe V-JEPA 2's two-stage training with the data scales for each stage.
flashcards.a: Stage 1 action-free: 1.2B-parameter ViT-g trained with masked latent prediction on VideoMix22M, over 1 million hours of internet video plus images, no actions, no rewards, no labels. Stage 2 action-conditioned: freeze the encoder, train a NEW predictor (V-JEPA 2-AC) mapping [repr(o_t), a_t] to repr(o_{t+1}) on FEWER THAN 62 HOURS of unlabelled Droid robot video.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: What are V-JEPA 2's benchmarked results?
flashcards.a: 77.3% top-1 on Something-Something-v2 (motion understanding), 39.7 recall-at-5 on Epic-Kitchens-100 action anticipation (reported SOTA, surpassing prior task-specific models). Aligned with an LLM at the 8B scale: 84.0 on PerceptionTest and 76.9 on TempCompass. arXiv 2506.09985, 11 June 2025, 48 pages.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: State the V-JEPA 2-AC robot result precisely, including what 'unlabelled' does and does not mean.
flashcards.a: Post-trained on under 62 hours of unlabelled Droid robot video, deployed ZERO-SHOT on Franka arms in TWO different labs with image goals, planning in latent space and replanning every step, at roughly 65-80% pick-and-place success on novel objects. 'Unlabelled' means no task labels, no rewards, no curated demonstrations for the target task, and no data from the deployment environments. It does NOT mean no actions: Droid trajectories carry proprioception and action logs.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: What does LeCun's 2022 position paper actually claim, and how much of it has been demonstrated?
flashcards.a: 'A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence' v0.9.2, 27 June 2022, OpenReview. A position paper with NO experiments. Six modules: configurator, perception, world model, cost (intrinsic + trainable critic), short-term memory, actor. JEPA implements the world model; H-JEPA (hierarchical, multi-timescale) is the proposal for long-horizon planning. Demonstrated: single-level JEPA as a representation learner, and single-level action-conditioned JEPA with inference-time action optimisation. NOT demonstrated at scale: the hierarchy, the configurator, the intrinsic cost module.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: How does JEPA differ from contrastive/invariance methods like SimCLR and DINO, and what is the honest downside?
flashcards.a: Contrastive methods pull together two AUGMENTED VIEWS of the same image (SimCLR: batch 4096, T=0.1, RN50 linear 69.3%; DINO ViT-B/8: 80.1% linear, 77.4% k-NN); JEPA predicts one part of the signal from another part, so the objective is prediction rather than invariance and no hand-designed augmentations are needed. Downside: DINOv2 (ViT-g/14, 1.1B params, curated LVD-142M) reports about 86.5% ImageNet linear probe against I-JEPA's roughly 79%.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: Resolve the apparent paradox: JEPA discards unpredictable detail, yet beats DINO on depth and object-counting probes.
flashcards.a: They discard along orthogonal axes. JEPA discards what is NOT PREDICTABLE FROM CONTEXT (grain, micro-texture, aleatoric noise) and has every incentive to keep spatial layout, object extent, depth ordering and motion, because those make the masked region predictable. Invariance methods discard what their AUGMENTATIONS DECLARE IRRELEVANT, and random resized crop plus colour jitter explicitly say position, scale and colour do not matter, which is exactly what a depth or counting probe needs.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: State the defensible position on 'is JEPA a fundamentally better path, or an elegant SSL method?'
flashcards.a: The narrow claim is supported: latent-space prediction is roughly 10x more compute-efficient than MAE, needs no augmentation design, gives the best low-level spatial and motion representations, and produced the only published zero-shot cross-lab robot planning result off under 62 hours of robot data. The broad claim is not: H-JEPA has no scaled demonstration as of August 2026, JEPA is not the default production frozen backbone, and no JEPA system has displaced a scaled generative model on a general benchmark. Validated as a representation-and-dynamics learner, unvalidated as an architecture thesis.

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: When should you NOT use JEPA?
flashcards.a: When you need to inspect or generate output (no decoder, so no samples and no synthetic data); when a strong curated-data backbone already exists for your modality (DINOv2/v3 or CLIP for general images); when training from scratch below roughly 100k samples (the anti-collapse argument depends on a long optimisation trajectory); when the task is genuinely invariance-shaped (same product under different lighting must be identical); and you must not call an action-free encoder a world model, since without an action-conditioned predictor there is no p(s'|s,a).

flashcards.topic: LeCun's JEPA & V-JEPA 2: Prediction in Latent Space, Not Pixels
flashcards.q: In video JEPA, why must the mask cover the same spatial region across all frames of the clip?
flashcards.a: Masking a random subset of patches per frame makes the task trivially solvable by copying from an adjacent frame, which is the video form of the identity-function failure: low loss, useless representation. Masking the same spatial region across all frames of the clip forces genuine motion inference.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: What are the three separable parts of the Cosmos platform?
flashcards.a: (1) A GPU-accelerated data-curation pipeline: 20M hours of raw video reduced to ~100M clips. (2) Open-weight world foundation models under the NVIDIA Open Model License: Predict (generation), Transfer (spatially-controlled translation), Reason (physical-commonsense VLM). (3) A tokenizer family, continuous and discrete, at up to 2048x total compression. It sits above Omniverse/OpenUSD/PhysX and Isaac Sim/Isaac Lab.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: Why is Cosmos not a simulator, mechanically?
flashcards.a: A simulator gives step(dt) -> state, reset(seed) -> exact state, deterministic replay, and queryable contact forces. A video WFM gives sampled pixels: no reset, no seed-to-state map, no forces, stochastic sampler. You can build a dataset from it; you cannot run an RL loop inside it. Throughput seals it: ~380 s on an H100 for 5 s of 7B video, about 76x slower than real time for ONE environment, against Isaac Lab running 2,048-4,096 environments each faster than real time.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: Cosmos 1.0 model sizes and output specification?
flashcards.a: Diffusion: 7B and 14B, each in Text2World and Video2World. Autoregressive: 4B and 12B base, 5B and 13B Video2World. Text2World emits 121 frames = 5 s at 24 fps at 1280x704; Video2World predicts the next 120 frames from one image. Ratios 960x960 / 960x704 / 704x960 / 1280x704 / 704x1280; fps configurable 12-40; prompts under 300 words; BF16 only, Linux only, Ampere/Hopper/Blackwell.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: Cosmos 7B and 14B Text2World inference time and peak VRAM by offload tier?
flashcards.a: One H100, end to end excluding init: 7B ~380 s, 14B ~590 s per clip. Peak VRAM 7B by offload tier: 74.0 (upsampler) -> 57.1 (+guardrails) -> 38.5 (+T5) -> 38.3 (+tokenizer) -> 24.4 GB (+diffusion model). 14B: >80 -> 70.5 -> 51.9 -> 51.7 -> 39.0 GB. The 24.4 GB figure is what makes a 24 GB RTX 4090 marginally viable.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: Decode the Cosmos tokenizer naming, and what does it buy?
flashcards.a: {C|D}{I|V}<temporal>x<spatial>x<spatial>: C continuous, D discrete, I image, V video. CV8x8x8 = continuous video, 8x temporal, 8x8 spatial. DV8x16x16 = discrete, 8x temporal, 16x16 spatial. Spatial 8x8 or 16x16, temporal 4x or 8x, max total 2048x. A 121-frame 1280x704 clip is 327M raw RGB values and about 211,200 latent tokens through CV8x8x8, roughly 1,550x fewer elements. Continuous feeds diffusion; discrete feeds autoregressive.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: How do you take apart NVIDIA's '9,000 trillion tokens' claim?
flashcards.a: 20M hours = 7.2e10 s, ~1.73e12 frames at 24 fps. 9e15 / 1.73e12 requires ~5,200 tokens per frame, which is the right order for 1280x704 at 8x8 spatial with 8x temporal pooling. So it is arithmetically reachable, but only by tokenising the ENTIRE UNCURATED 20M-hour corpus. The curated set is ~100M clips at ~211,200 tokens each = ~2.1e13, about 21 trillion. The headline is ~430x higher than the plausible training-token figure.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: What are the four Cosmos guardrail components and their thresholds?
flashcards.a: Pre-generation: a human-curated keyword blocklist, and Aegis (Aegis-AI-Content-Safety-LlamaGuard-LLM-Defensive-1.0, a Llama-Guard variant on Llama2-7B, 13 risk categories). Post-generation: a multi-class video content safety filter over SigLIP embeddings, and a RetinaFace face blur that pixelates any detection larger than 20x20 pixels. Offloading guardrails saves ~17 GB on the 7B path (74.0 -> 57.1 GB); it does not eliminate the compute.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: What does the NVIDIA Open Model License actually oblige you to do?
flashcards.a: Version dated 6 January 2025. Permits commercial use and derivatives; NVIDIA disclaims ownership of outputs. But: explicitly REVOCABLE; auto-terminates if you bypass, disable, reduce the efficacy of, or circumvent any safety guardrail or guardrail hyperparameter; auto-terminates on patent/copyright litigation against the model; requires 'Built on NVIDIA Cosmos' attribution that propagates to any AI model trained or fine-tuned on Cosmos OUTPUTS; Delaware law, exclusive jurisdiction Santa Clara County; NVIDIA may update it unilaterally.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: The two halves of the sim-to-real gap, and which one Cosmos addresses?
flashcards.a: Appearance gap: textures, lighting, lens, sensor noise, weather. Dynamics gap: friction, mass, compliance, actuator backlash, control latency, contact resolution. Cosmos Transfer addresses the appearance half well, because control conditioning on segmentation/depth preserves real geometry and changes only the look. It addresses the dynamics half essentially not at all: a video model has no representation of force and its objective contains no penalty for a violated contact constraint. In contact-rich manipulation the dynamics gap usually dominates.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: How do you measure which half of the sim-to-real gap you have?
flashcards.a: Three numbers. S_sim: train and evaluate entirely in simulation, the ceiling. S_realvision: keep dynamics simulated and swap in real imagery of the same scene; S_sim - S_realvision is the appearance gap. S_realdyn: run on hardware with vision out of the loop (state-based policy on proprioception plus fiducial/mocap object pose); S_sim - S_realdyn is the dynamics gap. Whichever drop is larger decides where the budget goes. Answering 'you just try it and see' is an admission of guessing.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: What synthetic-to-real ratio and volumes does the published DreamGen/GR00T work use?
flashcards.a: Co-training sampling ratio 1:1 neural trajectories to real trajectories. Volume: ~3,000 neural trajectories per task for RoboCasa simulation tasks, and only ~100 per task for real-world tasks. Effect: GR00T N1.5 reached 38.3% on a 12-task DreamGen suite versus 13.1% for GR00T N1; synthetic data helped consistently across 30/100/300-demo regimes and in a real-world 10%-data regime; up to +8.8% even when real demonstrations were already plentiful.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: What is the observable symptom of synthetic-data diversity collapse, and how do you measure it?
flashcards.a: Symptom: adding 10x more generated clips stops improving the policy and then makes it worse, while validation loss keeps dropping. Measure effective rank (exp of the entropy of the normalised singular-value spectrum) of synthetic versus real embeddings on a FROZEN third-party encoder such as DINOv2 or SigLIP; a synth/real ratio below about 0.6 is collapse. Also measure coverage: the fraction of real samples with a synthetic neighbour inside their own k-NN radius. Fix with stratified scenario prompting and embedding-level dedup, not by generating more.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: Why is the Cosmos data-curation pipeline arguably the real product, and what are its numbers?
flashcards.a: Stages: shot-boundary splitting, motion/quality/text-overlay filtering, deduplication, VLM captioning, uniform re-encode. 20M hours takes ~40 days on Hopper or ~14 days on Blackwell against a stated 3.4 years CPU-only, roughly 89x. The bottleneck is video decode/encode, not model inference, which is why fixed-function hardware wins. Systems detail: L40S has both NVDEC and NVENC while H100 has only NVDEC, so your most expensive training GPU is the wrong choice for the re-encode stage. Curation and search survive even if every WFM is replaced.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: What do OpenUSD, UsdPhysics, PhysX, Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab each contribute?
flashcards.a: OpenUSD is a layered composition system for scenes, not just a file format, which is what makes procedural scene generation tractable. UsdPhysics standardises rigid bodies, colliders, joints and materials inside USD so mass and friction travel with the asset. PhysX is the GPU rigid-body engine with a reduced-coordinate articulation solver. Isaac Sim adds RTX rendering, sensor models and ROS bridges. Isaac Lab is the vectorised RL/IL layer with a declarative randomisation manager. Isaac Sim 5.0 and Isaac Lab 2.2 went GA at SIGGRAPH, August 2025; Isaac Lab 3.0 adds multi-backend physics over PhysX, Newton and OVPhysX.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: Why does Isaac Lab get thousands of environments on one GPU, and what does that cost?
flashcards.a: The win is eliminating the serialisation boundary: physics stepping, observation assembly and the policy forward/backward all live in the same device memory as torch tensors, with no host copy and no process boundary. Typical locomotion configs run 2,048-4,096 parallel environments. Costs: all environments must step in lockstep at the same timestep; heterogeneous asset topologies are awkward; and rendering does NOT amortise like physics, so adding cameras collapses throughput. Train state-based first, add vision late.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: What is the Cosmos hardware floor, and why does it matter as an engineering constraint?
flashcards.a: Isaac Sim 5.1's stated minimum is an RTX 4080 with 16 GB VRAM and 32 GB system RAM. Isaac Lab benchmarks run on L40 (48 GB), RTX Pro 6000 (96 GB) and RTX 5090 (32 GB). Cosmos inference is tested only on Linux, only at BF16, only on Ampere/Hopper/Blackwell. There is no AMD path, no Apple path, no CPU-only CI path. Consequence: every engineer needs an NVIDIA GPU, CI needs GPU runners, and cloud spend is denominated in NVIDIA instance types. Price it rather than being annoyed by it.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: What are Cosmos Predict 2.5, Transfer 2.5 and Cosmos 3?
flashcards.a: Predict 2.5 (Oct 2025): 2B and 14B, unifying Text2World, Image2World and Video2World into one model, trained on 200M curated clips, using Cosmos Reason 1 (7B) as the text encoder, extending output to 30 seconds. Transfer 2.5: 2B, described as 3.5x smaller than Transfer1-7B, control modalities edge/blur/depth/segmentation, reporting up to 60% better 3D lane and cuboid detection than Transfer1-7B-Sample-AV (measured with LATR and BEVFormer). Cosmos 3 (arXiv:2606.02800, June 2026): omnimodal Mixture-of-Transformers over language, image, video, audio and action.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: What is the missing experiment that would settle whether synthetic data is worth the money?
flashcards.a: Fix a real-data budget N and total compute C. Arm A: N real + M synthetic. Arm B: N real + the same compute C on longer training and stronger classical augmentation. Arm C: the DOLLAR cost of generating M synthetic trajectories spent on more real demonstrations instead, so the comparison is budget-matched not data-matched. Evaluate on a held-out suite chosen by a disinterested party, >=20 trials/task, confidence intervals, >=3 seeds, with no eval contamination. DreamGen's ablations answer 'does adding synthetic data help?' (yes) but not 'is it the best use of this budget?' (unknown) because there is no Arm C.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: The synthetic-versus-teleop cost arithmetic (derived, not published)?
flashcards.a: At ~380 s per 5-second clip on one H100 for the 7B diffusion model, one H100-hour yields ~9.5 clips or ~47 seconds of video. 100 hours of generated video is therefore ~7,600 H100-hours, roughly $23k-30k at $3-4 per H100-hour, before curation, before discarding bad generations, before guardrail rejections. The same $30k buys roughly 400-750 fully-loaded teleoperator hours, or ~24,000-45,000 real demonstrations at 60 per hour. Not decisive, since synthetic covers scenarios you cannot safely stage, but a principal engineer should walk into the design review having done it.

flashcards.topic: NVIDIA Cosmos & Physical AI: World Foundation Models, Isaac Sim
flashcards.q: What is the contamination guard specific to neural-trajectory synthetic data?
flashcards.a: Neural trajectories are generated FROM real episodes, so a generated clip inherits its seed episode's scene. If that seed episode's scene later lands in your eval split, your synthetic training data is a paraphrase of your test set and the improvement is memorisation. Guard by tracking seed_episode_id through generation and asserting that no training sample's seed episode maps to an eval scene, in addition to the ordinary scene-overlap check and asserting zero generated samples in eval. This leak is invisible to every metric you would normally look at.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: What is a VLA in one sentence, and why does it always start from a pretrained VLM?
flashcards.a: A vision-language-action model is a VLM whose output space is robot actions instead of text. It starts from a pretrained VLM because robot data is four to five orders of magnitude smaller than language data: Open X-Embodiment is ~1M trajectories against Llama-3-class pretraining at ~15T tokens, so the semantics have to be imported rather than learned from robot demonstrations.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: How does RT-2 tokenise actions, and what is the trick with the vocabulary?
flashcards.a: Each continuous action dimension is discretised into 256 uniform bins over its training range (RT-1: 11 dims; RT-2 mobile manipulator: 8 dims = terminate flag, 6-DoF delta pose, gripper). Each bin index becomes a token, so an action is a string like "1 128 91 241 5 101 127 217". In PaLI-X, integers up to 1000 already have tokens so no vocab change is needed; in PaLM-E they overwrite the 256 least-frequently-used tokens. Nothing about the architecture, head, or loss changes, which is what enables co-fine-tuning on web VQA and robot data together.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: Name three concrete costs of discrete action tokens.
flashcards.a: 1) Sequential decoding: 7-11 tokens per action means 7-11 forward passes, the largest latency multiplier in the stack. 2) Quantisation floor: 256 bins is ~0.4% of the range per bin, so on a ±10 cm range one bin is 0.78 mm. 3) Per-dimension independence: parallel or poorly-conditioned decoding can pick mode A's Δy with mode B's Δz, producing an action in neither mode (the 'straight into the obstacle' failure).

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: Why does an L2 regression action head fail on real demonstration data?
flashcards.a: The minimiser of expected squared error is the conditional mean. If half the demonstrations go left around an obstacle and half go right, the mean goes through the obstacle. Same pathology as blurred video prediction: an averaging loss on multimodal data returns the average, which is not a valid sample. L1 gives the conditional median, which is somewhat better; diffusion and flow matching sample a mode and fix it properly.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: Describe π0's flow-matching action expert and its measured latency.
flashcards.a: π0 is 3.3B total: a 3B PaliGemma backbone (2.291B trainable) plus a 300M (0.315B) action expert with its own transformer weights processing proprioception and noisy action tokens. Training samples τ ~ Beta(1.5, 1) biased toward the noisy end, forms A^τ = τ·noise + (1-τ)·A_true, and regresses against velocity noise - A_true. Inference integrates τ from 1 to 0 with 10 forward-Euler steps, run on the 300M expert only while the backbone's KV cache is reused. Measured: ~73 ms for a 50-action chunk with three cameras.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: Give the four independent reasons action chunking helps.
flashcards.a: 1) Compounding error: BC error grows O(εT²); committing H steps per decision cuts decisions to T/H and shrinks the quadratic term by H². 2) Non-Markovian demonstrations: operator pauses map the same observation to both 'move' and 'don't move'; chunking absorbs the pause into the unit. 3) Inference amortisation: effective control rate = H / latency. 4) Temporal coherence, because the chunk is generated jointly rather than as H independent decisions.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: What is ACT's chunking ablation result, and what does temporal ensembling add?
flashcards.a: Success went from 1% at k=1 to 44% at k=100 on their simulated evaluation, averaged across settings, then tapered slightly for larger k. Temporal ensembling added about 3.3 percentage points in success plus a larger smoothness gain the metric does not capture. On real ALOHA hardware ACT reported 80-95% on tasks like battery slotting; that is a different suite from the 44% number and the two must not be plotted on the same axis.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: What is the cost of a large action chunk, quantitatively?
flashcards.a: A chunk is open loop. At 50 Hz with H=50 the final action executes 1.0 second after the observation that produced it, so anything changing in that second is invisible to the robot. H is bounded above by how fast the environment changes: static tabletop tolerates H=50, a handover with a moving human does not. GR00T N1 uses H=16 for that reason.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: What is temporal ensembling and why can't a 7B VLA use it?
flashcards.a: Run inference every timestep rather than every H timesteps, so at time t you hold H overlapping predictions for a_t from the last H chunks, combined with weights w_i ∝ exp(-m·i) over prediction age. Smaller m is smoother with more lag. It requires inference at the full control rate, which discards the entire amortisation benefit. A ~80M ACT model on 50 Hz hardware can afford it; a 7B VLA at 292 ms cannot. The substitute is asynchronous chunk overlap with a 4-10 step crossfade at the seam.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: Recite the measured control frequencies for the main VLAs.
flashcards.a: RT-1 (35M): 3 Hz. RT-2 on PaLI-X 55B: 1-3 Hz over a multi-TPU cloud endpoint. RT-2 5B variant: ~5 Hz. OpenVLA-7B: 292 ms on an A6000 (3.4 Hz), 405 ms on an L4 24GB (2.47 Hz), ~160 ms optimised (~6 Hz). π0 (3.3B): 73 ms for a 50-action chunk, giving 50 Hz effective. GR00T N1 System 1 DiT: 120 Hz.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: Why can't a 7B VLA run at 50 Hz, in hardware terms?
flashcards.a: 50 Hz is a 20 ms period, leaving ~5 ms of inference budget after camera and transport overhead. A 7B model in FP16 is 14 GB of weights; on ~2 TB/s HBM one full weight read is ~7 ms, and 7 action tokens means 7 of them, so ~49 ms is the hardware floor before any inefficiency. At batch size 1 (one robot) there is no arithmetic-intensity relief. Quantisation and compilation buy 2-3x, not 15x.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: Describe the two-system split and the four rules that make it work.
flashcards.a: System 2 (VLM, 1.3B-55B) runs at 1-10 Hz and emits a latent plan; System 1 (action expert, ~0.3B) runs at 50-200 Hz consuming that latent plus full-rate proprioception. GR00T N1 ships this explicitly with System 1 at 120 Hz. Rules: (1) the fast loop never blocks on the slow one, stale latent is fine; (2) the fast loop is pinned to an isolated core with SCHED_FIFO, no GC and no malloc in the hot path; (3) the slow system emits an intent/latent, not a target pose, because a stale pose is a wrong command while a stale intent is roughly right; (4) measure period jitter (std and p99), not just mean latency.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: Give the Open X-Embodiment headline numbers and the caveat that matters.
flashcards.a: 60 pooled datasets from 34 labs, 1M+ real trajectories, 22 embodiments, 527 skills, 160,266 tasks, released October 2023. RT-1-X beat the original per-dataset SOTA by ~50% on average across 5 evaluated datasets and RT-2-X showed ~3x improvement on emergent-skill evaluations. The caveat: on the datasets with the most data, RT-1-X was worse than the original single-embodiment model. Positive transfer for data-poor embodiments, negative transfer for data-rich ones.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: What did OpenVLA contribute, and what does its headline result imply about scale?
flashcards.a: OpenVLA is 7B, built on Llama-2-7B with a fused DINOv2 + SigLIP visual encoder, trained on 970k real robot episodes from Open X-Embodiment, with open weights and a LoRA fine-tuning path that fits on a single 24 GB consumer GPU. It outperformed the closed 55B RT-2-X by 16.5 percentage points absolute across 29 tasks with 7x fewer parameters, which implies that at these scales data quality, recipe, and action representation dominate parameter count, and every extra billion parameters is a direct control-frequency tax.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: Give the robot-data cost model and the scale gap against language pretraining.
flashcards.a: Every trajectory was produced by a human moving a robot in real time; there is no Common Crawl for torque. Realistic yield is 30-60 demonstrations per operator-hour for short tasks, and usable robot data lands roughly $50-200 per hour once hardware and supervision are included (order-of-magnitude estimate, not a published figure). π0's ~10,000 hours (~903M timesteps) is therefore a multi-million-dollar asset and about five person-years of teleoperation. Open X-Embodiment's ~1M trajectories is on the order of 10^8-10^9 timesteps against ~15T language tokens: a four-to-five-order-of-magnitude gap.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: What is the Wilson-interval arithmetic that invalidates most robotics success tables?
flashcards.a: A 90% observed success rate has a 95% Wilson interval of roughly [60%, 98%] at n=10, [79%, 96%] at n=50, and [85%, 94%] at n=200. Distinguishing an 80% policy from a 70% one at p<0.05 needs roughly n=300 per arm. At 30 s per trial plus 30 s of reset, 300 trials is ~5 hours of continuous robot time for one number, and a 10-task two-policy comparison is ~100 hours. Nobody runs that, so '+8 points over baseline' on n=20 is a measurement of noise.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: Policy stalls mid-trajectory: symptom, mechanism, fixes.
flashcards.a: Symptom: commanded deltas near zero for hundreds of consecutive steps while the observation is essentially static. Mechanism: operator pauses in the demonstrations mean the same observation is paired with both 'move' and 'don't move', so a regression head predicts the average, which near a pause is ~zero; it is self-reinforcing because predicting zero keeps the observation identical. Fixes in leverage order: increase the action chunk (ACT's 1% → 44%), filter or subsample near-zero-motion segments from training, switch from L2 to flow matching so you sample a mode. A consecutive-sub-threshold re-plan guard is a mitigation, not a fix.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: Policy only works from the training camera pose: mechanism and fixes.
flashcards.a: The policy learned pixels → actions in the robot frame and absorbed the camera extrinsics into its weights as a constant; nothing in BC forces a 3D-consistent representation and the data had one camera pose. Tell: predicted actions are systematically offset in one axis rather than randomly wrong. Real fix is a data-collection decision: randomise camera extrinsics at collection. Secondary: prefer a rigidly-mounted wrist camera, apply random-crop and photometric augmentation, feed proprioception. Check normalisation statistics first, since a stats mismatch produces the identical symptom and is a five-minute fix. Also lock auto-exposure and auto-white-balance.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: Control-loop jitter causing oscillation: cause and fix list.
flashcards.a: Cause: late commands. The controller either holds (velocity discontinuity) or extrapolates (overshoot), and near the arm's mechanical resonance the error reinforces each cycle. Ranked root causes: Python GC pause in the hot loop, GIL contention with the inference thread, non-isolated CPU core, chunk-boundary discontinuity with no crossfade, temporal-ensembling gain m set too high. Fixes: move the fast loop to C++/Rust or pre-allocate and gc.disable(); pin with SCHED_FIFO and isolcpus; crossfade 4-10 steps at chunk seams; add velocity/acceleration limits; export period std and p99 and alert on it. Fixed-frequency oscillation is the mechanical resonance: notch-filter it or lower gains.

flashcards.topic: Vision-Language-Action Models: GR00T, RT-2, π0, and Embodied Agents
flashcards.q: GR00T N1 versus π0: what is actually different?
flashcards.a: π0 is 3.3B (3B PaliGemma backbone, 2.291B trainable, plus a 300M flow-matching expert), H=50, 10 integration steps, ~73 ms/chunk, trained on ~10,000 hours mostly proprietary with ~9.1% open (OXE, Bridge, DROID). GR00T N1 is 2.2B total with a 1.34B Eagle-2 VLM as System 2 and a diffusion-transformer System 1 trained with flow matching, action horizon 16, System 1 at 120 Hz, plus an EmbodimentTag mechanism with per-embodiment encoders/decoders; N1.5 is the 3B successor. GR00T makes the two-system split architectural and is open-weights targeting humanoids; π0's data is proprietary and it targets tabletop and mobile manipulation. π0.5 adds knowledge insulation, 256-bin state tokens in the language prefix, and AdaRMSNorm timestep conditioning.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: Define a world model in one sentence, and say what disqualifies an unconditioned video generator from being one.
flashcards.a: A learned p(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t) that can be rolled forward without touching the real environment. An unconditioned video generator has no action input, so it is a prior over plausible futures, not a conditional next-state distribution you can act inside. The distinguishing test is counterfactual: fix the state, vary the action, check the difference between rollouts is coherent.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: What are the only two arguments for building a world model?
flashcards.a: (1) Sample efficiency: one real trajectory amortises into many imagined ones. PlaNet solved DMC image tasks in ~2,000 episodes where D4PG needed ~50x more on average and ~500x on Cheetah Run. (2) Off-system policy evaluation: score a candidate policy inside the model before it touches a robot, fleet or customer. Everything else is downstream. The trade being made is always: sample cost converted into model-error risk.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: Ha & Schmidhuber 2018: name the three components and their parameter counts.
flashcards.a: V = convolutional VAE (4,348,547 params, z in R^32 for CarRacing; 4,446,915 and z in R^64 for VizDoom). M = MDN-RNN, LSTM of 256 hidden units (512 for Doom) emitting a 5-component Gaussian mixture over z_{t+1} (422,368 / 1,678,785 params). C = LINEAR controller a = W[z;h]+b, 867 params for CarRacing and 1,088 for Doom, trained by CMA-ES with population 64. Data: 10,000 random rollouts. V and M never see the reward.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: What is the CarRacing ablation in Ha & Schmidhuber 2018 and why is it the most useful number in the paper?
flashcards.a: Controller seeing only z_t scored 632 +/- 251; adding a hidden layer got 788 +/- 141; giving it the RNN hidden state h_t as well scored 906 +/- 21 against a solve threshold of 900. h_t is the model's compressed belief about the future, so 274 points came purely from predictive representation with no rollout at decision time. This is the cheapest, lowest-risk way to get value from a world model and usually the only version that survives production.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: What did Ha & Schmidhuber's VizDoom experiment actually demonstrate, with numbers?
flashcards.a: The controller was trained entirely inside M's hallucination (M predicts z and done, so it exposes a fake gym.Env), then deployed cold on real VizDoom Take Cover. About 900 timesteps dreamed, about 1,100 real, against a 750 solve threshold, a 2,100-step episode cap, 210 +/- 108 for a random policy and 820 +/- 58 for the best Gym leaderboard entry. This is the origin datapoint for training a policy entirely in a learned simulator.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: What does the MDN-RNN temperature table show, and what is the counter-intuitive conclusion?
flashcards.a: tau=0.10 gave 2086 +/- 140 dreamed and 193 +/- 58 real (below the 210 random baseline). tau=1.00 gave 1145 / 868. tau=1.15 gave 918 dreamed and 1092 real, the best transfer. tau=1.30 gave 732 / 753. Conclusion: dreamed-to-real correlation is NOT monotonic, and best transfer occurred where the model was pessimistic (dream harder than reality), not where it was accurate. Same principle as domain randomisation.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: Give the compounding-error arithmetic: fidelity formula, a table, and the half-life.
flashcards.a: H-step rollout fidelity = (1-eps)^H, exponential. At eps=2%: 74% at H=15, 36% at H=50, 13% at H=100, 0.6% at H=250. Half-life H_1/2 ~= 0.693/eps, so eps=1% gives 69 steps, 5% gives 14, 10% gives 7. Planning 500 steps at 50% fidelity needs eps <= 0.14%, about 7x better than any published learned dynamics model. That is why Dreamer imagines 15 steps.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: Why is compounding error worse than the constant-eps exponential analysis suggests?
flashcards.a: eps is not constant. Drift pushes the rollout off the model's training distribution where its error is larger, so error causes distribution shift causes more error. Model it as eps_h = eps_0(1 + beta*h) and accumulated error picks up an eps_0*beta*H^2/2 term, quadratic in the horizon. With eps_0=1% and beta=0.05 the quadratic term overtakes the linear one around H=40. Same covariate-shift structure as the DAgger problem, seen from the model side.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: How does chaos bound the useful rollout horizon, and why is that a hard ceiling?
flashcards.a: With a positive Lyapunov exponent lambda, an initial discrepancy delta_0 grows as delta_0 * e^(lambda*H), so H_useful = (1/lambda) * ln(1/delta_0). At lambda=0.5/step and delta_0=1e-3 that is ~13.8 steps; improving to delta_0=1e-6 gives ~27.6. The dependence on model accuracy is LOGARITHMIC: a thousand-fold accuracy improvement only doubles the horizon. No amount of scaling changes this, so it is a physical ceiling rather than an engineering gap.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: What are the three standard mitigations for compounding error, and the one diagnostic everyone skips?
flashcards.a: (1) Keep H at or below the accuracy half-life and bootstrap the tail with a learned critic (Dreamer, H=15, lambda-returns). (2) Branch short rollouts (k=1..15) off real replay-buffer states rather than rolling long from an initial state (MBPO): 1,000 states x 5 steps gives error 5*eps for the same imagined-sample count as one 5,000-step rollout at 5000*eps. (3) Replan every step against fresh observations (MPC discipline). The skipped diagnostic: plot open-loop prediction error against horizon out to 4H, find the knee, plan below it. One-step error proves nothing about H-step error.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: What is model exploitation, and why is it not just noise?
flashcards.a: Optimising a policy against a learned model means searching for the argmax of the model's PREDICTED return, so the optimiser is actively drawn to regions where the model is optimistically wrong. Model error is not zero-mean noise from the optimiser's perspective; the search seeks it out, and it gets worse as the optimiser gets stronger. Ha & Schmidhuber's agent found a policy that made monsters never fire. Same structure as reward hacking and adversarial examples. Fixes: raised sampling temperature, uncertainty penalties (MOPO/MOReL), ensemble disagreement, domain randomisation.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: Why predict in latent space rather than pixel space, and what does it cost?
flashcards.a: Capacity: 1080p RGB is 6,220,800 numbers versus a latent 10^3-10^4x smaller; reconstruction loss allocates capacity where error mass is, which in natural video is texture no controller reads. Noise: much pixel content is aleatoric, and minimising squared error on unpredictable content converges to the conditional mean, i.e. blur, which is why pixel predictors go to mush in 10-20 frames. The cost: no external ground truth, so encoder and predictor can collude on a constant mapping. That is representation collapse. Defences: reconstruction anchor (Dreamer), EMA target encoder plus stop-gradient (JEPA), variance-covariance regulariser (VICReg).

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: State the representation-versus-dynamics split, including how each is tested and what the decoder is for.
flashcards.a: Representation q(z|x): compression with sufficiency; fails by dropping information; tested by linear-probing z for known state variables. Dynamics p(z'|z,a): accuracy over a horizon; fails by compounding error; tested with an H-step open-loop error curve. Reporting only reconstruction loss measures neither. The decoder is a third object that exists solely as an anti-collapse training anchor and is NEVER called during imagination; if your rollout needs to decode to pixels, you built a video model with an action input.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: PlaNet to DreamerV3: what did each of the four papers specifically fix?
flashcards.a: PlaNet (2019): RSSM splitting the latent into a deterministic GRU path and a stochastic variable, plus latent overshooting; planned with CEM every step. Dreamer (2020): replaced CEM with an actor-critic backpropagating imagined return through the differentiable dynamics at H=15 with a critic bootstrapping the tail, so the search amortises. DreamerV2 (2021): 32x32 categorical latents with straight-through gradients plus KL balancing; first human-level on 55-game Atari at 200M frames inside a world model. DreamerV3 (2023, Nature 2025): symlog, twohot over 255 buckets, percentile return normalisation, giving one fixed configuration across 150+ tasks and the first Minecraft diamonds from scratch.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: Why is DreamerV3's 'single configuration' the actual headline, not the 150+ tasks?
flashcards.a: Every prior model-based paper reported strong numbers after per-domain hyperparameter tuning, which silently excluded hundreds of tuning runs from the reported sample cost. A method needing 200 tuning runs at 10^6 steps each to demonstrate a 10^5-step result is not sample-efficient in any practical sense. Removing that hidden cost is what makes it applicable to a new domain out of the box. Secondary finding worth knowing: across 8M to 200M parameters, larger models were not only better asymptotically but MORE data-efficient per environment step.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: What do symlog and twohot actually solve in DreamerV3?
flashcards.a: Reward scales differ by orders of magnitude across domains (DMC returns in [0,1000], Atari 10 to 100,000, Minecraft almost always 0), so no fixed loss weight or learning rate works everywhere. symlog(x) = sign(x)*ln(|x|+1) compresses large magnitudes smoothly while staying well-behaved near zero. Twohot discretises the symlog-space target into 255 equally spaced buckets and predicts a categorical with mass split between the two adjacent buckets, making the loss scale-invariant and allowing multimodal value distributions under sparse reward. Percentile return normalisation bounds actor gradients when returns are usually zero and occasionally huge.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: What is the strongest published evidence that video generation does not learn physical law, with numbers?
flashcards.a: PhyWorld (Kang, Yue et al., ICML 2025, ByteDance Seed). Textureless 2D physics simulator, DiT-S through DiT-XL, 30K to 3M samples, measuring velocity error parsed from generated video against simulator ground truth. In-distribution error fell from 0.022 to 0.012 against a ground-truth-video floor of 0.010. Out-of-distribution error on the same DiT-L/3M model was 0.427, ~35x worse, and did not improve with scale: DiT-B OOD across 30K/300K/3M was 0.433, 0.328, 0.358. Mechanism: case-based retrieval of the nearest training example, with attribute priority colour > size > velocity > shape.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: Why are FVD, SSIM, PSNR and LPIPS blind to physics, and what is the concrete evidence?
flashcards.a: The training objective only requires each frame to be in-distribution; it contains no term penalising a physically impossible transition between individually plausible frames. Physical correctness is a property of trajectories, not frames, so no per-frame loss or metric can see it. Evidence: PhyWorld's PHYRE table reports SSIM 0.943-0.951 and PSNR 25.5-27.3 across out-of-template videos whose human-judged abnormal rate ranged from 67% down to 10%. Perceptual metrics barely moved while physical correctness changed by a factor of 6.7.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: Current physical-consistency benchmark numbers for video generation models.
flashcards.a: VideoPhy: best model tested (Pika) satisfied both caption and physical law on 19.7% of instances; CogVideoX-5B at 39.6%. VideoPhy-2 hard subset: best model 22% joint semantic-plus-physical adherence. PhyWorldBench: Sora-Turbo 20.8%, Kling-1.6 18.8%. The headline is that state of the art on physical adherence is 20-40%, not 90%, which is the number to have in mind when shown a beautiful demo reel.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: Sort Genie, Genie 3 and V-JEPA 2 into benchmarked versus demonstrated-but-unevaluated.
flashcards.a: Benchmarked: Genie (Bruce et al., ICML 2024), 11B params, 30,000 hours of 2D platformer video, an unsupervised latent action model via VQ-VAE with a codebook of only 8 discrete actions, with published controllability metrics. Also benchmarked: V-JEPA 2 (2025), ViT-g >1B params, >1M hours video, action-conditioned post-training on under 62 hours of unlabelled Droid robot video, 65-80% zero-shot pick-and-place on Franka arms in two unseen labs, which is a closed-loop real-hardware result. Demonstrated but unevaluated: Genie 3 (5 Aug 2025), 720p at 24fps consistent for a few minutes, with no technical report, no benchmark table and no agent-training result; self-declared limits of navigation-only actions and ~1 minute of memory.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: Give the seven-level ladder for testing whether a model 'understands physics', and which levels gate a launch.
flashcards.a: 1 in-distribution accuracy on extracted physical quantities, not pixels. 2 conservation-law adherence and object permanence. 3 OOD extrapolation holding out a contiguous parameter region. 4 counterfactual consistency: same state, different action. 5 compositional generalisation: all elements seen, no combinations seen. 6 closed-loop task success on the real system against a no-model baseline. 7 sim-to-real rank correlation over 10-20 candidate policies. Gate an acting system on level 6 and an evaluation harness on level 7; everything below is a proxy that can be excellent while the thing you care about is broken.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: When should you tell a team NOT to build a world model?
flashcards.a: When you can write the dynamics down (an explicit physics model plus MPC gives exact dynamics and analysable stability). When real samples are cheap, because the whole argument is the ratio c_real/c_sim and a 10,000-step-per-second simulator inverts it. In chaotic or adversarial domains, where useful horizon grows only logarithmically in model accuracy and the environment actively moves away from your model. When the cost of a wrong imagination is unbounded. And when two learned systems to train, version, monitor and debug are not justified by a measured win rather than an interesting architecture.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: What use of world models is actually deployed at scale today?
flashcards.a: Overwhelmingly three things, none of which is planning: representation learning (frozen RSSM or JEPA-style encoder feeding a small policy head, the 632 to 906 effect with zero rollout risk), synthetic data generation for robotics and AV (NVIDIA Cosmos, 20M hours of pretraining video, sold as a data product rather than as a simulator), and offline policy evaluation with a pessimism penalty and a live A/B as the real gate. Planning inside a learned generative model of a high-dimensional environment is a research capability with a small number of production instances, mostly in robotics, mostly at labs.

flashcards.topic: World Models: What They Are, Why They Matter, the Core Idea
flashcards.q: Objects vanish under occlusion in generated rollouts. Root cause, and why more data will not fix it.
flashcards.a: There is no representation whose job is 'this object exists and has these properties'. A frame-conditioned autoregressive model carries state only in its context window and recurrent activations, so occlusion removes the pixel evidence and nothing sustains the object. This is the same limit as Genie-class models having roughly one minute of effective memory. More data does not fix it because the objective is satisfied by any plausible continuation, and a continuation without the object is plausible frame-by-frame. Fixes: scripted occlusion tests scoring object count and identity, object-centric or slot latents, retrieval over a persistent scene buffer, or an explicit 3D representation.

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: How do you find the critical path in a trace waterfall?
flashcards.a: Start at the root and at every level descend into the child that FINISHES LAST. That chain, and only that chain, determines total duration. A span running in parallel with a longer sibling owns none of the latency: optimising it saves exactly 0ms. The widest bar and the responsible bar are frequently different bars.

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: Define span self time and give the three readings of it.
flashcards.a: self_time = span.duration - UNION of child intervals (union, not sum, so parallel children count once). ~100% with no children = leaf work. >50% WITH children = uninstrumented in-process time, go to a span-scoped profile. <10% = the service is a pure router, keep descending the critical path.

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: Self time sits BEFORE the first child vs AFTER the last child. What does each mean?
flashcards.a: Before the first child = a wait: connection-pool acquire, queue, scheduler, stop-the-world GC pause, or framework middleware. After the last child = response construction: serializing a large payload, compression, signing. A waterfall UI will not distinguish these; the arithmetic will.

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: What does a retry storm look like in a waterfall, precisely?
flashcards.a: 2-4 sibling spans, identical operation name and identical peer, durations UNIFORM to within a few percent and pinned at a round number (2000ms, 5000ms, 30000ms), all but the last errored, with growing jittered gaps between them. Uniformity is the tell: real work varies in duration, a timeout does not. Parent duration is about n x timeout + sum of backoffs. Seeing 3 attempts at two layers means 9 attempts for one logical call.

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: From trace data alone, how do you distinguish connection-pool exhaustion from a slow database?
flashcards.a: Pool exhaustion: the QUERY DURATION STAYS FLAT (4ms) while a gap of 200-900ms opens between the parent span's start and the first query span (the checkout wait). Slow database: the query span's own duration grows. Confirm with pool metrics (used at max, idle at zero, pending non-zero). A pool gap followed by NO DB span at all means the checkout timed out and the query never ran.

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: There is no span for a GC pause. What is its telemetry signature?
flashcards.a: Every span in flight on ONE POD lengthens by the SAME ABSOLUTE amount at the same instant, regardless of what it was doing (a 4ms cache read becomes 204ms; a 300ms DB call becomes 500ms). The affected endpoint differs every time and there is never a downstream span to blame. Group latency by pod, not by route; confirm with jvm.gc.duration or go_gc_pause_seconds.

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: Why is an N+1 across a service boundary invisible to every tool except distributed tracing?
flashcards.a: Each downstream call is genuinely fast (8ms) so the downstream service's p99, error rate, and CPU profile all look perfect. The 1.6 seconds exists only in the CALLER's round-trip accounting. Signature: a staircase of 50-500 serial near-identical short spans to the same peer. Fix: batch endpoint or DataLoader-style coalescing at the caller.

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: Head-based sampling: where is the decision made, and exactly what do you lose?
flashcards.a: At trace start, before anything interesting has happened; the decision rides the sampled flag of the traceparent header (00-<32hex traceid>-<16hex spanid>-<2hex flags>) so every service agrees. Stateless, constant memory, no infrastructure. You lose every RARE event: a failure affecting 1 in 10,000 requests at 1% sampling yields one stored trace per million requests. It also keeps only 1% of errors.

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: OTel Collector tail sampling: key defaults and the four costs.
flashcards.a: decision_wait default 30s; num_traces default 50,000. Costs: (1) all spans of a trace must reach the SAME Collector instance, requiring a two-tier deployment with loadbalancingexporter routing_key: traceID; (2) memory scales with in-flight traces x spans x window; (3) traces longer than decision_wait are truncated or split; (4) aggregates from sampled traces need a 1/p adjusted count, so generate span metrics BEFORE the sampler.

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: What is the number-one tail-sampling deployment error and its symptom?
flashcards.a: Running multiple Collector replicas behind a plain round-robin service. Each replica sees only a fraction of each trace and makes its sampling decision on a partial trace. Symptom: traces that exist but are silently and inconsistently missing their most interesting spans. Fix: a two-tier Collector with loadbalancingexporter and routing_key: traceID.

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: Why can't you put trace_id in a Prometheus label, and what is the purpose-built alternative?
flashcards.a: Every metric-name-plus-labelset is one time series, so a per-request label creates unbounded series and OOMs the server. Exemplars are the escape hatch: an out-of-band trace_id/span_id attached to an individual sample, stored PER BUCKET, contributing zero additional series. The exemplar on the TOP latency bucket is by construction a slow request, so you land in a guaranteed-interesting trace instead of a random one.

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: Three things that must ALL be true for Prometheus exemplars to work.
flashcards.a: (1) The SDK exemplar filter is TraceBased and the measurement is recorded inside an active span. (2) The scrape uses OpenMetrics exposition format; the classic Prometheus text format silently drops exemplars. (3) The Prometheus server runs with --enable-feature=exemplar-storage, which is off by default. Missing any one produces 'exemplars enabled but no jump link in Grafana'.

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: State the log cardinality rule and Loki's enforcing defaults.
flashcards.a: High-cardinality values go in the log BODY or structured attributes; only low-cardinality values go in index labels. Loki defaults: 15 index labels max, 10,000 streams per tenant and 50,000 global, label name 1024 chars, label value 2048. NEVER trace_id or order_id as a label. Query instead: {service="x",env="prod"} | json | trace_id="4bf92f35..."

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: Half your log lines have a null trace_id. What is the cause, and why is it disproportionately damaging?
flashcards.a: Context loss at a concurrency boundary: thread-pool handoff, asyncio task created without copying context, callback, Spring @Async, background queue consumer. Not a logging-config bug. Damaging because the uncorrelated half is the ASYNC half (retries, background writes, cleanup), which is exactly where the hard bugs live. Fix: propagate context explicitly (contextvars copy, capture Context.current() before submit, instrumented executor).

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: Why is avg(p99) across pods wrong, and what is the correct PromQL?
flashcards.a: Percentiles do not average. One pod at 8s among nineteen at 100ms averages under 500ms and the incident vanishes. Correct: sum the histogram buckets first, then take the quantile. histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: Map the four p50/p99/p99.9 divergence shapes to their causes.
flashcards.a: p50 flat + p99 up = a minority path got slower (cache miss, cold shard, one bad host, GC, one tenant). p50 up + p99 up proportionally = everything got slower (capacity, shared dependency, hot-path change). p99 up + p99.9 FLAT = a BOUNDED slow set, so group by tenant/shard/region. p50 up + p99 flat = almost always a measurement or traffic-mix change, not a system change.

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: Why is 'only 1% of requests are slow' a weaker statement than it sounds? Give the arithmetic.
flashcards.a: A user whose page load fires 100 backend requests has a 1 - 0.99^100 = 63.4% chance of hitting at least one p99-latency request. At 10 requests it is 9.6%. A percentile describes a sample of requests, not a population of users, and fan-out converts a rare request-level event into a common user-level one.

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: What is coordinated omission and what number illustrates it?
flashcards.a: A closed-loop load generator waits for each response before sending the next, so when the server stalls it stops issuing requests and the slow requests are never measured. The distortion is concentrated in p99 and beyond. One reported case: load test p99 = 47ms against production p99 = 1.8s for the same build, a 38x miss. Fix: an open-loop constant-arrival-rate workload that records intended send time, not actual send time.

flashcards.topic: Debugging From Traces & Logs Alone (When You Can't Attach)
flashcards.q: Your continuous CPU flame graph for the incident window looks completely normal. What does that actually tell you?
