Research (arXiv 2501.17858) showed coordinated voting with as few as a few hundred rigged votes, using output fingerprinting to identify a target model, can shift its ranking.

flashcards.q: What does METR's 'time horizon' metric measure, and how has its doubling rate changed?
flashcards.a: The length of task (measured in time a skilled human professional would take) a model can complete autonomously with 50% reliability. The doubling period compressed from roughly every 7 months (2019-2024) to roughly every 4 months (2024-2025). Measurements above ~16 hours are currently unreliable with METR's task suite.

flashcards.q: Compare Anthropic's RSP, OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, and Google DeepMind's FSF in one line each.
flashcards.a: Anthropic RSP: most prescriptive, ASL-1 through ASL-4+ with specific RAND weight-security-tier precommitments. OpenAI Preparedness: collapsed from four tiers to two qualitative bars (High/Critical), read by analysts as a weakening. Google FSF: most process-focused, specifies what will be measured/reviewed more than what action automatically follows.

flashcards.q: What regulatory milestone happened on 2 August 2026, and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: The EU AI Act's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice obligations began enforcement -- the first external enforcement mechanism on frontier model documentation and safety disclosure, as opposed to the three labs' voluntary, self-authored safety frameworks.

flashcards.q: What is the concrete licensing gotcha in Llama's license that a summary blog post typically undersells?
flashcards.a: A 700-million monthly-active-user cap measured at the parent corporate entity level, frozen at terms from a specific point in time rather than rolling forward, plus a separate exclusion of multimodal capabilities from the license grant specifically within the EU.

flashcards.q: Which open-weight model families use permissive MIT/Apache 2.0 licenses versus Llama's restrictive custom license?
flashcards.a: DeepSeek's V4 line (MIT), Qwen and Gemma (Apache 2.0) grant unrestricted commercial use, redistribution, and modification with no usage cap. Llama's custom license carries the 700M MAU cap and EU multimodal exclusion.

flashcards.q: What size of benchmark delta should be treated as noise rather than a real capability difference?
flashcards.a: Single-run accuracy deltas under roughly 2-3 points, and LM Arena Elo gaps under roughly 10 points, should be treated as ties until corroborated by repeated runs or a much larger sustained gap.

flashcards.q: What is the production-safe policy for adopting a new frontier model, versus 'always route to whatever tops the leaderboard'?
flashcards.a: Pin to a specific, immutable model version; migrate only after your own regression eval (on your task distribution, repeated runs) clears a stated bar, on a fixed review cadence -- never migrate the same day as a launch, since leaderboard rank reshuffles weekly and self-report/aggregator/Arena rankings frequently disagree.

flashcards.q: What's the structural difference between a model card and a system card?
flashcards.a: A model card documents the artifact (architecture, training data summary, context window, self-reported benchmarks). A system card documents the deployment (what tools/actions the model is wired to, what safeguards surround it, and the lab's own red-team findings, organized around risk categories like cyber, bio/chem uplift, persuasion, and model autonomy).

flashcards.q: What concrete result demonstrates test-time compute scaling is real, and at what cost?
flashcards.a: o3 scored 75.7% on ARC-AGI-1 at standard compute and 87.5% using roughly 172x more test-time compute, at an estimated cost of thousands of dollars per task at the high-compute setting.

flashcards.q: How does GRPO differ from standard PPO-based RLHF?
flashcards.a: GRPO removes the separate critic/value network entirely. It samples a group of G completions per prompt, scores each with a verifier, and computes each completion's advantage by normalizing its reward against the group's own mean and standard deviation, rather than against a learned baseline.

flashcards.q: Why do most 2025-26 production RLVR recipes use outcome-only rewards instead of process reward models?
flashcards.a: Outcome rewards (right/wrong final answer, tests pass/fail) are automatable and hard to game when the checker is genuinely objective. Process reward models are themselves learned and vulnerable to reward hacking -- the policy can learn to produce step-text that satisfies the PRM without the steps being logically load-bearing.

flashcards.q: Mechanically, why does chain-of-thought length grow over the course of RL training?
flashcards.a: The base RLVR recipe applies no length penalty -- a long completion that lands on the correct answer gets the same reward as a short correct one. Since longer, more careful chains empirically succeed more often on hard problems, the optimizer drifts toward greater length as a side effect of reinforcing correctness, not because length itself is rewarded.

flashcards.q: What did the NeurIPS 2025 pass@k study find about whether RLVR teaches genuinely new reasoning capability?
flashcards.a: RL-trained models beat their base model at small k (better first-try accuracy), but the base model matches or exceeds the RL-trained model at large k -- indicating RLVR mostly sharpens sampling toward correct paths the base model could already reach, rather than expanding what's reachable at all. Distillation from a stronger teacher's traces did expand capability, a different mechanism.

flashcards.q: Give the documented numbers for the 'overthinking' failure mode in reasoning models.
flashcards.a: Reasoning models can generate 7-10x more tokens than a standard model for comparable or worse accuracy on simple tasks; one model spent 17 seconds deliberating 'what is 1+1'; a measured production case showed latency doubling (18s to 38s) and cost rising ($1.70 to $2.59 per task) for zero accuracy gain.

flashcards.q: How are reasoning ('thinking') tokens billed, and what's the operational gotcha?
flashcards.a: They are billed at the output-token rate (often the most expensive pricing tier), whether or not they're shown to the caller. Teams that only track visible completion length in cost dashboards miss this and get blindsided by spend spikes; monitor the reasoning_tokens usage field and cap it via max_completion_tokens/budget_tokens/thinking_budget.

flashcards.q: What structurally distinguishes RL-trained native reasoning (o1/DeepSeek-R1) from prompting-era chain-of-thought (Wei et al., self-consistency)?
flashcards.a: Prompting-era CoT elicits multi-step text from a model with no training-time link between reasoning and reward -- self-consistency's majority vote over N samples hits diminishing returns fast since all samples come from the same distribution. RL-trained reasoning has reshaped the model's actual generation distribution via a reward tied to final-answer correctness, producing emergent behaviors (backtracking, self-correction) never explicitly demonstrated in training data.

flashcards.q: Why wasn't DeepSeek-R1-Zero (pure RL, no SFT) shipped directly as the product?
flashcards.a: R1-Zero's raw output was poorly formatted and sometimes mixed languages mid-reasoning, hard to read as a product. The shipped R1 added cold-start SFT for readable formatting, then RL, then rejection-sampling SFT, then a final RL phase -- targeting formatting/readability, not the reasoning behavior itself, which ablations show came from the RL phases.

flashcards.q: List the task properties that make a reasoning model the right tool versus the wrong tool.
flashcards.a: Right tool: multi-step, verifiable problems where a wrong intermediate step ruins the answer (math, code with tests, multi-hop synthesis), with latency/cost headroom. Wrong tool: simple/high-volume lookups and rewrites, hard latency budgets, tasks with no clean automated verifier, cost-sensitive high-volume paths, and anything needing a fully auditable answer path.

flashcards.q: What industry-wide compute shift is projected by 2030 regarding inference versus training?
flashcards.a: Inference compute is projected to represent roughly 75% of total AI compute by 2030, a full inversion from the training-dominated paradigm of the early 2020s.

flashcards.q: What did DiT (Peebles and Xie, 2022/2023) change about diffusion model architecture, and what was the key empirical claim?
flashcards.a: DiT replaced the U-Net backbone in latent diffusion with a ViT-style transformer operating on patchified latent tokens. The key claim: FID scales predictably as a function of transformer Gflops (depth, width, token count), the same shape as LLM scaling laws. DiT-XL/2 reached FID 2.27 on ImageNet 256x256.

flashcards.q: What is AdaLN-Zero and why is the gate initialized to zero?
flashcards.a: AdaLN-Zero conditions each DiT block on timestep+condition embeddings via a regressed scale, shift, and gate. The gate's final linear layer is zero-initialized so every block starts training as an exact identity function, giving DiT-scale models training stability from step one without careful warmup.

flashcards.q: How does video generation extend the DiT architecture, and why does this make video far more expensive than image generation?
flashcards.a: Video is compressed spatially and temporally by a VAE, then decomposed into spacetime patches that act as transformer tokens. Attention cost is quadratic in total token count, which scales with frames x spatial patches, so doubling duration at fixed resolution roughly quadruples attention cost, and doubling both duration and resolution multiplies cost by roughly 16x.

flashcards.q: What is flow matching, and how does its training objective differ from classic diffusion?
flashcards.a: Flow matching (Lipman et al. 2022) picks an explicit probability path between noise and data and regresses the velocity field along it via simulation-free L2 loss, rather than predicting the score of an implicit reverse-time SDE the way diffusion does. Diffusion is recoverable as one specific path choice within the flow-matching framework.

flashcards.q: What is rectified flow, and why does a straight-line path enable fewer sampling steps?
flashcards.a: Rectified flow prescribes a straight-line interpolation between noise and data (x_t = (1-t)x0 + t*x1) with a constant target velocity (x1-x0). A straight path has low curvature, so a coarse numerical integrator (even a single Euler step in the limit) tracks it accurately, unlike a curved diffusion path which needs many small steps to avoid discretization error.

flashcards.q: Why did the industry shift from DDPM-style diffusion training to flow matching by 2024-25 in production models like SD3.5, FLUX, Veo, and Movie Gen?
flashcards.a: Flow matching's low-curvature paths need far fewer sampling steps for comparable quality, and at the scale of serving millions of generations a day, a ~10x reduction in required sampling steps is a direct, large cut to serving cost and latency -- the primary driver of adoption.

flashcards.q: What is a consistency model, and how does it differ from simply running a diffusion model with fewer sampling steps?
flashcards.a: A consistency model (Song et al. 2023) is explicitly trained so any point along a deterministic noise-to-data trajectory maps to the same clean output, allowing generation in 1-4 evaluations. Simply truncating a standard diffusion/flow model's step count produces a blurry, degraded sample because it was never trained to be accurate at that coarse a step size.

flashcards.q: Give the concrete cost/quality numbers for Latent Consistency Model (LCM) distillation from Stable Diffusion.
flashcards.a: A 768x768, 2-4-step LCM distills from a pretrained SD checkpoint in roughly 32 A100-GPU-hours, delivers a 10-100x inference speedup, and matches 25-50-step DDIM sampling on FID/text-alignment at 2-4 steps -- but quality degrades sharply as step count is pushed toward true 1-step generation.

flashcards.q: What does VBench2 evaluate, and why does its physics-and-commonsense dimension matter for judging a video model release?
flashcards.a: VBench2 decomposes video generation quality into consistency (subject/background), physics-and-commonsense, human motion, and creative composition. The physics dimension matters because it shows every current model, including frontier ones, still has a real, measured gap between looking physically plausible and actually being physically consistent.

flashcards.q: What are the observed 2026 temporal-consistency failure modes for Sora 2 versus Veo 3 on longer generations?
flashcards.a: Independent 2026 comparisons report Sora 2 showing visible color jittering, brightness shifts, and frame freezing with static optical flow on longer clips, while Veo 3 produces sharper, more temporally stable frames with smoother motion -- both still show distinct, unresolved failure modes past short durations.

flashcards.q: Why is it a category error to use a video diffusion model as a physics-accurate world model or robot training data source?
flashcards.a: Video diffusion models optimize for visual plausibility under the training distribution, not an explicit physical constraint -- nothing in the DiT/flow-matching stack enforces physical consistency, only statistical resemblance to training footage. Actual physics simulators (Isaac Sim, MuJoCo) remain the correct source for physically-grounded training signal.

flashcards.q: What is the 2026 competitive differentiator among top video-gen vendors, and what does it look like in practice?
flashcards.a: Controllability, not raw fidelity, since fidelity has converged across top vendors. Examples: Kling 3.0's Motion Control and Omni Video (separating camera trajectory from character motion), Runway Gen-4.5's motion brush and reference-driven character consistency, Veo 3.1's reference images for consistency control.

flashcards.q: What is the structural difference between a cascaded voice pipeline and a unified speech-to-speech model like gpt-realtime?
flashcards.a: Cascaded: VAD -> streaming ASR -> LLM -> streaming TTS, each stage independent and swappable, with a text transcript as an auditable intermediate artifact. Unified: one model consumes and emits audio tokens directly over a persistent session with no intermediate text required, cutting a serialize-to-text-and-back hop and getting gpt-realtime to roughly 800ms voice-to-voice.

flashcards.q: Give the rough stage-by-stage latency budget for a cascaded voice agent at p50.
flashcards.a: Mic buffering/jitter 20-50ms, VAD endpoint wait 200-300ms, streaming ASR final-hypothesis lag 100-300ms, LLM time-to-first-token 200-500ms, TTS time-to-first-audio 90-300ms, network/jitter buffer 20-100ms, totaling roughly 800ms-1.5s.

flashcards.q: Why is roughly 300ms treated as a meaningful UX threshold for voice response latency?
flashcards.a: Natural human conversational turn-taking gaps average around 200ms; response latency under ~300ms reads as attentive, beyond ~500ms reads as the system thinking, and beyond ~1s reads as broken, independent of response accuracy. It's a perceptual threshold, which is why TTS providers compete on time-to-first-audio rather than total synthesis time.

flashcards.q: Why does Whisper process audio in fixed 30-second windows, and what problem does that cause for live use?
flashcards.a: Whisper's architecture chops 16kHz audio into non-overlapping 30-second chunks, each turned into an 80/128-channel log-mel spectrogram (25ms window, 10ms hop) fed to an encoder-decoder transformer -- a batch-shaped design. For live use it must be retrofitted with rolling short windows and overlap-and-stitch logic since it was not designed for streaming.

flashcards.q: What architectural change does Whisper large-v3-turbo make versus large-v3, and what's the tradeoff?
flashcards.a: Turbo prunes the decoder from 32 layers to 4, dropping parameters from 1.55B to 809M, running 2-5x faster with a small accuracy cost: 7.7% WER on LibriSpeech, roughly 8-12% on real-world meeting/phone audio.

flashcards.q: Why does Whisper hallucinate on silence or non-speech audio, and what fixes most of it in production?
flashcards.a: Its autoregressive decoder always emits plausible tokens even with no genuine speech signal, and a bad segment poisons the conditioning context for subsequent windows. Over 75% of hallucinations trace to three decoder self-attention heads (fixable via targeted fine-tuning, cutting hallucination rate from 99.97% to 15.51% on a non-speech benchmark). In production, gating ASR invocation behind VAD so it never runs on confirmed silence prevents most real-world instances.

flashcards.q: What is a typical production Silero VAD configuration, and what does the minimum-duration guard trade off?
flashcards.a: Energy gate around -40dBFS, classifier confidence threshold ~0.75, minimum sustained-voice duration 200-300ms before committing to 'voice detected'. The guard drops false-positive (barge-in or endpoint) triggers by 60-80%, at the direct cost of adding that same delay to every legitimate trigger's reaction time.

flashcards.q: What are the two distinct jobs a VAD signal is used for in a voice agent, and why can't one threshold serve both well?
flashcards.a: Endpointing ('has the user finished their turn?', fires on sustained silence) and barge-in detection ('has the user started talking while the agent is talking?', fires on sustained voice during agent playback). Tuning one threshold to be more sensitive for faster barge-in directly raises false-positive endpointing and vice versa, since both key off the same sustained-voice heuristic on the same signal.

flashcards.q: List the five steps a barge-in controller must execute atomically, and the 2026 production latency targets.
flashcards.a: 1) VAD fires on caller audio during agent TTS playback. 2) Flush TTS stream (target <60ms). 3) Cancel the in-flight LLM generation server-side. 4) Roll back conversation state to reflect the truncated agent utterance. 5) Re-enter listening state. Representative production numbers: TTS-flush p95 54ms, LLM-cancel p95 38ms, total barge-in handle p95 142ms, turn-taking gap p95 310ms.

flashcards.q: How does Cartesia's Sonic TTS architecture differ from a standard transformer-based TTS, and what latency does it achieve?
flashcards.a: Cartesia built Sonic on state-space models (SSMs) rather than transformers specifically for consistent low latency including at p99. Sonic 3.5 reports 75-90ms time-to-first-audio over WebSocket; Sonic Turbo claims sub-40ms.

flashcards.q: Why does 8kHz telephony audio hurt ASR accuracy compared to 16kHz, and can upsampling fix it?
flashcards.a: 8kHz sampling gives a 4kHz Nyquist limit, losing higher-frequency consonant detail (e.g. distinguishing 's' from 'f') that 16kHz-trained ASR models rely on, raising WER. Upsampling to 16kHz changes the sample rate but cannot recreate frequency content that was never captured, so the accuracy gap remains.

flashcards.q: Name four structural reasons voice agents are harder to engineer than text agents.
flashcards.a: 1) Full-duplex interaction with no clean turn boundary, requiring probabilistic endpointing. 2) No undo -- once audio plays, the user already heard it. 3) Barge-in requires actively cancelling and rolling back in-flight generation and synthesis under a tight deadline. 4) Latency is perceived directly and continuously, with no 'typing indicator' buffer to absorb it.

flashcards.q: Why might a compliance-sensitive voice flow stay on a cascaded pipeline instead of migrating to a unified speech-to-speech model?
flashcards.a: Unified models remove the intermediate text transcript as an auditable, injectable checkpoint, so you lose the ability to assert deterministic business logic (e.g. 'read this exact confirmation string verbatim') or produce a callback-verifiable record of exactly what was said -- a hard requirement for regulated flows, not just a nice-to-have.

flashcards.q: Which Compute Engine machine families are eligible for sustained-use discounts, and which current-generation families are NOT?
flashcards.a: Eligible: N1, N2, N2D, C2, M1, M2, sole-tenant nodes, GPUs attached to N1. NOT eligible (zero automatic discount): E2, C3/C3D, C4/C4A/C4D, N4/N4D/N4A, H3/H4D, Z3, T2A/T2D -- these require a CUD to get any discount regardless of runtime.

flashcards.q: How does the sustained-use discount ramp within a billing month?
flashcards.a: It ramps at usage thresholds of 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of the month. For a 30%-max resource: 50% month usage = ~10% effective discount, 75% = ~20%, 100% = the full 30%.

flashcards.q: What discount range do resource-based CUDs offer, and what's the tradeoff?
flashcards.a: Up to 55% off for most machine series, up to 70% for memory-optimized (M1-M4), for a 1- or 3-year commitment. Tradeoff: pinned to a specific machine type/region/quantity, billed whether used or not, and cannot be canceled.

flashcards.q: What is a compute flexible CUD and what's the memory-optimized 1-year trap?
flashcards.a: A spend-based commitment with no machine-type/region pinning, applying across Compute Engine, GKE, and Cloud Run. General purpose: 28% (1yr)/46% (3yr). Trap: memory-optimized (M1-M4) gets 0% discount at 1 year -- only a 3-year term unlocks any discount (63%).

flashcards.q: What is the GKE cluster management fee and what does the free tier cover?
flashcards.a: A flat $0.10/cluster/hour applies to every GKE cluster (Standard or Autopilot, zonal or regional). The free tier gives $74.40/month credit, roughly one free zonal Standard or Autopilot cluster -- it never applies to regional cluster fees or compute charges.

flashcards.q: Describe GKE Autopilot's two billing models and what triggers each.
flashcards.a: General-purpose Pods (default platform, Balanced/Scale-Out classes): Pod-based billing, charged for the resource REQUEST in 1-second increments with no minimum, only while Running/ContainerCreating. Pods requesting specific hardware (GPU, named machine series): node-based billing, charged for the whole provisioned node plus an Autopilot management premium.

flashcards.q: When should you choose GKE Standard over Autopilot?
flashcards.a: When the workload needs privileged containers/hostPath access, custom DaemonSets beyond what Autopilot permits, fine-grained node-level tuning, or specific GPU/TPU node topologies -- Autopilot enforces stricter security defaults and removes direct node control. Google's default recommendation for new clusters is Autopilot first.

flashcards.q: What happens to sustained-use discount accrual when a project moves between Cloud Billing accounts?
flashcards.a: Sustained resource usage time resets to zero on the new billing account -- it is not carried forward. Google recommends making billing account changes on the first day of a month to minimize the impact.

flashcards.q: Do sustained-use discounts and committed-use discounts stack on the same usage?
flashcards.a: No. SUDs don't apply to usage already covered by a CUD -- CUD coverage takes priority and SUD applies only to the remaining uncommitted usage on eligible machine families.

flashcards.q: How does GKE Autopilot's Pod-based billing differ from Fargate's task billing philosophically?
flashcards.a: Both bill for provisioned/requested capacity rather than measured consumption, but Autopilot bills only while a Pod is Running/ContainerCreating (not scheduled or terminated Pods) in 1-second increments with no minimum, while Fargate bills continuously for provisioned vCPU/memory per task regardless of load fluctuation, with per-second billing and a one-minute minimum on the underlying resource.

flashcards.q: What is GCP's resource hierarchy order, and how does allow-policy inheritance work?
flashcards.a: Organization -> Folder -> Project -> Resource. Allow policies are additive/union -- the effective policy on a resource is the union of its own bindings plus everything inherited from every ancestor. A child cannot remove or narrow a grant an ancestor made.

flashcards.q: How does GCP's IAM evaluation model differ fundamentally from AWS's?
flashcards.a: AWS evaluates identity policies plus resource policies with explicit Deny winning over any Allow. GCP has no explicit-deny-in-the-allow-policy concept -- it binds roles additively on a resource hierarchy, and the only override is a separate deny policy resource or Organization Policy (a different axis entirely).

flashcards.q: What is a GCP deny policy and what are its limits?
flashcards.a: A separate IAM v2 resource listing principals/permissions to block, evaluated at every hierarchy level, always wins over any allow grant. Limits: 500 deny policies/resource, 500 deny rules/resource, 2,500 total principal appearances/resource.

flashcards.q: What are the hard limits on GCP custom roles?
flashcards.a: 300 custom roles per organization and 300 per project (independent caps -- project-level roles don't count against org cap), up to 3,000 permissions per role, 64KB combined size of title+description+permission names.

flashcards.q: How does Organization Policy differ from IAM?
flashcards.a: IAM controls who can act (grants roles to principals). Organization Policy restricts what configuration is allowed to exist for everyone, regardless of identity (boolean or list constraints). Both must permit an action for it to succeed -- an Owner can still be blocked by an org policy constraint.

flashcards.q: Describe the Workload Identity Federation flow and its critical misconfiguration.
flashcards.a: External OIDC/SAML token -> workload identity pool -> provider (attribute mapping + CEL attribute_condition) -> short-lived STS token -> usually impersonates a real service account. The classic misconfig is a missing or too-broad attribute_condition: without it, any subject the IdP will vouch for (e.g. any repo in a GitHub org) is accepted.

flashcards.q: What are the limits on service account keys and access token lifetime?
flashcards.a: Max 10 keys per service account. Default access token lifetime is 3,600 seconds (1 hour), extendable to 43,200 seconds (12 hours) only via the iam.allowServiceAccountCredentialLifetimeExtension org policy list constraint naming specific service accounts.

flashcards.q: State the key numeric limits on a GCP allow policy.
flashcards.a: 1,500 total principal appearances per policy, 250 unique domains/groups, 12 logic operators per IAM Condition expression, up to 20 role bindings for the same role+principal pair with different condition expressions.

flashcards.q: Why can granting Viewer on a resource be a complete no-op?
flashcards.a: Basic roles are concentric: Owner contains Editor's permissions, Editor contains Viewer's. If a principal already has Editor inherited from a parent, granting Viewer at a child resource adds nothing -- the inherited Editor already includes every Viewer permission.

flashcards.q: What is a Principal Access Boundary (PAB) policy and how does it differ from a deny policy?
flashcards.a: A PAB policy is a hard ceiling on the maximum resources a principal can ever access, regardless of what any allow policy grants (conceptually close to an AWS permission boundary). A deny policy blocks specific permissions; a PAB policy caps overall scope. Limits: 500 rules/policy, 10 policies/resource, 1,000/org.

flashcards.q: What problem does Privileged Access Manager (PAM) solve on GCP?
flashcards.a: Just-in-time, time-boxed, approval-gated elevated access, replacing standing Owner/write grants for compliance-sensitive resources like production payment data. It provides an entitlement catalog, approval workflow, automatic expiry, and audit trail that static IAM Conditions with time bounds don't provide on their own.

flashcards.q: Does GCP support resource-based policies like AWS S3 bucket policies?
flashcards.a: Partially -- many services (Cloud Storage buckets, Pub/Sub topics, BigQuery datasets) support resource-level allow-policy bindings, but architecturally these are just another node in the same additive resource hierarchy, not a structurally separate policy type intersected against an identity policy the way AWS evaluates bucket policies.

flashcards.q: Why is a GCP VPC described as a global resource, and what changes as a result?
flashcards.a: A VPC's subnets are regional, but the VPC itself spans every region with no cross-region peering or transit gateway needed -- two subnets in different regions in the same VPC are reachable over Google's backbone by default. AWS/Azure networks are strictly regional and always need explicit cross-region plumbing.

flashcards.q: What is the default scope of a GCP firewall rule, and what's the common mistake it causes?
flashcards.a: VPC-scoped (global) by default -- applies to every matching instance in every region of the VPC unless explicitly scoped with target tags or service accounts. AWS engineers used to regionally-scoped security groups often assume implicit regional scoping that doesn't exist, creating unintentionally broad rules.

flashcards.q: How does Shared VPC work and what IAM role does a service project need?
flashcards.a: A host project owns the VPC, subnets, routes, and firewall rules; service projects attach and deploy resources INTO the host's subnets without owning networking resources. Requires roles/compute.networkUser granted per subnet (preferred) or project-wide on the host.

flashcards.q: How does GCP's global external Application Load Balancer route traffic, mechanically?
flashcards.a: A single global anycast IP is announced from every Google PoP simultaneously (BGP anycast). User traffic enters at the nearest PoP, travels Google's private backbone (Premium Tier), and reaches the nearest healthy backend in any region -- automatic geo-routing and instant health-check failover with no DNS TTL dependency.

flashcards.q: When should you choose a regional load balancer over the global anycast LB?
flashcards.a: Data-residency requirements, active-passive DR needing explicit regional control, genuinely single-region traffic where global's cost premium buys nothing, or Standard Tier (internet-routed, cheaper) networking instead of Premium Tier backbone routing.

flashcards.q: What are Cloud Armor's two pricing tiers and what does Enterprise add?
flashcards.a: Standard: pay-as-you-go, ~$1/rule/month, basic WAF/DDoS rules + rate limiting. Enterprise: ~$3,000/month, adds Adaptive Protection (ML-based anomaly detection tuned to backend traffic baseline) and DDoS bill protection (credits for attack-driven cost spikes).

flashcards.q: Why do static per-IP rate limits fail against a real botnet attack, and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: A distributed botnet uses thousands of rotating source IPs, so no single IP crosses the per-IP threshold even though aggregate backend load is severe. Fix: Adaptive Protection (Enterprise tier) does ML-based anomaly detection against the backend's aggregate traffic pattern rather than relying on any single per-IP dimension.

flashcards.q: What does Private Service Connect give you that VPC peering doesn't?
flashcards.a: Private IP access to a published service inside the consumer's own VPC without peering the two networks -- no IP-overlap coordination needed, no broad transitive-reachability exposure, and the producer controls exactly which consumers can connect via accept lists on the service attachment.

flashcards.q: Compare Dedicated, Partner, and Cross-Cloud Interconnect.
flashcards.a: Dedicated: direct physical circuit into Google colocation, 10Gbps/100Gbps ports, VLAN attachments 50Mbps-50Gbps, needs own colocation presence. Partner: via a supported service provider, sub-10Gbps, no colocation needed, faster provisioning, higher per-GiB egress at scale. Cross-Cloud Interconnect: direct Google-provisioned link straight to AWS/Azure, no third-party colocation partner.

flashcards.q: When do you use VPC Network Peering instead of Shared VPC?
flashcards.a: Peering connects two genuinely SEPARATE VPCs (different Shared VPC hosts, different orgs, M&A integration). Shared VPC is for one network with delegated usage rights across multiple teams/projects within the same org -- not a default multi-region pattern, since GCP's global VPC already gives cross-region reachability without either.

flashcards.q: What's the incomplete part of claiming 'Cloud Armor is just AWS WAF renamed'?
flashcards.a: Both provide comparable L7 WAF rules and rate limiting, but Cloud Armor sits in front of GCP's global anycast LB, so volumetric attacks are structurally absorbed/distributed across Google's entire edge before rules even fire. AWS WAF on a bare regional ALB doesn't get that dilution unless separately paired with CloudFront or Global Accelerator.

flashcards.q: What operationally changes migrating a two-region AWS Transit-Gateway topology to GCP?
flashcards.a: Transit Gateway's routing/attachment machinery mostly disappears -- same-org resources become subnets of one GCP VPC with default reachability. What replaces centralized routing control is disciplined firewall-rule scoping (default permissive-within-VPC) and Shared VPC with per-subnet IAM grants for team isolation. The model inverts: AWS = explicit reachability/implicit isolation; GCP = implicit reachability/explicit isolation.

flashcards.q: What are Cloud Run's two CPU allocation modes and what's the consequence of each?
flashcards.a: 'CPU only allocated during request processing' (default): throttles CPU to near-zero once no requests are in-flight, enabling scale-to-zero cost but silently starving detached background work after a response returns. 'CPU always allocated': behaves like an always-on box, billed continuously, background work keeps running.

flashcards.q: Why does Cloud Run scale to zero in a way Fargate structurally cannot match?
flashcards.a: Cloud Run's front door is an always-available request router that can hold an incoming request while spinning up a fresh instance on demand. Fargate has no built-in wake-on-request mechanism -- scaling to zero requires explicit Auto Scaling config, and scaling back up requires an external trigger, with a cold path (ENI + image pull) of tens of seconds to minutes.

flashcards.q: What is Cloud Run's default and maximum per-instance concurrency?
flashcards.a: Default 80 simultaneous requests per instance, configurable up to 1,000 per instance. Higher concurrency only helps for I/O-bound workloads; CPU-bound work contends for the same instance's CPU allocation at high concurrency.

flashcards.q: How long does Cloud Run keep an idle instance warm before tearing it down?
flashcards.a: Up to 15 minutes (10 minutes for GPU-backed instances) after the last request, then the instance is torn down back to zero.

flashcards.q: Contrast Cloud Functions 1st gen and 2nd gen (Cloud Run functions).
flashcards.a: 1st gen: bespoke pre-Cloud-Run engine, exactly 1 request per instance, max 9-minute timeout. 2nd gen: built on Cloud Run, concurrency up to 1,000/instance, up to 60-minute timeout, uses Eventarc triggers. Use 2nd gen for anything new.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between a direct Eventarc event and an audit-log-derived event, and which should you prefer?
flashcards.a: Direct events are emitted natively by ~100+ first-party GCP sources through a purpose-built stream, low latency. Audit-log-derived events are sourced from Cloud Audit Logs -- broader coverage (any API call) but more delivery lag. Prefer direct events whenever the source offers one.

flashcards.q: Does setting minScale >= 1 on a Cloud Run service eliminate all cold starts?
flashcards.a: No. It eliminates baseline cold starts for traffic within the warm instances' capacity, but a sudden spike beyond that capacity still triggers new cold-start instances to handle the overflow.

flashcards.q: What is the current recommended status of App Engine for new projects?
flashcards.a: App Engine is in maintenance mode and not recommended for new projects -- Cloud Run is its explicit successor for nearly every use case App Engine Standard used to serve.

flashcards.q: When should you choose GKE Autopilot over Cloud Run for a stateless-looking workload?
flashcards.a: Once it needs arbitrary long-lived non-HTTP TCP protocols, StatefulSet-style stable identity/persistent storage, complex sidecars beyond Cloud Run's limited multi-container support, or fine-grained custom scheduling/affinity -- capabilities Cloud Run doesn't offer natively.

flashcards.q: Why did Google rebuild Cloud Functions 2nd gen on top of Cloud Run instead of maintaining a separate engine?
flashcards.a: To converge scaling/cold-start engineering into one shared runtime -- every Cloud Run improvement automatically benefits Cloud Run functions -- while keeping the lighter function-first deployment experience as a product-level (not runtime-level) differentiator.

flashcards.q: List GCS's four storage classes with per-GB price, minimum storage duration, and retrieval fee.
flashcards.a: Standard: $0.020/GB-mo, no minimum, no retrieval fee. Nearline: $0.010/GB-mo, 30-day minimum, $0.01/GB retrieval. Coldline: $0.004/GB-mo, 90-day minimum, $0.02/GB retrieval. Archive: $0.0012/GB-mo, 365-day minimum, $0.05/GB retrieval.

flashcards.q: What does GCS Autoclass do and what's the key cost benefit over manual lifecycle rules?
flashcards.a: Monitors each object's actual access pattern and auto-transitions it between Standard/Nearline/Coldline/Archive, with no early-deletion fee for auto-migrated objects -- avoids the trap of manual lifecycle rules moving frequently-churned data into a class before its minimum duration, which bills the full minimum period anyway.

flashcards.q: What is TrueTime and what does it return?
flashcards.a: An API backed by GPS receivers and atomic clocks in Google datacenters that returns a bounded time INTERVAL [earliest, latest] guaranteed to contain true UTC time -- not a single point value. Typical uncertainty is under 7ms.

flashcards.q: What is commit-wait and why does Spanner need it?
flashcards.a: After assigning a transaction a commit timestamp drawn from TrueTime's interval, Spanner waits until TrueTime guarantees that timestamp is definitely in the past everywhere before exposing the write. This guarantees any transaction that committed earlier in real time gets a provably smaller timestamp than one that started later -- external consistency without a global lock.

flashcards.q: How is Spanner compute billed and what's the minimum?
flashcards.a: Processing Units (PU): 1 node = 1000 PU. Minimum purchase is 100 PU, provisioned in 100 PU increments up to 1000 PU then 1000 PU increments beyond. ~$0.90/node-hour regional on-demand; Standard edition ~$0.030/100PU/hr, Enterprise ~$0.041/100PU/hr. ~4TB storage per node.

flashcards.q: What are Spanner interleaved tables and what happens if the hierarchy is designed wrong?
flashcards.a: A child table's rows are physically co-located with the parent row on the same split (e.g. Orders interleaved in Customers), keeping cross-table reads/transactions cheap. Interleaving a high-write child under a low-cardinality/hot parent key recreates a hot-split problem, concentrating writes and defeating horizontal scale.

flashcards.topic: Spanner vs Aurora Global vs Cosmos DB
flashcards.q: Why is there no direct AWS/Azure equivalent to Spanner's external consistency?
flashcards.a: Aurora Global Database is asynchronous with real (if small) replica lag, no bounded ordering guarantee. Cosmos DB gives 5 tunable consistency levels but Strong isn't TrueTime-style global commit-wait and costs 2x RUs. Neither gives globally distributed multi-region WRITE availability with real-time external consistency backed by hardware time infrastructure.

flashcards.q: Why does a monotonically increasing Bigtable row key (timestamp, auto-increment) cause problems, and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: All recent writes concentrate on the tablet owning the newest key range -- a hot spot. Fix: salt/hash the key prefix or reverse the timestamp to spread writes across the key space, trading off some range-scan efficiency.

flashcards.q: State Bigtable's pricing and autoscaling storage-trigger defaults.
flashcards.a: ~$0.65/node-hour standard. Autoscaling adjusts nodes on a CPU-utilization target plus a storage-utilization target defaulting to 50% -- that's 2.5TB for SSD clusters, 8TB for HDD clusters, before triggering a scale event.

flashcards.q: What is Firestore's hard document size limit, and what's required for multi-field queries?
flashcards.a: 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes) per document in Native mode; 1,048,572 bytes for Datastore mode entities. Most multi-field queries require an explicit composite index pre-created before the query runs -- Firestore does not auto-index every field combination.

flashcards.q: What does AlloyDB's columnar engine do and what's its real limit?
flashcards.a: Maintains an automatically-updated in-memory columnar copy of frequently-scanned data alongside the row store, giving up to 100x faster analytical queries against LIVE transactional data without a separate ETL pipeline. It accelerates analytics on the operational dataset's current size -- it does not replace a data warehouse for many-TB historical aggregation at BigQuery scale.

flashcards.q: What is Cloud SQL's storage ceiling and what happens as an instance approaches it?
flashcards.a: Up to 64TB. Google's own docs flag that operations like backups get slower as storage approaches that ceiling -- a real operational degradation signal, not just a hard cutoff. Enterprise Plus edition adds read pools (pooled read replicas behind one endpoint) and near-zero-downtime maintenance.

flashcards.q: What changed when Vertex AI Agent Builder became Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (April 22, 2026)?
flashcards.a: Absorbed Vertex AI Agent Builder + Agentspace into one namespace, inverted console hierarchy (agents first-class, model training/AutoML/Endpoints now sub-features), made A2A v1.0 the default interop layer, added Agent Studio (low-code) + Agent Gateway. Console-level/organizational change -- underlying APIs, SDKs, and billing for existing Vertex AI workloads unchanged. 'Vertex AI' label gone from console as of 2026-05-21.

flashcards.q: How are Vertex AI / Gemini Enterprise prediction endpoints billed, and what's the common cost trap?
flashcards.a: Per hour for every model deployed to an endpoint, regardless of whether it's serving traffic -- you must explicitly undeploy to stop the charge. Common trap: a demo model gets deployed, demo ends, nobody undeploys, endpoint bills 24/7 indefinitely.

flashcards.q: State Gemini 3.1 Pro and 3.5 Flash pricing including the long-context surcharge.
flashcards.a: 3.1 Pro: 2M context, $2.00/$12.00 per 1M input/output tokens under 200K, rising to $2.50/$15.00 above 200K (surcharge applies to the WHOLE call, not just the excess). 3.5 Flash: 1M context, $1.50/$9.00. Flash-Lite: $0.10/$0.40, cheapest tier.

flashcards.q: What cost-saving levers do the Gemini Batch API and context caching offer?
flashcards.a: Batch API: flat 50% discount on any model with a 24-hour processing SLA -- default choice for non-synchronous workloads. Context caching: cuts cost of repeated large-context prompts (shared system prompt, reused document) by up to ~90%, since cached tokens bill at a steep discount vs fresh input tokens.

flashcards.q: What is the Agent Development Kit (ADK) and what are its core primitives?
flashcards.a: Open-source, code-first (Python/Go/Java) agent framework, explicitly model-agnostic and deployment-agnostic (optimized for Gemini, not locked to it). Core primitives: multi-agent hierarchy composition, rich tool ecosystem, graph-based workflow runtime (routing/fan-out/loops/retry/human-in-the-loop), ADK Web (local dev/debug UI with events/traces/artifacts/evals).

flashcards.q: Distinguish Agent Engine's Sessions from Memory Bank.
flashcards.a: Sessions: short-term, persists chronological interaction history within ONE conversation for contextual continuity. Memory Bank (GA early 2026): long-term, extracts salient facts across sessions and stores them for cross-session retrieval. Conflating them causes an agent to 'forget' facts from prior sessions if Memory Bank isn't enabled/populated.

flashcards.q: Contrast Vertex AI Vector Search's brute-force and tree-AH (ANN) index types.
flashcards.a: Brute force: exact linear search, no tunable parameters, appropriate only for small datasets or ground-truth baseline -- latency scales linearly with dataset size, breaks down at scale. Tree-AH/ANN (ScaNN-based): ~99% recall, sub-10ms latency even at billion-vector scale -- the production-appropriate choice. SOAR algorithm adds controlled redundancy for efficiency at smaller index sizes.

flashcards.q: When should you use Vector Search vs AlloyDB AI/Spanner's built-in vector index?
flashcards.a: Vector Search: dedicated, purpose-built for genuine large scale (millions-to-billions of vectors, high QPS) -- bills per-node-hour regardless of traffic, same undeploy trap as prediction endpoints. AlloyDB AI (ScaNN) or Spanner vector index: better when the vector workload can live alongside existing operational data at smaller scale, avoiding a second separately-billed system.

flashcards.q: Distinguish the A2A and MCP protocols.
flashcards.a: MCP (Model Context Protocol): agent-to-TOOL communication -- how an agent calls external tools/data sources. A2A (Agent2Agent): agent-to-AGENT communication -- how one agent hands off tasks to or communicates with another independent agent (task delegation, status, artifacts). Complementary, not substitutes; donated to Linux Foundation June 2025, v1.0 early 2026, 150+ supporting orgs claimed.

flashcards.q: Give the one-line honest positioning of Bedrock AgentCore, Azure AI Foundry, and Gemini Enterprise (ADK+Agent Engine).
flashcards.a: AgentCore: modular composable primitives (Runtime/Memory/Identity/Gateway/Policy), strongest zero-trust/multi-tenant story. Azure AI Foundry: bundled Agent Service, wins decisively for Microsoft 365-native orgs (one-click Teams/Copilot, days not months time-to-value). Gemini Enterprise: code-first ADK + managed Agent Engine, tightest GCP data-platform integration (BigQuery/Vector Search/Spanner), newest rebrand (docs churn risk).

flashcards.q: What is Model Garden and how does third-party model pricing work there?
flashcards.a: Vertex AI/Gemini Enterprise's catalog of 200+ models (Gemini, Claude, Llama, Mistral, Gemma, others) behind one deployment/billing surface. Third-party model pricing is set by the model vendor (e.g. Claude via Model Garden costs roughly what it costs via Bedrock) -- platform choice is rarely about that model's price, more about surrounding tooling fit.

flashcards.q: What changed about the Gemini API free tier on April 1, 2026?
flashcards.a: Free tier now covers only Flash and Flash-Lite models -- Pro-tier models became paid-only. A common gotcha for anyone assuming free-tier prototyping automatically covers the top model.

flashcards.q: How is BigQuery on-demand pricing calculated and what's the free tier?
flashcards.a: $6.25 per TiB of logical bytes scanned (columns actually read), with the first 1 TiB per project per month free. Columnar storage means SELECT * scans every column's bytes -- no buffer cache saves you the way it does on a row-store warehouse.

flashcards.q: What are BigQuery Editions and their pay-as-you-go slot-hour rates?
flashcards.a: Standard $0.04, Enterprise $0.06, Enterprise Plus $0.10 per slot-hour (US region), replacing flat-rate slots retired 2023-07-05. Autoscaling slots (baseline + max, 100-slot increments) are the default capacity model, billed only while in use.

flashcards.q: Roughly where does the on-demand-vs-Editions break-even point sit?
flashcards.a: Around 400-500 TiB scanned per month. Below that, on-demand's pay-per-scan model wins; above it, a slot commitment typically amortizes cheaper -- but only if partitioning/clustering already control scan volume first.

flashcards.q: What is BigQuery's partition column restriction and hard partition-count limit?
flashcards.a: One DATE/TIMESTAMP/DATETIME/INTEGER column (or ingestion time). Hard cap: 4,000 partitions per table. Daily partitioning gives ~11 years of runway; hourly burns through the cap in ~5 months.

flashcards.q: How does BigQuery clustering differ from partitioning mechanically?
flashcards.a: Clusters on up to 4 columns, sorted in specified order (order matters -- sorts by col1 then col2 within that...), no limit on cardinality/partition count, works on more types. STRING clustering only uses the first 1,024 characters. Only helps when WHERE clauses filter on the clustered columns.

flashcards.q: What breaks incremental refresh on a JOIN-based BigQuery materialized view?
flashcards.a: Only the LEFT-side table of the JOIN can have appended data and stay incremental. Any change (append/update/delete) to a right-side table forces a full non-incremental rebuild. Default refresh attempt: within 5 min if prior refresh was >30 min stale; configurable cap 1 min to 7 days.

flashcards.q: Name the three layered BigQuery cost controls and what each catches.
flashcards.a: maximum_bytes_billed: per-query, pre-execution byte estimate, fails free if over threshold. Custom quotas: project/user daily scan cap (200 TiB default since 2025-09-01, resets midnight PT), approximate safeguard. Partitioning/clustering: fixes the root cause (bytes scanned) rather than capping after the fact. None alone is sufficient.

flashcards.q: What does Dataflow's Streaming Engine offload, and what does the autoscaling hint control?
flashcards.a: Offloads windowing, state, and timer management from worker VMs to a managed backend, making workers near-stateless so horizontal autoscaling (1 to 1000+ workers) is fast and responsive to backlog changes. Autoscaling hint 0.3 favors minimal latency, 0.7 favors minimal cost.

flashcards.q: What is Pub/Sub's default delivery guarantee, and how does exactly-once differ?
flashcards.a: Default: at-least-once -- redelivery possible even after ack, consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once delivery (GA) guarantees no redelivery once a message is successfully acked, at the cost of added ack latency -- reserved for cases where idempotent consumer design is impractical, not the default.

flashcards.q: How do Pub/Sub ordering keys work and what's the failure mode?
flashcards.a: Opt-in: messages with the same ordering key deliver in publish order; all messages for one key must publish to the same region (subscribers can be anywhere). Since delivery is still at-least-once underneath, one unacked/failed message blocks (head-of-line-blocks) all subsequent messages for that key until resolved -- mitigate with a dead-letter topic.

flashcards.q: Contrast Pub/Sub's and Kinesis's default ordering/exactly-once posture.
flashcards.a: Kinesis: ordering is free per-shard by construction, but exactly-once is never provided -- consumer must always dedupe. Pub/Sub: ordering is opt-in via ordering keys (with a same-region publish constraint), exactly-once is a GA managed opt-in feature. Opposite defaults.

flashcards.q: Distinguish Looker from Looker Studio.
flashcards.a: Looker: enterprise semantic layer, LookML (modeling language compiled to governed SQL), no public pricing, real contracts land $60K-150K+/year, needs 1-2+ FTE to maintain. Looker Studio: free dashboard tool (Pro tier $9/user/month), no LookML, no governed semantic layer -- a lightweight reporting tool, not the enterprise product.

flashcards.q: State Cloud Logging's ingestion pricing, free tier, and retention rules.
flashcards.a: $0.50/GiB ingested, 50 GiB/month free per project. That charge includes 30 days of storage; extended retention beyond 30 days costs an additional $0.01/GiB-month.

flashcards.q: How do Cloud Logging exclusion filters save money, and what happens if the log is also exported via a sink?
flashcards.a: An exclusion filter stops a log from being ingested/billed at Logging's $0.50/GiB rate entirely. If a separate sink still exports that same log to Pub/Sub, GCS, or BigQuery, the export proceeds normally -- you pay that destination's (usually much cheaper) rate instead of Logging's ingestion charge.

flashcards.q: Name the four Cloud Audit Log types and which are free vs chargeable.
flashcards.a: Admin Activity (free, always on, can't disable) and System Event (free, Google-initiated actions) form the _Required bucket with free 400-day retention. Data Access (chargeable, off by default except a few services -- biggest cost-spike risk) and Policy Denied (chargeable, on by default) land in regular chargeable buckets.

flashcards.q: How is an error budget calculated, and what does a 99.9% SLO over 30 days yield?
flashcards.a: Error budget = (1 - SLO target) applied to the compliance period. A 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days yields roughly 43.2 minutes of allowed downtime for the period.

flashcards.q: What is a burn-rate alert and why does it beat a static error-rate threshold?
flashcards.a: Fires when X% of the error budget is consumed within a lookback window (default ~60 min), measuring consumption speed relative to a sustainable pace. Unlike a static threshold, it accounts for REMAINING budget -- avoiding both alert fatigue (firing on budget-cheap noise) and missed slow-burn incidents (steady degradation that never spikes dramatically).

flashcards.q: Describe a standard tiered burn-rate alerting setup.
flashcards.a: Fast-burn (e.g. 10x rate, exhausting the month's budget in ~3 days if sustained) pages on-call immediately. Slow-burn (e.g. 2x rate, longer lookback window) opens a ticket rather than paging -- catches gradual degradation a short fast-burn lookback would miss.

flashcards.q: State Cloud Trace pricing and contrast head-based vs tail-based sampling.
flashcards.a: 2.5M spans/month free, $0.20/million beyond -- near-free at typical scale, so sampling strategy is driven by signal quality, not cost. Head-based: fixed rate (5-10% typical), decision made before outcome known, cuts volume ~90% but drops a proportional share of errors. Tail-based: decision deferred until full trace seen, keeps errors/slow outliers preferentially -- needs an OpenTelemetry Collector, not native to Cloud Trace.

flashcards.q: What are Sustained Use Discounts (SUDs) and which machine families are eligible?
flashcards.a: Automatic, zero-commitment discount up to 30% off, applied once a VM runs more than 25% of the billing month. Only N1, N2, N2D, C2, M1, M2 are eligible -- E2, C3, C4, N4, and all accelerator-optimized families are explicitly excluded. No AWS/Azure equivalent (their discounts always require a commitment).

flashcards.q: State CUD terms and the 2026 scope change.
flashcards.a: Commit vCPU+memory in a region for 1 year (37% off) or 3 years (55% off), no-upfront-payment only (unlike AWS RIs which offer All/Partial-Upfront for deeper discounts). 2026 update: default scope moved from per-project to billing-account, so one commitment can apply across projects, fixing the classic stranded-commitment problem when one project's usage shrinks.

flashcards.q: What is the key limitation of the GCP CUD Recommender?
flashcards.a: It suggests coverage based on recent usage patterns but does not model growth uncertainty or protect against usage dropping after commitment -- a good free starting signal for early-stage FinOps, not a substitute for judgment-based sizing. Size commitments conservatively below historical minimum usage, not the raw recommendation.

flashcards.topic: GCP vs AWS Logging Free Tier
flashcards.q: Compare Cloud Logging's and CloudWatch Logs' free tiers and per-GB rates.
flashcards.a: Both charge roughly $0.50/GB ingestion. Cloud Logging's free tier is 50 GiB/month; CloudWatch Logs' free tier is only 5 GB/month -- a 10x difference giving GCP more headroom before logging costs become material at the same volume, though at high volume the deciding cost factor is operational hygiene (exclusion filters, log routing) on either platform, not the free tier.

flashcards.q: Should a dependency's outage that degrades your SLI be excluded from SLO calculation?
flashcards.a: No by default -- SLOs and error budgets are deliberately cause-agnostic, measuring actual user-observed impact regardless of root cause. Excluding dependency failures risks the SLO no longer reflecting real user experience. If a dependency's failures distort the SLO meaningfully, the better fix is improving resilience (retries, fallbacks, circuit breakers) or renegotiating the SLO target, not quietly excluding inconvenient data.

flashcards.q: In the Black-Scholes delta-hedge derivation, why does the real-world drift mu drop out of the result?
flashcards.a: Choosing Delta=dV/dS to cancel the random dW term in the hedged portfolio dPi simultaneously cancels the mu*S*(dV/dS-Delta) drift term, since it's the exact same bracket -- eliminating risk automatically eliminates dependence on mu.

flashcards.q: Write the Black-Scholes PDE and the closed-form European call formula.
flashcards.a: PDE: dV/dt + (1/2)sigma^2*S^2*d2V/dS2 + r*S*dV/dS - r*V = 0. Call: C = S*N(d1) - K*e^(-rT)*N(d2), d1=[ln(S/K)+(r+sigma^2/2)T]/(sigma*sqrt(T)), d2=d1-sigma*sqrt(T).

flashcards.q: Worked Black-Scholes: S=K=100, r=5%, sigma=20%, T=1. Compute d1, d2, C, P.
Define Delta, Gamma, Vega, Theta, Rho with their formulas.
flashcards.a: Delta=N(d1) (hedge ratio). Gamma=N'(d1)/(S*sigma*sqrt(T)) (rate of change of delta). Vega=S*N'(d1)*sqrt(T) (sensitivity to implied vol). Theta=-S*N'(d1)*sigma/(2*sqrt(T))-r*K*e^(-rT)*N(d2) (time decay). Rho=K*T*e^(-rT)*N(d2) (rate sensitivity).

flashcards.q: Why does a dealer who sold options ('short gamma') lose money from hedging in a volatile market?
flashcards.a: Short gamma means delta moves against the dealer as the stock moves: rising stock makes their (negative) delta more negative, forcing them to buy into the rally; falling stock forces selling into the decline -- mechanically buying high and selling low on every rehedge, compensated only by collected theta.

flashcards.q: Why does Monte Carlo option pricing simulate under drift r (risk-neutral), not the real-world expected return mu?
flashcards.a: The same no-arbitrage delta-hedging logic that eliminates mu from the PDE (Feynman-Kac connects the two) implies pricing equals the expected discounted payoff under the risk-neutral measure Q, where the underlying's drift is r -- simulating with mu would price under real-world probabilities, not a tradeable arbitrage-free price.

flashcards.q: What is antithetic variates and why prefer it over just adding more Monte Carlo paths?
flashcards.a: Pair each random draw Z with -Z; because option payoffs are locally smooth in Z, the pairing reduces variance essentially for free. Standard MC error shrinks only as 1/sqrt(n), so quadrupling paths only halves the CI -- antithetic variates is a cheaper first lever.

flashcards.q: How do you solve for implied volatility, and what's the update rule?
flashcards.a: Newton-Raphson inversion of the Black-Scholes formula: sigma_(n+1) = sigma_n - (C(sigma_n)-market_price)/Vega(sigma_n). Converges very fast (often 2-3 iterations) near-the-money since Vega is well-behaved there.

flashcards.q: Why is implied volatility typically higher than subsequently realized volatility?
flashcards.a: The variance risk premium: buyers of insurance-like protection pay implied vol above statistically expected realized vol, compensating sellers for bearing occasionally severe tail risk -- makes systematic option-selling a real average-return source but a structurally short-tail-risk position.

flashcards.q: What is the volatility smile/skew and why is it direct evidence against a core Black-Scholes assumption?
flashcards.a: Implied vol computed separately per strike is not flat -- equity index OTM puts typically show higher implied vol than ATM/OTM calls, pricing in fatter crash risk than lognormal returns imply. Since Black-Scholes assumes one constant sigma prices every strike, an observed non-flat curve directly contradicts that assumption.

flashcards.q: What production models replace flat Black-Scholes to handle the volatility smile, and what is flat BS still used for?
flashcards.a: Local volatility (Dupire, 1994, recovers sigma(S,t) consistent with observed prices) and stochastic volatility (Heston, 1993, volatility itself follows a random process). Flat Black-Scholes remains the universal quoting convention (implied vol) even though nobody prices exotic/skew-sensitive positions with it directly.

flashcards.q: Given asks 400@100.02, 600@100.03 and mid=100.00, what's the avg fill price and slippage for a 1000-share market buy?
flashcards.a: Avg fill = (400*100.02+600*100.03)/1000 = 100.026. Slippage vs mid = 2.6bps; vs best ask (100.02) = 0.6bps -- the marginal cost of walking past the first level.

flashcards.q: What three economic components decompose the bid-ask spread?
flashcards.a: Order-processing cost (fixed operating cost), inventory-holding risk (compensation for price exposure after a trade), and adverse selection (compensation for the risk the counterparty is informed).

flashcards.q: Define effective spread, realized spread, and price impact (adverse selection component), with formulas.
flashcards.a: Effective spread = 2*|exec_price - mid_at_trade|. Realized spread = 2*D*(exec_price - mid_later), D=+1 buy/-1 sell. Price impact = effective - realized (the adverse-selection/permanent-information component).

flashcards.q: State Kyle's (1985) lambda and beta formulas and what they depend on.
flashcards.a: lambda = sigma_v/(2*sigma_u) (price impact per unit order flow); beta = sigma_u/sigma_v (informed trader's optimal aggressiveness). Higher fundamental uncertainty sigma_v raises lambda; higher noise-trader volume sigma_u lowers it (informed flow easier to hide).

flashcards.q: Worked Kyle's lambda: sigma_v=$2, sigma_u=5000 shares. Compute lambda and the price impact of a 20,000-share net order flow.
Write the empirical square-root market impact law and a worked example.
flashcards.a: Impact = Y*sigma*sqrt(Q/V). Worked: Y=0.5, sigma=2% daily, V=5,000,000 shares ADV, Q=250,000 shares (5% ADV) -> impact = 0.5*0.02*sqrt(0.05) = 22.4bps.

flashcards.q: Why does sub-linear (square-root) impact scaling justify splitting large orders into smaller pieces?
flashcards.a: Doubling order size only multiplies impact by sqrt(2)~1.41x, not 2x, so executing n smaller pieces over time costs less in aggregate than one large market order -- the direct mathematical basis for execution algorithms.

flashcards.q: Distinguish TWAP, VWAP, POV, and Implementation Shortfall execution algorithms.
flashcards.a: TWAP: uniform time-based slices (simple, gameable). VWAP: slices by historical intraday volume profile (standard benchmark). POV: targets a fixed percent of LIVE real-time volume (adaptive). IS: directly optimizes the impact-vs-risk tradeoff (e.g. Almgren-Chriss) rather than targeting a volume benchmark.

flashcards.q: Write the Almgren-Chriss optimal execution trajectory formula and what kappa controls.
flashcards.a: x(t) = X*sinh(kappa*(T-t))/sinh(kappa*T), kappa = sqrt(risk_aversion*sigma^2/eta). kappa->0: trajectory approaches linear TWAP (minimize impact only). Large kappa: trajectory front-loads aggressively (cut price-risk exposure, accept more impact).

flashcards.q: Worked Almgren-Chriss contrast: at kappa*T=0.268 vs kappa*T=2.683, how much of a 1M-share order remains after the first 25% of the execution horizon?
flashcards.a: Low risk aversion (kappa*T=0.268): 74.6% remaining, close to linear TWAP's 75%. High risk aversion (kappa*T=2.683): only 50.5% remaining, roughly twice TWAP's execution rate early on.

flashcards.q: What is the Almgren-Chriss objective function being minimized?
flashcards.a: E[Cost] + lambda_risk*Var[Cost] -- a mean-variance tradeoff between expected market impact cost (grows with trading rate) and price risk from holding the unexecuted position exposed over time, structurally analogous to Markowitz portfolio optimization applied to an execution schedule.

flashcards.q: Derive the two-fund separation theorem from the mean-variance Lagrangian.
flashcards.a: Minimizing w'Sigma*w s.t. w'mu=r and w'1=1 gives FOC Sigma*w = lambda*mu + gamma*1, so w = lambda*Sigma^-1*mu + gamma*Sigma^-1*1 -- every efficient portfolio is a linear combination of exactly two fixed portfolios.

flashcards.q: Write the minimum-variance and tangency portfolio formulas.
flashcards.a: Min-variance: w = Sigma^-1*1 / (1'Sigma^-1*1), ignores mu entirely. Tangency (max Sharpe): w proportional to Sigma^-1*(mu-Rf*1), normalized to sum 1.

flashcards.q: Derive CAPM's E[Ri]=Rf+beta_i(E[Rm]-Rf) from the tangency portfolio.
flashcards.a: The tangency portfolio's own FOC is Sigma*w_tan proportional to mu-Rf*1, which per-asset rearranges to Cov(Ri,R_tan) proportional to mu_i-Rf. Under the equilibrium assumption that the market portfolio equals the tangency portfolio (two-fund separation + homogeneous expectations), substituting R_tan=Rm gives CAPM directly -- it's the tangency portfolio's optimality condition, not a separate assumption.

flashcards.q: Why are covariances estimated far more precisely than expected returns from the same data?
flashcards.a: A sample mean's standard error shrinks as sigma/sqrt(T) -- for 20% vol and 10 years, SE~6.3%, comparable to the entire equity risk premium. Covariances use every pairwise observation, not one number per asset, converging much faster -- risk inputs are far more trustworthy than return forecasts.

flashcards.q: Worked instability demo: two assets, both 15% vol, correlation 0.95. What happens to tangency weights when asset B's mu goes from 8% to 8.5%, then to 9%?
flashcards.a: 8.5% (50bp higher): tangency weights swing to (-28%, +128%). 9% (100bp higher): swings to (-100%, +200%). Covariance matrix condition number = 39, directly measuring this sensitivity amplification.

flashcards.q: What is Michaud's 'estimation-error maximization' (1989) and why does high asset correlation make it worse?
flashcards.a: Mean-variance optimization amplifies noise in mu via Sigma^-1, especially in directions of near-redundancy (highly correlated assets) where the optimizer perceives a long-short position as nearly risk-free, so any noise-driven return difference looks like a huge risk-adjusted opportunity, producing extreme leveraged positions.

flashcards.q: Define risk parity's equal risk contribution condition and why it avoids mean-variance instability.
flashcards.a: Risk contribution of asset i = w_i*(Sigma*w)_i/sigma_p; risk parity sets these equal across all i. Uses ONLY the covariance matrix, never mu, so it's completely insensitive to the return-estimate noise that destabilizes mean-variance optimization.

flashcards.q: Does naive inverse-volatility weighting (w_i proportional to 1/sigma_i) achieve exact risk parity?
flashcards.a: Only when assets are uncorrelated. With real correlation structure, naive inverse-vol weights give unequal risk-contribution fractions (worked example: 34.4%/25.0%/40.6% instead of equal thirds); a proper iterative solve using the full covariance matrix is needed for exact equal risk contribution.

flashcards.q: List the Fama-French three-factor and five-factor model factors.
flashcards.a: Three-factor (1992/93): market (Rm-Rf), SMB (small minus big, size), HML (high minus low, value). Five-factor (2015) adds: RMW (robust minus weak, profitability), CMA (conservative minus aggressive, investment).

flashcards.q: What is Roll's critique (1977) of CAPM and why does it still matter?
flashcards.a: CAPM's market portfolio is theoretically every risky asset in existence (unobservable); every practical test substitutes a tradeable proxy (S&P 500, MSCI World), so any empirical test is jointly testing 'CAPM plus that specific proxy,' and different reasonable proxies can give meaningfully different beta/required-return estimates.

flashcards.q: What is Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage and when is it needed?
flashcards.a: Blends a noisy sample covariance matrix with a simpler, well-conditioned structural target (e.g. single-factor or constant-correlation matrix) to reduce estimation error. Needed whenever N (assets) approaches or exceeds T (observations), making the raw sample covariance matrix singular or unstable to invert.

flashcards.q: State the three conditions for weak (covariance) stationarity.
flashcards.a: Constant mean E[y_t]=mu, constant variance Var(y_t)=sigma^2, and autocovariance Cov(y_t,y_t-k) depends only on lag k, never on t itself.

flashcards.q: What does one first-difference do to a random walk, and why?
flashcards.a: Converts it to white noise: dy_t = y_t - y_t-1 = e_t, since y_t = y_t-1 + e_t. This is exactly what d=1 means in ARIMA.

flashcards.q: ADF test: what is the null hypothesis and the regression it's based on?
flashcards.a: H0: unit root (gamma=0) in dy_t = alpha + beta*t + gamma*y_t-1 + sum(delta_i*dy_t-i) + e_t; test stat t_gamma = gamma_hat/SE(gamma_hat).

flashcards.q: Why are ADF critical values not from a standard t-table?
flashcards.a: Under H0, y_t-1 is itself non-stationary, breaking standard asymptotics; Dickey-Fuller simulated the actual distribution, giving more negative critical values (e.g. -2.86 at 5%, constant-only case) than the normal-theory -1.96.

flashcards.q: What is KPSS's null hypothesis, and why run it alongside ADF?
flashcards.a: KPSS's null is stationarity (opposite of ADF's unit-root null). ADF has low power near phi~1 (highly persistent stationary processes); running both and requiring agreement catches what either test alone would miss.

flashcards.q: Define ACF and PACF, and the key difference between them.
flashcards.a: ACF(k) = Cov(y_t,y_t-k)/Var(y_t), raw correlation including indirect paths through intermediate lags. PACF(k) is the direct effect of y_t-k on y_t after netting out lags 1..k-1 (Durbin-Levinson recursion).

flashcards.q: How do you identify AR(p) vs MA(q) from ACF/PACF shape?
flashcards.a: AR(p): PACF cuts off sharply after lag p, ACF decays (geometric or damped sine). MA(q): ACF cuts off after lag q, PACF decays. Both decaying gradually suggests ARMA(p,q).

flashcards.q: What is the 95% white-noise significance band for ACF/PACF at sample size n?
flashcards.a: +/- 1.96/sqrt(n). With n=200, that's about +/-0.139.

flashcards.q: What goes wrong if you difference a series that was already stationary?
flashcards.a: Over-differencing introduces artificial negative autocorrelation at lag 1 (theoretical ACF(1) = -0.5 for a differenced white-noise-like series) and inflates forecast variance unnecessarily.

flashcards.q: What is spurious regression (Granger-Newbold 1974) and how do you avoid it?
flashcards.a: Regressing one non-stationary (trending) series on another unrelated non-stationary series produces artificially high R^2 and 'significant' t-stats far above nominal rates. Test both series for stationarity before regressing; use cointegration testing if both have unit roots.

flashcards.q: Additive vs multiplicative decomposition: how do you choose?
flashcards.a: Additive (y=T+S+R) when seasonal swing is a constant absolute amount regardless of trend level; multiplicative (y=T*S*R, fit via logs) when the seasonal swing scales proportionally with the level. Check by plotting seasonal amplitude against trend over time.

flashcards.q: AIC vs BIC for ARIMA order selection: formula and when to prefer each.
flashcards.a: AIC = -2logL + 2k (asymptotically optimal for forecast accuracy); BIC = -2logL + k*ln(n) (heavier penalty, more conservative, better at recovering the true sparse model at large n). Prefer AIC for prediction, BIC for parsimony/interpretability.

flashcards.q: What does STL do differently from classical decomposition?
flashcards.a: STL (Cleveland et al. 1990) uses iteratively-refit Loess for both trend and seasonal components, letting the seasonal shape evolve over time; classical decomposition assumes one fixed seasonal profile across the whole series.

flashcards.q: Write GARCH(1,1) and its infinite-ARCH expansion.
flashcards.a: sigma^2_t = w + a*r^2_t-1 + b*sigma^2_t-1. Recursive substitution gives sigma^2_t = w/(1-b) + a*sum(i=1..inf) b^(i-1)*r^2_t-i -- an ARCH(inf) with exponentially decaying weights from only 2 parameters.

flashcards.q: GARCH(1,1) stationarity condition, unconditional variance, and half-life formulas.
flashcards.a: Stationary iff a+b<1. Unconditional variance = w/(1-a-b). Half-life of a shock = ln(0.5)/ln(a+b).

flashcards.q: With w=0.00001, a=0.08, b=0.90, what is the unconditional daily vol and shock half-life?
flashcards.a: Unconditional variance = 0.00001/0.02 = 0.0005, vol = sqrt(0.0005) = 2.236%. Half-life = ln(0.5)/ln(0.98) = 34.3 trading days.

flashcards.q: Why does plain GARCH miss the leverage effect, and what fixes it?
flashcards.a: r^2 discards the sign of the shock, so +4% and -4% days update variance identically. GJR-GARCH adds gamma*r^2_t-1*1[r_t-1<0]; EGARCH models log(sigma^2) with an asymmetric response term.

flashcards.q: State the Kalman filter predict and update equations for the local-level model.
flashcards.a: Predict: x_pred = x_est, P_pred = P + Q. Update: K = P_pred/(P_pred+R); x_est = x_pred + K*(z-x_pred); P = (1-K)*P_pred.

flashcards.q: What does the Kalman gain K represent, and what does K near 0 vs near 1 mean?
flashcards.a: K is the fraction of the observation 'surprise' (innovation) incorporated into the update; it's derived by minimizing posterior variance. K->0 when observation noise R is large relative to prediction uncertainty (trust the prior); K->1 when R is small (trust the new observation).

flashcards.q: When is the plain (linear-Gaussian) Kalman filter insufficient, and what replaces it?
flashcards.a: When dynamics are nonlinear or non-Gaussian. Extended Kalman Filter linearizes via Taylor expansion; Unscented Kalman Filter propagates sigma points without explicit linearization; particle filters represent the posterior with weighted samples for the most general case.

flashcards.q: What is Prophet's additive model formula and what are its three components?
flashcards.a: y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + noise: g(t) piecewise-linear/logistic trend with changepoints, s(t) Fourier-series seasonality, h(t) known holiday/event effects.

flashcards.q: What architectural idea makes N-BEATS notable, and what did it beat?
flashcards.a: Pure stacked fully-connected blocks with no RNN/attention, using learned or fixed basis functions (polynomial/Fourier) and doubly-residual backcast/forecast connections. Beat the M4-winning hybrid ES-RNN model by about 3%.

flashcards.q: What three input types does the Temporal Fusion Transformer combine, and via what mechanism?
flashcards.a: Static metadata, known future covariates, and observed-past-only covariates, combined via variable-selection gating networks plus an LSTM + multi-head attention encoder, producing quantile forecasts with attention-based interpretability.

flashcards.q: What is TimesFM and what makes it different from N-BEATS/TFT?
flashcards.a: A decoder-only transformer (Google, Feb 2024) pretrained on a large cross-domain corpus of time series and applied zero-shot to new series with no fine-tuning -- a foundation-model approach versus N-BEATS/TFT which are trained per-task.

flashcards.q: What did the M5 competition (2020) actually show about deep learning vs classical vs tree-based forecasting?
flashcards.a: LightGBM-based gradient-boosted tree approaches swept the top ranks in both accuracy and uncertainty tracks -- not deep learning, not classical ARIMA/exponential smoothing. 'Deep learning wins' is not a general truth; it depends on series count and covariate richness.

flashcards.q: Why is GARCH fit on ARIMA residuals rather than raw returns directly?
flashcards.a: GARCH's derivation assumes mean-zero, serially uncorrelated input shocks. ARIMA removes predictable conditional-mean structure first; skipping this conflates mean-misspecification with genuine variance clustering.

flashcards.q: Why do overlapping fixed-horizon labels cause k-fold to leak?
flashcards.a: label_t = sign(sum r_t+1..t+H) shares (H-k)/H of its terms with label_t+k, so nearby labels are highly correlated by construction with zero causal link. Random shuffling scatters these overlapping neighbors across train/test, letting any time-correlated feature 'predict' via near-duplicate match.

flashcards.q: Worked leakage demo result: naive shuffled 5-fold vs purged+embargoed vs walk-forward, on i.i.d. noise with true accuracy 50%.
flashcards.a: Naive shuffled 5-fold: 85.9% (pure leakage). Purged+embargoed shuffled 5-fold: 48.8% (had to purge ~98% of train). Sequential walk-forward+embargo: 50.2% (only 1-5% purged).

flashcards.q: Distinguish purging from embargo.
flashcards.a: Purging removes training samples BEFORE the test block whose feature-or-label window overlaps the test window. Embargo is an extra buffer AFTER the test block, needed because a later training sample's own lookback window could still reach backward into the test period's tail.

flashcards.q: How should embargo length be chosen?
flashcards.a: At least the maximum of the label horizon and the longest feature lookback window in the pipeline -- no universal formula, derived from the pipeline's actual windows.

flashcards.q: Expanding window vs rolling window walk-forward: tradeoff?
flashcards.a: Expanding window uses all history (more data, but early folds trained on much less data, stale data may hurt under regime shift). Rolling window uses a fixed-size recent window (comparable data per fold, tests regime-sensitivity, but window length must match the phenomenon's real timescale or it never sees enough of the pattern).

flashcards.q: Write the Sharpe ratio estimator variance formula and explain why it's not just 1/T.
flashcards.a: Var[SR_hat] = [1 - skew*SR + ((kurt-1)/4)*SR^2] / (T-1). Reduces to ~1/T only for normal returns (skew=0, kurt=3); real financial returns are skewed/fat-tailed, so the naive 1/T understates true uncertainty.

flashcards.q: Write the expected-maximum-Sharpe-from-N-trials formula (Bailey & Lopez de Prado).
flashcards.a: E[max_N SR] = sqrt(Var[SR]) * [(1-gamma)*Phi^-1(1-1/N) + gamma*Phi^-1(1-1/(N*e))], gamma = Euler-Mascheroni constant ~0.5772. This is the pure-chance benchmark a search of N trials would produce with zero real skill.

flashcards.q: Define the Deflated Sharpe Ratio and worked result for N=1000, T=250, observed annualized SR=1.5.
flashcards.a: DSR = PSR(SR* = E[max_N SR]) -- the probability the true Sharpe exceeds the pure-chance benchmark from N trials, not just 0. Worked: E[max SR|no skill]=3.27 annualized > observed 1.5, giving DSR=0.043 (4.3% chance of real skill).

flashcards.q: What is the most common practical failure in computing DSR correctly?
flashcards.a: Undercounting N -- only counting configurations that made the final report, not every variant actually explored (informal 'let's also try X' iterations), which understates the correction and defeats the metric's purpose.

flashcards.q: What is CPCV and what metric does it feed?
flashcards.a: Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation generates multiple purged train/test path combinations, producing a distribution of out-of-sample Sharpe ratios rather than one point estimate; feeds the Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO), the fraction of in-sample-best configurations that rank poorly out-of-sample.

flashcards.q: Does purged/embargoed walk-forward alone guarantee a strategy is production-ready?
