flashcards.a: Christoffersen tests whether exceptions CLUSTER in time (violating the iid assumption), fitting a two-state Markov chain to the exception sequence. Worked example: same 6 exceptions but 4 clustered -> pi11=0.50 vs pi01=0.0123, LR_ind=15.915, decisively rejecting independence (chi2(1) critical value 3.841) even though Kupiec alone nearly passed.

flashcards.q: Describe Basel's traffic-light backtesting zones and capital multipliers (250 days, 99% VaR).
flashcards.a: Green zone: 0-4 exceptions, multiplier k=3.00. Yellow zone: 5-9 exceptions, k steps up (5->3.40, 6->3.50, 7->3.65, 8->3.75, 9->3.85). Red zone: 10+ exceptions, k=4.00 and typically triggers supervisory review of the model.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between hypothetical (clean) P&L and actual (dirty) P&L in VaR backtesting, and why does FRTB require both?
flashcards.a: Hypothetical/clean P&L reprices yesterday's exact portfolio against today's actual market moves, holding positions fixed, isolating pure risk-model accuracy. Actual/dirty P&L includes intraday trading, fees, and other effects. FRTB requires tracking both because a clean-pass/dirty-fail pattern flags intraday risk-taking the end-of-day VaR snapshot doesn't capture.

flashcards.q: What is reverse stress testing, and how does it differ from ordinary scenario stress testing?
flashcards.a: Ordinary stress testing asks 'given this scenario, what's the loss.' Reverse stress testing flips the direction: 'what scenario would cause a loss large enough to threaten the firm's viability,' forcing risk teams to identify scenarios they might not have thought to construct forward.

flashcards.q: Why does per-seat pricing specifically break down for AI agents that substitute human labor?
flashcards.a: Per-seat pricing assumes value scales with headcount. A good AI agent reduces the number of humans needed, so a vendor pricing per seat is financially rewarded when their own product under-delivers -- the customer keeps (and pays for) more seats precisely because the AI isn't good enough to replace the work.

flashcards.q: What is the alignment gap in usage-based pricing for AI products specifically?
flashcards.a: Usage is a proxy for consumption, not value delivered -- a poorly-performing AI assistant needing 5 retries to get a correct answer generates 5x the revenue of a well-performing one, for delivering LESS value, not more.

flashcards.q: What's the biggest design risk in outcome-based AI pricing (e.g. charging per resolved support ticket)?
flashcards.a: Goodhart's Law baked into the pricing CONTRACT itself: a vague or gameable definition of 'outcome' creates a direct financial incentive to mark things resolved that aren't actually resolved -- more dangerous than an internal KPI being gamed because it's now commercial, not just organizational.

flashcards.q: What mitigations make an outcome-based pricing definition harder to game?
flashcards.a: A reopened-item clawback (credit/reversal if a 'resolved' ticket reopens within N days), customer confirmation of resolution, and independent audit sampling of billed outcomes against actual transcripts -- guardrails need independence from the party being paid based on the metric.

flashcards.q: Why has hybrid pricing (base fee + usage/outcome component) become the majority pattern for AI products?
flashcards.a: Pure usage-based pricing creates unpredictable bills enterprise procurement dislikes; pure outcome-based pricing requires a verifiable outcome definition many use cases don't have yet, and puts all demand-volatility risk on the vendor. A base fee gives predictability, the variable component gives incentive alignment -- Stripe data found hybrid associated with higher median growth than either pure model.

flashcards.q: What percentage of enterprise AI projects were approved on projected ROI that was never actually measured after launch?
flashcards.a: 61% (per 2025 MIT Sloan research) -- the project shipped and nobody checked whether the projected value materialized. This is a process failure, not a model-capability failure.

flashcards.q: What's the success-rate difference between AI projects with a quantified success metric defined upfront versus those without?
flashcards.a: Roughly 54% success rate with a defined metric upfront, versus roughly 12% without -- a 4-5x difference attributable to one specific, cheap, process-level practice. 73% of FAILED AI projects had no agreed success definition before starting.

flashcards.q: What percentage of organizations see measurable P&L return from their generative AI pilots, per 2025 MIT Sloan research?
flashcards.a: Only about 5% capture value at scale -- 95% see no measurable P&L return. The data attributes this overwhelmingly to undefined success criteria and unmeasured post-launch outcomes, not primarily to model capability failure.

flashcards.q: What connects the strategy module's 'AI wrapper is not a moat' point to real market outcomes?
flashcards.a: AI wrapper startups show roughly 80% failure rates, with 60-70% generating zero revenue ever -- the empirical outcome of lacking process power, switching costs, or a cornered resource: a fast-follower or the foundation-model provider itself can replicate the visible value proposition faster than the wrapper company can build a durable position.

flashcards.q: What did the 2026 buyer survey find about pricing model preference, and what does it mean for seat-only vendors?
flashcards.a: 43% of buyers prefer consumption-based pricing, 27% favor outcome-based. Seat-only vendors are increasingly disqualified from AI-product deals before they even reach a demo -- buyers have absorbed the 'seat pricing rewards under-delivery' argument.

flashcards.q: What question does Jobs To Be Done (JTBD) ask instead of 'who is our user'?
flashcards.a: What progress is someone trying to make in a specific circumstance, and what are they currently 'hiring' -- however clumsy -- to make that progress. This surfaces non-category competitors (e.g. a milkshake's real rival was a banana, hired for the same boring-commute job).

flashcards.q: What's the job story format and why is it preferred over a standard user story for discovery?
flashcards.a: 'When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome].' Unlike 'As a [persona], I want [feature]...', it avoids baking in a persona label or a specific solution before the need is understood.

flashcards.q: What's wrong with asking a user 'would you use a feature that does X?'
flashcards.a: It's a hypothetical about future behavior. People answer to be agreeable or because they can imagine a scenario where it'd help, with zero real cost for being wrong -- it produces expressed interest, not evidence of a real friction.

flashcards.q: What's the correct interview question format to get reliable signal?
flashcards.a: Ask about ONE specific, recent, real past event: 'Tell me about the last time you tried to [X]. Walk me through what happened.' People are unreliable predictors of future behavior but reliable narrators of a specific remembered event.

flashcards.q: Describe the four levels of Teresa Torres's opportunity solution tree.
flashcards.a: Outcome (metric to move) -> Opportunities (evidenced unmet needs, customer's language) -> Solutions (3-5 candidate ideas per opportunity) -> Assumption tests (cheapest experiment that could kill a solution before full build).

flashcards.q: How do you spot an 'opportunity' on a tree that's actually a disguised solution?
flashcards.a: Check if it names a specific technology or feature ('the opportunity is we need an AI chatbot'). If deleting that name breaks the sentence, it's a solution mislabeled as an opportunity, and it forecloses the 3-5 alternative solutions a real opportunity would generate.

flashcards.q: Name three types of assumption tests you can run before a full build.
flashcards.a: Fake-door test (button/CTA with no feature behind it yet, measures click-through), concierge/manual version (a human does by hand what the feature would automate), Wizard-of-Oz test (a human manually plays the role of the automated system, e.g. answering as 'the AI chatbot' for a week).

flashcards.q: What is the mechanical process for 'killing your own idea early'?
flashcards.a: 1) Write down, before building, what evidence would prove the idea wrong (a falsifiable, specific prediction). 2) Run the cheapest experiment that could produce that evidence. 3) Actually look at the result rather than rationalizing a bad one. 4) Pre-commit the kill threshold before seeing the data, not after.

flashcards.q: When are qualitative interviews the wrong tool, and what should you use instead?
flashcards.a: Interviews are strong for mechanism and depth (why/how) but weak for prevalence and magnitude (how many, how much). Use analytics, surveys, or an actual experiment to size a hypothesis interviews generated -- five consistent interviews justify building a cheap testable version, not skipping to a full build.

flashcards.q: What historical study is the canonical JTBD example, and what did it reveal?
flashcards.a: Clayton Christensen and Bob Moesta's fast-food milkshake study: commuters 'hired' the milkshake as a one-handed, slow-to-finish, boring-commute companion. Its real competition was a banana or candy bar, not competitors' milkshakes -- a functional-attribute lens (thicker? more flavors?) would have completely missed this.

flashcards.q: What happens to false-positive rate when you repeatedly peek at a fixed-horizon A/B test's p-value before its planned end?
flashcards.a: It inflates from the nominal ~5% to commonly cited estimates above 25% -- roughly one in four calls made this way is noise, not signal, because each look is an implicit additional hypothesis test.

flashcards.q: Name three fixes for the peeking problem, in order of how commonly they're implemented.
flashcards.a: 1) Lock the dashboard until the pre-committed sample size is reached (purely procedural). 2) Alpha-spending functions (pre-declared interim-analysis schedule, e.g. O'Brien-Fleming or Pocock). 3) Always-valid p-values / confidence sequences (mSPRT-based), valid at every sample size, safe to check continuously.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between the novelty effect and the primacy effect?
flashcards.a: Novelty effect: users respond MORE positively to a variant simply because it's new (a false positive that decays over days-weeks). Primacy effect (change aversion): users respond MORE negatively at first because they're accustomed to the old way (a false negative that recovers as they adjust).

flashcards.q: Why does a high-returning-traffic surface (SaaS product UI) need a longer test runtime than a high-new-visitor surface to catch novelty effects?
flashcards.a: On a high-new-visitor surface, most users see the change for the first time regardless of variant, so there's little novelty differential. On a high-returning-traffic surface, most of the treatment arm experiences a genuine change from an established habit, so novelty/primacy effects can be large and take weeks to wash out.

flashcards.q: How do you catch novelty/primacy decay concretely, rather than just running longer arbitrarily?
flashcards.a: Segment analysis by new-vs-returning traffic and by exposure count (1st vs Nth visit post-launch) within returning users -- a flattening or reversing trend as exposure count grows is the signature of decaying novelty/primacy, and it tells you when the effect has actually stabilized rather than guessing a fixed extra week.

flashcards.q: What is a holdback/haircut group and why use one even after a test has already 'won'?
flashcards.a: A small permanent control group kept running after a winning variant ships to 100% of remaining traffic, specifically to catch a lift that was partly or wholly novelty-driven and fades over subsequent weeks -- the most reliable way to confirm a launch decision was actually correct, reserved for high-stakes, hard-to-reverse launches.

flashcards.q: Why is 'no statistically significant difference' NOT the same claim as 'the feature has no effect'?
flashcards.a: A null result only rules out effects larger than the test's achieved MDE at the collected sample size -- it says nothing about smaller, still-meaningful effects the test wasn't powered to detect. Always report the achieved MDE alongside a null result.

flashcards.q: What is multiple-metric fishing and how is it the same underlying problem as peeking?
flashcards.a: Running one test but checking many metrics and reporting whichever crossed significance -- the same multiple-comparisons inflation as peeking, just applied across metrics instead of across time. Fix: pre-register ONE primary metric; treat other movements as directional/exploratory only.

flashcards.q: What's an always-valid p-value (mSPRT) and why do modern experimentation platforms default to it?
flashcards.a: A significance test constructed so Type I error is controlled simultaneously at every sample size, so looking any number of times -- including continuously -- never inflates the false-positive rate. Platforms default to it because users will look at live dashboards early and often regardless of documented warnings, so the correction is built into the statistic itself.

flashcards.q: What's the single cheapest, highest-value automated check every A/B test should have before its result is trusted?
flashcards.a: An automated sample ratio mismatch (SRM) check -- a chi-squared test on observed vs expected arm counts, run before any metric is displayed, hard-blocking the report if triggered. It's a few lines of code and catches the most common real-world experiment-invalidating bug. (Full root-cause treatment: T32-experiment-design.)

flashcards.q: Why does Amazon's PR/FAQ format start with a press release before any implementation detail?
flashcards.a: Writing the announcement first forces the author to articulate the customer-facing value proposition in plain language before getting lost in implementation detail -- if the value proposition can't be stated clearly, that's an early, cheap signal the idea isn't ready, delivered in hours instead of months.

flashcards.q: Why does a written one-pager/memo, read silently before discussion, produce better decisions than a live slide presentation?
flashcards.a: It produces a more independent read from each attendee, not anchored by who spoke first or delivery confidence. It also forces the author to resolve ambiguity in full sentences that a bullet-point deck lets slide -- the document has to stand on its own.

flashcards.q: What four vocabulary terms does a business case need to speak finance's language, beyond engineering merit?
flashcards.a: Payback period (comparable across different proposal types), NPV (fair comparison across different time horizons/risk), a risk-adjusted RANGE with stated confidence and source (not a fake-precise point estimate), and explicit opportunity cost (what else the resource could do).

flashcards.q: Describe the four roles in a stakeholder map for moving a decision you don't own.
flashcards.a: Decider (whose actual 'yes' approves it, often ONE person), Approver/Blocker (can green-light or veto a specific piece -- security, legal, a dependent team), Allies (amplify with minimal convincing), Skeptics (need real evidence, objections worth surfacing early).

flashcards.q: What is the correct pre-wiring order before a group decision meeting, and why?
flashcards.a: Allies first (cheap, low-stakes feedback that sharpens the pitch), then Skeptics in 1:1s (their objection caught privately is a gift you can address before it costs credibility live), then Approvers/Blockers, then the Decider -- who should ideally hear the substance informally before the formal room.

flashcards.q: What makes a proposal an 'easy yes' for a hesitant Decider?
flashcards.a: Minimizing what the Decider personally risks: propose the smallest reversible version first (a time-boxed pilot, not a year-long commitment), include your own kill criteria/checkpoint, and name competing priorities explicitly with a sequencing argument rather than pretending nothing else is competing for the resource.

flashcards.q: What is the 'how did you get there' or tactical-rebuttal technique, and when is it more effective than arguing directly?
flashcards.a: Asking a decision-maker to walk through their reasoning surfaces information/constraints you may not have, rather than risking an argument against a strawman of their actual position. More effective when you suspect they have context you don't (budget, other stakeholders, political factors) -- common in real orgs.

flashcards.q: You've made your case, been heard, and been overruled. What's the senior move, and why does it matter beyond this one decision?
flashcards.a: State disagreement once, clearly, then execute the decision fully with no relitigating or passive undermining. Credibility for future influence is a finite, reputational resource -- someone known for accepting a loss badly gets less benefit of the doubt next time they push back, exactly when it might matter more.

flashcards.q: Why does a risk-adjusted range with stated confidence beat a confident point estimate in a business case?
flashcards.a: Finance reviewers are professionally trained to distrust suspiciously precise, unsourced numbers. A range with a named basis ('likely $200-400K, moderate confidence, based on X') survives scrutiny because you can defend where it came from; a fabricated point estimate collapses the first time someone asks its source.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT spend your influence capital trying to change a decision, even if you disagree?
flashcards.a: When the decision is small and easily reversible (low cost of being wrong), when your own confidence isn't actually high, or when you've recently spent significant capital elsewhere -- influence capital is finite and reputational, and indiscriminate spending depletes it for the decision that actually matters most.

flashcards.q: What three properties make a good North Star metric?
flashcards.a: Reflects real customer value delivered (not company effort/output), acts as a leading indicator of durable business value fast enough to steer decisions by, and resists (though is never immune to) gaming.

flashcards.q: What does AARRR stand for and what mistake does it prevent?
flashcards.a: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue. It prevents celebrating a top-of-funnel win (e.g. signups) in isolation when Activation/Retention underneath are flat -- you can pay real CAC to acquire a cohort that behaves no differently than before.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between a leading and a lagging indicator, and what's the key trap?
flashcards.a: Leading indicators move first and are actionable; lagging indicators confirm the outcome later. The trap: a historical correlation between them isn't necessarily causal -- pumping the leading indicator directly can leave the lagging metric it 'predicts' completely untouched.

flashcards.q: What is a guardrail metric and what does it need to be effective?
flashcards.a: A metric you're prohibited from degrading while pursuing your actual target. It needs a threshold, an owner, and ideally an automated check -- and should be designed against a SPECIFIC known cheap way to game the target metric, not just tracked vaguely.

flashcards.q: State Goodhart's Law and why 'hire people with integrity' doesn't fix it.
flashcards.a: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure' (Goodhart, 1975). It describes a RATIONAL response to incentive structures, not bad actors -- a call center agent hanging up to protect average handle time is behaving rationally given what they're measured on. The fix has to be in measurement design, not personnel selection.

flashcards.q: Give a real, named example of Goodhart's Law causing organizational damage.
flashcards.a: Wells Fargo's 2016 scandal: cross-sell targets tied to compensation led employees to open millions of unauthorized accounts, completely decoupling the metric ('accounts opened') from what it was meant to proxy -- genuine customer relationship depth.

flashcards.q: What is the Soviet nail factory example illustrating about metric design?
flashcards.a: A factory measured on nail COUNT produces huge numbers of tiny useless nails; switched to a WEIGHT target, it produces a few enormous useless nails. Any single-number proxy for 'useful production' gets gamed the instant it becomes the target -- the failure reappears under a redefined metric, not just the first one.

flashcards.q: Why is 'time spent in app' a famously weak North Star metric?
flashcards.a: It's trivially inflated by addictive or harder-to-navigate design patterns that don't reflect real user value, and several major consumer platforms had to publicly walk it back once the correlation with actual well-being and long-term retention broke down.

flashcards.q: What's the actual mitigation for Goodhart's Law, since there's usually no ungameable metric?
flashcards.a: Combine guardrail metrics designed against specific known gaming vectors, periodic QUALITATIVE review (tracing through a sample of real 'wins' end to end, not just trusting the dashboard), and treat any metric that's been an explicit incentive target for 2+ quarters with elevated suspicion.

flashcards.q: Why is revenue usually a poor North Star for a single team to optimize day-to-day?
flashcards.a: It's downstream of pricing, sales motion, and market conditions the team doesn't control, and it moves too slowly to steer day-to-day decisions by. It's better used as a lagging validation check on a faster, more proximate team-level leading indicator.

flashcards.q: What are the three questions to ask before estimating a solution-shaped request?
flashcards.a: 1) What problem does this solve (specific, falsifiable)? 2) How would we know it worked (a number or observable behavior)? 3) Is the proposed solution the cheapest path to that number?

flashcards.q: Why do engineers jump straight to solutions instead of asking about the problem first?
flashcards.a: Solutions are legible, estimable, closeable work; asking 'what problem' can read as resistance; estimating feels safer than admitting uncertainty; and often nobody explicitly owns the problem/outcome layer, so no one in the room asks.

flashcards.q: How do you spot a 'disguised solution' pretending to be a problem statement?
flashcards.a: Delete the noun referring to the proposed fix from the problem sentence. 'The problem is we don't have a chatbot' becomes meaningless without 'chatbot' -- it was never a problem statement, it presupposed the answer.

flashcards.q: What is the shape of a reframe memo?
flashcards.a: Actor + moment (who, doing what, when) / current-state number (or 'not measured') / target-state number / requested solution / at least one alternative considered / one-line recommendation.

flashcards.q: When should you SKIP the formal reframe and just build what was asked?
flashcards.a: When the ask is cheap and reversible, externally mandated (compliance/contract/security), the requester already has solid data behind it, or the relationship cost of pushing back exceeds the expected value of reframing a low-stakes item.

flashcards.q: A VP hands you a fully-specified solution and says 'just build this.' What's the senior move?
flashcards.a: Build it, but write back a one-paragraph statement of the problem/outcome you believe it's meant to solve and confirm it takes 30 seconds and creates a record; it doesn't block delivery and often catches a misunderstanding early.

flashcards.q: How do you scale the problem/outcome reframe across a 20-engineer team without becoming a bottleneck?
flashcards.a: Bake the reframe fields (actor/moment, current state, target state, solution options) into the doc template itself so the format forces the question on every request, model it on a few high-stakes examples early, then let peer review enforce it -- and periodically spot-check whether shipped features' outcomes were actually measured.

flashcards.q: What's the cost-benefit rule for deciding how much reframe rigor a request deserves?
flashcards.a: Rigor should scale with (cost of being wrong) x (probability of being wrong). A two-day reversible fix rarely justifies a full reframe; a multi-week, hard-to-reverse bet almost always does.

flashcards.q: What historical shift named the failure mode of teams that are agile in process but still execute a pre-decided feature roadmap?
flashcards.a: Marty Cagan's 'empowered teams' framing (Inspired, 2008/2017) and Melissa Perri's 'build trap' (Escaping the Build Trap, 2018) -- both describe teams fully agile in cadence that still take solutions, not problems, from stakeholders.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between healthy pushback on a request and just being difficult?
flashcards.a: Healthy pushback asks the three questions, gets answers, and ends in a decision within one conversation, framed around the requester's success. Being difficult relitigates a decision after being overruled, or frames objections around your own preferences rather than the outcome.

flashcards.q: What are Porter's Five Forces and at what level (industry vs company) do they operate?
flashcards.a: Competitive rivalry, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers, threat of substitutes, threat of new entrants. They operate at the INDUSTRY level -- how much value can ANY participant in this category keep, largely independent of any one company's execution.

flashcards.q: List Hamilton Helmer's 7 Powers.
flashcards.a: Scale economies, network economies, counter-positioning, switching costs, branding, cornered resources, process power -- each a distinct COMPANY-level mechanism by which a specific advantage survives contact with a competitor.

flashcards.q: Why is 'we use GPT-5 / a specific foundation model' not a moat, even for a genuinely good product?
flashcards.a: The foundation-model layer is at product stage, moving toward commodity, with multiple credible competing providers and standardizing interfaces -- a competitor can switch to or already use an equivalent model with comparable ease. Real advantage has to live in a harder-to-replicate layer: process power, switching costs, or genuinely proprietary data.

flashcards.q: How has 'cornered resources' as a moat shifted meaning in the AI era?
flashcards.a: Raw proprietary datasets are less defensible now (foundation models train on enormous public/licensed corpora), but RIGHTS-CLEARED, CONTINUOUSLY REFRESHED, genuinely proprietary data -- updated faster than a competitor could re-derive it -- remains a strong cornered resource. Scarce talent and proprietary hardware/infra access are the other live examples.

flashcards.q: Why is process power specifically underestimated by teams building 'AI wrapper' products?
flashcards.a: The visible product (prompt, UI, wrapper) is genuinely easy to copy in a weekend, which makes teams assume the whole thing is easy to replicate. But getting a system to 99%+ reliable accuracy on a mission-critical task in production requires years of unglamorous edge-case engineering and eval infrastructure that a fast-follower can't shortcut by copying only what's externally visible.

flashcards.q: Describe Wardley mapping's evolution axis and its four stages.
flashcards.a: Genesis (novel, nobody's solved it) -> Custom-Built (maturing, still scarce/differentiating) -> Product (mature, multiple vendors) -> Commodity/Utility (standardized, interchangeable, rent it). Components move rightward over time driven by competition and standardization; compute took ~40 years to go from genesis to commodity.

flashcards.q: What is the build-vs-buy rule that follows from Wardley's evolution axis?
flashcards.a: Build at genesis (nobody's solved it, may be your differentiation). Build or carefully evaluate at custom-built. BUY at product stage (multiple vendors, comparison-shop). RENT/consume as utility at commodity -- building custom here is a strategic tax with no corresponding advantage.

flashcards.q: What real-world example illustrates the cost of ignoring a component's evolution DIRECTION, not just its current stage?
flashcards.a: Banking industry: billions invested in custom-built core-banking systems roughly 2010-2020, at the same time those systems were visibly transitioning toward the product stage -- the investment fought the evolution direction instead of riding it.

flashcards.q: What two conditions should be true before platform-izing a capability, rather than keeping it as a product?
flashcards.a: Evidenced third-party demand to actually build on top of it (not a hunch), and the underlying capability is differentiated enough (not racing toward commodity) to anchor real ecosystem value -- platform-izing carries real ongoing costs (API stability, backward compatibility, third-party support).

flashcards.q: What is the honest synthesis for what constitutes a durable moat in an AI product specifically?
flashcards.a: A thin prompt or wrapper around a foundation model is not a moat -- that layer commoditizes too fast. Durable advantage comes from process power (production reliability engineering) combined with switching costs (deep workflow embedding) and, where genuinely available, cornered resources (proprietary, refreshed, rights-cleared data) -- IN COMBINATION, not any single power alone.

flashcards.q: What are the current LTV:CAC ratio benchmarks?
flashcards.a: 3:1 is the conventional minimum viable ratio; 4:1-5:1 is considered strong (especially enterprise/post-Series B); below 2:1 signals a business model that isn't yet capital-efficient.

flashcards.q: What is CAC payback period and why does it matter more operationally than the LTV:CAC ratio?
flashcards.a: CAC / (monthly revenue per customer x gross margin %) -- months to recoup acquisition cost via contribution margin. It matters more operationally because a company can have a great ratio and still run out of cash if payback takes 18-24 months while acquiring the next cohort before the last one paid back -- it's the actual cash-flow constraint.

flashcards.q: What are current CAC payback benchmarks?
flashcards.a: Healthy B2B SaaS: 6-12 months. Elite: 80-90 days. Mid-market drifted from ~15 months (2023) to ~18 months (2026). Payback beyond 18 months usually signals real funding pressure.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't the 'near-zero marginal cost' assumption of classic SaaS gross margins transfer to AI features?
flashcards.a: AI features have real, non-trivial marginal cost per request -- inference tokens, retrieval, and especially human review scale with usage and with the model's error rate rather than approaching zero at scale. Margin can even decline as usage grows if review/escalation rates don't improve proportionally.

flashcards.q: List the four cost layers of a real AI feature's per-request cost, and which one is most consistently omitted from engineering estimates.
flashcards.a: Retrieval (vector search infra, reranking), generation (the token-priced call), evaluation (LLM-as-judge, sampled), and human review (escalated low-confidence cases). Human review is most consistently omitted and is often the LARGEST line item.

flashcards.q: In a worked RAG feature example, what multiple was the fully-loaded per-request cost versus the generation-only estimate?
flashcards.a: Roughly 3.5-7x. Generation-only was estimated at ~$0.007/request; the fully-loaded total (retrieval + generation + eval + human review) came to roughly $0.024-0.051/request.

flashcards.q: Why does human-review cost scale differently than generation cost as a model's error rate changes, and what's the implication for optimizing margin?
flashcards.a: Human review cost is driven by escalation RATE (tied to model error/uncertainty), not a fixed per-unit price -- a higher error rate directly inflates unit cost through review, often more than generation cost. The highest-leverage margin fix is usually reducing escalation rate (better calibration/retrieval) rather than negotiating token price.

flashcards.q: How does contribution margin mechanically connect to payback period, and what's a documented benchmark for the effect size?
flashcards.a: Contribution margin is the direct multiplier in payback period's denominator (CAC / (monthly revenue x margin%)) -- margin improvement directly compresses payback. Documented benchmark: moving gross margin from 72% to 78% shortens payback by roughly 4.3 months at typical SaaS unit economics.

flashcards.q: How do CAC benchmarks differ by go-to-market motion, and why does this matter when evaluating an AI feature?
flashcards.a: PLG/self-serve ~$420, mid-market/blended ~$1,680, enterprise sales-led ~$9,400 -- structurally different cost bases, not just different scale. An AI feature's economics must be evaluated against the motion-matched benchmark; blending across motions or comparing against the wrong one hides real problems.

flashcards.q: When should you run LLM-as-judge evaluation on 100% of production traffic versus sampling?
flashcards.a: 100% during a new feature's initial rollout, after a significant model/prompt change (re-establish quality baseline), or for a genuinely high-stakes surface. Once quality is stable, sample at 10-20% -- captures the same statistical signal at a fraction of the cost, since 100% eval roughly doubles the generation-layer cost.

flashcards.q: Why didn't downstream circuit breakers save AWS's and Cloudflare's customers during the 2025 outages?
flashcards.a: A breaker still needs to reach the dependency (or its health check) to decide whether to trip; when the control-plane failure breaks the addressing/discovery layer itself (DNS, proxy fleet), the breaker's own health-check path degrades along with the thing it's meant to protect against.

flashcards.q: What's the minimum viable retrofit to add blast-radius containment to an existing global control plane?
flashcards.a: A canary tier (small fleet %/one low-traffic region) that receives every push first, gated behind automated health signals with a bake time before wider rollout, plus rollback faster than full propagation — a checkpoint insertion, not a rearchitecture.

flashcards.q: What did Google's SRE book (2016) formalize, and why did it matter for postmortem quality?
flashcards.a: The 'blameless postmortem' — removing the incentive to stay vague to avoid blaming an individual, which made it safe to publish the actual mechanical failure chain in enough detail to be useful to people who weren't there, including future readers of the case study.

flashcards.q: How should you give leadership a project cost estimate without hiding the staged-gate structure inside one number?
flashcards.a: Give a firm number for the next gate only, plus a conditional range for what follows based on that gate's outcome, and name the abandonment branch explicitly — one collapsed total either overstates near-term spend or hides the real chance the project stops before production.

flashcards.q: Production reveals the MVP's core adoption assumption was wrong for the general population. What's the correct move?
flashcards.a: Treat it as the prototype gate's question (is this the right thing to build) failing retroactively, and re-run real user validation with a representative sample — not push forward with production hardening, which fixes an operational problem, not a product-fit one.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between Sealed Secrets and External Secrets Operator for keeping secrets out of plaintext Git?
flashcards.a: Sealed Secrets encrypts the value client-side with a cluster-specific public key before committing (only the in-cluster controller's private key can decrypt). External Secrets Operator commits only a reference (which key, which vault) and syncs the real value from an external secrets manager at reconcile time — Git never holds the value, encrypted or not.

flashcards.q: How do you guarantee a deployed image was actually built by CI, not manually pushed with the same tag?
flashcards.a: Sign the image at build time (cosign keyless signing via the CI workflow's OIDC identity) with an SLSA-style provenance attestation, then verify the signature and signing identity at admission time (Kyverno) — pinned to the immutable image digest, not the mutable tag, since a tag can be repointed after signing.

flashcards.q: Why can an EKS cluster fail to schedule pods on 'insufficient IP addresses' even with free CPU/memory on nodes?
flashcards.a: The default VPC CNI assigns each pod a real routable VPC IP, so pod density is bounded by ENI secondary-IP capacity and free subnet address space, independent of compute. Fix with larger subnets, prefix delegation (/28 prefixes instead of individual IPs), or an overlay-mode CNI.

flashcards.q: What's the core mechanical difference between Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter for EKS node provisioning?
flashcards.a: Cluster Autoscaler only scales pre-defined ASG node groups' size. Karpenter provisions nodes directly without ASGs, picking best-fit instance type/AZ per pending pod's actual resource requests at scheduling time, and actively consolidates underutilized nodes — faster scale-up, better bin-packing, bounded by NodePool/EC2NodeClass constraints.

flashcards.q: If the Jenkins controller's disk dies, what's lost that Jenkinsfiles in source control don't cover?
flashcards.a: Job configs, build history/artifacts, and credentials (encrypted via master.key — losing that key makes credentials.xml's values permanently unrecoverable) — Jenkinsfiles only define pipeline logic, not job config, credentials, or history.

flashcards.q: Does adopting JCasC (Jenkins Configuration as Code) remove the need to back up $JENKINS_HOME?
flashcards.a: No — JCasC makes system/job configuration reconstructable from version control, but credentials' encrypted values/key and build history/artifacts are runtime data JCasC doesn't cover, and still need their own backup and rotation strategy.

flashcards.q: Should you generally accept a counteroffer from your current employer after resigning to take another job?
flashcards.a: Usually no — a counteroffer typically fixes only the comp gap, not the underlying reasons (scope, growth, management) you started looking, which tend to resurface in 6-12 months; there's also a real trust cost once you've shown you were prepared to leave. Exception: a genuine structural fix (scope/role change), not just matched salary.

flashcards.q: How does negotiating an internal promotion-driven comp increase differ from negotiating a new external offer?
flashcards.a: External leverage comes from a competing offer or credible walk-away. Internal comp is bounded by the company's own leveling bands and a fixed budget cycle — the real lever is building the promotion case itself well before the comp conversation, since comp mostly follows once the level change is approved.

flashcards.q: Galinsky & Mussweiler's anchoring research found roughly what correlation between a negotiation's first stated offer and the final outcome, and what reduces that effect?
flashcards.a: A meta-analytic correlation of roughly 0.497. The effect is substantially reduced when the other party actively counters it by focusing on their own reservation price, alternatives, or target — not by passively deflecting alone.

flashcards.q: In a market downturn with scarce competing-offer leverage, what should shift in your negotiation approach?
flashcards.a: Weight shifts toward lower-friction levers that don't require a hard alternative to justify (sign-on bonus, start date, equity refresh terms), and toward market-data anchoring over a walk-away posture — the mechanics still apply, but the realistic ceiling is lower and asking as if conditions were a hot market reads as out of touch.

flashcards.q: As a manager advising a report on a lowball offer, what should you avoid doing even though you have relevant knowledge?
flashcards.a: Avoid using internal knowledge of another company's band in a way traceable back to you, and avoid negotiating on their behalf directly with the recruiter — coach on mechanics (vesting, comparable data, drafting a specific counter) and calibration/confidence, but it's their negotiation.

flashcards.q: In a blameless postmortem, how should a principal engineer separate accountability from blame?
flashcards.a: Own the outcome plainly without hedging, but pivot immediately to the structural question — what process/system gap let an individual action cause this — and drive toward a mechanism (a check, a changed default) rather than 'we'll be more careful,' which doesn't scale.

flashcards.q: Two peer principal engineers publicly disagree on technical direction with no shared decision-maker. What's the resolution mechanism?
flashcards.a: Reduce the disagreement to its actual empirical/risk-tolerance crux and get real evidence fast (a spike, small reversible pilot) rather than arguing from priors; if it's a genuine values tradeoff with no factual resolution, escalate explicitly to a documented decision-maker rather than letting it stall unresolved.

flashcards.q: How does AI coding agent delegation change what 'technical depth' signals at the principal level, versus Larson's 2021 framing?
flashcards.a: Depth increasingly shows in judgment about when to delegate implementation to an agent vs. do it by hand, and in critically reviewing AI-generated designs/code for plausible-but-subtly-wrong failure modes — the credibility signal shifts from 'wrote the hardest code' to 'right about when to trust agent output,' same underlying judgment, different venue.

flashcards.q: How should a candidate calibrate whether a 'principal engineer' title at a small company actually matches principal-level scope?
flashcards.a: Ask scope-revealing questions (what do other principal/staff engineers own, a recent cross-team decision the role drove) rather than trusting the title — a small company's whole engineering org can be a legitimate principal-scope problem even if it'd be staff-scope at a much larger company; the calibration is about problem shape, not headcount.

flashcards.q: How do subinterpreters (PEP 684, 3.12+) differ from both free-threading and multiprocessing?
flashcards.a: Each subinterpreter has its own GIL (true parallelism, unlike classic threading) and shares the OS process (no fork/pickling overhead, unlike multiprocessing), but doesn't share Python objects directly by default — communication goes through explicit restricted channels, closer to message-passing than shared-memory threading.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't CPython's RSS shrink proportionally after objects are freed?
flashcards.a: pymalloc manages small objects (<~512 bytes) in 256KB arenas; an arena can only be returned to the OS once every pool within it is completely empty, so one long-lived small object can pin an otherwise-empty arena resident even though CPython considers that memory free for reuse.

flashcards.q: How did the compact dict implementation (guaranteed ordering since 3.7) reduce memory instead of increasing it?
flashcards.a: It splits storage into a sparse array of small integer indices plus a dense, insertion-ordered array of the actual hash/key/value triples — indices are far smaller than full triples, shrinking the sparse portion by roughly 20-25% while adding an ordering guarantee as a side effect of the dense array being append-only.

flashcards.q: What does a Go write barrier do during concurrent GC marking, and why is it needed?
flashcards.a: Extra work on every pointer write during the concurrent mark phase to catch the mutator concurrently mutating the object graph in a way that could hide a live object from the collector (a tricolor-invariant violation) — the real, always-on cost of running marking concurrently with the mutator instead of stopping the world for it.

flashcards.q: Name V8's compilation tiers between Ignition and TurboFan, and why they exist.
flashcards.a: Sparkplug (fast baseline JIT, compiles Ignition bytecode to unoptimized machine code almost immediately) and Maglev (mid-tier optimizing compiler). They exist for the same reason the JVM's C1 exists between its interpreter and C2: TurboFan's compile cost is too slow to apply to every warm function, pure interpretation too slow for functions that run enough to matter.

flashcards.q: In Node.js, does a resolved Promise's .then() callback or an earlier-scheduled setTimeout(fn, 0) run first?
flashcards.a: The Promise callback always runs first — V8's microtask queue is fully drained after every callback the event loop runs, before it proceeds to the next macrotask (setTimeout, I/O, setImmediate), regardless of scheduling order. A recursively self-scheduling microtask chain can starve timers/I/O entirely.

flashcards.q: What is carrier-thread pinning with virtual threads (Project Loom), and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: A virtual thread inside a synchronized block can't unmount from its carrier thread when it blocks, since monitor ownership can't safely migrate carriers mid-hold — under load this starves the limited carrier pool. Fix: replace synchronized with ReentrantLock around the blocking call; locate pinning with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full or JFR pinning events.

flashcards.q: How do you confirm a Metaspace growth pattern is a classloader leak rather than legitimate dynamic class generation churn?
flashcards.a: Take heap dumps across two redeploys and diff classloader instance counts (Eclipse MAT has a dedicated classloader-leak report) — a count that grows by roughly one per redeploy and never drops is the leak signature; a framework properly releasing old classes on redeploy shows churn, not accumulation.

flashcards.q: Why isn't volatile a substitute for synchronized/AtomicInteger for a multi-threaded counter?
flashcards.a: volatile guarantees happens-before visibility/ordering for each individual read and write of that field, but no mutual exclusion — a compound read-modify-write (increment) can still race between threads exactly like CPython's x += 1, since volatile never made the multi-step operation atomic.

flashcards.q: Why does accessing memory on a remote NUMA node cost more than accessing local memory, and by roughly how much?
flashcards.a: Each CPU socket has its own locally-attached memory controller; remote access crosses an inter-socket interconnect (QPI/UPI, Infinity Fabric), commonly cited around 1.5-2x local DRAM latency or more. Fix: numactl --cpunodebind/--membind to keep threads and memory on the same node, or kernel NUMA balancing.

flashcards.q: Why do production runbooks for Redis/MongoDB commonly say to disable Transparent Huge Pages (THP)?
flashcards.a: THP's background page-promotion/compaction work can happen synchronously on the allocation path, and for workloads with frequent small allocations plus fork()-based background saves (Redis/MongoDB's pattern), that compaction stall causes multi-ms to multi-hundred-ms latency spikes — the opposite of THP's intended TLB-miss-reduction benefit for this specific allocation pattern.

flashcards.q: What two Linux kernel primitives actually implement container isolation, and how does this differ from VM isolation?
flashcards.a: Namespaces (PID, network, mount, UTS, IPC, user) give a process group its own view of kernel resources; cgroups enforce resource limits. Every container still runs on the SAME host kernel — no hypervisor-enforced hardware boundary — so a kernel escape compromises the whole host, unlike a VM escape which must break a much narrower hypervisor boundary.

flashcards.q: What mechanisms provide real hardware-backed isolation for genuinely untrusted multi-tenant workloads beyond plain containers?
flashcards.a: gVisor (a userspace kernel intercepting syscalls to shrink host kernel attack surface) or Firecracker/Kata Containers (lightweight VMs giving genuine hypervisor isolation at near-container startup speed) — used specifically because namespace/cgroup isolation alone is judged insufficient for adversarial multi-tenancy.

flashcards.q: Why is INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE safer under concurrency than a SELECT-then-INSERT-or-UPDATE pattern in application code?
flashcards.a: ON CONFLICT is atomic at the database level — the conflict check and resulting insert-or-update happen as one indivisible operation under the row's lock. A check-then-act pattern has a real race window: two concurrent transactions can both see 'no row exists' and both attempt an INSERT.

flashcards.q: A query slows drastically after a migration adds 10x rows to a joined table, with no query change. What's the first thing to check, before touching indexes?
flashcards.a: Whether table statistics are stale — if ANALYZE hasn't run since the migration, the planner may still cost-estimate against the old row count and pick a now-catastrophic join strategy (e.g. nested loop over a table that's no longer small). Stale statistics is the most common root cause of this exact symptom.

flashcards.q: When de-risking a 12-service distributed monolith, what's the actual unit you migrate — services or tables?
flashcards.a: Tables. Ownership, not the service diagram, is the real coupling graph; fix one table's ownership at a time (API or CDC replica cutover, reconciled in parallel, then old path removed) before revisiting whether the service boundaries themselves are wrong.

flashcards.q: What new failure mode does org-wide CDC (e.g. Debezium) introduce to fix dual writes?
flashcards.a: Every downstream consumer now implicitly depends on the source DB's WAL format and replication behavior — a schema change upstream can silently break every consumer at once, and replication lag creates new read-your-own-write bugs; the connector itself becomes a new operational single point of failure.

flashcards.q: Why is CDC still a net win over dual writes despite adding its own failure surface?
flashcards.a: Dual writes fail silently and randomly across many call sites (undetectable drift); CDC failures are visible (lag metrics, connector health, DLQ depth) and centralized in one place to monitor instead of N ad-hoc reconciliation jobs.

flashcards.q: Roughly how much cheaper is a budget-tier model than a frontier model for high-volume, low-risk content generation (early 2026 pricing)?
flashcards.a: Roughly 20-30x. Frontier models (GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6) run about $2.50-3/million input and ~$15/million output tokens; budget models (Gemini 1.5 Flash, GPT-4.1 Nano) run $0.075-0.10/$0.30-0.40 — making risk-tiered routing a cost lever, not just a quality one.

flashcards.q: By roughly how much does RAG-constrained generation reduce hallucination rates versus ungrounded generation, per published research?
flashcards.a: Roughly 30-70% across domains, with about a 40% aggregate improvement in factual accuracy; in structured-output tasks specifically, hallucinated fields drop from ~21% ungrounded to under 7.5% (steps) / under 4.5% (tables) with retrieval grounding.

flashcards.q: Why is Thompson Sampling generally a better default than UCB for a fast-moving, fatigue-prone creative portfolio?
flashcards.a: UCB's confidence bounds typically assume stationary rewards and stay tight (slow to react) as an arm accumulates observations even as true performance declines. Thompson Sampling's posterior naturally re-widens when combined with decayed/windowed observations, fitting the non-stationary fatigue pattern better.

flashcards.q: When is UCB still a reasonable choice over Thompson Sampling for ad creative allocation?
flashcards.a: When the portfolio refreshes frequently enough that non-stationarity isn't dominant, or when deterministic, easier-to-audit allocation behavior matters for stakeholder-facing reporting — the choice trades non-stationarity handling against auditability/simplicity, not a universal ranking.

flashcards.q: What's the mechanical process for translating a model's confusion matrix into a dollar figure for an executive?
flashcards.a: Attach a real cost or value to each confusion-matrix cell (TP value, FP cost, FN cost, TN value), multiply each by the count of that outcome at the chosen operating threshold and expected volume, and sum to get net expected value — report that, not AUC/precision/recall.

flashcards.q: What is the fixed shape of a 'one-slide result' per the Minto Pyramid Principle applied to ML reporting?
flashcards.a: Headline number (in the audience's currency) -> confidence/range -> the single biggest driver of uncertainty -> a clear ask. Everything else (methodology, full metric tables) goes in an appendix.

flashcards.q: When a room has two executives disagreeing before you've finished stating your headline number, what's the disciplined response?
flashcards.a: Finish stating the headline and range first, then reframe the disagreement as a concrete modeling question (which cost/timeline/risk assumption they differ on) rather than refereeing it live — and if the disagreement is genuinely non-quantifiable (politics, risk appetite), say so plainly rather than forcing it into the cost-table frame.

flashcards.q: With only 12 available markets, why is synthetic control preferred over simple difference-in-differences for a geo holdout?
flashcards.a: Synthetic control builds a weighted combination of untreated markets specifically chosen to reproduce the treated market's own pre-treatment trajectory, rather than assuming any single market or simple average is comparable -- at small N, simple DiD's parallel-trends assumption is hard to defend with few comparison units to check it against.

flashcards.q: What should you do if no combination of available control markets can reproduce a treated market's pre-treatment trend well in a synthetic control design?
flashcards.a: Report the poor pre-treatment fit explicitly rather than presenting the resulting estimate as ground truth -- a bad fit means no credible counterfactual exists among the available markets; fall back to a different design (longer-time-series MMM, or accepting the question can't be answered causally with the markets available).

flashcards.q: What accessibility concern does large-scale parallax/auto-playing animation raise that has nothing to do with screen readers or keyboards?
flashcards.a: Vestibular disorders — large-scale motion can trigger genuine physiological symptoms (dizziness, nausea). Fix by respecting prefers-reduced-motion and providing a substantially reduced/static alternative, not just slowing the animation down.

flashcards.q: Does prefers-reduced-motion: reduce mean disabling all CSS animation and transitions?
flashcards.a: No — it targets large-scale, parallax-style, or auto-playing motion affecting a significant portion of the viewport. Small functional motion (hover states, focus-ring transitions, loading spinners) is generally fine and often helps orientation; blanket-disabling all transitions is an over-application.

flashcards.q: Why isn't a bundler's code-splitting chunk boundary purely automatic for dynamically imported routes?
flashcards.a: Shared dependencies between two lazy-loaded routes force a real tradeoff: duplicate the shared module into both chunks (faster per-route initial load, wasted bytes) or extract a common chunk (no duplication, extra request/cache dependency) — a genuine tuning decision (splitChunks/manualChunks), not an automatic default.

flashcards.q: In a large multi-route app, a shared UI library re-downloads on every route navigation with no caching benefit. Likely cause?
flashcards.a: The bundler's automatic common-chunk extraction heuristic wasn't tuned for the app's actual sharing pattern, so the shared dependency is being duplicated into every route chunk instead of pulled into its own long-lived, independently-cached chunk — fix via explicit splitChunks.cacheGroups (webpack) or manualChunks (Rollup/Vite).

flashcards.q: Why do production JS bundles ship with content hashes in filenames instead of stable names?
flashcards.a: A content hash changes the filename whenever the bytes change, letting the deploy set an extremely long, aggressive cache lifetime (immutable) with zero staleness risk — a new deploy is simply a new URL, no cache invalidation needed. Stable filenames + cache-control alone create a real version-skew race during deploys.

flashcards.q: Does content-hashed asset naming eliminate version-skew risk entirely on its own?
flashcards.a: No — the entry HTML file referencing the hashed URLs must itself never be aggressively cached (Cache-Control: no-cache or very short-lived), since it's the one artifact that has to update every deploy to point at new hashes; long-lived HTML caching would serve stable HTML pointing at stale hashed assets indefinitely.

flashcards.q: How do design systems ship a breaking prop rename across hundreds of call sites without a coordinated big-bang migration?
flashcards.a: A codemod (an automated AST transformation, commonly jscodeshift) rewrites consuming code from the old shape to the new one mechanically, published with the new major version so each team migrates on its own schedule; a deprecation window supporting the old prop with a console warning decouples release from full migration.

flashcards.q: Beyond sentiment, what are concrete metrics for measuring design system success?
flashcards.a: % of UI built from system components vs custom one-offs (via static import analysis), frequency/size of style-prop escape-hatch usage (rising trend = eroding fit), time-to-ship vs pre-system baseline, and for federated systems, the ratio of external-team contributions to core-team contributions.

flashcards.q: Why is checking event.source instead of event.origin insufficient in a postMessage handler?
flashcards.a: event.source identifies which window object sent the message but says nothing about that window's origin (which can also change via navigation after the reference was captured) -- origin validation and source validation solve different problems; skipping the origin check leaves message forgery from any origin possible.

flashcards.q: What does Subresource Integrity (SRI) protect against for a third-party CDN-hosted script tag?
flashcards.a: A compromised CDN or vendor account silently swapping the script content. The browser computes a hash of the fetched script and refuses to execute it if it doesn't match the integrity attribute's hash, failing closed instead of silently executing tampered code.

flashcards.q: Why do large, full-component-tree Jest snapshots become low-value testing over time?
flashcards.a: They change on almost any legitimate change (a new class name, a wrapper div), so reviewers develop the habit of running --updateSnapshot and approving without reading the diff — the human verification step the snapshot depends on gets trained out by its own noisiness. Snapshots earn their keep on small, stable, low-churn output, not entire render trees.

flashcards.q: What does mutation testing measure that line coverage doesn't, and what's its practical cost tradeoff?
flashcards.a: Line coverage only confirms a line executed, not that a test asserted on its consequence correctly. Mutation testing (Stryker) introduces deliberate bugs and reports what % of mutants tests actually catch — a stronger signal, but computationally expensive, so typically run as a periodic/targeted audit rather than a per-PR blocking gate.

flashcards.q: Can a plain callback function be passed as a prop from a Server Component to a Client Component?
flashcards.a: No — a function is server-side code and code doesn't cross the RSC serialization boundary, only data does; passing one produces a runtime error. The one exception is a Server Action ('use server' function), which the framework serializes as an invokable reference, not literal function code.

flashcards.q: A Server Component renders a Client Component that needs an onClick handler. Where must that handler be authored?
flashcards.a: On the client side of the boundary, inside the Client Component itself — a Server Component can pass data props to a Client Component, but cannot author server-side and ship across an event-handling function as a prop, since functions don't serialize across the RSC payload.

flashcards.q: Why does useLayoutEffect fix a visible flicker that useEffect causes when measuring and repositioning DOM elements?
flashcards.a: useEffect runs asynchronously AFTER the browser paints, so a layout-changing update inside it causes a visible pre-update paint then a corrected second paint. useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM update but BEFORE paint, so the correction is reflected before anything is shown — one correct paint, no flicker.

flashcards.q: Why isn't useLayoutEffect the default over useEffect if it avoids flicker?
flashcards.a: It's synchronous and blocks the browser from painting until it completes, so using it for non-layout work (fetching, subscriptions, logging) adds unnecessary blocking to the critical rendering path. Reserve it specifically for synchronous DOM measurement-and-mutation that must be invisible to the user.

flashcards.q: In a TanStack Query optimistic update, what does onMutate need to do, in order, before the network request resolves?
flashcards.a: Cancel in-flight queries for the affected data (prevent a background refetch overwriting the optimistic value), snapshot the current cache value for rollback, then write the optimistic value into the cache with setQueryData so the UI updates immediately.

flashcards.q: Why does an optimistic mutation still trigger a refetch in onSettled even after the mutation succeeds?
flashcards.a: The optimistic value was a guess, not a guarantee — server-side side effects (a concurrent update, a server-computed field) the optimistic update couldn't know about can diverge from the guess even on success; a real refetch reconciles the cache with actual server truth, preventing drift from compounding across many optimistic mutations.
